native_language_example: Sometimes I ask myself what the meaning of life is.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" (to have) or "keinen ... haben" (to have no). You can describe how strong it is (e.g., "einen großartigen Sinn für Humor") or say you appreciate someone’s humor with "jemandes Sinn für Humor zu schätzen wissen".
target_language_example: Sie hat wirklich einen guten Sinn für Humor.
native_language_example: She really has a good sense of humor.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb „fahren“ (to ride/go) + „Ski“: „Ich kann Ski fahren.“ In the past, you often say „Ski gefahren“: „Ich bin Ski gefahren.“ You can also use it as an activity in comparisons: „lieber Ski fahren als …“, „genauso gut … wie …“, „besser … als …“.
target_language_example: Im Winter fahren wir jedes Wochenende Ski.
native_language_example: In winter, we go skiing every weekend.

additional_notes: Used to give a strong instruction to ensure something happens (or does not happen). Literally "take care (of it) that...". Often an imperative: "Sorge dafür, dass ..."; also possible: "Ich sorge dafür, dass ..." ("I’ll make sure that..."). The following clause uses normal verb position for a dass-clause (verb at the end).
target_language_example: Sorge dafür, dass die Tür abgeschlossen ist.
native_language_example: Make sure the door is locked.

meaning: worried (literally: “made worries”), used with "sich Sorgen machen".
additional_notes: Usually appears with a reflexive pronoun: „Er hat sich Sorgen gemacht.“ / „Ich habe mir Sorgen gemacht.“ You can intensify it with „große“: „Sie hat sich große Sorgen gemacht.“ Often followed by „um + Akkusativ“ to say what you’re worried about: „Ich habe mir Sorgen um dich gemacht.“
target_language_example: Ich habe mir Sorgen um dich gemacht.
native_language_example: I was worried about you.

additional_notes: Most often used in the pattern „sich Sorgen um + Akkusativ machen“: „Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.“ (I’m worried about you.) You can strengthen it with „große“: „große Sorgen um …“ = “big/serious worries about …”. The pronoun changes with the subject: „ich mache mir“, „du machst dir“, „wir machen uns“, etc.
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen um mich, alles ist in Ordnung.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about me, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase „sich Sorgen machen“ (to worry): „Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.“ = I’m worried about you. You can add adjectives like „große“ (big) to strengthen it: „große Sorgen um dich“.
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen um mich, mir geht’s gut.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about me, I’m fine.

additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed phrase **sich Sorgen um jemanden machen** (reflexive): *Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.* The person you worry about comes after **um** + accusative (mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/sie). You can also say **Sorgen um jemanden haben** (to have worries/concerns about someone).
target_language_example: Bitte mach dir keine Sorgen um mich.
native_language_example: Please don’t worry about me.

additional_notes: Usually used as the reflexive phrase **sich Sorgen machen**: **ich mache mir Sorgen** (I worry), **mach dir keine Sorgen** (don’t worry). Often with **um + Akkusativ** to say what you’re worried about: **sich um Geld Sorgen machen** (worry about money). You can intensify it with **große Sorgen** = “big worries.”
target_language_example: Ich mache mir Sorgen um dich.
native_language_example: I’m worried about you.

additional_notes: Usually used in the past with "haben": "(Etwas) hat (jemandem) Spaß gemacht" = "(Something) was fun (for someone)". The person who enjoyed it is in the dative: "mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen". Often used with "wirklich", "sehr" etc.: "Es hat wirklich Spaß gemacht."
target_language_example: Der Ausflug hat mir sehr Spaß gemacht.
native_language_example: I really enjoyed the trip.

meaning: to be fun (for someone); to enjoy doing something.
additional_notes: Used with a person in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) to say something is fun for them: „Das macht mir Spaß.“ With verbs/activities, German often uses „Spaß machen“ + infinitive clause: „Es macht mir Spaß, …“ or „[Etwas] macht mir Spaß.“ In your examples it appears with „scheinen“: „Es scheint ihm Spaß zu machen, …“ (= It seems he enjoys …).
target_language_example: Es macht mir Spaß, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I enjoy learning German.

additional_notes: Used with a relative pronoun to give more information about a noun: „eine Sprache, die …“ = “a language that …”. The relative pronoun „die“ refers back to „Sprache“ (feminine singular). In this pattern, „die“ can be the subject or object of the relative clause depending on the verb: „die man spricht“ = “that people speak”.
target_language_example: Deutsch ist eine Sprache, die viele Leute in Europa sprechen.
native_language_example: German is a language that many people in Europe speak.

meaning: the languages of the world; world languages.
additional_notes: A common phrase meaning all languages spoken worldwide. It’s often used after words like „alle“ (all) or in superlatives like „die meisten Sprachen der Welt“ (the most languages in the world). The genitive „der Welt“ means “of the world.”
target_language_example: Ich interessiere mich für die Sprachen der Welt.
native_language_example: I'm interested in the languages of the world.

additional_notes: "Sprachen" means "languages" and "zu lernen" is the infinitive "to learn" used like "to learn" in English. The whole phrase is often used as a subject or object: "Sprachen zu lernen ist ..." (Learning languages is ...), "Ich liebe es, Sprachen zu lernen" (I love learning languages). With "es fällt jemandem leicht, ..." it means "it’s easy for someone to ...".
target_language_example: Sprachen zu lernen macht mir Spaß.
native_language_example: Learning languages is fun for me.

additional_notes: Used in the passive voice to say that a text/book/etc. was translated. Typical pattern: „etw. ist in + Anzahl + Sprachen übersetzt worden“ (Perfekt passive: „ist … worden“). Often preceded by a number/quantity like „viele/mehrere/zehn“.
target_language_example: Der Roman ist in drei Sprachen übersetzt worden.
native_language_example: The novel has been translated into three languages.

additional_notes: Used to give advice by imagining yourself in the other person’s situation. Usually appears as: "An deiner Stelle würde ich …" (informal singular), "An Ihrer Stelle würde ich …" (formal), or "An eurer Stelle würde ich …" (informal plural). It’s often followed by an infinitive or another verb phrase (e.g., "… abwarten", "… das Gleiche tun").
target_language_example: An deiner Stelle würde ich heute früher nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d go home earlier today.

additional_notes: A common descriptive phrase for what you can see in the night sky. "am" is a contraction of "an dem" (literally “at the”), used with places like "am Himmel" (“in the sky”). Often used with verbs like "sehen" (to see) or "zu sehen sein" (to be visible): "Sterne am Himmel sehen" / "Sterne am Himmel zu sehen".
target_language_example: Heute Nacht sind viele Sterne am Himmel zu sehen.
native_language_example: Tonight, many stars can be seen in the sky.

meaning: “the pen that …” (a relative clause: *den* = “that/which” for a masculine object).
additional_notes: Used to add extra information about *der Stift* (“the pen”). Here *den* is the relative pronoun in the accusative masculine, because the pen is the direct object inside the relative clause (e.g., “Sarah gave **it** to me” → *den Sarah mir gegeben hat*). Common pattern: *Der Stift, den …, ist …*
target_language_example: Der Stift, den ich gestern gekauft habe, schreibt sehr gut.
native_language_example: The pen that I bought yesterday writes very well.

additional_notes: Used with a time amount + „lang“ to say how long something lasted (duration): „eine Stunde lang“, „zwei Tage lang“, „den ganzen Abend lang“. Often used with „eine ganze…“ (= a whole) to emphasize the length. Word order can vary: „Ich habe eine Stunde lang …“ or „… eine Stunde lang gesprochen“.
target_language_example: Wir haben eine Stunde lang auf den Bus gewartet.
native_language_example: We waited for the bus for an hour.

meaning: "(a number of) hours to (do something)"; used to say how long something takes.
additional_notes: Pattern: (jemand) braucht(e) + Zahl/mehrere/einige Stunden, um + infinitive. Use present (braucht) for general/now, past (brauchte/brauchten) for completed situations. Often translates as “It takes/took (someone) … hours to …”.
target_language_example: Ich brauche zwei Stunden, um meine Hausaufgaben zu machen.
native_language_example: I need two hours to do my homework.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. It often comes after a time expression: „ein paar Stunden lang“ (for a few hours), „mehrere Stunden lang“ (for several hours), „sechs Stunden lang“ (for six hours). You can also say „stundenlang“ as one word, meaning the same thing.
target_language_example: Wir haben stundenlang geredet.
native_language_example: We talked for hours.

additional_notes: Used with quantities: "ein/zwei/drei Stück Kreide" = "one/two/three pieces of chalk". In this counting expression, "Stück" often stays the same in the plural ("drei Stück", not *"drei Stücke"*).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir ein Stück Kreide geben?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of chalk?

meaning: a piece of cake (a slice/portion of cake).
additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article for an offer/request: „ein Stück Kuchen“ (a piece of cake). In sentences with a specific piece, you’ll often see the definite article or a possessive: „das letzte Stück Kuchen“ (the last piece of cake), „mein Stück Kuchen“ (my piece of cake). „Stück“ is a common word for a portion of food (e.g., „ein Stück Brot“, „ein Stück Pizza“).
target_language_example: Möchtest du ein Stück Kuchen?
native_language_example: Would you like a piece of cake?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single piece/sheet of paper. Often appears with an article and sometimes an adjective: ein Stück Papier, dieses Stück Papier, ein großes Stück Papier. Common with verbs like schreiben (write), geben (give), zerreißen (tear).
target_language_example: Ich habe deine Nummer auf ein Stück Papier geschrieben.
native_language_example: I wrote your number on a piece of paper.

additional_notes: A very common noun for this clothing item (borrowed from English). Neuter: das T-Shirt; plural: die T-Shirts. Often used with colors/adjectives (ein rotes/sauberes/altes T-Shirt). With the verb anziehen (to put on): sich ein T-Shirt anziehen; with ausziehen (to take off): sein T-Shirt ausziehen.
target_language_example: Ich ziehe ein blaues T-Shirt an.
native_language_example: I’m putting on a blue T-shirt.

additional_notes: Plural of „das T‑Shirt“. Refers to the casual short-sleeved shirt; often used with clothing words like „kurze Hosen und T‑Shirts“ or with quantities: „drei T‑Shirts“, „eines seiner T‑Shirts“.
target_language_example: Ich brauche zwei neue T-Shirts für den Sommer.
native_language_example: I need two new T-shirts for the summer.

additional_notes: Used with a form of the verb "nehmen" (to take) to talk about taking medication, often regularly. Common with reminders: "Daran gedacht, ... zu nehmen?" (Did you remember to take ...?). Possessive pronouns change with the person: "meine/deine/seine/ihre/eure Tabletten".
target_language_example: Ich habe vergessen, meine Tabletten zu nehmen.
native_language_example: I forgot to take my pills.

meaning: “the day when/on which” (introduces a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific day and add more information about it. The relative pronoun is usually **an dem** (dative), and it’s often shortened to **am** in everyday German: **der Tag, an dem … / der Tag, am dem …** (commonly written/said as **der Tag, an dem …** or **der Tag, an dem …**; **am** is especially common in speech). In your examples it follows expressions like **seit dem Tag, an dem …** (“since the day when …”).
target_language_example: Das war der Tag, an dem ich nach Berlin gezogen bin.
native_language_example: That was the day when I moved to Berlin.

meaning: "(the) day of my life" (used for the best/worst/most important day).
additional_notes: Usually used with a superlative to emphasize how special a day was: „der schönste/beste/glücklichste/schlimmste Tag meines Lebens“. „meines Lebens“ is the genitive form meaning “of my life.” You can use present („Das ist …“) for today, or past („Das war …“) for a past day.
target_language_example: Das war der aufregendste Tag meines Lebens.
native_language_example: That was the most exciting day of my life.

additional_notes: Used with a number (or a question like „Wie viele …?“) to say how often something happens in one week. Very common in questions: „Wie viele Tage die Woche …?“ You may also see the slightly more formal/explicit variant „Tage pro Woche“.
target_language_example: Ich gehe drei Tage die Woche ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three days a week.

additional_notes: Used with a number to say how long something lasts: „zwei/vier/sieben Tage lang“. It often goes with time expressions and verbs like „sein“, „dauern“, or weather/event descriptions: „Es schneite vier Tage lang.“ Similar patterns: „Wochen lang“, „Monate lang“.
target_language_example: Wir waren drei Tage lang in Berlin.
native_language_example: We were in Berlin for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens a certain number of days after an earlier event or time mentioned in context. Very often you add a number: „zwei/drei/vier Tage später“. It works on its own („Tage später …“) or with a number, and it doesn’t need an article.
target_language_example: Drei Tage später bekam ich eine Antwort.
native_language_example: Three days later I got an answer.

additional_notes: Often used with an indefinite article: „eine Tasse Kaffee“ = “a cup of coffee.” In invitations and suggestions you’ll often hear patterns like: „Was sagst du zu …?“ / „Was sagen Sie zu …?“ (“How about …?”) and „Wie wäre es mit …?“ (“How about …?”). It can also describe doing something while having coffee: „bei einer Tasse Kaffee“ (“over a cup of coffee”).
target_language_example: Wie wäre es mit einer Tasse Kaffee nach dem Essen?
native_language_example: How about a cup of coffee after the meal?

additional_notes: Often used when offering someone tea, especially in invitations like „Wie wäre es mit einer Tasse Tee?“ or „Was sagst du zu einer Tasse Tee?“ The phrase is usually „eine Tasse Tee“ (a cup of tea).
target_language_example: Möchtest du eine Tasse Tee?
native_language_example: Would you like a cup of tea?

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express a very large number (often not exact). It’s the plural of the noun "Tausend" used like a quantity: "Tausende von + [plural noun]". In writing you may also see the adjective form without "von" (e.g., "tausende Bilder"), but "Tausende von" is very common and clear.
target_language_example: In der Stadt gibt es Tausende von Möglichkeiten.
native_language_example: In the city there are thousands of possibilities.

additional_notes: A very common choice question (oder = “or”), often used by hosts, in cafés, or on planes. With a verb like möchten/wünschen/trinken, it means you’re offering or asking which drink someone prefers. You can answer with just one word: „Tee, bitte.“ / „Kaffee, bitte.“
target_language_example: Zum Frühstück nehme ich Tee oder Kaffee, je nachdem, wie müde ich bin.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have tea or coffee, depending on how tired I am.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to a larger whole or group. Often with a quantifier like ein Teil der (a part of), ein großer Teil der (a large part of), der größte Teil der (the largest part of). Also used without an article in fixed phrases like Teil der Gesellschaft sein (“to be part of society”).
target_language_example: Ich will Teil der Gruppe sein.
native_language_example: I want to be part of the group.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific area or neighborhood within a city. Very common with adjectives (e.g., alter/ältester Teil, feiner Teil) and with prepositions like „in diesem Teil der Stadt“, „im alten Teil der Stadt“.
target_language_example: In welchem Teil der Stadt wohnst du?
native_language_example: Which part of the city do you live in?

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to a larger whole. It’s usually followed by a genitive noun phrase (often with “des” for masculine/neuter singular), e.g., „Teil des Körpers“, „Teil des Problems“. In everyday German you may also hear „Teil von + Dativ“ (e.g., „Teil von dem Team“).
target_language_example: Das ist nur ein Teil des Plans.
native_language_example: That’s only part of the plan.

meaning: to use a phone (to make a call).
additional_notes: "benutzen" means "to use". "das Telefon benutzen" is a polite way to ask to borrow someone’s phone for a moment, often with modal verbs like "darf ich...?") / "dürfte ich...?" (more polite) / "könnte ich bitte...?". You can also say "Ihr Telefon" (your phone, formal) or "dein Telefon" (your phone, informal).
target_language_example: Kann ich kurz dein Telefon benutzen?
native_language_example: Can I use your phone for a moment?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" in the Perfekt to talk about a completed activity in the past: "Ich habe Tennis gespielt." The past participle "gespielt" goes at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Wir haben am Wochenende Tennis gespielt.
native_language_example: We played tennis on the weekend.

meaning: to play tennis (as an infinitive: “to play tennis”).
additional_notes: Used with other verbs that take an infinitive with **zu** (e.g., *Lust haben*, *genießen*, *pflegen*, *ausnutzen, um ...*, *daran hindern*). The **zu** normally goes right before the verb at the end: *Tennis zu spielen*.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, heute Tennis zu spielen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to play tennis today.

meaning: "animal god" (a god/deity in animal form, or a god connected to animals).
additional_notes: A hyphenated noun compound: Tier (animal) + Gott (god). Often used like a title/name for a specific deity (especially in fantasy contexts). It’s masculine: der Tier-Gott; accusative den Tier-Gott. With movement/direction you may see zum Tier-Gott (= zu dem Tier-Gott, “to the animal god”).
target_language_example: Wir müssen zum Tier-Gott gehen und ihn um Hilfe bitten.
native_language_example: We have to go to the animal god and ask him for help.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is about to cry or is crying lightly (from sadness, emotion, joy, etc.). Commonly used with haben: „Er/Sie hat/hatte Tränen in den Augen.“ Also used with other verbs to describe how someone does something: „Sie sprach mit Tränen in den Augen.“
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, hatte sie Tränen in den Augen.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she had tears in her eyes.

additional_notes: Often used as a short, direct command: „Tür auf!“ = „Open the door!“ You’ll also see it with separable verbs like aufmachen/aufgehen: „Mach die Tür auf.“ / „Die Tür geht auf.“ (The door opens.) Note: Sentence 3 uses a different verb: „auftauchen“ = „to show up/appear“ („an der Tür“ = at the door).
target_language_example: Tür auf, bitte!
native_language_example: Open the door, please!

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb phrase **an die/der Tür klopfen** (to knock on/at the door). In the past, you’ll often see **hat ... an die Tür geklopft** (Perfekt). **an die Tür** emphasizes the direction (onto the door); **an der Tür** is also common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich habe an die Tür geklopft, aber niemand hat aufgemacht.
native_language_example: I knocked on the door, but nobody opened up.

meaning: 'the door behind you/behind oneself' (usually in: die Tür hinter sich schließen = to close the door behind you).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like schließen (to close) or zumachen (to shut) to say you close the door after you enter or leave a room. The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject: hinter mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich. Often said as a polite instruction: „Bitte schließen Sie die Tür hinter sich.“
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte die Tür hinter dir schließen?
native_language_example: Can you please close the door behind you?

meaning: “close the door” / “shut the door”; also “(to/toward) the door”.
additional_notes: Common in separable-verb phrases like „die Tür zumachen“ (= to close/shut the door). In commands and many sentences, „zu“ goes to the end: „Mach die Tür zu!“, „Er knallte die Tür zu.“ Separately, „zu“ can be a preposition meaning “to/toward”: „Er ging der Tür zu.“ (= He walked toward the door; often also „zur Tür“).
target_language_example: Es zieht—mach bitte die Tür zu.
native_language_example: It’s drafty—please close the door.

additional_notes: Short for „Untergrundbahn“. Used for city train systems that run mostly underground. Common with the verb „fahren“ (to take/ride) and with lines/directions: „Welche U-Bahn fährt …?“
target_language_example: Wir nehmen die U-Bahn zum Hauptbahnhof.
native_language_example: We’re taking the subway to the main train station.

additional_notes: Short for **Unterseeboot** (“undersea boat”). It’s a **neuter** noun: **das U-Boot**. Plural: **die U-Boote**. In English, “U-boat” is also used, especially for German submarines (e.g., in WWII contexts).
target_language_example: Das U-Boot taucht ab.
native_language_example: The submarine dives down.

additional_notes: Used to say whether a clock/watch is working and whether it is slow or fast. Common patterns: „Die Uhr geht nach.“ = it’s slow (behind). „Die Uhr geht vor.“ = it’s fast (ahead). You often add how much: „Die Uhr geht fünf Minuten nach/vor.“ If it’s broken/not running: „Die Uhr geht nicht.“
target_language_example: Meine Uhr geht fünf Minuten vor.
native_language_example: My watch is five minutes fast.

meaning: “o’clock in the morning” (AM), used after a specific time.
additional_notes: Used to specify that a clock time is in the morning. Common pattern: **um + [time] + Uhr morgens** (e.g., *um sechs Uhr morgens*). You use **Uhr** with an exact hour; if you give minutes, you usually say **morgens** without **Uhr** (e.g., *um 6:30 morgens* / *um halb sieben morgens*).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um acht Uhr morgens am Bahnhof.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at the train station at eight o’clock in the morning.

meaning: to be convinced of someone’s innocence.
additional_notes: Used with **sein**: *Ich bin von … überzeugt.* The pattern is **von + dative** (e.g., *von seiner/ihrer Unschuld*). Common in legal/crime contexts when people believe someone did not do it.
target_language_example: Die Polizei ist von seiner Unschuld überzeugt.
native_language_example: The police are convinced of his innocence.

meaning: 'Father is' ("Vater" + the verb "sein" in 3rd person singular).
additional_notes: Used to state something about your father. In full sentences it’s usually followed by an adjective/noun phrase (e.g., "Vater ist müde" = Father is tired). You often also see "Der Vater ist ..." (the father) or "Mein Vater ist ..." (my father). Without an article ("Vater ist ...") it can sound like a general statement or a more headline-style/formal way of speaking.
target_language_example: Mein Vater ist heute sehr beschäftigt.
native_language_example: My father is very busy today.

additional_notes: A formal legal/political term for extremely serious crimes (e.g., torture, slavery, genocide), typically judged under international law. Usually used in the pattern „etw. ist ein Verbrechen gegen die Menschheit“ (something is a crime against humanity).
target_language_example: Die Anklage lautet: Verbrechen gegen die Menschheit.
native_language_example: The charge is: crimes against humanity.

additional_notes: Used for changing or improving video files (cutting, trimming, adding music/effects, etc.). Often appears with verbs like „wollen“ (to want) and „können“ (to be able to): „Videos bearbeiten wollen/können“. Also common: „ein Video bearbeiten“ (edit a video).
target_language_example: Ich muss das Video noch bearbeiten, bevor ich es hochlade.
native_language_example: I still have to edit the video before I upload it.

meaning: Polyjuice Potion (a potion that lets you take someone else’s appearance).
additional_notes: A fixed name from the Harry Potter universe. In the examples, it’s treated like a specific item you can look for, see, or have ready (“in ein paar Tagen fertig”). Grammatically masculine: der Vielsaft-Trank.
target_language_example: Der Vielsaft-Trank ist fast fertig, aber wir brauchen noch eine Zutat.
native_language_example: The Polyjuice Potion is almost ready, but we still need one ingredient.

meaning: pros and cons; advantages and disadvantages.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the positive and negative sides of an option or situation, often when comparing choices or making a decision. Common patterns: „Vor- und Nachteile haben“ (to have pros and cons), „über Vor- und Nachteile nachdenken“ (to think about the pros and cons), „die Vor- und Nachteile von + Dativ“ (the pros and cons of ...).
target_language_example: Lass uns die Vor- und Nachteile abwägen, bevor wir buchen.
native_language_example: Let’s weigh the pros and cons before we book.

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the phrase **die Wahrheit sagen** (“to tell the truth”). In the examples it appears in the perfect tense (**hat ... die Wahrheit gesagt**) and in hypothetical/conditional sentences (**hätte ... die Wahrheit gesagt**). You normally include the article: **die Wahrheit**.
target_language_example: Warum hast du mir nicht die Wahrheit gesagt?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me the truth?

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb **haben** in the **Perfekt** (present perfect/simple past in spoken German): **(ich/du/er …) habe/hast/hat … Wasser getrunken**. **getrunken** is the past participle of **trinken** (“to drink”). You can add amounts or time: **ein Glas**, **viel**, **heute**, **drei Liter**.
target_language_example: Ich habe nach dem Sport viel Wasser getrunken.
native_language_example: I drank a lot of water after exercising.

meaning: "Water is" (used to say what water is like or what it means).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **ist** ("is", 3rd person singular of **sein** = "to be") to make statements/definitions about water: **Wasser ist flüssig.** It can also appear in questions when **ist** comes before the subject: **Wie viel Wasser ist ...?** ("How much water is ...?").
target_language_example: Wasser ist wichtig für unsere Gesundheit.
native_language_example: Water is important for our health.

additional_notes: Commonly used with washing/cleaning verbs like „(sich) waschen“ (to wash) and „(sich) die Hände waschen“ (to wash your hands). Often appears after „mit“ (with): „mit Wasser und Seife“ = with water and soap. In everyday advice, it can mean simple, basic hygiene/cleaning.
target_language_example: Du brauchst nur Wasser und Seife, um die Flecken rauszubekommen.
native_language_example: You only need water and soap to get the stains out.

additional_notes: Used with destinations (usually cities/countries/regions): „der Weg nach Berlin“. Very common in phrases like „den Weg nach X nehmen“ (take the way to X) and „sich auf den Weg nach X machen“ (set off/head to X). Can also be figurative: „den Weg nach Europa finden“ = “make its way to Europe / become available in Europe.”
target_language_example: Wir suchen den schnellsten Weg nach Hause.
native_language_example: We’re looking for the fastest way home.

meaning: way home; the route back to your home.
additional_notes: Used with or without a preposition: often with "auf meinem Weg nach Hause" (= on my way home). "Weg" can mean a path/route or the act of going somewhere; here it’s specifically the trip back home. Also used in fixed phrases like "den Weg nach Hause finden" (= find your way home).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir den Weg nach Hause zeigen?
native_language_example: Can you show me the way home?

additional_notes: This is the noun + verb part of a sentence: **Welt** (world) + **ist** (is). It almost always appears with an article or possessive/demonstrative before it, e.g. **die Welt ist** (the world is), **unsere Welt ist** (our world is), **meine Welt ist** (my world is), **diese Welt ist** (this world is). In set phrases, it can be part of expressions like **das Ende der Welt ist nah** (“the end of the world is near”).
target_language_example: Die Welt ist manchmal laut, aber auch schön.
native_language_example: The world is sometimes loud, but also beautiful.

meaning: for a week; a week long.
additional_notes: Used with a time expression (often with an article or modifiers) to say how long something lasts: „eine Woche lang“, „die ganze Woche lang“, „zwei Wochen lang“. It usually goes after the time unit (Woche/Monat/Jahr) and can be used with durations like validity, weather, waiting, etc.
target_language_example: Wir waren eine Woche lang in Berlin.
native_language_example: We were in Berlin for a week.

meaning: to … for a week; (in/next week) to …
additional_notes: Used with movement/travel verbs (gehen, fahren, fliegen, müssen, wollen) and the destination preposition **nach** (typically for cities/countries without an article): **für eine Woche nach Berlin** = “to Berlin for a week.” With a time phrase like **in der nächsten Woche**, it means “(sometime) next week to …”. Note: **nach** here means “to,” not “after.”
target_language_example: Wir fliegen für eine Woche nach Spanien.
native_language_example: We’re flying to Spain for a week.

meaning: 'time (for you) to …' / 'it’s time that you …' (a prompt that you should do something now).
additional_notes: Usually used in the pattern **(Es ist) Zeit / an der Zeit, dass du …** + verb (often in the present tense): *Es ist Zeit, dass du gehst.* It often sounds like urging, reminding, or saying something is overdue; **allmählich** (“gradually/by now”) makes it stronger: *Es ist allmählich Zeit, dass du …*
target_language_example: Es ist Zeit, dass du nach Hause gehst.
native_language_example: It’s time for you to go home.

meaning: 'time to' / 'time in order to' (used before an action).
additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive clause: „Zeit, um … zu + Infinitiv“ (often with a comma). Common with verbs like „Zeit haben“ (to have time) or „Zeit geben“ (to give time): „Ich habe keine Zeit, um zu warten.“ / „Geben Sie mir Zeit, um …“.
target_language_example: Ich brauche Zeit, um das zu verstehen.
native_language_example: I need time to understand that.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has time available, or to say whether something is a good/bad moment for an activity. It’s followed by a noun phrase: Zeit für + accusative (e.g., Zeit für einen Besuch / ein Frühstück). Common in questions like „Haben Sie Zeit für …?“ and statements like „Ich habe (keine) Zeit für …“.
target_language_example: Hast du heute Abend Zeit für einen kurzen Spaziergang?
native_language_example: Do you have time for a short walk this evening?

meaning: “time with (someone)” (usually in: Zeit mit jemandem verbringen = to spend time with someone).
additional_notes:
Most commonly used with the verb **verbringen**: **Zeit mit + Dativ** (jemandem) **verbringen**.
- ich verbringe Zeit mit **dir**
- wir verbringen Zeit mit **Tom**
- Zeit mit **meiner Familie**
It’s about being together/doing things together. In sentence 7, a different expression is used: **die Zeit totschlagen** = “to kill time.”
target_language_example: Am Wochenende verbringe ich viel Zeit mit meinen Freunden.
native_language_example: On the weekend I spend a lot of time with my friends.

meaning: time to read / time for reading.
additional_notes: Used with (haben) to say you have (little/no/rarely) time to read: „Ich habe (kaum/keine/selten) Zeit zum Lesen.“ „zum“ = „zu dem“ and is used here to mean “for” doing an activity (reading). You can also say „Zeit zum + infinitive“ for other activities (e.g., „Zeit zum Kochen“).
target_language_example: Heute Abend habe ich endlich Zeit zum Lesen.
native_language_example: This evening I finally have time to read.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has successfully reached a goal (personal, work, travel, etc.). Often appears with haben + Ziel erreicht (e.g., Wir haben unser Ziel erreicht) or as a short status/message: Ziel erreicht!
target_language_example: Nach vielen Wochen Training habe ich mein Ziel erreicht.
native_language_example: After many weeks of training, I achieved my goal.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "haben" in the present perfect: "Ich habe mein Zimmer aufgeräumt" = "I tidied up my room / I have tidied up my room." The verb is "aufräumen" (separable: "räumen" + "auf"); the past participle is "aufgeräumt". Possessives change: mein/dein/ihr/sein/unser Zimmer.
target_language_example: Ich habe mein Zimmer aufgeräumt.
native_language_example: I tidied up my room.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase meaning to put things away and make your room neat. Usually used with a possessive: „mein/dein/unser/euer Zimmer aufräumen“. The separable verb is „aufräumen“ (e.g., „Ich räume mein Zimmer auf.“).
target_language_example: Ich räume heute mein Zimmer auf.
native_language_example: I’m tidying my room today.

meaning: to tidy/clean up (a) room (to put it in order).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase „(ein) Zimmer aufräumen“ = to tidy up a room. In your sentences it appears as „… das Zimmer aufzuräumen“ (zu + infinitive), used after phrases like „beschäftigt sein“, „brauchen“, or „helfen“: „Ich war damit beschäftigt, das Zimmer aufzuräumen.“ Word order: in main clauses you often say „Ich räume mein Zimmer auf.“ (separable verb: auf + räumen).
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine Stunde, um mein Zimmer aufzuräumen.
native_language_example: I need an hour to tidy up my room.

meaning: '(the) room is' / 'in the room there is…'.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" ("ist" = "is") to describe a room ("Mein Zimmer ist klein.") or, very often, after a place phrase to say what is in that place: "In meinem Zimmer ist …" = "In my room there is …". In this second use, German often uses "ist" (singular) even when English would say "there are"—German agrees with the thing that follows (e.g., "In meinem Zimmer ist keine Uhr."; plural would be "… sind zwei Stühle.").
target_language_example: In unserem Zimmer ist ein großes Fenster.
native_language_example: In our room there is a big window.

meaning: (to) keep the room clean / (to) clean the room.
additional_notes:
Usually used with a verb, especially: 
- „das Zimmer sauber machen“ = to clean/tidy the room (do the cleaning)
- „das Zimmer sauber halten“ = to keep the room clean (maintain cleanliness)
Used in commands and questions: „Halt dein Zimmer sauber!“ / „Ist dein Zimmer sauber?“
target_language_example: Ich muss mein Zimmer sauber machen.
native_language_example: I have to clean my room.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "fahren" with "Zug" (train). You’ll see it in schedules and questions like "Welcher Zug fährt ...?" (= Which train goes ...?). Note: With an object it can also mean "to drive/operate the train": "jemand fährt den Zug" (= someone drives the train).
target_language_example: Welcher Zug fährt zum Flughafen?
native_language_example: Which train goes to the airport?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **verpassen** (to miss) in the **Perfekt** tense: **Ich habe den Zug verpasst.** The train is usually in the accusative: **den Zug / meinen Zug**. Often used with **fast** (almost) or **vielleicht** (maybe): **Ich hätte fast meinen Zug verpasst. / Sie hat vielleicht ihren Zug verpasst.**
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich komme zu spät — ich habe meinen Zug verpasst.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm late — I missed my train.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can enter/reach a place or use a service/thing. "zur" = "zu der" and is used with feminine nouns (e.g., "zur Bibliothek"). With masculine/neuter nouns you usually use "zum" (= "zu dem"), e.g., "Zugang zum Internet".
target_language_example: Haben Sie Zugang zur Bibliothek?
native_language_example: Do you have access to the library?

additional_notes: Used with the verb „zur Welt bringen“ (= to give birth to). In the perfect tense, you’ll often see: „Sie hat Zwillinge zur Welt gebracht.“ In the simple past: „Sie brachte Zwillinge zur Welt.“ You can add details like „zwei Jungen / zwei Mädchen“ (two boys / two girls) or „eineiige Zwillinge“ (identical twins).
target_language_example: Sie hat letztes Jahr Zwillinge zur Welt gebracht.
native_language_example: She gave birth to twins last year.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "haben" (e.g., "hast du…?", "haben Sie…?") to talk about the completed action of brushing teeth. Often appears with "schon" (= already) and "das letzte Mal" (= the last time). With "deine" it means "your teeth"; without a possessive, "Zähne" is still understood as your own in everyday questions.
target_language_example: Ich habe mir heute Morgen schon die Zähne geputzt.
native_language_example: I already brushed my teeth this morning.

additional_notes: Common daily routine phrase, often used with "gehen" as an instruction: "Geh (dir/deine) Zähne putzen!". You’ll also hear "sich die Zähne putzen" (to brush one’s teeth). In commands, "dir" is common and "die" is often used instead of "deine".
target_language_example: Ich putze mir jeden Morgen und jeden Abend die Zähne.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth every morning and every evening.

meaning: "every now and then; occasionally" (ab und zu / ab und an).
additional_notes: On its own, "ab und" is usually incomplete; the fixed expressions are "ab und zu" and "ab und an" (= occasionally). In other sentences you may see "ab" as a separable verb prefix (e.g., "Er nahm die Brille ab und ..." = "He took his glasses off and ..."), where "ab" means "off/away" and is not the same as the time expression.
target_language_example: Wir gehen ab und zu ins Kino.
native_language_example: We go to the cinema every now and then.

meaning: to already have plans (for the evening).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is free at a certain time, often as a lead-in to an invitation. "schon" adds the idea of "already" (maybe you might have plans). The verb is "vorhaben" (separable in some forms): Ich habe … vor / Hast du … vor?
target_language_example: Hast du heute Abend schon etwas vor, oder hast du Zeit?
native_language_example: Do you already have plans this evening, or do you have time?

meaning: 'but that is…' (to add a contrast or correction).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information that contrasts with what was just said or expected. Very common in conversation and writing. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., „aber das ist nicht wichtig / nicht nötig / meine Kündigung“) or by an evaluation („aber das ist Selbstmord!“). In spoken German you may also hear it starting a new sentence to push back: „Aber das ist doch…“.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber das ist nicht mein Problem.
native_language_example: I understand you, but that's not my problem.

meaning: 'but you are …' (introduces a contrast or objection).
additional_notes: Used to push back against what was just said, or to point out a surprising/important fact about the other person. Often followed by an adjective, age, role, or group membership (e.g., "Aber du bist erst elf."). In speech, stress on "du" can add emphasis ("But YOU are...").
target_language_example: Ich dachte, du kommst nicht — aber du bist ja doch hier.
native_language_example: I thought you weren’t coming — but you’re actually here after all.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what comes before with something about a male person (er = he). Typically comes after a comma: „..., aber er ...“. You can swap in other pronouns: „aber sie“ (but she/they), „aber ich“ (but I).
target_language_example: Ich wollte gehen, aber er hatte keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but he didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast about a man/boy ("er"). Often follows a statement about him and adds a surprising or opposite detail: "Er sieht aus wie …, aber er ist …". In writing, a comma is typically used before "aber" when it connects two main clauses.
target_language_example: Er wirkt sehr freundlich, aber er ist sehr streng.
native_language_example: He seems very friendly, but he is very strict.

additional_notes: Used to start the next clause after a statement, to add a contrasting or limiting point about something referred to as "es" (= "it" / the situation). Very common in spoken and written German: first clause, then a comma + „aber es …“. „Es“ is a placeholder for an idea, event, or whole situation, not only a physical object.
target_language_example: Ich war müde, aber es ging mir besser als gestern.
native_language_example: I was tired, but I felt better than yesterday.

meaning: "but it is" (used to contrast or correct what came before).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast after a statement: something may seem one way, **but it is** actually/also another way. Very common in explanations and everyday speech. Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., *aber es ist interessant / sehr kalt / wahr*).
target_language_example: Es klingt komisch, aber es ist richtig.
native_language_example: It sounds strange, but it’s correct.

meaning: 'but it was …' (introduces a contrast about a past situation).
additional_notes: Used to add a contrasting fact after a previous statement. Very common pattern: "..., aber es war + Adjektiv/Adverb" ("..., but it was too late/occupied/over quickly"). Note that "war" is the simple past of "sein" ("to be").
target_language_example: Ich wollte dir helfen, aber es war schon zu spät.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but it was already too late.

meaning: 'but I' (used to contrast what you say about yourself).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or objection from the speaker’s point of view. Usually followed by a verb: "..., aber ich kann nicht" / "..., aber ich will ...". In writing, there’s typically a comma before "aber" when it connects two clauses.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber ich habe keine Zeit.
native_language_example: I understand you, but I don’t have time.

meaning: “but I am …” / “but I’m …” (used to contrast with what was just said).
additional_notes: Often comes after someone’s statement or an assumption to correct it or add a contrasting fact. Very common in conversation: “..., aber ich bin …” + adjective/noun/prepositional phrase (e.g., „unschuldig“, „der Auserwählte“, „noch nicht da“).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe dich, aber ich bin heute zu müde.
native_language_example: I understand you, but I’m too tired today.

meaning: “but I think …” / “but I believe …” (polite, slightly unsure disagreement or correction).
additional_notes: Used to soften a contradiction or to correct someone: you add a polite “but” (aber) and then your opinion/assumption (ich glaube). Often followed by a full clause ("…, aber ich glaube, dass …") or directly by a statement ("…, aber ich glaube, das ist …"). You can add words like "schon" or "eigentlich" to nuance it ("aber ich glaube schon" = “but I do think so”).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe, aber ich glaube, das ist nicht richtig.
native_language_example: I understand, but I think that’s not correct.

meaning: 'but I have …' (used to add a contrast).
additional_notes: Used to contradict, correct, or add an exception to what was just said. After "aber" in a main clause, the verb still stays in position 2, so you often get: "Aber ich habe …" + past participle (Perfekt) or an object (possession/experience).
target_language_example: Alle waren schon da, aber ich habe den Weg nicht gefunden.
native_language_example: Everyone was already there, but I couldn’t find the way.

meaning: 'but I have …' (used to add a contrast).
additional_notes: Used to contradict, correct, or add an exception to what was just said. After "aber" in a main clause, the verb still stays in position 2, so you often get: "Aber ich habe …" + past participle (Perfekt) or an object (possession/experience).
target_language_example: Alle waren schon da, aber ich habe den Weg nicht gefunden.
native_language_example: Everyone was already there, but I couldn’t find the way.

meaning: 'but I can …' (contrast: something is true, but you’re able to do something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or limitation after what was just said: “but I can/can’t …”. Often followed by an infinitive or phrase like helfen (help), bleiben (stay), zustimmen (agree). With a direct object, you may see it as: „aber ich kann es nicht tun“ (but I can’t do it).
target_language_example: Ich bin müde, aber ich kann noch ein bisschen arbeiten.
native_language_example: I’m tired, but I can still work a little.

additional_notes: Used to add a constraint or obligation after saying yes, agreeing, or stating a preference. Often used to politely decline or explain why you can’t do something: "Gerne, aber ich muss …". In everyday speech, German often uses "müssen" where English would say "have to".
target_language_example: Ich würde gern länger bleiben, aber ich muss morgen früh arbeiten.
native_language_example: I’d like to stay longer, but I have to work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to contrast a positive statement with a negation: something is true/possible in one respect, but it is not true/possible in another. Often appears after a clause ("..., aber nicht ...") or at the end of a sentence for emphasis ("..., aber nicht.").
target_language_example: Ich kann heute kommen, aber nicht lange bleiben.
native_language_example: I can come today, but I can't stay long.

additional_notes: Used to show a contrast: something happened or you expected a response, but no person did it (often after a comma). "Niemand" is singular, so the verb is singular: "aber niemand öffnete" / "aber niemand machte auf".
target_language_example: Ich habe dreimal angerufen, aber niemand ist rangegangen.
native_language_example: I called three times, but nobody picked up.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two statements. "Aber" is a coordinating conjunction, so you often put a comma before it when it connects two full clauses: "Ich wollte …, aber sie …". "Sie" can mean "she", "they", or formal "you"—in these examples it means "she" (e.g., Maria).
target_language_example: Ich wollte dir helfen, aber sie wollte es allein machen.
native_language_example: I wanted to help you, but she wanted to do it alone.

additional_notes: Used to contrast what “we” do/are with what was just said. Often comes after a comma (…, aber wir …) or at the start of a sentence (Aber wir …).
target_language_example: Sie haben mehr Geld, aber wir haben mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: They have more money, but we have more time.

additional_notes: Used to accuse or state that someone’s action was deliberate (not an accident). Often appears as: "Das hast du absichtlich getan" (informal "du") or "Das haben Sie absichtlich getan" (formal "Sie").
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht absichtlich getan.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

meaning: 'eight hours' in expressions like **acht Stunden am Tag** ('eight hours a day') or **acht Stunden am Stück** ('eight hours straight').
additional_notes: **am** is a contraction of **an dem** and is used here in time expressions. Most common completions are **am Tag** (= per day) and **am Stück** (= continuously/without a break). You can replace **acht** with other numbers: **sechs Stunden am Tag**, **zwei Stunden am Stück**, etc.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite acht Stunden am Tag.
native_language_example: I work eight hours a day.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to emphasize the whole group of nearby/mentioned things or people: all these roses/letters/people/questions/things. It’s a common combination of **all** (all) + **diese** (these). Often appears with a noun right after it: **all diese + Nomen (Plural)**.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe all diese Regeln nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t understand all these rules.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people as a whole. It often starts a sentence (e.g., „Alle Menschen sind …“). With an added phrase it can be more specific: „Alle Menschen dieser Erde“ = all people on Earth. In comparisons/generalizations you may see „Wie alle Menschen …“ = like everyone (else) / as most people do.
target_language_example: Alle Menschen brauchen Liebe und Respekt.
native_language_example: All people need love and respect.

meaning: all (the) students / every student (in a group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the entire group of students being talked about (e.g., at a school or in a class). Often followed by extra information like a place or group: „alle Schüler in der Klasse“, „alle Schüler an unserer Schule“. With negation, it means “not all students”: „Nicht alle Schüler …“.
target_language_example: Alle Schüler müssen pünktlich sein.
native_language_example: All students have to be on time.

additional_notes: "Alle" means "all" and "Türen" is the plural of "Tür" (door). It’s used literally for actual doors (e.g., in a house) and figuratively in phrases like "(etwas) öffnet alle Türen" = "(something) opens all doors" meaning it creates many opportunities or makes everything possible.
target_language_example: Ein gutes Netzwerk kann dir alle Türen öffnen.
native_language_example: A good network can open all doors for you.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like „zumachen“/„schließen“ (to close) or „verriegeln“ (to lock/bolt), often as an instruction for safety, noise, weather, or security. „Mach … zu“ = informal singular; „Macht … zu!“ = informal plural; „Schließen Sie …!“ = formal (Sie) command.
target_language_example: Bitte schließen Sie alle Türen und Fenster, bevor Sie gehen.
native_language_example: Please close all doors and windows before you leave.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean you include every one of your things/people: „alle meine Geschwister“ (all my siblings), „alle meine Lehrer“ (all my teachers). The forms can change with case: e.g. nominative/accusative plural „alle meine …“, dative plural „mit allen meinen …“. For singular, German often uses „mein ganzes / meine ganze / mein ganzer …“ (my whole …) instead of *alle meine*.
target_language_example: Alle meine Freunde sind schon da.
native_language_example: All my friends are already here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your entire group of friends. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis (Alle meine Freunde …). In a longer sentence it can also come after the verb: Ich habe alle meine Freunde eingeladen. (accusative object).
target_language_example: Alle meine Freunde kommen heute Abend zu mir.
native_language_example: All my friends are coming to my place tonight.

meaning: all sorts of; all kinds of; all manner of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “a wide variety of” things, often implying “many different types” (not literally every possible one). It commonly appears with rumors, names, ideas, books, insults, etc.: „alle möglichen Gerüchte / Bücher / Schimpfwörter“.
target_language_example: Im Internet findet man alle möglichen Tipps zum Deutschlernen.
native_language_example: On the internet you can find all kinds of tips for learning German.

meaning: every two days; every other day.
additional_notes: Used to describe a repeated schedule with a two-day interval (one day in between). Common with routines and appointments, often with a verb like kommen/gehen/anrufen/besuchen. Compare: „jeden zweiten Tag“ (same meaning).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns alle zwei Tage zum Lernen.
native_language_example: We meet every other day to study.

additional_notes: Used to say that a whole group is identical/similar in some way (often with verbs like „sein“ or „aussehen“) or that everyone has the same status/rights (e.g., „Vor dem Gesetz sind wir alle gleich.“ = equal before the law). In statements like „Frauen sind alle gleich“, it can sound like a sweeping generalization.
target_language_example: Für mich sehen sie alle gleich aus.
native_language_example: To me they all look the same.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or sending, especially **gehen** (to go) and **schicken** (to send): **Alle gehen nach Hause** = everyone goes home; **Jemand schickt alle nach Hause** = someone sends everyone home. In commands it often appears as **Geht alle nach Hause!** (“Everyone go home!”).
target_language_example: Es ist spät—wir gehen jetzt alle nach Hause.
native_language_example: It’s late—we’re all going home now.

additional_notes: “Alle” means “everyone” or “all (of them)”. “Waren” is the simple past (Präteritum) of “sein” (“to be”) for wir/sie/Sie: “we/they/you (formal) were”. Used to describe a past state of a whole group (often followed by an adjective or phrase): “Alle waren müde.”
target_language_example: Alle waren froh, als der Test vorbei war.
native_language_example: Everyone was happy when the test was over.

additional_notes: Used to say something is common knowledge. It’s typically followed by a subordinate clause introduced by **dass** (“that”). In German you usually write a comma before **dass**, and the verb in the **dass**-clause goes to the end: **Alle wissen, dass er heute kommt.**
target_language_example: Alle wissen, dass wir morgen eine Prüfung haben.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that we have an exam tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when talking about going somewhere without anyone else. "dorthin" means "to there" (to that place), and "allein" means "alone"—so it often appears with verbs of movement like "gehen" (to go) or "fahren" (to go/drive).
target_language_example: Ich möchte nicht allein dorthin gehen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go there alone.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with "zu" used after many verbs (e.g., "sich entschließen", "die Absicht haben", "zu jung sein, um … zu …"). "dorthin" means “to there” (to that place), and "allein" emphasizes you go without anyone else.
target_language_example: Ich traue mich nicht, allein dorthin zu gehen.
native_language_example: I don’t dare to go there alone.

meaning: alone in the forest (in the woods).
additional_notes: A common location phrase used with verbs like sein (to be), leben (to live), wohnen (to live/reside), or verbringen (to spend): „Er lebt allein im Wald.“ „im“ is a contraction of „in dem“ and „Wald“ means “forest/woods.”
target_language_example: Sie hat sich allein im Wald verlaufen.
native_language_example: She got lost alone in the woods.

additional_notes: Describes being at home with no other people there. Commonly used with verbs like „sein“ (to be) and „bleiben“ (to stay). Word order can vary: „allein zu Hause“ and „zu Hause allein“ both work, but „allein zu Hause“ is very common.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute Abend allein zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m home alone tonight.

meaning: "to ... alone / by yourself" (used before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say someone does an action without help or without other people. Pattern: "allein" + "zu" + infinitive (often at the end of the clause): "allein zu wohnen" = "to live alone". Can express being physically alone (no company) or doing something without assistance (on one’s own).
target_language_example: Kannst du das allein zu Ende bringen?
native_language_example: Can you finish that on your own?

additional_notes: Used to talk about being by yourself (without other people). Often used with phrases like „Ich mag es …“ (I like it…), „Ich wünsche …“ (I wish…), or „Macht es dir/Ihnen nichts aus …?“ (Do you mind…?).
target_language_example: Heute Abend möchte ich gern allein zu sein.
native_language_example: This evening I’d like to be alone.

meaning: apparently; it seems (based on what you can see/know).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re making a conclusion from appearances or available evidence, not stating a proven fact. It often comes at the beginning of the sentence, but can also be inserted later: „Tom hat allem Anschein nach …“. More formal than „anscheinend“.
target_language_example: Allem Anschein nach kommt der Bus heute zu spät.
native_language_example: Apparently, the bus is late today.

additional_notes: This is the dative form of **alles** (“everything”) + **was** (“that/which”) in a relative clause: **(mit/aus/nach) allem, was …** = “with/from/after everything that …”. The comma is standard before the relative clause (**was ...**). The case (allem / alles / allem, etc.) depends on the role in the main clause (often set by a preposition like **mit** or **aus**).
target_language_example: Ich bin mit allem, was du gesagt hast, einverstanden.
native_language_example: I agree with everything that you said.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **sagen** or **erzählen**: **jemandem (Dat.) sagen/erzählen, dass …**. Here **allen** means “to everyone” (dative plural of **alle**), and it’s followed by a **dass**-clause. Often used to report what someone told everybody.
target_language_example: Er hat allen gesagt, dass er morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He told everyone that he doesn’t have time tomorrow.

meaning: of the whole world; (with „aus“) from all over the world.
additional_notes: „aller Welt“ is genitive and is common in two patterns: (1) „aus aller Welt“ = “from all over the world” (people/things coming from many countries). (2) With a superlative: „der/die/das …ste … aller Welt“ = “the …est … in the whole world.”
target_language_example: In diesem Museum gibt es Kunst aus aller Welt.
native_language_example: This museum has art from all over the world.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has an allergy. Usually with a noun: „Ich bin allergisch gegen Milch.“ You can add contrasts with „aber nicht gegen …“ (but not to …). In everyday speech, people also say „allergisch auf“ with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Bist du allergisch gegen Katzen?
native_language_example: Are you allergic to cats?

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to wish someone well. Often used by itself ("Alles Gute!") or with a reason: "Alles Gute zum Geburtstag" (happy birthday) and "Alles Gute für ..." (all the best for ...). You can also say it more formally as part of a longer wish: "Ich wünsche Ihnen alles Gute."
target_language_example: Alles Gute für deine Prüfung morgen!
native_language_example: All the best for your exam tomorrow!

additional_notes: A common, friendly way to wish someone well. Often used by itself ("Alles Gute!") or with a reason: "Alles Gute zum Geburtstag" (happy birthday) and "Alles Gute für ..." (all the best for ...). You can also say it more formally as part of a longer wish: "Ich wünsche Ihnen alles Gute."
target_language_example: Alles Gute für deine Prüfung morgen!
native_language_example: All the best for your exam tomorrow!

additional_notes: Used to refer to the total set of things that meet a condition, often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): "alles, was ich will" = "everything (that) I want." The comma is typical because it introduces a relative clause with "was". In everyday speech, you may also hear "alles, was" without a pause, but the comma is still written.
target_language_example: Alles, was du brauchst, ist hier.
native_language_example: Everything you need is here.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause: **alles, was Sie + verb** = “everything (that) you + verb.” **Sie** is the formal “you” (for strangers, customers, etc.); with friends you’d usually say **alles, was du …**. Often appears in warnings, questions, and customer-service contexts.
target_language_example: Alles, was Sie hier unterschreiben, ist verbindlich.
native_language_example: Everything you sign here is binding.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to “everything” someone knows/has/does, etc. After "was du", the verb goes to the end of the clause (e.g., "alles, was du weißt"). Often followed by a prepositional phrase like "darüber" (about it) or "über ihn" (about him).
target_language_example: Erzähl mir alles, was du gehört hast.
native_language_example: Tell me everything that you heard.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or can find) all the things they need. "alles" = everything, and "was du brauchst" is a relative clause meaning "that you need" (literally: "what you need"). Often used in questions like "Hast du alles, was du brauchst?"
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—ich habe alles, was du brauchst.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—I have everything you need.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **alles, was** (“everything that/whatever”). The comma is required: **Alles, was er tut, …**. The verb in the relative clause goes to the end (e.g., **was er weiß**). Replace **er** with another subject as needed (sie, ich, Tom, etc.).
target_language_example: Alles, was er sagt, stimmt nicht immer.
native_language_example: Everything that he says isn’t always true.

additional_notes: Common pattern: "alles, was + subject + (verb in past)" = "everything that ...". Here, "besaß" is simple past of "besitzen" (to own/possess). Used when talking about all of someone’s belongings/property, often with verbs like "verkaufen" (sell), "verlieren" (lose), or "tragen" (carry). You can change the subject: "alles, was ich besaß" (everything I owned), "alles, was sie besaß" (everything she owned).
target_language_example: Nach dem Brand hatte er alles, was er besaß, verloren.
native_language_example: After the fire, he had lost everything he owned.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to “everything” (alles). The comma is required: „alles, was ich …“. After „was ich“, you usually continue with a verb at/near the end of the clause (e.g., „alles, was ich brauche“ = everything I need).
target_language_example: Das ist alles, was ich heute brauche.
native_language_example: That’s everything I need today.

additional_notes: Used to say you have (or don’t have) all necessary things. "alles, was ..." introduces a relative clause meaning "everything that ...". Often appears with verbs like "haben" (to have): "Ich habe alles, was ich brauche."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe alles, was ich brauche.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have everything I need.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **ihr** (= “you” plural/informal, or “you” formal in some dialects). **Alles** refers to a general set of things, and **was** links to what follows: *alles, was ihr gesehen habt* = “everything that you saw.” Often used to ask if something is the total amount: *Ist das alles, was ihr …?*
target_language_example: Erzähl mir alles, was ihr heute gemacht habt.
native_language_example: Tell me everything you (all) did today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with an indefinite subject (man = “one/you/people in general”). It refers to the total of things in a general sense: Alles, was man + VERB, … (“Everything that you eat/need/know/lose …”). Often followed by a verb at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Alles, was man braucht, ist ein bisschen Geduld.
native_language_example: Everything you need is a bit of patience.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause (comma + "was") referring back to "alles" (“everything”): "Alles, was sie sagt" = “Everything (that) she says.” The pronoun "sie" here can mean “she” or formal “you” (singular/plural), depending on context. The verb in the relative clause usually comes at the end: "Alles, was sie braucht, ist Zeit."
target_language_example: Ich glaube alles, was sie mir erzählt.
native_language_example: I believe everything she tells me.

additional_notes: Used when you refer to the total of things/actions connected to “we,” and then add more information with a verb at the end of the clause. Common patterns: “alles, was wir haben/tun/sagen/brauchen …”. In German, the verb in the “was”-clause typically comes last: “alles, was wir brauchen”.
target_language_example: Alles, was wir heute brauchen, ist Zeit.
native_language_example: Everything we need today is time.

additional_notes: Used to say/check that you have all necessary items or requirements. Often appears in questions (Hast du/Habt ihr …? Ist das …?) and can be used on its own as a short statement (e.g., on a checklist).
target_language_example: Okay, wir haben alles, was wir brauchen.
native_language_example: Okay, we have everything we need.

additional_notes: Used to contrast one thing with the rest: "X ist wichtig, alles andere ..." It can be the subject or object of a sentence. Often means "everything besides that" (everything else). In questions/negatives it can also mean "anything else" (e.g., "Hast du alles andere?" = "Do you have everything else?").
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit; alles andere muss warten.
native_language_example: I have no time; everything else has to wait.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is NOT the case (often with adjectives like sicher, unschuldig, glücklich). It suggests the opposite or that reality is very different from what’s being mentioned.
target_language_example: Der Film war alles andere als langweilig.
native_language_example: The movie was anything but boring.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is NOT the case (often with adjectives like sicher, unschuldig, glücklich). It suggests the opposite or that reality is very different from what’s being mentioned.
target_language_example: Der Film war alles andere als langweilig.
native_language_example: The movie was anything but boring.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is NOT the case (often with adjectives like sicher, unschuldig, glücklich). It suggests the opposite or that reality is very different from what’s being mentioned.
target_language_example: Der Film war alles andere als langweilig.
native_language_example: The movie was anything but boring.

additional_notes: Used with a relative clause starting with **was** (“that/what”) to say someone got everything they wanted/needed. Common in questions (**Habt ihr …?**) and statements (**Er hat …**). Note: **bekommen** means “to get/receive,” not “to become” (false friend).
target_language_example: Hast du alles bekommen, was du brauchst?
native_language_example: Did you get everything you need?

meaning: “did everything that …” (i.e., did all they could / did all that was necessary).
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause introduced by **was** to explain what “everything” refers to: **Ich habe alles getan, was ich konnte** = “I did everything I could.” Often followed by **um … zu** to give a goal/purpose: **… um jemanden zu retten** (“… to save someone”).
target_language_example: Ich habe alles getan, was ich konnte, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I did everything I could to help you.

additional_notes: Used with a relative clause: **alles tun, worum + person (Akk.) + bitten**. Here **worum** means “what/that which” referring back to **alles** (“everything”) and links to the verb **bitten** (“to ask/request”). The request is usually expressed as **jemanden um etwas bitten** (“to ask someone for something / to ask someone to do something”). Word order: *Hast du alles getan, worum ich dich gebeten habe?*
target_language_example: Danke, du hast alles getan, worum ich dich gebeten habe.
native_language_example: Thanks, you did everything I asked you to do.

additional_notes: Used in a subordinate clause with "dass" or "ob" to check or reassure that everything is fine. Often appears with "mit + Dativ" to mean "with (someone)" = regarding someone’s situation/health: "ob mit Tom alles in Ordnung ist" = "whether Tom is OK." The full main-clause version is: "Alles ist in Ordnung."
target_language_example: Sag mir bitte, ob alles in Ordnung ist.
native_language_example: Please tell me if everything is OK.

meaning: to do everything yourself / on your own.
additional_notes: Used when someone has to handle all tasks without help. "selbst" adds emphasis: no one else helps. Often appears with modal verbs like "müssen" (had to): "Ich muss alles selbst machen."
target_language_example: Ich muss heute alles selbst machen, weil niemand Zeit hat.
native_language_example: I have to do everything myself today because nobody has time.

additional_notes: Used with a relative clause ("was" + clause) to say you’ll allow or try to do whatever is possible/desired: "Alles tun, was in meiner Macht steht" = "do everything in my power." With "Lass/Lasst …" it means "Let … do whatever he/she wants."
target_language_example: Ich tue alles, was ich kann, um pünktlich zu sein.
native_language_example: I’m doing everything I can to be on time.

meaning: 'everything is under control' / 'I've got everything under control'.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a situation is handled and there’s no need to worry. You can say it alone as a short statement ("Alles unter Kontrolle."), or with a subject to emphasize who is managing things ("Ich habe alles unter Kontrolle.", "Hier ist alles unter Kontrolle.").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe alles unter Kontrolle.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ve got everything under control.

additional_notes: Used when you want to start a story or explanation at the very beginning, often with verbs like „erzählen“ (to tell) or „erklären“ (to explain): „Lass mich alles von Anfang an erzählen.“ It can also mean that something was already going wrong right from the start: „Alles ging von Anfang an schief.“
target_language_example: Wir müssen alles von Anfang an neu planen.
native_language_example: We have to plan everything again from the beginning.

additional_notes: Used with a noun or pronoun to say someone knows/tells/reports all details about a topic/person/thing: alles über den Plan, alles über mich. Common with verbs like wissen (to know), erzählen/berichten (to tell/report), erfahren (to find out).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir alles über die Stadt erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me everything about the city?

meaning: first (the first one to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone was the first to arrive/do something. It often answers “in what position/order?” and is common with verbs like kommen/ankommen/sein/überqueren/vorstellen. It changes for gender and case: als Erster (male), als Erste (female), als Erstes (neuter/“first of all”), plural: als Erste; with dative: als Erstem/Erster/Erstem.
target_language_example: Sie hat als Erste die richtige Antwort gefunden.
native_language_example: She was the first to find the correct answer.

additional_notes: Used with „als“ to describe the role/function of an animal (or even something unusual) in a situation: someone keeps/chooses something „als Haustier“ (= in the role of a pet). Often used with verbs like „halten“ (to keep), „sich halten“ (to keep for oneself), „sich (etw.) erwählen“ (to choose for oneself).
target_language_example: Ich möchte eine Katze als Haustier.
native_language_example: I want a cat as a pet.

meaning: as a child; when (I/you/etc.) was a child.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that was true or happened during someone’s childhood. Often followed by a verb in the past: "Als Kind war ich …" / "Als Kind habe ich …". You can also specify whose childhood with a possessive: "als mein Kind" is wrong—say "als Kind" (me) or "als Kind" + context, or "als Kind meines Bruders" (as my brother’s child) / "als Kind von …" (as the child of …).
target_language_example: Als Kind hatte ich Angst vor Hunden.
native_language_example: As a child, I was afraid of dogs.

meaning: "When I was a child, I ..." / "As a child, I ..."
additional_notes: Used to talk about things you regularly did or that happened to you in childhood. Often followed by the past tense (e.g., Perfekt: „bin ich … gegangen/geschwommen“ or passive: „bin ich … gestochen worden“). You can also use it with other persons: „Als Kind war er …“, „Als Kind habe ich …“.
target_language_example: Als Kind bin ich jeden Samstag zu meiner Oma gefahren.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I went to my grandma’s every Saturday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about habits, likes/dislikes, or beliefs from your childhood. "Als Kind" = "as a child" (time phrase) and is often placed at the beginning of the sentence; then the verb comes second: "Als Kind habe ich …". Typically followed by a past form (Perfekt: "habe ich + Partizip II"), but you can also use Präteritum in writing.
target_language_example: Als Kind habe ich jeden Sommer bei meinen Großeltern gewohnt.
native_language_example: As a child, I used to live with my grandparents every summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the next thing in a sequence or plan. Very common in questions like „Was kommt als Nächstes?“ (= What’s next?) and after verbs like „kommen“, „passieren“, or „zu tun sein“: „Ich frage mich, was als Nächstes passiert.“
target_language_example: Okay, und was machen wir als Nächstes?
native_language_example: Okay, and what are we doing next?

meaning: as the only one; the only person (who).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that one person (or thing) is the only one in a group with a certain situation or quality. It often comes right after the subject: „Tom war als einziger dort.“ For other genders/numbers it changes: „als einzige“ (female), „als einziges“ (neuter), „als einzige“ (plural = the only ones).
target_language_example: Sie war als einzige nicht müde.
native_language_example: She was the only one who wasn’t tired.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the first to do something. It changes to match the person’s gender/number/case: **als Erster** (male), **als Erste** (female), **als Erstes** (neuter/impersonal: “first of all”), **als Erste/Erste** (plural). Often followed by what happened (e.g., *als erster gehen/ankommen/gratulieren/erfahren*).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dir als Erster gratulieren.
native_language_example: I’d like to be the first to congratulate you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is last in a sequence (e.g., in a line, on a list, to fall asleep, to arrive/finish). It agrees with the person/thing: als letzter (masc.), als letzte (fem.), als letztes (neut.), als letzte(r) (plural). Often used with verbs like anstehen (to line up), einschlafen (to fall asleep), ankommen/ins Ziel kommen (to arrive), gehen (to leave), fertig werden (to finish).
target_language_example: Ich bin als Letzter angekommen.
native_language_example: I arrived last.

meaning: to do next; what to do next.
additional_notes: Used when planning the next step in a process. Very common in questions with "Was" (e.g., "Was soll ich als nächstes tun?") and after verbs like "wissen", "entscheiden" or "sagen" (e.g., "Ich weiß nicht, was ich als nächstes tun soll.").
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich als nächstes tun soll.
native_language_example: I don't know what I should do next.

meaning: "as well as" / part of "sowohl … als auch" = "both … and".
additional_notes: Most commonly used with "sowohl" to pair two (or more) items: "sowohl X als auch Y" = "both X and Y". It can link nouns, adjectives, or verbs (activities). Usually the same grammatical form follows on both sides (e.g., two nouns, two adjectives).
target_language_example: Wir haben sowohl Zeit als auch Lust.
native_language_example: We have both time and desire (we feel like it).

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr, weniger, größer, besser, länger, etc.) to compare something with men. In German, "als" = "than" in comparisons (not "as"). Example pattern: "X ist größer/besser/länger als Männer."
target_language_example: Frauen verdienen hier oft weniger als Männer.
native_language_example: Women often earn less than men here.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr, weniger, größer, schwieriger, klüger, älter, etc.) to say something is different from what the listener expects. Formal/polite because it uses "Sie"; informal is "als du denkst" (or plural "als ihr denkt"). Often preceded by intensifiers like "viel", "weitaus", or "wahrscheinlich".
target_language_example: Es dauert länger, als Sie denken.
native_language_example: It takes longer than you think.

meaning: “when the phone rang” (at that moment in the past).
additional_notes: Uses **als** to introduce a time clause for a **single, specific event in the past**. Often used with another past action that was in progress or had just (barely) happened (e.g., **gerade**, **kaum**, **mitten**). Word order: **Als das Telefon klingelte, ...** or **..., als das Telefon klingelte.**
target_language_example: Ich war gerade eingeschlafen, als das Telefon klingelte.
native_language_example: I had just fallen asleep when the phone rang.

additional_notes:
1) Time meaning: **als du + verb (at the end)** = *when you…* for a single event or time in the past. (Not used for repeated events—German usually uses **wenn** for that.)
2) Comparison meaning: **… größer/schneller … als du** = *… bigger/faster than you.* Here **als** means *than* (not *as*).
target_language_example: Als du angekommen bist, haben wir schon gegessen.
native_language_example: When you arrived, we had already eaten.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (e.g., besser, größer, klüger, reicher) to say someone/something is more/less X than the listener expects. Often follows a comma: „…, als du denkst.“
target_language_example: Das ist schwieriger, als du denkst.
native_language_example: That is harder than you think.

additional_notes:
"als" + subject "er" is used in two very common ways:
1) Time: "als er ..." = "when he ..." for a single event in the past (often with Präteritum or Perfekt). Example pattern: "Als er kam, ..."
2) Comparison: after a comparative, "... als er" = "... than he". Example pattern: "größer/jünger/besser ... als er".
Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Als er nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When he came home, nobody was there.

additional_notes: Uses **als** to mean **“when”** for a **single event in the past** (not repeated). It introduces a subordinate clause, so the **verb goes to the end**: *… den Polizisten sah*. The clause is usually separated by a **comma** and can come first or last: *Als er … sah, …* / *…, als er … sah.* Note: **als** can look like English “as,” but here it means “when.”
target_language_example: Als er den Polizisten sah, bekam er Angst.
native_language_example: When he saw the police officer, he got scared.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific moment in the past. "als" introduces a one-time past event; "er" = he; "starb" is the simple past of "sterben" (to die). You can swap the pronoun: "als sie starb" (when she died), or use a name: "als Tom starb".
