target_language_example: Er war bei seiner Mutter, als er starb.
native_language_example: He was with his mother when he died.

additional_notes: Used in storytelling with **als** to introduce a one-time event in the past: **…, als es zu regnen begann/anfing.** The verb is usually **beginnen** (more formal) or **anfangen** (more common in speech). Word order: main clause + comma + **als** + subject (**es**) + rest of the verb at the end (**… begann/anfing**).
target_language_example: Ich wollte gerade losfahren, als es zu regnen anfing.
native_language_example: I was just about to leave when it started to rain.

additional_notes: 1) Time: **als ich ...** introduces a past time clause for a single event or period (often translated as “when I ...”). For repeated situations, German usually uses **wenn ich ...**. 2) Comparison: **... als ich** means “... than I” after a comparative (e.g., *besser/größer/schneller*). Word order: the verb goes to the end in the **als**-clause (*Als ich zu Hause ankam, ...*).
target_language_example: Als ich klein war, wollte ich Pilot werden.
native_language_example: When I was little, I wanted to be a pilot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past time in your life. It often introduces a clause in the past tense (e.g., Präteritum or Perfekt) and is commonly followed by a comma: “Als ich Kind war, …”. You can also say “als ich ein Kind war” (a bit more explicit).
target_language_example: Als ich Kind war, habe ich jeden Sommer meine Großeltern besucht.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I visited my grandparents every summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single event in the past: **Als ich ankam, ...** = “When I arrived, ...”. Often sets the time for what happened next. In an **als**-clause, the verb goes to the end (**ankam**). Compare: **als** (one-time past) vs **wenn** (whenever / if, repeated or general).
target_language_example: Als ich ankam, war das Konzert schon vorbei.
native_language_example: When I arrived, the concert was already over.

meaning: "When I woke up, ..." (setting the scene for what was the case then).
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation in the past right after you woke up. "Als" introduces a past time point (“when”), and the verb comes second in the main clause, so you often get: "Als ich aufwachte, war ..." / "Als ich aufwachte, hatte ..." / "Als ich aufwachte, war er weg." You can follow it with a noun/adjective ("war ich müde"), a place ("war ich zu Hause"), or something that had happened/changed ("war mein Handy weg").
target_language_example: Als ich aufwachte, war es schon hell draußen.
native_language_example: When I woke up, it was already bright outside.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with words like einfacher/schwieriger, weniger/mehr, länger/kürzer, besser/schlechter) to say reality is different from your expectation. Common pattern: "(mehr/weniger/…)-er, als ich dachte."
target_language_example: Die Reise war teurer, als ich dachte.
native_language_example: The trip was more expensive than I thought.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause about a single event in the past (with **als**). The verb goes to the end of the clause: **als ich die Nachricht hörte**. Often paired with an emotional reaction in the main clause. Note: **als** can look like English “as,” but here it usually means “when” (in the past), not “as/like.”
target_language_example: Als ich die Nachricht hörte, war ich sprachlos.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I was speechless.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr, weniger, besser, leichter, teurer, etc.) to compare reality with what you expected in the past. In these sentences, als means “than” (not “when”). Often paired with “(nicht) so …, wie ich erwartet hatte” (= “(not) as … as I had expected”).
target_language_example: Der Test war schwieriger, als ich erwartet hatte.
native_language_example: The test was harder than I had expected.

meaning: "when I" / "than I" + "it" (referring back to something already mentioned).
additional_notes: This is a common chunk inside a longer clause. **Als** can mean **"when"** (for a one-time past event) or **"than"** (in comparisons). **Es** usually points back to a previously mentioned thing/idea, and in comparisons it often stands for an implied verb phrase: *geduldiger, als ich es bin* = “more patient than I am (patient)”; *besser ausgedrückt, als ich es könnte* = “better expressed than I could (express it).” Word order: the verb typically comes at the end of the *als*-clause (e.g., *als ich es bemerkte / als ich es bin / als ich es könnte*).
target_language_example: Das ist schwieriger, als ich es gedacht habe.
native_language_example: That is harder than I thought.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with a comparative adjective/adverb like billiger/teurer/länger) to say the reality was different from your expectation: „…, als ich gedacht hatte.“ It refers to what you previously assumed or expected.
target_language_example: Die Aufgabe war schwieriger, als ich gedacht hatte.
native_language_example: The task was harder than I had thought.

meaning: “when I … this morning” (talking about a past moment).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause in the past with als (“when” for a one-time past situation). You typically add a verb at the end of the clause: als ich heute Morgen aufgewacht bin / als ich heute Morgen angerufen habe. The main clause and als-clause often describe what was happening at that time.
target_language_example: Ich war noch müde, als ich heute Morgen das Haus verlassen habe.
native_language_example: I was still tired when I left the house this morning.

meaning: "when I (… ) him" (talking about a past moment).
additional_notes: Used to start a time clause about the past. **als** is used for a single time period/event in the past (“when”), not for repeated events (then you often use **wenn**). **ich** = “I”. **ihn** is the accusative form of “he” and means “him” (the direct object). The verb usually comes at the end of the **als**-clause: *Als ich ihn sah, …*
target_language_example: Als ich ihn gestern getroffen habe, war er sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: When I met him yesterday, he was very friendly.

meaning: "when I was in …" / "when I lived in …" (introduces a time in the past).
additional_notes: Used to start a subordinate clause with **als** for a single time period/event in the past. Word order: **Als ich in + place + verb …,** then the main clause follows (often with the verb in position 2). Common with **war** (was), **wohnte/lebte** (lived). Not used for repeated situations in the past (that’s usually **wenn**).
target_language_example: Als ich in Berlin war, habe ich jeden Tag Museen besucht.
native_language_example: When I was in Berlin, I visited museums every day.

meaning: “when I was young” / “back when I was young.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past period in your life. It’s a time clause introduced by **als** (for a single time/period in the past), often paired with the simple past (**war**) or past tense in the main clause (**habe … gespielt**, **lebte**, **konnte**). You can put it at the start of the sentence (then the verb comes second in the main clause) or later in the sentence.
target_language_example: Als ich jung war, wollte ich Feuerwehrmann werden.
native_language_example: When I was young, I wanted to be a firefighter.

meaning: when I was little / when I was young.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened regularly or at a specific time in your childhood. It often introduces a past situation (“Als ich klein war, …”) and commonly goes with past tense verbs (Perfekt or Präteritum). Word order can vary: “Als ich klein war, …” or “…, als ich klein war.”
target_language_example: Als ich klein war, wollte ich jeden Tag ein Eis essen.
native_language_example: When I was little, I wanted to eat ice cream every day.

additional_notes: Used with **als** to talk about a **single event in the past** (“when…”). It often starts a time clause, and the verb goes to the end in that clause: **Als ich nach Hause kam, …**. In the main clause, the verb comes right after this clause: **…, bemerkte ich / sah er / lernte Tom …**.
target_language_example: Als ich nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When I got home, nobody was there.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative to say something is more/less/different than the listener expects. Very common pattern: **(viel) + comparative + als ihr denkt** (e.g., *viel besser/mehr/länger … als ihr denkt*). **ihr** addresses more than one person informally; with one person you’d use **als du denkst**, and in formal speech **als Sie denken**.
target_language_example: Das ist schwieriger, als ihr denkt.
native_language_example: That is harder than you (all) think.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative ("-er" forms like größer, besser, schöner, schneller) to compare two people/things. German uses **als** for comparisons of inequality (bigger/better/etc.), where English uses **than**—not *as*. Common pattern: **X ist (nicht) ...-er als ihre Mutter** / **X ist nicht weniger ... als ihre Mutter**.
target_language_example: Er ist schneller als ihre Mutter.
native_language_example: He is faster than her mother.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr/besser/stärker/schöner, etc.) to mean that something is greater now than at any time in the past. Often paired with words like „mehr“, „besser“, „stärker“, etc.: „mehr als je zuvor“, „besser als je zuvor“.
target_language_example: Ich bin motivierter als je zuvor.
native_language_example: I’m more motivated than ever before.

meaning: than anyone else; than everyone else.
additional_notes: Used with comparatives (besser, schneller, mehr, usw.) to say someone does something more/better than all others. Often followed by extra information like „den ich kenne“ (“that I know”).
target_language_example: Sie kann das schneller lösen als jeder andere in der Klasse.
native_language_example: She can solve that faster than anyone else in the class.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined situation: “He talks as if he knew everything.” Very often followed by Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) to show it’s not (necessarily) true: wäre/wär’ (were), hätte (had), wüsste (knew). In everyday speech you may hear contractions like “wär’”.
target_language_example: Er schaut mich an, als ob er mich nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: He looks at me as if he didn’t know me.

additional_notes: Used to say that something seems a certain way, or that someone behaves/speaks in a way that isn’t really true. Very often followed by Konjunktiv II to show it’s unreal: „als ob ich verrückt wäre“ (not really crazy). You’ll also see it after feelings/perceptions like „Mir war, als ob …“ (“It felt as if …”).
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob ich ihn beleidigt hätte.
native_language_example: He acts as if I had insulted him.

additional_notes: Used to compare reality with an appearance, impression, or imagined situation. It’s often followed by Konjunktiv II (e.g., wäre/hätte) to show something is not real or is just assumed: "als ob sie reich wäre" = as if she were rich. In speech you may also hear "als wenn sie" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Er tut so, als ob sie ihn nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: He acts as if she didn’t know him.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (mehr, weniger, besser, größer, etc.) to compare two people/things. In German, **als** = “than” in comparisons (not “as”). The noun phrase can change: *als seine Schwester / als ihre Eltern* etc.
target_language_example: Sie ist größer als sein Bruder.
native_language_example: She is taller than his brother.

additional_notes: Used in two common patterns: (1) Comparisons: after comparatives like „besser“, „größer“, „schneller“ → „… als sie“ = “... than she/they.” (2) Time clause in the past: „als“ introduces a past moment or period (often a one-time event) → „als sie …“ = “when she/they …”. The meaning depends on whether it follows a comparative or introduces a time clause.
target_language_example: Ich war überrascht, als sie so früh angekommen ist.
native_language_example: I was surprised when she arrived so early.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a past event (often a one-time event) with **als** (“when” for past situations). The verb goes to the end of the **als**-clause: **als sie die Nachricht hörte**. Often sets the scene for an emotional reaction in the main clause.
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, konnte sie zuerst nichts sagen.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she couldn’t say anything at first.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a past time in someone’s life (here: a woman). With **als** you usually refer to a specific time period or one-time situation in the past. You can swap **sie** for another subject: **als ich/j er/wir jung war(en)** (“when I/he/we were young”).
target_language_example: Als sie jung war, hat sie in Berlin gelebt.
native_language_example: When she was young, she lived in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used with **als** to talk about a one-time period or situation in the past. Often appears in comparisons ("… schneller, als sie noch jung war") or to describe something that happened back then ("… als sie noch jung waren"). You’ll usually need the verb in the clause (e.g., **war/gewesen ist**).
target_language_example: Als sie noch jung war, ist sie jeden Tag schwimmen gegangen.
native_language_example: When she was still young, she went swimming every day.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative ("-er" forms or "mehr/weniger") to compare something to what is normal or typical: "länger als sonst", "voller als sonst", "später als sonst". You can also hear "nicht mehr als sonst (auch)" = "no more than usual".
target_language_example: Heute bin ich früher als sonst aufgestanden.
native_language_example: Today I got up earlier than usual.

meaning: "when we" (typically for a one-time event in the past).
additional_notes: Used to start a time clause about something that happened once in the past (Als wir ankamen, …). In the clause with "als", the verb goes to the end: "als wir angekommen sind" / "als wir ankamen". For repeated events or present/future, German usually uses "wenn" instead.
target_language_example: Als wir nach Hause kamen, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When we got home, nobody was there.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (länger, näher, schlimmer, ernster, reicher, etc.) to say reality is different from what you expected. Pattern: [comparative] + als wir dachten. In everyday speech you can also say: „als gedacht“ (“than expected”).
target_language_example: Der Weg war kürzer, als wir dachten.
native_language_example: The route was shorter than we thought.

additional_notes: Used with **als** to introduce a **one-time event in the past** (“when”). The clause is a **subordinate clause**, so the verb goes to the end: *als wir dort an**kamen***. Often used to set the time for another past action (e.g., something had already happened). Contrast: **wenn** = “when/if” for repeated events or general situations.
target_language_example: Als wir dort ankamen, war das Konzert schon angefangen.
native_language_example: When we arrived there, the concert had already started.

additional_notes: Used to compare something to an unreal or hypothetical situation: “(just) as if …”. It typically introduces a clause in the subjunctive (Konjunktiv II), most often with forms of sein: wäre (would be/weren’t). Common patterns: „als wäre nichts gewesen“ = “as if nothing had happened”; „als wäre ich …“ = “as if I were …”.
target_language_example: Er tut so, als wäre alles in Ordnung.
native_language_example: He acts as if everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used to make an unreal/imaginary comparison (often implying it’s not true). It uses Konjunktiv II (wäre = subjunctive of „sein“) and typically comes after a comma: „…, als wäre er …“ You can replace „er“ with other subjects: „als wäre ich/du/sie/wir/ihr/sie“.
target_language_example: Sie redet mit mir, als wäre er nicht im Raum.
native_language_example: She talks to me as if he weren’t in the room.

additional_notes: Used to open a question, often to move the conversation along or get to the point. Depending on tone, it can sound neutral (“So, what are we doing?”) or a bit impatient/expecting an explanation (“So, what’s this all about?”). Note: German „also“ usually means “so/well/therefore,” not English “also.”
target_language_example: Also, was machen wir jetzt?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing now?

meaning: "old enough to" (to be old enough to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has reached the age/maturity needed to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive clause with „zu“: „alt genug, um + zu + Verb“ (e.g., „alt genug, um allein zu reisen“).
target_language_example: Bist du alt genug, um Auto zu fahren?
native_language_example: Are you old enough to drive a car?

additional_notes: "alt" is an adjective meaning “old.” With "sein" (to be), you say someone/something “is old”: "Er/Sie/Es ist alt." Often used with an age comparison: "so alt wie" / "genauso alt wie" = “(just) as old as.” You can also specify an age: "fünf Jahre alt" = “five years old,” "wenige Monate alt" = “a few months old.”
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, wie alt er ist.
native_language_example: I don’t know how old he is.

meaning: “was … years/months old” (talking about someone’s age in the past).
additional_notes: Used in time clauses with **als** to mean “when I/he/she was … old.” The age phrase often comes before **alt**: **fünf Jahre alt**, **drei Monate alt**. Common pattern: **Als ich/er/sie … Jahre alt war, …**
target_language_example: Als sie zehn Jahre alt war, hat sie Klavier gelernt.
native_language_example: When she was ten years old, she learned piano.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons, often with adjectives like „gleich“, „so“, or „halb“: „gleich alt wie“ = the same age as; „so alt wie“ = as old as; „halb so alt wie“ = half as old as. Common alternative phrasing: „so alt wie“ or „genauso alt wie“.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht so alt wie du, aber wir sind ungefähr gleich alt wie Tom.
native_language_example: I’m not as old as you, but we’re about the same age as Tom.

additional_notes: Used to describe a female person who is old/elderly. It can sound blunt or disrespectful in some situations, especially when talking directly about someone; polite alternatives include "eine ältere Frau" (an older woman) or "eine Seniorin" (a senior woman).
target_language_example: Eine alte Frau sitzt auf der Bank und liest.
native_language_example: An old woman is sitting on the bench and reading.

additional_notes: Plural of „das Gebäude“ (building) with the adjective „alt“ (old). Often used for historic or traditional buildings in cities. In German, adjective endings change with the article/case: e.g., „viele alte Gebäude“ (many old buildings), „die alten Gebäude“ (the old buildings). Singular: „das alte Gebäude“.
target_language_example: In der Altstadt stehen viele alte Gebäude.
native_language_example: There are many old buildings in the old town (historic city center).

additional_notes: This is the accusative form of **(ein) alter Mann**. After verbs like **helfen** (to help), German often uses the **dative** (e.g., *hilf einem alten Mann*), but in other contexts you may see *einen alten Mann* as the direct object.
target_language_example: Ich sehe einen alten Mann im Park.
native_language_example: I see an old man in the park.

additional_notes: Means a car that is old/used. With the neuter noun „Auto“, the adjective often takes -es: „ein altes Auto“ (nominative/accusative). You can also specify age with a number: „ein acht Jahre altes Auto“ = “an eight-year-old car.”
target_language_example: Ich fahre noch ein altes Auto, aber es bringt mich überall hin.
native_language_example: I still drive an old car, but it gets me everywhere.

meaning: best; (often) best to / it’s best to.
additional_notes: Used to say something is the best option or works best (“am besten” = superlative of “gut”). Very common with “sein” + infinitive: “Es ist am besten, …” / “Am besten …” (= “It’s best to …”). Can also mean “(someone) knows (you) best”: “jemanden am besten kennen”.
target_language_example: Am besten gehst du jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: It’s best if you go home now.

meaning: to like best; to be your favorite (lit. “to please you the most”).
additional_notes: Used with the verb „gefallen“ (to please/appeal), so the person who likes something is in the dative: „mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/Ihnen“. Common in questions about preferences: „Was/Welcher Teil/Welches … hat dir am besten gefallen?“
target_language_example: Von allen Städten hat mir Berlin am besten gefallen.
native_language_example: Out of all the cities, I liked Berlin best.

additional_notes: Used to express your top preference among options (a superlative of "gern/lieber"). Common in questions like "Was machst du am liebsten?" (What do you like doing most?) or "Wie würdest du am liebsten …?" (How would you preferably …?). Often appears with verbs like "mögen", "gern haben", "hören", "machen".
target_language_example: Am liebsten trinke ich morgens Kaffee.
native_language_example: Most of all, I like to drink coffee in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to say what you like/prefer most or when something happens to the greatest degree. Often appears with verbs like „gefallen“ (to like) and with questions like „Was … am meisten?“ (What … the most?). It can also describe when something is strongest, e.g. „Montags bin ich am meisten beschäftigt“ (Mondays I’m the busiest).
target_language_example: Was magst du am meisten an Berlin?
native_language_example: What do you like most about Berlin?

additional_notes: Superlative form of "schnell" (fast). Used to say someone/something is the fastest, or which route/method is the quickest: "am schnellsten" = "fastest" (literally "at the fastest"). Often appears with questions like "Wie komme ich am schnellsten ...?" (What’s the fastest way for me to get ...?).
target_language_example: Wie komme ich am schnellsten ins Stadtzentrum?
native_language_example: What’s the fastest way to get to the city center?

additional_notes: Used to form the superlative of the adjective/adverb "schön" (beautiful, nice), often with seasons or places: "im Frühling am schönsten" = "most beautiful in spring." Common in the pattern "[Place] ist ... am schönsten" and the set phrase "Zu Hause ist’s am schönsten" (Home is nicest/best).
target_language_example: Die Stadt ist nachts am schönsten.
native_language_example: The city is most beautiful at night.

additional_notes: Superlative form of "wenig" (little). Used to compare three or more things: "am wenigsten interessant" = "the least interesting". Often appears with "von den ..." (of the ...): "von den dreien am wenigsten". With verbs/likes: "das mag ich am wenigsten" = "I like that the least". Also in the common phrase "wenn man es am wenigsten erwartet" = "when you least expect it".
target_language_example: Ich bin am Wochenende am wenigsten gestresst.
native_language_example: I’m least stressed on the weekend.

meaning: in the middle of nowhere; in a very remote place (vulgar).
additional_notes: A very informal, crude idiom used to complain that a place is extremely far away, hard to reach, or isolated. Often used with verbs like wohnen/leben (to live) or sich verirren (to get lost): „Wir haben uns … am Arsch der Welt verirrt.“ In polite situations, use something like „mitten im Nirgendwo“ instead.
target_language_example: Der Campingplatz liegt echt am Arsch der Welt.
native_language_example: The campsite is really in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: "am" = "an dem" and is used for locations (where something happens). Common with verbs like ankommen (arrive), abfahren (depart), treffen/begegnen (meet/run into).
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns morgen am Bahnhof um acht Uhr.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other tomorrow at the train station at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone feeling extremely upset after bad news, a breakup, disappointment, etc. Often used with "sein" (e.g., "Ich bin am Boden zerstört"). "Am Boden" literally means "on the ground" and emphasizes being knocked down emotionally.
target_language_example: Als ich die Nachricht hörte, war ich am Boden zerstört.
native_language_example: When I heard the news, I was devastated.

meaning: at the end of the (feminine genitive: der).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position at the far end of something (e.g., hallway, line) or something written at the bottom/end of a page. It’s the contraction of "an dem" → "am" + "Ende" + the genitive article "der" (because the next noun is feminine, e.g. "die Seite" → "der Seite"). With masculine/neuter nouns you’ll see "am Ende des" (e.g. "am Ende des Tages").
target_language_example: Am Ende der Straße gibt es einen Supermarkt.
native_language_example: At the end of the street there is a supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to point to the last part of something. It is followed by a genitive noun phrase (e.g., „des Konzerts“, „des Songs“, „des Flurs“). Common fixed expression: „(ein) Licht am Ende des Tunnels“ = hope after a difficult time.
target_language_example: Am Ende des Films waren alle ganz still.
native_language_example: At the end of the movie, everyone was completely quiet.

meaning: at the end of the sentence.
additional_notes: Used when talking about where something should be placed in a sentence (especially punctuation like a period) or about word order in grammar. Literally: “at the end of the sentence.”
target_language_example: Setz bitte ein Ausrufezeichen am Ende des Satzes.
native_language_example: Please put an exclamation mark at the end of the sentence.

additional_notes: "am" = "an dem" (dative), used for a specific place. You use it to say something happens at the airport (meeting someone there, being there, etc.). With location questions like "Wo?" it typically takes dative: "am Flughafen".
target_language_example: Wir sehen uns morgen am Flughafen.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other tomorrow at the airport.

additional_notes: Used to describe a place located at the bottom of something (often a mountain or hill). It is a fixed phrase with dative case: "am" = "an dem" and it’s followed by a genitive noun phrase (des + noun). For feminine nouns you use "am Fuße der" (e.g., am Fuße der Burg).
target_language_example: Am Fuße des Hügels gibt es ein kleines Café.
native_language_example: At the foot of the hill there is a small café.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happening up in the sky. Very common with verbs like sein (to be), fliegen (to fly), funkeln (to sparkle), and with things like stars, clouds, planes, birds. Literally "at the sky" (an + dem), but in English you usually say "in the sky."
target_language_example: Heute ist kein einziges Wölkchen am Himmel.
native_language_example: There isn’t a single cloud in the sky today.

additional_notes: Used to describe being alive (often with feelings like grateful, happy, or lucky), especially after danger or as a general appreciation of life. Common with adjectives like „froh/ glücklich/ dankbar“: „Ich bin froh/dankbar, am Leben zu sein.“
target_language_example: Nach der Operation war sie einfach nur dankbar, am Leben zu sein.
native_language_example: After the operation, she was simply grateful to be alive.

meaning: by the sea; at the seaside.
additional_notes: “am” = “an dem” (at/on the). “am Meer” is used for being located next to the sea (a town, a house, spending holidays there). Often contrasts with “im Meer” (= in the sea/water).
target_language_example: Im Sommer fahren viele Leute ans Meer und verbringen ein paar Tage am Meer.
native_language_example: In summer many people go to the sea and spend a few days at the seaside.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on Monday (a specific day/date). It’s a contraction of "an dem Montag" ("an" + "dem" → "am") and is used with days of the week (am Dienstag, am Mittwoch, etc.).
target_language_example: Am Montag arbeite ich bis spät.
native_language_example: On Monday I work until late.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the morning. It can refer to a specific morning (often with past/future context: "Am Morgen war...") or to a regular habit ("am Morgen" = in the mornings). It’s a contraction of "an dem Morgen" ("am" = "an dem").
target_language_example: Am Morgen habe ich oft keine Zeit für ein großes Frühstück.
native_language_example: In the morning, I often don’t have time for a big breakfast.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is planned during the afternoon. "am" = "an dem" (on/in the), so it often translates as "in the afternoon" in English.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns am Nachmittag im Park.
native_language_example: We’re meeting in the park in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific Saturday. "am" = "an dem" and is used with days of the week (am Montag, am Dienstag, etc.).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns am Samstag um 10 Uhr.
native_language_example: We’re meeting on Saturday at 10 o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on Sunday (a specific day of the week). It often answers the question "Wann?" (When?). Note: "am" = "an dem" and is used with days and dates (am Montag, am 3. Mai).
target_language_example: Am Sonntag haben wir Zeit.
native_language_example: On Sunday we have time.

meaning: at the wheel; in control (of something).
additional_notes: Used literally for driving a vehicle: „am Steuer sitzen“ = to be driving / to be behind the wheel. It can also be used figuratively to mean being in charge, especially with „das Steuer“ (e.g., „am Steuer des Landes“ = in control of the country).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute am Steuer, du kannst dich entspannen.
native_language_example: I’m driving today; you can relax.

additional_notes: "am" is a contraction of "an dem" and is used with places. With "Strand" it means being at the beach (on the sand/shore area). Often used to say where something happens: "am Strand spielen/liegen/laufen".
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns morgen am Strand.
native_language_example: We'll meet tomorrow at the beach.

meaning: to go for a walk on the beach.
additional_notes: Used with the verb „spazieren gehen“ (= to go for a walk). „am Strand“ means “at/on the beach” (literally: at the beach). Common in relaxed, leisure contexts; can be used in different tenses (e.g., „gingen“, „bin … gegangen“).
target_language_example: Wir gehen abends am Strand spazieren.
native_language_example: We go for a walk on the beach in the evening.

meaning: at the scene of the crime (at the location where it happened).
additional_notes: "Tatort" is the place where a crime happened; "am" = "an dem". Often used in police/news reports: "am Tatort gesehen" (seen at the crime scene), "am Tatort gestorben/verstorben" (died at the scene).
target_language_example: Die Polizei fand die Waffe am Tatort.
native_language_example: The police found the weapon at the crime scene.

meaning: on the phone; talking on the phone.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently on a phone call or to describe how someone sounds/what happens during a call. Common with verbs like sein (to be), klingen (to sound), sprechen (to talk), and phrases like Zeit am Telefon verbringen (to spend time on the phone).
target_language_example: Kannst du später anrufen? Ich bin gerade am Telefon.
native_language_example: Can you call later? I’m on the phone right now.

meaning: on the weekend; at the weekend.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening during the weekend in general, often as a repeated habit ("am Wochenende") or about plans for the upcoming weekend. "am" = "an dem" (at/on the).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende schlafe ich oft länger.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I often sleep in longer.

additional_notes: Adverbial superlative of „gut“ (good). Often answers “how (well)” or “what’s the best way”: „Wer kennt Sie am besten?“ = “Who knows you best?” It can also mean “preferably / it would be best (to) …”: „Am besten gehen wir jetzt.“ = “We’d better go now / Best we go now.” Not to be confused with English “at best” (= at most), which is usually „bestenfalls“ in German.
target_language_example: Am besten rufst du mich später an.
native_language_example: It’s best if you call me later.

meaning: all over the body; on the whole body.
additional_notes: Used to say something (itching, shaking, spots, bruises, pain, etc.) affects your body everywhere, not just one part. Often appears with verbs like „jucken“ (itch), „zittern“ (shiver), or with symptoms like „Flecken“ (spots) and „blaue Flecken“ (bruises).
target_language_example: Nach dem Insektenstich hatte ich am ganzen Körper Ausschlag.
native_language_example: After the insect bite, I had a rash all over my body.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened on the most recent weekend (Saturday/Sunday). It’s a time phrase: "am" = "an dem" (on the), "letzten" = last (dative). You can also say "letztes Wochenende" (without "am") depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Am letzten Wochenende habe ich meine Freunde besucht.
native_language_example: Last weekend I visited my friends.

additional_notes: Used to express your top preference among options (a superlative of "gern/lieber"). Common in questions like "Was machst du am liebsten?" (What do you like doing most?) or "Wie würdest du am liebsten …?" (How would you preferably …?). Often appears with verbs like "mögen", "gern haben", "hören", "machen".
target_language_example: Am liebsten trinke ich morgens Kaffee.
native_language_example: Most of all, I like to drink coffee in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to say what you like/prefer most or when something happens to the greatest degree. Often appears with verbs like „gefallen“ (to like) and with questions like „Was … am meisten?“ (What … the most?). It can also describe when something is strongest, e.g. „Montags bin ich am meisten beschäftigt“ (Mondays I’m the busiest).
target_language_example: Was magst du am meisten an Berlin?
native_language_example: What do you like most about Berlin?

additional_notes: Used with a noun to mean the next upcoming time or the next place in a sequence: am nächsten Bahnhof (at the next station), am nächsten Samstag/Dienstag (next Saturday/Tuesday), am nächsten Wochenende (next weekend). "Am" is a contraction of "an dem" + dative, so the noun is typically in the dative (e.g., Bahnhof → Bahnhof).
target_language_example: Am nächsten Halt steigen wir aus.
native_language_example: We get off at the next stop.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens on the morning of the next day (after what was just mentioned). Often starts a sentence as a time expression (position 1), but it can also appear later: „Ich rief Tom am nächsten Morgen an.“
target_language_example: Am nächsten Morgen gingen wir früh los.
native_language_example: The next morning we left early.

meaning: the next day; on the following day.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened one day after a time/event that was just mentioned. Very common for telling stories or describing sequences of events. Often appears at the start of a sentence: "Am nächsten Tag …"
target_language_example: Am nächsten Tag sind wir früh losgefahren.
native_language_example: The next day we set off early.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like (wieder) abfahren/abreisen/abfliegen to say someone departs the following day, often after a short visit. Word order: "am nächsten Tag" (time) + "wieder" (again) + separable prefix "ab" at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Wir sind nur kurz geblieben und fuhren am nächsten Tag wieder ab.
native_language_example: We only stayed briefly and left again the next day.

meaning: on the right leg (at the right leg).
additional_notes: Used to say where on the body something happens (e.g., get hit, injured, operated on). Grammatically it’s **an + dem = am** with dative: **am rechten Bein**. You’ll often see it with verbs like **treffen** (hit), **sich verletzen** (injure oneself), **operieren** (operate).
target_language_example: Er hat sich am rechten Bein verletzt.
native_language_example: He injured his right leg.

additional_notes: Used to say two events happen on the same calendar day as each other, or on the exact day already mentioned. Often refers back to a previous time expression (e.g., "he arrived on Monday" → "am selben Tag" = on that same Monday).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns getroffen und am selben Tag zusammen gegessen.
native_language_example: We met and ate together on the same day.

meaning: (the) most of all; most preferably; best of all.
additional_notes: Used to say what you like, prefer, or would rather do more than anything else. Common with questions like “Was … am allerliebsten?” (“What do you like best?”) and with verbs such as essen, kochen, mögen, or wäre(n) (“Where would you most like to be?”). It’s the superlative of gern/lieber/am liebsten (“gladly / rather / preferably”).
target_language_example: Ich trinke am allerliebsten Kaffee.
native_language_example: Most of all, I like to drink coffee.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine/neuter noun in the genitive case: an Bord des Schiffes, an Bord des Flugzeugs. It describes being on the vehicle (or going onto it). For feminine/plural nouns you use: an Bord der ...
target_language_example: Wir sind an Bord des Zuges und fahren gleich ab.
native_language_example: We’re on board the train and it’s about to depart.

meaning: to come aboard; to board (a ship/plane).
additional_notes: Used for getting onto a ship (and sometimes a plane). In formal/military-style speech you may hear it with a permission request, e.g. „Erlaubnis, an Bord kommen zu dürfen?“ (= “Permission to come aboard?”). With „lassen“ it means “to let someone come aboard”: „Lass/Lassen Sie ihn an Bord kommen.“
target_language_example: Dürfen wir jetzt an Bord kommen?
native_language_example: May we come aboard now?

additional_notes: Used to name the cause of illness or death, especially with verbs like „sterben“ (to die) and „erkranken“ (to fall ill): „an Krebs sterben“ = to die of/from cancer. In German, „an“ + dative is common for causes of death/illness (e.g., „an einer Krankheit“).
target_language_example: Leider ist ihr Vater an Krebs gestorben.
native_language_example: Sadly, her father died of cancer.

additional_notes: Used to say the cause of death: sterben + an + illness (e.g., an Krebs, an einer Krankheit). Often with time expressions like „letztes Jahr“, „vor einem Jahr“, or a month. You may also see „soll … gestorben sein“ to report something you heard (“is said to have died”).
target_language_example: Sie ist vor drei Jahren an Krebs gestorben.
native_language_example: She died of cancer three years ago.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "jemandem an allem die Schuld geben" = "to blame someone for everything." "an" + dative here means "for" (an allem = for everything).
target_language_example: Gib mir nicht an allem die Schuld!
native_language_example: Don’t blame me for everything!

meaning: to life in (as in: getting used to life in a place).
additional_notes: Most often used with the verb (sich) gewöhnen: „sich an das Leben in + Dativ gewöhnen“ = “to get used to life in …”. After „in“ you usually use the dative for location: „in der Stadt“, „in Tokio“, „in den USA“. Often appears with „gewöhnt sein“ (“to be used to”).
target_language_example: Ich muss mich erst an das Leben in Deutschland gewöhnen.
native_language_example: I first have to get used to life in Germany.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or say what you would do in someone else’s situation. Very common with the subjunctive for polite suggestions: „An deiner Stelle würde ich …“ You can change the pronoun: an meiner/seiner/ihrer/unserer/eurer Stelle.
target_language_example: An deiner Stelle würde ich den Arzt anrufen.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d call the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to give advice by imagining yourself in the other person’s situation (“in your place”). Very common in spoken German. It’s usually followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: „An deiner Stelle würde ich … machen/gehen/sagen.“ You can change the pronoun: „an Ihrer Stelle“ (formal), „an seiner/ihrer Stelle“ (his/her), „an eurer Stelle“ (you plural).
target_language_example: An deiner Stelle würde ich früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: If I were you, I would go to bed earlier.

additional_notes: Used when the preposition **an** requires the **dative** and the noun is **masculine/neuter** (**dem**). Very commonly contracted to **am** in everyday German: **an dem Turm** → **am Turm**. It appears in many fixed patterns with **an** (e.g., **teilnehmen an** = take part in, **Interesse/Vergnügen an** = interest/pleasure in, **unschuldig an** = not guilty of).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende nehmen wir an dem Kurs teil.
native_language_example: On the weekend we’re taking part in the course.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific day that’s already known from context or has been mentioned before. Often shortened to the contraction "am Tag"; with "dem" it points to a particular day (that day). Common in story-telling and when asking what happened on a certain day.
target_language_example: An dem Tag hatte ich meine erste Deutschstunde.
native_language_example: On that day, I had my first German lesson.

additional_notes: Used to link two parts of a sentence: it names a specific day ("an dem Tag") and then adds a relative clause that describes which day it was ("an dem ..."). Often appears as "An dem Tag, an dem ..." at the start of a sentence. In everyday speech it’s commonly shortened to "an dem Tag, als ..." or "an dem Tag, wo ..." (regional), but "an dem Tag, an dem" is standard.
target_language_example: An dem Tag, an dem wir umgezogen sind, hat es den ganzen Tag geregnet.
native_language_example: On the day when we moved, it rained all day.

additional_notes: Used when the preposition **an** takes the **dative** case: **an dem** + masculine/neuter noun. Very common with certain verbs/nouns that require **an** (e.g., **teilnehmen an** = take part in, **Interesse/Vergnügen an** = interest/pleasure in, **schuld sein an** = be to blame for). In everyday German, **an dem** is often contracted to **am** (e.g., *am Turm*, *am Wettbewerb*).
target_language_example: Am Samstag nehme ich an dem Kurs teil.
native_language_example: On Saturday I’m taking part in the course.

additional_notes: "An" describes contact or being right next to something (like *on* a surface or *at* a place). "An den" is used with **dative plural** (*an den Blumen*, *an den Türen*) or **accusative masculine** (*bis an den Horizont*). Dative often answers “where?” (location), accusative often answers “where to?” (movement/direction), especially with verbs like *riechen an* (to smell/sniff) or phrases like *bis an ...* (up to ...).
target_language_example: Er klopft an den Türen, aber niemand macht auf.
native_language_example: He knocks on the doors, but nobody opens up.

meaning: to the smell/odor (used with verbs like „sich gewöhnen an“ = to get used to).
additional_notes: Often appears in the phrase „sich an den Geruch gewöhnen“ (to get used to the smell). After „sich gewöhnen an“ you use the accusative, so: „an den Geruch“ (masc. der Geruch).
target_language_example: Ich habe mich schnell an den Geruch gewöhnt.
native_language_example: I got used to the smell quickly.

additional_notes: Used with motion verbs (e.g., gehen, fahren) to express going toward a specific beach area. Uses accusative (den Strand) because it answers “where to?” (wohin?). For being at the beach (no movement), German often uses “am Strand” (wo?).
target_language_example: Morgen gehen wir an den Strand, wenn das Wetter gut ist.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we're going to the beach if the weather is good.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *gehen* in the past (usually *Perfekt*): *ich bin / du bist / wir sind … an den Strand gegangen*. *An den Strand* means “to the beach” (direction/movement, accusative). For being located there (no movement), you say *am Strand* (“at the beach”).
target_language_example: Wir sind gestern nach der Arbeit an den Strand gegangen.
native_language_example: We went to the beach yesterday after work.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like gehen/fahren to mean going toward the beach as a destination. With this direction meaning it takes accusative: an den Strand. After you arrive and talk about being there (location), you often switch to dative: am Strand (= an dem Strand).
target_language_example: Heute Nachmittag gehen wir an den Strand.
native_language_example: This afternoon we’re going to the beach.

meaning: to/at the table (movement to a seated position).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion or change of position (especially "sich setzen") to mean going to the table and sitting down there. Often appears as "sich an den Tisch setzen" = "to sit down at the table." Contrast: "am Tisch" usually describes already being at the table (location).
target_language_example: Setz dich bitte an den Tisch.
native_language_example: Please sit down at the table.

meaning: to Santa Claus; in Santa Claus (believe in Santa).
additional_notes: A common phrase used with different verbs. With schreiben: „einen Brief an den Weihnachtsmann schreiben“ = to write a letter to Santa. With glauben: „an den Weihnachtsmann glauben“ = to believe in Santa. (The preposition „an“ changes case depending on the verb: movement/target → accusative „an den“, belief/attachment → dative „an dem“.)
target_language_example: Die Kinder glauben noch an den Weihnachtsmann.
native_language_example: The kids still believe in Santa Claus.

meaning: at/on the (feminine, dative); also “by” (e.g., by a feature).
additional_notes: “an der” is “an” + “der” (dative feminine singular; also dative plural in some contexts). It’s used for location near something (an der Ecke, an der Tankstelle) or contact with something (an der Wand). It can also mean “by” when you identify something using a feature: jemanden an der Stimme/Art/Bewegung erkennen (“recognize someone by their voice/style/movements”). Some fixed phrases use it too, e.g. an der Sache vorbei(gehen) (“to miss the point”).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns an der Haltestelle.
native_language_example: We'll meet at the bus stop.

additional_notes: Used with places where you are (stationary): warten/stehen/sein an der Bushaltestelle. Also common to describe a nearby location: „die Buchhandlung an der Bushaltestelle“ = the bookstore by/near the bus stop.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns an der Bushaltestelle um acht.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the bus stop at eight.

meaning: to be next / to be your turn.
additional_notes: Used when people take turns or wait in a line or sequence (e.g., at a counter, in a game, in class). Common with "sein": "Ich bin an der Reihe" (It’s my turn), "Wer ist als Nächster an der Reihe?" (Who’s next?).
target_language_example: Du bist jetzt an der Reihe.
native_language_example: It’s your turn now.

meaning: at the school (often: at/near the school building).
additional_notes: "An" + dative ("der Schule") commonly describes being at a place/location, often emphasizing the school as a site or meeting point (e.g., dropping someone off, working there, waiting outside). Often overlaps with "in der Schule" (in the school), but "an der Schule" can sound more like "at/near the school" rather than inside a classroom.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns an der Schule um acht Uhr.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the school at eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "berühren" (to touch) to say where someone was touched, and with injuries/pain to say the location: "sich an der Schulter verletzen" (to injure your shoulder). Often answers the question "Wo?" (Where?).
target_language_example: Tut dir die Schulter weh, oder hast du dich an der Schulter verletzt?
native_language_example: Does your shoulder hurt, or did you injure your shoulder?

meaning: at the meeting; in the meeting (often with teilnehmen = “to take part”).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb phrase „an der Sitzung teilnehmen“ (= to attend/participate in the meeting). „Sitzung“ is a formal word for a meeting/session (e.g., a team meeting, committee meeting). Note: „Sitzung“ looks like English “sitting,” but it does not mean sitting—here it means “meeting/session.”
target_language_example: Ich kann leider nicht an der Sitzung teilnehmen.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I can’t attend the meeting.

meaning: at the door; on the door.
additional_notes: Used with the dative (der Tür) after "an". It can mean a location next to the door (standing/waiting at the door, someone is at the door) or something attached to the door (a sign/lock on the door). You often see it with sounds/actions like "klingeln/läuten/klopfen an der Tür" (to ring/knock at the door).
target_language_example: Bitte warte an der Tür.
native_language_example: Please wait at the door.

additional_notes: Used to say someone studies, learns, works, or is physically located at a university. Often with verbs like „studieren“, „lernen“, „arbeiten“, or „sein“. „an der“ = „at the“ (dative feminine: die Universität → der Universität).
target_language_example: Ich studiere Informatik an der Universität.
native_language_example: I study computer science at the university.

meaning: on the wall; on the surface of the wall.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is located on/at the wall (e.g., hanging, painted, written, a spot/stain). With verbs like hängen/stehen/schreiben it often means something is displayed or written on the wall. Note: "an" is used where English often uses "on" because it expresses contact/attachment to a vertical surface.
target_language_example: Neben der Tür hängt ein Spiegel an der Wand.
native_language_example: Next to the door, there’s a mirror hanging on the wall.

meaning: "at the next" (at the next traffic light/stop/corner, etc.).
additional_notes: Used for directions and travel instructions. It’s usually followed by a feminine noun in the dative case: an der nächsten Ampel/Station/Straßenecke/Bushaltestelle/Kreuzung. (With a masculine or neuter noun you’d use: „am nächsten …“.)
target_language_example: An der nächsten Kreuzung gehen Sie geradeaus.
native_language_example: At the next intersection, go straight ahead.

additional_notes: Used for public transport (bus, tram, subway, train) to say where you want to get off or where someone should stop. Often used with verbs like aussteigen (get off), halten/stoppen (stop), and with requests like „Bitte …“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich möchte an der nächsten Haltestelle aussteigen.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’d like to get off at the next stop.

meaning: to you (informal singular) / about you (after certain verbs).
additional_notes: "an" + "dich" is used with the informal singular "you" (du). It can mean (1) direction/recipient: "für/zu dir" (e.g., a gift "to you"), and (2) the object of certain verbs that take "an" (e.g., "an dich denken" = think about you; "sich an dich erinnern" = remember you). With formal singular/plural "you", it becomes "an Sie"; with plural informal, "an euch".
target_language_example: Ich schicke dir morgen eine Nachricht an dich.
native_language_example: I'll send you a message tomorrow.

meaning: "in/at/to the" (feminine singular or plural after "an"), often "to" when "an" is used with verbs.
additional_notes: "An" is a preposition that can take either accusative (movement/direction, “to”) or dative (location, “at/on”). "An die" is accusative and is used with feminine singular nouns (die Tür) and plural nouns (die Touristen). Common with verbs like glauben an (believe in), sich anpassen an (adapt to), sich gewöhnen an (get used to), sich halten an (stick to/follow), klopfen an (knock on), herantreten an (approach). Contrast: "an der" (dative) = at/on the (feminine), e.g., "an der Tür" = at the door.
target_language_example: Ich muss mich an die neuen Regeln gewöhnen.
native_language_example: I have to get used to the new rules.

meaning: to get to work; to start working (on something).
additional_notes: Usually used with a reflexive pronoun: sich an die Arbeit machen (ich mache mich…, du machst dich…, wir machen uns…). It often suggests “stop delaying and begin now,” and is commonly followed by a reason or task (e.g., für die Prüfung).
target_language_example: Nach dem Kaffee machen wir uns an die Arbeit.
native_language_example: After the coffee, we’ll get to work.

meaning: (come) to power; into power (especially political power).
additional_notes: Most often used with verbs like **kommen** or **gelangen**: **an die Macht kommen/gelangen** = “to come to power” (e.g., a party/leader takes control of a government). Literally it’s “to the power,” but in English you usually say “to power / into power.” Not to be confused with **an die Macht glauben**—that’s usually **an die Macht (von …) glauben** = “to believe in the power (of …)” (e.g., *die Macht der Liebe*).
target_language_example: Die neue Partei kam nach der Wahl an die Macht.
native_language_example: The new party came to power after the election.

meaning: "(to) the rules" (used with sich an etw. halten = to follow/obey rules).
additional_notes: Most often appears in the phrase **sich an die Regeln halten**: *Ich halte mich an die Regeln* (I follow the rules). With **halten** it means “to stick to / comply with,” not the physical “hold.” The verb changes for the person: *ich halte mich*, *du hältst dich*, *wir halten uns*, *ihr haltet euch*, *Sie halten sich*.
target_language_example: Bitte halten Sie sich an die Regeln.
native_language_example: Please follow the rules.

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs of movement or contact directed at a door, e.g. klopfen an die Tür (knock on the door), klingeln an der/an die Tür (ring the doorbell), gehen an die Tür (go to the door to answer/open it). With location (no movement) you more often see an der Tür (“at the door”).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte an die Tür gehen?
native_language_example: Can you please go to the door?

meaning: 'against the wall' / 'to the wall' (placing something so it touches the wall).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/placement (stellen, lehnen, bringen, malen, hängen) to say something is put/leaned/painted onto the wall. Grammar note: "an" + accusative (an die Wand) = motion/direction; compare "an der Wand" (dative) = already located on/at the wall.
target_language_example: Kannst du das Regal an die Wand stellen?
native_language_example: Can you put the shelf against the wall?

meaning: to think about the future; to plan ahead.
additional_notes: Used when advising someone to be responsible and consider long-term consequences (often with müssen/sollen: „Du musst/solltest an die Zukunft denken.“). The verb is „denken an“ + accusative (an + die Zukunft).
target_language_example: Bevor du das Geld ausgibst, denk an die Zukunft.
native_language_example: Before you spend the money, think about the future.

additional_notes: "An diesem" is "an" + "diesem" (dative masculine/neuter), used before a noun: z.B. "an diesem Gerücht" (about this rumor), "an diesem Gebäude" (about/on this building). You often see it in patterns like "etwas dran an + Dativ" (there’s something to it) and "(jemandem) gefällt etwas an + Dativ" (someone likes something about…).
target_language_example: An diesem Plan gefällt mir, dass er so einfach ist.
native_language_example: What I like about this plan is that it’s so simple.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific morning already known from the context (often a particular day being talked about in a story). "An" here means "on" (time). You’ll also see the same pattern with other time words: "an diesem Tag" (that day), "an diesem Abend" (that evening).
target_language_example: An diesem Morgen hatte ich einen wichtigen Termin.
native_language_example: That morning I had an important appointment.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific day already known from context (often a particular date or occasion). With days/dates, German commonly uses "an" + dative: "an diesem Tag", "an dem Tag" (often shortened to "an dem" → "am").
target_language_example: An diesem Tag hat es den ganzen Tag geregnet.
native_language_example: It rained all day on that day.

meaning: this weekend (at some point during it).
additional_notes: Used to talk about plans, availability, or events happening at any time during the upcoming/current weekend. Often in questions like „Hast du an diesem Wochenende Zeit?“
target_language_example: Ich kann an diesem Wochenende leider nicht, ich bin unterwegs.
native_language_example: Unfortunately I can't this weekend; I'm traveling.

meaning: at this point; at this spot/place.
additional_notes: Used for either (1) a specific physical location (a particular spot along a river/road, etc.) or (2) a point in a text, conversation, or process (“at this point”). Often describes what changes or happens there: „Der Weg gabelt sich an dieser Stelle.“
target_language_example: An dieser Stelle müssen wir kurz anhalten.
native_language_example: We need to stop briefly at this point.

meaning: “on a” / “at a” (with a masculine or neuter noun in the dative).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition **an** + **einem** (= dative singular of *ein*) when something happens **at a time** (*an einem Mittwoch* = on a Wednesday), **at a place** (*an einem Ort* = at a place), or **on/against something** by contact (*an einem heißen Bügeleisen* = on a hot iron). Often contrasts with **in einem** (“in a”).
target_language_example: An einem Sonntag ist die Stadt viel ruhiger.
native_language_example: On a Sunday, the city is much quieter.

meaning: in one day; within a single day.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done in the time span of one day (often emphasizing speed or that it can/can’t be finished in a day). Contrast: "an einem Tag" = within one day vs. "an einem Tag" in the sense of "on a certain day" (less common without more context). Often interchangeable with "innerhalb eines Tages" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Ich muss das bis morgen schaffen, aber nicht an einem Tag.
native_language_example: I have to get it done by tomorrow, but not in one day.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition „an“ to say you are studying/working/doing something at an institution or place, especially with feminine nouns like „die Universität“, „die Schule“. Here „einer“ is the dative form of „eine“ (because „an“ often takes dative when it means location: where?).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet an einer Schule in Berlin.
native_language_example: She works at a school in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the most important thing. Very common with the verb „stehen“: „X steht an erster Stelle“ (= X comes first / is the top priority). Often appears with abstract nouns like „Sicherheit“ (safety) or „Klarheit“ (clarity).
target_language_example: Bei dieser Arbeit steht die Qualität an erster Stelle.
native_language_example: In this job, quality is the top priority.

additional_notes: Made of **an** + **ihrem** (dative: “her/its”). With **an + dative**, it often describes a position next to/at something (*an ihrem Platz*, *an ihrem Schreibtisch*) or being attached/close (*am/an ihrem Telefon*). It also appears after certain verbs/nouns that use **an**: **zweifeln an** (to doubt), **die Schuld an** (the blame for).
target_language_example: Er blieb an ihrem Tisch stehen.
native_language_example: He stopped at her table.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **an** + **dative** to mean that something happens/exists on each occasion or at each item in a set. Common with time expressions like **an jedem Freitag** (“every Friday”) and with parts/places like **an jedem Finger** (“on each finger”). The form **jedem** is the dative masculine/neuter form of **jeder**.
target_language_example: An jedem Montag gehe ich ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: Every Monday I go to the gym.

additional_notes: Used with a time word in the dative (e.g., Morgen/Abend/Nachmittag/Tag) to refer to a specific moment in the past or in a story: an jenem Abend = on that (particular) evening. Often points back to something already known from context (like “that evening” in a narrative).
target_language_example: An jenem Tag habe ich ihn zum ersten Mal getroffen.
native_language_example: On that day, I met him for the first time.

meaning: on that day (a specific day in the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a particular day that’s already known from the story/context, often in narration. "jenem" is a demonstrative form of "jener" (“that”), and it sounds a bit more literary/dramatic than the everyday "an dem Tag" or "an diesem Tag".
target_language_example: An jenem Tag habe ich zum ersten Mal Deutsch gesprochen.
native_language_example: On that day I spoke German for the first time.

meaning: on that day (back then; referring to a specific past day).
additional_notes: Points to a particular day in the past that’s known from the story/context (often a dramatic or important day). Very common in written/storytelling style; in everyday German you’ll more often hear: „an jenem Tag“ or simply „an dem Tag“/„an diesem Tag“ depending on meaning.
target_language_example: An jenem Tage begann für sie ein neues Leben.
native_language_example: On that day, a new life began for her.

meaning: (thinking) about my childhood; (reminds me) of my childhood.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **(sich) erinnern an** (to remember) and **jemanden an etwas erinnern** (to remind someone of something). With **an** + accusative: **an meine Kindheit** (accusative feminine). Examples: **Ich erinnere mich an meine Kindheit.** / **Das erinnert mich an meine Kindheit.**
target_language_example: Der Geruch von frisch gebackenem Brot erinnert mich an meine Kindheit.
native_language_example: The smell of freshly baked bread reminds me of my childhood.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **denken an** (to think of/about) and **sich erinnern an** (to remember / be reminded of). Here **an** takes the accusative (**meinen Vater**) and means “of/about,” not physical direction “to.”
target_language_example: Wenn ich das Lied höre, denke ich sofort an meinen Vater.
native_language_example: When I hear that song, I immediately think of my father.

meaning: "at/on my" or "to/with my" (with feminine nouns; dative).
additional_notes: “An” is a preposition that can take dative or accusative. “An meiner …” uses dative feminine (or dative singular feminine nouns like die Station, die Predigt, die Verbindung) and often means being at something or working on something: „an meiner Station“ (at my stop), „an meiner Predigt arbeiten“ (work on my sermon). For movement toward something, you’d usually use accusative: „an meine …“ (e.g., „Ich gehe an meine Station“ = I go to my stop).
target_language_example: Ich arbeite noch an meiner Hausaufgabe.
native_language_example: I'm still working on my homework.

meaning: by my side; next to me (physically or in support).
additional_notes: Literally “at my side.” It can mean someone is standing/sitting next to you, or (more often) that they stay with you and support you, especially in difficult moments. Common with verbs like sein (to be), bleiben (to stay), and haben/wollen … an meiner Seite haben (to have/want someone by your side). You can change the possessive: an deiner Seite, an seiner/ihrer Seite, an unserer/eurer Seite.
target_language_example: Danke, dass du in dieser schweren Zeit an meiner Seite bist.
native_language_example: Thank you for being by my side during this difficult time.

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone would do if they were in your situation (often with the conditional: „würdest … tun“, „wärst“). You can swap the pronoun: „an deiner Stelle“ (in your place), „an Ihrer Stelle“ (formal), „an seiner/ihrer Stelle“ (in his/her place), „an unserer/eurer Stelle“.
target_language_example: An deiner Stelle würde ich das Angebot annehmen.
native_language_example: In your place, I would accept the offer.

meaning: "about me" / "of me"; or "to me" (directed at me).
additional_notes: Used with different verbs where "an" takes different cases. With thinking/believing/remembering it’s usually **an + accusative**: *an mich denken* (think of me), *an mich glauben* (believe in me), *sich an mich erinnern* (remember me), *als Erinnerung an mich* (as a memory of me). With communication/turning to someone, it’s often **sich an + accusative wenden**: *Sie wandte sich an mich* (she addressed/turned to me). With movement toward someone, you’ll often see **an + accusative** too: *sich an mich heranschleichen* (sneak up to me).
target_language_example: Bitte denk ab und zu an mich.
native_language_example: Please think of me from time to time.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like **denken (an)** or **sich erinnern (an)** to say you can’t think of anything else—often because you’re obsessed or very focused. Common pattern: **an nichts anderes denken als an + Akkusativ** (“think of nothing else but …”).
target_language_example: Ich kann an nichts anderes denken als an dich.
native_language_example: I can’t think of anything else but you.

additional_notes: "an" + dative is used with masculine/neuter "sein-" forms: seinem (e.g., seinem Akzent, seinem Haus, seinem Kaffee). It can mean (1) "by/from" as the basis for recognizing something ("an seinem Akzent" = by his accent), (2) physical location/contact (at/on his house/arm), or (3) with some verbs, a point you are drinking/smoking from ("an seinem Kaffee schlürfen" = sip at/from his coffee).
target_language_example: An seinem Gesichtsausdruck sehe ich, dass er müde ist.
native_language_example: I can tell by his facial expression that he’s tired.

additional_notes: Describes someone’s location: being seated/working/eating at their desk. Often used with verbs like sitzen (to sit), essen (to eat), arbeiten (to work), or sein (to be). The preposition "an" + dative shows being at a place (not moving toward it). You can swap the possessive: an meinem/deinem/ihrem Schreibtisch = at my/your/her desk.
target_language_example: Ich sitze gerade an meinem Schreibtisch und schreibe eine E-Mail.
native_language_example: I'm sitting at my desk right now and writing an email.

meaning: on/at his …; in some phrases also “from/of his …” (e.g., dying from injuries).
additional_notes: “an” + “seinen” is usually “on/at his” with a following noun (often plural: an seinen Türen/Nägeln/Wunden = on/at his doors/nails/wounds). With certain verbs—especially health-related ones like “an … sterben/versterben”—“an” means “from” (cause): “an seinen Verletzungen” = from his injuries.
target_language_example: Die Bilder hängen an seinen Wänden.
native_language_example: The pictures are hanging on his walls.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens or exists at your school. Here, "an" means "at" (location/association), and "unserer Schule" is dative feminine ("die Schule" → "unserer Schule"). Common with institutions like schools/universities: "an der Schule", "an unserer Schule".
target_language_example: An unserer Schule gibt es eine große Bibliothek.
native_language_example: At our school there is a big library.

meaning: ..., when he ... (talking about a specific past time).
additional_notes: This pattern often appears with separable-prefix verbs that end in **an** (e.g. **anrufen**, **anfangen**, **anlächeln**, **sich anfreunden**): the **an** moves to the end of the clause, then a comma introduces a time clause with **als er**. **Als er** is used for a single event/time in the past (= “when he ...”), not for repeated events (use **wenn er** for that). Note: **als** looks like English “as”, but here it usually means “when”.
target_language_example: Ich fing an, als er ankam.
native_language_example: I started when he arrived.

meaning: Used with certain verbs to introduce a 'that…' clause (e.g., "Ich nehme an, dass…" = "I assume that…").
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. It’s the pattern you see when a separable-prefix verb with **an-** is split: the verb stem stays in position 2 and **an** goes to the end of the clause, right before a comma + **dass**-clause. Common ones: **annehmen, dass…** (to assume/think that), **jdm etw. ansehen, dass…** (to be able to tell/see from someone that), **damit angeben, dass…** (to brag that). The comma before **dass** is required.
target_language_example: Ich nehme an, dass wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: I assume that we’ll leave earlier tomorrow.

meaning: “to start/begin (to do something)” (often with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: This shows the common pattern with the separable verb **anfangen**: **fangen … an, (etwas) zu …**. In the present tense, **an** goes to the end: *Er fängt an …*; in the past: *Er fing an …*; participle: *hat angefangen*. Often followed by a reflexive verb with **sich** (e.g., *sich interessieren*, *sich lustig machen*, *sich küssen*).
target_language_example: Ich fange an, mich für Deutsch zu interessieren.
native_language_example: I’m starting to get interested in German.

additional_notes: Used to say that boredom begins after some time. Often with time phrases like „nach ein paar Minuten“ (after a few minutes) or „nach einer Viertelstunde“ (after a quarter of an hour). The reflexive verb „sich langweilen“ means “to be bored,” and with „anfangen“ it becomes “to start getting bored.”
target_language_example: Im Unterricht fange ich nach zehn Minuten an, mich zu langweilen.
native_language_example: In class, I start getting bored after ten minutes.

additional_notes: Most often seen as the pattern **anrufen / bei … anrufen, um … zu + infinitive** to say why you’re calling or contacting someone. **um … zu** expresses purpose (“in order to”). The comma is standard: *Er rief an, um …*
target_language_example: Ich rufe bei der Praxis an, um einen Termin zu vereinbaren.
native_language_example: I’m calling the doctor’s office to make an appointment.

meaning: Used with separable verbs like „anrufen/anfangen“ to mean “(do X) when … / if …”.
additional_notes: In many common verbs, **an-** is a separable prefix (e.g., **anrufen** = to call, **anfangen** = to start). In main clauses, **an** moves to the end: **Ruf mich an. / Wir fangen an.** A **wenn**-clause (“when/if”) adds the condition or time: **Ruf mich an, wenn …** (“Call me when/if …”). If the **wenn**-clause comes first, the main clause verb comes second: **Wenn Bob kommt, fangen wir an.**
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Call me when you have time.

additional_notes: Common with the separable verb **anrufen** (“to call”). In main clauses, the prefix **an** goes to the end: **Ruf mich an.** The **wenn du…** clause (“when you…”) often comes after it: **Ruf mich an, wenn du zu Hause bist.** If the **wenn** clause comes first, word order flips in the main clause: **Wenn du zu Hause bist, ruf mich an.**
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wenn du Zeit hast.
native_language_example: Call me when you have time.

meaning: Used when a separable verb with the prefix **an-** is split: the **an** goes to the end, often right before **und** (“and”).
additional_notes: In German main clauses, many verbs with **an-** are *separable*: the main verb stays in position 2 and the prefix **an** moves to the end. When you add another action with **und**, the **an** often appears immediately before **und**: **Ich rufe Tom an und erzähle …** (= *I call Tom and tell …*). Common verbs: **anrufen** (rufen … an = to call), **ankommen** (kommen … an = to arrive), **anziehen** (ziehen … an = to put on), **anlegen** (legen … an = to put on/put on equipment). In subordinate clauses, it usually stays together: **…, weil ich Tom anrufe.**
target_language_example: Ich mache das Licht an und lese noch ein bisschen.
native_language_example: I turn on the light and read a little more.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **anfangen** to say someone starts doing an action: **anfangen + zu + infinitive**. Because **anfangen** is separable, **an** often goes to the end: *Ich fange an zu laufen.* In 3rd person singular: *er/sie/es fängt an zu …*. (In everyday speech, **zu** is sometimes dropped: *Ich fange an zu lernen* / *Ich fange an, lerne…*).
target_language_example: Wir fangen an zu kochen, sobald die Gäste da sind.
native_language_example: We start cooking as soon as the guests are here.

meaning: to start laughing; to begin to laugh.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "anfangen" (to start): "anfangen, + zu + infinitive". In the present/past, the separable prefix "an" goes to the end: "Ich fange ... an, zu lachen." / "Ich fing ... an, zu lachen." In perfect tense: "Ich habe angefangen zu lachen."
target_language_example: Als er den Witz erzählte, fing ich an zu lachen.
native_language_example: When he told the joke, I started laughing.

meaning: to start raining (to begin to rain).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "anfangen" (or "beginnen"): "Es fängt/fing an zu regnen" = “It’s starting/started to rain.” Very common with weather and the dummy subject "es". In everyday speech you also often hear: "Es fängt an zu regnen" or shorter "Es fängt an zu regnen."
target_language_example: Nimm einen Schirm mit — es fängt gleich an zu regnen.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella — it’s about to start raining.

additional_notes: Used with the separable verb **anfangen** + **zu** + infinitive: **anfangen zu schreien** = “to start to scream”. In the past tense it often appears split: **Er fing an zu schreien.** / **Sie fingen an zu schreien.** You’ll also see **anfangen, zu schreien** with a comma.
target_language_example: Als er das hörte, fing er an zu schreien.
native_language_example: When he heard that, he started screaming.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „anfangen“/„beginnen“: „anfangen + an zu + infinitive“ (e.g., „Er fing an zu weinen.“). In modern German you’ll also often hear „anfangen zu weinen“ without the extra „an“.
target_language_example: Als sie die Nachricht hörte, fing sie an zu weinen.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she started to cry.

additional_notes: Used after comparisons with "als" ("better than", "faster than"): "besser/schneller als jeder andere, den ich kenne" = "better/faster than anyone else I know." The comma introduces a relative clause ("den ich kenne" = "(whom) I know") that describes "jeder andere". For a female person you can say "jede andere, die ich kenne"; for plural: "alle anderen, die ich kenne".
target_language_example: Du singst besser als jeder andere, den ich kenne.
native_language_example: You sing better than anyone else I know.

additional_notes: Usually used with a preposition like auf (on) and often with an indefinite article and adjective ending: auf anderen Planeten (on other planets) or auf einem anderen Planeten (on another planet). Also common in comparisons: wie auf einem anderen Planeten (“like on another planet”) to say a place feels alien/strange.
target_language_example: Auf anderen Planeten könnten ganz andere Bedingungen herrschen.
native_language_example: On other planets, completely different conditions could prevail.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "sein": "anderer Meinung sein" = to think differently / not share the same opinion. Common patterns: "Ich bin (da) anderer Meinung." (I disagree.), "Ich bin anderer Meinung als du." (I have a different opinion than you.), "Zu diesem Thema bin ich anderer Meinung." (On this topic, I disagree.).
target_language_example: Ich bin da anderer Meinung – ich finde, das ist keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: I disagree—I don't think that's a good idea.

meaning: to have a different opinion; to disagree.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone’s view is different from someone else’s. Often followed by „als + Person“: „Ich bin anderer Meinung als du.“ It’s fairly formal/neutral; in everyday speech you can also say „Ich sehe das anders“ or „Ich bin anderer Meinung.“
target_language_example: Ich bin anderer Meinung als du, aber ich verstehe deinen Punkt.
native_language_example: I disagree with you, but I understand your point.

meaning: to change your mind; to reconsider.
additional_notes: Usually used as the reflexive phrase **es sich anders überlegen** (e.g., *ich überlege es mir anders*, *du überlegst es dir anders*, *wir überlegen es uns anders*). It often comes with **noch/immer noch** to mean “you can still change your mind.”
target_language_example: Wenn du möchtest, kannst du es dir bis morgen noch anders überlegen.
native_language_example: If you want, you can still change your mind by tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the fixed reflexive phrase **es sich anders überlegen** = “to change one’s mind / decide differently.” The **sich** changes with the person: **ich überlege es mir anders**, **du überlegst es dir anders**, **er/sie überlegt es sich anders**, **wir überlegen es uns anders**, **ihr überlegt es euch anders**, **Sie überlegen es sich anders**. Often appears with **wieder** (“again”) or **plötzlich** (“suddenly”).
target_language_example: Ich habe es mir anders überlegt und komme doch mit.
native_language_example: I changed my mind and I’m coming along after all.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "anfangen" (= to start/begin) + a comma + an infinitive phrase ("... zu lernen" = to learn). Very common pattern: "anfangen, etwas zu tun" (to start doing something). Often said in the past with "haben" ("Ich habe angefangen, ...").
target_language_example: Ich habe letztes Jahr angefangen, Französisch zu lernen.
native_language_example: I started learning French last year.

additional_notes: Past form of the phrase "angeln gehen" (“to go fishing”). In the Perfekt, German uses **sein**: "Ich bin angeln gegangen" / "Wir sind angeln gegangen". Often used with time words like "letztes Wochenende" and with "nicht" to say you didn’t go: "Wir sind nicht angeln gegangen."
target_language_example: Wir sind gestern früh angeln gegangen.
native_language_example: We went fishing early yesterday.

additional_notes: A very common past-time sequence: one event happens first, and when someone arrives, the other situation has already happened. Typically used with **als** (= when, for one-time past events). **ankam** is Präteritum of *ankommen* (to arrive), and **war** is Präteritum of *sein* (to be). Often combined with **schon/bereits** (= already). Word order: **Als** + (subject) + **ankam**, **war** + (subject/complement) …
target_language_example: Als wir ankam(en), war das Restaurant schon voll.
native_language_example: When we arrived, the restaurant was already full.

meaning: to the phone; to answer/pick up the phone.
