additional_notes: Used in legal or formal contexts to say someone is allowed to protect themselves or to respond to accusations (e.g., in court). The verb phrase is reflexive: sich verteidigen = “to defend oneself.” Often appears with haben: jemand hat das Recht, sich zu verteidigen.
target_language_example: In einem Prozess hat jeder das Recht, sich zu verteidigen.
native_language_example: In a trial, everyone has the right to defend themselves.

additional_notes: Used for sporting races (running, cycling, car racing, etc.) and sometimes more generally for a contest to be first (e.g., elections, business). Common verbs: „ein Rennen gewinnen“ (to win a race), „ein Rennen anführen“ (to lead a race), „ein Rennen verfolgen/beobachten“ (to follow/watch a race).
target_language_example: Wir haben das Rennen im Fernsehen verfolgt.
native_language_example: We followed the race on TV.

additional_notes: Used in a subordinate clause (often an indirect question) meaning someone won a race. It’s in the Perfekt tense: "hat ... gewonnen" (has won). In subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb ("hat") goes at the end: "wer das Rennen gewonnen hat" = "who has won the race."
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, wer das Rennen gewonnen hat.
native_language_example: I don't know who has won the race.

meaning: “the right thing” / “the right one” (the correct or best choice).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like tun (“to do”) to mean doing what is morally right, or with sein (“to be”) to mean something is the right choice/fit. Often appears with genau (“exactly”) in phrases like genau das Richtige (“exactly the right thing/fit”). Capitalized like a noun (from the adjective richtig).
target_language_example: Dieser Kurs ist genau das Richtige für mich.
native_language_example: This course is exactly the right one for me.

additional_notes: Used for making a morally correct or appropriate choice (often implying it may be difficult). Common with verbs like versuchen (to try) or jemanden überzeugen (to convince someone).
target_language_example: Manchmal ist es nicht leicht, das Richtige zu tun.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s not easy to do the right thing.

additional_notes: Used to say someone acted correctly in a situation. It’s often used with the perfect tense: (ich habe / du hast / er-sie-es hat / wir haben / ihr habt / sie haben) + „das Richtige getan“. „das Richtige“ is a nominalized adjective meaning “the right thing” (literally “the right [one/thing]”). With „zu haben“ it appears in statements like „Ich hoffe, das Richtige getan zu haben“ (“I hope I did the right thing”).
target_language_example: Du hast das Richtige getan, indem du ihm geholfen hast.
native_language_example: You did the right thing by helping him.

additional_notes: Used at the table to ask someone to hand you the salt. It’s usually combined with an indirect object in the dative: „(Können/Könnten/Würden) Sie mir bitte das Salz reichen?“ You can swap „mir“ for „dir“ (to you) / „ihm/ihr“ (to him/her) etc. „reichen“ here means “hand over,” not “be enough.”
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte das Salz reichen?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the salt, please?

meaning: fate; destiny (what happens to you, often beyond your control).
additional_notes: A neutral noun used for the idea that life events are “meant to happen” or are decided by forces outside you. Common with verbs like: an das Schicksal glauben (to believe in fate), das Schicksal entscheidet (fate decides), das Schicksal herausfordern (to challenge fate). Metaphors are common, e.g. "Das Schicksal mischt die Karten" (fate deals the cards).
target_language_example: Manchmal fühlt es sich an, als würde das Schicksal alles bestimmen.
native_language_example: Sometimes it feels like fate decides everything.

additional_notes: A neuter noun: das Schiff (plural: die Schiffe). Often used with common shipping verbs like ablegen (to depart), auslaufen (to set sail/leave port), Anker setzen (to drop anchor), untergehen (to sink), and unter einer Flagge fahren (to sail under a country’s flag). Figuratively it can mean a “vehicle” for a place, e.g., das Schiff der Wüste (“ship of the desert” = camel).
target_language_example: Unser Schiff läuft um 18 Uhr aus.
native_language_example: Our ship leaves port at 6 p.m.

meaning: "the ship is" (used to describe the ship’s state, location, or direction).
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence: subject + verb "sein" (to be). "das Schiff" = "the ship" (neuter), and "ist" is the 3rd person singular present tense of "sein" ("is"). You often continue with an adjective (Das Schiff ist hübsch.), a place (Das Schiff ist auf See.), or movement/destination (Das Schiff ist unterwegs nach …).
target_language_example: Das Schiff ist heute im Hafen.
native_language_example: The ship is in the harbor today.

additional_notes: A simple past (Präteritum) statement describing that a ship went under water. "sank" is the Präteritum of "sinken" (to sink). In everyday spoken German, you’ll also often hear the perfect tense: "Das Schiff ist gesunken."
target_language_example: Zum Glück konnten sich alle retten, bevor das Schiff sank.
native_language_example: Luckily, everyone was able to get to safety before the ship sank.

additional_notes: Neuter superlative of schlimm (“bad/awful”). Used to talk about the worst aspect of something (Das Schlimmste am …), or about a situation being past or still ahead: Das Schlimmste ist vorbei (“the worst is over”), Das Schlimmste steht noch bevor (“the worst is still to come”). Often followed by a relative clause: Das ist das Schlimmste, was … (“That’s the worst thing that …”).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—das Schlimmste ist schon vorbei.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—the worst is already over.

additional_notes: "Schloss" has two common meanings. With doors/keys (Tür, Schlüssel, aufbrechen, klemmen), it means "lock". With visiting/sightseeing or descriptions of a building (Besuch wert, geöffnet, besichtigen, Graben, mitten in der Stadt), it means "castle/palace." Context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Wir haben das Schloss verloren, also kommen wir nicht rein.
native_language_example: We lost the key to the lock, so we can’t get in.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "jemandem etwas beibringen" = "to teach someone something" (often a skill). In the examples it’s in the perfect tense: "hat ... beigebracht". Word order: subject + "hat" + (indirect object in dative, e.g. "mir") + what was taught ("das Schwimmen") + "beigebracht" at the end.
target_language_example: Meine Mutter hat mir das Schwimmen beigebracht.
native_language_example: My mother taught me how to swim.

additional_notes: A noun meaning a rope used for climbing, rescuing, pulling, etc. Common with verbs like (fest)halten (hold tight), loslassen (let go), ergreifen (grab), hochklettern (climb up). Note the gender: das Seil (neuter).
target_language_example: Ich halte das Seil fest, damit du sicher hochklettern kannst.
native_language_example: I’m holding the rope tight so you can climb up safely.

additional_notes: Used for games in general (a board game, a children’s game) and for sports matches (especially football/soccer: „Das Spiel dauert neunzig Minuten.“). Common verbs: „stattfinden“ (to take place), „losgehen“ (to start), „dauern“ (to last), „gewinnen“ (to win), „beenden“ (to end).
target_language_example: Ich schaue mir das Spiel heute Abend im Fernsehen an.
native_language_example: I’m going to watch the match on TV tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gewinnen" (to win) in the perfect tense: "hat/haben ... gewonnen". "das Spiel" is the direct object (the game/match that was won). Common in questions: "Wer hat das Spiel gewonnen?" (Who won the game?).
target_language_example: Mein Bruder hat das Spiel gewonnen.
native_language_example: My brother won the game.

additional_notes: A neuter noun (das). Used for a physical telephone or a phone in general. Common with verbs like klingeln (to ring), (ab)nehmen (to pick up), hören (to hear).
target_language_example: Ich höre das Telefon, aber ich kann gerade nicht rangehen.
native_language_example: I hear the phone, but I can't pick up right now.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "Das Telefon klingelt". Used in narratives and written German to say that the phone rang (often with adverbs like "erneut" = again, "manchmal" = sometimes, "ziemlich lange" = quite a long time). In spoken German, people often use the perfect: "Das Telefon hat geklingelt."
target_language_example: Das Telefon klingelte, aber ich konnte nicht rangehen.
native_language_example: The phone rang, but I couldn’t answer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what you’re discussing or dealing with. Common with verbs like: über ein Thema sprechen (talk about a topic), ein Thema wechseln (change the subject), ein Thema kommt zur Sprache (a topic comes up). In the fixed phrase „Das Thema ist durch“ it means “That’s settled / We’re done with that topic.”
target_language_example: Können wir bitte das Thema wechseln?
native_language_example: Can we please change the subject?

additional_notes: Most commonly means a gate you can open/close (e.g., garden gate). Often used with verbs like aufschließen (unlock), schließen (close), and reparieren (repair). In sports (especially soccer), das Tor can also mean the goal or a scored goal (ein Tor schießen = to score a goal).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte das Tor hinter dir schließen?
native_language_example: Can you please close the gate behind you?

additional_notes: A noun meaning an organized meeting or planned get-together. Common with verbs like stattfinden (to take place), beginnen (to begin), absagen (to cancel), and verschieben (to postpone). Plural: die Treffen.
target_language_example: Können wir das Treffen auf Dienstag verschieben?
native_language_example: Can we postpone the meeting to Tuesday?

additional_notes: A neuter noun used for the whole cosmos/everything in space (stars, planets, galaxies). Often appears in general statements with verbs like „existieren“, „erschaffen“, or phrases like „keine Grenzen haben“ and „voller … sein“.
target_language_example: Wir wissen noch nicht viel über das Universum.
native_language_example: We still don’t know much about the universe.

meaning: a company; a business (also: an undertaking/project).
additional_notes: Most often means a company or business organization (especially in news or formal contexts). It can also mean an undertaking/venture (something you plan and carry out), but in your examples it’s mainly the business meaning (going bankrupt, changing owners, size of the company). Plural: die Unternehmen.
target_language_example: Das Unternehmen stellt dieses Jahr viele neue Mitarbeiter ein.
native_language_example: The company is hiring many new employees this year.

meaning: the video (a video clip or recording).
additional_notes: Neuter noun: das Video. Plural: die Videos. Used for a video file/clip or a recording (e.g., online video, movie on a device). With "leihen" it means to borrow/lend for a while: "jemandem etwas leihen" = to lend someone something; "sich etwas leihen" = to borrow something.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das Video später schicken?
native_language_example: Can you send me the video later?

meaning: the people (as a nation or population; often in a political sense).
additional_notes: Refers to the population of a country or group as a whole (like “the people”/“the populace”). Common in political speeches and statements about what people want or demand (e.g., “Das Volk hat gesprochen.” = “The people have spoken.”). It can sound formal, rhetorical, or propagandistic depending on context; for “people” in general you often use “Leute” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Die Regierung muss auf das Volk hören.
native_language_example: The government has to listen to the people.

additional_notes: A common neuter noun (das). Used with the definite article when referring to specific water in context (e.g., in a glass, a river, or water just mentioned). In many everyday situations you’ll also hear it without an article: „Wasser, bitte.“
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte das Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I have the water, please?

meaning: 'the water is' (used to describe the water).
additional_notes: "Das" makes "Wasser" definite: "the water". Use this phrase with an adjective or description: "Das Wasser ist heiß/kalt/warm". In "Das Wasser ist knapp", "knapp" means scarce/limited (e.g., during droughts or restrictions). In questions like "Wie tief das Wasser ist?", the verb goes at the end in the clause introduced by "wie".
target_language_example: Das Wasser ist zu kalt zum Schwimmen.
native_language_example: The water is too cold to swim.

additional_notes: Uses **war**, the simple past (Präteritum) of **sein** (“to be”), to describe what the water was like in the past (temperature, condition, depth, etc.). **Das Wasser** is neuter, so it goes with **es war** → **das Wasser war**. Note: **war** looks like English “war” but here it means **“was.”**
target_language_example: Das Wasser war nach dem Regen sehr schmutzig.
native_language_example: The water was very dirty after the rain.

additional_notes: A very common noun used to talk about weather conditions (warm/cold, sunny, rainy, etc.). Often used with verbs like sein (Das Wetter ist schön.), werden (Das Wetter wird kalt.), or bleiben (Das Wetter bleibt kalt.).
target_language_example: Wie wird das Wetter am Wochenende?
native_language_example: What will the weather be like on the weekend?

meaning: "the weather is" (used to describe the weather).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to talk about current weather conditions: Das Wetter ist schlecht/sonnig/trocken/wunderbar. Common alternatives: Es ist + adjective (Es ist kalt.) or Das Wetter ist + adjective. "Wetter" is neuter (das), so you say "das Wetter".
target_language_example: Das Wetter ist heute sehr warm, aber morgen ist es kühl.
native_language_example: The weather is very warm today, but tomorrow it’s cool.

additional_notes: Used to describe what the weather was like in the past. It’s the past tense (Präteritum) of "sein" (to be): "Das Wetter war ..." + adjective (angenehm, herrlich, perfekt). Common in written German and storytelling; in speech you also often hear: "Das Wetter ist ... gewesen."
target_language_example: Gestern war das Wetter warm und sonnig.
native_language_example: Yesterday the weather was warm and sunny.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about a specific word or expression (e.g., a word nobody uses anymore). It can also mean a person's spoken words in a more emotional or formal sense ("His words came from the heart"). In questions like "Wie ist das Wort?", it can mean "What’s the word again?" when you can’t remember the exact term.
target_language_example: Mir fällt das Wort gerade nicht ein.
native_language_example: I can't think of the word right now.

additional_notes: A neuter noun: das Zelt (plural: die Zelte). Often used with camping verbs like „ein Zelt aufbauen“ or „ein Zelt aufschlagen“ (= to pitch/set up a tent). Common prepositions: „im Zelt“ (in the tent), „vor dem Zelt“ (in front of the tent).
target_language_example: Wir schlafen heute Nacht im Zelt.
native_language_example: We’re sleeping in the tent tonight.

additional_notes:
A very general word for items/substances when you don’t want to name them precisely: "Kannst du das Zeug mitnehmen?" = “Can you take this stuff?”

Common fixed uses:
- "das Zeug dazu haben" = to have what it takes / to have the ability.
- "... was das Zeug hält" (idiom) = as much as possible, at full blast (e.g., feiern/arbeiten/musik hören).
target_language_example: Räum bitte das Zeug vom Tisch weg.
native_language_example: Please clear the stuff off the table.

additional_notes: Often used for a physical target you aim at (e.g., in shooting): aufs Ziel richten (aim at the target), das Ziel treffen (hit the target), das Ziel verfehlen (miss the target). It can also mean a goal/aim in a more general sense (e.g., ein Ziel erreichen = achieve a goal).
target_language_example: Ich habe mein Ziel erreicht.
native_language_example: I achieved my goal.

additional_notes: A neuter noun (das). Common for hotel rooms, bedrooms, or any room in a building. In phrases like „Das Zimmer dreht sich“ it can also mean “everything is spinning” (a dizziness feeling).
target_language_example: Ich bin gleich im Zimmer.
native_language_example: I’ll be in the room in a moment.

additional_notes: "betrat" is the simple past (Präteritum) of the verb "betreten" = "to enter". It’s often used in written narration and with time clauses like "als" (when) or "in dem Augenblick, in dem" (the moment when) to describe what was happening when someone entered.
target_language_example: Als sie das Zimmer betrat, verstummten alle.
native_language_example: When she entered the room, everyone fell silent.

additional_notes: Uses **war**, the simple past (Präteritum) form of **sein** (“to be”) for **er/sie/es**. Common in written German and when describing past states/conditions: **Das Zimmer war + adjective** (dunkel, warm, unordentlich) or **Das Zimmer war in + dative** (e.g., *in einem guten Zustand*).
target_language_example: Das Zimmer war sauber, aber sehr klein.
native_language_example: The room was clean, but very small.

meaning: “all that / all of that” (everything we’ve been talking about).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a whole set of things, events, or information already known from context. It often appears as an object: „Ich sollte dir das alles nicht erzählen.“ = “I shouldn’t tell you all that.” In questions it can emphasize the amount/effort: „Wie machst du das alles?“ = “How do you do all that?”
target_language_example: Ich kann das alles nicht alleine schaffen.
native_language_example: I can’t manage all of that on my own.

meaning: "the best" (neuter form), often meaning “the best one/thing”.
additional_notes: Used as the superlative of „gut“ (good). You’ll often see it with a noun: „das beste Restaurant“ (the best restaurant). It can also stand alone to mean “the best (option/model/poem/etc.)”: „Zeigen Sie mir das beste.“ (Show me the best one.). Note: without a noun, it can refer generally to “the best” rather than a specific item.
target_language_example: Von allen Optionen ist das beste zu teuer.
native_language_example: Of all the options, the best one is too expensive.

additional_notes: Used when there is just one option, item, or person. Often followed by a relative clause: "Das einzige, was ..." = "The only thing that ...". "einzige" changes to match gender/case (der/die/das einzige; das Einzige can also be used as a noun meaning "the only thing").
target_language_example: Das Einzige, was ich brauche, ist ein bisschen Zeit.
native_language_example: The only thing I need is a little time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is just one relevant thing (want, know, did, etc.). It’s often followed by a verb (will/weiß/habe) and then a form of "sein" (ist/war) to introduce what that one thing is: "Das Einzige, was ich will, ist …". Capitalize "Einzige" because it’s used as a noun here.
target_language_example: Das Einzige, was ich heute brauche, ist ein bisschen Ruhe.
native_language_example: The only thing I need today is a bit of peace and quiet.

additional_notes: Used to single out one person from a group, followed by a relative clause. Even though it refers to a girl, "Mädchen" is grammatically neuter, so the relative pronoun is often "das" (not "die"). The verb in the relative clause usually goes to the end: "... das Jeans trug."
target_language_example: Sie ist das einzige Mädchen, das heute Zeit hat.
native_language_example: She is the only girl who has time today.

additional_notes: Used when the adjective „erste“ is nominalized (used like a noun) and refers to the first person/thing in a sequence. It’s neuter here („das“), often meaning “the first thing.” Very common in fixed phrases like „das erste Mal“ = “the first time,” and in relative-clause patterns like „das erste (Lied/Buch), das …“.
target_language_example: Das erste, was ich morgens mache, ist Kaffee trinken.
native_language_example: The first thing I do in the morning is drink coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing (or did) something for the first time. It’s often used with a main clause like „Es ist/war …“ (it is/was …). After „dass“, the verb goes to the end of the clause: „… dass ich das Museum besuchte / gelesen habe“. The tense usually matches the time (present: „Es ist …“, past: „Es war …“).
target_language_example: Das ist das erste Mal, dass ich in Deutschland bin.
native_language_example: This is the first time that I’m in Germany.

meaning: “for the first time in …” / “the first time in (a place) …”.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens for the first time, either within a time period (e.g., “das erste Mal in zehn Jahren” = for the first time in ten years) or in a particular place/situation (e.g., “das erste Mal in London” = the first time in London). Often used with past tense when talking about when you first met/saw/experienced something.
target_language_example: Das ist das erste Mal in zwei Monaten, dass ich frei habe.
native_language_example: This is the first time in two months that I’ve had time off.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean you mean all of it: das ganze Dorf (the whole village), das ganze Wochenende (the whole weekend), das ganze Geschirr (all the dishes). It changes with gender/case: der ganze Tag, die ganze Woche, das ganze Jahr; im ganzen Haus (in the whole house). As a noun, "das Ganze" means "the whole thing / the whole matter" (e.g., Das Ganze ist schwierig.).
target_language_example: Ich habe das ganze Buch an einem Tag gelesen.
native_language_example: I read the whole book in one day.

additional_notes: Uses the neuter article "das" because "Geld" is neuter (das Geld). "Ganz" means "whole/entire"; with "das" it becomes "das ganze". Often refers to all the money available/mentioned in context (e.g., all your cash, all the money you were given, the full sum).
target_language_example: Ich habe leider nicht das ganze Geld dabei.
native_language_example: Unfortunately, I don't have all the money with me.

meaning: all year (round); throughout the whole year.
additional_notes: Used to say something is true for the entire year, not just in one season. Often with weather/temperature (warm/kalt) or ongoing situations (arbeiten). Word order: it typically sits in the middle of the sentence: „Es ist das ganze Jahr über …“ / „Sie mussten das ganze Jahr über …“.
target_language_example: In dieser Stadt gibt es das ganze Jahr über viele Touristen.
native_language_example: In this city there are lots of tourists all year round.

additional_notes: Means all parts of a country (nationwide). Often used to emphasize that something affects everyone or everywhere in the country. Grammar: "das" because "Land" is neuter; changes with case (e.g., nominative/accusative: "das ganze Land", dative: "dem ganzen Land").
target_language_example: Nach dem Finale feierte das ganze Land.
native_language_example: After the final, the whole country celebrated.

additional_notes: "Zeug" is an informal, vague word for things/items (often a pile or collection). "das ganze" means "all the" and refers to the whole amount. Used when you don’t want to name each item: buying it, selling it, or asking where it came from. In questions about price you often hear: "Was willst du für das ganze Zeug?" (informal) or "Wie viel wollen Sie für das ganze Zeug?" (more polite).
target_language_example: Ich räume später das ganze Zeug weg.
native_language_example: I’ll put all this stuff away later.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is identical to something else. Often appears with a comparison using **wie** (e.g., *das Gleiche wie ich* = “the same as me”). Capitalization can vary by function: **das gleiche** + noun (adjective: “the same ...”), but **das Gleiche** as a standalone noun (“the same thing”).
target_language_example: Ich habe das gleiche Problem wie du.
native_language_example: I have the same problem as you.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is identical to something else. Often appears with a comparison using **wie** (e.g., *das Gleiche wie ich* = “the same as me”). Capitalization can vary by function: **das gleiche** + noun (adjective: “the same ...”), but **das Gleiche** as a standalone noun (“the same thing”).
target_language_example: Ich habe das gleiche Problem wie du.
native_language_example: I have the same problem as you.

additional_notes: Used to say two people have/use an identical dictionary. Often appears with comparisons like “wie”: “das gleiche Wörterbuch wie ich” (“the same dictionary as me”). Note: In careful German, “das gleiche” can mean “the same kind of” (similar), while “dasselbe” means “the exact same one,” but many speakers use them interchangeably in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Wir haben das gleiche Wörterbuch für den Kurs.
native_language_example: We have the same dictionary for the course.

additional_notes: Used when the superlative adjective “größte” refers to a neuter noun with “das” (e.g., das größte Hotel) or when it’s used like a noun (“the greatest thing”), often with abstract nouns like „Glück“: „das größte Glück“. The form changes with gender/case (e.g., „der größte“, „die größte“, „im größten“).
target_language_example: Das größte Problem ist die Zeit.
native_language_example: The biggest problem is time.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you gave up something very important for someone. Often appears with a "für + Akkusativ" phrase: "für dich/Sie/euch" (= for you). "erbracht" is the past participle of "erbringen" (to perform/produce), so you’ll often see it as "ich habe ... erbracht" (present perfect).
target_language_example: Ich habe für dich das größte Opfer erbracht.
native_language_example: I made the greatest sacrifice for you.

additional_notes: A noun phrase: "das Wetter" (the weather) + adjective "kalt" (cold). The adjective ending changes depending on the article/case (e.g., "das kalte Wetter", "bei kaltem Wetter"). Common with verbs like "(an)halten" (to continue/last) and "sich an etwas gewöhnen" (to get used to something).
target_language_example: Bei dem kalten Wetter bleibe ich lieber zu Hause.
native_language_example: In this cold weather, I’d rather stay at home.

additional_notes: "Mädchen" is a neuter noun, so it uses "das" and pronouns like "es" (e.g., "warum es weine"). "kleine" is the adjective "klein" with the usual ending after "das" in the nominative/accusative: "das kleine Mädchen".
target_language_example: Das kleine Mädchen lacht, weil es ein Geschenk bekommen hat.
native_language_example: The little girl is laughing because she got a present.

additional_notes: Neuter, nominalized form of "letzt" used when "the last" stands on its own: "das letzte Stück" (the last piece), "das letzte Kapitel" (the last chapter). Very common in the pattern "Das Letzte, was ich will, ist ..." = "The last thing I want is ...".
target_language_example: Das Letzte, was ich brauche, ist noch mehr Stress.
native_language_example: The last thing I need is even more stress.

meaning: "(to have) seen (someone) the last time" / "last saw (someone)".
additional_notes: Used to ask or say when you most recently saw a person. Often appears in questions with "Wann ... das letzte Mal gesehen?" and takes an object in the accusative: "Ich habe ihn/sie dich/den Mann das letzte Mal gesehen ..." In casual speech, "hab" is common for "habe".
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn das letzte Mal gestern Abend gesehen.
native_language_example: I last saw him yesterday evening.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the most recent time you saw someone/something in the past. Often appears in time clauses like **als ich … das letzte Mal sah** (“when I last saw …”) or with **seit** (“since”): **seit ich dich das letzte Mal sah** (“since I last saw you”). The verb **sah** is simple past of **sehen** (“to see”), commonly used in writing and storytelling.
target_language_example: Als ich sie das letzte Mal sah, wohnte sie noch in Berlin.
native_language_example: When I last saw her, she still lived in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the most recent time something happened. Very common with the present perfect: „Wann bist du das letzte Mal … gegangen?“ (When was the last time you went …). Note the standard spelling is two words: „das letzte Mal“ (not *das letztemal*).
target_language_example: Ich war das letzte Mal vor zwei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: The last time I was in Berlin was two years ago.

additional_notes: Usually written as **„das letzte Mal gesehen“** (= “seen the last time”). Used in questions to ask **when/where someone last saw something/someone**, often with **haben** + **gesehen**: *Wo hast du es das letzte Mal gesehen?* = “Where did you last see it?”
target_language_example: Wo hast du deinen Pass das letzte Mal gesehen?
native_language_example: Where did you last see your passport?

meaning: 'the last time (you) … someone' (referring to a person in the dative).
additional_notes: Used to ask when something last happened involving another person (jemandem = “to/for someone,” dative). Often appears in questions like: „Wann hast du das letzte Mal jemandem …?“ Note the usual spelling is „das letzte Mal“ (two words, Mal is capitalized).
target_language_example: Wann hast du das letzte Mal jemandem geholfen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you helped someone?

meaning: 'the last time with' (i.e., the last time you did something with someone).
additional_notes: Used in questions like: „Wann war/bist/hast du das letzte Mal mit Tom …?“ to ask when you last did an activity with a specific person. Note spelling: usually „das letzte Mal“ (two words, „Mal“ capitalized). The verb comes later: „… mit Tom gestritten/angeln gewesen …“.
target_language_example: Wann warst du das letzte Mal mit deinen Freunden im Kino?
native_language_example: When was the last time you went to the movies with your friends?

additional_notes: Used when talking about pain, injuries, or medical issues involving the left leg. Common patterns: **Mir tut das linke Bein weh** (“My left leg hurts,” literally “To me the left leg hurts”) and **sich das linke Bein brechen** (“to break your left leg”). In medical contexts you may also see **sich das linke Bein abnehmen lassen** (“to have the left leg amputated”).
target_language_example: Nach dem Sturz konnte er das linke Bein kaum bewegen.
native_language_example: After the fall, he could hardly move his left leg.

meaning: most of that; most of what (…)
additional_notes: Used to say that the majority of something is true/known/taught, often followed by a relative clause: „das meiste von dem, was …“. It refers back to something already mentioned (e.g., what someone said). You’ll also see the close variant „das meiste davon“ = “most of it/that.”
target_language_example: Das meiste von dem, was sie erzählt hat, war hilfreich.
native_language_example: Most of what she told us was helpful.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific new thing with a neuter noun (e.g., das neue Haus, das neue Jahr, das neue Lied, das neue Modell). Note: you normally add the noun after it. If the noun is omitted and you mean “the new thing/the new (idea)”, German often capitalizes it: „das Neue“.
target_language_example: Ich mag das neue Kleid, das du gekauft hast.
native_language_example: I like the new dress you bought.

additional_notes: Uses the neuter definite article (das) because it often refers to an implied neuter noun like Jahr, Spiel, Zimmer, Flugzeug, Opfer, Geschäft, etc. You use it to talk about the next item in a sequence (next year, next game), the nearest/next location (the next shop/room), or the next occurrence/option (the next plane). The exact noun is often clear from context.
target_language_example: Wann ist das nächste Treffen?
native_language_example: When is the next meeting?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next occasion something happens (often with a condition like "wenn du ..." = "when you ..."). Common with verbs like "kommen" (come), "treffen" (meet), and in reminders or mild warnings (e.g., "Überprüfe es das nächste Mal ..." = "Check it more carefully next time").
target_language_example: Das nächste Mal rufe ich dich vorher an.
native_language_example: Next time I'll call you beforehand.

additional_notes: A noun phrase: "das" (the) + "rote" (red, with ending because it comes after "das") + "Kleid" (dress). Often used with verbs like "(sich) für etwas entscheiden" (to choose something) and "jemandem steht etwas" meaning "something suits someone / looks good on someone" (e.g., "Das rote Kleid steht ihr gut.").
target_language_example: Ich nehme das rote Kleid.
native_language_example: I’ll take the red dress.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific thing or content (often something said, done, or earned). It’s common before a clause: "Das, was du gesagt hast ..." = "What you said ...". In speech it’s often shortened to just "was" when the meaning is clear ("Was du gesagt hast, ..."), but "das, was" is more explicit.
target_language_example: Das, was ich meine, ist ganz einfach.
native_language_example: What I mean is quite simple.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to an unspecified thing (similar to English “what you said/did/want”). Often followed by a verb at the end of the clause: „das, was du gesagt hast“ = “what you said.” In writing, the commas are standard: „das, was du …“.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe das, was du meinst.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean.

meaning: "what he …" / "that which he …" (introduces a noun clause).
additional_notes: Used in the common structure "das, was + subject + …" to mean "what (someone) …". It refers to a thing/idea/action (not a person). The comma is part of the construction: "das, was er gesagt hat" = "what he said". In the following clause, the verb typically comes at the end.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe nicht das, was er meint.
native_language_example: I don't understand what he means.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a noun-like clause about something you do/think/have (a relative clause). It often comes before a verb phrase like „geschrieben habe“, „erwartet habe“, „trinke“, etc. Comma is normally used: „das, was ich …“.
target_language_example: Das, was ich gestern gesagt habe, tut mir leid.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what I said yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something in a general sense ("man" = one/you/people). It often introduces a relative clause: "Das ist das, was man … nennt" = "That’s what you call …". "das, was" refers to an idea or thing, and "man" makes it sound general rather than about a specific person.
target_language_example: Das ist das, was man im Urlaub braucht.
native_language_example: That’s what you need on vacation.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an event or situation (often something already known or being discussed). It’s a relative clause: **das** + **was passiert ist** (“that which happened”). The commas are common in writing when **was passiert ist** is inserted as extra information. You can change the tense: **das, was passiert war** (what had happened), **das, was passiert** (what is happening).
target_language_example: Ich möchte nicht mehr über das, was passiert ist, sprechen.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about what happened anymore.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a thing, action, or idea connected to “she” (sie). It’s a relative-clause structure: “das, was …” = “what/that which …”. A comma usually comes after “das” because the clause “was sie …” explains it: “das, was sie getan hat” = “what she did”.
target_language_example: Ich verstehe das, was sie meint.
native_language_example: I understand what she means.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause referring to an unspecified thing: "das, was wir + verb" = "what we + verb". Often separated by commas because it starts a relative clause (e.g., "Das, was wir brauchen, ...").
target_language_example: Das, was wir heute lernen, ist sehr wichtig.
native_language_example: What we’re learning today is very important.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did something deliberately (not by accident). Often appears with a form of **haben**: *Hast du das absichtlich getan?* (“Did you do that on purpose?”). **das** = “that,” **absichtlich** = “intentional(ly),” **getan** = “done” (past participle of *tun*).
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht absichtlich getan.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

meaning: 'that too / that as well' (also: 'that, too' in questions).
additional_notes: Used when referring back to a specific action/idea mentioned before ("das" = "that"). With "auch" it means the same action applies in addition ("too/as well"). In questions it often means “also/too” in the sense of “as well”: „Hast du dir das auch überlegt?“ = “Did you think that through as well?” Word order is usually „das auch“ when „das“ is the object: „Er wird das auch tun.“
target_language_example: Kannst du das auch machen, bitte?
native_language_example: Can you do that too, please?

additional_notes: Most commonly you’ll see just **auf jeden Fall** = “definitely / for sure / in any case.” In **das auf jeden Fall**, **das** refers back to a specific action/idea (“that”), and **auf jeden Fall** strongly emphasizes certainty or determination. It’s flexible in word order: *Ich mache das auf jeden Fall.* / *Das mache ich auf jeden Fall.*
target_language_example: Das mache ich auf jeden Fall morgen.
native_language_example: I’ll definitely do that tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to explain the meaning or consequence of something: "Das bedeutet X" = "That means X." With a person in the dative (mir/dir/ihm …), it means something is important to someone: "Das bedeutet mir viel" = "That means a lot to me." Often appears in questions like "Was bedeutet das?" or "Wissen Sie, was das bedeutet?"
target_language_example: Wenn du nicht kommst, bedeutet das, dass du keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: If you don’t come, that means you don’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to compare how well someone does something. Pattern: "[Person] macht/kann das besser als [comparison]" (e.g., besser als ich / besser als du / besser als jeder andere). "das" refers to the action or task being talked about.
target_language_example: Ich kann das besser als du.
native_language_example: I can do that better than you.

meaning: 'that/it, please' (polite request: asking someone to do that).
additional_notes: Used when you refer to a specific thing/action with **das** (“that/it”) and add **bitte** to make the request polite. Very common with verbs like *buchstabieren*, *zeigen*, *machen*, *lassen*: *Kannst du mir das bitte …?* / *Könnten Sie mir das bitte …?* In imperatives it softens the command: *Macht das bitte morgen!* The **das** usually refers to something already mentioned or clear from context.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das bitte kurz erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain that to me briefly, please?

meaning: “(that) just as well as …” / “(that) as well as …”.
additional_notes: Used to say that two people do something equally well, or that someone knows something just as well as someone else. It’s a comparison pattern: **[Person] weiß/kann das ebenso gut wie [Person]** (“[Person] knows/can do that just as well as [Person]”). Often used to point out that the other person already knows something: **Du weißt das ebenso gut wie ich.**
target_language_example: Sie spricht Deutsch ebenso gut wie ihre Schwester.
native_language_example: She speaks German just as well as her sister.

additional_notes:
Most common as the pattern **Was ist/sind das für + (ein/eine) + noun?** to ask about the type or nature of something: *Was sind das für Teile?* = “What kind of parts are those?” 

Be careful: **das + für** can also just be literal **“that” + “for”** in other sentences (e.g., *Haben Sie das für Tom getan?* = “Did you do that for Tom?”).
target_language_example: Was ist das für ein Film?
native_language_example: What kind of movie is that?

meaning: 'that for you' / 'it for you' (something done/bought/said for your benefit or from your perspective).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "machen/schreiben/kaufen" to mean doing something on someone’s behalf: "Ich kann das für dich kaufen" = "I can buy that for you." It can also mean "for you" in the sense of your opinion/needs: "Reicht das für dich aus?" (Is that enough for you?) or "Wie klingt das für dich?" (How does that sound to you?). Here, "dich" is the informal singular 'you'; with others it changes (e.g., "das für Sie", "das für euch").
target_language_example: Soll ich das für dich erklären?
native_language_example: Should I explain that for you?

meaning: "do that for you" (help you by doing it).
additional_notes: Used to offer help or say you’re willing/able to do something for someone. Often appears with modal verbs: „kann/könnte/wird … das für dich tun“ (can/could/will do that for you). „für dich“ = for you (singular, informal); with formal „you“ it becomes „das für Sie tun“.
target_language_example: Wenn du willst, kann ich das für dich tun.
native_language_example: If you want, I can do that for you.

meaning: (in “was … das für ein …?”) “what kind of …?” / “what a …!”
additional_notes: Used inside the common pattern **„Was ist/war … das für ein(e) + Nomen?“** to ask in surprise or to criticize: **„Was ist denn das für ein Mist?“** (“What kind of nonsense is that?”). It can also appear after **„wissen“**: **„Ich weiß, was das für ein Gefühl ist.“** (“I know what that feeling is like.”). **„ein“** changes with gender/case (ein/eine/einen/einem), and with plural you usually say **„was … für + Plural“** (no *ein*).
target_language_example: Was ist das für eine Idee?
native_language_example: What kind of idea is that?

meaning: 'that for me' / 'it for me' (for my benefit; on my behalf).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like kaufen, machen, tun, halten to say someone should do something for you or keep something for you: „Mach das für mich.“ = “Do that for me.” „Hältst du das für mich?“ = “Will you hold/keep that for me?” Often appears as „das für mich machen/tun“.
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte für mich erledigen?
native_language_example: Can you please take care of that for me?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone will do a task/favor for you. Very common with polite forms like „Können/Würden Sie das für mich tun?“ (formal) or „Kannst/Würdest du das für mich tun?“ (informal). „das“ refers to a specific thing already mentioned or clear from context; „für mich“ emphasizes it’s for your benefit.
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte für mich tun?
native_language_example: Can you please do that for me?

meaning: "that" / "it" (the thing) "for us"; "it for us / on our behalf".
additional_notes: Used when "das" refers to a specific task/thing already known from context, and "für uns" means someone does it for our benefit or in our place (on our behalf). Common with verbs like erledigen (take care of), tun (do), kaufen (buy). Word order: object "das" + "für uns" often stays together: "Kannst du das für uns machen?"
target_language_example: Kannst du das für uns erledigen?
native_language_example: Can you take care of that for us?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like bitten/fragen (to ask) or after phrases like „nett von dir/Ihnen“ (nice of you) to say that someone does something on our behalf. „das“ = “that/it” (a specific task), „für uns“ = “for us”, „zu tun“ = “to do” in an infinitive clause.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte das für uns tun?
native_language_example: Can you please do that for us?

meaning: 'did that' / 'done that' (referring to a specific action).
additional_notes: Used with the perfect tense (Perfekt): *ich habe das gemacht*, *du hast das gemacht*, etc. **das** means "that" and refers to something already known from context (a task, action, or thing someone did). Common in questions: *Wie hast du das gemacht?* (How did you do that?), *Wann/Warum hast du das gemacht?* (When/Why did you do that?).
target_language_example: Ich habe das gemacht, aber ich weiß nicht, ob es richtig war.
native_language_example: I did that, but I don't know if it was correct.

additional_notes: Used with a form of **haben** to refer back to a specific action already mentioned ("that"). Often appears in the Perfekt or Plusquamperfekt: **ich habe das getan** (I did that / I’ve done that), **ich hatte das getan** (I had done that).
target_language_example: Ich habe das schon getan.
native_language_example: I already did that / I’ve already done that.

additional_notes: Used when talking about an action (“that”) someone did. It’s the Perfekt tense of **tun** (“to do”): **hat … getan**. In subordinate clauses (after **wer**, **dass**, **die …**, etc.), the helping verb **hat** goes to the end: **wer das getan hat**, **dass Tom das getan hat**, **die Person, die das getan hat**.
target_language_example: Weißt du, wer das getan hat?
native_language_example: Do you know who did that?

additional_notes: Perfect infinitive: **etwas getan zu haben** = to have done something (earlier, before another moment). Often used after verbs like **bedauern** (regret), **bereuen** (regret), **sich erinnern** (remember), **bestreiten** (deny), especially in reported speech: *Er sagte, er bedauere, das getan zu haben.* Uses **haben** with most verbs; some verbs use **sein** (*gegangen zu sein*).
target_language_example: Sie gibt zu, das getan zu haben.
native_language_example: She admits to having done that.

meaning: “I have … (that) / I …ed that.” (used to form the past with *haben*)
additional_notes: This is the *Perfekt* (present perfect) with **haben**. **Das** (“that”) is moved to the front for emphasis, and a past participle usually comes later in the sentence: **Das habe ich schon gesehen** = “I’ve seen that already.” In normal word order you can also say: **Ich habe das schon gesehen.**
target_language_example: Das habe ich schon gehört.
native_language_example: I’ve heard that already.

meaning: 'you did that' / 'you said that' (introducing what someone did/said/thought).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle (e.g., gesagt, gemacht, getan, gedacht, erzählt) to refer to a specific action/statement/thought: "Das hast du gesagt" = "You said that." Often sounds accusatory ("Das hast du absichtlich gemacht"), surprised ("Das hast du doch nicht gedacht?"), or praising ("Das hast du gut gemacht"). Word order is typical for German perfect tense: "Das" (that) + "hast" (have) + "du" (you) + participle at the end.
target_language_example: Das hast du mir nie gesagt.
native_language_example: You never told me that.

meaning: "That has ...ed me" / "That really affected me" (introduces what something did to you).
additional_notes: Used when you talk about the effect something had on you, usually with a past participle or a result phrase: "Das hat mich beeindruckt" (That impressed me), "Das hat mich gerettet" (That saved me), "Das hat mich Stunden gekostet" (That cost me hours). Grammatically: "das" = that, "hat" = has, "mich" = me (accusative object).
target_language_example: Das hat mich sehr überrascht.
native_language_example: That really surprised me.

additional_notes: Usually used as: „Das hat nichts mit + Dativ + zu tun.“ It means something is not connected/related to something else, or it’s not someone’s business/responsibility (e.g., „Das hat nichts mit Ihnen zu tun.“ = “This has nothing to do with you.”). After „mit“, use the dative case (mit mir, mit dir, mit dem Thema, mit der Politik, etc.).
target_language_example: Das hat nichts mit dir zu tun.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with you.

meaning: “this (here)” — used to point to something nearby or just mentioned.
additional_notes: Common when you’re physically indicating an object/situation (“this right here”). Often stands alone as a pronoun: “Das hier ist …”. With a noun you’ll usually use a demonstrative like “dieses/ diese/ dieser … hier” (e.g., “dieses Buch hier”). For plural, use “die hier”.
target_language_example: Kannst du das hier bitte kurz festhalten?
native_language_example: Can you hold this here for a moment, please?

meaning: 'this here is…' / 'this is…' (introducing or pointing to something).
additional_notes: Used when you indicate something close by (physically or in a photo/on a screen) and identify or introduce it. Very common in spoken German. Often followed by a noun/name: "Das hier ist mein Freund." You can also use it more vaguely: "Was auch immer das hier ist…" = “Whatever this is…”.
target_language_example: Das hier ist meine Wohnung.
native_language_example: This is my apartment.

meaning: “this here is a …” / “this is a …” (introducing a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used when you’re pointing to something and identifying it. Common in explanations, presentations, or when showing someone an object/animal/place. It’s followed by a masculine noun in the nominative with the indefinite article "ein" (e.g., ein Brief, ein Igel). For feminine nouns use "Das hier ist eine …"; for neuter nouns "Das hier ist ein …"; for plurals "Das hier sind …".
target_language_example: Das hier ist ein Schlüssel.
native_language_example: This is a key.

additional_notes: Used to say something is conditional and depends on which option is true. Often followed by two alternatives with „oder (nicht)“, and the verb goes to the end of the „ob“-clause (e.g., „ob du Zeit hast“).
target_language_example: Das hängt davon ab, ob wir morgen genug Zeit haben.
native_language_example: That depends on whether we have enough time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Very common way to say something is conditional. It’s typically used with "ab": "Das hängt von X ab" = "It depends on X." After "von" you use the dative case (e.g., "von dir", "von euch", "von den Umständen").
target_language_example: Das hängt von der Situation ab.
native_language_example: That depends on the situation.

meaning: “you should have … / you would have …” (talking about what someone should have done in the past).
additional_notes: Used to criticize, advise, or express regret about a past action. It’s a short start of a sentence and is usually followed by a past participle at the end: “Das hättest du mir sagen müssen.” (= You should have told me.) Often appears with modal verbs like müssen/sollen and words like nicht, schon, eher, niemals.
target_language_example: Das hättest du mir vorher sagen sollen.
native_language_example: You should have told me earlier.

meaning: “You should have … (that) (to me).” / “You could have told me that.”
additional_notes: Common start of a complaint or criticism about something the other person didn’t do earlier. It uses Konjunktiv II in the past (hättest + past participle/infinitive) to express reproach: “you should/could have…”. It’s usually followed by a verb phrase, e.g. „…sagen sollen/können“, „…nicht antun sollen“. Word order: „Das“ refers to what just happened/was said, and „mir“ means “to me.”
target_language_example: Das hättest du mir vorher sagen sollen.
native_language_example: You should have told me that earlier.

meaning: “that sounds …” (how something seems based on what you hear).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective + "an" (e.g., "lustig an", "merkwürdig an") or with "nach" + noun ("nach einem Plan") to give your impression. In everyday speech you’ll often hear "Das hört sich … an" or "Das hört sich nach … an"; it can also be phrased as "Das klingt …".
target_language_example: Das hört sich nach einer guten Idee an.
native_language_example: That sounds like a good idea.

additional_notes: A relative clause: **das** refers back to a neuter noun like **das Geld** (“the money”) and introduces extra information about it. Word order: the past participle **gegeben** goes near the end, and the helping verb **habe** is at the very end. Often used with something like: **das Geld, das ich dir gegeben habe** = “the money that I gave you.”
target_language_example: Wo ist das Buch, das ich dir gegeben habe?
native_language_example: Where is the book that I gave you?

additional_notes: Used when asking for help translating something into French. "das" means "that/it" (the thing you want to translate). "ins Französische" is short for "in das Französische" (= into French). Often appears after verbs like "helfen" (to help) or in purpose phrases with "um ... zu".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir helfen, das ins Französische zu übersetzen?
native_language_example: Can you help me translate that into French?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (zu + verb) to politely ask someone to do something in a different place: „Würde es Ihnen/dir/euch etwas ausmachen, das irgendwo anders zu …?“ = “Would you mind … somewhere else?” Common verbs here are „machen“ and „tun“.
target_language_example: Würde es dir etwas ausmachen, das Gespräch irgendwo anders zu führen?
native_language_example: Would you mind having the conversation somewhere else?

additional_notes: Very common starter for statements. Used to describe or evaluate something (often followed by an adjective or phrase): "Das ist richtig" (That’s right), "Das ist zu klein" (That’s too small). In context it can mean "this" or "that" in English; German often uses "das" where English uses "it/that".
target_language_example: Das ist eine gute Idee.
native_language_example: That’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Literally “that is all.” Used to say there’s nothing more, or to emphasize that something is only/merely a certain thing. Very common with "nur" (only) + a noun: "Das ist alles nur Show." = “It’s all just a show.” Can also be used to downplay/explain something: "Das ist alles ganz spontan." = “It’s all completely spontaneous.”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das ist alles nur ein Missverständnis.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s all just a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing you have/know/want/can do, etc. It’s usually followed by a clause with a verb at the end: “Das ist alles, was ich habe.” Note the comma before “was” in writing. In English you often drop “that”: “That’s all I know.”
target_language_example: Das ist alles, was ich heute schaffen kann.
native_language_example: That’s all I can manage today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the complete amount/information/action you can or want to give. It’s typically followed by a verb phrase in the relative clause: “Das ist alles, was ich weiß/tun kann/tun möchte/brauche.”
target_language_example: Das ist alles, was ich heute sagen kann.
native_language_example: That’s all I can say today.

meaning: “That/this is the …” (used to point out or identify a specific thing).
additional_notes: Used when introducing or identifying a particular item: “Das ist das Wörterbuch …” = “This is the dictionary …”. Here, the second “das” is the definite article for a neuter noun (das Wörterbuch, das Tagebuch, das Protokoll). With other genders you change the article: “Das ist der … / Das ist die …”. Not the same as English “That’s that” (= end of discussion).
target_language_example: Das ist das Hotel, das ich dir empfohlen habe.
native_language_example: This is the hotel I recommended to you.

das ist das Haus, in dem

target_language_multi_word_term: das ist das Haus, in dem
meaning: “this is the house in which / where …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes “das Haus.” The phrase “in dem” is the dative relative form meaning “in which/that,” because the verb needs the preposition “in” + dative (location). It’s also a contraction of “in + dem.” Often translates naturally as “where” in English.
target_language_example: Das ist das Haus, in dem meine Großeltern früher gewohnt haben.
native_language_example: This is the house where my grandparents used to live.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the best in a group or category. It’s often followed by a noun: „Das ist das beste Restaurant …“. Note the ending „beste“ changes with the noun’s gender/case: „das beste Bild“ (neuter), „der beste Film“ (masculine), „die beste Idee“ (feminine).
target_language_example: Das ist das beste Hotel in der Nähe.
native_language_example: That’s the best hotel nearby.

meaning: "that is your …" (said before a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to point out or emphasize that something belongs to someone or is “their” thing: Das ist dein Weg. With feminine nouns you use **das ist deine …** (e.g., Das ist deine Farbe). With plural nouns: **das sind deine …**.
target_language_example: Das ist dein Platz.
native_language_example: That’s your seat.

meaning: "that is the" / "this is the" (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to point out or introduce a specific person/thing. "Der" is the masculine nominative form of "the" (e.g., der Mann, der Weg). In speech, it can sound emphatic depending on context ("This is THE one..."). For feminine or neuter nouns, use "das ist die" or "das ist das".
target_language_example: Das ist der Mann, der mir geholfen hat.
native_language_example: That is the man who helped me.

meaning: "that/this is the" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or point out something: "Das" = this/that, "ist" = is, "die" = the (feminine singular) or the plural article. Common pattern: "Das ist die + noun" (e.g., die Tastatur, die letzte Warnung). For masculine or neuter nouns, you use "Das ist der" / "Das ist das".
target_language_example: Das ist die Tür zum Garten.
native_language_example: That is the door to the garden.

meaning: "This/that really is …" / "Come on, that’s …" (emphatic; often surprise, annoyance, or ‘it’s obvious’).
additional_notes: Uses the modal particle **doch** to add emphasis. With **Das ist doch + noun/adjective!** it often expresses: (1) recognition/surprise (*Das ist doch Haku!* = “That’s Haku!”), (2) frustration (*Das ist doch Scheiße!* = “This is really crap!”), or (3) “as expected/typical” (*Das ist doch typisch.*). It doesn’t translate word-for-word; **doch** changes the tone more than the basic meaning.
target_language_example: Das ist doch unglaublich!
native_language_example: That’s really unbelievable!

meaning: "that is a/an" (used before a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something: "Das ist ein Anfang" = "That’s a start." Use "ein" only with masculine/neuter singular nouns (der/ein…, das/ein…). With feminine nouns, use "Das ist eine …" (e.g., "Das ist eine Idee."). You can add an adjective: "Das ist ein neues Buch."
target_language_example: Das ist ein guter Plan.
native_language_example: That is a good plan.

meaning: “That is a very …” (introducing a noun with a strong adjective).
additional_notes: Used at the start of sentences like: “Das ist ein sehr + adjective + noun.” The adjective must match the noun’s gender/case, e.g. masculine nominative: „ein sehr alter Stuhl“, neuter nominative: „ein sehr altes Buch“, feminine nominative: „eine sehr alte Lampe“.
target_language_example: Das ist ein sehr guter Film.
native_language_example: That’s a very good movie.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something: "Das" = "that/this", "ist" = "is", "eine" = "a/an" for feminine nouns (and also for plural nouns in the negative: "Das sind keine ..."). Often followed by a noun, sometimes with an adjective: "Das ist eine gute Idee." For masculine/neuter nouns you use "ein": "Das ist ein Hund./Das ist ein Haus."
target_language_example: Das ist eine sehr gute Idee.
native_language_example: That is a very good idea.

meaning: “That is a very …” (introducing a strong description).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective + noun: “Das ist eine sehr gute Idee.” The pattern shown (“eine”) is for feminine singular nouns in the nominative (e.g., die Idee, die Frage). With other nouns, the article changes: “Das ist ein sehr gutes Buch.” / “Das ist ein sehr guter Plan.”
target_language_example: Das ist eine sehr interessante Frage.
native_language_example: That is a very interesting question.

additional_notes: Used to point to or identify something and then add a relative clause with what you do/need/want/etc.: “Das ist es, was ich brauche.” Often followed by a verb at the end of the clause (brauche, will, meine, getan habe, etc.). You may also see the shorter “Das ist, was ich …” in speech, but “Das ist es, was ich …” is the more standard form.
target_language_example: Das ist es, was ich meine.
native_language_example: That’s what I mean.

additional_notes: Used to say who/what something is intended for. Common in giving/labeling things ("Das ist für Frodo!") and in general statements about suitability ("Das ist für jeden leicht zu machen" = easy for everyone to do). With people, use the dative: für mich/dich/ihn/sie/uns/euch/sie.
target_language_example: Das ist für meine Schwester.
native_language_example: This is for my sister.

meaning: "This/that is for you." (also: "That’s not right/suitable for you.")
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) to give or dedicate something to someone: "Das ist für dich, Tom." = “This is for you, Tom.” (2) to mean “for you / in your case” when judging what fits someone: "Das ist für dich der falsche Ort." = “That’s the wrong place for you.” Uses dative: für + dich (you), ihn, sie, uns, euch, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe ein Geschenk—das ist für dich.
native_language_example: I have a present—this is for you.

additional_notes: Used to point out a perfect match with what you mean, want, or were looking for. Often followed by a noun phrase with a relative clause: „Das ist genau das Buch, das …“. You can also use it with „so“ for emphasis: „Das ist genau so ein Auto, wie ich will.“
target_language_example: Das ist genau der Moment, auf den ich gewartet habe.
native_language_example: This is exactly the moment I’ve been waiting for.

additional_notes: “Ja” here is a modal particle, not the normal “yes.” It adds emotion like surprise, disbelief, admiration, or annoyance. Often used in spoken German before an adjective or noun phrase: “Das ist ja unglaublich!”, “Das ist ja Pech!”, “Das ist ja Geld!”
target_language_example: Das ist ja unglaublich!
native_language_example: Wow, that’s unbelievable!

meaning: “that is not a …” / “that is no …” (negation before a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something is not a certain thing: **Das ist kein Ausgang** (“That’s not an exit”). **kein** is used with masculine/neuter nouns in the singular (compare: **Das ist keine …** for feminine nouns, **Das sind keine …** for plural). Often used for emphasis in phrases like **Das ist kein Witz / Das ist kein Scherz** (“That’s no joke”).
target_language_example: Das ist kein Problem.
native_language_example: That’s not a problem.

meaning: "that is not a" (feminine noun) / "that is no".
additional_notes: Used to deny or correct what something is. Comes before a feminine singular noun (e.g., Bedrohung, Drohung, Hexerei, Mine, Liste) and uses the indefinite article with negation: "keine". For masculine/neuter nouns you’d use "kein" (Das ist kein Problem.), and for plural "keine" (Das sind keine Probleme.).
target_language_example: Das ist keine gute Idee.
native_language_example: That’s not a good idea.

meaning: 'This/that is my …' (shows that something belongs to you).
additional_notes: Used to point out or introduce something/someone that is yours. "mein" is used with masculine and neuter nouns in the nominative (e.g., mein Mantel, mein Notizbuch). With feminine or plural nouns you usually say "Das ist meine …" (e.g., meine Tasche, meine Freunde).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, das ist mein Platz.
native_language_example: Excuse me, this is my seat.

additional_notes: Used to identify something/someone as yours: “That is my …”. The word “meine” is the feminine (and plural) form of “my” (mein-). Use it with feminine nouns (e.g., die CD, die Puppe, die Schwester, die Meinung) and with plural nouns (e.g., Das sind meine Freunde.). For masculine/neuter singular you use “mein” (Das ist mein Bruder / mein Buch).
target_language_example: Das ist meine Tasche.
native_language_example: That is my bag.

meaning: 'that is not / this is not' (used to negate a statement about something).
additional_notes: Used to say something is not true, not the case, or not a certain thing. Often followed by a noun with an article ("Das ist nicht mein Auto."), an adjective ("Das ist nicht schwierig."), or a phrase like "der Fall" (= the case). In speech, it can refer to "this" or "that" depending on context.
target_language_example: Das ist nicht das, was ich meinte.
native_language_example: That's not what I meant.

meaning: “That’s not my …” (not mine / not my responsibility).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine/neuter noun to say something doesn’t belong to you or isn’t your responsibility: “Das ist nicht mein Fehler/Problem.” For feminine nouns use “meine” (Das ist nicht meine Tasche), and for plural use “meine” (Das sind nicht meine Schuhe). Often contrasts with someone else’s using “sondern …”: “nicht mein…, sondern dein…”
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, aber das ist nicht mein Problem.
native_language_example: Sorry, but that’s not my problem.

additional_notes: Used to comment on something with an adjective: "Das ist sehr + Adjektiv" (e.g., sehr nett/mutig/überraschend). You can also say "Das ist wirklich sehr …" to emphasize it more.
target_language_example: Das ist sehr hilfreich, danke.
native_language_example: That is very helpful, thank you.

meaning: “that’s so …” (used to emphasize an adjective or comparison).
additional_notes: Often followed by an adjective ("Das ist so aufregend!") or a comparison with "wie" ("… so schwer wie Blei"). It adds emphasis like English "so/really". In other contexts, "Das ist so" can also mean "That’s just how it is," but in these examples it’s an intensifier.
target_language_example: Das ist so langweilig!
native_language_example: That’s so boring!

additional_notes: Used to introduce something/someone that belongs to “us.” It’s usually followed by a noun: „Das ist unser Freund.“ Here „unser“ is the possessive “our” in the nominative with a masculine or neuter noun (e.g., unser Freund, unser Zuhause). For feminine or plural nouns you typically use „unsere“ (e.g., „Das ist unsere Mutter.“, „Das sind unsere Freunde.“).
target_language_example: Das ist unser Auto.
native_language_example: This is our car.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective or noun phrase to emphasize your reaction or opinion (positive or negative): Das ist wirklich schön / komisch / wichtig. In speech, the stress is usually on „wirklich“ to add extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Das ist wirklich eine tolle Idee.
native_language_example: That’s really a great idea.

additional_notes: "das" is a pronoun meaning "that/it" (something already known from context). "jeden Tag" means "every day" and usually comes after the verb: "Ich mache das jeden Tag." In questions, the verb comes first: "Machen Sie das jeden Tag?" In casual speech you may also hear "Musst du das jeden Tag (machen)?" where "machen" is understood.
target_language_example: Ich mache das jeden Tag nach der Arbeit.
native_language_example: I do that every day after work.

additional_notes: "das" refers to a specific thing/action already known from context (often translated as "it"), and "jetzt" adds emphasis that it’s happening (or should happen) immediately. Common in questions to show uncertainty or mild impatience: "Soll ich das jetzt ...?" (= "Am I supposed to ... now?") / "Was bedeutet das jetzt?" (= "So what does that mean now?").
target_language_example: Ich mache das jetzt, damit wir fertig werden.
native_language_example: I’m doing it now so we can be done.

meaning: to do that right now / immediately.
additional_notes: Used to stress urgency: you should do something without waiting. Common with modal verbs (müssen/should/should): „Du musst das jetzt gleich machen.“ Here, „gleich“ means “right away/straight away” (not “equal”).
target_language_example: Kannst du das jetzt gleich machen, bitte?
native_language_example: Can you do that right now, please?

additional_notes: Used to say you’re not able to do something or you refuse because it feels wrong or impossible. Often followed by an infinitive: "Das kann ich nicht machen." It can also stand alone for strong emphasis: "Das kann ich nicht!"
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, das kann ich nicht machen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't do that.

meaning: "you can do that" / "you’re able to do that".
additional_notes: Common pattern: **Das kannst du (nicht) + verb**. It can be used for ability (**Das kannst du noch viel besser.** = “You can do that much better.”), permission/encouragement (**Das kannst du ruhig schreiben.** = “You can go ahead and write that.”), or criticism (**Das kannst du nicht machen!** = “You can’t do that!”). Also appears in the fixed phrase **Das kannst du vergessen** = “Forget it / You can forget about that.”
target_language_example: Das kannst du morgen erledigen.
native_language_example: You can take care of that tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to react to information and give your impression: “That sounds + adjective.” Very common with adjectives like gut, einfach, interessant, super, komisch. Often followed by „nach + noun“ to mean “sounds like …” (e.g., „Das klingt nach einem Plan.“).
target_language_example: Das klingt nach einer guten Idee.
native_language_example: That sounds like a good idea.

additional_notes: Uses **könnte** (Konjunktiv II of *können*) to talk about a **possibility** or **potential result** (often a bit uncertain or cautious). Very common in warnings (*Das könnte Sie in Schwierigkeiten bringen.*) and guesses (*Das könnte ein Zufall sein.*). It can also be used for a **polite/softened** tone compared with *das kann*.
target_language_example: Das könnte heute noch regnen.
native_language_example: It might still rain today.

meaning: "that can be" / "that can be done" (or "that can’t be").
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say something is (or isn’t) possible or feasible: "Das lässt sich machen" = "That can be done." Very common with negatives and adverbs like "nicht" and "so leicht": "Das lässt sich nicht so leicht beantworten" = "That’s not so easy to answer." Often corresponds to English "can be" (passive meaning) or "can be arranged": "Das lässt sich einrichten/arrangieren."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, das lässt sich schnell lösen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, that can be solved quickly.

meaning: to do that; to do it.
additional_notes: Used when “das” refers to a specific action/task already known from context. Very common with modal verbs (können, müssen, wollen) and in questions (Könnt ihr das machen?). Also used with “lassen” to mean letting/making someone do it (Lass Tom das machen. / Tom ließ Maria das machen.).
target_language_example: Ich kann das machen, wenn du willst.
native_language_example: I can do that if you want.

additional_notes: "Das" means "that/this" and "macht" is 3rd-person singular present of "machen" (to do/to make). Use it when saying someone does something ("Tom does that") or when something has an effect ("That makes his speech more lively"). In questions, it often corresponds to English "do" ("How do you do that?").
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, Tom macht das.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, Tom will do it.

meaning: “that makes me …” (it causes me to feel …).
additional_notes: Used to say that something causes a certain feeling or reaction in you: “Das macht mich + adjective.” Common with emotions like neugierig (curious), glücklich (happy), wütend (angry), traurig (sad). Often intensified with sehr (very), wirklich (really), echt (really).
target_language_example: Deine Nachricht macht mich nervös.
native_language_example: Your message makes me nervous.

meaning: did that on purpose; did that intentionally.
additional_notes: Used to say (or ask) whether an action was intentional. Often appears as a full clause in the perfect tense: „Ich habe das mit Absicht getan.“ You can also ask: „Hast du das mit Absicht getan?“
target_language_example: Ich habe das nicht mit Absicht getan.
native_language_example: I didn’t do that on purpose.

meaning: “not that / don’t (do) that” (negating something referred to as “das”).
additional_notes: “Das” refers to a specific thing, idea, or action (“that/it”). Adding “nicht” negates it: *Ich glaube das nicht* = “I don’t believe that.” In commands and requests it often means “don’t do that”: *Tu mir das nicht an!* (“Don’t do that to me!”). It can also appear in questions/suggestions: *Könntest du das nicht auch?* (“Couldn’t you do that too?”). Word order depends on the rest of the sentence, so it doesn’t map 1:1 to an English phrase.
target_language_example: Bitte mach das nicht nochmal.
native_language_example: Please don’t do that again.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t do/want/tolerate something anymore. Often comes before the verb or before the infinitive with zu: „Du darfst das nicht mehr tun.“ / „…versprochen, das nicht mehr zu machen.“ With feelings/limits it can mean “I can’t take it anymore”: „Ich halte das nicht mehr aus.“
target_language_example: Ich will das nicht mehr hören.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hear that anymore.

meaning: “not to do that” / “not to do it.”
additional_notes: Uses **das** (“that/it”) to refer to an action mentioned in context, and **zu tun** (“to do”) as an infinitive phrase. Often follows verbs like **raten** (to advise), **auffordern** (to tell/urge), **überreden** (to persuade), **sich entschließen** (to decide).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihr gesagt, das nicht zu tun.
native_language_example: I told her not to do that.

additional_notes: "das" is a pronoun meaning "that" or "it" (referring to an action/idea). "nie" means "never". Together you often see it in sentences like "(jemand) hat das nie gemacht/getan" = "(someone) never did that" or with modal verbs/conditional: "würde das nie tun/glauben" = "would never do/believe that."
target_language_example: Ich würde das nie machen.
native_language_example: I would never do that.

additional_notes: Used when warning or promising that a specific action (das = “that”) should not happen again. Often followed by an infinitive with zu: „das nie wieder zu tun“ (“to never do that again”). As an imperative, it’s common as: „Mach das nie wieder!“
target_language_example: Bitte erinnere mich daran, das nie wieder zu sagen.
native_language_example: Please remind me to never say that again.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to repeat an action, a sentence, or an explanation. Very common with requests like „Bitte …“ and questions like „Kannst du …?“ or polite „Könnten Sie …?“. Often means “again” in the sense of “repeat it” (not necessarily “once more in addition”).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe das nicht verstanden—können Sie das noch einmal sagen?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand that—could you say that again?

additional_notes: Used with a verb to ask for repetition (“Say that again!”), to talk about doing something again (“try again”), or to suggest reconsidering something (“Let’s think about that again”). Often also written/pronounced as **das nochmal**; more formal: **das noch einmal**.
target_language_example: Kannst du das noch mal wiederholen, bitte?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that again, please?

additional_notes: Uses Konjunktiv II ("würde" + infinitive) to talk about something expected/hypothetical from a past viewpoint, often after verbs like "wissen" or in indirect speech: „Ich wusste, dass das passieren würde.“ = “I knew that would happen.”
target_language_example: Sie hat nicht gedacht, dass das passieren würde.
native_language_example: She didn’t think that would happen.

additional_notes: Uses **lassen + infinitive** to mean you arrange for someone else to do it (e.g., a mechanic or repair shop). **das** can be replaced with **etwas** or a specific item: *das Auto reparieren lassen*, *mein Handy reparieren lassen*. Often used with modal verbs: *Du solltest…*, *Wir müssen…*; and with questions like *Wo kann ich das reparieren lassen?*.
target_language_example: Ich lasse mein Fahrrad reparieren.
native_language_example: I’m having my bike repaired.

additional_notes: Used when referring back to a fact or action with "das" (= that/it) and saying it is already known, already happened, or has been the case for some time. Very common in questions like "Wusstest du das schon?" (= Did you already know that?) and time expressions like "Wie lange ist das schon her?" (= How long ago was that?). In rhetorical questions like "Wen kümmert das schon?", it can imply "Who cares anyway?"
target_language_example: Ich habe dir das schon gestern erklärt.
native_language_example: I already explained that to you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out multiple people/things. It’s the plural form of “das ist” (“that/this is”). Often followed by a plural noun or a plural subject complement: “Das sind Geschenke.” = “Those are gifts.” It can also appear at the end of an embedded clause: “Rate mal, wessen Kinder das sind.” = “Guess whose children those are.”
target_language_example: Das sind meine Freunde aus Berlin.
native_language_example: Those are my friends from Berlin.

meaning: 'Those are my …' (introducing or pointing to things/people that belong to you).
additional_notes: Used when you’re talking about more than one person/thing (plural): *das sind* = “those are.” *meine* changes to match the noun that follows (plural here). Common for introductions: *Das sind meine Freunde.* You can also use it for a group right in front of you.
target_language_example: Hallo! Das sind meine Kolleginnen und Kollegen.
native_language_example: Hi! These are my coworkers.

meaning: to do it the way (that) …; to do it like …
additional_notes: Used to give instructions or say how something should be done. After „wie“ you often have a full clause: „… wie Tom es dir gezeigt hat“ (“… the way Tom showed you”). „das“ refers to what you’re doing (“it/that”), and „so“ emphasizes “in this way.”
target_language_example: Mach das so, wie ich es dir erklärt habe.
native_language_example: Do it the way I explained it to you.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific action that is already known from context ("das" = "that"). Very common with modal verbs like müssen, wollen, sollen: „Ich muss das tun.“ = “I have to do that.”
target_language_example: Ich will das nicht tun.
native_language_example: I don't want to do that.

das tun lassen, was sie will

target_language_multi_word_term: das tun lassen, was sie will
meaning: to let her do what she wants.
additional_notes: Used with someone as the person you allow to act: jemanden (Akk.) + das tun lassen, was sie/er will. Often appears after modal verbs like „solltest/solltet/sollten“ to give advice: „Du solltest … (You should …)“. You can swap the pronoun: „… was er will“ (what he wants), „… was du willst“ (what you want).
