additional_notes: Common in sports contexts (football/soccer, etc.) and with movement verbs like fliegen (to fly), rollen (to roll), prallen/klatschen (to bounce/hit), and treffen (to hit). Plural: die Bälle. Not to confuse with der Ball meaning a formal dance/ball (event).
target_language_example: Der Ball rollt ins Tor.
native_language_example: The ball rolls into the goal.

meaning: 'the bank' (financial institution) or 'the bench' (a seat) — in the dative/genitive form.
additional_notes: The base form is **die Bank** (feminine). You see **der Bank** mainly after prepositions like **bei** (at/with), **von** (from), **unter** (under), **auf** (on), or after **vor** when it answers “where?” (location): **bei der Bank** = at the bank; **unter der Bank** = under the bench; **auf der Bank** = on the bench. Context tells you whether it means a financial bank or a bench.
target_language_example: Ich warte bei der Bank auf dich.
native_language_example: I’ll wait for you at the bank.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: der Baum (plural: die Bäume). Used for a tree in nature; common with location words (z.B. da drüben) and comparisons (höher als …). Common verbs: stehen (stand), Schatten werfen, (um)fallen, fällen (to cut down).
target_language_example: Im Sommer spendet der Baum viel Schatten.
native_language_example: In summer, the tree provides a lot of shade.

additional_notes: Superlative of „gut“ (good). Used to say someone is the best, often as praise: „Du bist der Beste!“ For women, use „die Beste“; for plural: „die Besten“. Often appears with comparisons like „der Beste von uns“ (the best of us) or in sayings like „Möge der Beste (oder die Beste) gewinnen!“ (May the best (man/woman) win!).
target_language_example: Danke für deine Hilfe — du bist der Beste!
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — you’re the best!

additional_notes: “Bibliothek” is feminine: die Bibliothek. “der Bibliothek” is the dative form, used after many prepositions and verbs, e.g. in/bei/zu/nahe an/vor + der Bibliothek (“in/at/to/near/in front of the library”). In “Ich erinnere mich, der Bibliothek das Buch zurückgegeben zu haben”, it means “to the library” (recipient of the book).
target_language_example: Ich treffe dich um drei vor der Bibliothek.
native_language_example: I’ll meet you at three in front of the library.

meaning: “the bridge” (in dative/genitive: “to/on the bridge” or “of the bridge”).
additional_notes: “Brücke” is feminine: **die Brücke** (nominative). In the examples, **der Brücke** is usually either **dative** after a preposition (e.g., *auf der Brücke* = on the bridge; *von der Brücke* = from the bridge) or **genitive** (e.g., *der Bau der Brücke* = the construction of the bridge).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns auf der Brücke.
native_language_example: We’ll meet on the bridge.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: der Bus. Common with verbs like fahren (to go/drive), bringen (to take/bring), halten/anhalten (to stop), and weg sein (to be gone). Used to talk about routes and destinations: Der Bus fährt zum Zoo. Plural: die Busse.
target_language_example: Der Bus kommt gleich, wir müssen noch kurz warten.
native_language_example: The bus is coming soon; we still have to wait a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say that a bus stops (makes a stop) at a particular place. Often followed by a location phrase like "vor ..." (in front of), "nahe (an) ..." (near), or "direkt" (right/directly). In everyday speech you’ll also hear: "Der Bus hält hier." / "Wo hält der Bus?"
target_language_example: Der Bus hält an der nächsten Haltestelle.
native_language_example: The bus stops at the next stop.

meaning: the boss; the manager; the person in charge.
additional_notes: Used for someone who leads or is responsible (at work: your boss/manager; more generally: the person in charge). With a group/department, you often say: „der Chef von + Dativ“ (e.g., „der Chef von unserer Abteilung“). In informal speech, „Chef“ can also be a friendly way to address someone (like “boss”), but in the examples it’s literal.
target_language_example: Ich muss erst meinen Chef fragen.
native_language_example: I have to ask my boss first.

additional_notes: A noun for a person who steals. Often used in news/police contexts (Der Dieb entkam / flüchtete / rannte weg). Feminine form: die Diebin. Plural: die Diebe. Common structure: „jdn./etw. stehlen“ (to steal) and „Der Dieb machte sich mit … davon“ (the thief got away with …).
target_language_example: Der Dieb hat mein Fahrrad gestohlen.
native_language_example: The thief stole my bike.

additional_notes:
This is a case form of **die Dunkelheit** (“the darkness”). You often see it after prepositions:
- **aus der Dunkelheit** = “out of the darkness” (dative)
- **unter dem Schutz der Dunkelheit** = “under cover of darkness” (genitive after *Schutz*).
target_language_example: Sie warteten in der Dunkelheit, bis es ruhig war.
native_language_example: They waited in the darkness until it was quiet.

meaning: "the Dark Lord" (a powerful evil ruler in fantasy).
additional_notes: Used as a title/nickname for the main villain in fantasy stories (e.g., like “the Dark Lord”). The adjective is often capitalized here ("Dunkle") because it’s part of the title/name. In German, the article changes with case: nominative "der Dunkle Lord", accusative "den Dunklen Lord" (e.g., "Ich fürchte den Dunklen Lord").
target_language_example: Alle hatten Angst vor dem Dunklen Lord.
native_language_example: Everyone was afraid of the Dark Lord.

additional_notes: You see *der Dusche* after certain prepositions that take the dative, especially when talking about location or where something comes from: *in der Dusche* (“in the shower”), *aus der Dusche* (“out of/from the shower”). The base noun is *die Dusche* (feminine); in dative singular it becomes *der Dusche*.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch in der Dusche.
native_language_example: I’m still in the shower.

additional_notes: Used with masculine nouns/people. In other cases: die Einzige (female), das Einzige (neuter/thing), die Einzigen (plural). Often followed by a relative clause: der Einzige, der/dem ...
target_language_example: Er ist der Einzige, der mir helfen kann.
native_language_example: He’s the only one who can help me.

additional_notes: Used to say that just one person does something. It’s masculine; for women: „die Einzige, die“. For plural groups: „die Einzigen, die“. Often followed by a relative clause (with „der/die“) and the verb at the end: „… der/die … kann/konnte/war“.
target_language_example: Er ist der Einzige, der mir helfen kann.
native_language_example: He is the only one who can help me.

additional_notes: "der Erde" is the genitive ("of the Earth") or dative ("to/on the Earth") form of "die Erde". You see it after many prepositions and in set phrases: "über der Erde" (above the Earth), "unter der Erde" (under the ground/underground), "von der Erde aus" (from Earth / as seen from Earth), "der Mond ist von der Erde entfernt" (from the Earth). In sentence 2 it means "on Earth" in the sense of "the biggest animal on Earth".
target_language_example: Gibt es Leben außerhalb der Erde?
native_language_example: Is there life outside of Earth?

meaning: 'the first (person) who' (followed by a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is the first to do something. It’s the masculine form; other forms are common: die Erste, die (female), das Erste, das (neuter/thing), die Ersten, die (plural). Often followed by a verb at the end of the clause: „der Erste, der ankam / der das gesagt hat“.
target_language_example: Sie war die Erste, die mir geholfen hat.
native_language_example: She was the first one who helped me.

additional_notes: Used to say whether something is true in a given situation: "Das ist der Fall" = "That’s the case"; "Das ist nicht der Fall" = "That’s not the case". Very common in fixed expressions like "Das Gegenteil ist der Fall" (the opposite is true) and "Wie oft der Fall" (as is often the case).
target_language_example: Bei mir ist das nicht der Fall.
native_language_example: That’s not the case for me.

meaning: 'is the case' / 'is true' (often: "das ist der Fall" = "that’s the case").
additional_notes: Used to state or check whether something is true: "Ich glaube nicht, dass das der Fall ist" = "I don’t think that’s the case." Very common in the pattern "wie es bei ihm oft der Fall ist" = "as is often the case with him" (i.e., this happens frequently). Also used literally with "Fall" meaning a case (e.g., police/legal): "Der Fall ist geschlossen/erledigt" = "The case is closed/finished."
target_language_example: Ich denke nicht, dass das der Fall ist.
native_language_example: I don’t think that’s the case.

meaning: 'the celebration / the party' (dative/genitive form of *die Feier*).
additional_notes: *Die Feier* means a celebration, party, or event. **Der Feier** is used when grammar requires **dative** (common after certain prepositions) or **genitive**. Very common patterns: **nach der Feier** = after the party; **an der Feier teilnehmen** = to take part in the celebration; **mit der Feier anfangen** = to start the celebration. (The base form is: **die Feier**.)
target_language_example: Nach der Feier fahren wir nach Hause.
native_language_example: After the party, we’re going home.

additional_notes: Used for a person, group, or army you are fighting against (often in war/military contexts). It can also be used more generally for someone who is against you. Plural: die Feinde.
target_language_example: Wir müssen den Feind finden, bevor er uns findet.
native_language_example: We have to find the enemy before he finds us.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Commonly used for movies in the cinema or on TV/streaming. Often appears with verbs like anfangen/beginnen (to start), spielen (to be set/take place), gefallen (to like), and ausgehen (to end/turn out).
target_language_example: Der Film dauert zwei Stunden.
native_language_example: The movie lasts two hours.

additional_notes: Used to describe a film in the past with an adjective or phrase: „Der Film war lustig / interessant / drei Stunden lang.“ Here „war“ is the simple past of „sein“ (to be). You’ll often use it to give opinions or comparisons about a movie.
target_language_example: Der Film war richtig spannend, aber ein bisschen zu lang.
native_language_example: The movie was really exciting, but a bit too long.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Plural: die Flüsse. Used for a natural flowing body of water; common with location/direction phrases (z.B. "nach links") and descriptions of water level ("Hochwasser führen" = to be in flood).
target_language_example: Wir gehen am Fluss spazieren.
native_language_example: We’re going for a walk by the river.

meaning: “the river is …” (used to describe the river’s state/condition).
additional_notes: Use this as the start of a sentence before an adjective or description: Der Fluss ist trocken/ausgetrocknet (dry), tief (deep), breit (wide), über die Ufer getreten (overflowed its banks), dabei, über die Ufer zu treten (about to overflow). Note: “Fluss” is masculine, so it takes “der.”
target_language_example: Der Fluss ist heute sehr hoch und tritt fast über die Ufer.
native_language_example: The river is very high today and is almost overflowing its banks.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning the season after winter and before summer. Often used with seasonal expressions like „im Frühling“ (in spring), „Frühling in der Luft“ (spring is in the air), or in sequences like „Nach dem Winter kommt der Frühling“ (after winter comes spring). Plural: „die Frühlinge“ (rare; usually you talk about spring in the singular).
target_language_example: Im Frühling wird das Wetter oft wärmer.
native_language_example: In spring, the weather often gets warmer.

additional_notes: Used to say that spring has arrived or that spring is over/past, often with words like "da" (here), "endlich" (finally), "vergangen" (gone/past), or "vorüber" (over). The verb "ist" changes with the noun (e.g., "Der Sommer ist …", "Der Winter ist …").
target_language_example: Der Frühling ist schon da, aber es ist noch kalt.
native_language_example: Spring is already here, but it’s still cold.

additional_notes: You see **der Hand** because *Hand* is feminine (*die Hand*) and many common prepositions take the **dative** case, e.g. **mit der Hand** (“with the hand”), **in der Hand** (“in the hand”). It also appears in the fixed expression **auf der Hand liegen** = “to be obvious / to be clear.”
target_language_example: Der Schlüssel ist in der Hand.
native_language_example: The key is in (my/the) hand.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the sky” (weather, clouds, getting dark/bright). It can also mean “heaven” in religious/poetic contexts. In German it’s masculine: der Himmel (genitive: des Himmels).
target_language_example: Heute ist der Himmel ganz blau.
native_language_example: Today the sky is completely blue.

additional_notes: Used to describe what the sky looks like (color, weather, clouds). It’s the start of a sentence and is followed by an adjective (grau, heiter, orange) or a phrase like „voll von …“.
target_language_example: Der Himmel ist blau, und die Sonne scheint.
native_language_example: The sky is blue, and the sun is shining.

additional_notes: Used to describe what the sky was like in the past, usually followed by an adjective (e.g., blau, grau, bewölkt, klar, dunkel). Note: “Himmel” can also mean “heaven,” but in weather descriptions it means “sky.”
target_language_example: Gestern Abend war der Himmel voller Sterne.
native_language_example: Yesterday evening the sky was full of stars.

additional_notes: "Hitze" means heat, especially from hot weather. "der Hitze" is the dative form, used after certain prepositions and phrases (e.g., "in der Hitze" = in the heat; "aus der Hitze" = out of the heat; "aufgrund der Hitze" = because of the heat). It’s also used with verbs like "zurechtkommen (mit)" (to cope with).
target_language_example: In der Hitze trinke ich viel Wasser.
native_language_example: In the heat, I drink a lot of water.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: der Hund (singular), die Hunde (plural). Used for pet dogs and dogs in general. In stories it often appears as a subject doing an action (e.g., chasing something).
target_language_example: Der Hund läuft im Park.
native_language_example: The dog is running in the park.

additional_notes: Used to describe the dog (with an adjective), say where it is (often with a location phrase like auf/unter), or state what it has become/turned into (e.g., Teil der Familie). In a clause with a question word like „wo“ (where), German often puts the verb at the end: „… wo der Hund ist.“
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, wo der Hund ist.
native_language_example: I don’t know where the dog is.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning a (male) child or young boy. Used with the definite article der (nominative singular); changes in other cases (e.g., den Jungen in accusative: Ich sehe den Jungen). Plural: die Jungen.
target_language_example: Der Junge spielt im Park.
native_language_example: The boy is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Used to identify a specific boy by adding extra information. "der" is the relative pronoun for a masculine noun (der Junge) in the nominative case; the verb in the relative clause usually goes to the end: "Der Junge, der dort steht, …" (If the boy is the object, you’ll often see "der Junge, den …" instead.)
target_language_example: Der Junge, der neben mir sitzt, heißt Tim.
native_language_example: The boy who is sitting next to me is called Tim.

meaning: “the boy has” (or “the boy is …” with certain states like hunger/thirst).
additional_notes: “Der Junge” = “the boy” (subject). “hat” is the 3rd-person singular form of “haben” (to have). It’s used for possession (Der Junge hat einen Apfel.), for conditions/states like hunger and thirst (Der Junge hat Durst./Hunger.), and in common expressions like “recht haben” = “to be right” (Der Junge hat recht.). Note: German “hat” does NOT mean an English “hat” (that’s “der Hut”).
target_language_example: Der Junge hat Hunger, aber er hat kein Brot.
native_language_example: The boy is hungry, but he doesn’t have any bread.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a boy (subject in the nominative case: der Junge) and then describe him or say what is happening. Common patterns: **Der Junge ist + adjective** (müde, nett, erschrocken) or **Der Junge ist + phrase** (oft bei mir vorbeigekommen; verrückt nach …; zu nichts mehr zu gebrauchen).
target_language_example: Der Junge ist heute krank.
native_language_example: The boy is sick today.

meaning: the captain (e.g., of a ship, plane, or team).
additional_notes: Used for the person in command (especially on a ship) or the leader of a sports team ("Kapitän der Mannschaft"). In German it’s a masculine noun: der Kapitän (plural: die Kapitäne).
target_language_example: Der Kapitän der Mannschaft spricht mit dem Trainer.
native_language_example: The team captain is talking to the coach.

meaning: “of the class” / “(to, from, in) the class” (forms of **die Klasse**).
additional_notes:
**der Klasse** is a case form of **die Klasse**:
- **Genitive (“of the class”)**: *der Rest der Klasse* = “the rest of the class.”
- **Dative (“to/in the class”)** in certain set phrases: *vor der Klasse* = “in front of the class.”
- **With prepositions** you may also see it meaning “from the class”: *aus der Klasse* = “out of the class.”
So the exact English translation depends on the preposition and context.
target_language_example: Sie ist die Beste der Klasse in Mathe.
native_language_example: She is the best in the class in math.

additional_notes: A masculine noun: der Krieg (genitive: des Krieges/des Kriegs, plural: die Kriege). Often used with prepositions like in: "der Krieg in Europa" (the war in Europe), mit: "der Krieg mit Frankreich" (the war with France), and expressions like "Der Krieg ist vorbei" (the war is over).
target_language_example: Viele Menschen wünschen sich, dass der Krieg endlich endet.
native_language_example: Many people hope that the war will finally end.

additional_notes: A masculine noun. In religious or very formal language you may see it in phrases like „König der Könige“ (“King of Kings”).
target_language_example: Der König wohnt im Schloss.
native_language_example: The king lives in the castle.

meaning: “the kitchen” (dative form of *die Küche*), often meaning “in/to/from the kitchen” depending on the preposition.
additional_notes: *Die Küche* is feminine. In the dative case it becomes **der Küche**. You’ll often see it after prepositions like **in der Küche** (in the kitchen), **aus der Küche** (out of the kitchen), **zu(r) Küche** is uncommon (more common: *in die Küche* = into the kitchen), and in fixed phrases like **Raus aus der Küche!** (“Out of the kitchen!”). The preposition tells you the exact English meaning; **der Küche** itself is just “the kitchen” in dative.
target_language_example: Wir essen heute in der Küche.
native_language_example: We’re eating in the kitchen today.

meaning: the coast / the shoreline (dative: along/at/by the coast).
additional_notes: "Küste" means the coast (where land meets the sea). In the examples it appears as "an der Küste" (= on/along the coast, near the sea) or "vor der Küste" (= off the coast, out at sea but near land). It’s feminine: die Küste; dative singular after many prepositions is der Küste.
target_language_example: Wir machen Urlaub an der Küste.
native_language_example: We’re going on vacation on the coast.

additional_notes: Common everyday word for a shop or store, often used when talking about location and opening hours (öffnet/schließt, geöffnet/geschlossen). It can also refer more generally to a business or establishment (“the place”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich gehe schnell in den Laden und kaufe Brot.
native_language_example: I’m quickly going to the shop and buying bread.

additional_notes:
Used to describe a shop/store (or sometimes a business/place in general) with an adjective or phrase: 
- Der Laden ist teuer. (The store is expensive.)
- Der Laden ist riesig. (The store is huge.)
Note: “Laden” can be a regular store, but in everyday speech it can also mean “this place/this joint” when talking about a business.
target_language_example: Der Laden ist heute geschlossen.
native_language_example: The store is closed today.

meaning: “of the situation” / “of the position” (genitive of *die Lage*).
additional_notes: *Der Lage* is most often used as a genitive form meaning “of the situation/position,” especially in set phrases like **der Ernst der Lage** (“the seriousness/gravity of the situation”) and **Herr der Lage sein** (“to be in control of the situation”). Note: *die Lage* = “situation” or “position/location,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Er war sich des Ernstes der Lage bewusst.
native_language_example: He was aware of the seriousness of the situation.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning “teacher” (male, or a teacher when gender isn’t specified). For a female teacher, say “die Lehrerin.” Plural: “die Lehrer” (male/mixed group) or “die Lehrerinnen” (female). Used with verbs like “sagen,” “begrüßen,” “befehlen,” “lassen.”
target_language_example: Der Lehrer erklärt die Grammatik sehr langsam.
native_language_example: The teacher explains the grammar very slowly.

meaning: 'the last person who' (often: 'the least likely to').
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause: „Er ist der Letzte, der …“ can mean literally that someone was last in order/time, or more commonly that it would be very unlike them to do something (they’re the least likely person). It changes for gender/number/case (e.g., „die Letzte, die …“, „der Letzte, den …“).
target_language_example: Sie ist die Letzte, die sich beschweren würde.
native_language_example: She’s the last person who would complain. / She’s the least likely to complain.

additional_notes: You see **der Liste** when *Liste* is feminine and used in the **dative** (often after prepositions like **auf/in/von**) or **genitive**. Common patterns: **auf der Liste stehen** = to be on the list; **etw. der Liste hinzufügen** = to add something to the list; **von der Liste entfernen** = to remove from the list.
target_language_example: Steht mein Name schon auf der Liste?
native_language_example: Is my name already on the list?

additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Often used for noise that bothers people or keeps them awake. Common verbs: Lärm machen (to make noise), jdn. durch Lärm wach halten (to keep someone awake because of noise), jdn. durch Lärm wecken (to wake someone up with noise), jdn. stören (to disturb someone).
target_language_example: Bitte mach nicht so viel Lärm, ich muss morgen früh aufstehen.
native_language_example: Please don’t make so much noise; I have to get up early tomorrow.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning an adult male person. Often used with the definite article: „der Mann“ = “the man.” In everyday German, „mein Mann“ can mean “my husband.” Plural: „die Männer“.
target_language_example: Der Mann steht vor der Tür.
native_language_example: The man is standing in front of the door.

additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause describing a specific man. "den" is the accusative relative pronoun (referring back to "der Mann") and is used when the man is the direct object in the relative clause: *der Mann, den ich suche* (= I’m looking for him). If the man is the subject, you use *der Mann, der …* instead.
target_language_example: Der Mann, den ich angerufen habe, kommt heute vorbei.
native_language_example: The man (whom/that) I called is coming by today.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe a specific man by adding extra information in a relative clause. German uses a comma before the relative pronoun: „Der Mann, der …“. Here „der“ means “who/that” (not the article “the” in this position) and it changes with gender/case: e.g. „der Mann, den ich kenne“ (whom/that I know), „der Mann, dem ich helfe“ (to whom I’m helping).
target_language_example: Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Nachbar.
native_language_example: The man who is standing there is my neighbor.

meaning: 'the man is' (introduces what the man is like or what he is).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man with an adjective (Der Mann ist alt.), a profession/noun (Der Mann ist Arzt.), or a past participle for events/state (Der Mann ist gestorben.). "Mann" is a masculine noun, so it takes the article "der" and is always capitalized in German.
target_language_example: Der Mann ist müde, aber freundlich.
native_language_example: The man is tired but friendly.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your opinion or belief, usually as part of the pattern „(Ich) bin/war der Meinung, dass …“. With „war der Meinung“ it can mean you believed something in the past (sometimes later found out it wasn’t true). Often interchangeable with „ich glaube, dass …“ in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich bin der Meinung, dass wir jetzt gehen sollten.
native_language_example: I think we should go now.

meaning: the human being; a person; humankind.
additional_notes: Often used in a general, universal sense (“people/humans in general”), especially in sayings and general statements. Singular with the article (der Mensch) can mean “humankind” rather than one specific person, depending on context. Plural: die Menschen (“people”).
target_language_example: Der Mensch braucht soziale Kontakte.
native_language_example: Humans need social contact.

meaning: 'humans are…' / 'the human being is…' (a general statement about people).
additional_notes: Used to make broad, general statements about human nature or people in general. Grammatically it’s the subject “der Mensch” (humankind / the human being) + the verb “ist” (is). Often followed by an adjective or a noun phrase: “Der Mensch ist sterblich.” / “Der Mensch ist ein soziales Wesen.” In English this is usually translated with “humans are …” rather than “the human is …” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Der Mensch ist nicht perfekt, aber er kann dazulernen.
native_language_example: Humans aren’t perfect, but they can learn.

der Mensch ist das einzige Tier, das

target_language_multi_word_term: der Mensch ist das einzige Tier, das
additional_notes: Used to introduce a general statement about a unique human ability or behavior. After „das“, you add a relative clause describing what humans can/do (often with a verb at the end). Example patterns: „…, das + Verb“ or „…, das + Verb + kann“ (can/is able to).
target_language_example: Der Mensch ist das einzige Tier, das Musik machen kann.
native_language_example: Humans are the only animal that can make music.

meaning: "The human being is a…" / "Humans are…" (general statement).
additional_notes: Used to make a general statement about people/humans. Grammatically it’s: subject (Der Mensch) + verb (ist) + predicate noun/adjective phrase. Because "Mensch" is masculine singular, you use "ein" before a noun (e.g., "ein Teil", "ein soziales Tier"). In English this is often translated as "Humans are…" rather than "The human is…".
target_language_example: Der Mensch ist ein Gewohnheitstier.
native_language_example: Humans are creatures of habit.

additional_notes: Masculine noun: der Mond (genitive: des Mondes, plural: die Monde—rare in everyday speech). Common with verbs like scheinen (to shine) and aussehen (to look/appear): „Der Mond scheint.“ / „Der Mond sieht schön aus.“ Often used when talking about night, the sky, seasons, or weather.
target_language_example: Heute ist Vollmond, und der Mond scheint sehr hell.
native_language_example: Tonight is a full moon, and the moon is shining very brightly.

additional_notes: Used to describe the moon’s state/location (often followed by an adjective or a place phrase): Der Mond ist hell. / Der Mond ist hinter den Wolken. Also appears in the Perfekt with certain intransitive verbs like aufgehen (“to rise”): Der Mond ist aufgegangen (“The moon has risen”).
target_language_example: Der Mond ist heute Nacht besonders hell.
native_language_example: The moon is especially bright tonight.

additional_notes: Used after another noun to mean “of the night” (genitive case), often in fixed phrases: *die Mitte der Nacht* (the middle of the night), *die Stille der Nacht* (the stillness of the night), *im Dunkel der Nacht* (in the darkness of the night). Also appears in time expressions with prepositions: *in der Nacht* = at night/during the night; *im Laufe der Nacht* = in the course of the night.
target_language_example: In der Stille der Nacht konnte ich endlich einschlafen.
native_language_example: In the stillness of the night, I could finally fall asleep.

meaning: “of nature” / “(in) nature” (genitive or dative form of "die Natur").
additional_notes: "der Natur" is the form of "die Natur" used most often after certain prepositions (e.g., "in der Natur" = in nature/outdoors, "näher an der Natur" = closer to nature) and to show possession/description (genitive), e.g., "Teil der Natur" = part of nature, "Produkte der Natur" = nature’s products. It’s also used in the phrase "in der Natur von …" = “in the nature of … / typical of …”.
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehen wir raus in die Natur und genießen die Ruhe der Natur.
native_language_example: On the weekend we go out into nature and enjoy the peace of nature.

additional_notes: Usually used in the fixed phrase **in der Nähe** = “nearby.” You can add what it’s near to with **in der Nähe von + dative** (common in speech) or **in der Nähe + genitive** (more formal/written): *in der Nähe von der U-Bahn-Station* / *in der Nähe der U-Bahn-Station*. **Nähe** is the noun “nearness”; **der** is the case form used here (dative after *in*, or genitive in more formal structures).
target_language_example: Gibt es hier in der Nähe einen Supermarkt?
native_language_example: Is there a supermarket nearby?

additional_notes: Used after dative prepositions like "zu" (to) and "bei" (at), or after certain verbs that take dative. "die Party" is feminine; in the dative singular it becomes "der Party" (e.g., "zu der Party" = "to the party", often shortened to "zur Party"). After "von" (from), you use dative too: "von der Party" = "from the party".
target_language_example: Kommst du mit zur Party?
native_language_example: Are you coming with me to the party?

meaning: the patient (a person receiving medical care).
additional_notes: Used for someone who is being treated by a doctor or in a hospital (e.g., before an operation, recovering from an illness). Plural: die Patienten. Usually refers to medical situations (not just any “patient” person).
target_language_example: Der Patient wartet im Wartezimmer.
native_language_example: The patient is waiting in the waiting room.

additional_notes: Used to describe a (male) patient’s condition, location, or status. "der Patient" = "the patient" (masculine noun); "ist" is the 3rd person singular form of "sein" (to be). Common in medical or hospital contexts. For a female patient: "die Patientin ist…"
target_language_example: Der Patient ist müde, aber stabil.
native_language_example: The patient is tired, but stable.

meaning: the plan; an idea/strategy for what to do.
additional_notes: A very common noun for a plan or strategy (often a concrete set of steps). Used with verbs like funktionieren (to work), scheitern (to fail), and sein (to be). In phrases like „auf Eis liegen“ it means a plan is on hold/paused.
target_language_example: Wir brauchen einen Plan für morgen.
native_language_example: We need a plan for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when "die Polizei" is the indirect object (dative), often after verbs like "helfen" (to help), "vertrauen" (to trust), "glauben" (to believe), "etwas sagen/nennen" (to tell/name), or in phrases like "von der Polizei" (by the police). The base word is "die Polizei" (the police); in dative singular it becomes "der Polizei".
target_language_example: Kannst du der Polizei beschreiben, was passiert ist?
native_language_example: Can you describe to the police what happened?

additional_notes: Masculine noun (plural: die Polizisten). Used for a male police officer; for mixed/unspecified gender you’ll also see the gender-neutral form: die Polizei (the police) or the pair der Polizist / die Polizistin. Common with verbs like anhalten (stop), festnehmen (arrest), verdächtigen (suspect), verfolgen (chase).
target_language_example: Der Polizist kontrolliert meine Ausweise.
native_language_example: The police officer is checking my ID documents.

meaning: the post office; the postal service (mail).
additional_notes: Used for both the place (post office) and the organization/service that delivers mail. Often appears with prepositions in the dative: bei der Post (at/with the post office), neben der Post (next to the post office), an der Post vorbei (past the post office).
target_language_example: Ich muss schnell zur Post, um ein Paket zu schicken.
native_language_example: I need to quickly go to the post office to send a package.

additional_notes: Most commonly means the amount of money something costs (Der Preis ist 300 Euro.). In some contexts it means a prize/award that is given to someone (e.g., in a competition or at school): Der Preis wird verliehen. Context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Wie hoch ist der Preis für das Ticket?
native_language_example: How much is the price for the ticket?

additional_notes: A male member of a royal family, often (but not always) the son of a king or queen. Used in fairy tales and formal/historical contexts. Plural: „die Prinzen“.
target_language_example: Der Prinz wohnt im Schloss.
native_language_example: The prince lives in the castle.

meaning: the president (head of a country or organization).
additional_notes: A masculine noun: der Präsident (plural: die Präsidenten). Used for the head of a state (e.g., the U.S.) as well as the leader of an organization or company. Often followed by a genitive phrase: „der Präsident der USA“ (= the president of the USA).
target_language_example: Der Präsident hält heute Abend eine Rede.
native_language_example: The president is giving a speech tonight.

meaning: 'the exam' / 'the test' (genitive or dative form of *die Prüfung*).
additional_notes: *Prüfung* means an exam, test, or assessment. Because *Prüfung* is feminine (*die Prüfung*), **der Prüfung** appears in the **genitive** (e.g., *wegen der Prüfung* = because of the exam) and in the **dative** after certain prepositions (e.g., *in der Prüfung* = in the exam).
target_language_example: Ich kann heute nicht, weil ich morgen in der Prüfung bin.
native_language_example: I can’t today because I have an exam tomorrow.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Commonly used with verbs like regnen (to rain) and schlagen/klatschen gegen + Akkusativ (“to beat/patter against”), e.g., gegen das Fenster / gegen die Fenster. In sentences like „Der Regen hinderte uns daran, …“, it’s the thing preventing you from doing something.
target_language_example: Der Regen hört endlich auf.
native_language_example: The rain is finally stopping.

additional_notes: Used to comment on a sentence (for example in writing, language learning, or grammar discussions). **Der Satz** = “the sentence” (masculine, nominative), **ist** = “is” (3rd person singular of *sein*). Typically followed by an adjective or phrase: *Der Satz ist gut / in Ordnung / zu kurz / unklar.*
target_language_example: Der Satz ist unklar, kannst du ihn anders formulieren?
native_language_example: The sentence is unclear—can you phrase it differently?

additional_notes: Commonly used for physical pain (e.g., headache, stomach pain) but can also mean emotional pain. Often appears with verbs like beginnen (start), weg sein (be gone), nachlassen (ease), and with questions like „Wo ist der Schmerz?“ to locate pain. Plural: „die Schmerzen“ (pains, aches).
target_language_example: Ich habe starke Schmerzen im Rücken.
native_language_example: I have bad back pain.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Often used with winter/weather verbs like: „Der Schnee ist geschmolzen.“ (melted), „Der Schnee ist verschwunden.“ (disappeared), „Der Schnee lag … hoch.“ (was lying … high/deep), „Der Schnee gefror …“ (froze). In comparisons: „Der Schnee ist noch weißer.“ (even whiter).
target_language_example: Heute fällt der Schnee schon wieder.
native_language_example: It’s snowing again today.

meaning: 'of the school' or 'at/from the school' (depending on the case).
additional_notes: This is the noun phrase "die Schule" (school) in a different case: **Genitive**: *der Schule* = "of the school" (e.g., *der Star der Schule* = "the star of the school"). **Dative**: *der Schule* = "at/to/from the school" after many prepositions like *neben* (next to), *von* (from), *bei* (at). Note: beginners often say *auf der Schule*, but standard German is usually *in der Schule* (at school) or *auf die Schule gehen* (to go to school).
target_language_example: Ich warte vor der Schule auf dich.
native_language_example: I'll wait for you in front of the school.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "verweisen" in the passive: "(jemand) wird von/der Schule verwiesen" = someone is expelled from school. In the active: "Die Schule verweist jemanden der Schule" (more common: "Die Schule verweist jemanden von der Schule"). It often implies the person is no longer allowed to attend, typically because of bad behavior.
target_language_example: Er wurde wegen seines Verhaltens von der Schule verwiesen.
native_language_example: He was expelled from school because of his behavior.

additional_notes: Used to describe a lake (der See) with an adjective or phrase: Der See ist blau / tief / zugefroren. Watch out: der See = “lake”, while das Meer = “sea/ocean”. (Also, die See can mean “the sea” in some contexts, especially in nautical language.)
target_language_example: Der See ist heute sehr ruhig.
native_language_example: The lake is very calm today.

additional_notes: “der Sitzung” is the dative (or genitive) singular form of **die Sitzung** (“meeting/session”), often used for official or formal meetings (e.g., a committee meeting). Common with prepositions like **bei** (at/during), **nach** (after), and **mit** (with): *bei der Sitzung*, *nach der Sitzung*, *mit der Sitzung anfangen*.
target_language_example: Während der Sitzung dürfen wir keine Handys benutzen.
native_language_example: During the meeting/session, we’re not allowed to use phones.

additional_notes: A masculine noun for someone who serves in the army. Plural: die Soldaten. Female form: die Soldatin. Commonly used when talking about war, fighting, weapons, injuries, and military life.
target_language_example: Der Soldat kommt morgen zurück.
native_language_example: The soldier is coming back tomorrow.

meaning: “the sun” (in the dative or genitive case).
additional_notes:
“Die Sonne” is feminine. You’ll often see “der Sonne” after certain prepositions and in common phrases:
- Dative (location/after some prepositions): in der Sonne = “in the sun”, vor der Sonne = “from/before the sun”.
- Genitive (possession/description): die Wärme der Sonne = “the warmth of the sun”.
So “der” here doesn’t mean masculine—it’s the case form of “die Sonne.”
target_language_example: Wir sitzen in der Sonne und trinken Kaffee.
native_language_example: We’re sitting in the sun and drinking coffee.

meaning: “of the city/town” (genitive), or “to/at the city” (dative, with certain prepositions).
additional_notes: “Stadt” is feminine: die Stadt. “der Stadt” is an inflected form used mainly (1) for possession/description in the genitive: „das Zentrum der Stadt“ = “the city center / the center of the city”, and (2) after some prepositions that take the dative (e.g., „in der Stadt“ = “in the city”, „aus der Stadt“ = “out of the city”). It can also appear in fixed phrases like „das Gespräch der Stadt“ = “the talk of the town.”
target_language_example: Das Rathaus der Stadt ist sehr alt.
native_language_example: The city’s town hall is very old.

meaning: 'the street' / 'the road' (genitive or dative form of *die Straße*).
additional_notes: *Die Straße* is feminine. **der Straße** is used in the **dative** (often after prepositions like *in*, *auf*, *von*: *in der Straße*, *auf der Straße*, *von der Straße*) and in the **genitive** to show belonging (*beiden Seiten der Straße* = “both sides of the street”). Note: *in der Straße* can mean “on that street” (i.e., along that street), while *auf der Straße* means “in/on the roadway” (outside, on the street).
target_language_example: Die Apotheke ist in der Straße gleich um die Ecke.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is on this street, just around the corner.

meaning: a storm (strong wind, often with bad weather).
additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Used for severe weather with strong winds; it often appears with verbs like „vorüber sein“ (be over), „weitergehen“ (continue), „Schäden anrichten/verursachen“ (cause damage), and „Verluste mit sich bringen“ (bring losses).
target_language_example: Der Sturm hat viele Bäume umgeworfen.
native_language_example: The storm knocked down many trees.

meaning: part of fixed phrases like “in der Tat” (= indeed/in fact) and “ein Mann der Tat” (= a man of action).
additional_notes:
“Tat” means “deed/act.” You’ll often see it in the genitive “der Tat” in set expressions: 
- “in der Tat” is a common, fairly formal way to say “indeed / in fact.” 
- “(ein) Mann der Tat” means someone who acts instead of just talking (a “man of action”). 
- With “zu der Tat,” it can mean “to the act/deed,” e.g. “Grund zu der Tat haben” = “have reason to do it / have reason for the act.”
target_language_example: In der Tat habe ich heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: In fact, I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Refers to the devil/Satan in religion, fairy tales, and everyday expressions. It also appears in curses or strong exclamations (e.g., "Der Teufel soll ...!" = "The devil can ...!" / "To hell with ...!") and in proverbs about greed or bad intentions.
target_language_example: Was hat der Teufel dich geritten?
native_language_example: What on earth got into you? (lit. “What devil rode you?”)

meaning: the animal god / animal spirit (a deity in a story).
additional_notes: Used mainly in fantasy/myth contexts for a powerful animal deity or guardian spirit (often capitalized as a title/name). "Tier" in German means "animal" (not English "tier" = level).
target_language_example: Alle fürchten den Tier-Gott im Wald.
native_language_example: Everyone fears the animal god in the forest.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Used for death in general (Der Tod ist sicher.) or a specific person’s death (Der Tod seiner Tochter). In literature it can be personified as “Death” (Der Tod war gnadenlos.).
target_language_example: Der Tod seines Vaters hat ihn sehr getroffen.
native_language_example: His father's death affected him a lot.

additional_notes: Common in spoken German to refer to a man whose name you don’t know or don’t want to say (often like “that guy”). It can sound casual and sometimes slightly dismissive depending on tone and context. Not the same as English “type” in most everyday uses.
target_language_example: Wer ist der Typ da drüben?
native_language_example: Who is that guy over there?

additional_notes: You’ll see **der Tür** instead of **die Tür** when the noun is in the **dative** or **genitive** case. Common patterns: **von der Tür** (away/from the door), **in der Nähe der Tür** (near the door), **hinter der Tür** (behind the door), **an der Tür** (at/by the door). In everyday speech, **genitive** is often replaced by **von + dative** (e.g., *die Nähe von der Tür* instead of *die Nähe der Tür*).
target_language_example: Bitte warte an der Tür.
native_language_example: Please wait at the door.

additional_notes: Short for "die Untergrundbahn". In practice you’ll most often see it as "die U-Bahn" (feminine). It’s commonly used with public-transport phrases like "mit der U-Bahn fahren" (to take the subway) and in compounds such as "U-Bahn-Station" (subway station) or "U-Bahn-Haltestelle" (subway stop).
target_language_example: Wir fahren mit der U-Bahn in die Innenstadt.
native_language_example: We’re taking the subway to downtown.

meaning: accident (usually an unexpected harmful event, e.g., a traffic accident).
additional_notes: Masculine noun: der Unfall (plural: die Unfälle). Very commonly used for road/traffic accidents, but can also refer to accidents in general (e.g., at work). Often appears with verbs like passieren/geschehen/sich ereignen (“to happen”) and in phrases like „einen Unfall haben“ (to have an accident) or „bei einem Unfall“ (in an accident).
target_language_example: Zum Glück wurde bei dem Unfall niemand verletzt.
native_language_example: Luckily, nobody was injured in the accident.

additional_notes: Used to say that an accident occurred. Often followed by a place ("an einer Kreuzung" = at an intersection) or by a time clause with "als" ("als der Unfall passierte" = when the accident happened). "passieren" is a common verb for "to happen"; in speech you also often hear "Der Unfall ist passiert."
target_language_example: Ich war gerade unterwegs, als der Unfall passierte.
native_language_example: I was on my way when the accident happened.

meaning: 'the university' (feminine singular in the dative or genitive case).
additional_notes: German changes the article depending on the case. With the feminine noun *die Universität*, the article becomes *der* in the dative (after many prepositions, e.g. *an/auf/in/vor/von/mit der Universität*) and also in the genitive (meaning “of the university”). In everyday speech, genitive is often replaced by *von + dative* (e.g. *ein Abschluss von der Universität*).
target_language_example: Ich studiere an der Universität Berlin.
native_language_example: I study at the University of Berlin.

additional_notes: “Die Vergangenheit” means “the past.” You often see it as **der Vergangenheit** because some common patterns require dative or genitive, e.g. **etw. gehört der Vergangenheit an** = “something is a thing of the past,” and **Verben der Vergangenheit** = “verbs in the past (past-tense verbs).” Also common: **in der Vergangenheit** = “in the past,” and **in der Vergangenheit leben** = “to live in the past.”
target_language_example: Zum Glück gehören diese Probleme der Vergangenheit an.
native_language_example: Luckily, those problems are a thing of the past.

additional_notes: A common masculine noun for a bird (animal). Plural: die Vögel. Often used with basic verbs like sein (Der Vogel ist auf dem Dach.), haben (Der Vogel hat Durst.), and with body parts like die Flügel (wings).
target_language_example: Im Garten sitzt ein Vogel auf dem Zaun.
native_language_example: In the garden, a bird is sitting on the fence.

meaning: “the wall” (dative form, used after certain prepositions).
additional_notes: This is the dative form of **die Wand** (“the wall”). You often see it after prepositions like **in**, **an**, **auf**, etc.: **in der Wand** can mean “in the wall” (inside/within it, e.g., a cable), while **an der Wand** means “on/against the wall.”
target_language_example: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
native_language_example: The picture is hanging on the wall.

meaning: “of the world” / “to the world” (the word “world” in genitive or dative).
additional_notes:
“Welt” is feminine (die Welt). “der Welt” is either:
- Genitive singular = “of the world” (common after nouns and in superlatives): der Rest der Welt (the rest of the world), der schnellste … der Welt (the fastest … in the world), viele Länder der Welt (many countries of the world).
- Dative singular = “to/in the world” after certain prepositions (e.g., in der Welt = in the world). The case depends on the surrounding words, but the form stays “der Welt.”
target_language_example: Das ist das beste Restaurant der Welt.
native_language_example: That’s the best restaurant in the world.

additional_notes: A common masculine noun used for weather. Often appears with verbs like: **(der Wind) bläst** (the wind blows), **lässt nach** (dies down), **nimmt zu** (picks up/gets stronger). It can also be used poetically as if the wind could "whisper" something.
target_language_example: Heute ist der Wind sehr stark.
native_language_example: Today the wind is very strong.

additional_notes: Used to describe the weather. With directions you often see: „Der Wind weht nach Süden“ (toward the south) and „Der Wind weht von Norden (her)“ (from the north; „her“ emphasizes ‘from that direction toward here’ but is often optional). You can also just say „Der Wind weht“ as a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Heute ist es kalt, und der Wind weht stark.
native_language_example: Today it's cold, and the wind is blowing strongly.

additional_notes: Used with **sein** (“to be”) to describe the state of winter or to say that winter is (not) over. Common patterns: **Der Winter ist kalt.** (Winter is cold.) / **Der Winter ist vorbei/vorüber.** (Winter is over.) / **Der Winter ist sehr kalt gewesen.** (The winter was very cold — using *gewesen* to talk about the past.)
target_language_example: Der Winter ist endlich vorbei.
native_language_example: Winter is finally over.

additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to a week or is a part of a week, often after nouns like "Ende" (end) or "Tag" (day): "bis zum Ende der Woche" = "by the end of the week", "der dritte Tag der Woche" = "the third day of the week".
target_language_example: Ich brauche den Bericht bis zum Ende der Woche.
native_language_example: I need the report by the end of the week.

additional_notes: "der Zeit" is the genitive form of "die Zeit" and often means "of time" (e.g., "das Rad der Zeit" = "the wheel of time"). You’ll also see it in common phrases like "mit der Zeit" (= "over time") and "in der Zeit" (= "in that time period"), where "der Zeit" can also be dative after certain prepositions.
target_language_example: Mit der Zeit wird alles leichter.
native_language_example: Over time, everything gets easier.

meaning: 'the newspaper' (in the dative or genitive case).
additional_notes: “Zeitung” is feminine: die Zeitung (nom./acc.). “der Zeitung” is the dative (“with/to the newspaper”) or genitive (“of the newspaper”) form. Common patterns: **mit der Zeitung** = with the newspaper; **neben der Zeitung** = next to the newspaper; **aus der Zeitung** = out of/from the newspaper. Also used in the fixed expressions **der Zeitung nach** / **der Zeitung zufolge** = according to the newspaper.
target_language_example: Der Zeitung zufolge beginnt der Streik am Montag.
native_language_example: According to the newspaper, the strike starts on Monday.

additional_notes: A masculine noun (der). Common with travel verbs like abfahren (to depart), kommen (to arrive), verlassen (to leave), and verkehren (to run/operate on a route). Often used with Bahnhof (train station).
target_language_example: Der Zug fährt um 8 Uhr ab.
native_language_example: The train departs at 8 o'clock.

meaning: “the train goes/is running” (i.e., it travels or departs).
additional_notes: A common way to talk about train schedules. With a time, it often means “departs/leaves”: Der Zug fährt in zehn Minuten / um sechs Uhr. With ab it’s explicitly “departs”: Der Zug fährt vom Bahnhof ab. With every/each (jede halbe Stunde) it means “runs”: “The train runs every half hour.”
target_language_example: Der Zug fährt um 8:15 Uhr ab.
native_language_example: The train leaves at 8:15.

additional_notes: Uses Präteritum (simple past) of "kommen" (kam). Often used with place words like "am Bahnhof" (at the station) and with "an" to emphasize arrival: "Der Zug kam ... an." In everyday speech, many speakers also use Perfekt: "Der Zug ist gekommen" / more commonly "Der Zug ist angekommen."
target_language_example: Der Zug kam gestern Abend pünktlich an.
native_language_example: The train arrived on time yesterday evening.

meaning: 'the train was' (talking about the train’s state/condition in the past).
additional_notes: Used to describe what the train was like (e.g., empty/full/on time/delayed) or what had happened to it at a specific time. "Der Zug" = the train (masculine); "war" is the simple past of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective (leer, pünktlich, überfüllt) or a phrase like "schon weg" (already gone).
target_language_example: Der Zug war zu spät, also haben wir ein Taxi genommen.
native_language_example: The train was late, so we took a taxi.

additional_notes: A normal, neutral noun phrase for an elderly man. It takes adjective endings: nominative der alte Mann, accusative den alten Mann, dative dem alten Mann. Plural: die alten Männer.
target_language_example: Ich habe den alten Mann im Park gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw the old man in the park.

meaning: 'the old man is …' (introduces a description/state of an old man).
additional_notes: Used as the subject phrase "der alte Mann" (the old man) + the verb "ist" (is). After "ist" you typically add an adjective (e.g., krank, verrückt), a noun phrase (e.g., ein Arzt), or other information describing his state/situation.
target_language_example: Der alte Mann ist sehr müde.
native_language_example: The old man is very tired.

additional_notes: This is the dative form of "die alte Dame". You often see it after verbs that take the dative, especially "helfen" (to help): "jdm. helfen" = "help someone". "Dame" is a polite word for a woman (often used for an older woman).
target_language_example: Kannst du der alten Dame bitte die Tür aufhalten?
native_language_example: Can you please hold the door open for the old lady?

meaning: “the best” (masculine singular), or “best” used as a noun (e.g., “the best one/person”).
additional_notes: Superlative form of „gut“ (good). Used when you compare and say something is number 1. It changes with gender/case: „der beste“ (masc.), „die beste“ (fem.), „das beste“ (neut.), plural „die besten“. Often followed by a noun (e.g., „der beste Kuchen“) or used alone (“Er ist der Beste.”).
target_language_example: Welches ist der beste Weg zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: Which is the best way to the train station?

meaning: the best way / the best route.
additional_notes: Used for the most effective method to do something (often with an infinitive clause: „der beste Weg, ... zu ...“) or for the best route from one place to another („der beste Weg von ... nach ...“). It can also mean “the best way forward” in a situation.
target_language_example: Der beste Weg, Deutsch zu lernen, ist jeden Tag ein bisschen zu üben.
native_language_example: The best way to learn German is to practice a little every day.

additional_notes: Used to say there is just one person/thing of that kind. It often comes before a noun: „der einzige Eingang“ = “the only entrance.” It can also be used like a pronoun for a person: „Ich bin der Einzige.“ = “I’m the only one.” The form changes with gender/case: der/die/das einzige, den einzigen, dem einzigen, etc. You may also see it with a following clause: „der einzige, den …“ (“the only one whom/that …”).
target_language_example: Bist du der einzige, der Deutsch spricht?
native_language_example: Are you the only one who speaks German?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the only person who does/knows something. It’s often followed by a verb in a relative clause: „der einzige, der …“. For a female person: „die einzige, die …“. For plural: „die einzigen, die …“. The verb in the relative clause matches the real subject (e.g., „Ich bin der einzige, der weiß …“).
target_language_example: Sie ist die einzige, die heute Zeit hat.
native_language_example: She’s the only one who has time today.

meaning: “the first (one)” (masculine), also used for “the first” + a masculine noun.
additional_notes: Use **der Erste** when the “first” is a masculine person/thing standing on its own (a nominalized adjective): *Er war der Erste.* If a noun follows, it acts like an adjective and takes the matching ending: *der erste Tag* (masc.), *die erste Idee* (fem.), *das erste Mal* (neut.), *die ersten Schritte* (plural).
target_language_example: Ich war heute der Erste im Büro.
native_language_example: I was the first one in the office today.

meaning: 'the biggest' / 'the greatest' (masculine singular superlative of groß).
additional_notes: Used to compare more than two things/people: the one that is biggest, greatest, or often tallest. You’ll see it either before a noun ("der größte Teil" = the largest part) or after "sein" as a predicate ("Er ist der größte" = He is the biggest/tallest). For other genders/cases it changes (e.g., die größte, das größte, den größten).
target_language_example: Von allen Spielern ist er der größte.
native_language_example: Of all the players, he is the biggest/tallest.

meaning: 'the young man' (a male person, usually young).
additional_notes: Common, neutral way to refer to a young male person. Used when you don’t know the person’s name or when pointing someone out. Declension changes with case (e.g., nominative: der junge Mann; accusative: den jungen Mann; dative: dem jungen Mann).
target_language_example: Ich habe den jungen Mann gestern im Park gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw the young man in the park yesterday.

meaning: the little boy / the young boy.
additional_notes: A noun phrase with the definite article: **der** (masculine, nominative). With **der**, the adjective often takes **-e**: **der klein-e Junge**. Used to refer to a specific boy known from context (or as a “storybook-style” way to introduce a character). In other cases you might see different endings depending on case: e.g., **den kleinen Jungen** (accusative), **dem kleinen Jungen** (dative).
target_language_example: Der kleine Junge spielt im Park.
native_language_example: The little boy is playing in the park.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the final one in a sequence (time, order, etc.). It’s the masculine form in nominative case (e.g., der letzte Bus/Zug/Kunde). With other genders/cases it changes: die letzte Bahn, das letzte Mal, den letzten Zug. Common fixed phrase: "der letzte Schrei" = "the latest fashion/craze" (not literally “the last scream”).
target_language_example: Wann fährt der letzte Bus?
native_language_example: When does the last bus leave?

additional_notes: Used to identify the final person in a sequence who did something: „Ich war der letzte, der ging.“ It’s also common in a more idiomatic sense meaning someone is the least likely to do something (often with Konjunktiv II): „Er wäre der letzte, der lügen würde.“
target_language_example: Sie wäre die Letzte, die so etwas sagen würde.
native_language_example: She would be the last person to say something like that.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun: "der neue Plan / der neue Papst / der neue Wagen". It can also be used as a noun meaning "the new guy/one": "Der Neue ist schon da." The ending (-e) is the adjective ending for nominative masculine with "der"; it changes in other cases (e.g., "Ich kenne den Neuen."). For feminine nouns you’d say "die neue ..." (e.g., "die neue Sängerin").
target_language_example: Der Neue arbeitet seit heute bei uns.
native_language_example: The new guy has been working with us since today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the next person/thing in a sequence (often like a pronoun: "the next one"). It changes with gender and case: der nächste (masc.), die nächste (fem.), das nächste (neut.); e.g., "der nächste Bus" = "the next bus".
target_language_example: Der nächste Bus kommt in zehn Minuten.
native_language_example: The next bus comes in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used when talking about the following train in the schedule (the one coming/arriving after the current time). Often appears in questions with verbs like „kommen“ (to come), „ankommen“ (to arrive), or „eintreffen“ (to arrive). Note the adjective ending: „der nächste Zug“ (masculine nominative); in other cases you’ll see e.g. „Wann kommt der nächste Zug?“ but „Ich warte auf den nächsten Zug.“
target_language_example: Wann fährt der nächste Zug nach Berlin?
native_language_example: When does the next train to Berlin leave?

meaning: the richest man in the world.
additional_notes: Used to describe a man who has the most money (highest wealth) worldwide. Superlative form: reich (rich) → reicher → der reichste. Often used with "sein" (to be): "Er ist der reichste Mann der Welt." Also commonly appears in news or rankings; "angeblich" adds uncertainty (“allegedly”).
target_language_example: Viele sagen, er sei der reichste Mann der Welt.
native_language_example: Many people say he is the richest man in the world.

meaning: the right time (the best moment to do something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about whether it’s a good or appropriate moment for an action or decision. Often used with "jetzt" (now) and with questions like "Ist jetzt der richtige Zeitpunkt?". Grammatically masculine: "der Zeitpunkt".
target_language_example: Vielleicht ist morgen der richtige Zeitpunkt, um darüber zu reden.
native_language_example: Maybe tomorrow is the right time to talk about it.

additional_notes: Uses the superlative of „schnell“ (schnell → schneller → am schnellsten / der schnellste). Often followed by a genitive („der schnellste Läufer seiner Klasse“ = of his class) or a phrase with „aus“ („der schnellste Läufer aus unserer Klasse“ = the fastest runner in/from our class).
target_language_example: Sie ist die schnellste Läuferin im Team.
native_language_example: She is the fastest runner on the team.

additional_notes: Means a lot of rain coming down hard (often used when the rain causes problems or prevents plans). It’s a noun phrase: der Regen (rain) + stark (strong) → strong/heavy. Common with verbs like bringen/verursachen (cause), abhalten/ davon abhalten (keep someone from doing something), and zwingen (force someone to do something).
target_language_example: Wegen des starken Regens fällt das Spiel heute aus.
native_language_example: Because of the heavy rain, the game is canceled today.

additional_notes: Used to specify a particular person/thing: “der …” = “the one …”. In the relative clause, the pronoun changes case depending on its role there. Very common pattern: **der, den ich** … when it’s the **direct object** of *ich* (I): *den ich gekauft/gesucht habe* = “that/who I bought/was looking for”. If it’s the subject in the relative clause, you’d use **der, der …** (*der, der hier wohnt* = “the one who lives here”).
target_language_example: Ist das der, den ich gestern im Laden gesehen habe?
native_language_example: Is that the one I saw in the store yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to identify a specific male person by adding a relative clause: „der, der + Verb …“. The first „der“ is a demonstrative/pronoun (“the one”), and the second „der“ starts the relative clause (“who”). Often used in contrasts like „nicht mehr der, der …“ = “no longer the person (he) used to be.” Feminine: „die, die …“, plural: „die, die …“, neuter: „das, das …“.
target_language_example: Er ist der, der immer die Wahrheit sagt.
native_language_example: He’s the one who always tells the truth.

meaning: "that one (over there)" (masculine) / "that (one)" when pointing to a man or object.
additional_notes: A common pointing phrase used with the masculine demonstrative pronoun/article: der ("that one", masculine) + da ("there"). Often used with a gesture or in contrast: "dieser ... ist besser als der da" (= this one ... is better than that one). It can also appear in a relative clause meaning "who/that is there": "der Mann, der da steht" (= the man who is standing there). For other genders: "die da" (feminine/plural), "das da" (neuter).
target_language_example: Wer ist der da neben der Tür?
native_language_example: Who is that guy (over there) next to the door?

meaning: “who did that” / “the one who did that” (referring to a man).
additional_notes: This is a relative clause meaning “who did that,” using **der** (masculine singular). It often follows words like **derjenige** (“the one”) or **den** (“the one [him]”) depending on the grammar: e.g. **Tom war derjenige, der das getan hat** (“Tom was the one who did that”) and **Ich finde den, der das getan hat** (“I’ll find the one who did that”). For other genders/numbers you’d change **der** (e.g. **die das getan hat**, **die das getan haben**).
target_language_example: Die Polizei sucht den Mann, der das getan hat.
native_language_example: The police are looking for the man who did that.

meaning: "the one who" (referring to a specific male person).
additional_notes: Used to point out or identify a particular person: "X is the one who ...". The pronoun agrees with the person you mean: derjenige (masc.), diejenige (fem.), dasjenige (neut.), diejenigen (plural). Often used in questions or accusations to identify who did something.
target_language_example: Ich war nicht derjenige, der das Fenster geöffnet hat.
native_language_example: I wasn't the one who opened the window.

additional_notes: Used to show possession/relationship, often after another noun: "die Seite des Buches" (the page of the book), "der Titel des Buches" (the title of the book). It’s the genitive singular form: "das Buch" → "des Buches".
target_language_example: Ich habe das Ende des Buches nicht verstanden.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand the ending of the book.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or relation: "der Anfang des Films" (the beginning of the movie), "das Ende des Films" (the end of the movie), "ein Teil des Films" (a part of the movie). You also see it after certain prepositions that take the genitive, especially "während": "während des Films" = during the movie. "Film" is masculine (der Film), so in the genitive singular it becomes "des Films".
target_language_example: Am Ende des Films waren alle ganz still.
native_language_example: At the end of the movie, everyone was completely quiet.

additional_notes: Used with the genitive case to mean “of the river,” often after nouns like Seite (side), Ufer (bank), Tiefe (depth), Lauf (course). Fluss is masculine (der Fluss), so the genitive is des Flusses (often with -es on the noun).
target_language_example: Die Farbe des Flusses ändert sich nach dem Regen.
native_language_example: The color of the river changes after the rain.

additional_notes: This is the genitive singular of *das Geld*. You often see it after genitive expressions like **wegen** (because of) and nouns like **die Frage** (the question/issue): *wegen des Geldes* = “because of the money”, *eine Frage des Geldes* = “a matter of money”. In everyday speech, many speakers also use dative with *wegen* (*wegen dem Geld*), but *wegen des Geldes* is the more standard/formal form.
target_language_example: Sie streiten sich wegen des Geldes.
native_language_example: They’re arguing because of the money.

meaning: because of the money; for money’s sake.
additional_notes: Used to give a (often critical) reason/motive: doing something primarily for financial reasons. It’s the formal genitive form with "wegen" ("des Geldes" = "of the money"). Very common with "nur" ("nur des Geldes wegen" = "only because of the money").
target_language_example: Sie macht den Job nicht des Geldes wegen, sondern weil er ihr Spaß macht.
native_language_example: She doesn’t do the job for the money, but because she enjoys it.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to the house or is part of it (e.g., "die Türen des Hauses" = "the doors of the house"). "des" is the genitive form of "der" for masculine/neuter nouns; "Haus" is neuter (das Haus), and it often adds -(e)s in the genitive: "des Hauses". Common in more formal/written German; in speech people often use "von dem Haus" / "vom Haus" instead.
target_language_example: Die Fenster des Hauses sind neu.
native_language_example: The windows of the house are new.

additional_notes: Used with the genitive case of "das Jahr" to express time within a year (e.g., "am Ende des Jahres" = "at the end of the year", "der erste Tag des Jahres" = "the first day of the year"). Often appears after time words like "Anfang" (beginning), "Ende" (end), "Rest" (rest), "Tag" (day), "Zeit" (time).
target_language_example: Am Anfang des Jahres mache ich immer neue Pläne.
native_language_example: At the beginning of the year I always make new plans.

additional_notes: *Des Krieges* is the genitive singular of *der Krieg* (“the war”). It’s used to show possession/relationship, often after nouns like *Ende* (end), *Schrecken* (horrors), *Fortsetzung* (continuation): *das Ende des Krieges* = “the end of the war.” In many everyday contexts, German also uses *von + dative* instead of the genitive, but fixed phrases like *das Ende des Krieges* are very common.
target_language_example: Nach dem Ende des Krieges begann der Wiederaufbau.
native_language_example: After the end of the war, reconstruction began.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to or is connected with the king. It’s the genitive form of **der König**. Common after another noun: **die Tochter des Königs** (the king’s daughter), **eine Einladung des Königs** (an invitation from/of the king).
target_language_example: Die Krone des Königs ist aus Gold.
native_language_example: The king’s crown is made of gold.

meaning: "of the country" (or "of the land/region"), in the genitive case.
additional_notes: "des Landes" is the genitive form of "das Land" and is used to show possession/connection: something belongs to or relates to the country/land/region. Common in fixed phrases like "Hauptstadt des Landes" (capital of the country) or "die beste … des Landes" (the best … in the country).
target_language_example: Die Wirtschaft des Landes wächst schnell.
native_language_example: The country's economy is growing quickly.

additional_notes: "des Lebens" is the genitive singular form of "das Leben" and is used to show possession or a close relationship, often in formal or fixed phrases (e.g., "die Quelle des Lebens" = "the source of life", "die Grundlage des Lebens" = "the basis/foundation of life"). It commonly follows nouns like "Weg" (path), "Quelle" (source), "Grundlage" (foundation), etc.
target_language_example: Er suchte nach dem Sinn des Lebens.
native_language_example: He was searching for the meaning of life.

meaning: 'of the sea' (genitive: belonging to/related to the sea).
additional_notes: "des Meeres" is the genitive form of "das Meer" and is used after another noun to show a relationship like possession, origin, or description (e.g., "das Geräusch des Meeres" = the sound of the sea). It often appears in written/literary style; in everyday speech people also use "vom Meer" (from/of the sea) in some contexts, but the meaning can shift depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Die Ruhe des Meeres hilft mir beim Einschlafen.
native_language_example: The calm of the sea helps me fall asleep.

additional_notes: Used to specify a point within a particular month, especially in common time expressions: am Anfang/Ende des Monats (“at the beginning/end of the month”), der erste/letzte Tag des Monats (“the first/last day of the month”), or der Erste des Monats (“the first day of the month”). Here, Monats is the genitive singular of der Monat.
target_language_example: Am Ende des Monats bezahle ich die Miete.
native_language_example: At the end of the month I pay the rent.

meaning: 'of murder' (used with schuldig/for schuldig befunden = 'guilty of murder').
additional_notes: Genitive form of „der Mord“ used in formal/legal language, especially after „schuldig sein“ (to be guilty) and in court-style phrases like „für schuldig befunden werden“ (to be found guilty). In everyday speech you may also hear „wegen Mordes“ (for murder) depending on context.
target_language_example: Der Angeklagte wurde des Mordes für schuldig befunden.
native_language_example: The defendant was found guilty of murder.

additional_notes: An (older/literary) way to say "nachts" or "in der Nacht". It uses the genitive form ("of the night") and often appears in written language, reports, or storytelling.
target_language_example: Des Nachts ist es in dieser Stadt sehr ruhig.
native_language_example: At night it’s very quiet in this city.

additional_notes: Used to show possession/relationship: *die Lösung des Problems* = “the solution to/of the problem”, *ein Teil des Problems* = “part of the problem”. Also used with some expressions/adjectives, e.g. *sich (Genitiv) bewusst sein*: *Ich war mir des Problems nicht bewusst* = “I wasn’t aware of the problem.” In everyday speech, German often replaces the genitive with *von + dative* (e.g. *die Lösung von dem Problem*), but the genitive (*des Problems*) is common and standard.
target_language_example: Wir müssen zuerst die Ursache des Problems finden.
native_language_example: We first have to find the cause of the problem.

additional_notes: "Des Regens" is the genitive singular of "der Regen". You often see it after genitive prepositions like "wegen" (because of) and "aufgrund" (due to): "wegen/aufgrund des Regens". It can also be used with nouns to mean "the ... of the rain", e.g. "das Geräusch des Regens" (the sound of the rain).
target_language_example: Wir bleiben wegen des Regens zu Hause.
native_language_example: We’re staying home because of the rain.

additional_notes: Used when *Schnee* is in the genitive case (masculine/neuter: *des* + noun usually with -(e)s). Common in phrases like *der größte Teil des Schnees* (“most of the snow”) and after prepositions such as *wegen* and *aufgrund* (“because of”), e.g. *wegen/aufgrund des Schnees*.
target_language_example: Wegen des Schnees bleiben wir heute zu Hause.
native_language_example: Because of the snow, we’re staying home today.

additional_notes: "Des Sturms" is the genitive form of the masculine noun "der Sturm" (storm). You often see it after prepositions that take the genitive, especially in formal/written German, e.g. "während des Sturms" (during the storm), "wegen des Sturms" (because of the storm), "trotz des Sturms" (despite the storm).
target_language_example: Wegen des Sturms fällt der Flug aus.
native_language_example: Because of the storm, the flight is cancelled.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to express "... of the day" (genitive), often in set phrases like "Ende des Tages" (end of the day), "(größter) Teil des Tages" (most of the day), "die meiste Zeit des Tages" (most of the day), or "die größte Mahlzeit des Tages" (the biggest meal of the day).
target_language_example: Ich bin den ganzen Rest des Tages beschäftigt.
native_language_example: I’m busy for the rest of the day.

additional_notes: "des Todes" is the genitive form of "der Tod" and is used to mean "of death" in fixed expressions and titles, e.g. "der Gott des Todes" (the god of death) or "im Angesicht des Todes" (in the face of death). It often sounds formal/literary and is common after nouns ("Anfang des Todes") or in set phrases.
target_language_example: Sie hatte im Angesicht des Todes keine Angst.
native_language_example: In the face of death, she wasn’t afraid.

additional_notes: Genitive singular of **das Universum** (neuter). Used to show possession/relationship, often after nouns like **das Zentrum**, **der Mittelpunkt**, **ein Teil**: *das Zentrum des Universums* = “the center of the universe.”
target_language_example: Wir sind nur ein kleiner Teil des Universums.
native_language_example: We are only a small part of the universe.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an idea or content and express it in the genitive case. Common after nouns or expressions that require genitive, e.g. "die Bedeutung dessen, was ...", "das Gegenteil dessen, was ...", or with prepositions like "bezüglich dessen, was ...". It’s written with a comma: "dessen, was ...".
target_language_example: Ich verstehe die Gründe dessen, was gestern passiert ist, noch nicht.
native_language_example: I still don’t understand the reasons for what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: „dich“ is the accusative form of „du“ (yourself/you), used with many reflexive verbs that take „an + Akkusativ“. Common patterns from the examples: „sich an etwas halten“ = to stick to/adhere to (a plan, rules, the truth); „sich an etwas beteiligen“ = to take part in; „sich an etwas erinnern“ = to remember. The exact English meaning depends on the verb + what comes after „an“.
target_language_example: Bitte halte dich an die Abmachung.
native_language_example: Please stick to the agreement.

meaning: "you" + "the last time" (i.e., “the last time you… / the last time I… you…”).
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about the most recent previous occasion something happened. In sentences like "Wann habe ich dich das letzte Mal besucht?", "dich" is the object (“you”), and "das letzte Mal" means “the last time.” Very often you’ll also see the reflexive version: "dich das letzte Mal" ↔ "mich/dich/sich … das letzte Mal" (e.g., "Wann hast du dich das letzte Mal beteiligt?" = “When did you last take part?”).
target_language_example: Wann habe ich dich das letzte Mal angerufen?
native_language_example: When did I last call you?

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase used to express (often pleasant) surprise or coincidence about seeing someone in this place. Common with expressions like „Ich freue mich (sehr), …“, „Was für ein Zufall, …“, „Was für ein Glück(sfall), …“, or „(Welch) angenehme Überraschung, …“.
target_language_example: Was für ein Zufall, dich hier zu treffen!
native_language_example: What a coincidence to meet you here!

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an accusative object (dich = “you”). Always refers to one person you address as du. Immer noch means “still” in the sense of “up to now / despite time passing.” Word order: dich often comes before immer noch: Ich liebe dich immer noch. It can also appear later for emphasis: Ich liebe dich noch immer.
target_language_example: Ich denke immer noch an dich.
native_language_example: I still think about you.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/transport (e.g., begleiten, bringen, fahren) to mean taking someone to their home. “dich” is the accusative form of “du” (you), used here as the direct object (“you”), and “nach Hause” means “(to) home.” Often appears as “dich nach Hause begleiten/bringen/fahren.”
target_language_example: Soll ich dich nach Hause bringen?
native_language_example: Should I take you home?

meaning: “not you/yourself” — used to negate a verb phrase with (reflexive) “dich”.
additional_notes: “dich” is the accusative form of “du” (“you”) and is often used reflexively (“yourself”) with verbs like „sich bewegen“ (to move), „sich erinnern“ (to remember), „sich abhängig machen“ (to become dependent). „nicht“ negates what follows or the verb phrase; in commands it often becomes „… dich nicht!“ = “don’t …!”. Example pattern: „Beweg dich nicht!“ = “Don’t move!”
target_language_example: Bitte setz dich nicht auf meinen Platz.
native_language_example: Please don’t sit in my seat.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the intensity of a feeling or how much something affects someone. Often appears with verbs like lieben (love), hassen (hate), interessieren (interest), and kümmern (care/matter). Word order changes with grammar: e.g., Ich liebe dich so sehr. / Es interessiert dich so sehr, weil …
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, dass es dich so sehr verletzt hat.
