additional_notes: Used to compare two people: Person A goes to/attends the same school as Person B. Very common with **auf dieselbe Schule gehen** (“to go to the same school”) or **dieselbe Schule besuchen** (“to attend the same school”). You can also use it in past tense: **hat dieselbe Schule wie ich besucht** (“attended the same school as me”).
target_language_example: Ich gehe auf dieselbe Schule wie meine Schwester.
native_language_example: I go to the same school as my sister.

additional_notes: „Diesem Buch“ is used when the noun „Buch“ is in the dative case, often after common dative prepositions like „mit“ (with), „von“ (from/about), and „unter“ (under, in a location sense), or in expressions like „viel von etwas halten“ (to think highly of something).
target_language_example: Ich lerne gerade mit diesem Buch für die Prüfung.
native_language_example: I’m studying for the exam with this book.

additional_notes: Dative form of "dieses Gebiet" (from "das Gebiet" = area/region; also used figuratively for a subject area or professional field). Common after prepositions like "in" or "auf" when they indicate location/area: "in diesem Gebiet" = in this area; "auf diesem Gebiet" = in this field.
target_language_example: In diesem Gebiet gibt es viele Wanderwege.
native_language_example: In this area there are many hiking trails.

additional_notes: Used when "Haus" is in the dative case, often after certain prepositions. Common patterns: "in diesem Haus" = "in this house" (location), "von diesem Haus" = "of/from this house." The base form is "dieses Haus" (nominative/accusative).
target_language_example: In diesem Haus gibt es drei Wohnungen.
native_language_example: There are three apartments in this house.

additional_notes: “Diesem Land” is the dative form of “dieses Land” (“this country/land”). It often appears after certain prepositions (e.g., in, aus, zu) and with verbs like “gefallen” (to like/appeal to): “Was gefällt dir an diesem Land?” = “What do you like about this country?”
target_language_example: In diesem Land spricht man Deutsch.
native_language_example: In this country people speak German.

additional_notes: "diesem Thema" is the dative form of "dieses Thema". It’s often used after prepositions like "bei" (with/when it comes to), "zu" (on the topic of), and some verbs that take dative (e.g., "sich mit etwas auskennen" = to know a lot about something).
target_language_example: Bei diesem Thema bin ich mir nicht sicher.
native_language_example: I’m not sure about this topic.

additional_notes: Used when "this room" is the object of a dative-taking preposition (common here: "aus diesem Zimmer" = out of/from this room, "zu diesem Zimmer" = to this room) or when the sentence requires dative. Base form: "dieses Zimmer" (nominative/accusative). "diesem" is the dative form of "dieses" for neuter nouns like "das Zimmer".
target_language_example: Ich komme gerade aus diesem Zimmer.
native_language_example: I'm just coming out of this room.

additional_notes: A verb phrase using the past participle **gepflanzt** (from **pflanzen** = “to plant”). In the **Perfekt** past tense it’s usually **hat ... gepflanzt** (with **haben**): *Er hat diesen Baum gepflanzt.* **Diesen Baum** is accusative (“this tree” as the direct object). Often used in questions like **Wer hat diesen Baum gepflanzt?** (“Who planted this tree?”).
target_language_example: Ich habe diesen Baum vor drei Jahren gepflanzt.
native_language_example: I planted this tree three years ago.

additional_notes: Used when "der Bericht" (report) is the direct object of the verb (e.g., write, correct, translate, discuss). "diesen" is the accusative masculine form of "dieser" (this). In the nominative you’d say "dieser Bericht" (this report).
target_language_example: Ich habe diesen Bericht gestern fertig geschrieben.
native_language_example: I finished writing this report yesterday.

additional_notes: Used when the letter is the direct object (what you give, read, send, answer, etc.). It’s the accusative masculine form of the demonstrative/article: der Brief → diesen Brief. Common with verbs like geben (to give), lesen (to read), schicken/senden (to send), beantworten (to answer).
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Brief bitte zur Post bringen?
native_language_example: Can you take this letter to the post office, please?

meaning: "this letter for me" / "this letter on my behalf".
additional_notes: Used as the object in polite requests asking someone to mail a specific letter for you. "Diesen Brief" is accusative (direct object). "für mich" here means "for me / on my behalf" (i.e., you want the other person to do the mailing). Often used with verbs like "abschicken", "abschicken/absenden", or with "aufgeben" (to post at the post office) and separable forms like "abschicken"/"abschicken" and "abschicken" with "ab" (e.g., "Schick ... ab!").
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Brief für mich abschicken?
native_language_example: Can you mail this letter for me?

additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt tense: **haben** + **geschrieben**. **Diesen Brief** is the direct object (accusative) meaning “this letter.” Common question words with it: **Für wen/Wem ... geschrieben?** (“for whom/to whom did you write...?”) and **Wo ... geschrieben?** (“where did you write...?”). Note: **Brief** means “letter,” not “brief” (false friend).
target_language_example: Ich habe diesen Brief gestern Abend geschrieben.
native_language_example: I wrote this letter yesterday evening.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is the direct object of the verb (e.g., sehen, mögen, hassen): *Ich sehe diesen Film.* Depending on context, *Film* can mean a movie or a roll of photographic film; in a photo shop/lab, *diesen Film entwickeln und drucken* means “develop and print this roll of film.”
target_language_example: Ich möchte diesen Film heute Abend sehen.
native_language_example: I want to watch this movie tonight.

additional_notes: Used when the course is the direct object of the verb (e.g., pass/complete/take/buy a textbook for this course). It’s the accusative form of “dieser Kurs.” Common with verbs like “bestehen” (to pass) and “schaffen” (to manage/complete).
target_language_example: Ich muss für diesen Kurs viel lernen.
native_language_example: I have to study a lot for this course.

meaning: "this place" (accusative: the place as the object of the sentence).
additional_notes: "Diesen" is the masculine accusative form of "dieser" (this), used with "der Ort" (place/location). You use "diesen Ort" after many verbs that take a direct object (e.g., besuchen, kennen, hassen, beschreiben). If it’s the subject, you’d say "dieser Ort" (e.g., "Dieser Ort ist schön.").
target_language_example: Ich möchte diesen Ort noch einmal besuchen.
native_language_example: I’d like to visit this place one more time.

additional_notes: Used when the sentence is the direct object of the verb (accusative), often with requests/commands: „Diesen Satz bitte …“ (e.g., delete/rewrite/translate this sentence). In nominative it’s „dieser Satz“ (this sentence as the subject).
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Satz bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Can you repeat this sentence, please?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „lernen“ or „können“ to mean memorizing something so you can say it without looking. „auswendig“ = from memory/by heart; „diesen Satz“ is accusative ('this sentence' as the direct object). Often appears as „… auswendig lernen“ or „… auswendig können“.
target_language_example: Ich muss diesen Satz für die Prüfung auswendig lernen.
native_language_example: I have to memorize this sentence for the exam.

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to translate a specific sentence. Common in questions with polite forms: "Könnten Sie diesen Satz übersetzen?" (formal) vs. "Könntest du diesen Satz übersetzen?" (informal). You can add a person in the dative with "mir/uns": "Könntest du mir diesen Satz übersetzen?" = "Could you translate this sentence for me?"
target_language_example: Kannst du diesen Satz bitte übersetzen?
native_language_example: Can you please translate this sentence?

meaning: this summer (referring to the current/coming summer).
additional_notes: Accusative time phrase meaning “this summer.” Used to say when something happens or is planned (often about plans for the upcoming summer, but it can also refer to the summer that just happened in context). Common with future intentions: „Ich will/werde diesen Sommer …“
target_language_example: Diesen Sommer fahren wir nach Italien.
native_language_example: This summer we’re going to Italy.

additional_notes: "Angelegenheit" means a matter/issue/affair (often something practical or official). "dieser" is the dative feminine form of "dies-" because it’s used after "bei" (bei + dative). Common pattern: "bei dieser Angelegenheit" = "with/on this matter".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bei dieser Angelegenheit bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Can you please help me with this matter?

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific apple. **dieser** = “this” (masculine, nominative) and **ist** = “is”. Often followed by an adjective (groß, rot, schlecht, etc.).
target_language_example: Dieser Apfel ist süß.
native_language_example: This apple is sweet.

additional_notes: "dieser" is the masculine nominative form of "this" (used with masculine nouns like "der Baum"). Often used while pointing something out ("hier" = "here"). In questions: "Wie alt ist dieser Baum?" = "How old is this tree?"
target_language_example: Schau mal, dieser Baum hat schon keine Blätter mehr.
native_language_example: Look, this tree doesn’t have any leaves anymore.

additional_notes: Used to describe or compare a specific tree. "dieser" means "this" (masculine nominative singular, agreeing with "der Baum"). Often followed by an adjective, age/height information, or a comparison like "so … wie" (as … as) or "… als" (… than).
target_language_example: Dieser Baum ist sehr hoch.
native_language_example: This tree is very tall.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific letter you’re talking about or holding. "dieser" is the masculine nominative form of "dies-" (this), because "Brief" is masculine (der Brief). In other cases it changes: z.B. "Ich habe diesen Brief bekommen" (accusative).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte diesen Brief zur Post bringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take this letter to the post office?

meaning: "this movie/this film" (referring to a specific film).
additional_notes: Used to point out or refer back to a particular movie that’s clear from the context (e.g., the one you’re watching or just mentioned). "Dieser" is the masculine nominative form of "dies-" (this) because "der Film" is masculine. In other cases you’ll see forms like "diesen Film" (accusative) or "diesem Film" (dative).
target_language_example: Dieser Film ist viel besser als der letzte.
native_language_example: This movie is much better than the last one.

additional_notes: "Gegend" means an area or region (often like a neighborhood or part of a city). "dieser Gegend" is the dative form of "diese Gegend" and is commonly used after prepositions like "in" (in this area) and "aus" (from this area), and in expressions like "sich in dieser Gegend auskennen" (to know your way around this area).
target_language_example: Ich wohne schon lange in dieser Gegend.
native_language_example: I've lived in this area for a long time.

meaning: "this dog is" (used to describe a dog).
additional_notes: Used to make statements about a specific dog. "dieser" = "this" (masculine, nominative singular, used with "Hund"); "ist" is the 3rd person singular of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective or description: "Dieser Hund ist groß / nicht zu verkaufen / voller Zecken."
target_language_example: Dieser Hund ist sehr freundlich.
native_language_example: This dog is very friendly.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative pronoun "dieser" (= this) with the masculine noun "Mann". It points to a particular man you mean (often someone present, visible, or already mentioned). In questions you often hear: "Wer ist dieser Mann?". For other cases: "diesem Mann" (to/for this man), "diesen Mann" (this man as the direct object).
target_language_example: Dieser Mann dort ist mein Nachbar.
native_language_example: That man over there is my neighbor.

meaning: 'this man is …' (introducing/identifying a man and describing him).
additional_notes: Used before a noun (often without an article for jobs/nationalities: „Dieser Mann ist Chinese/Anwalt.“), a name („… ist Tom.“), an adjective („… ist lebendig/unfähig.“), or a state/condition („… ist in Panik.“ / „… ist seit fünf Jahren blind.“). „Dieser“ points to a specific man (often one you can see or have mentioned).
target_language_example: Dieser Mann ist mein Nachbar.
native_language_example: This man is my neighbor.

additional_notes: Used to describe or evaluate a specific coat. It’s typically followed by an adjective (e.g., „altmodisch“, „wasserdicht“) or by „zu + adjective“ meaning “too …” (e.g., „zu klein“, „zu teuer“). In „Dieser Mantel ist mir zu klein“, „mir“ (dative) means “for me” = “It’s too small for me.”
target_language_example: Dieser Mantel ist sehr warm.
native_language_example: This coat is very warm.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article "dieser" with the masculine noun "Roman" (a book/novel). "Dieser" changes with case (e.g., "Ich lese diesen Roman" = accusative; "in diesem Roman" = dative). Note: German "Roman" means "novel" (not something "Roman" as in Ancient Rome).
target_language_example: Ich habe diesen Roman letzte Woche gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought this novel last week.

meaning: 'this novel is …' (used to describe or compare a novel).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to give an opinion or a fact about a specific novel. "Dieser" is masculine nominative for "Roman" and points to a particular novel (often "this" one here / the one we’re talking about). Common patterns: "Dieser Roman ist langweilig/interessant/schwer zu verstehen", and comparisons with "… interessanter als …".
target_language_example: Dieser Roman ist spannend, aber manchmal schwer zu verstehen.
native_language_example: This novel is exciting, but sometimes hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used when pointing to a particular sentence (spoken, written, or shown on a page/screen). 'Dieser' is the masculine nominative form of 'this' and matches 'Satz' (masculine). Often appears with extra words like 'hier' to emphasize the exact sentence being referred to.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte diesen Satz ins Englische übersetzen?
native_language_example: Can you please translate this sentence into English?

meaning: "This sentence is …" (introduces a description or judgment about a sentence).
additional_notes: Used when talking about a specific sentence (often in grammar, writing, or tests). After „ist“ you typically add an adjective (falsch, langweilig, verkehrt) or a phrase like an instruction (z. B. „mit einem Fragezeichen abzuschließen“ = “to be ended with a question mark”). „Satz“ can also mean “set” (math/tennis), but here it means “sentence”.
target_language_example: Dieser Satz ist zu lang.
native_language_example: This sentence is too long.

additional_notes: Used to describe or compare a specific desk that’s close by or clearly identified. "dieser" is a demonstrative meaning "this" (masculine nominative singular: der Schreibtisch), and "ist" is the 3rd-person singular form of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective or comparison: "… ist besser/defekt/anders als …".
target_language_example: Dieser Schreibtisch ist zu klein für mein Zimmer.
native_language_example: This desk is too small for my room.

meaning: “of this city/town” (genitive: belonging to this city).
additional_notes: “dieser” is the genitive singular feminine form of “dies-” used with “die Stadt”. It’s used to show possession/association, often after another noun: “der Name dieser Stadt” = “the name of this city”. In everyday speech, Germans also often use “von dieser Stadt” instead of the genitive (“der Name von dieser Stadt”).
target_language_example: Ich kenne die Geschichte dieser Stadt nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t know the history of this city.

meaning: “this street” (in/on this street; along this street).
additional_notes:
This is the form of **diese Straße** (“this street”) used in certain cases:
- **Dative** (often after prepositions or with directions): *in dieser Straße* = “on/in this street”; *Folgen Sie dieser Straße* = “Follow this street.”
- **Genitive** (showing “of this street”): *der Name dieser Straße* = “the name of this street.”
In everyday speech, people sometimes also say *der Name von dieser Straße*.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wo ist die Apotheke in dieser Straße?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the pharmacy on this street?

additional_notes: Used to describe or compare a specific chair that’s close by or clearly identified. “dieser” is the masculine nominative form of “this,” matching “der Stuhl.” It’s usually followed by an adjective (bequem, hässlich, klein) or a phrase like “aus Plastik” or a comparison like “besser als …”.
target_language_example: Dieser Stuhl ist zu unbequem für mich.
native_language_example: This chair is too uncomfortable for me.

additional_notes: Used to describe or compare a specific table. “dieser” is the masculine nominative form of “this” (because “der Tisch” is masculine). “ist” is “is” (3rd person singular of “sein”). Often followed by an adjective (sauber, schwer) or a comparison (so groß wie …).
target_language_example: Dieser Tisch ist zu klein für vier Personen.
native_language_example: This table is too small for four people.

additional_notes: A noun phrase with the demonstrative "dieser" (masculine nominative singular) + adjective "alt" + noun "Mann". Used to point to a specific old man (often someone you can see or have just mentioned). In other cases you’ll see different case forms like "diesem alten Mann" (dative) or "diesen alten Mann" (accusative).
target_language_example: Dieser alte Mann wohnt allein in dem Haus am Fluss.
native_language_example: This old man lives alone in the house by the river.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article "dieses" (neuter nominative/accusative) with the noun "Auto" (neuter). Common when pointing to or talking about a particular car you mean (e.g., in a comparison, description, question, or advice).
target_language_example: Dieses Auto ist sehr sparsam.
native_language_example: This car is very fuel-efficient.

additional_notes: Used to describe a specific car that’s close by or clearly identified. Add an adjective or a phrase after **ist** (e.g., a color, condition, value, or features). Note the verb agrees with **Auto** (singular): **ist**.
target_language_example: Dieses Auto ist sehr sparsam.
native_language_example: This car is very fuel-efficient.

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the neuter form of "this" (for "das Bild"). Used when pointing to or referring to a specific picture/photo/painting. In speech it’s often used with a gesture or context (e.g., on a screen, in a book, in a gallery).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir etwas über dieses Bild erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me something about this picture?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "malen" (to paint). Often appears in the perfect tense as "hat dieses Bild gemalt" (has painted this picture) or in the passive voice as "wurde dieses Bild gemalt" (was this picture painted). In questions, it’s commonly used to ask who created a painting: "Wer hat dieses Bild gemalt?"
target_language_example: Wer hat dieses Bild gemalt?
native_language_example: Who painted this picture?

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article "dieses" (neuter nominative/accusative) to point to a specific book. You’ll also hear it in other cases, e.g. "mit diesem Buch" (with this book) or "in diesem Buch" (in this book).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dieses Buch kaufen.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy this book.

additional_notes: Used to say who owns something. After gehört, the owner is in the dative case: Dieses Buch gehört Paul / der Bibliothek / euch / ihr (= to her). Note: gehört can also mean 'heard' (Ich habe das gehört), so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: Dieses Buch gehört meiner Schwester.
native_language_example: This book belongs to my sister.

additional_notes: Used with the Perfekt tense: (ich/du/er...) habe/hast/hat + dieses Buch + gekauft. "dieses Buch" is accusative (the direct object). In questions with "Wo ...?" (Where?), the verb "gekauft" usually stays at the end: "Wo hast du dieses Buch gekauft?"
target_language_example: Ich habe dieses Buch gestern online gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought this book online yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haben" to form the Perfekt (past) tense: "Ich habe dieses Buch geschrieben." In questions you often hear it as "Hast du dieses Buch geschrieben?" (informal) or "Haben Sie dieses Buch geschrieben?" (formal). "geschrieben" is the past participle of "schreiben" (to write), and "dieses Buch" means "this book" (accusative object).
target_language_example: Ich habe dieses Buch geschrieben.
native_language_example: I wrote this book / I have written this book.

additional_notes: Used to describe what a book (or story, film, article, etc.) is about. The verb is **handeln von + dative**: *Das Buch handelt von einem König.* You can swap *dieses Buch* for another subject: *Der Film handelt von ...*
target_language_example: Dieses Buch handelt von einer Familie, die in die Berge zieht.
native_language_example: This book is about a family that moves to the mountains.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a specific book. "Dieses" means "this" and agrees with the noun: "das Buch" (neuter, nominative) → "dieses Buch". "ist" is the 3rd-person singular form of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective ("interessant"), a noun/pronoun ("meins"), or a phrase like "auf Englisch" / "in einfachem Englisch".
target_language_example: Dieses Buch ist sehr hilfreich für Anfänger.
native_language_example: This book is very helpful for beginners.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with „zu“ used to talk about the action in general (often with verbs like „dauern“ = to take, „lohnen“ = to be worth it, „brauchen“ = to need, or in questions). Pattern: „Es dauert …, [etwas] zu lesen“ = “It takes … to read …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, dieses Buch zu lesen.
native_language_example: I don't have time to read this book.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase with **zu** (“to …”) often used after verbs like **brauchen** (to need/take [time]) and **kosten** (to cost [someone time/effort]): *Wie lange hast du gebraucht, dieses Buch zu schreiben?* = “How long did it take you to write this book?”
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch ein paar Wochen, um dieses Buch zu schreiben.
native_language_example: I still need a few weeks to write this book.

additional_notes: This is the genitive singular of "dieses Buch". It’s used to show possession/relationship, often after another noun: "der Preis dieses Buches" (the price of this book), "die letzte Seite dieses Buches" (the last page of this book). You also see it in set phrases like "mit Hilfe dieses Buches" (with the help of this book).
target_language_example: Die Bedeutung dieses Buches ist heute noch groß.
native_language_example: The importance of this book is still great today.

meaning: 'this document' (a specific document you’re referring to).
additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative article meaning “this” (neuter singular), used with the noun "Dokument" (neuter). It changes with the case: nominative/accusative "dieses Dokument"; dative "diesem Dokument"; genitive "dieses Dokuments". Common in formal contexts (forms, contracts, official papers), often with verbs like "unterschreiben" (sign), "ausdrucken" (print), "abschicken" (send).
target_language_example: Bitte lesen Sie dieses Dokument sorgfältig durch.
native_language_example: Please read this document carefully.

meaning: "this form" (a document you need to fill out).
additional_notes: "Dieses" is the neuter form of "this" and is used with "das Formular" (the form). Very common in offices, applications, registrations, and appointments, often with the verb "(ein) Formular ausfüllen" = "to fill out a form."
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wo soll ich dieses Formular abgeben?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where should I hand in this form?

additional_notes: Common in offices, doctor’s visits, hotels, and government services. Often used in polite requests with "Bitte" or "Würden Sie bitte ...?" and with "müssen" to show that it’s required. "ausfüllen" is separable (ich fülle ... aus).
target_language_example: Könnten Sie bitte dieses Formular ausfüllen und unterschreiben?
native_language_example: Could you please fill out this form and sign it?

meaning: “this building” (a specific building nearby or being talked about).
additional_notes: “Dieses” is the neuter form of “this” (for nouns like “das Gebäude”). Used with a noun to point out or refer to a particular building; often appears with descriptions (alt/neu, hoch) or extra details (mit dem grünen Dach).
target_language_example: Kennen Sie dieses Gebäude?
native_language_example: Do you know this building?

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative article meaning "this" (neuter nominative/accusative), used to point to a particular poem that’s being discussed, shown, or just mentioned. "Gedicht" means "poem". Common with verbs like schreiben/verfassen (to write/compose), übersetzen (to translate), and with questions like "Wer hat dieses Gedicht geschrieben?"
target_language_example: Dieses Gedicht gefällt mir sehr.
native_language_example: I like this poem a lot.

additional_notes: Used in restaurants or when talking about food on a menu. "Gericht" here means a dish (not a court of law). "Dieses" is the demonstrative "this" and changes with gender/case (e.g., "dieses Gericht" because "Gericht" is neuter).
target_language_example: Ich nehme dieses Gericht, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have this dish, please.

meaning: "this house" (a specific house near/known in the context).
additional_notes: "dieses" is the demonstrative word "this" used with a noun. With "Haus" (neuter), it becomes "dieses" in the nominative and accusative (e.g., "Dieses Haus ist groß." / "Ich sehe dieses Haus."). In other cases it changes: "in diesem Haus" (dative), "wegen dieses Hauses" (genitive). Often used to point out or compare one particular house.
target_language_example: Ich mag dieses Haus, aber es ist zu teuer.
native_language_example: I like this house, but it’s too expensive.

meaning: 'this house is …' (used to describe this house).
additional_notes: Use it to start a sentence describing a specific house that is close by, visible, or already known. "Dieses" is the neuter nominative form of "dieser" to match "das Haus". What follows after "ist" is typically an adjective (berühmt, unbewohnt, wunderschön), an age/measure phrase (fünfhundert Jahre alt), or something with "zu" + adjective (zu groß/zu klein).
target_language_example: Dieses Haus ist sehr teuer.
native_language_example: This house is very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific shirt that’s near you, in your hand, or otherwise clear from context. "dieses" is the neuter form of "this" (for nouns like "das Hemd"). In other cases you’ll see: "dieser" (masculine), "diese" (feminine/plural).
target_language_example: Kann ich dieses Hemd anprobieren?
native_language_example: Can I try on this shirt?

additional_notes: Refers to the current calendar year. Often used to talk about plans, experiences, or comparisons within the same year (e.g., weather, travel, how many times something happened). You can place it at the beginning or end of a sentence: „Dieses Jahr fahre ich nach Berlin.“ / „Ich fahre dieses Jahr nach Berlin.“
target_language_example: Dieses Jahr lerne ich mehr Deutsch.
native_language_example: This year I’m learning more German.

additional_notes: Used with the perfect tense: **(jemand) hat/habt/haben dieses Jahr Weihnachtsgeschenke gekauft**. **dieses Jahr** (“this year”) is a time expression and can move around in the sentence; **Weihnachtsgeschenke** means “Christmas presents/gifts”; **gekauft** is the past participle of **kaufen** (“to buy”). Often used when asking **Für wie viele Leute …?** (“For how many people …?”) or **Für wen …?** (“For whom …?”).
target_language_example: Ich habe dieses Jahr Weihnachtsgeschenke für meine Familie gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought Christmas presents for my family this year.

meaning: “this dress” (referring to a specific dress near you or just mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to point out one particular dress. In a sentence, the form changes with case: nominative/accusative: „dieses Kleid“, dative: „diesem Kleid“ (e.g., „mit diesem Kleid“).
target_language_example: Ich mag dieses Kleid sehr.
native_language_example: I like this dress a lot.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative article/pronoun "dieses" (neuter) to point to a specific place you mean (nearby, just mentioned, or obvious from context). "Land" can mean both "land" (territory) and "country"; the exact meaning depends on context. In these examples it appears as nominative or accusative: "Dieses Land gehört mir" (subject) vs. "Ich liebe dieses Land" (object).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dieses Land besser kennenlernen.
native_language_example: I want to get to know this country better.

additional_notes: A noun phrase: "dieses" (this, referring to a specific song) + "Lied" (song). Used when pointing out one particular song in the situation or one that’s already known from context. With "singen" it means "to sing this song"; with "hören" it means "to hear/listen to this song".
target_language_example: Ich mag dieses Lied sehr.
native_language_example: I like this song a lot.

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative "this" for a neuter noun (das Medikament). Used to point to a specific medicine already known from the situation (e.g., a prescription or something the doctor is referring to). In advice/medical instructions you’ll often see it with "nehmen" (to take): "Nehmen Sie dieses Medikament …"
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie dieses Medikament zweimal täglich.
native_language_example: Take this medication twice a day.

meaning: "this medicine will" (used to say what the medicine is expected to do).
additional_notes: Often followed by a verb describing the effect of the medicine (e.g., heilen = cure, lindern = relieve, (den Schmerz) beseitigen/nehmen = remove (the pain), verschwinden lassen = make (pain) go away). It’s a neutral, common way to talk about expected results.
target_language_example: Dieses Medikament wird dir helfen, besser zu schlafen.
native_language_example: This medicine will help you sleep better.

meaning: “this girl” (referring to a specific girl nearby or just mentioned).
additional_notes: “Dieses” is the demonstrative article “this” and changes with case and gender. “Mädchen” is neuter (das Mädchen), so you get forms like: nominative/accusative: dieses Mädchen; dative: diesem Mädchen; genitive: dieses Mädchens. Used to point out or identify a particular girl (“this girl is Maria”) or to refer back to someone in context.
target_language_example: Kennst du dieses Mädchen da drüben?
native_language_example: Do you know that/this girl over there?

meaning: "this problem" (a specific issue being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular problem that’s already known in the conversation or situation. Often appears with case endings depending on its role: nominative/accusative: „dieses Problem“; genitive: „dieses Problems“ (e.g., „die Lösung dieses Problems“); dative: „diesem Problem“ (e.g., „bei diesem Problem“).
target_language_example: Wir müssen dieses Problem heute lösen.
native_language_example: We need to solve this problem today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a statement about a specific problem. "dieses" is the demonstrative "this" (nominative neuter, matching "das Problem"), and "ist" is the 3rd person singular of "sein" (to be). Often followed by an adjective or comparison: "Dieses Problem ist zu schwer" (too difficult), "Dieses Problem ist ebenso ... wie ..." (just as ... as ...).
target_language_example: Dieses Problem ist nicht so schwierig, wie es aussieht.
native_language_example: This problem isn’t as difficult as it looks.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „lösen“ (to solve) plus an object in the accusative: „ein/dieses Problem lösen“. In questions, German often places the verb first: „Kannst du dieses Problem lösen?“ You can swap in another object: „das Rätsel lösen“ (solve the riddle), „den Konflikt lösen“ (resolve the conflict).
target_language_example: Wir müssen dieses Problem schnell lösen.
native_language_example: We need to solve this problem quickly.

additional_notes: "Zu lösen" is the infinitive phrase of "lösen" (to solve), used after adjectives and expressions like "schwierig/schwer", "Mühe haben", "helfen", or with time limits: "Ich gebe dir fünf Minuten, ...". You can replace "dieses Problem" with another noun phrase (e.g., "die Aufgabe", "das Rätsel").
target_language_example: Ich brauche Hilfe, dieses Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: I need help to solve this problem.

meaning: "this program" (a software program, TV show, or a planned program).
additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative "this" for neuter nouns (das Programm). Use it to point to a specific program that’s clear from context: "dieses Programm" (this program) vs. "das Programm" (the program). In the examples, it refers to a particular program you like, pay for, or can use (e.g., for editing videos).
target_language_example: Dieses Programm ist sehr einfach zu benutzen.
native_language_example: This program is very easy to use.

additional_notes: Common in instructions and help texts. The verb is **benutzen** (“to use”). You’ll often see it with different forms of “you”: **du kannst** (informal singular), **Sie können** (formal), **ihr könnt** (informal plural).
target_language_example: Um die Datei zu öffnen, kannst du dieses Programm benutzen.
native_language_example: To open the file, you can use this program.

additional_notes: Used with masculine/neuter nouns in the genitive singular after a genitive article/pronoun like „dieses“. Here the base noun is „der Satz“ (masculine), so it becomes „des/dieses Satzes“ in the genitive. Common in formal/written German, often after nouns like „Übersetzung“, „Subjekt“, or when talking about reading/meaning of a sentence.
target_language_example: Die Bedeutung dieses Satzes ist nicht ganz klar.
native_language_example: The meaning of this sentence isn’t completely clear.

additional_notes: "dieses" is the demonstrative determiner "this" used with a neuter noun in the nominative/accusative singular. Use it to point out a specific game (e.g., the one you’re looking at or talking about).
target_language_example: Magst du dieses Spiel auch?
native_language_example: Do you like this game too?

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative "this" used with neuter nouns like "das T-Shirt". It often points to a specific item you mean or are holding/looking at (e.g., in a shop). In other cases you’ll see: "dieses T-Shirts" (genitive), "diesem T-Shirt" (dative), "dieses T-Shirt" (accusative).
target_language_example: Ich nehme dieses T-Shirt, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll take this T-shirt, please.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific video that’s nearby, being shown, or already known from context. "Dieses" is the demonstrative/article for neuter nouns (das Video) in nominative/accusative singular. Often used when recommending or referring back to something someone should watch (e.g., online).
target_language_example: Kennst du dieses Video schon?
native_language_example: Do you already know this video?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the upcoming (or the current) weekend close to now. It answers questions like "When?" and can be placed early or later in the sentence: "Dieses Wochenende habe ich frei" / "Ich habe dieses Wochenende frei."
target_language_example: Ich kann dieses Wochenende nicht, aber nächste Woche habe ich Zeit.
native_language_example: I can't this weekend, but next week I have time.

meaning: "this word" (the specific word being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular word in a text or conversation. It changes with the noun’s gender/case (e.g., "dieses Wort" for neuter "das Wort"; "dieser Satz" = "this sentence"). Common when asking about spelling, meaning, correctness, or dictionary entries.
target_language_example: Wie schreibt man dieses Wort richtig?
native_language_example: How do you spell this word correctly?

additional_notes: "Dieses" is the demonstrative "this" for a neuter noun (das Wörterbuch). In these examples it’s used when pointing to a specific dictionary or the one already being talked about. Common verbs with it: "benutzen" (to use), "leihen" (to lend), "auskommen ohne" (to manage without).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte dieses Wörterbuch geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me this dictionary?

additional_notes: Used to describe or evaluate a specific dictionary. "dieses" = "this" (neuter nominative), "Wörterbuch" = "dictionary" (neuter), "ist" = "is" (3rd person singular of "sein"). Often followed by an adjective (teuer, nützlich, nutzlos) or a phrase like "für + Akk" (für Schüler) or "von großem Wert".
target_language_example: Dieses Wörterbuch ist sehr hilfreich.
native_language_example: This dictionary is very helpful.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific room that’s near, present, or already known from context. "dieses" is the neuter form of "dies-" (this/that) and matches "das Zimmer". It can appear in different cases depending on the sentence (e.g., nominative: "Dieses Zimmer ist..."; accusative after many verbs/prepositions: "in dieses Zimmer").
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte dieses Zimmer nehmen?
native_language_example: Can I take this room, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe or evaluate a specific room (size, condition, price, availability, etc.). "Dieses" changes with gender/case (e.g., "dieser Raum ist …", "dieses Apartment ist …"). Common patterns: "… zu klein/groß" (= too small/big), "… nicht so groß" (= not that big), "… zu vermieten" (= for rent).
target_language_example: Dieses Zimmer ist sehr hell und ruhig.
native_language_example: This room is very bright and quiet.

additional_notes: "dir" is the dative form of "du" (= to/for you). "dabei" refers to what the other person is doing or trying to do ("with it/with that"). Very common in offers of help and questions: "Soll ich dir dabei helfen?" / "Lass mich dir dabei helfen!"
target_language_example: Ich kann dir dabei helfen, das Formular auszufüllen.
native_language_example: I can help you fill out the form.

meaning: 'you (dative) ... it/that (accusative)'; often "to you that/it" as in "I'll give you that."
additional_notes: Common pronoun combination with verbs like geben/zeigen/sagen/schicken: **dir** = "to you" (informal singular, dative), **das** = "that/it" (neuter, accusative). Typical word order is **verb + dir + das**: *Ich gebe dir das.* (If you stress *das*, you can also say: *Das gebe ich dir.*)
target_language_example: Ich kann dir das morgen schicken.
native_language_example: I can send you that tomorrow.

meaning: 'you (dative) ... it/that (accusative)'; often "to you that/it" as in "I'll give you that."
additional_notes: Common pronoun combination with verbs like geben/zeigen/sagen/schicken: **dir** = "to you" (informal singular, dative), **das** = "that/it" (neuter, accusative). Typical word order is **verb + dir + das**: *Ich gebe dir das.* (If you stress *das*, you can also say: *Das gebe ich dir.*)
target_language_example: Ich kann dir das morgen schicken.
native_language_example: I can send you that tomorrow.

meaning: (in „schau/guck/sieh dir das an“) “look at that / take a look at that.”
additional_notes:
This chunk appears with the separable verb **sich (etwas) ansehen** (“to look at / to watch / to check out”).
- **dir** = “to yourself” (reflexive dative)
- **das** = “that/it” (the thing you’re looking at)
- **an** = the separable prefix (goes to the end)
Common forms: **Schau dir das an! / Guck dir das an! / Sieh dir das an!** (imperative). In questions: **Warum siehst du dir das an?** = “Why are you looking at that?”
target_language_example: Schau dir das mal an, das ist total neu.
native_language_example: Take a look at that—it's totally new.

additional_notes: Used when someone does something to/for you, or when you do something to/for yourself. **dir** is the dative “to/for you” (often reflexive), and **deine** is “your” (feminine/plural, depending on the noun: *deine Tasche* / *deine Zähne*). Common with verbs like *sich die Zähne putzen* (to brush one’s teeth), *sich die Schuhe anziehen* (to put on one’s shoes), and with requests like *Soll ich dir deine … tragen?*
target_language_example: Kannst du dir deine Hände waschen?
native_language_example: Can you wash your hands?

meaning: “to you, then?” (adds surprise/curiosity in a question).
additional_notes: Used in questions with the dative pronoun dir (“to you”) plus the modal particle denn. Here denn doesn’t mean “then” (time); it makes the question sound more interested, surprised, or like you’re asking for an explanation: “So how did that happen?” / “What’s that about?” Often optional, but changes the tone.
target_language_example: Wie ist dir denn das passiert?
native_language_example: How did that happen to you (then)? / So how did that happen to you?

meaning: 'to you the' / 'for yourself the' (dative pronoun + definite article).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression; it’s a common combination of **dir** ("to you" / "for yourself", dative) + **die** ("the" for feminine singular or plural nouns). You’ll often see it when someone does something **for you**: *Ich gebe dir die Erlaubnis* (I give you the permission). With some verbs it can mean doing something **to/for yourself** (an “ethical dative”), especially in commands: *Lies dir die Anleitung durch!* = “Read the instructions (for yourself), carefully.”
target_language_example: Ich erkläre dir die Aufgabe noch einmal.
native_language_example: I’ll explain the task to you again.

meaning: “your hair” (used with verbs like cut/wash/do; literally “to yourself the hair”).
additional_notes: Common pattern with body parts in German: use a dative pronoun (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) + the body part, especially with actions you do to yourself: sich die Haare schneiden/waschen/föhnen, sich die Zähne putzen, etc. Also appears in the idiom „da stehen dir die Haare (zu Berge)“ = “your hair stands on end” (you’re shocked/scared).
target_language_example: Ich muss mir noch schnell die Haare waschen.
native_language_example: I still have to quickly wash my hair.

additional_notes: Used when you want to be honest or direct with someone. Grammar: **jemandem (Dat.) die Wahrheit sagen** = to tell someone the truth; **dir** is dative “to you.” Often appears with modal verbs: **Ich will/möchte/werde dir die Wahrheit sagen** (“I want to / would like to / will tell you the truth”).
target_language_example: Ich muss dir die Wahrheit sagen: Ich habe es vergessen.
native_language_example: I have to tell you the truth: I forgot it.

additional_notes: Common, polite way to introduce a question. The person you ask is in the dative case: mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen. Often used with modal verbs for politeness or necessity: „Darf/Dürfte ich dir eine Frage stellen?“ (May I ask you a question?) or „Ich muss dir eine Frage stellen.“ (I have to ask you a question).
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, darf ich dir eine Frage stellen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask you a question?

additional_notes: Common pattern with verbs that take a recipient in the dative (dir = to you) and a thing in the accusative (einen = a + masculine noun). Often used with nouns like Rat (advice), Antrag (proposal), Gürtel (belt), etc.: „Ich gebe dir einen Rat.“ = “I’m giving you some advice.” Word order can vary (e.g., „Lass mich dir einen Rat geben.“).
target_language_example: Ich kaufe dir einen Kaffee.
native_language_example: I’m buying you a coffee.

additional_notes: Used when 'dir' (informal singular 'to you') is the dative object and 'etwas' is an indefinite direct object: e.g., jemandem etwas geben/erzählen/sagen/vorsingen ('to give/tell/say/sing something to someone'). Word order can vary, but a common pattern is: verb + dir + etwas. Contrast: euch etwas (to you all), Ihnen etwas (formal to you).
target_language_example: Ich gebe dir etwas zu trinken.
native_language_example: I'll give you something to drink.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say or reveal some information to someone. "dir" is the informal dative form of "to you" (to one person you address as du). You can swap in other pronouns/nouns: "Ich muss Ihnen etwas sagen" (formal), "Ich muss meinem Bruder etwas sagen" (my brother).
target_language_example: Kann ich dir etwas sagen?
native_language_example: Can I tell you something?

meaning: to have something to tell you; to want/need to say something to you.
additional_notes: Often used with a form of "haben" (e.g., "Ich habe dir etwas zu sagen") to introduce a message—sometimes something important, serious, or private. "dir" is dative = "to you," and "zu sagen" is an infinitive construction (literally "to say").
target_language_example: Ich habe dir etwas zu sagen, aber nicht hier.
native_language_example: I have something to tell you, but not here.

additional_notes: "dir" is the dative form of "du" (= to you). "gesagt" is the past participle of "sagen" (to say/tell). You’ll often see it with an auxiliary verb, e.g. Perfekt: "Er hat dir gesagt, dass …" (He told you that …), or passive: "Es wurde dir gesagt, dass …" / "Was wurde dir gesagt?" (You were told … / What were you told?).
target_language_example: Hat er dir gesagt, wann er kommt?
native_language_example: Did he tell you when he's coming?

meaning: "(that) I told you" / "(that) I said to you".
additional_notes: This is the Perfekt form of **jemandem etwas sagen** (“to tell someone something”). **dir** is dative = “to you,” and **gesagt habe** = “have said/told.” It often appears in a subordinate clause with **dass** (“that”) or **wie** (“as”), where the conjugated verb (**habe**) goes to the end: **wie/dass ich dir gesagt habe**. In main clauses you’d usually say: **Ich habe es dir gesagt.**
target_language_example: Mach es so, wie ich dir gesagt habe.
native_language_example: Do it the way I told you.

additional_notes: "dir" is the dative form of "du" (informal "you"). Use it when someone receives help: "Ich helfe dir" (I help you). With other people: "Ihnen helfen" (help you, formal), "euch helfen" (help you all, informal), "ihm/ihr helfen" (help him/her). "helfen" is followed by the dative, not the accusative.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich kann dir helfen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can help you.

additional_notes: Common with questions in the Perfekt or simple past to ask about earlier experiences or whether something has happened before (often like English “ever”): e.g., “Habe ich dir schon einmal … gesagt?” = “Have I ever told you …?” and “Ist dir schon einmal aufgefallen …?” = “Have you ever noticed …?” Here, “dir” is the dative pronoun (“to you”), and “schon einmal” emphasizes “at least once before/already once.”
target_language_example: Habe ich dir schon einmal erzählt, dass ich hier gewohnt habe?
native_language_example: Have I ever told you that I used to live here?

additional_notes: Means helping the person you’re speaking to (dir = “you” informal singular, dative). Used with an infinitive clause: e.g., after verbs like versuchen (“try”), or with um … zu (“in order to”) and phrases like in der Lage sein (“to be able”). For formal “you,” use Ihnen zu helfen.
target_language_example: Ich bin hier, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I’m here to help you.

meaning: “(you know / I told you) that …” (adds emphasis: it was already known, expected, or previously said).
additional_notes: This is the modal particle **doch** used before a **dass**-clause. It often expresses mild insistence, reminder, or “See? I knew it!” feelings: **Du weißt doch, dass …** (“You know that …”), **Ich sagte dir doch, dass …** (“I told you that …”), **Ich wusste doch, dass …** (“I knew that …”). In English, **doch** is often not translated with one fixed word; it’s conveyed through tone or phrases like “after all,” “you know,” or “I told you.”
target_language_example: Ich habe dir doch gesagt, dass es heute regnen wird.
native_language_example: I told you that it was going to rain today.

meaning: please (go ahead and) get a chair.
additional_notes: Used in requests/imperatives (often with holen/bringen: „Hol/Brинг … doch bitte einen Stuhl!“). „bitte“ = “please”. „doch“ softens the command and adds a friendly push (“please do / go ahead and”), sometimes with a hint of “come on”. Word order: verb first in imperatives (Hol/Holt/Holen Sie …), then the person (Tom), then „doch bitte“, then the thing (einen Stuhl).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir doch bitte einen Stuhl holen?
native_language_example: Could you please get me a chair?

meaning: “(I) did tell you that …” / “I told you (after all) that …” (often as a reminder or mild reproach).
additional_notes: Used when repeating something you already said, often to emphasize “See, I was right” or “You should have listened.” Typically appears as: „Ich habe dir/Ihnen/euch doch gesagt, dass …“ (with the correct pronoun for the listener). „doch“ adds emphasis and can sound a bit annoyed depending on tone.
target_language_example: Ich habe dir doch gesagt, dass der Zug um acht Uhr abfährt.
native_language_example: I told you (I really did) that the train leaves at eight o’clock.

meaning: 'if only' / 'I wish …' (often expressing regret or longing); sometimes 'just' (emphatic contrast).
additional_notes: Common in wish sentences, especially with „wenn“ + Konjunktiv II / hätte/wäre: „Wenn es doch nur so einfach wäre!“ = “If only it were that easy!” It adds emotional emphasis (regret, frustration, longing). It can also appear in statements like „… aber bist doch nur …“ to stress a contrast: “but you’re just … after all / really only …”.
target_language_example: Wenn ich doch nur mehr Zeit hätte!
native_language_example: If only I had more time!

meaning: “surely not…?” / “after all, not …” (contrary to what you expect).
additional_notes:
Often used with **nicht** to express surprise, doubt, or reassurance that something is probably *not* the case. 
- In **questions**, it’s like “You’re not seriously…?, right?” (the speaker expects/hope the answer is no): *Das unterschreibst du doch nicht?*
- In **statements**, it means “actually/after all, not …” when plans or assumptions change: *Wir können doch nicht nach London fahren.*
target_language_example: Du hast doch nicht vergessen, den Herd auszuschalten?
native_language_example: You didn’t forget to turn off the stove, did you?

meaning: 'if only' / 'I wish …' (often expressing regret or longing); sometimes 'just' (emphatic contrast).
additional_notes: Common in wish sentences, especially with „wenn“ + Konjunktiv II / hätte/wäre: „Wenn es doch nur so einfach wäre!“ = “If only it were that easy!” It adds emotional emphasis (regret, frustration, longing). It can also appear in statements like „… aber bist doch nur …“ to stress a contrast: “but you’re just … after all / really only …”.
target_language_example: Wenn ich doch nur mehr Zeit hätte!
native_language_example: If only I had more time!

additional_notes: Used with comparisons, often in patterns like: "doppelt so + Adjektiv/Adverb + wie" (doppelt so schnell wie … = twice as fast as …) or "doppelt so viele + Nomen + wie" / "doppelt so viel + uncountable + wie" (doppelt so viele Bücher wie … = twice as many books as …).
target_language_example: Heute bin ich doppelt so müde wie gestern.
native_language_example: Today I’m twice as tired as yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to compare sizes: **X ist doppelt so groß wie Y** = X has double the size of Y. You can replace **groß** with other adjectives (e.g., **doppelt so teuer wie** = twice as expensive as). Often used with **fast** (almost) or **mehr als** (more than) for approximate comparisons.
target_language_example: Das neue Sofa ist doppelt so groß wie das alte.
native_language_example: The new sofa is twice as big as the old one.

meaning: twice as high as; double the amount/level of.
additional_notes: Used to compare heights, amounts, prices, weights, salaries, etc. Pattern: **A ist (etwa) doppelt so hoch wie B** (“A is about twice as high as B”). With time comparisons: **doppelt so hoch wie vor … Jahren** (“twice as high as … years ago”). Often interchangeable with **doppelt so teuer wie** when talking about prices.
target_language_example: Die Miete ist jetzt doppelt so hoch wie letztes Jahr.
native_language_example: The rent is now twice as high as last year.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities: someone has/earns/does 2× the amount. Very often followed by a comparison clause with „wie“ (than/as): „doppelt so viel wie ich/du/er…“. You can also compare with „als“ when referring back to a stated amount: „…doppelt so viel, als ich gesagt habe.“
target_language_example: Sie hat doppelt so viel Geld wie ich.
native_language_example: She has twice as much money as I do.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific place and then describe it with a clause: "dort, wo + (subject + verb...)". Common in statements and instructions (e.g., "Leave it where it is"). Also appears as "von dort, wo..." (= "from where..."). Often interchangeable with just "wo"; "dort" adds emphasis: "there, where...".
target_language_example: Stell die Tasche dort, wo du sie gefunden hast.
native_language_example: Put the bag where you found it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone was at a specific place at some time in the past. It’s the past participle phrase of "dort sein" and is typically used with "sein" in the Perfekt: "Ich bin dort gewesen." It can also appear in reported speech/subjunctive: "Sie sagt, sie sei dort gewesen."
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nie dort gewesen.
native_language_example: I’ve never been there.

additional_notes: Infinitive perfect with **sein** (*gewesen sein*) used after verbs like **leugnen** (deny), **bestreiten/abstreiten** (deny), **zugeben** (admit), **sich erinnern** (remember). Often follows statements about whether someone was present somewhere in the past: *Er bestreitet, dort gewesen zu sein.*
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht beweisen, dort gewesen zu sein.
native_language_example: I can't prove that I was there.

meaning: to be there; to be at that place (often: to have arrived).
additional_notes: Used with a specific place that’s understood from context ("dort" = over there/at that place). Often implies arriving or needing to arrive by a certain time: "Ich muss um 8 Uhr dort sein" = "I have to be there at 8." With "schon" it often means "already there".
target_language_example: Wenn wir uns beeilen, können wir in zehn Minuten dort sein.
native_language_example: If we hurry, we can be there in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Uses the direction word **dorthin** (“to there”) with **gegangen** (past of *gehen*, “to go”). Commonly used with **sein** in the Perfekt tense: *Ich bin dorthin gegangen* = “I went there.” It refers to a specific place that’s already known from context.
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern dorthin gegangen, aber niemand war da.
native_language_example: I went there yesterday, but nobody was there.

additional_notes: "dorthin" means "to there" (motion toward a place), often referring to a place already known from context. Use it with verbs of movement like "gehen". Contrast: "dort" = there (location), "dahin" = to there (often more general), "hierhin" = to here.
target_language_example: Ich möchte heute Abend dorthin gehen.
native_language_example: I want to go there tonight.

additional_notes: Used with an object + infinitive: jemanden (nicht) dorthin gehen lassen = (not) allow someone to go there. Often implies permission rather than physically escorting them. Word order: pronoun object usually comes before “dorthin” (e.g., Ich habe ihn dorthin gehen lassen.).
target_language_example: Ich lasse dich nicht allein dorthin gehen.
native_language_example: I’m not letting you go there alone.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase used after other verbs (often with modal/attitude verbs like „zögern“, „versuchen“, „planen“). „dorthin“ means “to there” (movement toward a specific place, usually away from the speaker).
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst, dorthin zu gehen.
native_language_example: I’m afraid to go there.

meaning: “turns/rotates” (literally); also in “es dreht sich um …” = “it’s about …”
additional_notes: Literal use: something spins/turns (often a wheel, the Earth, etc.). Very common fixed pattern: **Es dreht sich um + Akkusativ** / **Es dreht sich nicht um …** = “It’s (not) about …” (topic/what matters). In speech you often see contractions: **um das → ums** (e.g., *nicht ums Geld*). Another idiom: **sich im Grab umdrehen** = “to turn in one’s grave” (be very shocked/disapproving).
target_language_example: In dem Gespräch dreht sich alles um die Arbeit.
native_language_example: In the conversation, everything is about work.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of reflexive "sich umdrehen" = to turn around (your body) to face the other direction, often in reaction to something (a sound, someone calling you). You can add a reason with "als" (when) or "weil" (because): "Sie drehte sich um, als sie...".
target_language_example: Er drehte sich um, weil jemand seinen Namen rief.
native_language_example: He turned around because someone called his name.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of time (duration) or a time difference. Common patterns: „drei Jahre lang“ (for three years), „seit drei Jahren“ (for three years / since three years ago), „vor drei Jahren“ (three years ago), „drei Jahre später“ (three years later), „drei Jahre alt“ (three years old), „drei Jahre jünger/älter“ (three years younger/older).
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit drei Jahren Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for three years.

additional_notes: Used to state the age of people, animals, or things. The number changes: ein Jahr alt, zwei Jahre alt, vier Jahre alt, etc. With a person/thing as the subject, you often use the verb „sein“: „Er ist drei Jahre alt.“ You can also use it with „schon“ to mean “already”: „Der Computer ist schon drei Jahre alt.“
target_language_example: Mein Hund ist drei Jahre alt.
native_language_example: My dog is three years old.

additional_notes: Used to say how long someone lived/stayed in a place. Often appears with verbs like „leben“, „wohnen“, „bleiben“ or „(Zeit) verbringen“: „Ich habe drei Jahre in Boston gelebt.“ You can swap the number and time unit (e.g., „zwei Monate“, „fünf Wochen“) and the place after „in“.
target_language_example: Wir haben drei Jahre in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: We lived in Berlin for three years.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasted. It often comes after the time expression ("drei Jahre") and emphasizes the length of time ("lang" = "for/long"). You can replace the number: "zwei Jahre lang", "fünf Monate lang", etc.
target_language_example: Wir haben drei Jahre lang in Berlin gewohnt.
native_language_example: We lived in Berlin for three years.

meaning: three years (dative plural), used for durations/time periods.
additional_notes: You often see it with prepositions that take the dative: **seit drei Jahren** (“for/since three years”), **vor drei Jahren** (“three years ago”), **in drei Jahren** (“in three years”). Also common in fixed patterns like **zu drei Jahren (Gefängnis) verurteilt** (“sentenced to three years (in prison)”).
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I've been living in Berlin for three years.

meaning: “(for) three years in …” (talking about time spent in a place).
additional_notes: Usually used with a time preposition like **seit** (“for/since”) or **nach** (“after”): **seit drei Jahren in Berlin** = “for three years in Berlin.” With **seit**, German typically uses the present tense: **Er ist seit drei Jahren in Berlin** (“He has been in Berlin for three years”). The noun takes dative plural here: **drei Jahren**.
target_language_example: Ich bin seit drei Jahren in Deutschland.
native_language_example: I’ve been in Germany for three years.

additional_notes: Used to say the number of children (often in a family): „Tom hat drei Kinder.“ In German, number words are usually written as digits in formal writing (3 Kinder), but spelled out is also common. With a specific group, you’ll often see it with a case ending: „der drei Kinder“ (genitive: “of the three children”), „den drei Kindern“ (dative: “to/with the three children”).
target_language_example: Wir haben drei Kinder.
native_language_example: We have three children.

additional_notes: A time duration or amount of time. Often used with words like „dauern“ (to last), „unter“ (for a time: „unter Wasser“), „später“ (later), or with clocks: „Die Uhr geht drei Minuten nach/vor“ = the clock is three minutes slow/fast.
target_language_example: Warte bitte drei Minuten, dann bin ich fertig.
native_language_example: Please wait three minutes, then I’ll be finished.

additional_notes: A time expression used to say how long something lasts or how much time has passed (often with verbs like „dauern“, „vergehen“, „warten“). You can also use it with „seit“ (for a period up to now) or „in“ (within/after a period), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich bin seit drei Monaten in Berlin.
native_language_example: I've been in Berlin for three months.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a period of time spent in a location. The duration (drei Monate) is an accusative time expression, and the place after in is usually dative for location (in Australien, in Boston). Common with verbs like leben/wohnen (live), bleiben (stay), and verbringen (spend).
target_language_example: Wir waren drei Monate in Berlin.
native_language_example: We were in Berlin for three months.

meaning: three months (dative form, used in time expressions).
additional_notes: You usually see **drei Monaten** after prepositions like **in** and **seit** because they require the dative: **in drei Monaten** = “in three months (from now)”; **seit drei Monaten** = “for three months / since three months ago” (up to now). Without a dative preposition, it’s often **drei Monate** (e.g., *Drei Monate sind vergangen.*).
target_language_example: Ich lerne seit drei Monaten Deutsch.
native_language_example: I’ve been learning German for three months.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something takes/lasts, how long you wait, or how long you sleep/study. Often answers the question „Wie lange?“ (How long?). It can also be used with prepositions like „in drei Stunden“ (in three hours) or „unter drei Stunden“ (in under three hours).
target_language_example: Der Flug dauert drei Stunden.
native_language_example: The flight takes three hours.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. Put the time amount before **lang** (e.g., **eine Stunde lang**, **zwei Tage lang**). Often comes after the verb or at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Wir sind drei Stunden lang durch die Stadt gelaufen.
native_language_example: We walked through the city for three hours.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has three male children. After numbers like „drei“, plural nouns are used: „Söhne“ (plural of „Sohn“). In possessive statements you’ll often see it with „haben“: „Er/Ich hat/habe drei Söhne …“.
target_language_example: Meine Nachbarin hat drei Söhne.
native_language_example: My neighbor has three sons.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (how long something lasts) or a time period someone is away/not present. Often answers the question „Wie lange?“ (How long?).
target_language_example: Ich bleibe nur drei Tage in Berlin.
native_language_example: I'm only staying in Berlin for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say how long someone stays somewhere: duration (drei Tage) + location with „in“ + dative (e.g., „in Boston“, „in Australien“, „in Prag“). Often with verbs like „sein“ (to be), „bleiben“ (to stay), or „verbringen“ (to spend).
target_language_example: Wir sind drei Tage in Berlin.
native_language_example: We are in Berlin for three days.

meaning: for three days; three days long.
additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. Often follows the time expression ("drei Tage") and can be used with states ("bewusstlos"), actions ("geholfen"), or events/weather ("geregnet"). Similar pattern: "eine Woche lang", "zwei Stunden lang".
target_language_example: Wir waren drei Tage lang in Berlin.
native_language_example: We were in Berlin for three days.

meaning: 'three days' (in time expressions, usually after a preposition).
additional_notes:
This is the dative plural form of "drei Tage". It commonly appears with time prepositions like: 
- "in drei Tagen" = in three days (from now)
- "seit drei Tagen" = for three days (up to now)
- "vor drei Tagen" = three days ago
- "nach drei Tagen" = after three days
Without a preposition you often see "drei Tage" (e.g., "Ich bleibe drei Tage.").
target_language_example: Ich bin seit drei Tagen krank.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick for three days.

additional_notes: A simple quantity phrase: number + (Tasse/Tassen) + drink in the genitive or without an article. "drei" (three) takes the plural "Tassen". Common in orders (Bitte …) or when talking about how much someone drinks (am Tag, jeden Morgen, mindestens, mehr als).
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern drei Tassen Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like three cups of coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or time period. Often appears with prepositions/expressions like „seit drei Wochen“ (for three weeks, up to now), „die letzten drei Wochen“ (the last three weeks), or without a preposition to show how long something lasted (e.g., „Er war drei Wochen im Krankenhaus.“).
target_language_example: Ich bin seit drei Wochen in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been in Berlin for three weeks.

meaning: “three weeks in (a place)” (duration of a stay).
additional_notes: Used to say how long someone stays/spends somewhere: duration + location. Often with verbs like **bleiben** (to stay) or **(Zeit) verbringen** (to spend time). The duration is typically in the accusative: **drei Wochen**.
target_language_example: Wir waren drei Wochen in Spanien.
native_language_example: We were in Spain for three weeks.

meaning: for three weeks (for a duration of three weeks).
additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. It often comes after the time expression ("drei Wochen lang"), but you can also place it earlier for emphasis ("Drei Wochen lang aß er nichts"). "lang" here means "for (that long)".
target_language_example: Ich habe drei Wochen lang in Berlin gearbeitet.
native_language_example: I worked in Berlin for three weeks.

additional_notes: A specific amount of money. Used with prices (kostete dreihundert Dollar), costs (kostete mich dreihundert Dollar), or pay rates (dreihundert Dollar pro Tag). In German it’s common to write this as a number too: 300 Dollar. "Dollar" is often used in the plural (Dollar) after numbers.
target_language_example: Das hat dreihundert Dollar gekostet.
native_language_example: That cost three hundred dollars.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in one day. Common with routines (e.g., eat, take medicine, go for a walk). You can swap the number: „zweimal am Tag“ (twice a day), „viermal am Tag“ (four times a day).
target_language_example: Ich nehme dieses Medikament dreimal am Tag.
native_language_example: I take this medicine three times a day.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in a typical month. Often comes after the verb (or near the end of the sentence). Similar patterns: „einmal/zweimal/viermal im Monat“. You can add emphasis with words like „mindestens“ (at least) or „ungefähr“ (about).
target_language_example: Ich gehe dreimal im Monat ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a month.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in a typical week. Often follows the verb (e.g., „Ich trainiere dreimal in der Woche.“). Variations: „zweimal …“, „viermal …“, etc.
target_language_example: Ich koche dreimal in der Woche zu Hause.
native_language_example: I cook at home three times a week.

meaning: three times as much money as.
additional_notes: Used to compare amounts of money: X hat/verdient dreimal so viel Geld wie Y (“X has/earns three times as much money as Y”). The person after wie is in the same case as it would be without the comparison (e.g., wie ich/du/ihr/Sie). Often used with haben (to have) or verdienen (to earn).
target_language_example: Sie verdient dreimal so viel Geld wie er.
native_language_example: She earns three times as much money as he does.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities with a multiple. Pattern: "X hat (etwa) dreimal so viele + Pluralnomen + wie Y" = X has (about) three times as many [noun] as Y. "so viele" is the plural form used with countable nouns; you can replace "Bücher" with other plural nouns (z.B. "dreimal so viele Freunde wie").
target_language_example: Wir haben dreimal so viele Gäste wie letztes Jahr.
native_language_example: We have three times as many guests as last year.

additional_notes: Used with “sein” (to be) to state someone’s age: „Ich bin dreizehn Jahre alt.“ Often appears with time words like „damals“ (back then) or „als …“ (when …), and with adverbs like „erst“ (only), „bereits“ (already), „immer noch“ (still).
target_language_example: Als ich dreizehn Jahre alt war, bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: When I was thirteen years old, I moved to Berlin.

additional_notes: A money amount. Used with common verbs like kaufen/bezahlen/ausgeben (to buy/pay/spend) and schulden (to owe). After "für" (for) it often means the price: "für dreißig Dollar" = "for thirty dollars".
target_language_example: Das kostet dreißig Dollar.
native_language_example: That costs thirty dollars.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s age. Pattern: “[Name/Pronoun] ist … Jahre alt” (is … years old). With time words you may also see “wird … Jahre alt” (turns … years old) or “war … Jahre alt” (was … years old).
target_language_example: Ich bin dreißig Jahre alt.
native_language_example: I am thirty years old.

additional_notes: This is the dative plural form of "dreißig Jahre" and commonly appears after prepositions like "seit" (for/since), "vor" (ago), and in age expressions like "im Alter von" or "mit" (at age). Examples: "seit dreißig Jahren" = for thirty years; "vor dreißig Jahren" = thirty years ago; "mit/im Alter von dreißig Jahren" = at age 30.
target_language_example: Sie wohnen seit dreißig Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: They have lived in Berlin for thirty years.

additional_notes:
A time duration. Common with:
- **vor dreißig Minuten** = thirty minutes ago
- **seit dreißig Minuten** = for thirty minutes (up to now)
- **in dreißig Minuten** = in thirty minutes / within thirty minutes
- **ungefähr dreißig Minuten** = about thirty minutes
Also used for delays: **dreißig Minuten Verspätung** = a 30-minute delay.
target_language_example: Wir brauchen ungefähr dreißig Minuten bis zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: We need about thirty minutes to get to the train station.

meaning: “you … that …” (you + a dass-clause, often: “Do you want/say/know that …?”).
additional_notes: This is not a fixed expression, but a very common pattern: a main clause with „du“ (often a question) plus a subordinate clause introduced by „dass“ (= “that”). The comma is required before „dass“. In the „dass“-clause, the verb usually goes to the end: „Willst du, dass er kommt?“ = “Do you want him to come?”
target_language_example: Glaubst du, dass es heute regnet?
native_language_example: Do you think it will rain today?

meaning: "do you think that…?" (asking for someone’s opinion).
additional_notes: This pattern appears in questions like "Findest du, dass …?" or "Meinst du, dass …?" The comma comes before "dass/daß" because it introduces a subordinate clause. Modern spelling is usually "dass" (older: "daß").
target_language_example: Glaubst du, dass er morgen kommt?
native_language_example: Do you think he’s coming tomorrow?

meaning: “you … where …” — used to introduce an indirect question with *wo* (“where”).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom; it’s a common sentence pattern: a main clause with *du* (“you”) + a comma, then a *wo*-clause that gives the information being asked/known. Often used after verbs like *wissen* (to know): *Wusstest du, wo …?* = “Did you know where …?” In indirect questions, German keeps *wo* (not *ob*) and sends the verb to the end of the *wo*-clause.
target_language_example: Wusstest du, wo das Restaurant ist?
native_language_example: Did you know where the restaurant is?

additional_notes: Used with "du" to talk to one person you address informally (friends, family, children). It’s the 2nd person singular form of "sein" (to be). For formal "you are" to one person, use "Sie sind".
target_language_example: Du bist heute sehr müde.
native_language_example: You are very tired today.

additional_notes: Used to label/identify someone with a noun in the nominative (a compliment, accusation, role, etc.): *Du bist der Beste / der Grund / der Lügner.* The article must match the noun’s gender and number: **du bist der** (masc.), **du bist die** (fem.), **du bist das** (neut.), **ihr seid die** (plural). Often sounds emphatic or dramatic depending on the noun.
target_language_example: Du bist der Beste in unserem Team.
native_language_example: You’re the best on our team.

meaning: "you are (surely/...right?)" / "but you are..." (seeking confirmation or emphasizing what the speaker believes).
additional_notes: Used when the speaker thinks something is obvious or already known and wants confirmation or stresses it. Often sounds like: “Come on, you are…”, “You *are* … though/after all”. In questions it can mean “You’re not… are you?” or “Surely you’re not…”. The particle "doch" adds this expectation/contrast; it’s hard to translate with one fixed English word.
target_language_example: Du bist doch mein Nachbar, oder?
native_language_example: You’re my neighbor, right?

additional_notes: Common in spoken German to strongly emphasize what you say next (a compliment or an insult): "Du bist echt toll." / "Du bist echt nervig." Often carries an emotional tone and can also be sarcastic depending on context and intonation.
target_language_example: Du bist echt mutig, das so zu sagen.
native_language_example: You’re really brave to say that.

meaning: "you are a" (addressing one person; with a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone with a noun in the nominative case: "Du bist ein Feigling." With feminine nouns, use "du bist eine …" (e.g., "Du bist eine Heldin."). If there’s an adjective before the noun, it usually takes the ending -er after "ein" in nominative masculine: "Du bist ein guter Freund." It can be positive ("ein Schatz") or insulting ("ein Idiot").
target_language_example: Du bist ein guter Freund.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

meaning: “you are a good …” (talking about a man/masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone by saying they are a good friend/driver/etc. It normally needs a noun after it: „Du bist ein guter Freund.“ The adjective ending „-er“ is because it’s masculine nominative with „ein“. For feminine: „Du bist eine gute …“ (e.g., „eine gute Freundin“). For plural: „Ihr seid gute …“
target_language_example: Du bist ein guter Lehrer.
native_language_example: You’re a good teacher.

meaning: “you are a …” (to a woman/girl, with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the informal “du” and introduces a feminine predicate noun (often an insult or a compliment): Du bist eine Nervensäge. / Du bist eine Wucht! For masculine nouns, you’d say “Du bist ein …”. For a polite/formal address, use “Sie sind ein/e …”.
target_language_example: Du bist eine gute Freundin.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

meaning: "you are not a" (used before a masculine or neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to negate a noun with the verb "sein" (to be): "Du bist kein + Nomen". "Kein" is for masculine/neuter nouns in the nominative singular (e.g., "kein Student", "kein Genie"). For feminine nouns use "keine" ("Du bist keine Lehrerin"), and for plural use "keine" ("Ihr seid keine Studenten"). Often corresponds to English "not a/an" rather than the literal-sounding "no".
target_language_example: Du bist kein Arzt, oder?
native_language_example: You're not a doctor, are you?

additional_notes: Used with the informal singular pronoun "du" to say someone belongs to you in a relationship sense (e.g., "mein Schatz") or, more commonly, to state a connection/role: "mein Nachbar" (my neighbor), "mein Kind" (my child), "mein Stuntdouble" (my stunt double). "Mein" must match the noun’s gender/case, so it may change (e.g., "du bist meine Freundin", "du bist mein Bruder").
target_language_example: Du bist mein Freund.
native_language_example: You are my friend.

additional_notes: Used to negate a statement about “you” (singular, informal). Put “nicht” after the verb “bist” and typically before what is being negated (e.g., an adjective or noun phrase): “Du bist nicht müde.” / “Du bist nicht der Erste …”. For formal “you,” use “Sie sind nicht …”.
target_language_example: Du bist nicht allein.
native_language_example: You are not alone.

meaning: 'you are so …' (used to emphasize a description).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective ("Du bist so hübsch." = “You’re so pretty.”) or before "ein/eine" + noun ("Du bist so ein Lügner!" = “You’re such a liar!”). Often expresses strong emotion (praise, surprise, annoyance). Can also be said as a question to show disbelief or surprise: "Du bist so schlau?" = “You’re that smart?” / “You’re so smart?”
target_language_example: Du bist so nett, dass du mir hilfst.
native_language_example: You’re so nice to help me.

additional_notes: Use **zu** before an adjective/adverb to say someone has an excessive amount of a quality: **Du bist zu langsam / zu aggressiv / zu dünn.** It often sounds critical or rude, so use carefully (you can soften it with words like **ein bisschen**).
target_language_example: Du bist zu müde, geh lieber ins Bett.
native_language_example: You’re too tired; you’d better go to bed.
