additional_notes: Common start of a sentence in the Perfekt (present perfect): **er hat** + past participle (often later in the sentence). **seinen** is the possessive "his" used with a **masculine accusative** noun (e.g., *seinen Fehler, seinen Kopf, seinen Traum, seinen Wagen*). For a neuter noun it’s also **sein** in accusative (*sein Auto*), and for feminine/plural it changes (*seine Tasche / seine Freunde*).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: He lost his key.

meaning: “he has … himself” — used to form the present perfect with reflexive verbs (“he …”).
additional_notes: This is the Perfekt (present perfect) for a reflexive verb: **er hat** + **sich** + past participle/verb phrase. In English you usually don’t translate **sich** as “himself” unless it’s truly reflexive (e.g., **Er hat sich den Arm gebrochen.** = “He broke his arm.”). Word order often puts **sich** right after **hat**: **Er hat sich beklagt / Sorgen gemacht / umgebracht.**
target_language_example: Er hat sich heute bei der Arbeit verletzt.
native_language_example: He got injured at work today.

meaning: “he has her/them” (often the start of a past/perfect sentence: “he … her/them”).
additional_notes: Common pattern in the Perfekt (conversational past): **Er hat sie + past participle** (e.g., *geliebt, bedroht, verachtet*). **sie** can mean **“her”** (singular, feminine) or **“them”** (plural)—context tells you which. By itself, **er hat sie** sounds incomplete; it usually needs the main verb at the end.
target_language_example: Er hat sie gestern angerufen.
native_language_example: He called her/them yesterday.

additional_notes: Common sentence start in the German Perfekt (spoken past). Pattern: "Er hat uns" + past participle / infinitive phrase. Examples: "Er hat uns gefunden" = he found us; "Er hat uns geholfen" = he helped us (note: with "helfen", "uns" is dative = to us); "Er hat uns arbeiten lassen" = he made/let us work ("lassen" + infinitive). Not the same as English "he has us" (possession).
target_language_example: Er hat uns gestern angerufen.
native_language_example: He called us yesterday.

meaning: “he has” / “he has (done)” (3rd person singular of haben).
additional_notes: Used with **haben** for (1) **possession**: *Er hat ein Auto.* (“He has a car.”) and (2) the **Perfekt (present perfect / past)** with a past participle: *Er hat Gemüse gekauft.* (“He bought vegetables.”). In many contexts, German **Perfekt** is the normal way to talk about the past in everyday speech. Note: **hat** is pronounced like “hutt” and is unrelated to the English noun “hat.”
target_language_example: Er hat heute lange gearbeitet.
native_language_example: He worked for a long time today.

meaning: he is afraid of (…); he fears (…).
additional_notes: Used to say that a male person is scared of something or someone. Pattern: „jemand hat Angst vor + Dativ“ (e.g., „vor dem Hund“, „vor Katzen“). With feminine nouns: „vor der …“; plural often has no article: „vor Katzen“.
target_language_example: Er hat Angst vor der Spinne.
native_language_example: He is afraid of the spider.

meaning: 'he has a' / 'he has (done) a …' (with a noun, often in the perfect past).
additional_notes: Often used with a noun object (ein Fenster, ein Ticket, ein Verbrechen, ein Kind) and a past participle to talk about something completed: "Er hat ein Fenster kaputtgemacht" = "He broke a window." The verb "hat" is the auxiliary for the perfect tense, and "ein" is the indefinite article for a masculine/neuter noun. If the noun is feminine, use "eine" ("Er hat eine Wohnung gemietet").
target_language_example: Er hat ein neues Handy gekauft.
native_language_example: He bought a new phone.

meaning: “he has a …” (with a feminine noun), or “he has one.”
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun in the accusative (direct object): *Er hat eine Kamera / eine kurze Antwort / eine Klasse.* It can also mean “he has one (of them)” when the noun is understood from context. In speaking, **hat er** can sound like *hatter*, but it’s still written separately: *Er hat eine …*
target_language_example: Er hat eine neue Jacke gekauft.
native_language_example: He bought a new jacket.

meaning: "he has a" / "he ... a" (with a masculine object in the accusative).
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence in the Perfekt (present perfect): **Er hat + Partizip II**. **einen** is the accusative form of **ein** for masculine nouns (e.g., *einen Big Mac, einen Fahrschein, einen Tiger, einen Fotoapparat*). In English, you usually translate the whole structure as simple past ("He ate/bought/got/found...") depending on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Er hat einen Termin gemacht.
native_language_example: He made an appointment.

meaning: “he has no / he doesn’t have any …” (used before a neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy (er) does not have something. The negative article **kein** changes like *ein* depending on the noun: **kein** (neuter: *kein Geld*), **keine** (feminine/plural: *keine Zeit / keine Freunde*), **keinen** (masculine accusative: *keinen Job*). Often followed by a noun, sometimes with an extra phrase like **um … zu …** (“in order to …”) or a relative clause (**…, in dem …**).
target_language_example: Er hat kein Auto, also fährt er mit dem Bus.
native_language_example: He doesn’t have a car, so he takes the bus.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy doesn’t have something. "keine" is the negation used with nouns ("no / not any") and is used here with feminine singular nouns (e.g., keine Kraft, keine Fantasie) or plural nouns (e.g., keine Geschwister, keine Einwände). With masculine/neuter singular nouns you use "keinen/kein" instead (e.g., er hat keinen Bruder; er hat kein Geld).
target_language_example: Er hat keine Zeit für ein Treffen.
native_language_example: He has no time to meet.

meaning: “he has no…” / “he doesn’t have any…” (with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a noun after "haben" to say someone doesn’t have something. "keinen" is the accusative form for masculine nouns (e.g., keinen Freund, keinen Hut, keinen Sinn). With other genders it changes: "er hat keine Zeit" (feminine), "er hat kein Geld" (neuter/plural as a mass noun), "er hat keine Freunde" (plural).
target_language_example: Er hat keinen Schlüssel dabei.
native_language_example: He doesn’t have a key with him.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy possesses or has a large number of things (or abstract things like talents or debts). It’s typically followed by a plural noun: „Er hat viele Bilder.“ = “He has many pictures.” (With an uncountable noun, you’d usually use „viel“ instead of „viele“.)
target_language_example: Er hat viele Freunde in Berlin.
native_language_example: He has many friends in Berlin.

additional_notes: Uses *hatte* (Präteritum/simple past), common in written German and storytelling to describe past states/possession. In speech you also often hear *Er hat ... gehabt* (perfect), especially in southern Germany/Austria/Switzerland. In phrases like *Er hatte doch recht*, *doch* adds emphasis: “he actually/after all was right.”
target_language_example: Er hatte keine Zeit, deshalb blieb er zu Hause.
native_language_example: He had no time, so he stayed at home.

additional_notes: "Angst haben" means "to be afraid." "Er hatte Angst" is past tense (Präteritum) and is common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech you often hear "Er hat Angst" (present/perfect). It’s frequently followed by a clause with "zu" + infinitive (e.g., "allein dorthin zu gehen") or by "vor" + dative to say what someone is afraid of (e.g., "Er hatte Angst vor Hunden").
target_language_example: Er hatte Angst, im Dunkeln nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: He was afraid to walk home in the dark.

meaning: "he had a" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is the simple past (Präteritum) of "er hat" ("he has"). It’s followed by a feminine noun in the accusative case: "Er hatte eine + [feminine noun]". In context, it can be literal (e.g., having/holding something) or part of fixed expressions like "eine Operation haben" (= to have/undergo an operation) or "eine Fahne haben" (= to have a hangover / smell of alcohol).
target_language_example: Er hatte eine Idee.
native_language_example: He had an idea.

additional_notes: "Er" means "he" and "isst" is the 3rd-person singular present of "essen" (to eat). Used to say what a man/boy eats or when/where he eats; it can also appear before a subordinate clause (e.g., "Er isst, bevor...").
target_language_example: Er isst heute keine Süßigkeiten.
native_language_example: He isn't eating any sweets today.

additional_notes: Present tense of "sein" (to be) with "er" (he). Used to describe identity (Er ist Lehrer.), qualities (Er ist müde.), and location (Er ist in der Küche.). "Er ist" is also used as the auxiliary verb in the Perfekt with some verbs (especially movement/change of state), e.g. "Er ist nach London gekommen."
target_language_example: Er ist heute krank.
native_language_example: He is sick today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has reached the necessary age/maturity to do something. The verb after "um" goes in the infinitive (e.g., "um allein zu reisen"). You can change the subject: "ich bin alt genug, um…", "sie ist alt genug, um…", etc.
target_language_example: Er ist alt genug, um allein zu wohnen.
native_language_example: He is old enough to live alone.

additional_notes: Used with **bei + dative** to say where someone is (often at someone’s place): **Er ist bei seinen Freunden.** It can also describe a situation/condition: **bei schlechter Gesundheit** = “in poor health.” In religious contexts, **Er ist bei Gott** is a common euphemism meaning “He is with God” (i.e., he has died).
target_language_example: Er ist bei seiner Schwester zu Besuch.
native_language_example: He is visiting his sister (at his sister’s place).

meaning: "he is the" (used to identify or describe a male person).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine noun or a masculine adjective used like a noun: "Er ist der Sohn ..." (the son), "Er ist der Auserwählte" (the chosen one). Very common with superlatives/comparisons: "Er ist der Größere (von beiden)" (the bigger one), "Er ist der Jüngste" (the youngest). If the person is female or plural, you use different forms: "sie ist die", "es ist das", "sie sind die".
target_language_example: Er ist der beste Spieler im Team.
native_language_example: He is the best player on the team.

meaning: "he is a" (used to say what someone is: a person, type, nationality, etc.).
additional_notes: Use "Er ist ein" before a masculine noun phrase in the nominative (often a job/role, type of person, or nationality): "Er ist ein Dieb." With feminine nouns use "Er ist eine ..." ("Er ist eine Lehrerin" is unlikely because of gender; more typical: "Er ist ein Lehrer"). With plural: "Er ist (kein) ..." (no article) or "Er ist ein/einer von den ..." depending on meaning. Adjectives go between the article and noun: "Er ist ein aggressiver Mensch."
target_language_example: Er ist ein guter Freund.
native_language_example: He is a good friend.

additional_notes: Often used as the start of a description of someone’s character or qualities, followed by an add-on like: „ein Mann der …“ (a man of …, e.g. „der Tat“ = action), „ein Mann mit …“ (a man with …), „ein Mann von …“ (a man of …), or a relative clause: „ein Mann, mit dem man rechnen muss“ (someone you have to take seriously / reckon with).
target_language_example: Er ist ein Mann mit großen Plänen.
native_language_example: He is a man with big plans.

meaning: “he is a good …” (before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used as a starter phrase with a masculine noun in the nominative: **Er ist ein guter + Nomen** (e.g., *Esser, Koch, Zuhörer*). **guter** is the adjective ending for **ein guter** + masculine noun. For feminine nouns, you’d say **Sie ist eine gute …**; for plural: **Sie sind gute …**.
target_language_example: Er ist ein guter Lehrer.
native_language_example: He is a good teacher.

meaning: "he is a very ..." (used before an adjective + noun).
additional_notes: This is the start of a common description pattern: "Er ist ein sehr + adjective + noun" (e.g., Mann/Junge). After "ein" in the nominative masculine, the adjective usually ends in -er: "ein sehr netter Mann", "ein sehr kluger Junge". You can swap in many adjectives (attraktiv, gefährlich, intelligent, nett, freundlich, etc.).
target_language_example: Er ist ein sehr netter Mann.
native_language_example: He is a very nice man.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things when they are not equal. German uses **als** (not *wie*) for “than” in comparisons: **größer als** = “bigger/taller than”. You can replace **er** with other subjects (sie/du/ich) and **größer** with other comparative adjectives (z.B. *schneller als*, *älter als*).
target_language_example: Er ist größer als ich.
native_language_example: He is taller than me.

additional_notes: "im" is a contraction of "in dem" and is used with masculine/neuter nouns in the dative case. It often means being located in something ("im See" = in the lake) or being in a state/phase ("im Alpha-Schlaf" = in alpha sleep; "im ersten Studienjahr" = in the first year of studies).
target_language_example: Er ist im Büro.
native_language_example: He is in the office.

additional_notes: Used to describe a habitual, constant, or repeated situation about a man/boy. It’s commonly followed by an adjective ("Er ist immer ehrlich."), a state ("beschäftigt"), or a phrase with a preposition ("an meiner Seite", "mit ... unterwegs"). For other people: "sie ist immer" (she), "du bist immer" (you), "ich bin immer" (I).
target_language_example: Er ist immer pünktlich.
native_language_example: He is always on time.

meaning: 'he is in …' / 'he is at …' (location); also in fixed phrases like 'in jemanden verknallt sein' = 'to have a crush on someone'.
additional_notes: Used with a place or country to say where he is ("Er ist in Tokyo.") or where something happened: "in Australien groß geworden" = grew up in Australia; "in Osaka geboren" = born in Osaka. With feelings it can appear in set expressions: "in dieses Mädchen verknallt" means he has a crush on this girl (not a physical location).
target_language_example: Er ist in Berlin, aber er ist in niemanden verknallt.
native_language_example: He is in Berlin, but he doesn't have a crush on anyone.

additional_notes: Used to say that a male person does not belong to a category (nationality, job, role, type). "kein" is the negative form of "ein" (a/an) and agrees with the noun’s gender/case (e.g., "Er ist kein Student"; with feminine nouns: "Sie ist keine Lehrerin"). Often contrasted with "sondern" to correct a statement: "Er ist kein X, sondern Y."
target_language_example: Er ist kein Arzt, sondern Krankenpfleger.
native_language_example: He isn't a doctor; he's a nurse.

meaning: "he is my" (used to say who a male person is to you, or what he is for you).
additional_notes: Use this to introduce or identify a man/boy by his relationship/role: a family member ("Er ist mein Ehemann."), a work connection ("Er ist mein Kollege."), or someone you’re dating/into ("Er ist mein Typ!" is more colloquial). It’s followed by a masculine noun in the nominative case. For feminine nouns, you need "Sie ist meine …"; for neuter nouns, "Er ist mein …" is still possible if you’re talking about a male person and the noun is neuter (e.g., "Er ist mein Kind.").
target_language_example: Er ist mein Bruder.
native_language_example: He is my brother.

meaning: “he is with … / he is occupied with … / he is (at age) … / he is certainly …” (using **mit**).
additional_notes:
**mit** is a very common preposition meaning “with” and it takes the **dative** case.

Common patterns you see with **Er ist mit …**:
- **mit + person/thing** = “with” (together with): *Er ist mit Maria nach Boston gefahren.*
- **mit + activity/task** = “busy/occupied with”: *Er ist mit seiner Arbeit beschäftigt.* / *Er ist mit Englischlernen beschäftigt.*
- **mit Sicherheit** = “certainly/for sure” (fixed expression; not literal “with security” in English).
- **mit + age/number** = “at (the age of) …”: *Er ist mit zwölf von Zuhause weggelaufen.*
target_language_example: Er ist mit dem Bericht beschäftigt.
native_language_example: He is busy with the report.

meaning: "he is with his" / "he is using his" (and often: "he is satisfied with his").
additional_notes: "mit seinem" means "with his" (dative, masculine/neuter). It’s used (1) for being together with someone/thing: "Er ist mit seinem Freund." (2) for the means you use, especially transport: "Er ist mit seinem Fahrrad gefahren" = "He went by bike." (3) with "zufrieden": "Er ist mit seinem Auto zufrieden" = "He is satisfied with his car."
target_language_example: Er ist mit seinem neuen Handy sehr zufrieden.
native_language_example: He is very satisfied with his new phone.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not true about a male person ("er"). "nicht" usually comes after the verb "ist" to negate it: "Er ist nicht ..." It can be used with nouns (Er ist nicht mein Sohn.), adjectives (Er ist nicht freundlich.), or phrases like "nicht ... als" in comparisons ("not less ... than"). In yes/no questions, the word order stays the same and you raise your voice at the end: "Er ist nicht da?"
target_language_example: Er ist nicht zu Hause.
native_language_example: He is not at home.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective, noun, or role to say that something is no longer true about him (a past state has ended). In German, this is built with **nicht mehr** (“no longer / not anymore”) after the verb: *Er ist nicht mehr jung.* It can also mean he’s not the same person as before: *Er ist nicht mehr der Alte.*
target_language_example: Seit dem Unfall ist er nicht mehr derselbe.
native_language_example: Since the accident, he hasn’t been the same.

additional_notes: Used with "schon" to say something has happened earlier than expected or by now ("already"). Depending on context, "schon" can also add emphasis like "indeed" or "quite" (e.g., "Er ist schon ein ..." = "He really is / He’s quite a ..."). Often followed by a place/state/time phrase: "da/oben", or "seit ...".
target_language_example: Er ist schon zu Hause.
native_language_example: He is already at home.

additional_notes: Used to describe a male person with an adjective: "Er ist sehr + Adjektiv" (e.g., freundlich, vorsichtig, mutig). It's a common sentence starter when talking about someone's personality or behavior.
target_language_example: Er ist sehr freundlich zu allen.
native_language_example: He is very friendly to everyone.

er ist zwei Jahre älter als

target_language_multi_word_term: er ist zwei Jahre älter als
additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Structure: [Person/subject] + ist + [number] + Jahr(e) + älter + als + [person/pronoun]. With 1 you usually say "ein Jahr"; with 2+ you use "Jahre". Pronouns can change: als ich/du/Sie/ihr.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist drei Jahre älter als ich.
native_language_example: My sister is three years older than me.

additional_notes: *Kam* is the **simple past (Präteritum)** of *kommen* (“to come”). It’s common in **writing and storytelling**; in everyday spoken German you often hear **"er ist gekommen"** (present perfect) instead. You can add details like **position** (*als Erster* = “first”), **state** (*vorbereitet* = “prepared”), or **destination** (*nach Hause* = “home”).
target_language_example: Er kam gestern Abend spät nach Hause.
native_language_example: He came home late last night.

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb **können** in the 3rd person singular (**er kann**). It’s followed by another verb in the **infinitive**, which usually goes to the **end of the clause**: *Er kann schwimmen.* It can express ability/skill or possibility (depending on context).
target_language_example: Er kann heute nicht kommen.
native_language_example: He can’t come today.

additional_notes: "kaufte" is the Präteritum (simple past) form of "kaufen". It’s common in writing, stories, and news; in everyday conversation people often use the perfect tense instead: "Er hat ... gekauft." You can add what was bought (accusative): "Er kaufte ein Brot." With an extra person, it often uses dative + accusative: "Er kaufte mir (dative) ein Wörterbuch (accusative)."
target_language_example: Er kaufte seiner Mutter Blumen.
native_language_example: He bought his mother flowers.

additional_notes: From the verb **kennen** (to know/be familiar with people, places, things, or skills). Often used for familiarity or experience (e.g., a city, languages, dances). Compare: **kennen** = know (be acquainted with), **wissen** = know a fact/information. You may also see **Er kennt sich … aus** = “He knows his way around / he knows a lot about …”.
target_language_example: Er kennt meine Schwester schon lange.
native_language_example: He has known my sister for a long time.

additional_notes: Present tense of **kommen** with **er** (“he”). Often used for habits/frequency (**Er kommt oft…**) or scheduled/expected arrival (**Er kommt später…**). In German, **kommen** can mean “come” or “arrive,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Er kommt morgen um acht Uhr.
native_language_example: He’s coming tomorrow at eight o’clock.

meaning: 'I think he's from …' / 'He comes from …, I think.'
additional_notes: Used to say someone is from a place, while adding uncertainty with the parenthetical phrase "denke ich" (= "I think"). In German, "denke ich" can be placed in the middle of the sentence with commas. Often followed by a country/city: "… aus China/Italien/Berlin".
target_language_example: Er kommt, denke ich, aus Spanien.
native_language_example: I think he's from Spain.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s origin (country/city/region) or background (e.g., a family or a town). Often followed by a place name or a noun phrase in the dative with "aus" (e.g., aus Frankreich, aus einer großen Familie). You can change the subject: "Ich komme aus …", "Sie kommt aus …", "Wir kommen aus …".
target_language_example: Er kommt aus Kanada, aber jetzt wohnt er in Berlin.
native_language_example: He comes from Canada, but he lives in Berlin now.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of the modal verb "können". Used for ability, possibility, or permission in the past. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Er konnte das Buch lesen." It also appears in set expressions like "nicht leiden können" = "can’t stand".
target_language_example: Er konnte gestern nicht kommen, weil er arbeiten musste.
native_language_example: He couldn’t come yesterday because he had to work.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of the modal verb "können". Used for ability, possibility, or permission in the past. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Er konnte das Buch lesen." It also appears in set expressions like "nicht leiden können" = "can’t stand".
target_language_example: Er konnte gestern nicht kommen, weil er arbeiten musste.
native_language_example: He couldn’t come yesterday because he had to work.

meaning: "he was lying on the" (on top of something).
additional_notes: Used to describe where a man/boy was lying. "liegen" (lag, hat gelegen) is the verb “to lie (down)”. With "auf" meaning location (not movement), German uses dative: "auf dem" (masculine/neuter) = often shortened to "auf'm" in speech; for feminine it’s "auf der". If there is movement onto something, German uses accusative: "Er legte sich auf das Bett" (He lay down onto the bed).
target_language_example: Er lag auf dem Teppich und schlief.
native_language_example: He was lying on the carpet and sleeping.

meaning: 'he lives' (where he lives / he is alive).
additional_notes: Most often used to say where someone lives (their place of residence), especially with "wo" (where): "wo er lebt". Depending on context, it can also mean "he is alive" (e.g., after an accident). In the example "Er lebt jwd.", "jwd" is informal slang (Berlin) for "janz weit draußen" = far out / in the middle of nowhere.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht genau, wo er lebt.
native_language_example: I don't know exactly where he lives.

meaning: “he lives in” (he resides in a place).
additional_notes: Used to say where a man/boy lives. The verb is **leben** (“to live”). It’s often interchangeable with **er wohnt in** (“he lives/resides in”), with **wohnen** being more common for addresses. **in** is followed by the dative case for location (e.g., **in Berlin**, **in der Schweiz**). Cities usually have no article; some regions/countries do (e.g., **in den USA**, **in der Türkei**).
target_language_example: Er lebt in Berlin.
native_language_example: He lives in Berlin.

additional_notes:
**legte** is the simple past (Präteritum) of **legen** (“to put/lay/place”). It often appears with separable prefixes or prepositions that change the meaning:
- **er legte auf** = “he hung up (the phone)”
- **er legte seinen Arm um sie** = “he put his arm around her”.
You can swap **er** for another subject (ich legte, sie legte, etc.).
target_language_example: Er legte das Buch auf den Tisch.
native_language_example: He put the book on the table.

additional_notes: "Er" = "he". "liebt" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "lieben" (to love). It’s used with an accusative object: "Er liebt Kaffee / dich / sie." Depending on context, it can mean romantic love ("Er liebt dich") or strong liking ("Er liebt Kaffee").
target_language_example: Er liebt seine Familie sehr.
native_language_example: He loves his family very much.

meaning: "he let" / "he left" / "he had (something) done" (simple past of *lassen*).
additional_notes: *Lassen* is a very common verb with several meanings. **Er ließ + object + infinitive** often means “he had (someone) do something” (e.g., *Er ließ einen Arzt rufen* = he had a doctor called). **Er ließ + object** can mean “he let (something happen)” or “he dropped” (*Er ließ eine Vase fallen*). It can also mean “he left (something behind/for someone)” (*Er ließ mir nur ein paar Bissen übrig*). With **jemanden/nicht in die Nähe lassen** it means “allow/permit.” With a reflexive pronoun (**er ließ sich …**) it often means “he let himself … / he sank/settled …” (*Er ließ sich in den Sessel sinken*). Some fixed uses are slang, e.g. *einen fahren lassen* = “to fart,” but *er ließ* itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Er ließ mich nicht rein.
native_language_example: He wouldn’t let me in.

meaning: “he left his … / he let his … / he had his … (done)” (depending on context).
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence with **lassen** (past: **ließ**). With **lassen**, German often expresses: (1) **leave** something somewhere: *Er ließ seine Sonnenbrille im Auto.* (2) **let/allow**: *Er ließ seine Hunde von der Leine.* (3) **have something done (by someone else)**: *Er ließ seine Klarinette stimmen.* / *Er ließ seine Sekretärin den Bericht tippen.* The object after **seine** changes with gender/number (e.g., *sein/seine/seinen*).
target_language_example: Er ließ seine Haare schneiden.
native_language_example: He had his hair cut.

meaning: 'he does' / 'he makes' (often: 'he is doing ...', 'he is making ...').
additional_notes: From the verb "machen". Used with many common expressions where English might use different verbs (e.g., "Fehler machen" = make a mistake; "Fortschritte machen" = make progress; "Hausaufgaben machen" = do homework; "Spaß machen" = joke / have fun; "Eindruck machen" = make an impression; "jemandem das Leben zur Hölle machen" = make someone’s life hell). Can also appear reflexive: "Er macht sich gut" = he’s doing well / he looks good (in a situation).
target_language_example: Er macht heute seine Hausaufgaben nach dem Abendessen.
native_language_example: He’s doing his homework after dinner today.

additional_notes: *Er machte* is the **Präteritum** (simple past) of **machen** and is common in writing and storytelling. It can mean **did** (an action) or **made** (created/prepared), depending on what follows: *Er machte es zum Spaß* = he did it for fun; *Er machte ihr einen neuen Mantel* = he made her a new coat. It also appears in fixed expressions like *sich über etwas lustig machen* (to make fun of something) and with actions like closing something: *die Tür zumachen* (to close the door).
target_language_example: Er machte die Aufgabe in zehn Minuten.
native_language_example: He did the task in ten minutes.

meaning: "he made/took a …" (used with a masculine noun in the accusative, e.g. Schritt, Witz, Eindruck).
additional_notes: This is the start of a very common pattern: **machen + einen + noun**. The exact English translation depends on the noun: **einen Schritt machen** = “take a step”, **einen Witz machen** = “make a joke”, **einen (guten/sympathischen) Eindruck machen** = “make a (good/nice) impression”. After **einen**, the noun is masculine (der Schritt, der Witz, der Eindruck).
target_language_example: Er machte einen Fehler.
native_language_example: He made a mistake.

meaning: he started (doing something) / he made himself (something) / he set off (left).
additional_notes:
This is the past tense of the reflexive verb phrase **sich machen**. The meaning depends on what comes next:
- **sich an etw. machen / sich daran machen** = to start doing something ("He set about ...").
- **sich etw. machen** = to make oneself something (often food): *Er machte sich ein Sandwich.*
- **sich auf den Weg / nach Hause aufmachen** = to set off, head somewhere.
- **sich aus dem Staub machen** = to leave quickly / sneak off (idiomatic, fairly informal).
target_language_example: Er machte sich sofort auf den Weg.
native_language_example: He set off right away.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy likes something. It’s usually followed by a direct object in the accusative (e.g., Er mag Kaffee.). You can add intensity with sehr (“a lot”). You can also describe how he likes something: Er mag seinen Kaffee schwarz (“He likes his coffee black”).
target_language_example: Er mag Pizza, aber er mag keinen Fisch.
native_language_example: He likes pizza, but he doesn’t like fish.

meaning: 'he must' / 'he has to' (necessity or strong assumption).
additional_notes: "Er muss" is "er" (he) + "muss" (must/has to) from the verb "müssen". It can express (1) obligation/necessity: "Er muss fleißig studieren." (He has to study hard.) and (2) a strong guess based on evidence, often with a past infinitive: "Er muss den Zug verpasst haben." (He must have missed the train.)
target_language_example: Er muss heute länger arbeiten.
native_language_example: He has to work longer today.

additional_notes: "musste" is the simple past of "müssen" (to have to). It expresses obligation/necessity in the past. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Er musste arbeiten" (He had to work). It can also be used with nouns: "Er musste ihrer Entscheidung gehorchen" (He had to obey their decision).
target_language_example: Er musste früh nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: He had to go home early.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (especially gehen/kommen/fahren): „nach Hause gehen“ = to go home, „nach Hause kommen“ = to come/get home. Note the difference: „nach Hause“ (movement/direction) vs. „zu Hause“ (location: at home). „Hause“ is capitalized in this set phrase.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: I'm going home now.

additional_notes: *Er nahm* is the **simple past (Präteritum)** of *er nimmt* (“he takes”). It’s common in written German and storytelling. *Nehmen* is used in several everyday patterns: **a means of transport** (*Er nahm ein Taxi.* = “He took a taxi.”) and in fixed expressions like **keine Notiz nehmen (von)** (“to take no notice (of)”), **jdn in den Arm nehmen** (“to hug someone”), and **Mühen auf sich nehmen** (“to go to a lot of trouble / make a big effort”).
target_language_example: Er nahm meinen Schlüssel und ging zur Tür hinaus.
native_language_example: He took my key and walked out the door.

additional_notes: *Er rief … an* is very common and means “he called … (on the phone)”. Without *an*, *rufen* often means “to shout/call out” (e.g., a name). Related forms you may see: *Er rief zurück* (“he called back”) and *Er rief bei X an* (“he called X” / “he phoned X”).
target_language_example: Er rief mich gestern Abend an.
native_language_example: He called me last night.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sagen** (“to say/tell”) in the **present tense** for **er** (“he”): **er sagt**. Often followed by what someone says (e.g., **Er sagt, dass …** / “He says that …”) or a direct object (e.g., **Er sagt die Wahrheit.**).
target_language_example: Er sagt, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He says that he doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy claims or says. The comma is required before the subordinate clause with **dass**. In the **dass**-clause, the conjugated verb usually goes to the end (e.g., „… dass er morgen **kommt**.“).
target_language_example: Er sagt, dass er keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He says that he doesn’t have time.

meaning: “he says (that) he …” (reporting what a man says).
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported/indirect speech. After the comma, German often uses Konjunktiv I (e.g., „er habe“, „er kenne“) in more formal reporting, but in everyday speech you also hear the normal forms (e.g., „er hat“, „er kennt“). Often interchangeable with „Er sagt, dass er …“.
target_language_example: Er sagt, er könne morgen nicht kommen.
native_language_example: He says he can’t come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "sagen" used in narration and reported speech. Often followed by a clause with "dass" or with no conjunction: "Er sagte, (dass) er krank sei." With an object it can mean "told": "Er sagte ihm alles" = "He told him everything."
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass er morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He said that he doesn’t have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy said. After "dass" (“that”), German often uses a subordinate-clause word order (the verb tends to go to the end): "Er sagte, dass er allein wäre." In everyday speech, people sometimes drop "dass" ("Er sagte, er wäre allein."), but the meaning is the same.
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass er keine Zeit hätte.
native_language_example: He said that he didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said. It introduces a **dass**-clause (a subordinate clause), so the **main verb goes to the end**: „Er sagte, dass er morgen **kommt**.“ In reported speech you may also see **Konjunktiv I** (e.g., „er **habe**“, „er **sei**“) to show you’re reporting someone else’s words.
target_language_example: Er sagte, dass er heute keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: He said that he didn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy said. In German, reported speech often uses the subjunctive (Konjunktiv): e.g., „er hasse“, „er kenne“, „er könne“, „er wäre“, „er würde“. In everyday speech you may also hear the indicative: „Er sagte, er ist hungrig.“ Note the comma after „sagte“.
target_language_example: Er sagte, er hätte keine Zeit.
native_language_example: He said he didn’t have time.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone else said. After verbs like „sagen“ (to say), German often uses Konjunktiv I to show reported speech; „er habe“ is the Konjunktiv I form of „er hat“. In everyday speech people also often say „Er sagte, er hat …“, but „er habe“ is common in news, police reports, and more formal writing.
target_language_example: Er sagte, er habe den Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: He said he had lost the key.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone else said. After verbs like „sagen“ (to say), German often uses Konjunktiv I to show reported speech; „er habe“ is the Konjunktiv I form of „er hat“. In everyday speech people also often say „Er sagte, er hat …“, but „er habe“ is common in news, police reports, and more formal writing.
target_language_example: Er sagte, er habe den Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: He said he had lost the key.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said without quoting them directly. "sei" is Konjunktiv I of "sein" and is common in news, reports, and more formal writing. In everyday speech, people often use indicative instead: "Er sagte, er ist/war …".
target_language_example: Er sagte, er sei krank.
native_language_example: He said (that) he was sick.

meaning: “he said that he wanted to / would …” (reported speech).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (indirect/reported speech). The verb form **wolle** is **Konjunktiv I** of **wollen** and is common in news/reporting to show it’s someone else’s statement (not necessarily a fact). Often followed by an infinitive: *er wolle helfen / gehen / Geld haben*.
target_language_example: Er sagte, er wolle morgen anrufen.
native_language_example: He said he wanted to call tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone promised/claimed/said they would do. The verb form **würde** is **Konjunktiv II** and often corresponds to English **“would”** in reported speech (a kind of “future from the past”). The main verb usually comes at the end of the clause: *Er sagte, er würde kommen.*
target_language_example: Er sagte, er würde morgen anrufen.
native_language_example: He said he would call tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **sagen**: **er sagte** = “he said/told.” **mir** is dative = “to me.” Often followed by a comma and a clause with **dass** implied or omitted (e.g., *Er sagte mir, (dass) das Buch interessant sei.*). In reported speech, German often uses **Konjunktiv** forms like **sei** or **gefalle** after *er sagte mir*.
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, dass er morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn’t have time tomorrow.

meaning: "he told me that" / "he said to me that".
additional_notes: Used to report what a man said (indirect/reported speech). After „dass“ (“that”), German often puts the verb at the end of the clause: „Er sagte mir, dass du recht hattest.“ (literally: “that you right had”). You can swap in other subjects and objects: „Sie sagte mir, dass …“ (she told me that…), „Er sagte ihm/ihr, dass …“ (he told him/her that…).
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, dass er heute keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn't have time today.

meaning: “he told me that he …” (introduces what he said).
additional_notes: Used to report someone’s words with a **dass**-clause. In indirect/reported speech, German often uses **Konjunktiv** (e.g., *sei, wäre, würde*) to show it’s reported rather than the speaker’s own statement.
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, dass er keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: He told me that he didn’t have time.

meaning: “he told me that he …” / “he said to me that he …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech (what someone said). In modern spelling you’ll usually see **dass** instead of **daß**. The verb in the **dass**-clause typically goes to the end: *Er sagte mir, dass er keine Zeit habe.*
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, dass er morgen keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn’t have time tomorrow.

meaning: 'he told me that he …' (introduces reported speech).
additional_notes: Used to report what a man said. After this phrase, German often uses the subjunctive for reported speech: Konjunktiv I (e.g., „er arbeite“, „er habe“, „er kenne“) or sometimes Konjunktiv II (e.g., „er würde …“), especially when Konjunktiv I sounds the same as the normal present tense.
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, er könne heute nicht kommen.
native_language_example: He told me that he couldn't come today.

meaning: “he told me that he was …” (reported speech).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone else said. The part **„er sei …“** is **Konjunktiv I** (subjunctive I), common in news/reporting and more formal writing, to show it’s reported information (not the speaker’s own statement). In everyday speech people often use **„er sagte mir, dass er … ist/war“** instead.
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, er sei morgen nicht da.
native_language_example: He told me that he wouldn’t be there tomorrow.

meaning: "he told me (that) I should …" (reporting advice or an instruction).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone told you to do. "ich solle" is the reported-speech form (Konjunktiv I) of "ich soll" from "sollen". In everyday speech you may also hear: "Er sagte (mir), dass ich … soll."
target_language_example: Er sagte mir, ich solle früher kommen.
native_language_example: He told me I should come earlier.

meaning: "he saw" (simple past of *sehen*); often also "he looked" in phrases like *er sah ... aus*.
additional_notes: Used with what someone sees (*Er sah sie.* = He saw her), with a clause (*Er sah, dass ...* = He saw/realized that ...), and in common patterns like *er sah ... aus* (he looked ...), *er sah jemanden nie wieder* (he never saw someone again), and *er sah sich gezwungen, ...* (he felt/was forced to ...).
target_language_example: Er sah, dass sie traurig war.
native_language_example: He saw (realized) that she was sad.

meaning: “he sat / he was sitting” (simple past of *sitzen*).
additional_notes: *Saß* is the **simple past (Präteritum)** form of *sitzen* (“to sit”). It’s very common in **written stories and reports** to describe a past situation (similar to “he was sitting”). In everyday spoken German, you may also hear the perfect tense: *Er hat (da) gesessen.* It can be used literally (*Er saß da…* = “He sat there…”) and in fixed expressions like *am Steuer sitzen* (“to be at the wheel / driving”).
target_language_example: Er saß am Fenster und wartete auf den Bus.
native_language_example: He sat by the window and waited for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to express an impression or assumption (not a certain fact). Common patterns: **Er scheint + Adjektiv** (Er scheint müde.), **Er scheint + zu + Infinitiv** (Er scheint nett zu sein.), and **Er scheint + etwas getan zu haben** to talk about the past (Er scheint es nicht gewusst zu haben.).
target_language_example: Er scheint heute keine Zeit zu haben.
native_language_example: He seems to have no time today.

additional_notes: Present tense in German can describe a habit ("he writes books") or something happening now ("he is writing"). Common patterns: "Er schreibt + object" (He writes + something) and "Er schreibt jemandem" (He writes to someone), often with "einen Brief / eine E-Mail" implied.
target_language_example: Er schreibt gerade eine E-Mail.
native_language_example: He is writing an email right now.

additional_notes: "schreiben" often takes the person you write to in the dative case (here: "seinen Eltern" = to his parents). You can add what he’s writing (e.g., "einen Brief" = a letter) or leave it implied: "Er schreibt seinen Eltern."
target_language_example: Er schreibt seinen Eltern heute Abend eine Nachricht.
native_language_example: He’s writing his parents a message this evening.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a completed action in the past. Common in written German (stories, reports); in everyday speech many people prefer the present perfect: "Er hat (einen Brief) geschrieben." Often followed by what he wrote (einen Brief/einen Bericht), to whom (ihm/ihr/Ihnen), or combined with "auf" meaning "to write down": "Er schrieb es auf."
target_language_example: Gestern schrieb er mir eine E-Mail.
native_language_example: Yesterday he wrote me an email.

additional_notes: "Er sei" uses *sein* in **Konjunktiv I** (subjunctive I), which is common in **reported speech** to show you’re repeating what someone said or what is claimed (often with verbs like *sagen, erzählen, hören, annehmen, es heißt*). It often implies: “according to what was said,” without confirming it’s true. In everyday speech, people also often use *er ist* instead, but *er sei* is especially common in news reports and more formal writing.
target_language_example: Die Polizei teilte mit, er sei bereits festgenommen worden.
native_language_example: The police announced that he had already been arrested.

meaning: he sat down; he took a seat.
additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of the reflexive verb „sich setzen“ (to sit down). Often used with a place: „Er setzte sich an den Tisch“ (at the table). With „hin“ it emphasizes the action of sitting down: „Er setzte sich hin“.
target_language_example: Er setzte sich neben mich und schwieg.
native_language_example: He sat down next to me and stayed silent.

additional_notes: Not a fixed phrase by itself: it’s the subject pronoun "er" (he) plus the reflexive pronoun "sich" (himself). You see it with reflexive verbs like "sich befinden" (to be located), "sich aussuchen" (to choose for oneself), "sich verirren" (to get lost). In the past tense, "sich" can appear after the auxiliary: "Er hat sich ...".
target_language_example: Er hat sich schnell entschuldigt.
native_language_example: He apologized quickly.

meaning: “he looks …” / “he appears …” (often used as **er sieht … aus**).
additional_notes: In these examples, **sieht** is part of the separable verb **aussehen** (“to look/appear”). You’ll usually hear it as **Er sieht + adjective + aus** (Er sieht müde aus. = He looks tired.) or **Er sieht (genau) wie + person + aus** (Er sieht wie sein Vater aus. = He looks like his father.). On its own, **er sieht** can also literally mean “he sees,” but with **aus** it’s about appearance.
target_language_example: Er sieht heute sehr müde aus.
native_language_example: He looks very tired today.

meaning: 'he should' / 'tell him to …' (reported instruction, request, or expectation).
additional_notes: Used with the verb in the infinitive ("er soll + Infinitiv") to pass on what someone wants/asks/expects him to do: "Sag ihm, er soll …" = "Tell him to …". It can also report hearsay/claims about him: "Er soll verrückt sein" = "They say he's crazy / He's supposedly crazy." (This use is common in news or gossip.)
target_language_example: Sag ihm, er soll mich später anrufen.
native_language_example: Tell him to call me later.

meaning: 'he plays' (a sport/game or a musical instrument).
additional_notes: "Er" = "he". "spielt" is the 3rd-person singular present tense of "spielen" (to play). Use it with sports and games (often without an article: "Er spielt Golf.") and with musical instruments (often with an instrument name: "Er spielt Harfe."). Adverbs like "ziemlich schlecht" can describe how well someone plays.
target_language_example: Er spielt jeden Samstag Fußball.
native_language_example: He plays soccer every Saturday.

additional_notes: Used to say that a male person is good at playing something. With **spielen**, German uses the same verb for **sports** (Baseball spielen), **musical instruments** (Gitarre spielen), and **games** (Schach/Poker spielen). You can replace **er** with another subject (e.g., **sie**, **ich**) and add what he plays after it.
target_language_example: Er spielt sehr gut Klavier.
native_language_example: He plays the piano very well.

additional_notes: Used with languages to say what someone can speak (often with adverbs like „fließend“, „ziemlich gut“, or negatives like „kein“: „Er spricht kein Englisch.“). It can also mean someone is currently talking/speaking, often with „mit“ + dative: „Er spricht mit seinem Hund.“
target_language_example: Er spricht heute nicht, weil er krank ist.
native_language_example: He isn't speaking today because he is sick.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **aufstehen** for **er**. Used for rising from a sitting/lying position (e.g., from a chair or bed). Often followed by **um ... zu + infinitive** to say the purpose: *Er stand auf, um ... zu ...*.
target_language_example: Er stand auf, um die Tür zu öffnen.
native_language_example: He stood up to open the door.

additional_notes: *Er* = “he”. *Starb* is the **Präteritum** (simple past) form of *sterben* (“to die”), often used in written stories, reports, and biographies. In everyday conversation, German more often uses the perfect tense: *Er ist gestorben* (“He died / He has died”).
target_language_example: Er starb im Krankenhaus nach einer langen Krankheit.
native_language_example: He died in the hospital after a long illness.

additional_notes: Uses the Präteritum (simple past), common in written German and storytelling. In everyday speech, people often use the perfect tense instead (er hat … getan). Often appears with an object or fixed phrases like „sein Bestes tun“ (to do one’s best) or with a clause describing what he did.
target_language_example: Er tat alles, um pünktlich anzukommen.
native_language_example: He did everything to arrive on time.

meaning: he acted as if / he pretended (that).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone pretending something is true. Very often followed by **als ob** ("as if"), and the verb in the following clause is commonly in the **subjunctive** (Konjunktiv I/II): *als sei/als wäre…, als sähe…, als schliefe…*. In everyday speech, you may also hear indicative forms, but the subjunctive is common in writing and careful speech.
target_language_example: Er tat so, als ob er nichts gehört hätte.
native_language_example: He acted as if he hadn’t heard anything.

additional_notes: Used to talk about you and a male person together. Because it’s two people, German uses the plural verb: "sein" → "wir sind" / "er und ich sind" (not *"ist"*). Often followed by a noun describing your relationship (e.g., "Brüder", "Freunde", "Klassenkameraden").
target_language_example: Er und ich sind Freunde.
native_language_example: He and I are friends.

additional_notes: "verdienen" has two common meanings. (1) Money/job context: "earn" (often with an amount: "Er verdient zwanzig Dollar pro Tag."). (2) With "es" or in moral/justice contexts: "deserve" ("Er verdient es." / "Jeder hat, was er verdient."). "seinen Lebensunterhalt verdienen" = "to earn a living"; "sich seinen Lebensunterhalt verdienen" emphasizes earning it oneself.
target_language_example: Er verdient als Kellner genug, um die Miete zu bezahlen.
native_language_example: He earns enough as a waiter to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Past tense (simple past) of the reflexive verb phrase „sich verlieben in“ (= to fall in love with). Used with the accusative after „in“: „in + Akk.“ (e.g., „in das Mädchen“, „in sie“). In the present tense: „Er verliebt sich in …“; in perfect tense: „Er hat sich in … verliebt.“
target_language_example: Er verliebte sich in sie.
native_language_example: He fell in love with her.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of **verlieren** for **er** (“he”). Used for losing objects (keys, a book), possessions, or in a serious sense like **sein Leben verlieren** (“to lose his life”). In spoken German, people often use the present perfect instead: **Er hat ... verloren**.
target_language_example: Er verlor seinen Schlüssel und musste ein neues Schloss kaufen.
native_language_example: He lost his key and had to buy a new lock.

additional_notes: Past tense (simple past) of "versuchen" = "to try" with "er" (he). Often followed by an infinitive with "zu" ("Er versuchte, sie zu beruhigen.") or by "es" as a placeholder object ("Er versuchte es ihr auszureden." = he tried to talk her out of it). In conversation, you may also hear the perfect tense: "Er hat versucht …"
target_language_example: Er versuchte, pünktlich zu sein, aber der Bus kam zu spät.
native_language_example: He tried to be on time, but the bus came too late.

additional_notes: "Er" means "he". "war" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "sein" and is very common in writing and storytelling, and also used in speech for descriptions and states. Often followed by an adjective or noun: "Er war allein." (He was alone.) / "Er war unser Held." (He was our hero.)
target_language_example: Er war sehr müde, aber er half trotzdem.
native_language_example: He was very tired, but he helped anyway.

meaning: 'he was the …' (introducing who/what he was, often with an adjective like 'the youngest', 'the only', 'the born …').
additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun phrase in the nominative: **Er war der + (adjective) + noun** (e.g., *der geborene Künstler*, *der jüngste*). It often describes someone’s role/identity or points out a unique/superlative quality. For feminine/neuter/plural, the article changes: *sie war die …*, *es war das …*, *sie waren die …*.
target_language_example: Er war der beste Spieler im Team.
native_language_example: He was the best player on the team.

meaning: "he was a" (introduces what he was: a person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone in the past, followed by a noun phrase in the nominative (a role, type of person, description): "Er war ein Kriegsheld." With masculine/neuter singular nouns you typically use "ein"; any adjectives take the "ein-" endings (e.g., "ein gutaussehender Mann"). With some labels like jobs/religion/nationality, German can sometimes omit the article (e.g., "Er war Lehrer"), but "Er war ein ..." is common when you’re describing the person as a type or emphasizing the description.
target_language_example: Er war ein guter Freund.
native_language_example: He was a good friend.

meaning: 'he was in' (in a place or in a state/situation).
additional_notes: Used with **in + dative** for being in a place (no movement): *Er war in Amerika/England/Frankreich.* It can also describe being in a condition or situation: *in finanziellen Schwierigkeiten* (“in financial trouble”), *in sie verknallt* (“crushing on her”), *in einen Skandal verwickelt* (“involved in a scandal”). With **in + accusative** you often see fixed phrases like *in einen Skandal verwickelt* (literally “into a scandal”).
target_language_example: Er war in großer Gefahr.
native_language_example: He was in great danger.

additional_notes: Used to describe how someone was in the past: **er** = “he”, **war** = past tense of *sein* (“was”), **sehr** = “very”. It’s normally followed by an adjective (e.g., *nett, arm, reich, höflich*). With predicate adjectives after *sein*, the adjective usually has **no ending**: *Er war sehr nett.*
target_language_example: Er war sehr müde nach der Arbeit.
native_language_example: He was very tired after work.

meaning: “he was so …” (used to strongly emphasize an adjective/feeling).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective (er war so müde = he was so tired). Common patterns: **so + Adjektiv, dass …** (“so … that …”) and **so + Adjektiv, (zu) …** to describe a consequence/behavior (e.g., so unvorsichtig, die Tür offen zu lassen = so careless as to leave the door open).
target_language_example: Er war so müde, dass er im Zug eingeschlafen ist.
native_language_example: He was so tired that he fell asleep on the train.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of **werfen** = “to throw”. Often used in stories/writing; in everyday speech many people prefer **er hat einen Stein geworfen** (present perfect). Common prepositions: **auf** (+ accusative) “onto/at” a target, **in** (+ accusative) “into” (direction), **nach** (+ dative) “at/toward” (throwing in someone’s direction).
target_language_example: Er warf einen Stein ins Wasser.
native_language_example: He threw a stone into the water.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb „sich weigern“ (= to refuse). It’s typically followed by „zu“ + infinitive: „Er weigerte sich, zu kommen.“ You can also add what someone refuses to do: „Er weigerte sich, mir zu helfen.“
target_language_example: Er weigerte sich, den Vertrag zu unterschreiben.
native_language_example: He refused to sign the contract.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man/boy has knowledge or is aware of something. Often followed by a clause with "dass" (that) or a question word (e.g., "was", "wie"). Note: "weiß" can also be the adjective meaning "white" (e.g., "ein weißes Hemd"), but in "er weiß" it’s the verb "to know".
target_language_example: Er weiß, dass ich heute keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: He knows that I don’t have time today.

meaning: "he knows how to ..." (he knows the way to do something).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an embedded question with **wie** (“how”). What follows is a normal clause with the verb near the end: **Er weiß, wie er ... macht / ... ausgibt / ... verbindet.** Often implies that he has the skill/know-how or a method.
target_language_example: Er weiß, wie er das Problem schnell lösen kann.
native_language_example: He knows how to solve the problem quickly.

additional_notes: Used to say that a man knows the method/skill for doing something. After „wie man“, German often uses the verb at the end: „Er weiß, wie man ein Radio baut.“ You can swap the subject: „Ich weiß, wie man …“, „Sie weiß, wie man …“.
target_language_example: Er weiß, wie man ein Fahrrad repariert.
native_language_example: He knows how to repair a bike.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a lot of knowledge about a subject. The verb is *wissen* (to know facts), and it’s followed by **über + accusative** (e.g., *über Blumen*). You can change the subject: *Ich weiß viel über… / Sie weiß viel über… / Wir wissen viel über…*.
target_language_example: Er weiß viel über Geschichte.
native_language_example: He knows a lot about history.

meaning: “he dedicated his …” (gave his time/effort/work to something or someone).
additional_notes: Used with **widmen** to say someone dedicates something (a book, time, a whole life) to a person or cause. Typical pattern: **Er widmete sein + [thing] + (Dativ)**, e.g. *seiner Frau / der Wissenschaft*. You can also use **um … zu** to express a purpose, but very often German prefers the dative form (*Er widmete sein Leben der Hilfe für arme Menschen.*).
target_language_example: Er widmete seine Karriere der Erforschung neuer Medikamente.
native_language_example: He dedicated his career to researching new medicines.

additional_notes: "Er" = "he". "will" is the 3rd-person singular of "wollen" (to want). It’s used with an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Er will kochen lernen." Note: German "will" usually means "wants", not English future "will".
target_language_example: Er will heute Abend mit dir sprechen.
native_language_example: He wants to talk to you this evening.

additional_notes: "Er" = "he". "will" is the 3rd-person singular of "wollen" (to want). It’s used with an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Er will kochen lernen." Note: German "will" usually means "wants", not English future "will".
target_language_example: Er will heute Abend mit dir sprechen.
native_language_example: He wants to talk to you this evening.

meaning: "he will" (future) or "he is being" (passive); sometimes "he becomes".
additional_notes:
“Er wird” is the start of a verb phrase with werden. 
- Future: er wird + infinitive (Er wird kommen. = He will come.)
- Passive: er wird + past participle (Er wird angegriffen. = He is being attacked.)
- Change of state: er wird + adjective/noun (Er wird müde. = He becomes tired.)
Which meaning it has depends on what comes after “wird”.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, er wird dir helfen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, he will help you.

additional_notes: "Er" = he, and "wohnt" is the 3rd-person singular of "wohnen" (to live). Used to say where someone lives or that they live (or don’t live) somewhere. Often followed by a place phrase with "in" (in/near), "neben"/"nebenan" (next to/next door), or distance phrases like "zwei Häuser weiter" (two houses down).
target_language_example: Er wohnt seit einem Jahr in Berlin.
native_language_example: He has been living in Berlin for a year.

additional_notes: Used to say where a man/boy lives. "wohnen" = to live/reside; it’s usually followed by "in" + the dative case: "in Chile", "in Rom", "in dieser Straße". You can swap "er" for other subjects: "ich wohne in…" (I live in…), "sie wohnt in…" (she lives in…).
target_language_example: Er wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: He lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: "Wolle" is Konjunktiv I of "wollen" and is mainly used after verbs like "sagen" (to say) to report what someone said or claimed: "Er sagte, er wolle ...". In everyday speech, many people also use the indicative instead: "Er sagte, er will ...".
target_language_example: Sie sagte, er wolle später anrufen.
native_language_example: She said he wanted to call later.

meaning: "he wanted" (or "he was going to" / "he intended to").
additional_notes: “Er” = “he”. “wollte” is the simple past of “wollen” (to want). It’s used for past wishes/plans/intentions: *Er wollte Arzt werden* = he wanted to become a doctor; *Er wollte nicht …* = he didn’t want to …. With another verb, the other verb usually goes to the end in the infinitive (e.g., *werden, hören, sein*).
target_language_example: Er wollte heute früher nach Hause gehen, aber es hat nicht geklappt.
native_language_example: He wanted to go home earlier today, but it didn’t work out.

meaning: "he wanted" (or "he was going to" / "he intended to").
additional_notes: “Er” = “he”. “wollte” is the simple past of “wollen” (to want). It’s used for past wishes/plans/intentions: *Er wollte Arzt werden* = he wanted to become a doctor; *Er wollte nicht …* = he didn’t want to …. With another verb, the other verb usually goes to the end in the infinitive (e.g., *werden, hören, sein*).
target_language_example: Er wollte heute früher nach Hause gehen, aber es hat nicht geklappt.
native_language_example: He wanted to go home earlier today, but it didn’t work out.

meaning: “he became” or “he was” (past tense of werden).
additional_notes: “Er wurde …” is the simple past (Präteritum) of **werden** for **er** (“he”). It’s used in two very common ways: (1) **change of state** = “he became …” (e.g., *Er wurde sehr böse.*), and (2) **passive voice** = “he was …” + past participle (e.g., *Er wurde gerettet / verwechselt / bestraft / überfahren.*). In everyday speech, people also often use the perfect tense (*Er ist … geworden* / *Er ist … worden*), but in writing and news the Präteritum (*er wurde*) is very common.
target_language_example: Er wurde plötzlich nervös, als das Telefon klingelte.
native_language_example: He suddenly became nervous when the phone rang.

additional_notes: Pattern: "Er wurde in + Dativ (place) + Partizip II". Common with passive verbs like "geboren" (born), "großgezogen" (raised), "gedreht" (filmed). For a feminine subject: "Sie wurde in ..."; plural: "Sie wurden in ...".
target_language_example: Er wurde in Berlin geboren.
native_language_example: He was born in Berlin.

meaning: "he was ... by" (passive voice: the doer is introduced with "von").
additional_notes: Used in the passive with "werden": **Er wurde + Partizip II + von + Dativ** to say who did the action. Example pattern: *Er wurde von Maria geliebt.* (Maria is the agent/doer, in the dative after "von").
target_language_example: Er wurde von seinem Chef gelobt.
native_language_example: He was praised by his boss.

meaning: "he was ... because of / for (the reason of)" (introduces the reason).
additional_notes: Used in passive sentences to give the reason for what happened to him: "Er wurde wegen X ..." (e.g., fired/charged/rejected). The preposition "wegen" means "because of" and is often followed by the genitive in formal German ("wegen Diebstahls"), but many speakers use dative in everyday speech ("wegen dem Diebstahl"). After "wegen" you usually name a noun (a crime, illness, problem, etc.).
target_language_example: Er wurde wegen Betrugs verhaftet.
native_language_example: He was arrested for fraud.

meaning: "he was made/appointed/elected/promoted to" (a role or position).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine noun ("zum" = "zu dem") to say someone received a new status or position: *jemand wird zum + Nomen*. Often appears in the passive with *werden* for official actions (elected, appointed, promoted, knighted). For feminine nouns, use *zur* (e.g., *Er wurde zur Direktorin ernannt*).
target_language_example: Er wurde zum Abteilungsleiter befördert.
native_language_example: He was promoted to department head.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (Präteritum) of **zeigen** (“to show”), common in storytelling and written German. **mir** is the dative pronoun “to me.” In everyday speech, you may also hear **Er hat mir … gezeigt** (present perfect).
target_language_example: Er zeigte mir den Weg zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: He showed me the way to the train station.

additional_notes: *Er zog* is the Präteritum (simple past) form of *er zieht* (“he pulls/draws”). With separable-prefix verbs, the prefix comes at the end: *Er zog seine Jacke aus* = “He took off his jacket” (*ausziehen* = to take off clothes). In other contexts, *ziehen* can also mean “to move/drag” or “to draw (a line)”.
target_language_example: Er zog die Tür zu.
native_language_example: He pulled the door shut.

additional_notes: Used to say that a sentence, story, idea, plan, or situation is illogical or doesn't add up. The verb is usually conjugated: *Das ergibt keinen Sinn.* (that makes no sense), *Das ergibt doch keinen Sinn!* (that still doesn’t make sense), *Das hat keinen Sinn.* is also common and means “there’s no point.”
target_language_example: Das ergibt keinen Sinn, lass uns noch mal von vorne anfangen.
native_language_example: That doesn’t make sense—let’s start again from the beginning.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of **sich erheben**. Common in written/narrative German to mean that someone stands up (often from a chair/bed) or rises. In everyday spoken German you often hear **(sie) stand auf** instead. Often used with **von + dative**: *Sie erhob sich von ihrem Stuhl.*
target_language_example: Er erhob sich langsam und ging zur Tür.
native_language_example: He slowly stood up and went to the door.

additional_notes: Used when the thing you remember is a whole clause introduced by „was“ (what). The verb is usually reflexive: „ich erinnere mich … / erinnerst du dich …“. With a noun, you often say „sich an etw. erinnern“ (e.g., „Ich erinnere mich an den Tag.“), but with a „was“-clause you commonly just use „sich erinnern, was …“.
target_language_example: Ich kann mich nicht erinnern, was du gestern gesagt hast.
native_language_example: I can’t remember what you said yesterday.

additional_notes: Formal (Sie) form of the reflexive verb **sich erinnern**. Often used as a question (**Erinnern Sie sich noch an …?** = “Do you still remember …?”) or as a prompt/imperative (**Erinnern Sie sich daran …!** = “Remember that …!”). It commonly takes **an + accusative** (e.g., **an Tom**) or **daran** (“about that/that”).
target_language_example: Erinnern Sie sich an den Namen des Arztes?
native_language_example: Do you remember the doctor’s name?

additional_notes: 2nd person singular question form of **sich erinnern** (“to remember”). Very often used with **an + Akkusativ**: *Erinnerst du dich an mich / an den Tag?* It can also be followed by a clause: *Erinnerst du dich, was sie sagte?* With question words you’ll see: *Woran / an wen erinnerst du dich?*
target_language_example: Erinnerst du dich an unseren ersten Schultag?
native_language_example: Do you remember our first day of school?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **sich an etwas erinnern** = “to remember something.” It’s reflexive: **du erinnerst dich** (you remember), and what you remember comes after **an** (usually with the accusative): **an das**, **an die**, **an früher**, **an unsere Treffen**. You can change the person: **Erinnern Sie sich an …?** (formal), **Erinnert ihr euch an …?** (you all), **Erinnert er/sie sich an …?** (he/she).
target_language_example: Erinnerst du dich an meinen Namen?
native_language_example: Do you remember my name?

additional_notes: A common way to ask someone if they remember something from the past. Uses the reflexive verb **sich erinnern** (“to remember”). Often followed by **an + accusative** (*Erinnerst du dich noch an unseren Urlaub?*) or by a clause (*Erinnerst du dich noch, als …?*). **noch** adds the idea of “still / anymore” (checking if the memory is still there).
target_language_example: Erinnerst du dich noch an meinen Namen?
native_language_example: Do you still remember my name?

meaning: 'Do you still remember …?' / 'Do you remember … (from before)?'
additional_notes: A common way to ask someone if they remember something from the past. Literally it’s the verb phrase "sich an etw. erinnern" (to remember something) in the form "erinnerst du dich" (do you remember), plus "noch" (still) and "an" (about/of). It’s usually followed by a noun or a clause introduced by "dass": "Erinnerst du dich noch daran, dass …?" You can swap the person: "Erinnert ihr euch noch an …?", "Erinnern Sie sich noch an …?"
target_language_example: Erinnerst du dich noch an den Film, den wir gestern gesehen haben?
native_language_example: Do you still remember the movie we watched yesterday?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to a group of people you address with **ihr** (informal plural “you”). It’s the verb **(sich) erinnern** (“to remember”), usually with **an + accusative**: **Erinnert ihr euch an …?** = “Do you remember …?” / **Ich erinnere mich an …** = “I remember …”.
target_language_example: Erinnert ihr euch an meinen Bruder?
native_language_example: Do you all remember my brother?

additional_notes: From the verb „jemanden an etwas erinnern“ = “to remind someone of something.” The person being reminded is in the accusative („mich“, „dich“, „ihn“…), and what it reminds you of comes with „an“ + accusative (often a thing/place/person: „an zuhause“, „an meine Kindheit“, „an John“). You can change the subject: „Das erinnert mich an …“ / „Er/Sie erinnert mich an …“.
target_language_example: Der Geruch erinnert mich an den Sommer bei meinen Großeltern.
native_language_example: The smell reminds me of the summer at my grandparents’ place.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „(sich) erinnern“ in the pattern „X erinnert mich an Y“ = “X reminds me of Y.” Here, „jemanden“ is accusative (“someone”). Often used when a person, song, smell, place, etc. makes you think of another person. Don’t confuse it with English “to remember”: „Ich erinnere mich an …“ = “I remember …”
target_language_example: Deine Stimme erinnert mich an jemanden, den ich früher kannte.
native_language_example: Your voice reminds me of someone I used to know.

additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb „sich erinnern“ (= to remember). Often used with „an“ + accusative: „Er erinnert sich an dich.“ = “He remembers you.” You can also use „daran“ to refer back to something: „Er erinnert sich nicht daran.“ / „Er erinnert sich daran, das gesagt zu haben.“ In questions: „Erinnert sich jemand …?“ = “Does anyone remember …?” (Note: „erinnern“ without „sich“ often means “to remind someone,” which can be confusing.)
target_language_example: Sie erinnert sich nicht, wo sie den Schlüssel hingelegt hat.
native_language_example: She doesn't remember where she put the key.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **erkennen** used before a **dass**-clause. Common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech you may also hear **hat erkannt, dass …** (Perfekt). Often best translated as “realized that …” when it’s about suddenly understanding something.
target_language_example: Er erkannte, dass er einen Fehler gemacht hatte.
native_language_example: He realized that he had made a mistake.

additional_notes: Präteritum (simple past) of **erkennen** (“to recognize”): **ich erkannte**. Often used after an opening time/condition word like **als/da/obwohl**, which makes the verb come early in the clause (word order inversion): **Als ich Tom sah, erkannte ich ihn sofort.** **ihn** = “him” (accusative object). **sofort** = “immediately/right away.”
target_language_example: Als sie reinkam, erkannte ich sie sofort.
native_language_example: When she came in, I recognized her immediately.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "nachdenken" (or "denken") in the pattern "(über etw.) ernsthaft darüber nachdenken" = to seriously consider something. "darüber" refers back to the thing you’re considering; you’ll often see it together with "über" + what you’re thinking about ("über X ... darüber"). Common in questions that show surprise or doubt: "Denkst du ernsthaft darüber nach …?"
target_language_example: Denkst du ernsthaft darüber nach, deinen Job zu kündigen?
native_language_example: Are you seriously thinking about quitting your job?

meaning: to feed on; to live on (as a diet).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (ich ernähre mich, du ernährst dich, er/sie/es ernährt sich, wir ernähren uns, ihr ernährt euch, sie/Sie ernähren sich) plus von + dative to say what someone/something eats as their regular food. Common for animals and general diets; for a specific meal you’d more often use essen.
target_language_example: Ich ernähre mich meistens von Gemüse und Vollkornprodukten.
native_language_example: I mostly live on vegetables and whole-grain products.

meaning: for now; first (of all); to start with.
additional_notes: Very common in spoken German. It can mean (1) “for the moment/temporarily” (Der Plan liegt erst mal auf Eis. = The plan is on hold for now), or (2) “first, before anything else” when doing something step by step (Lass mich erst mal Luft holen. = Let me catch my breath first). Often used to soften requests: Könnte ich erst mal …? = Could I have … first/for now?
target_language_example: Ich schaue erst mal, was es kostet.
native_language_example: I'll first see how much it costs.

additional_notes: Used to say that something repeatedly surprises you, even though you’ve seen it before. The subject can be a person or thing: "Tom erstaunt mich immer wieder" = "Tom keeps surprising me." Often expresses positive admiration, but it can also be neutral depending on context.
target_language_example: Wie ruhig du bleibst, erstaunt mich immer wieder.
native_language_example: How calm you stay keeps surprising me.

meaning: “the first time” (usually in phrases like „zum/beim ersten Mal“ = “for the first time”).
additional_notes: „ersten Mal“ is the dative form of „erstes Mal“ and is very commonly used with prepositions: „zum ersten Mal“ (for the first time), „beim ersten Mal“ (the first time / on the first try), „vom ersten Mal an“ (from the very first time on). You’ll often see it with verbs like „treffen“ (meet), „sehen“ (see), „probieren“ (try), etc.
target_language_example: Ich bin zum ersten Mal in Deutschland.
native_language_example: I’m in Germany for the first time.

additional_notes: Used literally (a child takes their first step) and figuratively (someone initiates an action, starts a process, or makes the first move). Often appears with an article/possessive: „den ersten Schritt getan“ / „seinen ersten Schritt getan“.
target_language_example: Ich habe den ersten Schritt getan und sie angerufen.
native_language_example: I took the first step and called her.

additional_notes:
Used to say it’s your first time visiting a place. Often appears with:
- **in + dative** for countries/cities: *mein erster Besuch in Japan / in Berlin*
- **(Genitive) dieser Stadt** (more formal): *mein erster Besuch dieser Stadt* (common alternative: *mein erster Besuch in dieser Stadt*).
target_language_example: Das ist mein erster Besuch in Deutschland.
native_language_example: This is my first visit to Germany.

additional_notes: Question form of **du erwartest** (“you expect/are expecting”). Used for expecting a person (e.g., a guest), expecting someone at a certain time, or expecting someone to do something (**Was erwartest du, dass …?** = “What do you expect (that) …?”). In questions, the verb comes first: **Erwartest du …?**
target_language_example: Erwartest du heute Abend Gäste?
native_language_example: Are you expecting guests this evening?

meaning: 'expect that' (to think something will happen / someone will do something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *erwarten* plus a *dass*-clause. The *dass*-clause is a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb goes to the end (e.g., *dass das Konzert länger dauern würde*). You can use it for expectations about events (*Ich erwarte, dass es regnet.*) or people (*Man erwartet, dass ihr die Prüfung besteht.* = “People expect you to pass the exam.”).
target_language_example: Ich erwarte, dass du pünktlich kommst.
native_language_example: I expect you to come on time.

additional_notes: Past perfect of *erwarten* (to expect): *ich/er/sie hatte erwartet* = “I/he/she had expected.” Often used in comparisons with **wie** or **als**: **nicht so …, wie/als ich erwartet hatte** (“not as … as I had expected”), or **viel … als sie erwartet hatte** (“much … than she had expected”). In subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb (**hatte**) goes at the end.
target_language_example: Es war viel teurer, als ich erwartet hatte.
native_language_example: It was much more expensive than I had expected.

additional_notes: Used to say that after checking or with time, something was revealed to be true (often unexpectedly). It’s the past tense (Präteritum) of the reflexive verb phrase „sich als … erweisen“. Typical pattern: „X erwies sich als + adjective/noun“ (e.g., eine Lüge, unschuldig, wahr, ein Fehler, zu kompliziert).
target_language_example: Der Plan erwies sich als Erfolg.
native_language_example: The plan turned out to be a success.

additional_notes: Imperative of "erzählen" + "mir" (to me). Used to ask someone informally to tell or narrate something; often followed by what you want to hear ("Erzähl mir die Geschichte") or a clause with "was/wie/wo" ("Erzähl mir, was du getan hast"). More formal: "Erzählen Sie mir …"
target_language_example: Erzähl mir bitte, warum du so spät bist.
native_language_example: Tell me, please, why you’re so late.

additional_notes: This is the formal (Sie) imperative of *erzählen* + *mir* (“to me”). Use it when speaking politely to strangers, customers, or in professional situations. Often followed by: **von + dative** (“tell me about…”): *Erzählen Sie mir von Ihrem Vater.* Or by a clause with **was/wohin/warum** etc.: *Erzählen Sie mir, was Sie wollen.* If you’re speaking informally to one person, use **Erzähl mir …**
target_language_example: Erzählen Sie mir bitte, wie ich zum Bahnhof komme.
native_language_example: Please tell me how to get to the train station.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone told you. "erzählte" is the simple past of "erzählen" (to tell), "mir" means "to me," and "dass" introduces a subordinate clause (the verb in that clause usually goes to the end). In spoken German, you often hear "hat mir erzählt, dass ..." instead of the simple past.
target_language_example: Er erzählte mir, dass er morgen keine Zeit hat.
native_language_example: He told me that he doesn’t have time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when a verb or expression needs an object/subject, but the real content comes in a “dass …” clause. Very common with verbs like mögen (Niemand mag es, dass …), bereuen (Er bereute es, dass …), and expressions like Wie kam es, dass … / Für wie wahrscheinlich hältst du es, dass … . In writing, there is usually a comma before “dass”.
target_language_example: Ich hasse es, dass der Bus immer zu spät kommt.
