meaning: is as good as; is practically/virtually.
additional_notes: Used to say something is effectively the same as something else, or almost true/complete ("practically"). Common patterns: "X ist so gut wie Y" (= X is basically the same as Y) and "so gut wie nichts/kein(e)" (= almost nothing/ hardly any).
target_language_example: Ohne Ausweis ist der Vertrag so gut wie ungültig.
native_language_example: Without an ID, the contract is practically invalid.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sein** (to be) + **stolz** (proud) + **auf** + **accusative** to say you’re proud of a person or thing. The possessive changes with gender/case (e.g., **auf seinen Sohn**, **auf seine Familie**, **auf ihre Arbeit**).
target_language_example: Ich bin stolz auf dich.
native_language_example: I’m proud of you.

additional_notes: Used to compare strength (physical strength, ability, or power): X ist stärker als Y. It’s the comparative form of stark (strong). You can replace X with other subjects and use other forms (e.g., war stärker als = was stronger than; wird stärker als = will become stronger than).
target_language_example: Diese Lösung ist stärker als die andere.
native_language_example: This solution is stronger than the other one.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sein** to state that someone (or an animal) has died: **X ist tot.** It’s a direct, matter-of-fact statement; in sensitive contexts people may use softer phrases like **ist gestorben** (“has died”). Note: German **tot** looks like English **tot** (a small child), but it means **dead**.
target_language_example: Der Vogel ist tot.
native_language_example: The bird is dead.

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to “us” (our + noun), or that someone/something is part of our group/relationship (e.g., our neighbor, our customer). “Unser” changes with the noun: unser Vater, unsere Mutter, unser Haus, unsere Kinder. In questions you often see inversion: “Was ist unser Problem?”
target_language_example: Das ist unser Auto.
native_language_example: That is our car.

additional_notes: Often used to mean “much/a lot” as an intensifier. Common patterns: (1) with comparatives: „ist viel + -er“ = “is much …er” (e.g., „viel höher“, „viel interessanter“); (2) with change: „ist viel wärmer geworden“ = “has gotten much warmer”; (3) with events/amount: „Es ist viel passiert.“ = “A lot happened.” In English you usually translate it as “much” (before comparatives) or “a lot” (with verbs like „passieren“).
target_language_example: Heute ist viel mehr los als gestern.
native_language_example: There’s a lot more going on today than yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things. Pattern: [X] ist viel besser als [Y]. "viel" intensifies "besser" (= better) to mean "much/a lot better". The word after "als" is in the same case as it would be without the comparison (often nominative with "sein": "Er ist besser als ich/du", but in everyday speech you’ll also hear "als mich/dich").
target_language_example: Dein Vorschlag ist viel besser als meiner.
native_language_example: Your suggestion is much better than mine.

additional_notes: Used to compare size (or height) and emphasize a big difference. Pattern: [X] ist viel größer als [Y]. The adjective can change for other comparisons (e.g., viel kleiner als = much smaller than). Note the forms after „als“: Tom ist viel größer als ich. / … als Sie.
target_language_example: Dieser Tisch ist viel größer als der andere.
native_language_example: This table is much bigger than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Pattern: [Person/thing] ist viel älter als [person/thing]. “viel” intensifies the comparison (much/a lot). With people, “älter als ich/du/er …” is common; in casual speech you may also hear “älter als mich/dich/ihn …”.
target_language_example: Mein Bruder ist viel älter als ich.
native_language_example: My brother is much older than me.

additional_notes: Used to say a place/thing contains a lot of something: “X ist voller Y.” Here, **voller** is not the English “fuller” (comparative), but the form used with **genitive** after *voll* (common in writing). In everyday speech you’ll also hear **ist voll von …** or simply **ist voll …**.
target_language_example: Die Stadt ist voller Touristen im Sommer.
native_language_example: The city is full of tourists in the summer.

meaning: “(he/she/it) was … three months ago” (happened three months ago).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened a certain time ago. Pattern: **[subject] ist vor + time period (dative) + past participle** (Perfekt), e.g. *ist vor drei Monaten gestorben/ gegangen/ verschwunden*. **vor** means “ago” here (literally “before”). You can also change the time: *vor einer Woche*, *vor zwei Jahren*.
target_language_example: Sie ist vor drei Monaten nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: She moved to Berlin three months ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three weeks ago. The key time phrase is **vor drei Wochen** (“three weeks ago”), with **vor** + **dative**: *vor einer Woche, vor zwei Wochen, vor drei Wochen*. You can use it with many verbs in the **Perfekt** (*ist … abgereist / gestorben / weggelaufen*) or with the **passive** (*ist … gemeldet worden*).
target_language_example: Sie ist vor drei Wochen nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: She moved to Berlin three weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used with a noun + sein to say something has ended: "Der Sommer ist vorbei". "Es ist vorbei" means "It’s over" (often with an emotional tone, e.g., a relationship, a fight, a difficult time). Past participle "vorbei" works like an adjective here with "sein".
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, der Test ist vorbei.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, the test is over.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a judgment or description, usually followed by an adjective (ist völlig richtig/falsch/harmlos) or a phrase like „einer Meinung“ (to fully agree). In German it often sounds a bit stronger than just „sehr“ (“very”).
target_language_example: Das ist völlig normal.
native_language_example: That’s completely normal.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement is true or correct. It can stand alone after a noun/pronoun (“Das ist wahr.”) or introduce a clause (“Es ist wahr, dass …” = “It’s true that …”). In the first example, “wahr geworden” means “come true” (said about dreams/wishes).
target_language_example: Das ist wahr, aber nicht die ganze Wahrheit.
native_language_example: That’s true, but not the whole truth.

additional_notes: Used to say that something matters or has priority. Often follows a noun (“Die Wahrheit ist wichtig.”) or a clause introduced by “was” (“Was du tust, ist wichtig.”). You can also add “für + Akkusativ” to say “important for …” (“Das ist wichtig für mich.”).
target_language_example: Pünktlichkeit ist wichtig für den Job.
native_language_example: Punctuality is important for the job.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things and say the first one matters more. Pattern: **[Thing A] ist wichtiger als [Thing B]**. The verb changes with the subject (e.g., **sind wichtiger als** for plural). You can also use it in longer sentences: **Was du tust ist wichtiger als …**.
target_language_example: Familie ist wichtiger als Arbeit.
native_language_example: Family is more important than work.

meaning: “is like a …” (used to compare something to something else).
additional_notes: Used to make comparisons: **X ist wie ein Y** (“X is like a Y”). The article changes with the noun: **wie ein** (masc.), **wie eine** (fem.), **wie ein** (neut.), **wie (keine) + plural**. Often followed by a noun phrase, and you can add adjectives: *Er ist wie ein guter Freund.*
target_language_example: Dein neues Handy ist wie ein kleiner Computer.
native_language_example: Your new phone is like a small computer.

additional_notes: Used to say a person or thing has come back after being away. Often heard as an announcement or reassurance (e.g., someone arrives home again). Literal word-for-word is “is again there,” but natural English is “is back.”
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, Mama ist wieder da.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, Mom is back.

meaning: “is really” (used to emphasize that something is true or strong).
additional_notes: Used with the verb **sein** (“to be”) + **wirklich** (“really”) to add emphasis: *X ist wirklich + adjective/noun*. In speech you can stress **wirklich** to show strong opinion. Similar to English “really”/“truly,” and often just adds emphasis rather than new information.
target_language_example: Das ist wirklich wichtig.
native_language_example: That’s really important.

additional_notes: Used to soften or moderate an adjective: it means “fairly/quite,” not “very.” It can sound casual in everyday speech. Word order: subject + ist + ziemlich + adjective (e.g., Er ist ziemlich müde).
target_language_example: Das Wetter ist ziemlich gut heute.
native_language_example: The weather is pretty good today.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (event/activity/time period) in the present tense: "X ist zu Ende" = X has come to an end. Common with things like "der Unterricht" (class), "die Pause" (break), "die Schule" (school/day of school), "der Film" (movie), "der Traum" (dream). You can also say "zu Ende sein" in other tenses: "Die Pause war zu Ende" (was over).
target_language_example: Der Tag ist zu Ende.
native_language_example: The day is over.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or adverb to say something is more than acceptable/possible: „Er ist zu langsam.“ = “He’s too slow.” You’ll often see it as „zu + adjective/adverb“ (e.g., „zu schwer“, „zu betrunken“, „zu mager“, „zu schwach“). It can also appear with „zu sehr“ (“too much/too strongly”), often followed by what it relates to: „zu sehr von Maria abhängig“ = “too dependent on Maria.”
target_language_example: Die Tasche ist zu schwer für mich.
native_language_example: The bag is too heavy for me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" (to be) to say something is bigger than desired/needed. Common for clothes and objects: "Die Jacke ist zu groß." You can swap in other adjectives: "ist zu klein" (too small), "ist zu teuer" (too expensive).
target_language_example: Der Pullover ist zu groß, ich brauche eine kleinere Größe.
native_language_example: The sweater is too big; I need a smaller size.

additional_notes: Used to say something’s temperature is higher than it should be (often: too hot to touch, drink, or use). Common pattern: „X ist zu heiß (zum + Infinitiv)“ = “X is too hot (to + verb)” (e.g., „zu heiß zum Trinken“ = “too hot to drink”).
target_language_example: Die Suppe ist zu heiß zum Essen.
native_language_example: The soup is too hot to eat.

additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t have the right age/ maturity for an action. Pattern: „[Person] ist zu jung, um + zu + Infinitiv“ (e.g., „Er ist zu jung, um zu arbeiten.“). The verb goes to the end in the „um … zu“ clause.
target_language_example: Sie ist zu jung, um Auto zu fahren.
native_language_example: She is too young to drive a car.

additional_notes: Used to say that something’s size/amount isn’t enough. Often followed by **für + accusative** to say who it’s too small for: *Die Mütze ist zu klein für mich.* You can change **ist** to match the subject (e.g., *sind zu klein*).
target_language_example: Der Tisch ist zu klein für vier Personen.
native_language_example: The table is too small for four people.

additional_notes: Used to say something’s length (or duration) isn’t enough. It’s the verb "sein" (to be) + "zu" (too) + "kurz" (short). It changes with the subject and tense (e.g., "Der Rock ist zu kurz.", "Die Sätze sind zu kurz.").
target_language_example: Das Kabel ist zu kurz, ich brauche ein längeres.
native_language_example: The cable is too short; I need a longer one.

additional_notes: Used to say something has an excessive length (hair, clothes, a sentence, etc.). Often followed by “für + accusative” to mean “too long for someone”: “Die Hose ist zu lang für mich.” You can also use it as an exclamation: “Der Satz ist zu lang!”
target_language_example: Der Film ist zu lang.
native_language_example: The movie is too long.

additional_notes: Used to say something costs more than you think is acceptable. Structure: [thing] + ist + zu + teuer (e.g., „Das ist zu teuer.“). You can replace „ist“ with other forms of „sein“: „sind zu teuer“, „war zu teuer“, etc.
target_language_example: Das Ticket ist zu teuer, wir gehen lieber zu Fuß.
native_language_example: The ticket is too expensive; we’d rather walk.

meaning: has gone too far (crossed a line).
additional_notes: Used to criticize someone’s actions, words, or behavior as excessive or unacceptable (often morally or socially). Can also be literal about going too far in distance, but it’s very common in the figurative sense. Often said with: „Ich finde, …“ / „Er/Sie ist zu weit gegangen.“
target_language_example: Mit diesem Witz bist du zu weit gegangen.
native_language_example: You went too far with that joke.

ist zwei Jahre älter als ich

target_language_multi_word_term: ist zwei Jahre älter als ich
meaning: is two years older than me.
additional_notes: Used to compare ages: **X ist [number] Jahre älter als Y**. You can change the number (ein, drei, fünf …) and the person (**als ich/du/er/sie/wir/ihr/sie**). You can also make the opposite with **jünger** (younger): *zwei Jahre jünger als ich*.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist drei Jahre älter als ich.
native_language_example: My sister is three years older than me.

additional_notes: Used to make a comparison with the comparative adjective „älter“ (older) + „als“ (than). If „als“ introduces a full clause (with a subject + verb), you usually use a comma and the verb goes to the end: „Er ist älter, als ich dachte.“ Without a full clause, no comma: „Er ist älter als Tom.“
target_language_example: Sie ist älter, als sie aussieht.
native_language_example: She is older than she looks.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: **[Person/thing] ist älter als [person/thing]**. The verb changes with the subject (e.g., **ich bin älter als…**, **du bist älter als…**, **wir sind älter als…**). Often used with a number: **älter als fünfzig** = older than fifty.
target_language_example: Mein Bruder ist älter als ich.
native_language_example: My brother is older than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages (people, things, songs, cars, etc.). Pattern: **X ist älter als ich** = X is older than I am. You can swap **ich** for another person: **älter als du/er/sie/wir/ihr/Sie**.
target_language_example: Dieser Film ist älter als ich.
native_language_example: This movie is older than me.

meaning: “is extremely / is very” (used to strongly describe someone or something).
additional_notes: “äußerst” is an intensifier meaning “extremely/very,” placed before an adjective or adverb: “Er ist äußerst freundlich.” It often sounds a bit more formal than “sehr.” The form “ist” is just the 3rd-person singular of “sein” (to be), so you’ll also see: “ich bin äußerst…”, “wir sind äußerst…”, etc.
target_language_example: Der Film ist äußerst spannend.
native_language_example: The movie is extremely exciting.

meaning: “is not at all” / “isn’t … in the slightest” (strong negation).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a negation. Often appears with **sein + adjective** (e.g., *ist überhaupt nicht glücklich*), but **überhaupt nicht** can also negate other verbs: *Ich habe überhaupt nicht geschlafen* (“I didn’t sleep at all”). In a sentence it typically comes after the verb and before what it negates (an adjective, participle, or verb phrase).
target_language_example: Das ist überhaupt nicht schlimm.
native_language_example: That’s not bad at all.

meaning: "(I) told you that …" (reminding someone; “as I already said”).
additional_notes: Used when you’re reminding someone of something you previously said. The particle "ja" adds emphasis like “you know / as you know / I did tell you.” Very common pattern: "Ich habe dir/Ihnen ja gesagt, dass …" ("dir" = to you, informal; "Ihnen" = to you, formal). Often in a slightly annoyed or “see?” tone.
target_language_example: Ich habe dir ja gesagt, dass es heute regnen wird.
native_language_example: I told you it was going to rain today.

additional_notes: Used with **sich freuen** (“to be happy / to look forward to”) to strongly emphasize your feeling. In sentences like **Ich habe mich ja so gefreut, dich zu sehen!**, **ja** is a modal particle adding extra emphasis (like “really/you know”), and **so** intensifies it (“so much”). Usually appears as **(ich) habe mich ja so gefreut, …** or **(wir) haben uns ja so gefreut, …**.
target_language_example: Ich habe mich ja so gefreut, dich endlich wiederzusehen!
native_language_example: I was so happy to finally see you again!

meaning: “Yes, sir.” (polite/obedient reply to a man in authority).
additional_notes: Used when addressing a man respectfully (often someone in charge). In German, this is common in films, the military, or when copying an English-style way of speaking; in everyday German you more often hear “Ja, Herr …” or simply “Ja.”
target_language_example: Ja, Sir, ich mache das sofort.
native_language_example: Yes, sir, I'll do that right away.

additional_notes: Used to acknowledge what someone said (“ja”), then immediately introduce a counterpoint or limitation (“aber”). Very common in conversations and arguments; the speaker often wants to correct, qualify, or bring up a problem.
target_language_example: Ja, aber so einfach ist das nicht.
native_language_example: Yes, but it’s not that simple.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to confirm what was said or to agree with a situation or suggestion. It often introduces a full clause: "Ja, das habe ich…", "Ja, das ist…", "Ja, das wäre…". In speech it can sound like English "Yeah, that…" or "Yes, that’s right."
target_language_example: Ja, das stimmt, ich habe es vergessen.
native_language_example: Yes, that's true—I forgot it.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with what someone just said/asked, often when identifying a person/thing (“Ja, das ist mein Haus.”) or confirming a statement (“Ja, das ist eine gute Idee.”). You can replace “das” with “er/sie” for people (“Ja, das ist sie.” = “Yes, that’s her / yes, it’s her.”).
target_language_example: Ja, das ist genau das, was ich meine.
native_language_example: Yes, that’s exactly what I mean.

meaning: “Yes, it …” (starting an answer with “yes” and referring to “it”).
additional_notes: Used to answer a question or confirm something: **Ja** = “yes” and **es** = “it” (often referring back to something already mentioned, or a general “it” like in *es funktioniert* = “it works”). In speech, there’s usually a short pause after *ja* (written as a comma).
target_language_example: Ja, es ist schon spät.
native_language_example: Yes, it’s already late.

meaning: “yes, I …” (agreeing and then speaking about yourself).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to confirm something (“ja”) and immediately continue with a statement about yourself (“ich …” + verb). Often followed by a verb like „denke“, „habe“, „verstehe“ in normal sentence word order.
target_language_example: Ja, ich komme gleich.
native_language_example: Yes, I’m coming right away.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or agree with a statement about yourself. Often followed by an adjective or phrase: “Ja, ich bin müde.” (Yes, I’m tired.), “Ja, ich bin so weit.” (Yes, I’m ready.). You can also add “es” for emphasis or to refer back to what was said: “Ja, ich bin es.” (Yes, I am / Yes, that’s me.).
target_language_example: Ja, ich bin müde, aber ich kann noch helfen.
native_language_example: Yes, I’m tired, but I can still help.

additional_notes: Used to confirm something about yourself. Often followed by an object ("…das Buch") or by a past participle to form the present perfect ("Ich habe … gelesen / verpasst / gestimmt"). In English this can sound like "I have" or "I did" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ja, ich habe die E-Mail schon beantwortet.
native_language_example: Yes, I already answered the email.

meaning: "yeah, and…" / "yes, and…" (often: "so what?" or "what about it?")
additional_notes: Used to continue a point ("Yes, and…") or—very often in spoken German—to sound impatient or dismissive, like "Yeah, and?" / "So what?". Tone depends on context and intonation; it can be neutral or sarcastic.
target_language_example: Ja, und was hat das mit mir zu tun?
native_language_example: Yeah, and what does that have to do with me?

meaning: "yes, we…" (agreeing and then saying what "we" do/did).
additional_notes: Used at the start of an answer to confirm something and then continue with a statement about a group including the speaker ("wir" = we). Often heard in conversations/interviews: "Ja, wir …" + verb. The comma reflects a pause in speech; in writing you may also see "Ja, wir ..." at the beginning of a sentence.
target_language_example: Ja, wir können Ihnen morgen helfen.
native_language_example: Yes, we can help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to stress a correction, surprise, or realization that something is not the case. Here, **ja** is a modal particle (often like “you know / actually”), and **gar nicht** strengthens the negation (“not at all”). Common in spoken German when contradicting an assumption: *Ich muss ja gar nicht …* = “Wait, I actually don’t have to …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe ja gar nicht gesagt, dass ich komme.
native_language_example: I didn’t say at all that I was coming (actually).

additional_notes: Often used to make a warning or command very strong, especially in imperatives: "Fass das ja nicht an!" = “Don’t touch that (whatever you do)!” In statements, "ja" can also mean “as you know / anyway,” and "ja nicht" emphasizes that something is not the case: "Sie kommen ja nicht weg" = “They’re not going anywhere anyway.” Tone can sound strict or threatening depending on context.
target_language_example: Sag das ja nicht zu deiner Mutter!
native_language_example: Don’t you dare tell your mother that!

additional_notes:
Used (often in questions) to ask whether someone has ever considered something: „Hast du je darüber nachgedacht, …?“ = “Have you ever thought about …?”
- „je“ = “ever” (not “every”).
- „darüber“ refers back to a topic/idea (“about it/that”).
- „nachgedacht“ is the past participle of „nachdenken“ and is commonly used with „haben“: „Ich habe darüber nachgedacht.“
target_language_example: Hast du je darüber nachgedacht, den Job zu wechseln?
native_language_example: Have you ever thought about changing jobs?

meaning: 'the sooner / the earlier' (in the pattern 'je …, desto …').
additional_notes: Used in the correlative comparative structure **je …, desto/umso …** to say that one thing changes depending on another: **Je eher du gehst, desto besser.** = “The sooner you leave, the better.” *Je* introduces the condition (with a comparative like **eher**), and **desto/umso** introduces the result (often also with a comparative like **besser**, **mehr**, **weniger**). You can also use it as a shortened phrase: **Je eher, desto besser.**
target_language_example: Je eher wir losfahren, desto schneller sind wir da.
native_language_example: The sooner we leave, the faster we’ll be there.

additional_notes: Used in a correlative comparison with a second clause, often with **desto** or **umso**: **Je mehr …, desto/umso …**. The **je-** clause is treated like a subordinate clause, so the conjugated verb typically goes to the end (e.g., *Je mehr du lernst,* …). You can also repeat **je mehr** in the second clause instead of using **desto/umso** (more literary/old-fashioned).
target_language_example: Je mehr ich übe, desto besser spreche ich Deutsch.
native_language_example: The more I practice, the better I speak German.

meaning: "the more I …" (used in a 'the more…, the …' sentence).
additional_notes: Used in the correlative comparative pattern: „Je + comparative + ich …, desto/umso + comparative …“. It expresses that as one thing increases, another thing also increases (or decreases). Example: „Je mehr ich lerne, desto besser werde ich.“
target_language_example: Je mehr ich Deutsch spreche, desto sicherer fühle ich mich.
native_language_example: The more I speak German, the more confident I feel.

additional_notes: Used in the comparative correlative structure **je …, desto/umso …** to show that when one thing increases/decreases, another changes too: **Je mehr man X (verb), desto/umso mehr/weniger Y (verb).** Here **man** means “one/people in general.”
target_language_example: Je mehr man übt, desto besser wird man.
native_language_example: The more you practice, the better you become.

meaning: lots of people; a whole bunch of people.
additional_notes: “Jede Menge” is a very common way to say “a lot of” with emphasis. It’s used with uncountable nouns (“jede Menge Zeit” = lots of time) and with plural countable nouns like “Leute”. It often appears in sentences like “Es sind … da” (There are … here) or “Draußen warten …” (Outside … are waiting).
target_language_example: Vor dem Kino stehen jede Menge Leute.
native_language_example: There are lots of people standing in front of the movie theater.

meaning: plenty of time; lots of time.
additional_notes: Used to say you have more than enough time and don’t need to hurry. Very common in everyday speech. Often appears with "noch" (still): "Ich habe noch jede Menge Zeit."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, wir haben noch jede Menge Zeit, bevor das Konzert anfängt.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we still have plenty of time before the concert starts.

meaning: to have lots to do; a lot to do.
additional_notes: Common, everyday phrase meaning you’re very busy. Often used with forms of "haben" (ich habe/wir haben/ich hatte …) or "es gibt" ("there is/are"). "jede Menge" = "lots/plenty"; "zu tun" = "to do".
target_language_example: Heute habe ich jede Menge zu tun, deshalb kann ich nicht mitkommen.
native_language_example: Today I have lots to do, so I can't come along.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens nightly as a regular habit or repeated event. Often goes with the present tense for routines ("Ich schlafe jede Nacht …") or with past tense to describe a repeated action in the past ("Sie telefonierten jede Nacht …").
target_language_example: Ich lese jede Nacht vor dem Schlafengehen.
native_language_example: I read every night before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens weekly or to ask about a weekly amount/frequency. It can answer “how often?” (Wie oft?) or set a time frame for quantities (e.g., how much per week).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jede Woche dreimal ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym three times a week.

meaning: everyone who / anyone who (in a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used to refer to any person that fits a description: "jedem" is dative (often after verbs like helfen, danken, geben), and the comma introduces a relative clause. The relative pronoun is often "der" (nominative) because it is the subject inside the relative clause, even though "jedem" is dative in the main clause: "Hilf jedem, der Hilfe braucht."
target_language_example: Ich helfe jedem, der mich darum bittet.
native_language_example: I help anyone who asks me for it.

meaning: every evening; each night (in the evening).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a regular, repeated action that happens in the evening. You can place it in different positions: at the beginning for emphasis ("Jeden Abend …") or later in the sentence ("… jeden Abend"). With masculine nouns like "Abend", "jeden" is accusative because it answers “when/how often?”.
target_language_example: Wir sehen jeden Abend eine Serie.
native_language_example: We watch a series every evening.

additional_notes: Means something happens once a month on a regular basis. It can appear mid-sentence (Ich bezahle jeden Monat ...) or at the start for emphasis (Jeden Monat ...). The form changes with gender/case: jeden Monat (masculine, accusative), jeden Tag, jede Woche, jedes Jahr.
target_language_example: Jeden Monat überweise ich die Miete.
native_language_example: Every month I transfer the rent.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens as a regular routine each day in the morning (often with the present tense). Similar to "jeden Tag" (every day) and can be emphasized with words like "gewöhnlich" (usually) or "immer" (always).
target_language_example: Ich trinke jeden Morgen einen Kaffee.
native_language_example: I drink a coffee every morning.

additional_notes: Used in routines, usually with the verb "(sich) die Zähne putzen" = "to brush (your) teeth". German often uses "sich" (reflexive) with body-care actions, and uses the definite article "die" (the) instead of a possessive: "Ich putze mir die Zähne" = "I brush my teeth." Word order is flexible: "jeden Morgen putze ich mir die Zähne" / "ich putze mir jeden Morgen die Zähne."
target_language_example: Ich putze mir jeden Morgen die Zähne.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth every morning.

additional_notes: A time expression meaning something happens on all Sundays (a regular habit). It uses the accusative form "jeden" (masculine accusative of "jeder") because it's used as an adverbial of time: "jeden + day" (e.g., "jeden Tag", "jeden Montag").
target_language_example: Wir gehen jeden Sonntag spazieren.
native_language_example: We go for a walk every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "gehen" (to go): "(Ich/Wir) gehe(n) jeden Sonntag in die Kirche" = going to church every Sunday (regular habit). "jeden Sonntag" means "every Sunday" (accusative time expression), and "in die Kirche" indicates movement/direction (into/to the church).
target_language_example: Meine Großeltern gehen jeden Sonntag in die Kirche.
native_language_example: My grandparents go to church every Sunday.

additional_notes: Means that you do something related to the French language every day (e.g., speak, learn, read). Often used with verbs like sprechen (to speak), lernen (to learn/study), lesen (to read). Grammar note: jeden Tag = "every day" (accusative, used for frequency).
target_language_example: Ich lerne jeden Tag Französisch.
native_language_example: I study French every day.

additional_notes: Used with a verb like **Klavier üben** (to practice piano) or **Klavier spielen** (to play piano). **jeden Tag** = every day; **Klavier** = piano (the instrument).
target_language_example: Ich spiele jeden Tag Klavier, auch am Wochenende.
native_language_example: I play the piano every day, even on the weekend.

meaning: "every day with" (to do/spend time with someone every day).
additional_notes: Used to say you do something every day together with someone, or you spend time every day on something. "mit" takes the dative case: mit Tom, mit meiner Mutter, mit Maria. Often appears with verbs like "sprechen" (jeden Tag mit jemandem sprechen) or "Zeit verbringen" (jeden Tag mit etwas Zeit verbringen).
target_language_example: Ich verbringe jeden Tag mit meinen Kindern Zeit.
native_language_example: I spend time with my kids every day.

meaning: to go for a walk every day.
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "gehen": "jeden Tag spazieren gehen" (to go for a walk every day). "Spazieren" here functions like "spazieren gehen" = "to take/go for a walk" (often for leisure or exercise).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden Tag spazieren.
native_language_example: I go for a walk every day.

additional_notes: Used to express a repeating schedule with one day in between (day 1 yes, day 2 no, day 3 yes, etc.). Often placed in the sentence as a time expression (usually near the beginning or after the verb).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden zweiten Tag ins Fitnessstudio.
native_language_example: I go to the gym every other day.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause about people: "jeder" (everyone/anyone) + "der" (who). The verb in the clause goes to the end: "Jeder, der kommen möchte, …". It can also appear as "ein jeder, der …" (more formal/literary). For feminine/plural you’ll see "jede, die …" / "alle, die …".
target_language_example: Jeder, der Deutsch lernen will, braucht Geduld.
native_language_example: Everyone who wants to learn German needs patience.

additional_notes: Used to say that all people (each individual) possess something or have a certain situation. Often followed by a noun phrase ("jeder hat eine Meinung") or by a clause ("jeder hat, was …"). Note: "jeder" = everyone/each (masculine nominative); you may also see "jede" (feminine) or "jeder" (feminine dative/genitive) depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Jeder hat seine eigenen Probleme.
native_language_example: Everyone has their own problems.

additional_notes:
Used to state a general right that applies to all people. Often followed by:
- "auf" + noun (e.g., "das Recht auf freie Meinungsäußerung" = the right to freedom of expression)
- "zu" + infinitive (e.g., "das Recht zu sagen" = the right to say)
- a comma + infinitive with "zu" (e.g., "das Recht, ... zu ...")
target_language_example: Jeder hat das Recht, Nein zu sagen.
native_language_example: Everyone has the right to say no.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with a well-known fact or something considered obvious. Often followed by a subordinate clause with verb at the end (…, dass du sie liebst). You can also use it for emphasis or to suggest something is common knowledge.
target_language_example: Jeder weiß, dass es heute regnet.
native_language_example: Everyone knows that it’s raining today.

additional_notes: "jedes" means "every/each" and agrees with the noun. "Buch" is neuter, so you often see "jedes Buch" (nominative/accusative singular) in general statements or when you don’t care which one (e.g., "Mir ist jedes Buch recht" = "Any book is fine with me").
target_language_example: Nicht jedes Buch ist spannend.
native_language_example: Not every book is exciting.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens annually or repeatedly once per year. Often paired with a time marker like a season or date (e.g., „jedes Jahr im Herbst“, „jedes Jahr am selben Tag“).
target_language_example: Wir besuchen unsere Großeltern jedes Jahr zu Weihnachten.
native_language_example: We visit our grandparents every year at Christmas.

additional_notes: Introduces a time clause meaning that something happens repeatedly whenever the other action/event happens. Often followed by verb-last word order in the clause (e.g., „wenn er hierher kommt …“).
target_language_example: Jedes Mal, wenn es regnet, nehme ich einen Regenschirm mit.
native_language_example: Every time it rains, I take an umbrella with me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a repeated situation: a main clause + "jedes Mal, wenn ich" + a verb-at-the-end clause. Often followed by common verbs like "sehe" (see), "denke" (think), "mich erinnere" (I remember). You can also start the sentence with it: "Jedes Mal, wenn ich …, …".
target_language_example: Jedes Mal, wenn ich ihn anrufe, ist er beschäftigt.
native_language_example: Every time I call him, he’s busy.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens regularly on Saturdays/Sundays. Often comes with present tense to talk about routines (e.g., "Ich arbeite jedes Wochenende.").
target_language_example: Ich besuche meine Eltern jedes Wochenende.
native_language_example: I visit my parents every weekend.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something applies to all the words (none are excluded). Often comes up with verbs like kennen/lernen (to know), glauben (to believe), lesen (to read), and in set phrases like „Jedes Wort zählt.“ (“Every word counts.”). You can also use it figuratively, e.g., „jedes Wort aus deinem Mund“ (“every word out of your mouth”).
target_language_example: Ich habe dir jedes Wort geglaubt.
native_language_example: I believed every word you said.

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to ask whether someone has ever been in a place or done something in a place. It often goes with verbs like **sein** (Seid/Sind ... gewesen? / Wart/Waren ...?), **leben** (Hast du ... gelebt?), or **sitzen** (Hast du ... gesessen?). **schon jemals in ...** adds extra emphasis, like 'ever (at all)'.
target_language_example: Bist du jemals in Berlin gewesen?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to describe an unknown/unspecified person and add more information with a relative clause. The relative pronoun changes with gender and case: jemand, der (masc.), jemand, die (fem.), jemand, das (neut., rare); e.g., Ich suche jemanden, der mir hilft. / Ich brauche jemanden, den ich vertrauen kann.
target_language_example: Ich suche jemanden, der mir beim Umzug hilft.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone who can help me move.

meaning: someone else; another person (to/for someone else).
additional_notes: "Jemand" means "someone". "Anderem" is the dative form of "ander-" ("other") and is used after many verbs/prepositions that take the dative (often implying 'to/for' someone). It commonly appears with verbs like "geben" (Gib es jemand anderem), "sagen" (zu jemand anderem), or "übertragen" (jemand anderem übertragen).
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte jemand anderem erklären?
native_language_example: Can you please explain that to someone else?

meaning: someone else; another person (not me/you/that person).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a different person than the one expected or mentioned. This form is typically accusative (direct object): „Ich frage jemand anderen.“ In other cases you may see different endings, e.g. nominative „jemand anderer“ or dative „jemand anderem“.
target_language_example: Frag bitte jemand anderen um Hilfe.
native_language_example: Please ask someone else for help.

additional_notes: "Jemand" means an unspecified person (someone). "Hat" is the 3rd-person singular of "haben" (to have) and is very often used to form the past tense (Perfekt): "jemand hat" + past participle (e.g., "jemand hat das gesagt" = someone said that).
target_language_example: Jemand hat mein Handy gefunden.
native_language_example: Someone found my phone.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action is necessary or that a certain person is required to do something. With a perfect infinitive ("... genommen haben", "... gesagt haben"), it often expresses a logical guess: "someone must have...".
target_language_example: Jemand muss das Fenster offen gelassen haben.
native_language_example: Someone must have left the window open.

additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause about a person: "jemanden" = "someone" (accusative), and "den" is the relative pronoun referring back to that person (masculine singular, accusative). Common with verbs like "treffen" (meet), "kennen" (know), "sehen" (see): „jemanden, den ich kenne/getroffen habe“. For a woman you’d use: „jemanden, die ich …“; for plural: „jemanden, die ich …“.
target_language_example: Ich suche jemanden, den ich gut kenne.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone I know well.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing the person you need/are looking for. You’ll often see it with a verb at the end of the clause: „jemanden, der mir hilft“ / „jemanden, der mir helfen kann“. (Changes with case/gender: jemanden, der; jemandem, der; jemand, der; etc.)
target_language_example: Ich suche jemanden, der Deutsch spricht.
native_language_example: I’m looking for someone who speaks German.

additional_notes:
Used to introduce a relative clause describing a person: jemanden (someone) + mit dem (with whom). 
- "mit dem" refers to a masculine/neuter singular person (e.g., der Mann / das Kind). 
- For feminine: "jemanden, mit der ..." (die Frau). 
- For plural: "jemanden, mit denen ..." (die Leute). 
Common with verbs like "reden", "lernen", "arbeiten", "üben".
target_language_example: Ich suche jemanden, mit dem ich Deutsch sprechen kann.
native_language_example: I'm looking for someone I can speak German with.

meaning: (you) paid someone for it / to do that.
additional_notes: Used with the verb **bezahlen** in the Perfekt (**haben ... bezahlt**). **jemanden** is the person being paid (accusative). **dafür** means “for it/for that” and often points to an action mentioned next (e.g., **dafür, das zu tun** = “to do that”). You can change the subject and tense: **Ich habe jemanden dafür bezahlt...**, **Hast du jemanden dafür bezahlt...?**
target_language_example: Ich habe jemanden dafür bezahlt, meine Bewerbung zu korrigieren.
native_language_example: I paid someone to correct my job application.

additional_notes: Used with "haben" in the Perfekt (past tense): "Hast/Haben Sie jemanden gesehen?" = "Did you see anyone?". "jemanden" is the accusative form of "jemand" (someone), often used in questions and negatives (like English "anyone").
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern jemanden gesehen, den ich aus der Schule kenne.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw someone I know from school.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like haben/brauchen/suchen/finden: „jemanden zum Reden haben“ = to have someone to talk to (often for company or emotional support). The structure „jemanden + zum + Verb(noun)“ means “someone to (do something with)”, here „zum Reden“ = “to talk”.
target_language_example: Ich bin neu hier und kenne niemanden, aber ich hätte gern jemanden zum Reden.
native_language_example: I'm new here and I don't know anyone, but I'd like someone to talk to.

additional_notes: Used with a place name to say where someone is or lives at the moment. Often follows a form of “sein” (to be) or “wohnen/leben” (to live): „Ich bin jetzt in …“, „Ich wohne jetzt in …“.
target_language_example: Wir sind jetzt in Berlin.
native_language_example: We are in Berlin now.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion like gehen/fahren/kommen to say that someone is heading home at this moment. Often used as an order (Geh jetzt nach Hause!) or a question (Gehst du jetzt nach Hause?). Word order can vary for emphasis (e.g., Ich gehe jetzt nach Hause / Jetzt gehe ich nach Hause).
target_language_example: Wir fahren jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: We’re going home now.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase for asking, offering permission, or stating that someone will leave and go home at this moment. "jetzt" = now, "nach Hause" = (to) home (direction), "gehen" = to go/walk. Often used with modal verbs like "können" (can), "dürfen" (be allowed to), and "müssen" (have to): "Kann/Darf/Muss ich jetzt nach Hause gehen?"
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt nach Hause gehen, es ist schon spät.
native_language_example: I have to go home now; it's already late.

additional_notes: Used to say that something that was true/needed before is no longer true/needed from now on. Often contrasts with a past state (e.g., “früher …, aber jetzt nicht mehr”) and can be used as a short standalone reply: “Jetzt nicht mehr.”
target_language_example: Früher hatte ich Angst, aber jetzt nicht mehr.
native_language_example: I used to be afraid, but not anymore.

additional_notes: Used when you’ve just understood something (after an explanation or new information). Often followed by what you understand: „Jetzt verstehe ich das (alles).“ You can also use it ironically/negatively with a comparison: „Jetzt verstehe ich noch weniger als zuvor.“
target_language_example: Ah, jetzt verstehe ich, warum du so spät bist.
native_language_example: Oh, now I understand why you’re so late.

additional_notes: Used to say you understand something now (often after learning/experiencing it). In German word order, the time word "jetzt" comes first, so the verb comes second: "Jetzt weiß ich ...". Often followed by a comma and a clause with "wie/was/warum": "Jetzt weiß ich, wie ...".
target_language_example: Jetzt weiß ich, warum du so müde bist.
native_language_example: Now I know why you’re so tired.

additional_notes: Used with a subject to describe someone’s earlier life, very often in a time clause with **als** (“when” for one past time period): **Als ich (noch) jung war, …**. **war** is the simple past (Präteritum) of **sein** (“to be”).
target_language_example: Als wir jung waren, hatten wir keinen Fernseher.
native_language_example: When we were young, we didn’t have a TV.

meaning: young lady (polite way to address or describe a young woman).
additional_notes: Used with an article to describe someone ("eine/die junge Dame") or without an article as a direct form of address ("junge Dame!"). Sounds polite and a bit formal/old-fashioned; when used as an address it can also sound admonishing or strict, especially in phrases like "Nicht so schnell, junge Dame!".
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, junge Dame, haben Sie das hier verloren?
native_language_example: Excuse me, young lady, did you lose this here?

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for a female person who is young (roughly late teens to early adulthood). Often used with the definite article in stories/descriptions: „die junge Frau …“. It’s neutral and not slang. Note: „junge“ changes for case/article (e.g., „eine junge Frau“, „der jungen Frau“).
target_language_example: Ich habe mit der jungen Frau gesprochen.
native_language_example: I spoke with the young woman.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to talk about young people as a group (often teens/young adults). It’s the plural of „der/die Jugendliche“ in meaning, but formed from adjective + noun: „jung“ + „die Leute“ (people). Usually used in general statements: „Junge Leute …“.
target_language_example: In dieser Stadt gibt es viele Angebote für junge Leute.
native_language_example: In this city there are many activities/services for young people.

additional_notes: “Junge Leute” means “young people.” The form “jungen Leuten” is the dative plural, used after many prepositions (e.g., bei = among/with, von = by/from) and with some verbs like „gefallen“ (to be pleasing to): „Das gefällt jungen Leuten“ = “Young people like that.”
target_language_example: Die App ist bei jungen Leuten sehr beliebt.
native_language_example: The app is very popular with young people.

meaning: young man; a young male (often a polite form of address).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a young adult male. It can also be used to address someone directly, often to get their attention or to warn/reprimand them (e.g., „Immer langsam, junger Mann!“ = “Easy there, young man!”). Watch adjective endings: as a subject with „dieser“, you usually say „dieser junge Mann“ (not „dieser junger Mann“).
target_language_example: Entschuldigen Sie, junger Mann, können Sie mir helfen?
native_language_example: Excuse me, young man, can you help me?

additional_notes: Used to compare ages (or how old someone looks): **X ist jünger als Y** (“X is younger than Y”). Often used with intensifiers like **viel/jede Menge/um einiges** (“much/a lot”) or with **aussehen** (“to look”): **jünger als er aussieht** (“younger than he looks”).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester ist jünger als ich.
native_language_example: My sister is younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: **jünger** is the comparative of **jung** (“young”), and **als** introduces the comparison (“than”). In careful/standard German, the pronoun after **als** is often in the nominative (**als ich**), though in everyday speech many people also say **als mich**.
target_language_example: Sie ist fünf Jahre jünger als ich.
native_language_example: She is five years younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to specify a sister who is younger than you or younger than another sibling being compared. Often used with a possessive ("meine/deine/seine jüngere Schwester"). In German, "jüngere" takes the -e ending because it comes before the noun (attributive adjective).
target_language_example: Meine jüngere Schwester wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: My younger sister lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to specify that someone’s brother is younger than the person being talked about (often the speaker: „mein jüngerer Bruder“). „Jüngerer“ is the comparative form of „jung“ (young) and takes the -er ending before a noun (e.g., „mein jüngerer Bruder“).
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute mit meinem jüngeren Bruder ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m going to the movies today with my younger brother.

additional_notes: Literally refers to water at a low temperature, often mentioned in everyday situations (drinking, cooling off, washing your face). It’s also used in expressions like „Kaltes Wasser bringt Sie zur Vernunft“ (cold water makes you come to your senses), meaning a shock can snap someone back to reality.
target_language_example: Nach dem Sport trinke ich gern ein Glas kaltes Wasser.
native_language_example: After sports, I like to drink a glass of cold water.

additional_notes:
Used with an infinitive clause: **kam, um + zu + infinitive** to say someone came with a purpose.

Pattern: **jemand kam, um etwas zu tun** = “someone came to do something / in order to do something.”

Note: **kam** is the simple past of **kommen** (“to come”).
target_language_example: Ich kam, um dir zu danken.
native_language_example: I came to thank you.

additional_notes: Often used in storytelling to describe two past events: one event happens (ich kam = I came/arrived), and at that time something was the case (es war = it was). Very common after time words like **als** (when, for a single past moment) or **bis** (until).
target_language_example: Als ich nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When I came home, nobody was there.

meaning: 'came out of (the)' / 'came from (the)' (simple past of *kommen aus*).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something emerged from a place or came from a source. *aus dem* = *aus* + *dem* (dative masculine/neuter), often used with places like *aus dem Haus, aus dem Gebäude, aus dem Theater*. If the noun is feminine, you use *aus der*; if plural, *aus den*.
target_language_example: Plötzlich kam ein Hund aus dem Garten.
native_language_example: Suddenly a dog came out of the garden.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of the separable verb **hereinkommen** (= to come in). **herein** emphasizes movement *into this room/inside, toward the speaker’s location* ("in here"). In other tenses you’ll often see: **kommt herein!** (Come in!), **ist hereingekommen** (has/had come in).
target_language_example: Plötzlich kam ein Mann herein.
native_language_example: Suddenly a man came in.

meaning: "(I) came here to / in order to" (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say the purpose of coming somewhere. It’s past tense (Präteritum) of "kommen": ich kam, du kamst, er/sie kam. Very common pattern: "(Person) kam hierher, um + zu + Infinitiv" (e.g., "um zu studieren"). In everyday speech, people often use Perfekt instead: "Ich bin hierhergekommen, um …"
target_language_example: Wir kamen hierher, um dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: We came here to help you.

additional_notes: Past tense (ich/er/sie) of **kommen** used with **mit**. **mit + Dativ** can mean (1) accompaniment: *Tom kam mit mir / mit seinen Freunden* (“Tom came with me / his friends”), or (2) means of transport: *Ich kam mit dem Auto / Taxi* (“I came by car / by taxi”). It can also describe a feature someone came in with: *Sie kam mit leuchtenden Augen herein* (“She came in with shining eyes”). Don’t confuse this with the separable verb **mitkommen** (“to come along”).
target_language_example: Sie kam mit ihrer Schwester zur Party.
native_language_example: She came to the party with her sister.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (Präteritum) of **kommen**: *ich kam, du kamst, er/sie/es kam*. Common in written stories and narration to say someone arrived home and then did something next. With people’s names: *Maria kam ...*, *Tom kam ...*.
target_language_example: Ich kam nach Hause und rief meine Mutter an.
native_language_example: I came home and called my mother.

additional_notes: Simple past (Präteritum) of "kommen" used to say someone/something arrived late. Often followed by "zu" + place/event: "kam zu spät zur Schule/zum Bahnhof". With "ankommen" you can also say "kam ... an" (prefix goes to the end): "Er kam zu spät an."
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich kam zu spät zum Treffen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was late to the meeting.

additional_notes: Common in news reports to say that people died in an accident, disaster, conflict, etc. It’s the past tense (plural) of **ums Leben kommen**; singular: **kam ums Leben**.
target_language_example: Bei dem Unfall kamen zwei Menschen ums Leben.
native_language_example: Two people lost their lives in the accident.

additional_notes: Uses the modal verb „können“ (here: „kann“ = he/she/it can) + infinitive at the end („sprechen“). Swap the subject as needed: „Ich kann …“, „Du kannst …“, „Wir können …“. You can replace „Französisch“ with other languages (e.g., „Deutsch“, „Englisch“).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester kann Französisch sprechen, aber ich nicht.
native_language_example: My sister can speak French, but I can’t.

additional_notes: Used with the verb können (here: kann = “can”, 3rd person singular present) plus the formal pronoun Ihnen (“to/for you”). Common in polite speech when someone can help, tell, show, or give advice: „Ich kann Ihnen helfen.“ / „Tom kann Ihnen sagen …“. In questions, the verb often comes first: „Kann Ihnen jemand helfen?“ = “Can someone help you?”
target_language_example: Ich kann Ihnen morgen dabei helfen.
native_language_example: I can help you with that tomorrow.

meaning: “can do that” / “is able to do that.”
additional_notes: From **können** (“can/to be able to”) + **das** (“that/it”). Used to say someone has the ability/skill to do something: **Er kann das.** (“He can do it.”). In questions it asks if something is possible: **Kann das gewaschen werden?** (“Can that be washed?”). Often **das** refers to an action mentioned before or understood from context; you may also see an extra verb later: **Tom kann das (immer noch) machen.**
target_language_example: Ich kann das nicht allein machen.
native_language_example: I can’t do that alone.

meaning: “can imitate the human voice” / “can mimic a human voice” (usually with a verb like *imitieren* or *nachmachen*).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment: *kann* (“can”) + *die menschliche Stimme* (“the human voice”). In full sentences you normally add what the subject can do with the voice, e.g. *die menschliche Stimme imitieren/nachmachen* (“to imitate/mimic the human voice”). *menschliche Stimme* can also mean “a human voice” in general, depending on context.
target_language_example: Manche Vögel können die menschliche Stimme erstaunlich gut nachmachen.
native_language_example: Some birds can mimic the human voice amazingly well.

additional_notes: Used with the dative pronoun **dir** (“to you”) after **kann** (“can”). It often appears with verbs like **helfen** (help), **sagen** (tell), **zeigen** (show), **beibringen** (teach): *Ich kann dir helfen* = “I can help you.” Word order changes in main clauses: *Tom kann dir sagen …* / *Kann dir jemand helfen?*
target_language_example: Ich kann dir morgen beim Umzug helfen.
native_language_example: I can help you move tomorrow.

additional_notes: "kann" is the 3rd person singular of "können" (can, to be able to). "es" is often a pronoun meaning “it/that” and can refer to something mentioned earlier (e.g., a task: "Sie kann es erklären."). In questions it often means “can it be…?” ("Was kann es sein?") or “how bad can it be?” ("Wie schlimm kann es sein?"). Sometimes "es" is just a placeholder (dummy) pronoun with "sein" (to be): "kann es sein" = “can it be…?”.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich kann es morgen erledigen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express strong excitement or impatience. The "es" is a dummy object (not a specific “it”). Common patterns: "Ich kann es kaum erwarten, dich zu sehen" (with an infinitive clause) or "Ich kann es kaum erwarten, auf den Urlaub" / "… den Urlaub zu erleben" (often with "auf" + accusative). Conjugate "können": "Ich kann…", "du kannst…", "er/sie kann…", "wir können…", "ihr könnt…", "sie/Sie können…".
target_language_example: Ich kann es kaum erwarten, endlich Urlaub zu haben.
native_language_example: I can’t wait to finally be on vacation.

additional_notes: Used when the subject (often a person or thing) is not able to do something or when something is impossible. The pronoun **es** usually refers to an action/idea mentioned before (like “it” in English), or it can be a placeholder in expressions like **Das kann es nicht geben** (“That can’t be true/That’s impossible”). You’ll also see it with another verb: **kann es nicht verhindern** (“can’t prevent it”), **kann es nicht lassen** (“can’t stop it / can’t help it”).
target_language_example: Ich kann es nicht glauben.
native_language_example: I can’t believe it.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is a 3rd-person singular (er/sie/es, a name, jemand, etc.) and **euch** is the object meaning **you all** (informal plural). The word order can vary (e.g., in main clauses: "X kann euch …"; in questions: "Kann X euch …?").
target_language_example: Niemand kann euch helfen.
native_language_example: Nobody can help you (all).

meaning: “can be quite possible” / “is good at (doing something)”
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- **Es kann gut sein, dass …** = “It’s quite possible that …” (expresses possibility).
- **jemand kann gut + Verb** = “someone is good at + verb-ing” (ability/skill), e.g. *gut malen, gut lügen, gut vorlesen*.
In the skill meaning, **gut** describes *how well* someone can do something.
target_language_example: Es kann gut sein, dass ich heute später komme, aber ich kann gut allein arbeiten.
native_language_example: It’s quite possible that I’ll come later today, but I’m good at working alone.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has the ability to swim and does it well. The verb is "können" (can/to be able to): ich kann, du kannst, er/sie/es kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie/Sie können. "gut" = well, and "schwimmen" = to swim (infinitive goes to the end).
target_language_example: Ich kann gut schwimmen, aber mein Bruder nicht.
native_language_example: I can swim well, but my brother can't.

meaning: "can I" / "may I" (asking permission or offering to do something).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. With a verb: ask permission ("Kann ich Ihren Radiergummi ausleihen?") or make an offer ("Kann ich Ihnen etwas bringen?"). With polite pronouns like "Ihnen/Sie" it sounds formal and respectful. In shops you can also use it with what you want to see/try: "Kann ich diese Bluse mal sehen?".
target_language_example: Kann ich hier mit Karte bezahlen?
native_language_example: Can I pay by card here?

meaning: “can I … for you?” / “can I … you?” (polite, formal).
additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun Sie (dative: Ihnen) when speaking politely to a customer, stranger, etc. Often starts a question offering help or asking permission: “Kann ich Ihnen helfen?” (Can I help you?), “Kann ich Ihnen etwas bringen?” (Can I bring you something?). It can also appear in statements like “Da kann ich Ihnen nicht helfen.” (I can’t help you with that.)
target_language_example: Kann ich Ihnen heute irgendwie helfen?
native_language_example: Can I help you with anything today?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask for permission or to request something. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., „…benutzen?“) or by what you want (e.g., „…Ihre Nummer haben?“). „Ihre“ is formal (to a stranger), „deine“ is informal (to a friend).
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte ein Glas Wasser bekommen?
native_language_example: Could I please get a glass of water?

meaning: "Can I …?" / "May I …?" (asking if something is allowed or possible).
additional_notes: Used to ask permission or possibility. "das" means "that/it" and refers to an object or action already understood from context. It’s usually followed by another verb in the infinitive at the end: "Kann ich das behalten?" (keep it), "Kann ich das essen?" (eat it), "Kann ich das später erledigen?" (do it later).
target_language_example: Kann ich das fotografieren?
native_language_example: Can I take a photo of that?

meaning: 'can I … you?' (used to start a request like “Can I ask you …?”).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question with another verb: “Kann ich dich + Verb …?” In everyday speech you’ll often hear “Kann ich dich was fragen?” (= “Can I ask you something?”). More standard: “Kann ich dich etwas fragen?”
target_language_example: Kann ich dich kurz etwas fragen?
native_language_example: Can I ask you something quickly?

meaning: "can I ... for you?" / "can I ... you?" (offering help or something).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to offer something or offer help. "dir" means "to you" (informal singular, dative). The verb usually comes at the end: "Kann ich dir helfen?", "Kann ich dir etwas anbieten?".
target_language_example: Kann ich dir mit den Taschen helfen?
native_language_example: Can I help you with the bags?

meaning: “Can I help you?” / “Can I help you (with something)?”
additional_notes: Common, polite offer of help. Used in shops, at work, or when someone seems to need assistance. Often followed by a question word to specify the help: „Womit kann ich dir helfen?“ (With what can I help you?) or „Wie genau kann ich dir helfen?“ (How exactly can I help you?). „dir“ is informal “you” (to one person you address as du); formal is „Kann ich Ihnen helfen?“
target_language_example: Kann ich dir helfen, die Kisten zu tragen?
native_language_example: Can I help you carry the boxes?

meaning: “Can I … a/an …?” (asking for permission or possibility).
additional_notes: Used to start a polite yes/no question. After the object with **eine** (feminine noun) or **ein** (masculine/neuter), the main verb usually comes at the end: **Kann ich eine Kopie davon haben?** (“Can I have a copy of that?”). Also used for “Can I use/open/visit …?” depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Kann ich eine Flasche Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I have a bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used to start a question or offer with the verb in 1st position: "Kann ich euch + [verb/infinitive or object]?". "euch" is the object form of "ihr" (you all) and is used when speaking to a group you address with "du" (friends, family, kids). For a formal group, use "Kann ich Ihnen ...?"
target_language_example: Kann ich euch kurz etwas fragen?
native_language_example: Can I ask you (all) something quickly?

meaning: "Can I here…?" / "Can I … here?" (asking permission or possibility in this place).
additional_notes: Used to ask whether something is allowed or possible at the current location. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the sentence: "Kann ich hier + [object] + [verb]?" (e.g., "Kann ich hier parken?"). It can also be part of questions like "Was kann ich hier tun?" (“What can I do here?”).
target_language_example: Kann ich hier mit Karte zahlen?
native_language_example: Can I pay by card here?

meaning: "Can I …?" (used with reflexive verbs, literally "can I myself …?")
additional_notes: Used when the main verb is reflexive and needs the pronoun "mich" ("myself/me"): e.g., "mich anschließen" (join), "mich unterhalten" (chat), "mich hinlegen" (lie down), "mich verstecken" (hide). In questions it often starts the sentence: "Kann ich mich …?" In formal situations you’ll often see it with "Ihnen/Sie" (you, formal).
target_language_example: Kann ich mich kurz vorstellen?
native_language_example: Can I introduce myself briefly?

meaning: "can I" / "am I able to" (for myself), often used when asking permission or talking about what you can do/afford/imagine.
additional_notes:
"Kann ich" = "can I". Adding "mir" (dative reflexive: "to/for myself") is very common with certain verbs:
- "sich (Dat.) leisten" → "kann ich mir das leisten?" = can I afford that?
- "sich (Dat.) vorstellen" → "kann ich mir (gut/lebhaft) vorstellen" = I can imagine that (well/vividly).
- "sich (Dat.) etw. leihen/ausleihen" → "kann ich mir das ausleihen?" = can I borrow that?
- "sich (Dat.) etw. ansehen" → "kann ich mir das ansehen?" = can I take a look at that?
- "sich (Dat.) etw. aussuchen" → "kann ich mir etwas aussuchen?" = can I choose (something) for myself?
Often used as a polite question to ask permission.
target_language_example: Kann ich mir das kurz ansehen?
native_language_example: Can I take a quick look at that?

meaning: "I can't" / "I cannot" (I’m not able to / not allowed to).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to do something (because it’s too hard, impossible, or you don’t have the ability), or that you’re not permitted to do it. Word order changes depending on the sentence: in main clauses with a modal verb, the conjugated verb comes in position 2 (Ich kann nicht …), but after something comes first (Warum/Wieso/Das/So vieles), you often get inversion: … kann ich nicht …
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, heute kann ich nicht kommen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come today.

meaning: "one can" / "can you?" (general possibility or polite question).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal pronoun "man" (= "one/people/you" in a general sense). "kann man" often talks about what is possible or typical in general (e.g., "In Boston kann man..."), or it can be a polite way to ask if something is possible/helpful ("Kann man...?"). In the past tense, it becomes "konnte man".
target_language_example: Hier kann man sehr gut essen.
native_language_example: You can eat very well here.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal pronoun „man“ (= people/one/you in general) plus negation „nicht“. It’s used for general impossibility, not being allowed, or something that doesn’t work that way: „Ohne X kann man nicht …“ (= Without X, you can’t …). It can also be a short reply meaning “You can’t (know/do that).”
target_language_example: Ohne Internet kann man nicht alles nachschlagen.
native_language_example: Without internet, you can’t look everything up.

meaning: “you can only …” / “one can only …” (it’s only possible in this way).
additional_notes: Used to say something is possible only under a certain condition or in a certain way. Very common with an infinitive at the end: „Das kann man nur + Infinitiv“ (e.g., „kaufen“, „lesen“). „man“ is the general “you/one” (not a specific person).
target_language_example: Den Code kann man nur mit der App scannen.
native_language_example: You can scan the code only with the app.

additional_notes: Used with "man" (= people in general / you) to make a general statement about what is possible or typical. The "sich" is the reflexive pronoun and belongs to a reflexive verb (e.g., sich vorstellen, sich fürchten, sich entschuldigen, sich ausleihen). With "man" it stays "sich" (not "mir/dir"). In English it’s often translated as "you can" or "one can" rather than literally.
target_language_example: Das kann man sich gut merken.
native_language_example: You can remember that easily.

additional_notes: Used to ask the group if anyone is willing/able to do something for you. The pronoun **mir** is dative (“to/for me”), so it often comes before **jemand** in this pattern. Typically followed by an infinitive or another verb phrase: **Kann mir jemand helfen / sagen / geben …?**
target_language_example: Kann mir jemand erklären, wie das funktioniert?
native_language_example: Can someone explain to me how that works?

meaning: "can't / cannot" (is not able to; is not possible).
additional_notes: Used with the modal verb "können" + "nicht" to say someone cannot do something or something cannot happen. Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Er kann nicht kommen." It can also be used with passive forms: "Er kann nicht gerettet werden" (= he cannot be saved). For other persons/tenses, the form changes (e.g., "ich kann nicht", "du kannst nicht", "wir können nicht").
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht kommen, ich muss arbeiten.
native_language_example: I can't come; I have to work.

meaning: "can (do something) very well" / "is very good at (something)".
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (often at the end of the clause): "Er kann sehr gut schwimmen." In spoken German you can also use it as a short answer meaning "That works very well": "Kann sehr gut!" (short for "Das kann sehr gut klappen.").
target_language_example: Ich kann sehr gut Deutsch verstehen, aber ich spreche noch nicht so gut.
native_language_example: I can understand German very well, but I don't speak it that well yet.

additional_notes: Used to compare ability/skill. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (often placed at the end): „Er kann viel besser schwimmen.“ Very often used with „als“ (“than”): „… als ich/du/sie.“ You can also use it without „als“ when the comparison is implied.
target_language_example: Ich kann viel besser Deutsch sprechen als letztes Jahr.
native_language_example: I can speak German much better than last year.

additional_notes: Used in a conditional sentence pattern: **Wenn** + someone **das kann**, **dann** + someone else **das auch**. It expresses a consequence or comparison (often meaning “so can I/you”). In everyday speech, **dann** is sometimes optional, but it’s common and clear for beginners.
target_language_example: Wenn sie das kann, dann kann ich das auch.
native_language_example: If she can do that, then I can do that too.

meaning: "can you" (asking about ability) or "could you" (a request).
additional_notes: Literally "are you able (to)" from *können* (to be able to) + *du* (you, informal singular). Very common to ask someone to do something: **Kannst du …?** In questions about skill/ability, it means "can you": *Kannst du malen?*; with a favor/request it often corresponds to English "could you": *Kannst du den Fernseher ausschalten?* The verb comes first in questions: **Kannst du + infinitive …?**
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte helfen?
native_language_example: Could you please help me?

meaning: “can you … in/on …?” (often: in a language); also appears with a person/thing meaning “can you look after …?”
additional_notes:
This is an incomplete phrase that needs something after **auf**.
- **Kannst du auf + Sprache + Verb?** = “Can you (do/say something) in + language?”: *Kannst du auf Italienisch zählen?* (“Can you count in Italian?”)
- With an object/person, **auf** is often used with verbs like **achten** or **aufpassen**: *Kannst du auf meinen Hund aufpassen?* (“Can you look after my dog?”)
In writing, the language is usually capitalized: **auf Englisch/Deutsch/Italienisch**.
target_language_example: Kannst du auf Deutsch etwas bestellen?
native_language_example: Can you order something in German?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone informally (du) to do something. It’s a common, polite way to request an action: "Kannst du bitte + infinitive" (e.g., machen/ausmachen/warten/sprechen). For a more formal request to someone you address as Sie, use "Können Sie bitte …?".
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte mir kurz helfen?
native_language_example: Can you please help me quickly?

additional_notes: Common question starter with "/können/" to ask if someone is able (or willing) to do something. "das" refers to a specific thing or task already known from context (money, a text, a file, a problem, etc.). It’s often followed by an infinitive: "Kannst du das erklären/reparieren/holen?"
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte wiederholen?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that, please?

additional_notes: A polite way to ask someone to do something (often again). It’s the start of a request; you usually add a verb/infinitive phrase after it (e.g., „… wiederholen“, „… noch mal sagen“, „… wiegen“).
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte langsamer sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you please speak that more slowly?

meaning: “can you … the …?” (asking if someone is able to do something with a masculine direct object).
additional_notes: Used to start a question with **können** (“can / to be able to”). **kannst** = “can (you)” (informal singular **du**). **den** is the masculine **accusative** form of “the” (**der** → **den**) because it’s usually the direct object: *Kannst du den Koffer tragen?* = “Can you carry the suitcase?” Often followed by a noun (*den Deckel, den Koffer*) and then a verb or verb phrase.
target_language_example: Kannst du den Stuhl kurz zur Seite stellen?
native_language_example: Can you move the chair to the side for a moment?

additional_notes: Used when the verb needs the reflexive pronoun “dich” (e.g., sich erinnern = to remember, sich widersetzen = to resist). Word order: Kannst du dich + infinitive …? (Often with extra words after “dich”, like “noch” or “daran”.) In statements: Du kannst dich …
target_language_example: Kannst du dich an seinen Namen erinnern?
native_language_example: Can you remember his name?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone remembers something. It comes from the verb phrase **sich an + Akkusativ erinnern** (“to remember”). Word order: **Kannst du dich an X erinnern?** (the verb **erinnern** often goes to the end of the clause).
target_language_example: Kannst du dich an unseren ersten Schultag erinnern?
native_language_example: Can you remember our first day of school?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone you address as du to do something or if they are able to do it. die is the definite article for feminine singular or plural nouns, and in these examples it’s often in the accusative (direct object): Kannst du die Glühbirnen austauschen? = Can you replace the light bulbs? For formal situations use: Können Sie die ...?
target_language_example: Kannst du die Tür bitte zumachen?
native_language_example: Can you please close the door?

meaning: “can you … (for yourself)”; often used in set phrases like “kannst du dir vorstellen …?” = “can you imagine …?”
additional_notes:
This is “kannst du” + the dative reflexive pronoun “dir” (to/for yourself). It commonly appears with reflexive verbs/expressions where German uses “sich”:
- sich vorstellen: Kannst du dir vorstellen …? = Can you imagine …?
- sich sparen: Das kannst du dir sparen. = You can spare yourself that / Don’t bother with that.
- sich denken: Das kannst du dir ja denken. = You can probably guess/figure that.
- sich freinehmen: Kannst du dir einen Tag freinehmen? = Can you take a day off?
- sich (etw.) selbst …: Kannst du dir selbst die Schuhe flicken? = Can you mend your shoes yourself?
target_language_example: Kannst du dir vorstellen, nächste Woche umzuziehen?
native_language_example: Can you imagine moving next week?

meaning: “can you (… a …)?” (asking if someone is able to do something).
additional_notes: Used to start a yes/no question about ability/skills. The main verb often comes at the end in the infinitive: “Kannst du ein Auto fahren?” (“Can you drive a car?”). “ein” is the indefinite article (“a/an”) and changes depending on the noun (ein/eine/einen, etc.). In many everyday cases, German can also omit the article: “Kannst du Auto fahren?”
target_language_example: Kannst du ein Fahrrad reparieren?
native_language_example: Can you repair a bicycle?

meaning: "Can you" (asking if someone is able to do something with a masculine object).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question with the verb "können" (to be able to/can): "Kannst du …?" = "Can you …?". "Einen" is the accusative form of "ein" for masculine nouns (e.g., einen Computer, einen Reifen). With feminine nouns you use "eine" (eine Pizza), with neuter "ein" (ein Auto), and in the plural no article or "welche" etc. The full pattern is often: "Kannst du einen + Nomen + Verb?".
target_language_example: Kannst du einen Brief auf Deutsch schreiben?
native_language_example: Can you write a letter in German?

meaning: "can you (do) it" / "are you able to (do) it".
additional_notes: Used with the informal singular "du" to ask if someone can do something, with "es" referring to a specific task/thing already known from context (e.g., "Can you do it alone?", "Can you figure it out?"). In statements, it can also mean "you can have it" depending on context ("kannst du es haben"). Word order changes in subordinate clauses: "..., ob du es kannst."
target_language_example: Kannst du es morgen erledigen?
native_language_example: Can you get it done tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s ability or skill at doing something. It’s followed by an activity (often a verb phrase): „Kannst du gut + [verb]?“ or „Kannst du + [noun] + gut + [verb]?“ For example: „Kannst du gut schwimmen?“ / „Kannst du gut Witze erzählen?“
target_language_example: Kannst du gut Deutsch sprechen?
native_language_example: Are you good at speaking German?

meaning: "can you" + "me" (asking if someone can do something for you / can hear you).
additional_notes: Used to start a question to one person (du) with a request involving you (mich). Often followed by an infinitive at the end: „Kannst du mich … bringen/beschützen/halten/hören?“ In phone/video calls it commonly means “Can you hear me?”
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte abholen?
native_language_example: Can you pick me up, please?

additional_notes: Used to check whether someone can hear you (on the phone, in a video call, over a radio, or across a distance). Informal because it uses "du" (to a friend, family member, child, etc.); the formal version is "Können Sie mich hören?". You can also add a name after it: "Kannst du mich hören, Tom?".
target_language_example: Kannst du mich hören? Die Verbindung ist schlecht.
native_language_example: Can you hear me? The connection is bad.

meaning: “can you (… ) for me?” / “could you (… ) for me?”
additional_notes: Used to ask someone for help or a favor. Literally “can you to me…”, but in English you usually translate it as “can/could you … for me?” It’s followed by what you want the person to do (often with an object like “das” or an infinitive like “helfen”). Often paired with “bitte” to be more polite.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte den Weg zum Bahnhof zeigen?
native_language_example: Could you please show me the way to the train station?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone politely to do something for you. It’s made of: kannst (can/are you able to) + du (you) + mir (to me/for me) + bitte (please). Often followed by an infinitive verb (helfen, sagen, geben, empfehlen) or by what you’re asking for.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte sagen, wie spät es ist?
native_language_example: Could you please tell me what time it is?

additional_notes: Used to start a request with **du** (informal). It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb: **Kannst du mir das erklären/aufschreiben/buchstabieren/leihen?** Here **mir** = “to/for me” and **das** = “that/it” (something already known from context). For a formal/polite version, use **Können Sie mir das …?**
target_language_example: Kannst du mir das kurz erklären?
native_language_example: Can you explain that to me quickly?

meaning: “can you … for me / can you please …?” (starting a request, with a feminine or plural direct object: “die …”).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something for you.
