target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich mit meinem Bruder schwimmen.
native_language_example: On the weekend I’m going swimming with my brother.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your son or doing something accompanied by him. "mit" is followed by the dative case, so "mein Sohn" becomes "meinem Sohn". Often used with verbs like gehen (to go), treffen (to meet), or müssen (must/need to).
target_language_example: Ich koche heute Abend mit meinem Sohn.
native_language_example: I’m cooking with my son this evening.

additional_notes: "Mit" takes the dative case, so "mein" becomes "meinen" when it’s plural (e.g., mit meinen Freunden = with my friends). It’s used for (1) being together/communicating with someone (mit meinen Nachbarn sprechen), and (2) tools/body parts/instruments (mit meinen Augen sehen). For feminine singular you’d say "mit meiner" (mit meiner Mutter), and for neuter/masculine singular "mit meinem" (mit meinem Bruder / mit meinem Handy).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich mit meinen Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: On the weekend I go to the movies with my friends.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (“with”), which takes the **dative** case: **meinen Eltern** (dative plural). Common with verbs like **sprechen** (to talk), **leben/wohnen** (to live), or activities: **mit meinen Eltern wandern** (go hiking with my parents). In questions like **Was ist mit meinen Eltern?**, **mit** can mean “about/with (regarding)”: “What’s going on with my parents?” / “What about my parents?”
target_language_example: Am Wochenende esse ich oft mit meinen Eltern zu Abend.
native_language_example: On the weekend I often have dinner with my parents.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (“with”), which takes the **dative** case. That’s why it’s **meinen Freunden** (dative plural). Often used to say who you are doing something with (going out, playing, traveling, etc.).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende gehe ich mit meinen Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: On the weekend I’m going to the cinema with my friends.

meaning: "with my" (used with feminine nouns in the dative case).
additional_notes: Used after the preposition "mit" (with), which always takes the dative. "meiner" is the dative form of "meine" for feminine nouns (e.g., "mit meiner Schwester", "mit meiner Uhr"). It’s also used in fixed expressions like "stimmt etwas mit meiner ... nicht" = "something is wrong with my ...".
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute Abend mit meiner Schwester ins Kino.
native_language_example: I’m going to the cinema with my sister tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your family or doing something in their company. "mit" takes the dative case, so "meine Familie" becomes "meiner Familie" (feminine dative). You can swap in other possessives: "mit deiner/seiner/ihrer/unserer/eurer Familie".
target_language_example: Am Wochenende esse ich oft mit meiner Familie zu Abend.
native_language_example: On the weekend I often have dinner with my family.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (“with”), which takes the **dative** case: **meiner Schwester**. It can mean doing something together (e.g., *Ich esse mit meiner Schwester.*). In the common question **Was ist mit ...?**, it often means “What’s wrong with ...?” or “What about ...?” depending on context (e.g., *Was ist mit meiner Schwester?*).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende treffe ich mich mit meiner Schwester.
native_language_example: On the weekend I’m meeting up with my sister.

additional_notes: Literally means you are together/accompanying your daughter (e.g., going somewhere with her, speaking with her). Used with the dative case after "mit": "meiner Tochter" (from "meine Tochter"). In "mit meiner Tochter ausgehen," it can mean "to go out with my daughter" in the sense of dating.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute mit meiner Tochter ins Kino.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movie theater with my daughter today.

meaning: "with me" / "to me" (used with verbs that take "mit" + dative).
additional_notes: "Mir" is the dative form of "ich" (me). "Mit mir" is used for: (1) being together/doing something together: „Kommst du mit mir?“ (2) talking/interacting with you: „Er spricht mit mir.“ (3) having/carrying something on you: „Ich habe kein Geld mit mir.“ (meaning you don’t have it with you). (4) something happening/being done to you: „Was passiert mit mir?“ / „Was macht das mit mir?“
target_language_example: Hast du deinen Ausweis mit mir dabei?
native_language_example: Do you have your ID with you (with me) ?

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **Schluss machen (mit jemandem)** = “to break up (with someone)” or more generally “to end it.” In the perfect tense: **Er/Sie hat mit mir Schluss gemacht.** Often used for romantic relationships.
target_language_example: Ich kann es nicht glauben: Er hat gestern mit mir Schluss gemacht.
native_language_example: I can’t believe it: he broke up with me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with **sprechen mit + dative** (mit mir = with me) to say someone spoke to you. Often appears in the **Perfekt** tense: **hat mit mir gesprochen** = “(he/she) has talked to me.” You can also use it in questions: **Hast du mit mir gesprochen?** = “Did you talk to me?”
target_language_example: Warum hast du nicht mit mir gesprochen?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you talk to me?

meaning: to go to the movies/cinema with me.
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to the cinema with you. Commonly appears as a question ("Möchtest du …?", "Würdest du …?") or after "ob" in reported speech ("Ich fragte, ob …"). "ins" = "in das" (into/to the).
target_language_example: Hast du Lust, am Samstag mit mir ins Kino zu gehen?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going to the movies with me on Saturday?

meaning: to talk to me (to speak with me).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "reden" + "mit" + dative pronoun (mir). Common in requests or suggestions: "Red(e) mit mir!" (Talk to me!). "sprechen" is a slightly more formal alternative: "mit mir sprechen". In sentences, the verb changes form and position: "Du solltest mit mir reden." / "Sie sagte, sie müsse mit mir reden."
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte kurz mit mir reden?
native_language_example: Can you please talk to me for a moment?

meaning: to talk to me / speak with me.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants to have a conversation with you. With "sprechen" you can also add a topic using "über" (or "worüber" in a question): "mit mir über ... sprechen" = "talk to me about ...".
target_language_example: Kannst du nach dem Unterricht kurz mit mir sprechen?
native_language_example: Can you talk to me briefly after class?

meaning: to talk to me; to speak with me.
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **mit jemandem reden** (“to talk to someone”). In sentences like **(sich) weigern, mit mir zu reden** it means “to refuse to talk to me.” With **so mit mir reden** it means “talk to me like that / in that way” and is often used when someone feels spoken to rudely. Common pattern: **um mit mir zu reden** = “in order to talk to me.”
target_language_example: Bitte hör auf, so mit mir zu reden.
native_language_example: Please stop talking to me like that.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **mit** (“with”), which always takes the **dative** case. **Seinem** is the dative form of **sein** (“his”) for **masculine/neuter** nouns: *mit seinem Bruder* (with his brother), *mit seinem Geld* (with his money). For feminine/plural you use different forms: *mit seiner Schwester*, *mit seinen Freunden*.
target_language_example: Ich gehe mit seinem Bruder nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m going home with his brother.

additional_notes: A common prepositional phrase using **mit** (“with”) + **dative**: **seinem Bruder** (his brother). Used to say someone does something together with his brother (e.g., share a room, go somewhere). The possessive **seinem** changes with gender/case; here it’s masculine dative (der Bruder → mit seinem Bruder).
target_language_example: Ich gehe morgen mit seinem Bruder ins Kino.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the cinema with his brother.

additional_notes: Means someone is together/doing something together with his dog. After **mit**, German uses the **dative** case: **sein Hund** → **seinem Hund**. (For other owners: **mit meinem Hund** = with my dog, **mit deinem Hund** = with your dog, **mit ihrem Hund** = with her/their dog.) Often used with activities like **Gassi gehen** (to walk the dog) or **spielen** (to play).
target_language_example: Ich gehe am Abend mit meinem Hund spazieren.
native_language_example: In the evening, I go for a walk with my dog.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their father (going somewhere/doing an activity), living together, or describing a relationship/comparison (e.g., similarity) involving the father. Case note: after **mit**, **sein Vater** becomes dative: **mit seinem Vater**.
target_language_example: Er hat gestern mit seinem Vater Fußball gespielt.
native_language_example: He played soccer with his father yesterday.

additional_notes: A prepositional phrase with **mit** + **dative**. Here **seinem** is dative (masculine/neuter), agreeing with **Wagen** (“car”). It’s used to say someone does something involving/using/related to his new car (e.g., boasting about it, being satisfied with it, having trouble with it).
target_language_example: Er fährt jeden Tag mit seinem neuen Wagen zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: He drives to work every day with his new car.

additional_notes: "Mit" takes the dative case, so the possessive pronoun changes form: mit seinem (masc./neut. singular), mit seiner (fem. singular), mit seinen (plural). Used to say someone does something together with his people/things, or uses his body parts/tools (e.g., mit seinen Händen/Flügeln/Augen).
target_language_example: Er spricht oft mit seinen Freunden über die Schule.
native_language_example: He often talks with his friends about school.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something together/along with his friends. After "mit" you use the dative case: "seinen Freunden" (plural dative). The possessive changes with gender/number: "mit seiner Freundin" (with his girlfriend), "mit seinen Freundinnen" (with his (female) friends).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende geht er oft mit seinen Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: On the weekend, he often goes to the cinema with his friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/doing something with the other students in the same class. The pronoun changes with the person and case: mit meinen/deinen/ihren/unseren Klassenkameraden; for one classmate: mit seinem Klassenkameraden.
target_language_example: Er spricht in der Pause oft mit seinen Klassenkameraden.
native_language_example: He often talks with his classmates during the break.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "mit" (with), which always takes the dative case. "Seiner" is the masculine/neuter possessive form used in the dative feminine singular (e.g., "mit seiner Geduld" = with his patience; "mit seiner Position" = with his position). The ending changes with gender/number: "mit seinem" (dative masc/neut), "mit seinen" (dative plural), "mit seiner" can also be used with feminine nouns for "her" ("mit ihrer" = with her).
target_language_example: Er hilft mir mit seiner Erfahrung.
native_language_example: He helps me with his experience.

additional_notes: Means someone is accompanied by his wife (Er kommt mit seiner Frau.), or that something happens involving her (sprechen/reden mit seiner Frau = talk to his wife; sich streiten mit seiner Frau = argue with his wife). The form changes with gender/number/case (e.g., mit seiner Freundin, mit seinem Mann, mit seinen Kindern). After "mit" you use the dative: "seiner Frau".
target_language_example: Er fährt am Wochenende mit seiner Frau ans Meer.
native_language_example: He’s going to the sea with his wife on the weekend.

additional_notes: “mit” means “with” and is followed by the dative case. “seiner” is the dative form of “sein” (his) to match “Freundin” (girlfriend). Used both for being together/doing something together (Er war mit seiner Freundin da.) and in fixed verb phrases like “mit jemandem Schluss machen” (break up with someone), “mit jemandem sprechen/telefonieren” (talk on the phone with someone), and “sich mit jemandem streiten” (argue with someone). Don’t confuse this with “Was ist mit seiner Freundin?” which means “What about his girlfriend?/What’s going on with his girlfriend?”—here “mit” is part of “was ist mit …”.
target_language_example: Ich war gestern mit seiner Freundin im Restaurant.
native_language_example: I was at the restaurant yesterday with his girlfriend.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their mother or doing something with her. After "mit" you use the dative case: "seiner Mutter" (= "his mother" in dative, feminine). For "with her mother" you’d say "mit ihrer Mutter".
target_language_example: Er fährt am Wochenende mit seiner Mutter in die Stadt.
native_language_example: He goes into the city with his mother on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to include the speaker’s group ("us") when doing something together. "mit" takes the dative, so it’s always "mit uns" (not *mit wir*). Common with verbs like "kommen/gehen" (to come/go with us) and "spielen" (to play with us).
target_language_example: Willst du heute Abend mit uns essen gehen?
native_language_example: Do you want to go eat with us this evening?

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to join you (and your group) for swimming. Common with "möchten"/"will"/"wollen": "Möchtest du …?" (informal), "Möchten Sie …?" (formal), "Er will …" (he wants to). Word order is flexible with time words: "heute Nachmittag" can come before or after the phrase.
target_language_example: Willst du morgen mit uns schwimmen gehen?
native_language_example: Do you want to go swimming with us tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to join you for the evening meal (dinner/supper). Often appears with polite or modal verbs like „möchten“ (would like) and „sollten“ (should). Word order stays the same when you change who you’re talking to: „Möchtest du / Möchtet ihr / Möchten Sie …?“
target_language_example: Komm doch vorbei und iss mit uns zu Abend.
native_language_example: Come by and have dinner with us.

additional_notes: Used to talk about speaking while you still have food in your mouth; often in etiquette rules or admonitions like „Sprich nicht mit vollem Mund.“ It can also describe someone’s behavior: „Er sprach mit vollem Mund.“
target_language_example: Bitte sprich nicht mit vollem Mund.
native_language_example: Please don’t talk with your mouth full.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state the person someone is with. Very common in indirect questions after verbs like wissen (to know) or fragen (to ask): „Ich weiß nicht, mit wem er kommt.“ In casual speech people often say „mit wem“ (or even „mit wem denn?“), while more formal writing may use „mit wem“ as well (English often avoids “whom”).
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, mit wem sie heute Abend ausgeht.
native_language_example: I don’t know who she’s going out with tonight.

meaning: “who are you with?” / “with whom are you …?”
additional_notes:
Used to ask which person someone is accompanied by. It’s typically followed by a verb or context: 
- Mit wem bist du gegangen/gekommen? = Who did you go/come with?
- Mit wem bist du zu dem Tanz gegangen? = Who did you go to the dance with?
- Mit wem bist du gerade zusammen? = Who are you dating/with (as a couple) right now?
In English you usually say “Who are you with?” (not “With whom are you?” in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Mit wem bist du heute Abend unterwegs?
native_language_example: Who are you out with tonight?

additional_notes: A question using **mit wem** (“with whom/with who”) + **gehst du** (“are you going”). Often followed by a place or activity: **Mit wem gehst du ins Kino / angeln / in die Bibliothek?** In everyday speech, **mit wem** is common; it can sound a bit more formal than **mit wem gehst du denn?** (“So who are you going with?”).
target_language_example: Mit wem gehst du heute Abend essen?
native_language_example: Who are you going out to eat with tonight?

meaning: (to take/bring) along home; home with you.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like nehmen/bringen to say you take something or someone with you to your home (often from the current place). With people, it can mean “to take someone home” / “to bring someone back to your place.” Word order is often split: "Nimm das mit nach Hause." / "Ich nehme es mit nach Hause."
target_language_example: Ich nehme das Buch mit nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m taking the book home with me.

meaning: right in the middle of the street/road.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is (often inconveniently or dangerously) blocking the street. Common with verbs like stehen (to stand), halten/anhalten (to stop), parken (to park), and eine Panne haben (to break down).
target_language_example: Ein Fahrrad lag mitten auf der Straße.
native_language_example: A bicycle was lying right in the middle of the street.

meaning: in the middle of the night.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens very late at night, often unexpectedly or at an unusual time. It’s a fixed phrase: "mitten" (right in the middle) + "in der Nacht" (at night).
target_language_example: Ich bin mitten in der Nacht aufgewacht.
native_language_example: I woke up in the middle of the night.

additional_notes: Time expression meaning the evening of the next day (usually from late afternoon through night). Often used to make plans or say when something will happen; you can also say "morgen Abend" or "am morgen Abend" (less common) depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich kann morgen Abend nicht, aber übermorgen schon.
native_language_example: I can’t tomorrow evening, but I can the day after tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morning of the next day; often implies ‘early in the morning.’ It can be used with plans, travel, appointments, or questions about availability.
target_language_example: Ich rufe dich morgen früh an.
native_language_example: I’ll call you tomorrow morning.

meaning: “tomorrow it will …” (talking about what will happen tomorrow).
additional_notes: Common starter for weather forecasts and predictions. German uses an impersonal subject "es" (“it”) with weather and some events: "Morgen wird es kalt." Word order: the time word "morgen" is in position 1, so the verb "wird" comes second, then "es".
target_language_example: Morgen wird es den ganzen Tag bewölkt sein.
native_language_example: Tomorrow it will be cloudy all day.

meaning: "do I have to?" / "I have to" (I must).
additional_notes: From the verb "müssen" (to have to / must) + "ich" (I). In statements it often means obligation/necessity: "… muss ich …". In yes/no questions it’s commonly used at the start: "Muss ich …?" (= Do I have to …?).
target_language_example: Muss ich das heute noch machen?
native_language_example: Do I have to do that today?

meaning: 'has to now' / 'must now' (sometimes: 'must be by now').
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb **müssen** (here: **muss** = 'must/has to') with **jetzt** ('now'). Often followed by an infinitive: **Er muss jetzt gehen.** It can also be used with a destination: **Ich muss jetzt nach Hause.** With **sein** + age/time, it can express an assumption/inference: **Er muss jetzt über dreißig sein.** (= 'He must be over 30 by now.').
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt los.
native_language_example: I have to go now.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say that something is necessary in general (not aimed at one specific person). Common in advice, rules, or general statements: „muss man + Infinitiv“ (e.g., „muss man vorsichtig sein“, „muss man tun“). In questions/answers it can also sound like “that’s just what you have to do.”
target_language_example: In Deutschland muss man oft lange Formulare ausfüllen.
native_language_example: In Germany, you often have to fill out long forms.

additional_notes: Used to say that something needs fixing. It’s a common structure: **[thing] + muss + past participle + werden** (a passive form meaning “must be done”). Example: *Die Tür muss ersetzt werden.* = “The door must be replaced.”
target_language_example: Der Computer muss repariert werden.
native_language_example: The computer must be repaired.

meaning: “you must / you have to” (talking to one person).
additional_notes: From the verb **müssen** (to have to). You’ll often see **musst du** after another word or clause because German puts the conjugated verb in position 2: **Jetzt musst du …** = “Now you have to …”, **Wenn …, musst du …** = “If …, you have to …”. It’s usually followed by another verb in the infinitive at the end: **Du musst lernen.**
target_language_example: Du musst du nicht alles allein machen.
native_language_example: You don’t have to do everything on your own.

meaning: 'Do you have to (do/say/ask) that?'; 'Do you really need to (do that)?'
additional_notes: Used to question whether something is necessary or appropriate. "musst" is from "müssen" (to have to), "du" is 'you' (informal singular), and "das" refers to 'that/it'—the thing just mentioned or understood from context. Often has an annoyed, skeptical, or critical tone depending on voice and situation.
target_language_example: Musst du das jetzt wirklich machen?
native_language_example: Do you really have to do that right now?

meaning: “you must / you have to” (or in questions: “must you…?”).
additional_notes: Used with the verb „müssen“ + „du“ to express obligation, necessity, or strong advice. In statements it often appears as „du mußt …“ or „du musst …“ (new spelling: „musst“; „mußt“ is older but still seen). In questions the verb comes first: „Mußt du …?“
target_language_example: Mußt du heute so früh aufstehen?
native_language_example: Do you have to get up so early today?

meaning: “would like to (do something with) you” / “wants to (… ) you.”
additional_notes: Common pattern: **(Subject) möchte dich + infinitive** (e.g., *sehen, treffen, kennenlernen*). **dich** is the informal singular “you” in the accusative case (used as the direct object). Polite/formal version: **möchte Sie**.
target_language_example: Ich möchte dich morgen treffen.
native_language_example: I’d like to meet you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „möchten“ (a polite way to say „wollen“ = to want) plus the indefinite article „ein/eine“ before a singular noun. Changes by subject and gender: ich möchte, du möchtest, er/sie/es möchte, wir möchten…; and „ein“ (masc./neut.) vs. „eine“ (fem.). Often followed by an infinitive verb: „möchte ein Buch lesen“ = would like to read a book.
target_language_example: Ich möchte ein Wasser, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like a water, please.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say someone wants to do something together with someone else. In real sentences, you usually get: **möchte + infinitive** and **mit + Dative** (e.g., *mit uns, mit dir, mit meiner Freundin*): *Ich möchte mit dir kommen.* / *Er möchte mit uns reden.*
target_language_example: Ich möchte mit dir ins Kino gehen.
native_language_example: I’d like to go to the movies with you.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish/request with a "dass" clause. The subject after "dass" is the person who should do the action: "Ich möchte, dass du kommst." = "I’d like you to come." In the "dass" clause, the verb goes to the end.
target_language_example: Ich möchte, dass du mir hilfst.
native_language_example: I’d like you to help me.

additional_notes: Used with a comma and a subordinate clause: „(Person) möchte, dass Sie + verb …“. The verb goes to the end of the clause (e.g., „… dass Sie kommen.“). „Sie“ is the formal/polite “you” (singular or plural). In everyday speech, many speakers also use „möchte, dass …“ where English would say “want (someone) to …”, but it’s generally a bit softer/more polite than „will, dass …“.
target_language_example: Ich möchte, dass Sie mir bitte helfen.
native_language_example: I would like you to help me, please.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish or request about what another person should do. It introduces a "dass"-clause: the verb in the second clause goes to the end (e.g., „… dass du morgen kommst“). „möchte“ is softer/more polite than „will“ (which can sound more demanding).
target_language_example: Ich möchte, dass du mir morgen hilfst.
native_language_example: I’d like you to help me tomorrow.

meaning: (I) want/would like you to do that.
additional_notes: Uses the pattern „möchte, dass …“ to express what someone wants another person to do. „möchte“ (Konjunktiv II of „mögen“) is a polite/softer way to say „will“. The verb in the „dass“-clause goes to the end: „…, dass du das tust.“ You can swap the subject: „Er/Sie möchte, dass …“.
target_language_example: Ich möchte, dass du mir hilfst.
native_language_example: I’d like you to help me.

meaning: polite way to ask: “would you like (to)…?” / “do you want (to)…?”
additional_notes: Used with "Sie" (formal "you") when speaking politely to strangers, customers, or in formal situations. "möchten" is the subjunctive of "mögen" and sounds softer than "wollen" (which can sound too direct). Often followed by an infinitive: "Möchten Sie … machen/gehen/hören?" or by a noun: "Möchten Sie einen Kaffee?"
target_language_example: Möchten Sie etwas trinken?
native_language_example: Would you like something to drink?

meaning: polite way to ask: “would you like (to)…?” / “do you want (to)…?”
additional_notes: Used with "Sie" (formal "you") when speaking politely to strangers, customers, or in formal situations. "möchten" is the subjunctive of "mögen" and sounds softer than "wollen" (which can sound too direct). Often followed by an infinitive: "Möchten Sie … machen/gehen/hören?" or by a noun: "Möchten Sie einen Kaffee?"
target_language_example: Möchten Sie etwas trinken?
native_language_example: Would you like something to drink?

additional_notes: Used to politely offer to do something for someone you address as Sie (customers, strangers, in formal situations). The verb in the dass-clause goes to the end: „Möchten Sie, dass ich Ihnen helfe?“ You can often replace it with the simpler offer: „Soll ich …?“ (still polite, a bit more direct).
target_language_example: Möchten Sie, dass ich Ihnen dabei helfe?
native_language_example: Would you like me to help you with that?

additional_notes:
Used to politely ask if someone wants an additional thing or to do something else. "möchten Sie" is the formal (Sie) form of "möchten" (= would like). "noch" often means "another / some more" or "else" depending on context: 
- Möchten Sie noch einen Kaffee? = another/more coffee 
- Möchten Sie noch etwas sagen? = anything else to say 
Often followed by a noun (with an article) or "etwas" + noun/infinitive.
target_language_example: Möchten Sie noch ein Stück Kuchen?
native_language_example: Would you like another piece of cake?

meaning: “would you like…?” / “do you want…?” (addressing one person informally).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone (du = informal “you”, singular) what they want or would prefer. Comes from the verb “möchten” (polite ‘would like’), and is often used to make offers or ask about plans. Word order can vary (e.g., “Wo möchtest du hin?”).
target_language_example: Möchtest du heute Abend ins Kino gehen?
native_language_example: Would you like to go to the movies tonight?

meaning: “Would you like me to…?” / “Do you want me to…?”
additional_notes: Used to offer to do something for someone or ask for instructions. It’s a polite question: "Möchtest du" (would you like) + "dass ich" (that I) + a verb at the end of the clause: "…dass ich es mache" (…that I do it). You can also use the formal version with "Sie": "Möchten Sie, dass ich …?"
target_language_example: Möchtest du, dass ich dir dabei helfe?
native_language_example: Would you like me to help you with that?

additional_notes: Used to politely offer someone something (drink, food, item). It’s the start of a question and is followed by a noun: "Möchtest du ein Wasser?" The article changes with the noun’s gender/case (e.g., "möchtest du einen… / eine… / ein…").
target_language_example: Möchtest du ein Stück Kuchen?
native_language_example: Would you like a piece of cake?

meaning: “Would you like a …?” (offering one item; for feminine nouns).
additional_notes: Used to offer someone something politely. It’s the 2nd-person singular form of "möchten" (a polite way to say "want/would like"). "eine" is used with feminine nouns (die Banane, die Brezel, die Nachspeise, die Orange, die Wurst, die Schokolade). For masculine nouns use "möchtest du einen …?" and for neuter nouns "möchtest du ein …?".
target_language_example: Möchtest du eine Tasse Tee?
native_language_example: Would you like a cup of tea?

additional_notes: Used to offer someone a small amount of food or drink. It’s the polite question form of “du möchtest” (you would like), with “etwas” meaning “some/anything.” Usually followed by a noun: “Möchtest du etwas Wasser?” You can also say “Möchtest du etwas?” (“Would you like something?”).
target_language_example: Möchtest du etwas Kaffee?
native_language_example: Would you like some coffee?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s preference, often when giving two (or more) options: „Möchtest du lieber A oder B?“. „möchtest“ is the polite/soft form of „wollen“ (to want), and „lieber“ means “rather / preferably”. You can also use it with just one option to check a preference (e.g., „Möchtest du lieber Englisch sprechen?“).
target_language_example: Möchtest du lieber drinnen sitzen oder draußen?
native_language_example: Would you rather sit inside or outside?

meaning: “Would you like (some) more…?” / “Do you still want…?”
additional_notes: Used to offer someone another serving (food/drinks) or to ask if they want to do something additional. The key word is **noch** = “(any) more / another / still”. Often followed by a noun ("…noch Kaffee?") or by another phrase with a verb ("…noch irgendwo anders hin?").
target_language_example: Möchtest du noch etwas trinken?
native_language_example: Would you like something more to drink?

meaning: "Would you like anything else?" / "Do you want anything else?"
additional_notes: A very common, polite question (using möchten) to ask if someone wants additional items or has any other requests—often in shops, restaurants, or at the end of a conversation. "sonst noch" means "anything else / otherwise," and "etwas" is "something/anything". You can add a verb to be specific: "... essen/sagen/tun/wissen?"
target_language_example: Möchtest du sonst noch etwas trinken?
native_language_example: Would you like anything else to drink?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a person’s identity ("who"). The verb comes first in the main question ("Möchtest du …?"), and the person-question starts with "wer". Often followed by a normal statement word order after "wer" (e.g., "wer das gemacht hat").
target_language_example: Möchtest du wissen, wer dir diese Nachricht geschickt hat?
native_language_example: Would you like to know who sent you this message?

meaning: “would you like…?” / “do you want…?” (addressing one person informally).
additional_notes: Used to ask someone (du = informal “you”, singular) what they want or would prefer. Comes from the verb “möchten” (polite ‘would like’), and is often used to make offers or ask about plans. Word order can vary (e.g., “Wo möchtest du hin?”).
target_language_example: Möchtest du heute Abend ins Kino gehen?
native_language_example: Would you like to go to the movies tonight?

meaning: “would you like (to)?” (addressing two or more people).
additional_notes: "Möchtet ihr" is the polite/softer way to ask a group ("ihr" = you plural) what they want or would like to do. It’s the 2nd person plural form of "möchten" (from "mögen"). Often followed by an infinitive: "Möchtet ihr mitkommen?" or a noun: "Möchtet ihr Kaffee?" In questions it typically comes first.
target_language_example: Möchtet ihr noch etwas trinken?
native_language_example: Would you like something else to drink?

meaning: “Would you like me to …?” (asking a group).
additional_notes: Used to offer to do something for more than one person (“ihr” = you plural). Often followed by an infinitive clause: „Möchtet ihr, dass ich das mache?“ You can also use the singular form with one person: „Möchtest du, dass ich …?“
target_language_example: Möchtet ihr, dass ich euch dabei helfe?
native_language_example: Would you like me to help you with that?

additional_notes: "Mögen" means "to like" (or "to be fond of."), and "Sie" is the formal "you." Used in polite questions and statements, often about preferences (people, animals, music, food, etc.). In questions: "Mögen Sie …?" = "Do you like …?" You can negate it with "nicht": "Mögen Sie … nicht?" or "Was mögen Sie nicht?"
target_language_example: Mögen Sie Kaffee oder Tee?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee or tea?

additional_notes: Used with a "dass"-clause to say something may be true or may happen. Very common patterns: "Es ist möglich, dass ..." / "Ist es möglich, dass ...?" In the dass-clause, the conjugated verb goes to the end ("..., dass ich Unrecht habe"). Often interchangeable with "vielleicht" or "kann sein, dass".
target_language_example: Es ist möglich, dass der Zug heute später kommt.
native_language_example: It’s possible that the train will arrive later today.

additional_notes: From the verb **mögen** (“to like”). **ihr** is the informal plural “you” (talking to two or more people). Used in questions about preferences: *Mögt ihr Pizza?* = “Do you all like pizza?” In some contexts it can sound a bit formal/old-fashioned for “like”; learners often also hear **mögt ihr … gern?** or **Habt ihr … gern?** for “Do you like …?”
target_language_example: Mögt ihr Kaffee oder Tee?
native_language_example: Do you (all) like coffee or tea?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "aussehen" (to look/appear): "müde aussehen" = to look tired. It often appears as a separable verb form like "Du siehst müde aus" (you look tired) or in past tense "Er sah müde aus" (he looked tired).
target_language_example: Ich sehe heute wirklich müde aus.
native_language_example: I really look tired today.

additional_notes: This is a common two-clause pattern: a subordinating conjunction (weil/da/als) introduces a clause where the verb goes to the end (… ich müde war). Then you use a comma, and the main clause follows with the verb in 2nd position (ging ich …). Use **weil/da** for a reason (“because/since”), and **als** for a past one-time situation (“when”).
target_language_example: Weil ich müde war, ging ich früh nach Hause.
native_language_example: Because I was tired, I went home early.

additional_notes: Used with the formal pronoun **Sie** to say someone is required/obliged to do something. In statements it often follows another element: **Dann müssen Sie …** (“Then you have to …”). In yes/no questions, the verb comes first: **Müssen Sie …?** (“Do you have to …?”).
target_language_example: Müssen Sie heute arbeiten?
native_language_example: Do you have to work today?

additional_notes: From the modal verb "müssen" (to have to, must) + "wir" (we). In statements, "müssen" is in position 2: "Das müssen wir besser machen." In yes/no questions, it comes first: "Müssen wir ...?" The main action stays in the infinitive at the end: "Müssen wir Französisch lernen?"
target_language_example: Müssen wir heute so früh aufstehen?
native_language_example: Do we have to get up so early today?

additional_notes: "Müsst" is the 2nd-person plural form of the modal verb "müssen" (to have to / must), used with "ihr" (you all). Often appears at the start of a question: "Müsst ihr …?" = "Do you all have to …?" In a normal statement, the order is usually "Ihr müsst …".
target_language_example: Müsst ihr morgen so früh aufstehen?
native_language_example: Do you all have to get up so early tomorrow?

additional_notes: Form of the modal verb **müssen** with **ihr** (“you all”). Used to say something is necessary/required: **Ihr müsst …** (“You have to …”). In modern spelling it’s usually written **müsst ihr** (with **ss**); **müßt** is an older spelling. Word order changes in questions: **Müsst ihr …?** (“Do you have to …?”).
target_language_example: Müsst ihr morgen früh aufstehen?
native_language_example: Do you (all) have to get up early tomorrow?

additional_notes: Common, informal reaction used to agree, give in, or end a discussion and move on. Often said with a sigh or slightly annoyed tone: accepting something even if you don’t love it. Can be used alone ("Na gut!") or followed by what you’ll do next ("Na gut, dann …").
target_language_example: Na gut, dann machen wir es so.
native_language_example: Fine, then we’ll do it that way.

meaning: 'Come on!' / 'Get going!' (urging someone to do something).
additional_notes: Used to encourage, push, or hurry someone along—often when you’re impatient or trying to motivate them. Common before commands or suggestions: “Na los, mach schon!” (“Come on, do it already!”). Can also be said alone to mean “Come on!”
target_language_example: Na los, beeil dich, sonst verpassen wir den Bus!
native_language_example: Come on, hurry up, or we'll miss the bus!

additional_notes: Used to say something happens once it has become dark outside. Fairly formal phrasing; in everyday speech you can also say „nach Einbruch der Nacht“ or simply „nach Einbruch“ when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Nach Einbruch der Dunkelheit gehe ich nicht mehr allein spazieren.
native_language_example: After dark, I don't go for walks alone anymore.

meaning: to bring (someone/something) home; to deliver to someone’s home.
additional_notes: Used when you take a person to their home (e.g., by car) or when you deliver something to a home address. Often used with a person as the object ("Ich bringe dich nach Hause") or with "es" for an item being delivered.
target_language_example: Kannst du mich nach Hause bringen?
native_language_example: Can you take me home?

additional_notes: Used with a means of transport (especially by car): someone drives themselves or someone else home. "nach Hause" = "home" (direction), and "fahren" = to travel/drive. You can change the pronoun depending on who is being taken home: mich (me), dich (you), euch (you all).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich nach Hause fahren?
native_language_example: Can you drive me home?

additional_notes: Past participle of **(jemanden) nach Hause bringen**. Used in the perfect tense (**hat ... nach Hause gebracht**) and in the passive (**muss nach Hause gebracht werden** = “must be brought home / taken home”). **nach Hause** means “(to) home” with motion, not “at home” (that’s **zu Hause**).
target_language_example: Der Nachbar hat mich nach Hause gebracht.
native_language_example: The neighbor brought me home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **fahren** (to drive/ride/go by vehicle) in the past (Perfekt): **(sein/hat) … nach Hause gefahren**. Use **sein** when you mean you went home yourself (**Ich bin nach Hause gefahren.**), and **haben** when someone drove someone else (**Er hat mich nach Hause gefahren.**). Often appears in passive forms: **nach Hause gefahren zu werden** (“to be driven home”). **bis nach Hause** emphasizes “all the way home.”
target_language_example: Kannst du mich nach Hause fahren? Ich bin gestern spät nach Hause gefahren.
native_language_example: Can you drive me home? I rode home late yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with **sein** to form the past tense (Perfekt/Plusquamperfekt) of **nach Hause gehen** (“to go home”): **Ich bin nach Hause gegangen.** It describes returning to your home (not just going to a house). Often used after **schon / bereits** (“already”) or in questions: **Bist du nach Hause gegangen?**
target_language_example: Ich bin nach der Arbeit nach Hause gegangen.
native_language_example: I went home after work.

additional_notes: Used for the action of returning home. "nach Hause" is used with movement verbs (gehen, fahren, laufen, kommen). With "sein" (no movement), you typically say "zu Hause" (at home).
target_language_example: Ich gehe jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m going home now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "kommen" (to come): "nach Hause kommen" = to come/get home. It typically implies arriving home (often safely), especially in questions like "Bist du gut nach Hause gekommen?" (= Did you get home okay?). In the past, it’s usually formed with "sein": "Ich bin nach Hause gekommen", "Wir sind nach Hause gekommen".
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern spät nach Hause gekommen.
native_language_example: I got home late yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the verb phrase „nach Hause kommen“ (“to come home”). Commonly used in time clauses with „als“ for a one-time event in the past (e.g., „Als er nach Hause kam, …“). Note: „nach Hause“ is often written as two words; „zuhause“ usually means “at home” (location), not “to home” (movement).
target_language_example: Als ich gestern nach Hause kam, war niemand da.
native_language_example: When I came home yesterday, nobody was there.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like kommen, gehen, fahren) to express going/coming back to your home. Often appears with modal verbs (können, müssen, möchten, werden) to talk about ability, obligation, desire, or future plans. Note: It’s usually written as two words here: „nach Hause“.
target_language_example: Ich komme heute spät nach Hause.
native_language_example: I’m coming home late today.

additional_notes: "nach Hause" expresses movement/direction (going/coming home) and is often used with motion verbs like "kommen" (to come) or "gehen" (to go). Don’t confuse it with "zu Hause", which means being at home (location), e.g., "Ich bin zu Hause."
target_language_example: Ruf mich an, wenn du nach Hause kommst.
native_language_example: Call me when you come home.

additional_notes: Used to link two actions in sequence: first going/coming home ("nach Hause" = motion/direction), then doing something else ("und"). Common after verbs of movement like gehen/kommen/laufen/fahren. Contrast: "zu Hause" means "at home" (no movement).
target_language_example: Ich gehe nach Hause und rufe dich später an.
native_language_example: I’m going home and I’ll call you later.

meaning: to drive home (to go back to where you live).
additional_notes: Used with movement verbs like fahren/gehen/laufen to mean going to your home. Note the difference: „nach Hause“ = (going) home (direction), but „zu Hause“ = at home (location). You can also add someone: „jemanden nach Hause fahren“ = to drive someone home.
target_language_example: Ich fahre nach der Arbeit nach Hause.
native_language_example: I drive home after work.

additional_notes: Used as an infinitive phrase ("zu gehen") after many verbs and expressions (e.g., erlauben, raten, Angst haben, es steht dir frei). "nach Hause" means "(to) home" and is used without an article.
target_language_example: Ich habe beschlossen, nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: I decided to go home.

meaning: to come home; to get back home.
additional_notes: Uses motion toward home: "nach Hause" = (to) home. Often used with verbs like "versuchen" (try), "jemanden bitten" (ask someone), "überzeugen" (convince), or "es eilig haben" (be in a hurry) + "..., nach Hause zu kommen". In a full sentence you’ll conjugate "kommen" (e.g., "Ich komme nach Hause").
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, heute früh nach Hause zu kommen.
native_language_example: I hope to get home early today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion like kommen/kehren/fahren/gehen to mean going back to your home. Very common word order is: "nach Hause" + "zurück" (e.g., "Ich fahre nach Hause zurück"), but you’ll also hear it without "zurück" when the idea of returning is already clear ("Ich gehe nach Hause").
target_language_example: Wir gehen jetzt nach Hause zurück.
native_language_example: We’re going back home now.

additional_notes: Used to say a time is later than 12:00 a.m. Often with adverbs like „kurz“ (shortly) or „deutlich“ (well/clearly): „kurz nach Mitternacht“ = shortly after midnight. You can also use it with „gehen“/„ins Bett gehen“ to talk about going to bed after midnight.
target_language_example: Wir haben uns erst nach Mitternacht auf den Heimweg gemacht.
native_language_example: We didn’t start heading home until after midnight.

additional_notes: Used with directions, movement, wind, migration, or orientation (e.g., a road or windows facing south). With verbs like gehen/fahren/fliegen it means “to the south”; with showing/facing (zeigen/schauen) it means “facing south.”
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen nach Süden, weil es dort wärmer ist.
native_language_example: We’re driving south tomorrow because it’s warmer there.

meaning: based on everything that …; as far as … (from what is known).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a conclusion or judgment drawn from all available information, experience, or achievements. Often followed by a verb like „wissen“, „lesen“, „hören“: „Nach allem, was ich weiß/gehört habe …“. It can also refer to what has been done so far: „Nach allem, was wir erreicht haben …“.
target_language_example: Nach allem, was ich gehört habe, kommt der Zug zu spät.
native_language_example: Based on everything I’ve heard, the train is going to be late.

meaning: after the; according to the (based on the).
additional_notes: „nach“ + „dem“ (dative masculine/neuter singular). Most often it means time: something happens after an event (e.g., nach dem Unterricht = after class). It can also mean “according to/based on” with judgments or criteria (e.g., nach dem Ergebnis urteilen = judge by the result).
target_language_example: Nach dem Essen rufe ich dich an.
native_language_example: After the meal, I’ll call you.

additional_notes: A common time phrase meaning something happens later than dinner. Uses the dative case after the preposition "nach" → "dem Abendessen" (not *nach das Abendessen*). Often placed at the beginning or end of a sentence: "Nach dem Abendessen ..." or "... nach dem Abendessen."
target_language_example: Nach dem Abendessen räume ich die Küche auf.
native_language_example: After dinner, I tidy up the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than the meal (often right afterward). It’s a common time phrase in everyday instructions and routines: „nach dem Essen“ + verb (e.g., brush teeth, do dishes).
target_language_example: Nach dem Essen gehen wir noch spazieren.
native_language_example: After the meal, we’re going for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than lunch (after the meal). With "nach" + dative: "dem" because "das Mittagessen" is neuter. Similar: "nach dem Frühstück" (after breakfast), "nach dem Abendessen" (after dinner).
target_language_example: Nach dem Mittagessen mache ich oft einen kurzen Spaziergang.
native_language_example: After lunch, I often go for a short walk.

additional_notes: Used with "nach" + dative to say something happens/feels/is true after a rain shower. It can start a sentence ("Nach dem Regen ...") or be placed later ("... nach dem Regen").
target_language_example: Nach dem Regen riecht es oft nach frischer Erde.
native_language_example: After the rain, it often smells like fresh earth.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what happens once a storm is over. Often followed by a past-tense verb: "Nach dem Sturm war ..." / "Nach dem Sturm wurde ...". You can use the same pattern with other events: "nach dem Essen" (after the meal), "nach der Arbeit" (after work).
target_language_example: Nach dem Sturm räumten wir die Äste aus dem Garten.
native_language_example: After the storm, we cleared the branches out of the garden.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the time following someone’s death (often with the genitive: „nach dem Tod seiner Frau“ = after the death of his wife). It can also refer more generally to what happens in an afterlife: „Was passiert nach dem Tod?“
target_language_example: Nach dem Tod ihres Großvaters zog die Familie in ein anderes Haus.
native_language_example: After their grandfather’s death, the family moved to another house.

additional_notes: Time phrase: used to say something happened later than an accident (often a specific one already known). Grammar: "nach" + dative → "dem Unfall" (der Unfall). Can also mean "about the accident" with certain verbs (e.g., "jemanden nach dem Unfall fragen" = to ask someone about the accident).
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall konnte sie erst nach einigen Tagen wieder arbeiten.
native_language_example: After the accident, she could only work again after a few days.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „fragen“: „jemanden nach dem Weg fragen“ = to ask someone for directions. „Weg“ here means the route/path, not “way” in a general sense. Common in polite questions, e.g. „Entschuldigung, können Sie mir sagen, wie ich zum Bahnhof komme? Ich möchte nach dem Weg fragen.“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich wollte Sie nach dem Weg zum Bahnhof fragen.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I wanted to ask you for directions to the train station.

meaning: one after another; one at a time.
additional_notes: Used to show that things happen in sequence, repeatedly. Often used with numbers/pronouns like "eins" (or "eine/einer/eines") or with a noun: "eins nach dem anderen" (one after another), "einen Fehler nach dem anderen" (one mistake after another). It commonly appears in negative contexts (problems, mistakes), but can be neutral too (checking parts one by one).
target_language_example: Bitte nimm die Aufgaben eine nach der anderen.
native_language_example: Please do the tasks one after another (one at a time).

meaning: 'after the' (feminine dative); sometimes 'to the' in set directions.
additional_notes: "Nach" takes the dative case. "Nach der" is used with feminine nouns (e.g., nach der Wahl = after the election; nach der Ecke = after/at the corner when giving directions). Also appears in fixed expressions like "nach der anderen" = "one after another."
target_language_example: Nach der Arbeit gehe ich nach Hause.
native_language_example: After work, I go home.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone does when their workday is over. It can refer to after work in general or after a specific shift/day. Often follows time expressions like „jeden Tag“ (every day) or starts questions like „Was machst du …?“
target_language_example: Nach der Arbeit gehe ich oft noch einkaufen.
native_language_example: After work, I often go shopping.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens after the school day ends. It often answers the question "Wann?" (When?) and is followed by what you do or where you go: "nach der Schule nach Hause gehen" (go home after school), "nach der Schule Hausaufgaben machen" (do homework after school).
target_language_example: Nach der Schule gehe ich meistens nach Hause und mache Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: After school I usually go home and do homework.

additional_notes: Used with a verb like **spielen**: **nach der Schule Tennis spielen**. **nach der Schule** = “after school” (time phrase) and it often comes before the activity. You can swap in other activities: **nach der Schule Fußball/Basketball spielen**, etc.
target_language_example: Wir spielen nach der Schule Tennis.
native_language_example: We play tennis after school.

meaning: to take/bring (someone or something) outside; to show someone out.
additional_notes: Used with an object (e.g., jemanden/etwas) to mean moving them from inside to outside. In polite/formal situations (e.g., an office), it often means “to escort/show someone out” (e.g., a secretary leads a visitor outside).
target_language_example: Ich bringe dich nach draußen.
native_language_example: I'll take you outside.

additional_notes: Used for leaving a building/room and going out into the open air. Very common with pets, smoking, getting fresh air, or taking a short break. Often answers the question „Wohin gehst du?“ (Where are you going?): „nach draußen“.
target_language_example: Ich gehe kurz nach draußen, um frische Luft zu schnappen.
native_language_example: I’m going outside for a moment to get some fresh air.

additional_notes: “Nach” is a preposition that takes the dative case, so you often see it as “nach einem” (masculine/neuter dative: “einem”). Common uses: time/sequence = “after a …” (Nach einem kurzen Besuch …); searching/requesting = “for a …” with verbs like “suchen nach …”, “sich umsehen nach …”, “nach … schicken” (send for). It can also mean “looks like a …” with “nach etwas aussehen” (Sieht nach einem Versehen aus?).
target_language_example: Ich suche nach einem Parkplatz.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a parking space.

meaning: to look for a parking space (spot).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "suchen" (to search/look for) with "nach" + dative: "nach einem Parkplatz". Often used with time words like "lange" (for a long time) or "ewig" (forever) to emphasize how hard it was to find parking.
target_language_example: Am Samstag mussten wir lange nach einem Parkplatz suchen.
native_language_example: On Saturday we had to look for a parking space for a long time.

meaning: "after a" (period of time); also "for a" (longing for something).
additional_notes: "Nach" takes the dative case, so with a feminine noun you often get "nach einer ..." (e.g., nach einer Weile = after a while; sich sehnen nach einer Tätigkeit = to long for an activity/job). It’s a common pattern: nach + time expression for "after", and verbs like "sich sehnen" use "nach" to mean "for".
target_language_example: Nach einer Stunde sind wir endlich angekommen.
native_language_example: After an hour, we finally arrived.

additional_notes: **Nach** takes the dative case. **Ihrem** is the dative form of **ihr** (= her / their). It’s very common in set verb + preposition phrases, e.g. **jemanden nach etwas fragen** = to ask someone about something (*nach ihrem Alter* = about her age), and **süchtig nach etwas** = addicted to something (*süchtig nach ihrem Telefon* = addicted to her phone). Don’t confuse it with **Ihrem** (capital I), which is formal “your” (dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe sie nach ihrem Namen gefragt.
native_language_example: I asked her about her name.

meaning: after every meal (your) teeth — usually in “die Zähne putzen” (“to brush your teeth”).
additional_notes: A common timing phrase used with reflexive “sich die Zähne putzen” (to brush one’s teeth). Word order is flexible: “Nach jeder Mahlzeit solltet ihr euch die Zähne putzen.” / “Ihr solltet euch nach jeder Mahlzeit die Zähne putzen.”
target_language_example: Ich putze mir nach jeder Mahlzeit die Zähne.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth after every meal.

meaning: after his; for/asking about his (with „fragen“); addicted to his (with „süchtig“).
additional_notes: „nach“ takes the dative, so you often see it with dative possessives like „seinem“ (= his, masc./neut.). Common patterns: (1) time: „nach seinem Abschluss“ = after his graduation; (2) asking for/about: „nach seinem Namen/Anwalt fragen“ = ask for/about his name/lawyer; (3) fixed expression: „süchtig nach seinem Telefon“ = addicted to his phone.
target_language_example: Nach seinem Essen ist er sofort eingeschlafen.
native_language_example: After his meal, he fell asleep immediately.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „(jdn.) nennen“ or „benennen“ to say someone was given the same name as an older family member. Here, „nach“ means “after” in the sense of “in honor of / following the name of,” not “afterwards in time.”
target_language_example: Er wurde nach seinem Großvater benannt.
native_language_example: He was named after his grandfather.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re making a conclusion from evidence or an impression. Often follows a noun in the dative + „nach“ (e.g., „dem Himmel nach zu urteilen“ = judging by the sky). You can also use it with „nach dem, was …“ (judging by what …).
target_language_example: Dem Verkehr nach zu urteilen, kommen wir zu spät.
native_language_example: Judging by the traffic, we’re going to be late.

meaning: according to what; based on what.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **denken über ... nach** (to think about) or **(sich) richten nach** (to go by/follow). It introduces a clause that says what your action/thought is based on: **nach dem, was + clause**. Common fixed form: **nach dem, was ich weiß** (“according to what I know”).
target_language_example: Wir entscheiden nach dem, was wir heute wissen.
native_language_example: We’ll decide based on what we know today.

additional_notes: Used to start a dependent clause (subordinate clause) about something that happened before the main action. In this clause, the verb goes to the end: „Nachdem er gegangen war, …“. Often paired with past perfect (Plusquamperfekt) to show the earlier action: „Nachdem er gegessen hatte, ging er …“.
target_language_example: Nachdem er gegessen hatte, ging er schlafen.
native_language_example: After he had eaten, he went to sleep.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **annehmen, dass ...**. Used to express an assumption or belief (often without being sure). Common in writing and storytelling; in everyday speech people also often use **habe angenommen, dass ...** (Perfekt). Word order: **Ich nahm an, dass + verb at the end** (e.g., „… dass er kommt“).
target_language_example: Ich nahm an, dass du heute keine Zeit hast.
native_language_example: I assumed you don’t have time today.

meaning: “took a …” (simple past of *nehmen* + a masculine direct object).
additional_notes: *nahm* is the simple past of *nehmen* (“to take”). It’s used with an object in the accusative: *nahm einen* + masculine noun (e.g., *einen Zug*, *einen Kredit*). Often it appears with separable verbs where another part comes later, e.g. *einen Kredit aufnehmen* → *Er nahm einen Kredit auf* (“He took out a loan”).
target_language_example: Sie nahm einen Schluck Wasser.
native_language_example: She took a sip of water.

additional_notes: Used in narratives to say that a man/boy took something that belongs to him. In many common phrases you’ll see it with a separable prefix later in the sentence, e.g. **nahm seine Brille ab** = “took off his glasses.” Word order: **nahm** (verb) + **seine** + noun, and the prefix (**ab**) comes at the end of the clause.
target_language_example: Er nahm seine Jacke ab, weil es warm war.
native_language_example: He took off his jacket because it was warm.

meaning: “took (for oneself)”; in these examples: “took time off / took a day off.”
additional_notes: Simple past of the reflexive verb phrase **sich nehmen** (“to take for oneself”). Very common with **frei**: **sich frei nehmen** = to take time off (work/school). Often used with a time expression: **einen Tag / eine Woche frei**.
target_language_example: Ich nahm mir gestern frei.
native_language_example: I took yesterday off.

meaning: soaking wet; wet to the skin.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone or something is completely wet (usually from rain, getting splashed, falling in water, etc.). Often follows forms of „sein/werden“ (e.g., „Ich bin …“, „Er wurde …“).
target_language_example: Nach dem Spaziergang im Sturm waren wir nass bis auf die Haut.
native_language_example: After the walk in the storm, we were soaking wet.

meaning: to take off your wet clothes.
additional_notes: Uses the separable verb „ausziehen“ (to take off clothes). In the present tense, „aus“ often goes to the end: „Zieh dir die nassen Sachen aus.“ Often paired with „… und trockene anziehen“ (…and put on dry ones). „ausziehen“ can also mean “to move out,” but with clothes it means “to take off.”
target_language_example: Nach dem Regen habe ich mir die nassen Sachen ausgezogen.
native_language_example: After the rain, I took off my wet clothes.

meaning: next to / beside the (masculine or neuter noun, dative).
additional_notes: Used to say something is located next to something else. It uses the dative form of “der/das” → “dem” (e.g., neben dem Kühlschrank, neben dem Hotel). With feminine nouns you’ll often see “neben der …”, and with plural “neben den …”.
target_language_example: Mein Fahrrad steht neben dem Eingang.
native_language_example: My bike is standing next to the entrance.

additional_notes: “Nehmen Sie …” is the polite/formal imperative (addressing someone as Sie). It’s common in instructions and requests: medicine (“Nehmen Sie Ihre Tabletten!”), directions (“Nehmen Sie die nächste Straße rechts!”), and set phrases like “Nehmen Sie Platz!” = “Have a seat.” It also combines with prefixes/particles: “mitnehmen” → “Nehmen Sie … mit!” (“take … along”), “annehmen” → “Nehmen Sie … an!” (“accept …”).
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie bitte noch ein Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: Please have another glass of water.

meaning: formal command: “take your …” / “put your …” (for a masculine thing).
additional_notes: Used with **Sie** (formal “you”) in instructions/requests. **Ihren** is the accusative form of “your” for a **masculine** noun (e.g., *Ihren Hut, Ihren Mantel*). The exact meaning of *nehmen* depends on context: it can mean “take” (*Nehmen Sie Ihren Mantel!*), or “take off” when paired with **ab** (*Nehmen Sie Ihren Hut ab!*), or “put/leash” in set phrases (*Nehmen Sie Ihren Hund an die Leine!*).
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie Ihren Mantel bitte mit.
native_language_example: Please take your coat with you.

additional_notes: This is the formal (Sie) imperative of **sich nehmen** (“to take for oneself”). It’s used with an object: **Nehmen Sie sich das Geld** (take the money), **Nehmen Sie sich die Zeit** (take the time), **Nehmen Sie sich so viel, wie Sie brauchen** (take as much as you need / help yourself). In the fixed phrase **sich ein Beispiel an jemandem nehmen**, it means “to follow someone’s example.”
target_language_example: Nehmen Sie sich ruhig noch ein Stück Kuchen.
native_language_example: Go ahead and help yourself to another piece of cake.

meaning: to tend to (do something); to be prone to.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a typical habit or general tendency. It’s often followed by an infinitive with „zu“: „… neigt dazu, zu + Infinitiv“ (e.g., „Sie neigt dazu, zu spät zu kommen.“). Can also refer to groups: „Wir/Die Leute neigen dazu …“.
target_language_example: Ich neige dazu, zu viel zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: I tend to work too much.

meaning: tends to (has a habit/likelihood of doing something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause: „jemand/etwas neigt dazu, + zu + Verb“. It describes a typical tendency or behavior, not a one-time action. Often translates to “tends to” or “is prone to”.
target_language_example: Ich neige dazu, zu viel nachzudenken.
native_language_example: I tend to overthink.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to reject or correct what was just said or assumed. Often followed by a verb phrase: “Nein, das ist … / das gibt es … / das wird …”. In speech there’s usually a pause after “Nein”.
target_language_example: Nein, das stimmt nicht.
native_language_example: No, that's not true.

meaning: "No, that is…" (used to deny/correct or clarify).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a reply to say something is not true or to correct information: "Nein, das ist es nicht." (= "No, it isn’t."). You can follow it with an adjective ("… furchtbar", "… zu groß"), a noun phrase ("… sein Name"), or "kein" + noun ("… kein Problem").
target_language_example: Nein, das ist nicht richtig.
native_language_example: No, that’s not correct.

meaning: "No, you…" (an emphatic way to contradict or stop someone and tell them what they must/should do).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to someone (du = informal "you") to strongly disagree, correct them, or give a firm instruction. Often followed by a statement or command: "Nein, du bleibst …" / "Nein, du sollst …". In writing, it’s commonly separated by a comma to show a pause and emphasis.
target_language_example: Nein, du gehst jetzt nach Hause.
native_language_example: No, you’re going home now.

meaning: "No, it’s …" (used to correct or disagree, then add information).
additional_notes: Used when you want to say “no” and then explain what the situation really is. Common with adjectives or short statements: “Nein, es ist alles gut.” / “Nein, es ist fertig.” You can also use it with negation: “Nein, es ist nicht …”. In speech, there’s often a pause after “Nein”.
target_language_example: Nein, es ist nicht teuer.
native_language_example: No, it’s not expensive.

meaning: "No, I …" (used to start a negative reply about yourself).
additional_notes: Used when answering a question or correcting someone: you begin with "Nein," and then continue with "ich" + verb (e.g., "Nein, ich bin …", "Nein, ich bleibe …"). The comma is common in writing; in speech there’s usually a short pause.
target_language_example: Nein, ich habe heute keine Zeit.
native_language_example: No, I don’t have time today.

meaning: "No, I am …" (used to deny or correct, then say what you are/feel).
additional_notes: Used when replying to something and correcting it: start with "Nein" and follow with a statement about yourself using "ich bin". "bin" is the 1st-person singular of "sein" (to be). It’s followed by an adjective (alleine, zufrieden) or a noun with an article/possessive (sein Freund).
target_language_example: Nein, ich bin müde.
native_language_example: No, I am tired.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse, correct someone, or stop/interrupt them (often like “no, no—”). Can also sound reassuring when calming someone down (tone matters). Often followed by an instruction: “Nein, nein, bleib hier.”
target_language_example: Nein, nein, das ist nicht nötig.
native_language_example: No, no, that’s not necessary.

additional_notes: Saying "nein" three times is a common way to make the refusal or warning much stronger. Depending on tone, it can mean: a firm rejection ("Absolutely not"), alarm ("Oh no"), or stopping someone ("Don’t do that"). You can repeat it more or fewer times: "Nein, nein!" / "Nein, nein, nein, nein!"
target_language_example: Nein, nein, nein — das machen wir auf keinen Fall.
native_language_example: No, no, no — we’re definitely not doing that.

additional_notes: Used to strongly refuse, correct, or stop something: "Nein" rejects, and "nicht" negates what follows. Common in spoken German when you interrupt or contradict someone: "Nein, nicht so!" (= No, not like that!). It can also mean "No, not really" when followed by an adverb like "wirklich".
target_language_example: Nein, nicht so laut sprechen!
native_language_example: No, don't speak so loudly!

additional_notes: Used with an indefinite subject “man” (= “one/people”). Common patterns: (1) “Wie nennt man …?” = “What do you call …?” (asking for the word/name). (2) “Das nennt man …” = “That’s what you call …” (often to praise or comment on something).
target_language_example: Wie nennt man das auf Deutsch?
native_language_example: What do you call that in German?

additional_notes: Used with the verb „sein“ (to be) to describe someone’s emotional state (feeling anxious/uneasy). It often appears after verbs like „scheinen“ (to seem): „Er scheint nervös zu sein.“ You can add intensifiers like „ein wenig“ (a little), „sehr“ (very), or „überaus“ (extremely).
target_language_example: Ich bin nervös, weil ich gleich ein Gespräch habe.
native_language_example: I'm nervous because I have an interview in a moment.

additional_notes: Used to comment on or thank someone for a kind action: **(Das ist) nett von dir/euch/ihm/ihr/ihnen.** Often appears with **Wie nett von …!** (“How nice of …!”). The person is introduced with **von** + dative pronoun/name.
target_language_example: Das ist sehr nett von dir, dass du mich abholst.
native_language_example: That’s very nice of you to pick me up.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something kind they did or said. "Ihnen" is the formal “you” (to one person or a group). Common patterns: "Das ist (sehr/unheimlich) nett von Ihnen" and "Es war nett von Ihnen, …".
target_language_example: Das war wirklich nett von Ihnen, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: That was really nice of you to help me.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone or show appreciation for a kind action or comment. Often appears as: „(Es war) nett von dir, … zu …“ (“It was nice of you to …”) or as an exclamation: „Wie nett von dir!“ (“How nice of you!”).
target_language_example: Das ist echt nett von dir, mir zu helfen.
native_language_example: That’s really nice of you to help me.

meaning: 'nice of you (to do something) for me' / 'kind of you (to help me)'.
additional_notes: Used to thank someone or show appreciation for something they do for you. Pattern: (Das/Es) ist/war (sehr) nett von dir, mir + zu-infinitive ("… zu helfen") or + noun phrase ("mir ein Geschenk zu machen"). In exclamations you can also say: "Wie nett von dir, mir zu helfen!"
target_language_example: Es ist wirklich nett von dir, mir beim Umzug zu helfen.
native_language_example: It’s really nice of you to help me with the move.

additional_notes: Used with a person (often in dative): "nett zu + jemandem". It describes how you behave toward someone: "Sei nett zu ihr" = "Be nice to her."
target_language_example: Bitte sei nett zu deinem Bruder.
native_language_example: Please be nice to your brother.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" (or "war", "bist", etc.): "jemand ist nett zu mir" = someone is kind toward me. "zu" here means "to/toward" a person (often "nett zu + dative").
target_language_example: Danke, dass du immer nett zu mir bist.
native_language_example: Thanks for always being nice to me.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone's character or behavior as friendly, kind, or pleasant. Often appears after another verb (e.g., scheinen, versuchen) and in the structure „nett zu jemandem sein“ (= to be nice to someone).
target_language_example: Versuch bitte, nett zu mir zu sein.
native_language_example: Please try to be nice to me.

meaning: a nice person; a kind person.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s personality in a friendly, polite way. Often appears with "ein" and intensifiers like "sehr" (very) or "wirklich" (really): "ein sehr netter Mensch". Note the ending changes: "ein netter Mensch" (masculine nominative) but "eine nette Person" (feminine).
target_language_example: Danke für Ihre Hilfe — Sie sind ein wirklich netter Mensch.
native_language_example: Thanks for your help — you’re a really nice person.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "versuchen" (to try) or "probieren" (to try): "Hast du versucht, den Router neu zu starten?" It means turning a device off and on again, or restarting it so it starts fresh. The separable verb is "neu starten"; in an infinitive construction with "zu" it becomes "neu zu starten".
target_language_example: Ich versuche, mein Handy neu zu starten.
native_language_example: I’m trying to restart my phone.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a new job/position (“eine neue Arbeit haben”). In some contexts it can also mean new work/tasks, but for jobs German often also uses “ein neuer Job” or “eine neue Stelle”. “Arbeit” is feminine: die Arbeit, eine neue Arbeit, seine neue Arbeit.
target_language_example: Ich fange nächste Woche eine neue Arbeit an.
native_language_example: I’m starting a new job next week.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "(neue) Freundschaften schließen" = "to make new friends / form new friendships." It often comes up when talking about moving somewhere new, starting school, or meeting people.
target_language_example: In einer neuen Stadt ist es nicht immer leicht, neue Freundschaften zu schließen.
native_language_example: In a new city, it’s not always easy to make new friends.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **treffen** (“to meet”) in the **present perfect**: **(jemanden) treffen → ich habe … getroffen**. **Nachbarn** can be plural (“neighbors”) or singular (“neighbor”), depending on the article/pronoun: **meine neuen Nachbarn** (plural) vs. **meinen neuen Nachbarn** (singular, masculine). After **treffen**, the person is in the **accusative** case.
target_language_example: Ich habe unsere neuen Nachbarn gestern im Treppenhaus getroffen.
native_language_example: I met our new neighbors yesterday in the stairwell.

additional_notes: Used with masculine accusative articles/pronouns (e.g., "einen/meinen/den neuen Wagen") because "Wagen" is masculine (der Wagen). Often means a (new) car, though "Wagen" can also mean a vehicle/wagon in some contexts. In the nominative it’s "ein neuer Wagen"; in the dative: "mit einem neuen Wagen".
target_language_example: Ich habe mir gestern einen neuen Wagen gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new car yesterday.

additional_notes: Means a car that is new (often: newly bought). In German, adjectives change endings: with "ein" you say "ein neues Auto" (neuter noun "das Auto"); with "sein" you say "sein neues Auto".
target_language_example: Ich habe mir ein neues Auto gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a new car.

additional_notes: "Neues" is the neuter form of "neu" (new) to match "das Buch" (neuter). Often used with an article or possessive: "ein neues Buch" (a new book), "mein/dein/sein neues Buch" (my/your/his new book).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein neues Buch gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought a new book.

additional_notes: "Neues" is the neuter form of "neu" (new) to match "das Fahrrad" (bike). Often used with verbs like "kaufen" (to buy), "haben" (to have), and "(sich) leisten" (to afford), e.g., "Ich kann mir kein neues Fahrrad leisten."
target_language_example: Ich spare für ein neues Fahrrad.
native_language_example: I'm saving for a new bike.

additional_notes: Used with the adjective "neu" (new) plus the neuter noun "das Haus" (house/home). In the nominative/accusative with no article, it becomes "neues Haus" ("-es" ending). With an article or possessive, the ending changes: "das neue Haus", "sein neues Haus", "unser neues Haus".
target_language_example: Wir ziehen nächste Woche in unser neues Haus ein.
native_language_example: We’re moving into our new house next week.

additional_notes: "Kleid" means "dress" (a noun). "Neu" is an adjective; with "ein" it becomes "ein neues Kleid" (neuter: das Kleid). With a possessive (mein/ihr/sein…) it’s also "mein/ihr neues Kleid". You can change the adjective: "ein schönes Kleid" (a nice dress).
target_language_example: Ich habe ein neues Kleid gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought a new dress.

additional_notes: Used to state a time. Often with **um** for “at” (e.g., *um neun Uhr*). In time ranges you’ll see **von … bis …** (“from … to …”), and you can also see it without **um**, especially in informal speech (e.g., *Ich komme neun Uhr*).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um neun Uhr vor dem Museum.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at nine o’clock in front of the museum.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s age. With "sein" it describes how old someone is ("Er ist neunzig Jahre alt"). With "werden" it means to turn/reach that age ("Er wird neunzig Jahre alt"), and in the past it can mean someone lived to that age ("Er wurde neunzig Jahre alt").
target_language_example: Meine Nachbarin ist neunzig Jahre alt und sehr aktiv.
native_language_example: My neighbor is ninety years old and very active.

meaning: 'not that …' / 'so that … not' (to prevent a misunderstanding or warn about a possible outcome).
additional_notes: Used to add a clarification like English “not that …” (often with Konjunktiv II: „Nicht, dass du denkst, …“). It can also introduce a warning meaning “so that you don’t … / in case …” (common in spoken German: „Beeil dich, nicht dass du den Zug verpasst.“).
target_language_example: Nicht, dass du denkst, ich hätte keine Lust – ich bin nur müde.
native_language_example: Not that you think I don’t feel like it—I’m just tired.

meaning: "that you ... not" / "that you don't ..." (used to introduce a 'dass'-clause).
additional_notes: Used before a subordinate clause with **dass** when the main verb expresses things like **not believing** or **not wanting** something: *Ich fasse es nicht, dass du ...* = “I can’t believe (that) you ...”; *Ich wollte nicht, dass du ...* = “I didn’t want you to ...”. In writing there is usually a comma before **dass**: *Ich fasse es nicht, dass du ...*. In the **dass**-clause, the conjugated verb typically goes to the end: *... dass du morgen kommst*.
target_language_example: Ich will nicht, dass du so spät nach Hause gehst.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to go home so late.

meaning: “not that it …” / “(did) not … that it …” (with dass = “that”).
additional_notes: Used with the conjunction **dass** to introduce a subordinate clause. With verbs like **sagen / wissen / wollen**, it means “not (say/know/want) that it …”. The clause usually has **verb at the end** (e.g., *… dass es so schlimm ist*). A comma typically comes before **dass**.
target_language_example: Ich hoffe nicht, dass es heute regnet.
native_language_example: I hope it doesn’t rain today.

meaning: "not that she/they …" (used to say you don’t think/want/claim that she/they …).
additional_notes: Often introduces a subordinate clause with "dass" after verbs like "denken" (to think), "glauben" (to believe), "wollen" (to want), or "sich beklagen" (to complain): "Ich denke nicht, dass sie …" = "I don’t think she …". "sie" can mean "she" (singular) or "they" (plural)—the verb form in the clause helps you tell which.
target_language_example: Ich glaube nicht, dass sie heute kommt.
native_language_example: I don’t think she’s coming today.

additional_notes: This is the combination of the negation **nicht** with the question/relative word **was** (“what”). It commonly appears in sentences with verbs like **wissen** (to know), **denken** (to think), **erzählen** (to tell): **Ich weiß nicht, was …** = “I don’t know what …”. It can also start a short correction/contrast: **Nicht, was wir uns erhofft hatten.** = “Not what we had hoped for.”
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich tun soll.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect clause starting with **was ich …** ("what I …"). In German, indirect questions/clauses use **verb at the end**: *Ich wusste nicht, was ich sagen sollte.* It can also be used in commands to push back: *Sag/Erzähl mir nicht, was ich …* ("Don’t tell me what to …").
target_language_example: Sag mir nicht, was ich fühlen soll!
native_language_example: Don’t tell me what I should feel!

additional_notes: Used before an adjective/adverb (or a quantity phrase like "viele") to soften it: "not too/that". Often implies something is limited or moderate (e.g., not many, not big, not important).
target_language_example: Die Aufgabe war nicht allzu schwierig.
native_language_example: The task wasn’t too difficult.
