additional_notes: Used with a following infinitive clause (often with „zu“), e.g. „nicht die Absicht, … zu + infinitive“. It’s a formal/neutral way to say you don’t plan to do something, or that you didn’t mean to do something (often in apologies: „Ich hatte nicht die Absicht, … zu verletzen.“).
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht die Absicht, heute länger zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I have no intention of staying longer today.

additional_notes:
A "zu"-infinitive clause with negation (nicht) and the adverb dorthin (“to there”). Often used after verbs like bitten (to ask/request) or brauchen (to need): 
- jemanden bitten, nicht dorthin zu gehen = to ask someone not to go there
- Du brauchst nicht dorthin zu gehen = You don’t need to go there. 
Word order stays: nicht + dorthin + zu + gehen.
target_language_example: Ich rate dir, nicht dorthin zu gehen.
native_language_example: I advise you not to go there.

additional_notes: Often used to say something is difficult, challenging, or complicated. It can describe a task (Es war nicht einfach, ...), a situation (Das wird nicht einfach sein.), or people/behavior (Sie sind nicht einfach = “They’re difficult / not straightforward”). In speech you can stress it for emphasis: Das ist wirklich nicht einfach.
target_language_example: Es ist nicht einfach, eine neue Sprache zu lernen.
native_language_example: It’s not easy to learn a new language.

additional_notes: Used to soften a statement or say something is only partly true/finished (often with adjectives or verbs): „nicht ganz verstanden“ = didn’t fully understand; „nicht ganz ehrlich“ = not entirely honest; „nicht ganz unrecht“ = not completely wrong. In fixed phrases like „nicht ganz auf dem Damm“ it means someone isn’t feeling well / isn’t back to normal.
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht ganz sicher, ob das stimmt.
native_language_example: I’m not quite sure if that’s true.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t like/approve of something (Das ist nicht gut), that something is bad/poor quality (Seine Anweisungen waren nicht gut), or that you don’t feel well/it hurts (Es fühlt sich nicht gut an). With “sein + nicht gut in + Dativ” it means “to be not good at” something: Ich bin nicht gut im Abschiednehmen.
target_language_example: Mir geht's heute nicht gut, ich bleibe zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m not feeling well today, I’m staying home.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t like/approve of something (Das ist nicht gut), that something is bad/poor quality (Seine Anweisungen waren nicht gut), or that you don’t feel well/it hurts (Es fühlt sich nicht gut an). With “sein + nicht gut in + Dativ” it means “to be not good at” something: Ich bin nicht gut im Abschiednehmen.
target_language_example: Mir geht's heute nicht gut, ich bleibe zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’m not feeling well today, I’m staying home.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only sometimes (not in every case). Often appears with general statements ("X ist nicht immer …") or habits/routines ("Er macht das nicht immer"). In questions like "Können Sie das nicht immer?", it can suggest surprise/complaint: “Can’t you always do that?”.
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht immer Zeit, dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I don't always have time to help you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not located somewhere ("not in" + dative: nicht in Boston) or is not going/moving into a place ("not into" + accusative: nicht in die Schule). German often uses "nicht" directly before the prepositional phrase to negate it.
target_language_example: Bitte geh nicht in dieses Zimmer.
native_language_example: Please don’t go into this room.

meaning: “out of the question” / “no way” (not an option).
additional_notes: Usually used in the set phrase **(gar/überhaupt) nicht in Frage kommen** (“to be completely out of the question”), often to strongly refuse an idea or say something is not possible/acceptable. Can also be used alone as **Kommt nicht in Frage!**
target_language_example: Für mich kommt das nicht in Frage.
native_language_example: That’s out of the question for me.

meaning: 'not in the' / 'not within' (used before a feminine noun in the dative).
additional_notes: Often appears in set expressions that describe something being outside a scope, power, reach, or state. Common patterns: „nicht in der Geschichte“ (= not part of the story), „nicht in der Macht von …“ (= not in someone’s power), „nicht in der Reichweite von …“ (= not within someone’s reach), „nicht in der Stimmung (für) …“ (= not in the mood (for) …). It’s literally „nicht“ + „in“ + „der“ (feminine dative: in der + noun).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute nicht in der Stimmung für ein langes Gespräch.
native_language_example: I’m not in the mood for a long conversation today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone cannot do something (because of ability, circumstances, health, etc.). Very common with an infinitive clause: „nicht in der Lage sein, + zu + Infinitiv“ (e.g., „Er ist nicht in der Lage, zu kommen.“). It can also be used without a verb in the phrase, relying on context: „Er ist nicht in der Lage dazu.“
target_language_example: Ich bin heute nicht in der Lage, dir zu helfen.
native_language_example: I'm not able to help you today.

meaning: not at school; absent from school.
additional_notes: Used to say someone didn’t attend school on a particular day/period. Very common with forms of "sein" (war, bist, wart): "Ich war nicht in der Schule" = "I wasn’t at school." Often followed by a reason with "weil" (because) or "wegen" + Genitive/Dative (because of).
target_language_example: Heute bin ich nicht in der Schule, weil ich einen Arzttermin habe.
native_language_example: Today I’m not at school because I have a doctor’s appointment.

meaning: not in town; out of town.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not currently in the city/town (often because they’re traveling). Common with time expressions like "diese Woche" or "letzte Woche". You can also use it in longer clauses like "solange ich nicht in der Stadt bin" (“as long as I’m out of town”).
target_language_example: Ich bin am Wochenende nicht in der Stadt.
native_language_example: I’m out of town this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to say something is hard to do or hard to deal with. Very common in the pattern: „Es ist/war nicht leicht (für jdn), …“ = “It’s/was not easy (for someone) to …”. Also: „jdn/etw macht es (jdm) nicht leicht“ = “someone/something doesn’t make it easy (for someone)” (i.e., makes it harder).
target_language_example: Es ist nicht leicht für mich, so früh aufzustehen.
native_language_example: It’s not easy for me to get up so early.

meaning: to not like; to not be able to stand (someone/something).
additional_notes: Most often used with "können" ("Ich kann … nicht leiden") to express strong dislike or intolerance. It can be about a person ("Ich kann ihn nicht leiden"), a thing/food ("Ich kann Kaffee nicht leiden"), or a situation introduced with "wenn"/"dass" ("Ich kann es nicht leiden, wenn …" / "…, dass …"). Stronger than simple "nicht mögen" and often close to "can't stand".
target_language_example: Ich kann es nicht leiden, wenn man zu spät kommt.
native_language_example: I can’t stand it when people are late.

additional_notes: Used to say a state, situation, or rule has ended. Often placed before the part it negates (e.g., adjective/verb phrase): „Ich bin nicht länger müde.“ / „Er kann das nicht länger ertragen.“ Common in writing and formal speech; in everyday conversation people also say „nicht mehr“.
target_language_example: Wir können nicht länger warten.
native_language_example: We can’t wait any longer.

additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit: "nicht mehr als zehn" = at most ten. You can also use it in comparisons: "nicht mehr als dir" = no more than you (do). Often followed by a number, an amount of money, or expressions like "nötig" (necessary).
target_language_example: Ich brauche nicht mehr als fünf Minuten.
native_language_example: I need no more than five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say something has changed and isn’t the same as before, often with forms of "sein" (ist/war): "X ist nicht mehr das, was es (einmal/früher) war." The clause after "was" often uses "war" to refer to the past state.
target_language_example: Meine Lieblingsband ist nicht mehr das, was sie früher war.
native_language_example: My favorite band is no longer what it used to be.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is not in a place (or situation) anymore. The key part is "nicht mehr" = "no longer / not anymore"; it often comes right before a prepositional phrase like "in + Dativ" (in Australia, in public, etc.). Word order: subject + verb + nicht mehr in + place.
target_language_example: Wir sind nicht mehr in der Innenstadt.
native_language_example: We’re no longer in the city center.

additional_notes: Used to say something is no longer the same degree as before. Often followed by an adjective/adverb or a comparison: “nicht mehr so + Adjektiv/Adverb (wie früher / wie …)”. Example patterns: “nicht mehr so stark”, “nicht mehr so oft”, “nicht mehr so bitter”. Sometimes “so” refers back to a situation already mentioned: “Jetzt ist es nicht mehr so” = “Now it’s not like that anymore.”
target_language_example: Ich bin nicht mehr so müde wie gestern.
native_language_example: I’m not as tired as yesterday anymore.

additional_notes: Used before a "zu"-infinitive to say something is not possible anymore or won’t happen anymore. Very common with an implied passive meaning: "nicht mehr zu reparieren/erkennen" = "can’t be repaired/recognized anymore". With a normal verb it can simply mean "not to (do something) anymore" (e.g., "ihm nicht mehr zu begegnen" = "not to run into him anymore"). The infinitive goes to the end: "… nicht mehr zu + Infinitiv".
target_language_example: Die Tür ist nicht mehr zu öffnen.
native_language_example: The door can’t be opened anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say something should not happen a second time. Common in warnings and instructions (often with a strong, annoyed tone): "Nicht noch einmal!" = "Not again!" / "Don’t do that again!" Can also appear in longer sentences with verbs like "vorkommen" (happen) or "tun" (do).
target_language_example: Mach das bitte nicht noch einmal.
native_language_example: Please don’t do that again.

additional_notes: Used to add extra information: 'not only X, (but) also Y'. Very often paired with "sondern auch" (or just "sondern") in the same sentence. Can also be used more generally to mean 'not just' (e.g., "Es geht nicht nur mir so" = 'It’s not just me').
target_language_example: Das ist nicht nur teuer, sondern auch schlecht gemacht.
native_language_example: That’s not only expensive, but also badly made.

nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Französisch

target_language_multi_word_term: nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Französisch
meaning: not only English, but also French.
additional_notes: Pattern: "nicht nur X, sondern auch Y" = "not only X, but also Y". Use it to add a second item that is also true (languages, skills, facts, etc.). Often used with verbs like "sprechen" or "können" when talking about languages.
target_language_example: Ich spreche nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Französisch.
native_language_example: I speak not only English, but also French.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something is necessary or must be included before an action happens. Often followed by a noun/pronoun: „nicht ohne meinen Ausweis“, „nicht ohne dich“. It can also be used as a short/elliptical warning or condition: „Nicht ohne den Fahrer.“ (= not without the driver).
target_language_example: Ich gehe nicht ohne meinen Ausweis ins Hotel.
native_language_example: I’m not going into the hotel without my ID.

additional_notes: Used to give mild praise or say something is better than expected. Can stand alone as a reaction ("Nicht schlecht!"). Often means "quite good" rather than literally "not bad."
target_language_example: Die Idee ist nicht schlecht, aber wir brauchen noch mehr Zeit.
native_language_example: The idea isn’t bad, but we still need more time.

meaning: "not so" / "not that" / "not like that" (often: "not as … as …").
additional_notes: Common in comparisons with "wie": "nicht so + adjective/adverb + wie …" = "not as … as …" (e.g., "nicht so schwierig wie …"). Also used to tell someone to stop doing something in a certain way, especially with imperatives: "Nicht so!" / "Red nicht so" = "Don’t (talk/act) like that."
target_language_example: Mach das bitte nicht so laut.
native_language_example: Please don’t do it so loudly.

additional_notes: Used to say something is smaller (in size) or shorter (in height) than expected or than something/someone else. Often appears in comparisons with **wie** (“as … as”): **nicht so groß wie …** = “not as big/tall as …”. You can also use it without a comparison: **Das Zimmer ist nicht so groß.**
target_language_example: Der Koffer ist nicht so groß wie meiner.
native_language_example: The suitcase isn’t as big as mine.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is going poorly or less good than expected, often with verbs like *gehen* (to be doing/feeling) and *laufen* (to be going). It can also be used for comparisons: *nicht so gut wie …* (“not as good as …”).
target_language_example: Mir geht es heute nicht so gut.
native_language_example: I’m not feeling so well today.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone they shouldn’t (advice) or aren’t allowed to (rule) stay up late. Common with modal verbs like sollen (should) and dürfen (be allowed to). The verb aufbleiben (“to stay up”) is separable: Ich bleibe auf / Du bleibst auf / …, but in the infinitive it stays together: aufbleiben.
target_language_example: Bleib heute Abend nicht so lange auf!
native_language_example: Don’t stay up so late tonight!

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or downplay a problem: "Das ist nicht so schlimm" = "It’s not that bad." Often used in comparisons: "nicht so schlimm wie ..." = "not as bad as ..." You can also say it alone as a response: "Nicht so schlimm!" = "No worries!/It’s okay!"
target_language_example: Mach dir keine Sorgen — das ist nicht so schlimm.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it’s not that bad.

additional_notes: Used with a dative person: jemandem nicht trauen = “not trust someone.” Common in advice/warnings (often with sollen: Du sollst ihm nicht trauen.). Don’t confuse with sich trauen (“to dare”) or sich trauen lassen (“to get married”).
target_language_example: Ich traue ihm nicht.
native_language_example: I don’t trust him.

meaning: no less than; nothing less than.
additional_notes: Used for emphasis to say a number/amount is surprisingly large, or that something is exactly as serious/extreme as stated ("nothing less than..."). Often placed at the start of a sentence for dramatic emphasis, especially with numbers.
target_language_example: Es waren nicht weniger als zwanzig Leute auf der Party.
native_language_example: There were no less than twenty people at the party.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" or "war" to say someone isn’t/wasn’t at home (e.g., not in their house/apartment). It can also be used more generally to mean someone is absent/unavailable. Common warning: "Mach(t) das nicht zu Hause nach!" = “Don’t try this at home!”
target_language_example: Ich rufe später noch mal an, weil er gerade nicht zu Hause ist.
native_language_example: I’ll call again later because he isn’t at home right now.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective/adverb or an adverbial phrase to say something shouldn’t be too much/too strong: "Nicht zu aggressiv" = "Not too aggressive." With "nah/nahe" it means "not too close": "Komm mir nicht zu nah!" It can also go with frequency/time words: "nicht zu oft" = "not too often."
target_language_example: Mach die Musik nicht zu laut.
native_language_example: Don’t make the music too loud.

additional_notes: Used to say or ask that someone should arrive on time (or at least not after the expected time). Often with the purpose phrase "um nicht zu spät zu kommen" ("so as not to be late"). With a destination you typically use: "(nicht) zu spät + zu/zur/zum + [place/event]" (e.g., "nicht zu spät zur Schule/zum Termin"). In questions it can be a reminder: "Kommst du nicht zu spät?" ≈ "You’re not going to be late, are you?"
target_language_example: Wir müssen jetzt los, damit wir nicht zu spät zum Termin kommen.
native_language_example: We have to leave now so that we don’t arrive too late for the appointment.

additional_notes: Used before an adjective/adverb or an adverbial phrase to say something shouldn’t be too much/too strong: "Nicht zu aggressiv" = "Not too aggressive." With "nah/nahe" it means "not too close": "Komm mir nicht zu nah!" It can also go with frequency/time words: "nicht zu oft" = "not too often."
target_language_example: Mach die Musik nicht zu laut.
native_language_example: Don’t make the music too loud.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive + zu after verbs like versprechen (to promise), bitten (to ask), erlauben (to allow), or in polite requests (Würde es dir/euch etwas ausmachen …?). Often means “please don’t smoke (here)” when talking about a place (e.g., in diesem Zimmer).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte daran denken, hier nicht zu rauchen?
native_language_example: Can you please remember not to smoke here?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (usually with a previous “das/es” = “it/that”) to say that something should not be done. Common after verbs like raten (to advise), brauchen (to need), beschließen (to decide), bitten (to ask), auffordern (to tell/urge). Word order: “… das nicht zu tun.” or with es: “… es nicht zu tun.”
target_language_example: Bitte vergiss nicht, das nicht zu tun.
native_language_example: Please don’t forget not to do that.

meaning: “not allow/permit that …” (refuse to let something happen).
additional_notes: Used to say you will not allow a certain action or situation. It’s often followed by a clause with “dass” describing what must not happen. Common with “Ich werde … nicht zulassen, dass …” (I won’t allow …) or “Wir dürfen/können … nicht zulassen, dass …” (we must/can’t allow …).
target_language_example: Ich lasse nicht zu, dass du so mit ihr redest.
native_language_example: I won’t let you talk to her like that.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/going (especially "gehen" and "kommen"): "nicht zur Schule gehen/kommen" = to not go/come to school. "zur" = "zu der" (to the), and with "Schule" it usually means going to school (attending) rather than going into the school building.
target_language_example: Ich gehe heute nicht zur Schule, weil ich krank bin.
native_language_example: I’m not going to school today because I’m sick.

meaning: to not agree; to disagree (not give approval).
additional_notes: Used to politely say you don’t agree with someone or you won’t approve something. Very common with „kann“ in formal contexts: „Ich kann dem/ Ihnen nicht zustimmen“ (= I can’t agree with that/with you). „zustimmen“ often takes the dative: „jemandem zustimmen“ (agree with someone) or „etwas zustimmen“ (approve/agree to something).
target_language_example: Ich kann dem Plan nicht zustimmen.
native_language_example: I can’t agree to the plan.

additional_notes: Used when you negate an entire group of things and then describe that group with a relative clause: "Es gibt nichts, was ..." = "There is nothing that ..." Often followed by a verb at the end of the clause (e.g., "... was ich tun kann"). You can also use it at the start of a sentence for emphasis: "Nichts, was du sagst, ...".
target_language_example: Es gibt nichts, was ich heute noch erledigen muss.
native_language_example: There’s nothing I still have to do today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone does only one thing (and no other activity). Often appears with verbs like "tun" (e.g., "Er tut nichts anderes, als …") followed by "als" + infinitive: "… als fernzusehen / sich zu beschweren / an sie zu denken". In everyday speech, you may also hear it without the comma.
target_language_example: Ich tue heute nichts anderes, als zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: Today I’m doing nothing but staying at home.

meaning: 'nothing but / nothing other than'; emphasizes that something is simply that (and not more).
additional_notes: Used to stress that someone/something does only one thing or that something is essentially just that thing. Often followed by an infinitive with "zu" ("nichts anderes als zu + Infinitiv": Das Baby tut nichts anderes als zu weinen.) or by a noun ("nichts anderes als + Nomen": Ein Lebenslauf ist nichts anderes als Werbung.). In past tense you may see "tat" (ich tat nichts anderes als ...).
target_language_example: Am Wochenende habe ich nichts anderes als geschlafen.
native_language_example: On the weekend I did nothing but sleep.

additional_notes: Used with bleiben (e.g., „Es bleibt mir/dir/uns nichts anderes übrig, als …“) to say there is only one possible option left. After „als“ you usually use an infinitive with „zu“ (e.g., „als zu warten“, „als dich zu entschuldigen“).
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall blieb uns nichts anderes übrig, als die Polizei zu rufen.
native_language_example: After the accident, we had no choice but to call the police.

meaning: "nothing against it" / "don’t mind"; also in set phrases: "can’t do anything about it".
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- (etwas) nichts dagegen haben + dass/zu… = to not mind / to have no objection ("Ich habe nichts dagegen, dass du kommst.")
- nichts dagegen einzuwenden haben = to have nothing to object to (more formal)
- nichts dagegen tun/machen können = to be unable to change the situation / can’t do anything about it. "dagegen" refers to a specific thing/situation mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts dagegen, wenn du das Fenster aufmachst.
native_language_example: I don’t mind if you open the window.

meaning: to have nothing to do with it; to not be involved.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not connected to a situation, decision, or problem. Often appears as: „Ich habe nichts damit zu tun.“ (I have nothing to do with it.) You can also use it with past tense: „Er hatte nichts damit zu tun.“ (He had nothing to do with it.)
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts damit zu tun, dass die Tür kaputt ist.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with the door being broken.

meaning: "none of it / nothing of it"; "not any of that".
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned (an idea, plan, facts, etc.). Common with verbs like wissen/verstehen/sagen: „nichts davon wissen“ (to know nothing about it), „nichts davon verstehen“ (to understand none of it), „nichts davon sagen“ (to say nothing about it). It can also mean “you get nothing out of it” with haben: „Du hast nichts davon, …“ = “It doesn’t benefit you to …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts davon gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard anything about it.

additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone isn’t at fault or hasn’t made a mistake. Built from: "nichts" (nothing) + "falsch" (wrong) + "gemacht" (done/made, past participle of "machen"). Often appears with "haben": "Ich habe nichts falsch gemacht." / "Er hat nichts falsch gemacht."
target_language_example: Keine Sorge — du hast nichts falsch gemacht.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — you did nothing wrong.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **geschehen** (“to happen”) with **nichts** (“nothing”). Often used to reassure someone with **jemandem wird nichts geschehen** (“nothing will happen to someone,” dative: *mir/dir/ihr/ihm/uns/euch/ihnen*). Very common in the phrase **als ob nichts geschehen wäre** (“as if nothing had happened”).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, dir wird nichts geschehen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, nothing will happen to you.

meaning: “nothing more / nothing else / no longer anything.”
additional_notes: Used with **mehr** (“more/anymore”) to say that there is nothing left, nothing else to add, or that something doesn’t happen anymore. Common patterns: **nichts mehr + Verb** (Ich weiß nichts mehr. = I don’t know anything anymore.), **von jemandem nichts mehr hören** (not hear from someone anymore), **nichts mehr zu + Infinitiv** (nichts mehr zu essen = nothing left to eat).
target_language_example: Ich kann dir nichts mehr helfen.
native_language_example: I can’t help you anymore.

meaning: haven’t heard from him anymore / since then.
additional_notes: Used to say there has been no news or contact from him after a certain time or event. Common with time expressions like „seitdem“, „seit“, „seither“, „schon seit …“.
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug habe ich nichts mehr von ihm gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard from him since he moved.

meaning: “nothing left to …” / “no more … to …” (with an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive at the end of the clause to say there is nothing remaining to do, say, fear, discover, etc. Common pattern: “Es gibt nichts mehr zu + Infinitiv” (There’s nothing left to + verb), “Du hast nichts mehr zu + Infinitiv” (You have nothing left to + verb), “Wir haben nichts mehr zu + Infinitiv” (We have nothing more to + verb).
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts mehr zu sagen.
native_language_example: I have nothing left to say.

additional_notes: Used to say there are no more tasks or actions needed. Common with forms like: „Es gibt nichts mehr zu tun.“ (There’s nothing left to do.) or „Ich habe nichts mehr zu tun.“ (I have nothing left to do.) „mehr“ = “any more / left”. The verb is „tun“ (to do); with „zu tun“ it’s an infinitive phrase (“to do”).
target_language_example: Wir sind fertig – es gibt nichts mehr zu tun.
native_language_example: We’re finished—there’s nothing left to do.

additional_notes: Used to say that no incident occurred, often to reassure someone (e.g., after a scare): „Es ist nichts passiert.“ It can also be used in the present as an exclamation meaning “Nothing’s happening!” or “Nothing happened!” (depending on context). With dative pronouns it can mean “nothing happened to him/her/etc.”: „Ihm ist nichts passiert.“
target_language_example: Keine Sorge—mir ist nichts passiert.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—nothing happened to me.

meaning: "nothing about" / "nothing from" (i.e., no news/contact from someone; or no knowledge of something).
additional_notes: Used mainly in two ways: (1) with verbs like "hören" or "sehen" to mean you haven’t heard/seen anything from someone (= no news/contact): "Ich habe nichts von ihm gehört." (2) with verbs like "wissen" to mean you know nothing about a plan/idea/topic: "Ich wusste nichts von Ihrem Plan." It can also refer to parts of a set: "Nichts von beiden" (= neither), "Nichts von dem, was …" (= nothing of what …).
target_language_example: Seit Wochen habe ich nichts von meiner Freundin gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard from my friend in weeks.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say there is nothing to do/fear/forgive, etc.: „nichts zu + Infinitiv“ = “nothing to + verb.” Common fixed phrase: „Nichts zu danken.“ = “Don’t mention it / You’re welcome.”
target_language_example: Du hast nichts zu befürchten.
native_language_example: You have nothing to fear.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no food available, or that someone has no food. Grammatically it’s the negation "nichts" + "zu" + infinitive (here: "essen") meaning “nothing to [do]”. Common with verbs like haben/geben: "Ich habe nichts zu essen" (I have nothing to eat), "Es gibt nichts zu essen" (There’s nothing to eat).
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe heute nichts zu essen.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have nothing to eat today.

meaning: to say nothing; to have nothing to say.
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) choosing not to tell someone something: „jemandem nichts sagen“ (often with promises/oaths: „versprechen/schwören, jemandem nichts zu sagen“). (2) having no comment or nothing to contribute: „Ich habe (dazu) nichts zu sagen.“ You can also use it as a question: „Habt ihr nichts zu sagen?“ = “Don’t you have anything to say?”
target_language_example: Bitte sag ihm nichts zu sagen, bis ich da bin.
native_language_example: Please tell him to say nothing until I’m there.

meaning: “nothing to do” / “not to be involved (with something)”.
additional_notes: Common in two situations: (1) having no tasks/being idle: „Ich habe heute nichts zu tun.“ (2) denying involvement or responsibility, often with „damit“ or „mit + Dativ“: „Damit habe ich nichts zu tun.“ / „Ich habe mit der Sache nichts zu tun.“
target_language_example: Am Wochenende finde ich es schön, einfach nichts zu tun.
native_language_example: On the weekend, I think it’s nice to just do nothing.

additional_notes: Used to say you aren’t hiding any secrets or doing anything wrong, often as a reassurance or defense. Very common with forms of haben (e.g., Ich habe/du hast/er hat …) and also in reported speech with Konjunktiv (e.g., er sagte, er habe/hätte nichts zu verbergen).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich habe nichts zu verbergen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I have nothing to hide.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "haben" (e.g., "Ich habe nichts zu verlieren") to say there’s no real risk or nothing left that could be lost—often to encourage taking a chance or because the situation can’t get much worse.
target_language_example: Probier es ruhig—du hast doch nichts zu verlieren.
native_language_example: Go ahead and try it—you’ve got nothing to lose.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „wissen“ (to know), „erzählen“ (to tell), „verraten“ (to reveal), „sagen“ (to say) to mean you have (or share) no information about a person/thing/topic. Common pattern: „(jemand) weiß nichts über (jemanden/etwas)“.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nichts über diesen Film.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about this movie.

additional_notes: This is a common sentence pattern: a main clause with **nie** (“never”) is followed by a comma and a subordinate clause starting with **was** (“what”). It often appears after verbs like **wissen** (to know), **sagen** (to say/tell), or **tun** (to do): *Ich weiß nie, was …* / *Er sagt nie, was …*.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nie, was ich als Nächstes tun soll.
native_language_example: I never know what I should do next.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not happen at any time (nie) and with any thing/information (etwas). Often appears with a verb: "Er sagt mir nie etwas" = he never tells me anything. In German you usually don’t add another "nicht" with this: "nie etwas" already makes the sentence negative.
target_language_example: Ich vergesse nie etwas Wichtiges.
native_language_example: I never forget anything important.

meaning: "never said" (used to deny having said something).
additional_notes: Often appears in the present perfect: "Das habe ich nie gesagt" = "I never said that." Used to contradict someone or to emphasize that something was not mentioned. With "hätte" it can appear as reported/conditional speech: "Er behauptet, dass er das nie gesagt hätte" = "He claims he would never have said that / that he never said that."
target_language_example: Das habe ich nie gesagt – du hast mich falsch verstanden.
native_language_example: I never said that—you misunderstood me.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object in the dative (jemandem = “to someone”). Often appears in the middle of the sentence: subject + auxiliary + nie + jemandem + (object) + past participle (e.g., „Er hat es nie jemandem gesagt.“). The words don’t have to be right next to each other, but this is a very common pairing.
target_language_example: Ich habe nie jemandem davon erzählt.
native_language_example: I never told anyone about it.

additional_notes: Used to promise, vow, or strongly say you won’t repeat an action. It often appears with a direct object like „das“/„es“: „Das/Es werde ich nie wieder tun.“ You can change tense or add modals: „Ich will/muss/darf … nie wieder tun.“
target_language_example: Das mache ich nie wieder!
native_language_example: I’ll never do that again!

additional_notes: Used to express that you don’t want to meet or see a person anymore. Often said strongly or emotionally (e.g., after an argument). The core verb is "wiedersehen" (“to see again”); "nie" (“never”) makes it final.
target_language_example: Nach dem Streit wollte sie ihn nie wiedersehen.
native_language_example: After the argument, she never wanted to see him again.

additional_notes: Used to say something has not happened/been seen/experienced at any time earlier. Often appears with the past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum), and it can be placed before the verb phrase: „Ich habe das nie zuvor gesehen.“
target_language_example: So etwas habe ich nie zuvor erlebt.
native_language_example: I have never experienced something like that before.

meaning: "nobody I know" / "no one that I know."
additional_notes: Used to say that none of the people you personally know do something. The part "den ich kenne" is a relative clause meaning "(whom) I know"; "den" is the accusative relative pronoun referring to "niemand" (masculine), even though in English you usually just say "nobody I know." Often used with "noch" to mean "anymore / still."
target_language_example: Niemand, den ich kenne, benutzt noch Facebook.
native_language_example: Nobody I know uses Facebook anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person did something (often in the Perfekt tense): **niemand** (nobody) + **hat** (has) + past participle at the end of the clause. Common with verbs that form the Perfekt with **haben** (e.g., *angerufen, gefragt, gesehen, besucht*).
target_language_example: Niemand hat mir heute geantwortet.
native_language_example: No one answered me today.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is no person who is able to do something. In statements, the conjugated verb (here: "kann") stays in 2nd position, so "Niemand" often comes first: "Niemand kann ...". The infinitive usually goes to the end: "Niemand kann alles wissen."
target_language_example: Niemand kann heute kommen.
native_language_example: No one can come today.

additional_notes: Used to say that at this point in time there is no person who does something anymore, or that no person remains in a place. Often comes after the verb or at the end of the clause: „Hier wohnt niemand mehr.“ / „Ich kenne niemanden mehr hier.“ (With the accusative form „niemanden“ when it’s the object.)
target_language_example: Nach dem Umzug kannte sie in der Stadt niemanden mehr.
native_language_example: After the move, she didn’t know anyone in the city anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say that no one wants a certain thing to happen. It’s followed by a subordinate clause with **dass** (“that”), and the verb in that clause goes to the end (e.g., **…, dass du das machst/tust**). **möchte** is the polite/soft form of **will** (“wants / would like”).
target_language_example: Niemand möchte, dass wir zu spät kommen.
native_language_example: Nobody wants us to be late.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in your group ("uns") did something or are something. It’s usually the subject of the sentence and is followed by a verb in 3rd person singular: "Niemand von uns hat/ist/weiß ...". You can also use it with reflexive verbs: "..., dass niemand von uns sich setzen konnte."
target_language_example: Niemand von uns kann heute kommen.
native_language_example: None of us can come today.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person has the information. Often followed by a statement (Niemand weiß das.) or by a clause starting with **dass/ob/wie/warum** etc.: **Niemand weiß, ob… / dass… / wie…**. In these clauses, the verb goes to the end (**…dauern wird**).
target_language_example: Niemand weiß, wann der Zug ankommt.
native_language_example: Nobody knows when the train will arrive.

meaning: “no one knows what …” (introduces an unknown outcome or situation).
additional_notes: Often used to say the result, future, or situation is uncertain. The comma is standard before the clause with “was”. Common continuations include: “... als Nächstes passieren wird” (will happen next), “... die Zukunft bringt” (the future holds), “... mit ihm geschehen ist” (what happened to him), “... aus ihm geworden ist” (what became of him).
target_language_example: Niemand weiß, was morgen passieren wird.
native_language_example: No one knows what will happen tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a person (often the one you’re talking to) has the most knowledge or experience about something. Very common as a lead-in to add what they know best: “Niemand weiß das besser als du: Wie funktioniert das?” You can change the pronoun (Sie/du/er/sie/wir/ihr) or replace it with a name.
target_language_example: Niemand weiß das besser als du: Wie läuft der Kurs wirklich ab?
native_language_example: No one knows that better than you: what is the course really like?

additional_notes: Used to say that no one wants something to happen or to do something. After "will" (from "wollen" = to want), German typically uses an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Niemand will gehen." = "Nobody wants to go."
target_language_example: Niemand will heute arbeiten.
native_language_example: Nobody wants to work today.

additional_notes: Used with the future meaning of **werden** (“will”). The main verb usually goes to the end: **Niemand wird dich verstehen.** (“No one will understand you.”). It can also be used with a past participle to form the passive: **Niemand wird verletzt.** (“No one will be hurt.”).
target_language_example: Niemand wird dir helfen, wenn du nicht fragst.
native_language_example: No one will help you if you don’t ask.

meaning: "no one (to) whom" / "no one to turn to."
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause to refer back to "niemanden" (nobody): "niemanden, an den ..." = "no one (that) ... to." The preposition depends on the verb; with sich an jdn wenden (to turn to someone), it’s an + accusative: an den (masc.), an die (fem.), an das (neut.), an die (pl.). Often used with Hilfe/um Hilfe: "niemanden, an den er sich um Hilfe wenden kann" = "no one he can turn to for help."
target_language_example: Ich habe niemanden, an den ich mich wenden kann.
native_language_example: I have no one I can turn to.

meaning: “no one who …” (referring to a male person: “no one who …”).
additional_notes: Used with a relative clause to say there is nobody who does/can do something. Grammar: "niemanden" is accusative (object). The relative pronoun agrees with the missing person: der (masc.), die (fem.), das (neut.), die (plural). Examples: "Ich habe niemanden, der mir hilft." / "Ich habe niemanden, die mir hilft." (for a woman).
target_language_example: Wir haben niemanden, der uns heute fahren kann.
native_language_example: We have no one who can drive us today.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say you don’t have a person to do something with. It commonly appears with a relative clause: „Ich habe niemanden, mit dem ich …“ (= I have no one to/with whom I can …). The form changes with gender/case: „niemanden, mit dem“ (masc./neut. dative), „niemanden, mit der“ (fem. dative), „niemanden, mit denen“ (plural dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe niemanden, mit dem ich heute Abend ins Kino gehen kann.
native_language_example: I have no one to go to the movies with tonight.

additional_notes: Imperative of the reflexive verb phrase „sich (etwas) nehmen“: „Nimm dir …“ = “help yourself / go ahead and take …”. Common with food/drinks („Nimm dir etwas vom Kuchen!“) and with time or breaks: „Nimm dir Zeit“ = “take your time”, „Nimm dir ein paar Tage frei“ = “take a few days off”. The „dir“ is a dative pronoun (“for yourself”).
target_language_example: Nimm dir ruhig noch ein Stück Brot.
native_language_example: Go ahead and take another piece of bread.

additional_notes: From the verb **nehmen** (“to take”), **nimmst du** asks what someone takes/uses/chooses. Common meanings in everyday German: taking/bringing someone along (**Nimmst du mich mit?**), taking medicine (**Nimmst du deine Medikamente?**), taking/using transport (**Nimmst du den Zug? / ein Taxi?**), choosing one option (**Nimmst du die rote oder die blaue?**). It’s addressed to one person you say **du** to (friends, family, kids).
target_language_example: Nimmst du heute das Auto oder den Bus?
native_language_example: Are you taking the car or the bus today?

additional_notes: "nippen an" means to sip slowly, usually from a drink. It’s often used with "an" + dative, so you’ll see forms like: an meinem/deinem/ihrem/seinem … (e.g., "an ihrem Kaffee"). "nippte" is simple past (Präteritum) of "nippen".
target_language_example: Sie nippte an ihrem Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: She sipped at her glass of water.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **nippen an + dative** to mean taking small, slow sips from a drink. **nippte** is simple past (Präteritum) of *nippen*; **seinem** changes to match gender/case: *an seinem Kaffee/Wein* (masc./neut.), *an seiner Cola* (fem.), *an seinem Getränk* (neut.).
target_language_example: Sie nippte an ihrem Tee und lächelte.
native_language_example: She sipped her tea and smiled.

meaning: used like “(still) remember what …” / “do you remember what …?”
additional_notes: Often used in the pattern **(Weißt/Wisst) du/ihr noch, was …?** to ask if someone remembers a specific detail. With **ich weiß noch, was …**, it means “I still remember what …”. With **immer noch** it means “still” in the sense of “even now” (e.g., *Fragst du dich immer noch, was …?* = “Are you still wondering what …?”).
target_language_example: Weißt du noch, was der Arzt gesagt hat?
native_language_example: Do you remember what the doctor said?

meaning: 'still (remember/know) how …' / 'do you still remember what … was like?'.
additional_notes: Used when you’re asking or stating that someone still remembers something from the past. Often appears with verbs like (sich) erinnern and wissen: „Erinnerst du dich noch, wie …?“ / „Ich weiß noch, wie …“. The comma before „wie“ is typical because „wie …“ introduces an embedded (indirect) question/clause.
target_language_example: Weißt du noch, wie wir uns kennengelernt haben?
native_language_example: Do you still remember how we met?

additional_notes: Used to say someone hasn’t died (often after an accident, illness, or danger). Common with verbs like „sein“: „Er ist noch am Leben.“ Also used with „Glück haben“ to mean someone survived: „Er hat Glück, noch am Leben zu sein.“
target_language_example: Nach dem Unfall ist sie zum Glück noch am Leben.
native_language_example: After the accident, luckily she is still alive.

meaning: still / yet … (with an = on/about; often: still remember/think of).
additional_notes:
Used when something is still true or still happens, with a phrase introduced by **an**.
- With **denken an + Akk.** / **sich erinnern an + Akk.**: **noch an** = “still (think of / remember)”.
  Example pattern: *Denkst du noch an …?* / *Erinnern Sie sich noch an …?*
- With time expressions: **noch an + Dat.** can mean “not (even) on … yet/ever”: *noch an keinem Tag* = “not on a single day (ever)”.
- With **beteiligt an + Dat.**: *noch an … beteiligt* = “still involved in …”.
target_language_example: Denkst du noch an mich?
native_language_example: Do you still think of me?

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about more items beyond the ones already mentioned. Often comes before a plural noun: „noch andere Hobbys/Symptome/Gedichte“. Can also appear with articles/pronouns: „noch andere(n)“ depending on case (e.g., „Kennst du noch andere?“).
target_language_example: Gibt es noch andere Fragen?
native_language_example: Are there any other questions?

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb: **sich (an etw.) erinnern** = “to remember (something)”. **noch** adds the idea of “still” (you remember it even now). **daran** refers back to something (“to it/that”) and often introduces a clause with **wie/wo/was** etc. Common pattern: **Kannst du dich noch daran erinnern, ...?** (informal **du**) / **Können Sie sich noch daran erinnern, ...?** (formal **Sie**).
target_language_example: Kannst du dich noch daran erinnern, wie er heißt?
native_language_example: Do you still remember what his name is?

meaning: another three days; three more days.
additional_notes: Used with time periods to mean an additional amount of time from now or from a reference point (often with verbs like bleiben, warten, dauern). It implies the time continues beyond what was expected or already counted. You can add words like „länger“ to stress the extension: „noch drei Tage länger“ = “three more days longer.”
target_language_example: Ich muss noch drei Tage hier bleiben.
native_language_example: I have to stay here for another three days.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine or neuter singular noun (ein) to ask for or mention an additional one: „noch ein Kaffee“ = another coffee. With amounts: „noch ein paar Fragen“ = a few more questions. In set phrases like „noch ein Mal“ or „noch ein letztes Mal“ it means “once more / one last time.” (For feminine nouns: „noch eine …“.)
target_language_example: Kann ich noch ein Stück Kuchen haben?
native_language_example: Can I have another piece of cake?

additional_notes: Used when you want an additional beer (after you’ve already had one, or you’re adding one more to an order). Very common in restaurants/bars. Word order can vary: "noch ein Bier, bitte"; polite requests often use "Könnte ich bitte …?" or "Ich hätte gern …". In casual speech you may hear "Hol mir mal noch ein Bier!" (informal, can sound like an order).
target_language_example: Könnte ich bitte noch ein Bier haben?
native_language_example: Could I please have another beer?

additional_notes: Most often used with **sein**: **(Er/Ich war) noch ein Kind** = “(He/I was) still a child / just a child (at that time).” Depending on context, **noch ein** can also mean “another” (one more), e.g. **noch ein Kind verlieren** can mean “to lose another child.”
target_language_example: Ich war damals noch ein Kind und habe das nicht verstanden.
native_language_example: Back then I was still a child and didn’t understand that.

meaning: another piece of cake (one more piece).
additional_notes: Used when offering or asking for an additional serving of cake. "noch" = "another/one more" here; "ein Stück" means "a piece" (common with food like cake, pizza, bread). Often appears in polite requests with "Darf ich/Kann ich ... haben?" or when offering with "Möchtest du/Wollen Sie ...?".
target_language_example: Ich nehme noch ein Stück Kuchen, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have another piece of cake, please.

meaning: “a little more / a bit longer” (still some).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to continue for a short time or have some extra amount. Common with verbs (noch ein bisschen schlafen = sleep a bit longer) and with food/drink (noch ein bisschen Salat = a little more salad).
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein bisschen warten?
native_language_example: Can you wait a little longer?

meaning: “a little more / a bit longer” (still some).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to continue for a short time or have some extra amount. Common with verbs (noch ein bisschen schlafen = sleep a bit longer) and with food/drink (noch ein bisschen Salat = a little more salad).
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein bisschen warten?
native_language_example: Can you wait a little longer?

meaning: a little longer; a bit more.
additional_notes: Used with time or actions to mean “just a little more / a little longer.” Common with verbs like bleiben/dableiben (“stay”), warten (“wait”), nachdenken (“think about it”). In modern spelling you’ll often see: „noch ein bisschen“.
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein bißchen warten?
native_language_example: Can you wait a little longer?

additional_notes: Used to say there are some items/amount left or still to do. Common with plural nouns: noch ein paar Karten/Termine/Briefe. Often implies an additional small number rather than an exact amount.
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein paar Minuten warten?
native_language_example: Can you wait a few more minutes?

additional_notes: Used to say you will wait/stay for an additional short time. Common with verbs like bleiben (to stay) and warten (to wait). In speech you’ll also hear: noch ein paar Tage lang (“for a few more days”).
target_language_example: Können wir noch ein paar Tage hier bleiben?
native_language_example: Can we stay here for a few more days?

additional_notes: Used to say there are some items/amount left or still to do. Common with plural nouns: noch ein paar Karten/Termine/Briefe. Often implies an additional small number rather than an exact amount.
target_language_example: Kannst du noch ein paar Minuten warten?
native_language_example: Can you wait a few more minutes?

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (eine) to mean an additional one: *noch eine Kopie / Flasche / Nacht / Chance*. It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: *Bitte noch eine.* Often means “one more” in requests (*Noch eine Flasche, bitte.*) or “another” in the sense of “an additional/different one” (*Es wird sich noch eine Gelegenheit ergeben.*).
target_language_example: Können wir noch eine Flasche Wasser kaufen?
native_language_example: Can we buy another bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used when asking for or offering an additional opportunity to try again, often after a mistake. Very common with verbs like „geben“ (to give): „Jemandem noch eine Chance geben“ = “to give someone another chance.” „Noch“ here means “still/yet/another,” emphasizing “one more.”
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte noch eine Chance geben?
native_language_example: Can you please give me another chance?

additional_notes: Used when offering or suggesting an extra serving, often coffee or tea. “noch” = “another/one more” in this context. You’ll often hear it in polite questions with Sie (Möchten/Trinken Sie …?) or casual with du (Möchtest/Trink …?).
target_language_example: Möchtest du noch eine Tasse Tee?
native_language_example: Would you like another cup of tea?

meaning: another cup of coffee; one more cup of coffee.
additional_notes: Used when offering or asking for an additional serving. Here, "noch" means "another / one more" (not "still"), especially with food and drinks. Common in polite questions like "Möchten Sie noch …?"
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern noch eine Tasse Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like another cup of coffee, please.

meaning: another cup of tea (one more cup).
additional_notes: "noch" means "another/one more" here, used to ask for or offer an extra serving. Common in polite questions with "Möchtest du …?" or "Wollt ihr …?" and in requests like "Gib mir …".
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte noch eine Tasse Tee haben?
native_language_example: Could I please have another cup of tea?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine accusative noun (einen + noun), e.g. „noch einen Tee“, „noch einen Tag“. With „noch“ it can mean (1) adding one more (“one more/another”), or (2) something is still available/left (“still a”), especially in questions and statements like „Gibt es noch einen…?“ / „Wir haben noch einen…“. For other genders/cases you’ll see forms like „noch eine“, „noch ein“, „noch einem“, etc.
target_language_example: Ich nehme noch einen Kaffee, bitte.
native_language_example: I’ll have another coffee, please.

meaning: again from the beginning; redo it (anew).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "schreiben" (write) or "anfangen" (start) to say something has to be done over completely. "noch einmal" = once again, and "neu" adds the sense of starting fresh/from scratch.
target_language_example: Kannst du das bitte noch einmal neu erklären?
native_language_example: Can you please explain that again from the beginning?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "überdenken" (to rethink / to think over). "noch einmal" adds the idea of doing it again—often after getting new information or having doubts. Common with decisions, plans, and offers: "den Plan / das Angebot noch einmal überdenken".
target_language_example: Ich habe die Entscheidung noch einmal überdacht.
native_language_example: I’ve rethought the decision.

additional_notes: Used when you want an additional item (often something already mentioned), e.g. another beer, another comment, another of those. Very common when ordering or offering things: „Ich nehme/Willst du noch eins?“ In the pattern „nur noch eins …“, it means “only one (thing) left”: „Uns bleibt nur noch eins zu tun.“
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern noch eins, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like another one, please.

meaning: a little longer; a bit longer.
additional_notes: Used to say someone should continue doing something for a short additional time. "noch" adds the idea of "still/yet" (additional time), and "etwas" softens it to mean "a little/a bit". Common with verbs like bleiben (stay), warten (wait), schlafen (sleep), halten (hold).
target_language_example: Können wir noch etwas länger warten?
native_language_example: Can we wait a little longer?

additional_notes: Used when you want an additional amount of something or to ask if there is more available. Common in offers and requests (especially food/drink): „Möchten Sie noch etwas …?“ / „Könnte ich noch etwas … bekommen?“ / „Haben wir noch etwas …?“ It can also mean “anything else?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern noch etwas Wasser, bitte.
native_language_example: I’d like some more water, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about an additional item, idea, or option besides what’s already mentioned. Often in questions: "Gibt es noch etwas anderes ...?" (= Is there anything else ...?). "noch" adds the sense of "still/yet/in addition," and "etwas anderes" means "something else".
target_language_example: Hast du noch etwas anderes, das du sagen möchtest?
native_language_example: Do you have anything else you’d like to say?

additional_notes: Used to say there is still an extra five minutes left, or to suggest waiting/sleeping a bit longer. Often used with verbs like schlafen (sleep) or warten (wait): „noch fünf Minuten schlafen/warten“. „Noch“ here means “still/yet/more,” and the exact meaning depends on context (remaining time vs. additional time).
target_language_example: Können wir noch fünf Minuten warten?
native_language_example: Can we wait another five minutes?

additional_notes: Used to say someone hasn’t gotten up yet (often later than expected). Common in questions with "sein" (to be): "Bist du noch im Bett?" It can sound mildly surprised or impatient depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch im Bett, ich stehe gleich auf.
native_language_example: I’m still in bed; I’ll get up in a moment.

meaning: still; even now (continuing up to the present).
additional_notes: Used when something has not changed and is continuing longer than expected or compared to an earlier time. Often interchangeable with "immer noch" (same meaning; word order varies by emphasis). Common with present tense: "Er zweifelt noch immer."
target_language_example: Ich warte noch immer auf deine Antwort.
native_language_example: I’m still waiting for your reply.

additional_notes: Used with the common pattern **Angst haben** (“to be afraid”): **noch immer Angst haben** = “to still be afraid.” You can add what you’re afraid of with **vor + dative** (e.g., *vor Spinnen*) or with **davor, … zu + infinitive** (e.g., *davor, nach Hause zu gehen*). **Noch immer** emphasizes that the fear continues up to now.
target_language_example: Ich habe noch immer Angst, allein nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: I'm still afraid to go home alone.

additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to the present. Often followed by a state with **in + dative**, e.g. **noch immer in jemanden verliebt/verknallt sein** (“still in love with someone”), or with fixed phrases like **noch immer in Gebrauch sein** (“still in use”). Similar to **immer noch**, but **noch immer** can sound a bit more emphatic (“still, after all this time”).
target_language_example: Bist du noch immer in ihn verliebt?
native_language_example: Are you still in love with him?

additional_notes: Used to say something continues up to now involving another person. Very common in questions: „Bist du noch immer mit Tom befreundet?“ (= Are you still friends with Tom?). „noch immer“ usually comes before the part you’re emphasizing (often the verb phrase), and „mit“ is the preposition used with verbs like „arbeiten“, „befreundet sein“, „sich treffen“ (to meet up).
target_language_example: Triffst du dich noch immer mit Anna?
native_language_example: Are you still meeting up with Anna?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a negative situation continues up to the present moment. Common with verbs like wissen, verstehen, können, or with states like klar/überzeugt/verheiratet. Word order: it often sits before the main verb or adjective it negates (e.g., „ist noch immer nicht klar“, „kann noch immer nicht …“).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch immer nicht verstanden, was du meinst.
native_language_example: I still haven't understood what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to repeat an action: *Kannst du das noch mal machen?* = “Can you do that again?” Often written/spoken as **noch mal** or **nochmal**. **das** = “that” (the action), and **es** = “it”. Works in informal (**du/ihr**) and formal (**Sie**) situations.
target_language_example: Können Sie das bitte noch mal machen?
native_language_example: Could you please do that again?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or emphasize an additional amount/number beyond what there already is. Often follows a verb ("Ich will noch mehr …") or stands as an exclamation ("Noch mehr …!").
target_language_example: Kann ich noch mehr Wasser haben?
native_language_example: Can I have some more water?

additional_notes: "noch" adds the idea of "still/yet" (there are additional ones), and "mehr" means "more". Often used at the end of an explanation or meeting: "Haben Sie noch mehr Fragen?" (formal) / "Habt ihr noch mehr Fragen?" (to a group) / "Hast du noch mehr Fragen?" (to one person, informal). You can also use it as a statement: "Ich habe noch mehr Fragen."
target_language_example: Haben Sie noch mehr Fragen, oder soll ich weitermachen?
native_language_example: Do you have any more questions, or should I continue?

additional_notes: Used when you already have/need/ask for money and you want an extra amount beyond that. Often sounds like an emphasis: "more than before" or "more than expected" ("wirklich noch mehr Geld?" = "really even more money?").
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch mehr Geld, um die Rechnung zu bezahlen.
native_language_example: I need even more money to pay the bill.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect or past perfect to say something has never happened up to now/that point in time: "Ich habe noch nie einen …" / "Er hatte noch nie einen …". The key part is "noch nie" = "never (yet)". "einen" is just the masculine accusative form of "ein"; depending on the noun it can change to "noch nie eine" (feminine) or "noch nie ein" (neuter).
target_language_example: Ich habe noch nie einen Herzinfarkt gehabt.
native_language_example: I have never had a heart attack.

additional_notes: Uses the passive voice: **geküsst worden** = “been kissed” (literally “kissed been”). It’s often used with **sein** in the past: **Ich war noch nie geküsst worden.** = “I had never been kissed.” With **so** (“like that / that way”), it emphasizes the manner: **So bin/war ich noch nie geküsst worden.** = “I’ve never been kissed like that before.”
target_language_example: Sie war noch nie geküsst worden, bis sie ihn traf.
native_language_example: She had never been kissed until she met him.

additional_notes: Used with the present perfect (Perfekt) to say that something has not happened at any time up to now: (ich) habe … noch nie gesehen. Often appears with etwas/so etwas (“something like that”): So etwas habe ich noch nie gesehen. “Noch nie” is stronger than just “nie” because it emphasizes “up to now”.
target_language_example: Ich habe das noch nie gesehen.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen that before.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something has never happened before, often with the present perfect ("Ich habe …") or past perfect ("Ich hatte …"). "Im Leben" adds extra emphasis to "noch nie". Sometimes "(in) meinem" is implied rather than said: "Noch nie im Leben …". (Note: if you see this phrase in sentences containing insults/slurs, that offensive language is separate from the phrase itself.)
target_language_example: So etwas habe ich noch nie im Leben gesehen.
native_language_example: I have never seen anything like that in my life.

meaning: “never (before) in / to” (has never been to a place; has never seen something in a situation).
additional_notes: Used to say something has not happened at any time up to now. Often with the present perfect for life experience ("Ich war/Ich bin noch nie in ... gewesen") and with the past perfect to talk about an earlier point in the past ("hatte noch nie in ... gesehen"). Word order: "noch nie" usually comes before the place phrase with "in" ("noch nie in Frankreich").
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nie in Deutschland gewesen.
native_language_example: I have never been to Germany.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has never happened or been experienced to this degree before. Very common in comparisons with adjectives/adverbs: "noch nie so + adjective/adverb" (e.g., "noch nie so klar", "noch nie so sauer"). Often paired with "in meinem ganzen Leben" (“in my whole life”) for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Ich war noch nie so müde wie heute.
native_language_example: I’ve never been this tired before.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something has not happened at any time in the past until that moment: *Ich habe das noch nie zuvor gemacht* = “I’ve never done that before.” Often appears with past tenses (Perfekt/Präteritum) and can be placed in the middle of the sentence near the verb.
target_language_example: Ich habe so etwas noch nie zuvor gesehen.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen anything like that before.

meaning: still in time; just in time (before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used when there is (or was) a deadline or danger of being too late. "noch" emphasizes that there’s still time left; "rechtzeitig" means on time/in good time. Very common with verbs like "schaffen" (manage), "kommen" (arrive), or "helfen" (help) in urgent situations.
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, wir sind noch rechtzeitig angekommen.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, we arrived just in time.

meaning: to still have a lot to learn.
additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t finished learning yet (often about school, skills, or personal growth). Common with müssen: „Ich muss noch viel lernen.“ = “I still have to learn a lot.” The word order can change: „Ich habe noch viel zu lernen.“
target_language_example: Wir haben noch viel zu lernen, bevor die Prüfung beginnt.
native_language_example: We still have a lot to learn before the exam starts.

additional_notes: Used to say that a lot of work/tasks are not finished yet. Very common with verbs like „haben“ (Ich habe noch viel zu tun), „bleiben“ (Es bleibt noch viel zu tun), or „geben“ (Es gibt noch viel zu tun).
target_language_example: Wir können noch nicht gehen – wir haben noch viel zu tun.
native_language_example: We can’t leave yet—we still have a lot to do.

meaning: still (go) to school; still in school (not graduated yet).
additional_notes: Used with a verb like gehen/fahren to say someone is still attending school (as opposed to having finished school). Word order: "Gehst du noch zur Schule?" = "Are you still in school?"
target_language_example: Ich gehe noch zur Schule, aber nächstes Jahr mache ich meinen Abschluss.
native_language_example: I still go to school, but next year I’ll graduate.

meaning: “only that … / just that …” (introduces a limited condition or statement).
additional_notes: Used before a dass-clause to express that one thing is the only point/requirement: „Ich will nur, dass …“ = “All I want is that …”. It can also be used to clarify or correct something in conversation: „Nur, dass …“ = “It’s just that … / Except that …”. Often implies “this is the only important thing.”
target_language_example: Mir ist nur wichtig, dass du pünktlich bist.
native_language_example: The only thing that matters to me is that you’re on time.

meaning: “just/only that you …” (often: “I just want you to …”).
additional_notes: Used with a clause starting with **dass du ...** to limit what someone wants/says to one point: **Ich will nur, dass du ...** = “I only want you to ... / I just want you to ...”. In questions like **Wie kam es nur, dass du ...?**, **nur** works as an intensifier meaning “(how) on earth / ever”.
target_language_example: Ich will nur, dass du mir Bescheid gibst.
native_language_example: I just want you to let me know.

additional_notes: Used to limit something strictly to a specific thing, followed by a relative clause with "was" (often with a comma): "nur das, was ich will" = "only what I want". Often expresses emphasis: not more than that.
target_language_example: Ich sage nur das, was ich sicher weiß.
native_language_example: I only say what I know for sure.

meaning: “just/only the red button” (i.e., you only need to press the red button).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **drücken** (to press) and often after **nur** with **müssen** or **brauchen** to mean “all you have to do is…”. Common patterns: **Du musst nur den roten Knopf drücken.** / **Du brauchst nur den roten Knopf zu drücken.** (with *brauchen* you typically use **zu + infinitive**).
target_language_example: Sie müssen nur den roten Knopf drücken, dann geht es los.
native_language_example: You just have to press the red button, then it starts.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the number is small or limited. Often answers “how many/how long?” and can refer to a quantity (nur drei Brote) or a duration (nur drei Monate). Word order: usually “nur” directly before the number it limits.
target_language_example: Ich habe nur drei Fragen.
native_language_example: I only have three questions.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or limit what someone/something is: “I’m just a …”. It usually comes right before an indefinite article + noun. The form changes with gender/case, e.g. nur ein Mann, nur eine Person, nur einen Moment, nur einem Kind.
target_language_example: Ich bin nur ein Student.
native_language_example: I’m just a student.

meaning: only a little (bit); just a bit.
additional_notes: Used to say the amount is small or limited. Often used when requesting a small quantity ("Geben Sie mir nur ein bisschen.") or when emphasizing that only a small amount is needed/left ("nur ein bisschen Milch"). "nur" = only/just, "ein bisschen" = a little bit. You can also add what you want: "nur ein bisschen Zeit", "nur ein bisschen mehr".
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur ein bisschen Hilfe.
native_language_example: I only need a little help.

meaning: only a few; just a couple (of).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the number/amount is small. Typically followed by a plural noun: „nur ein paar Bissen/Lieder/Sätze/Antworten“. „Nur“ adds the sense of “only/just.” You can strengthen it with „nur ein paar wenige …“ (= only a very few).
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: I only need a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say something takes a short time or that you can stay for a short time. Often with verbs like dauern (to take), bleiben (to stay), warten (to wait). Note: vor Ihnen/euch = “before you” (formal/plural informal), often meaning “a few minutes earlier than you.”
target_language_example: Warte bitte, es sind nur ein paar Minuten.
native_language_example: Please wait, it’s only a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that there is exactly a single item/instance. "Eine" is the feminine form of "one/a" and is used with feminine nouns (often the noun is understood from context, e.g., "nur eine (Sache/Frage/Socke)"). With other genders/cases you’ll see forms like "nur ein" (masc./neut.), "nur einen" (acc. masc.), "nur einem" (dat.).
target_language_example: Ich brauche nur eine Minute.
native_language_example: I only need one minute.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s only one question left (“Es bleibt nur eine Frage.”) or to soften what you’re asking (“Ich habe nur eine Frage …”). In replies like “War ja nur eine Frage.” it downplays the question: “It was just a question,” often after someone reacts strongly.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich habe nur eine Frage: Wo ist die Toilette?
native_language_example: Sorry, I just have one question: where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used to say there is just one of something. "Nur" = "only/just" and "einen" is the masculine accusative form of "ein" (e.g., einen Mond, einen Bruder, einen Muffin). For feminine/neuter or different cases, the form changes (e.g., "nur eine" Idee, "nur ein" Kind, "nur einem" Freund).
target_language_example: Ich habe nur einen Euro dabei.
native_language_example: I only have one euro with me.

additional_notes: Used to compare amounts or degree, usually in the pattern „nur halb so + adjective/adverb + wie …“ (only half as … as …) or „nur halb so viel(e) + noun + wie …“ (only half as much/many … as …). Often implies something is 50% of someone else’s amount/degree.
target_language_example: Ich bin nur halb so schnell wie du.
native_language_example: I’m only half as fast as you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is possible/true only if a certain thing is included or available. Common in phrases like "nur mit Mühe" / "nur mit großen Schwierigkeiten" (= only with difficulty). Can also mean you are speaking/communicating exclusively with someone/something: "Ich rede nur mit dir" (= I’m only talking to you).
target_language_example: Ohne Passwort kommst du nur mit Hilfe rein.
native_language_example: Without a password, you can only get in with help.

meaning: only ... left/remaining; just ... more (and then no more).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a number/amount/time has become very small compared to before: *Es sind nur noch drei da* (“There are only three left”). Often refers to what remains after a reduction, or what will happen from now on (sometimes like “only anymore”): *Ich trinke nur noch Wasser* (“I only drink water now”). Word order: usually placed before the quantity/time/thing that remains.
target_language_example: Wir haben nur noch zehn Minuten.
native_language_example: We only have ten minutes left.

additional_notes: “nur noch + time/amount” is a very common pattern meaning “only … left” or “just … more.” It often appears with “bis + event” (Nur noch drei Tage bis Weihnachten.) or with an infinitive phrase like “zu leben” (to live): “nur noch drei Tage zu leben haben” = “to have only three days left to live.” You can swap the number/time unit: nur noch zwei Wochen, nur noch fünf Minuten, etc.
target_language_example: Ich habe nur noch drei Tage Zeit, das Projekt fertig zu machen.
native_language_example: I only have three days left to finish the project.

meaning: only very rarely anymore; hardly ever now.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens much less often than before. �nur noch� = �only� / �only anymore� (now compared to earlier), and �sehr selten� = �very rarely�. Often used with everyday habits or repeated actions.
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug sehen wir uns nur noch sehr selten.
native_language_example: Since the move, we only see each other very rarely anymore.

meaning: only rarely now / not often anymore.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens less often than before. "nur" = only, "noch" = still/anymore (change over time), "selten" = rarely. Often answers "Wie oft?" (How often?) and implies a decrease in frequency.
target_language_example: Seit dem Umzug sehe ich meine Freunde nur noch selten.
native_language_example: Since moving, I only see my friends rarely now (not often anymore).

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like (sich) lassen, können, or kommen to say something is difficult to do or happens only slowly. It means “not easily,” and can also express that something is hard to imagine or understand ("Ich kann mir das nur schwer vorstellen").
target_language_example: Der Text ist nur schwer zu verstehen.
native_language_example: The text is hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens infrequently. Common in statements about habits or general frequency (often with the present tense). Word order: it can go after the verb or later in the sentence depending on what you emphasize (e.g., „Er schreibt nur selten.“ / „…aber ich sehe sie nur selten.“).
target_language_example: Ich esse nur selten Fleisch.
native_language_example: I only rarely eat meat.

meaning: (in exclamations) ‘ever/possibly’ to express disbelief or reproach: “How could … be so …?”
additional_notes: Often used in emotional questions with "Wie konnte/könntest du/Sie/ich/wir nur so … sein?" It adds emphasis (surprise, shock, criticism) and doesn’t mean “only so” here. Common with adjectives like "blind", "grausam", "dumm", "naiv".
target_language_example: Wie konntest du nur so unhöflich sein?
native_language_example: How could you possibly be so rude?

meaning: to be so stupid (said in shock/criticism: “How could … be so stupid?”)
additional_notes: Most often used in the pattern „Wie konnte(n/st) … nur so dumm sein?“ to express disbelief, frustration, or criticism about someone’s mistake. „nur“ here doesn’t mean “only” literally; it intensifies the question (like “ever/possibly”). „dumm“ is quite blunt, so it can sound rude if said directly to someone.
target_language_example: Wie konntet ihr nur so dumm sein und das Passwort weitergeben?
native_language_example: How could you be so stupid and give out the password?

additional_notes: Used with plural countable nouns to emphasize that the number is small. Often followed by a plural noun (e.g., „nur wenige Studenten“) and the verb is typically plural. Can also stand alone when the noun is clear from context: „Nur wenige haben es geschafft.“
target_language_example: Nur wenige Leute wissen davon.
native_language_example: Only a few people know about it.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the number of people is small. Often followed by a verb in plural (e.g., „nur wenige Menschen wissen …“). You can also use it with other nouns: „nur wenige Bücher“, „nur wenige Tage“ (only a few books/days).
target_language_example: Nur wenige Menschen haben genug Zeit für ihre Freunde.
native_language_example: Only a few people have enough time for their friends.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that the number is small/limited. Often followed by a noun ("nur zwei Minuten", "nur zwei Restaurants") or used on its own when the noun is understood ("Es gibt nur zwei.").
target_language_example: Wir haben nur zwei Tickets, also können nur zwei Leute mitkommen.
native_language_example: We only have two tickets, so only two people can come along.

additional_notes: Used when saying you will go/travel somewhere next week: **nächste Woche** (next week) + **nach** + destination. **nach** is used with most cities and many countries **without an article** (nach Berlin, nach Kanada). With countries/places that take an article, you usually use **in** + article instead (e.g., *nächste Woche in die Schweiz*). Often appears with verbs like **fahren**, **reisen**, **fliegen**, **müssen**.
target_language_example: Wir fliegen nächste Woche nach Spanien.
native_language_example: We’re flying to Spain next week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Often appears without an article as a time expression: „nächsten Monat“ (= next month). You can also say „im nächsten Monat“ (in the next month), but „nächsten Monat“ is the most common for plans. With „bis zum nächsten Monat“ it means “by next month” / “until next month”.
target_language_example: Nächsten Monat fange ich einen neuen Job an.
native_language_example: Next month I’m starting a new job.

meaning: “next month to (a destination)” / “going/traveling to … next month”.
additional_notes: Used when you mention a time + a destination: **nächsten Monat** (next month) + **nach** + place. **Nach** is used mainly with **cities** and **most countries** (usually **without an article**): *nach Boston, nach Australien*. If the place has an article, you typically use **in**: *in die Schweiz*, *in die USA*. In the examples it often appears with verbs like **fahren** (to go/drive/travel) or **müssen** (to have to).
target_language_example: Ich fliege nächsten Monat nach Berlin.
native_language_example: I’m flying to Berlin next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a point in time. Often appears without a preposition: „nächsten Montag“ (common in everyday speech). With a preposition it’s usually „am nächsten Montag“ (literally “on the next Monday”). Depending on context, it can mean the nearest upcoming Monday.
target_language_example: Ich habe nächsten Montag einen Arzttermin.
native_language_example: I have a doctor’s appointment next Monday.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will happen (or someone will be) on the next Monday, in a specific location. Word order: time phrase first ("nächsten Montag"), then location with "in" + place (e.g., "in Berlin", "in Boston"). "Nächsten" is the accusative form because "Montag" is implied as the time when something happens.
target_language_example: Wir sind nächsten Montag in Berlin.
native_language_example: We’ll be in Berlin next Monday.

additional_notes: Refers to the Sunday that comes next (often the upcoming Sunday). You can use it without an article as a time expression: „nächsten Sonntag“. With prepositions like „auf“ (postponed to), it’s common to use the accusative: „auf den nächsten Sonntag verschieben“.
target_language_example: Können wir uns nächsten Sonntag treffen?
native_language_example: Can we meet next Sunday?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the year after the current one. Often used with future plans or predictions; it can appear at the beginning of the sentence ("Nächstes Jahr ...") or later ("... nächstes Jahr ..."). Capitalize "Jahr" because it’s a noun; "nächstes" changes depending on gender/case (e.g., "nächsten Monat").
target_language_example: Nächstes Jahr mache ich einen Deutschkurs.
native_language_example: Next year I’m taking a German course.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going/moving/traveling to a place next year. Typically followed by a place name with **nach** (e.g., nach Frankreich, nach Boston, nach Australien). Often used with verbs like **fahren**, **gehen**, **ziehen**.
target_language_example: Wir fliegen nächstes Jahr nach Spanien.
native_language_example: We’re flying to Spain next year.
