target_language_example: Seien Sie vorsichtig, wenn Sie die Treppe hinuntergehen.
native_language_example: Be careful when you go down the stairs.

meaning: “to be [adjective] to do that” (e.g., “to be tempted/interested to do it”).
additional_notes: A common pattern: **[adjective] sein + das zu tun**. It describes how doing something would feel or what it would be like. In your examples: **versucht sein, das zu tun** = “to be tempted to do it”; **interessant sein, das zu tun** = “to be interesting to do (it)”. Often used with modal verbs (e.g., **müssen/sollte/dürfte**) to express necessity or probability.
target_language_example: Es wäre spannend, das zu tun.
native_language_example: It would be exciting to do that.

meaning: to be [adjective] that … / to be [adjective] about the fact that …
additional_notes: Very common pattern: **[Adjective/participle] + sein + dass + clause**. The **dass-clause** explains *what* you’re sure/aware/clear/happy/angry about, etc. Often used with adjectives like **sicher, klar, bewusst, froh, traurig, überrascht**. The verb in the **dass-clause** goes to the end: *Ich bin sicher, dass er kommt.*
target_language_example: Bist du sicher, dass wir den richtigen Weg nehmen?
native_language_example: Are you sure that we’re taking the right way?

additional_notes: Used to connect a state (often an adjective like stinksauer, zufrieden, frei, enttäuscht, hungrig) with a condition or time introduced by wenn. Very common in the future with "wird ... sein, wenn ..." ("will be ... when/if ..."). It can also express a conclusion about someone: "Er muss dumm sein, wenn ..." = "He must be stupid if ...".
target_language_example: Ich werde froh sein, wenn du wieder da bist.
native_language_example: I’ll be happy when you’re back.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what something/someone will be like in the future. Very common in sentences with **dass/ob/was** where the conjugated verb (**wird**) often comes at the end: *Ich hoffe, dass es besser sein wird.* (Main clause: *Es wird besser sein.*).
target_language_example: Ich denke, dass es morgen kalt sein wird.
native_language_example: I think it will be cold tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “his age” (age of a male person) and is used when talking about how old someone is (guessing it, lying about it, considering it, etc.). The possessive changes with the person: sein Alter (his), ihr Alter (her/their), dein Alter (your, informal), mein Alter (my).
target_language_example: Niemand kennt sein Alter genau.
native_language_example: Nobody knows his age exactly.

meaning: his car (also: its car; or formal: your car).
additional_notes: "sein" is a possessive determiner meaning "his/its" (and sometimes "your" when addressing someone formally: "Ihr Auto" is more common for formal "your"). "Auto" is neuter (das Auto), so you say "sein Auto" in both nominative and accusative (e.g., "Er verkauft sein Auto").
target_language_example: Er parkt sein Auto vor dem Haus.
native_language_example: He parks his car in front of the house.

meaning: "his best"; doing the best he can.
additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like „sein Bestes tun“ or „sein Bestes geben“ to say someone tried as hard as possible or made their best effort. It changes with the person/possessor: „mein Bestes“, „dein Bestes“, „ihr Bestes“, „unser Bestes“, etc.
target_language_example: Ich gebe mein Bestes, aber ich brauche noch etwas Zeit.
native_language_example: I’m doing my best, but I still need a bit of time.

additional_notes: Means “his brother” (a male sibling belonging to a man/boy mentioned or understood from context). "sein" changes depending on the owner: "mein Bruder" (my brother), "dein Bruder" (your brother), "ihr Bruder" (her/their brother), "unser Bruder" (our brother), "euer Bruder" (your [plural] brother).
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern seinen Bruder kennengelernt.
native_language_example: I met his brother yesterday.

additional_notes: "sein" is the possessive for "er" (he) and "es" (it). So "sein Geld" usually means "his money" (or "its money" for things/animals). The noun "Geld" is neuter (das Geld), so you get: sein Geld, dein Geld, ihr Geld, unser Geld, etc. It can be the subject or object without changing form: "Sein Geld ist weg." / "Er hat sein Geld verloren."
target_language_example: Er hat sein Geld im Portemonnaie.
native_language_example: He has his money in his wallet.

additional_notes: Literally “his face.” Often appears in sentences describing someone’s facial expression or how it changes (e.g., “sein Gesicht hellte sich auf” = his face/expression brightened) or with reflexive verbs like „sich das Gesicht reiben“ (to rub one’s face). Case changes with the role in the sentence (sein Gesicht = nominative/accusative; seines Gesichts = genitive; seinem Gesicht = dative).
target_language_example: Als er die gute Nachricht hörte, hellte sich sein Gesicht sofort auf.
native_language_example: When he heard the good news, his face (expression) brightened immediately.

additional_notes: Means the hair belonging to a male person (often referring to the hair on his head). In German, "Haar" is often used like a mass noun (similar to "hair" in English), especially when talking about hair length, color, or style. You may also see the plural "seine Haare" when talking about individual hairs or hair in general.
target_language_example: Er wäscht sein Haar jeden Abend.
native_language_example: He washes his hair every evening.

additional_notes: "sein" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (also "its" for things with neuter grammatical gender). It changes depending on case: nominative/accusative neuter "sein Haus"; dative "seinem Haus" (e.g., "in seinem Haus"). Used to show that the house belongs to a male person (or to refer back to "er").
target_language_example: Er hat sein Haus letztes Jahr verkauft.
native_language_example: He sold his house last year.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: **sein** = “his” (or “its”) and **Hemd** = “shirt”. The possessive changes with gender/case: e.g. **sein Hemd** (his shirt, nominative/accusative), **seinem Hemd** (to/with his shirt, dative).
target_language_example: Er hat sein Hemd vergessen.
native_language_example: He forgot his shirt.

meaning: his heart (literal or figurative: feelings/inner self).
additional_notes: Literally refers to a male person’s physical heart (often with verbs like „schlagen“ = to beat). Very often it’s used figuratively for emotions, love, courage, or one’s inner self (e.g., „jemandem sein Herz offenbaren“ = to reveal/open up one’s heart). In stories it can also be used literally in a fantasy way („sein Herz stehlen“ = steal his heart).
target_language_example: Als er die Nachricht hörte, schlug sein Herz schneller.
native_language_example: When he heard the news, his heart beat faster.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive pronoun "sein" (= his/its). It changes depending on the person: "mein Leben" (my life), "dein Leben" (your life), "ihr Leben" (her/their life), "unser Leben" (our life). Common with verbs like "riskieren" (to risk), "verlieren" (to lose), and "ändern" (to change).
target_language_example: Er will sein Leben verbessern.
native_language_example: He wants to improve his life.

additional_notes: Means “his name” (referring to a male person). Often used in patterns like: „Wie ist sein Name?“ (What is his name?), „Sein Name ist …“ (His name is …), and „Das ist sein Name.“ (That is his name.). Note: „sein“ changes depending on the person’s gender/number: „ihr Name“ (her name), „dein Name“ (your name), „mein Name“ (my name), „sein/ihr Name“ (their name, formal).
target_language_example: Sein Name ist Daniel.
native_language_example: His name is Daniel.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify a male person's name. The possessive "sein" agrees with masculine nouns like "der Name" (so it’s always "sein Name", even when talking about a woman’s name you would say "ihr Name"). Often followed by the person’s name: "Sein Name ist …"
target_language_example: Sein Name ist Tobias.
native_language_example: His name is Tobias.

additional_notes: "sein" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (or sometimes "its"), used before a masculine noun like "Sohn" (son). In the nominative it’s "sein Sohn"; in the accusative it becomes "seinen Sohn" (e.g., "Ich sehe seinen Sohn."). The meaning can also be "his own son" when the context makes the relationship important.
target_language_example: Er holt sein(en) Sohn von der Schule ab.
native_language_example: He picks up his son from school.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive determiner **sein** with a masculine noun (**der Vater**). In the nominative it’s **sein Vater** (“his father” as the subject). In other cases it changes: **seinen Vater** (accusative), **seinem Vater** (dative), **seines Vaters** (genitive). Can also mean “its father” depending on context.
target_language_example: Sein Vater arbeitet in Berlin.
native_language_example: His father works in Berlin.

meaning: his behavior; the way he acts.
additional_notes: "Sein" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (for a masculine/neuter owner). "Verhalten" means "behavior/conduct" and is often used when judging or describing how someone acted (e.g., polite/rude, surprising, annoying). Common patterns: "sein Verhalten verstehen" (understand his behavior), "sich über sein Verhalten ärgern" (be annoyed about his behavior), "sich für sein Verhalten entschuldigen" (apologize for his behavior).
target_language_example: Ich verstehe sein Verhalten nicht, aber ich möchte ruhig bleiben.
native_language_example: I don’t understand his behavior, but I want to stay calm.

additional_notes: A noun phrase with the possessive pronoun „sein“ (his/its). It changes with gender/number and case (e.g., „sein Versprechen“ nominative/accusative; „seines Versprechens“ genitive; „seinem Versprechen“ dative). Common with verbs like „ein Versprechen brechen“ (to break a promise) and „ein Versprechen vergessen“ (to forget a promise).
target_language_example: Er hat sein Versprechen gehalten.
native_language_example: He kept his promise.

additional_notes: Often used with common verbs: **sein Wort geben** = to give one’s word / promise; **sein Wort halten** = to keep one’s word; **sein Wort brechen** = to break one’s word. The pronoun changes with the person: *mein Wort, dein Wort, sein/ihr Wort, unser/euer Wort*.
target_language_example: Ich gebe dir mein Wort, dass ich pünktlich bin.
native_language_example: I give you my word that I’ll be on time.

additional_notes: Used for both an abstract aim (a goal in life/work) and a physical target (e.g., what an arrow hits). It’s the possessive pronoun + noun: **sein** (his/its) + **Ziel** (goal/target). You can swap the possessive: **mein Ziel** (my goal), **ihr Ziel** (her goal / their goal), etc.
target_language_example: Er hat sein Ziel erreicht.
native_language_example: He achieved his goal.

additional_notes: "sein" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (also "its" for neuter nouns). "Zimmer" means "room"; in everyday use, "sein Zimmer" often refers to someone’s bedroom, especially when talking about keeping it clean or tidying up. Changes with the person: mein Zimmer (my), dein Zimmer (your), ihr Zimmer (her), unser Zimmer (our), euer Zimmer (your pl.), ihr Zimmer (their/your formal).
target_language_example: Er geht in sein Zimmer und macht die Tür zu.
native_language_example: He goes into his room and closes the door.

meaning: to tidy up/clean up your room.
additional_notes: "aufräumen" means to tidy up (put things away, make the room neat). With "sein Zimmer" it usually means cleaning and organizing your room. Often used with modal verbs like "müssen/sollen/sollte" to say someone has to/should tidy their room.
target_language_example: Ich muss heute mein Zimmer aufräumen.
native_language_example: I have to tidy up my room today.

meaning: 'his own' (emphatic: something belongs to him / is his personally).
additional_notes: Used when you want to emphasize that something is someone’s own. It’s a combination of the possessive determiner (sein = his) + adjective (eigen = own). It must match the noun’s gender/case, so you’ll also see forms like „sein eigener Hund“, „seine eigene Wohnung“, „sein eigenes Leben“ or with other people: „mein eigenes…“, „ihr eigenes…“, „unser eigenes…“.
target_language_example: Sie hat ihr eigenes Zimmer.
native_language_example: She has her own room.

meaning: (to) dig your own grave; to bring about your own downfall.
additional_notes: Literally means “his/your own grave,” and is commonly used as an idiom with verbs like **(sein eigenes Grab) graben** or **(sein eigenes Grab) schaufeln**. Often used with **sich** (reflexive) to show the person is causing their own trouble: **Er schaufelt sich sein eigenes Grab.**
target_language_example: Mit dieser Lüge schaufelt er sich sein eigenes Grab.
native_language_example: With that lie, he’s digging his own grave.

additional_notes: Used with a neuter singular noun (e.g., Geld, Land): „sein ganzes Geld“ = “all his money”, „sein ganzes Land“ = “his whole country/land.” It’s the possessive „sein“ (his/its) + „ganz“ (whole/all) with the adjective ending (-es). For feminine nouns you’ll see „seine ganze …“ (e.g., „seine ganze Zeit“), and for plural nouns „seine ganzen …“ (e.g., „seine ganzen Freunde“).
target_language_example: Er hat sein ganzes Leben in Berlin verbracht.
native_language_example: He spent his whole life in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine person (sein = “his”). It emphasizes that the person has no money left. For a woman, use „ihr ganzes Geld“ (all her money). You can swap the possessive: „mein/dein/unser/euer/ihr ganzes Geld“. Often used with verbs like „verlieren“ (to lose), „rauben“ (to rob), or „ausgeben“ (to spend).
target_language_example: Er hat bei dem Betrug sein ganzes Geld verloren.
native_language_example: He lost all his money in the scam.

meaning: his whole life; his entire life.
additional_notes: Used to say that something was true for the entire duration of a man’s life. It’s a phrase with a possessive pronoun that changes with the person: sein ganzes Leben (his), ihr ganzes Leben (her/their), mein ganzes Leben (my), dein ganzes Leben (your). Often appears with verbs like widmen (devote), bestehen aus (consist of), bleiben (remain), or leben (live), and can be expanded with “über” for emphasis: sein ganzes Leben über.
target_language_example: Er hat sein ganzes Leben in dieser Stadt gearbeitet.
native_language_example: He worked in this city his whole life.

meaning: for his whole life; all his life (long).
additional_notes: Used to say something is true for someone’s entire life up to now, or for their entire lifetime in general. It changes with the person: sein (his), ihr (her/their), mein (my), dein (your), unser (our), euer (your plural), etc. Often used with states (e.g., unmarried, a gentleman) or with verbs like sich erinnern (“to remember”) to mean “for the rest of his life.”
target_language_example: Sie hat sich sein ganzes Leben lang um ihre Mutter gekümmert.
native_language_example: She took care of her mother her whole life.

additional_notes: A noun phrase with the possessive pronoun **sein** (“his”) + an adjective: **neuer** is the masculine nominative form of **neu** before **Roman**. Commonly used as the subject of sentences with verbs like **erscheinen** (“to be released/published”) or **veröffentlicht werden** (“to be published”). Note: German **Roman** means “novel,” not “romance” (potential false friend).
target_language_example: Sein neuer Roman wird im Frühjahr veröffentlicht.
native_language_example: His new novel will be published in the spring.

meaning: to be [adjective] that … / to be [adjective] about the fact that …
additional_notes: Very common pattern: **[Adjective/participle] + sein + dass + clause**. The **dass-clause** explains *what* you’re sure/aware/clear/happy/angry about, etc. Often used with adjectives like **sicher, klar, bewusst, froh, traurig, überrascht**. The verb in the **dass-clause** goes to the end: *Ich bin sicher, dass er kommt.*
target_language_example: Bist du sicher, dass wir den richtigen Weg nehmen?
native_language_example: Are you sure that we’re taking the right way?

meaning: his work (his job / what he is working on).
additional_notes: "seine" means "his" and changes with the noun’s case and gender. Here, "Arbeit" is usually feminine: nominative/accusative "seine Arbeit" (Ich sehe seine Arbeit), dative "seiner Arbeit" (bei seiner Arbeit), genitive "seiner Arbeit". It can mean either someone’s job in general or the task/work they are doing at the moment; context shows which.
target_language_example: Er ist stolz auf seine Arbeit.
native_language_example: He is proud of his work.

additional_notes: "Seine" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (or "its") and changes depending on case and the noun. With "Brille" you’ll commonly see: nominative/accusative "seine Brille" (his glasses), dative "seiner Brille" (with/to his glasses). Used in everyday situations like losing, forgetting, taking off, or adjusting glasses.
target_language_example: Er kann ohne seine Brille nicht lesen.
native_language_example: He can’t read without his glasses.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a male person’s parents. The possessive word changes with case: e.g., nominative/accusative plural is often **seine Eltern**, but dative is **seinen Eltern** ("with/to his parents").
target_language_example: Er besucht seine Eltern am Wochenende.
native_language_example: He visits his parents on the weekend.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: „seine“ (his) + „Familie“ (family). Used when the family belongs to a male person or to someone/thing grammatically masculine or neuter in the sentence (even if the person is female). For a female person as owner, use „ihre Familie“ (her family).
target_language_example: Er telefoniert jeden Sonntag mit seiner Familie.
native_language_example: He calls his family every Sunday.

additional_notes: "Seine" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (or "its"), and "Frau" means "woman/wife". Most often it means "his wife" in context. Grammar note: it changes with case—Nominative/Accusative: "seine Frau"; Dative/Genitive: "seiner Frau" (e.g., "Er hilft seiner Frau.").
target_language_example: Er geht heute Abend mit seiner Frau ins Kino.
native_language_example: He’s going to the cinema with his wife this evening.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify a man’s wife. Here, "seine" is the possessive pronoun meaning "his" and agrees with "Frau" (feminine, nominative). With other cases it can change (e.g., „Ich sehe seine Frau.“ = accusative; „Ich helfe seiner Frau.“ = dative).
target_language_example: Seine Frau ist Ärztin und arbeitet im Krankenhaus.
native_language_example: His wife is a doctor and works at the hospital.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: "seine" = "his" (and also "their" in some contexts), "Freunde" = "friends" (plural). It changes with the owner and grammatical case, e.g. nominative/accusative: "seine Freunde", dative: "seinen Freunden" (to/with his friends), genitive: "seiner Freunde" (of his friends).
target_language_example: Er geht heute Abend mit seinen Freunden ins Kino.
native_language_example: He’s going to the movies with his friends tonight.

meaning: 'his girlfriend' (often), or 'his (female) friend' depending on context.
additional_notes: "Seine" is the possessive pronoun "his" and changes with the gender/case of the noun (here feminine nominative/accusative: "seine Freundin"). "Freundin" can mean either a romantic partner (girlfriend) or a female friend; in many everyday contexts it’s understood as "girlfriend" unless the context clearly shows it’s just a friend.
target_language_example: Er geht heute Abend mit seiner Freundin ins Kino.
native_language_example: He’s going to the movies with his girlfriend tonight.

additional_notes: "Seine" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (it changes depending on case and the noun). "Gefühle" is plural: "feelings". Very common with verbs like "zeigen" (show), "verbergen" (hide), "verletzen" (hurt), "über ... sprechen" (talk about), "(jdm.) eingestehen" (admit/confess). Variants: "meine/deine/ihre/unsere Gefühle".
target_language_example: Er zeigt seine Gefühle nicht gern.
native_language_example: He doesn’t like to show his feelings.

additional_notes: Means someone’s health (here: a man’s). Often used with common verbs like auf seine Gesundheit achten (to look after his health), um seine Gesundheit besorgt sein (to be worried about his health), seine Gesundheit zurückbekommen/zurückgeben (to get/regain his health), and seine Gesundheit lässt nach (his health is declining). Change the possessive for other people: meine/deine/ihre/unsere/eure Gesundheit.
target_language_example: Er muss besser auf seine Gesundheit achten.
native_language_example: He has to take better care of his health.

additional_notes: "Hausaufgaben" is usually plural in German (even when English uses uncountable "homework"). "seine" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (or "its"), used here in the accusative plural: "Er macht seine Hausaufgaben."
target_language_example: Er hat seine Hausaufgaben schon gemacht.
native_language_example: He has already done his homework.

additional_notes: "Seine" means "his" and changes depending on the case and the noun (e.g., nominative/accusative: "seine Hilfe"; dative: "mit seiner Hilfe" = "with his help"). Common patterns: "um seine Hilfe bitten" (to ask for his help), "seine Hilfe anbieten" (to offer his help), "seine Hilfe ablehnen" (to refuse his help), "für seine Hilfe danken" (to thank him for his help), "sich auf seine Hilfe verlassen" (to rely on his help).
target_language_example: Ohne seine Hilfe hätte ich das nicht geschafft.
native_language_example: Without his help, I wouldn’t have managed that.

additional_notes: "Seine" is the possessive determiner for "his" (also "its") and changes form depending on the case and gender/number of the noun. With the plural noun "Kinder", it’s usually "seine Kinder" in nominative or accusative (e.g., "Er liebt seine Kinder"), and "seinen Kindern" in dative (e.g., "Er hilft seinen Kindern").
target_language_example: Am Wochenende besucht er oft seine Kinder.
native_language_example: On weekends, he often visits his children.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: „seine“ = “his” (also “its” for neuter nouns). Usually used with verbs like „(nicht) zählen“ (to (not) count/matter), „ändern“ (to change), and „teilen“ (to share/agree with). With other people you change the possessive: „meine Meinung“ (my), „deine Meinung“ (your), „ihre Meinung“ (her/their), etc.
target_language_example: Ich respektiere seine Meinung, aber ich bin anderer Meinung.
native_language_example: I respect his opinion, but I have a different opinion.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: **seine** = “his” (also “its”), **Mutter** = “mother”. Used to say who someone’s mother is or to talk about caring for/mentioning someone’s mother. With formal address you might ask: **Sind Sie seine Mutter?** (“Are you his mother?”). Changes with gender/case, e.g. **seiner Mutter** (to/of his mother), **seine Mutter** (his mother, as subject or direct object).
target_language_example: Er ruft seine Mutter jeden Sonntag an.
native_language_example: He calls his mother every Sunday.

additional_notes: Literally refers to a male person’s nose (body part). It also appears in common idioms, especially: „seine Nase in etw. stecken“ = “to stick/poke his nose into something” (to interfere or be nosy).
target_language_example: Er soll seine Nase nicht in meine Angelegenheiten stecken.
native_language_example: He shouldn't poke his nose into my business.

additional_notes: Used when talking about a speech given by a male person. The possessive changes with the speaker: seine Rede (his), ihre Rede (her/their), meine Rede (my), etc. "Rede" is often used for formal speeches (e.g., at an event or in politics).
target_language_example: Nach seiner Rede haben alle applaudiert.
native_language_example: After his speech, everyone applauded.

additional_notes: "seine" is the possessive determiner meaning "his" (also "their" when referring to "they"). "Schlüssel" usually means physical keys (house/car keys). In these examples it’s in the accusative plural as the direct object (e.g., finden, im Auto lassen, auf den Tisch legen, sich seine Schlüssel schnappen).
target_language_example: Ich habe seine Schlüssel auf dem Sofa gefunden.
native_language_example: I found his keys on the couch.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: „sein-“ = “his” (or “its”), „Schwester“ = “sister”. The ending changes with the case: nominative/accusative „seine Schwester“ (Ich sehe seine Schwester), dative „seiner Schwester“ (Ich helfe seiner Schwester). It can also refer to a male person’s sister; for a female person you’d use „ihre Schwester“ (“her sister”).
target_language_example: Ich kenne seine Schwester schon lange.
native_language_example: I’ve known his sister for a long time.

additional_notes: “Seine” is the possessive determiner for “his” (from *sein*). It changes with the gender/case of the noun. With *Tasche* (feminine), it’s often **seine Tasche** (e.g., nominative/accusative: *Er nimmt seine Tasche.*). In other cases it changes, e.g. dative: *mit seiner Tasche*. Used to show that the bag belongs to a male person being talked about.
target_language_example: Er hat seine Tasche im Bus vergessen.
native_language_example: He forgot his bag on the bus.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: „sein-“ = “his” (changes with case and gender). With the feminine noun „Tochter“, nominative is „seine Tochter“ (“his daughter” as the subject). In the accusative it’s also often „seine Tochter“ (“his daughter” as the direct object), e.g., „Er besucht seine Tochter.“
target_language_example: Seine Tochter wohnt in Berlin.
native_language_example: His daughter lives in Berlin.

additional_notes: Means what a man has said/written. Often used when judging or describing what he said (e.g., whether it is logical, believable, encouraging, etc.). You can swap the possessive: „meine Worte“ (my words), „deine Worte“ (your words), „ihre Worte“ (her/their words).
target_language_example: Seine Worte haben mich beruhigt.
native_language_example: His words calmed me down.

meaning: his own (emphasizing that it belongs to him personally).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun (or in certain cases as a standalone phrase) to stress “his own” in contrast to others. It changes with gender/case: e.g., „sein eigener Wagen“ (masc.), „sein eigenes Haus“ (neut.), „seine eigenen Freunde“ (plural).
target_language_example: Er hat seine eigene Meinung dazu.
native_language_example: He has his own opinion about it.

additional_notes: “Seinem Bruder” is the dative form of “sein Bruder” (his brother). You use it when the verb or a preposition requires the dative case (often meaning “to/for” someone, or “with” after “mit”). Note the ending: sein → seinem (masculine/neuter dative singular).
target_language_example: Ich helfe seinem Bruder bei den Hausaufgaben.
native_language_example: I help his brother with the homework.

meaning: “his office” (dative form, often after a preposition like *in* or *aus*).
additional_notes: *Seinem* is the dative form of *sein* (“his”) used with the neuter noun *das Büro*. You’ll often see it after prepositions that take dative for location (e.g., *in seinem Büro* = “in his office”) and after *aus* (always dative) for movement out of somewhere (*aus seinem Büro* = “out of his office”).
target_language_example: Er sitzt in seinem Büro und telefoniert.
native_language_example: He’s sitting in his office and talking on the phone.

additional_notes: “Seinem” is the masculine/neuter dative form of “sein” (“his”). You use “seinem Hund” after many verbs that take the dative (e.g., geben, helfen) or to express “to/for his dog.” The base form is “sein Hund” (nominative: “his dog”).
target_language_example: Er hilft seinem Hund jeden Tag.
native_language_example: He helps his dog every day.

additional_notes: Used when the noun "Schreibtisch" is in the dative case (masculine/neuter: seinem), often after prepositions like von (from), auf (on/at), hinter (behind), or neben (next to). It typically translates as "at/from/behind/next to his desk," depending on the preposition.
target_language_example: Er sitzt an seinem Schreibtisch und arbeitet.
native_language_example: He is sitting at his desk and working.

additional_notes: Used when someone (usually a male person) gives, writes, transfers, or leaves something to his son. Grammatically it’s the dative form of „sein Sohn“ after verbs that take a recipient (e.g., „jemandem einen Brief schreiben“, „jemandem etwas übertragen“, „jemandem etwas hinterlassen“). The base form is „sein Sohn“ (his son); dative masculine/neuter singular becomes „seinem“.
target_language_example: Sie gab seinem Sohn das Geld.
native_language_example: She gave the money to her son.

meaning: to/with/from his father (dative of “sein Vater” = “his father”).
additional_notes: “Seinem Vater” is the dative form used after many prepositions (e.g., zu, vor, mit) and with verbs that take a dative object (e.g., jemandem schreiben = to write to someone). The base form is “sein Vater” (his father).
target_language_example: Er spricht oft mit seinem Vater.
native_language_example: He often talks with his father.

meaning: “his room” (dative form: “to/in/on his room,” depending on the preposition).
additional_notes: “Seinem” is the dative masculine/neuter form of “sein” (“his”). You’ll often see it after prepositions that take the dative when describing location, e.g. “in seinem Zimmer” = “in his room.” With “auf” you can also get “auf seinem Zimmer,” which in some contexts (e.g., hospital/boarding school) means he’s staying/remaining in his room. With “nach,” it can be part of phrases like “nach seinem Zimmer suchen” = “to look for his room.”
target_language_example: Ich bin gerade in seinem Zimmer.
native_language_example: I’m in his room right now.

additional_notes: Often used with **machen**: **seinen Abschluss machen** = “to graduate” / “to get one’s degree” (from school, university, etc.). With **von/an** you can mention the institution: **sein Abschluss von der Universität** / **sein Abschluss an einer Universität**.
target_language_example: Er hat letztes Jahr seinen Abschluss an der Universität gemacht.
native_language_example: He graduated from the university last year.

meaning: 'his parents' (often in the dative: 'to/for his parents').
additional_notes: „seinen Eltern“ is the plural form of „seine Eltern“ (= his parents). The -n often appears because it’s commonly used in the dative case (e.g., „mit seinen Eltern“, „es seinen Eltern sagen“). Depending on the verb/preposition, it can also be accusative (e.g., „seinen Eltern besuchen“ = to visit his parents). For other possessors: „ihren Eltern“ (her/their parents), „meinen Eltern“ (my parents), „deinen Eltern“ (your parents).
target_language_example: Ich telefoniere jeden Sonntag mit seinen Eltern.
native_language_example: I talk on the phone with his parents every Sunday.

meaning: his friends (dative plural: to/for/with his friends).
additional_notes: "Seinen" is the masculine/neuter possessive pronoun "his" in the dative plural, and "Freunden" is the dative plural of "Freund". You often see this after dative prepositions (e.g., "bei seinen Freunden" = at his friends’ place/with his friends) or with verbs that take an indirect object (e.g., "seinen Freunden helfen" = help his friends).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Freunden ein Geschenk gekauft.
native_language_example: He bought his friends a present.

meaning: “his dog” (accusative: his dog as the object).
additional_notes: “Seinen” is the masculine accusative form of “sein” (his). You use “seinen Hund” when the dog is what someone has, brings, feeds, names, looks for, ties up, etc. In the nominative (subject) it’s “sein Hund” (e.g., “Sein Hund ist süß.”).
target_language_example: Er sucht seinen Hund im Park.
native_language_example: He’s looking for his dog in the park.

meaning: "his hat"; in "seinen Hut ziehen (vor …)": to take off your hat (to …) / to show respect.
additional_notes: Most often it’s simply a possessive phrase (sein + Hut): "his hat" (accusative), e.g. after verbs like "holen" (to fetch) or "bürsten" (to brush). In the fixed expression "(vor jemandem) seinen Hut ziehen" it means showing admiration or respect for someone (sometimes "vor" is implied by context).
target_language_example: Vor deiner Leistung ziehe ich meinen Hut.
native_language_example: I take my hat off to your achievement.

meaning: "his coffee" (as the object of a verb).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like trinken (to drink), mögen (to like), geben (to put/add), or austrinken (to finish). It’s the accusative form: sein Kaffee (his coffee, subject) → seinen Kaffee (his coffee, direct object). Often appears with descriptions like schwarz (black: no milk) and ohne Zucker (without sugar). You can swap the possessive: meinen Kaffee (my), deinen Kaffee (your), ihren Kaffee (her/their), etc.
target_language_example: Ich trinke meinen Kaffee immer schwarz.
native_language_example: I always drink my coffee black.

additional_notes: Used when 'his children' is in the dative case, often after common patterns like: jemandem etwas geben (Er gab seinen Kindern …), zu + Dativ (streng zu seinen Kindern), and mit + Dativ (mit seinen Kindern). The base form is seine Kinder (accusative/nom.), but it becomes seinen Kindern in the dative.
target_language_example: Er liest seinen Kindern jeden Abend eine Geschichte vor.
native_language_example: He reads his children a story every evening.

meaning: his suitcase (accusative: the suitcase is the object).
additional_notes: "Seinen" is the masculine accusative form of "sein" (his). You use it when "Koffer" is the direct object: jemanden bitten, seinen Koffer zu tragen (to carry his suitcase); seinen Koffer abstellen (to set/put it down); seinen Koffer auf das Bett stellen (to put it onto the bed); seinen Koffer auspacken (to unpack it).
target_language_example: Er trägt seinen Koffer zum Auto.
native_language_example: He carries his suitcase to the car.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with **verdienen**: **seinen Lebensunterhalt verdienen** = “to earn a living.” Often followed by **mit + Dativ** to say how you earn it: **seinen Lebensunterhalt mit etwas verdienen** (e.g., *mit Singen*).
target_language_example: Sie verdient ihren Lebensunterhalt als Lehrerin.
native_language_example: She earns her living as a teacher.

additional_notes: "seinen" is the masculine accusative possessive determiner for "sein" (his). You often see it after verbs that take a direct object, especially with actions you do to/with a coat: anziehen (put on), ausziehen (take off), aufhängen (hang up), zuknöpfen (button up). The noun is "der Mantel" (coat).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Mantel vergessen.
native_language_example: He forgot his coat.

additional_notes: “Seinen” is the masculine accusative form of “sein” (“his”). You use “seinen Namen” when “name” is the direct object (e.g., write/know/remember/say his name). Common patterns: „seinen Namen schreiben“, „seinen Namen kennen“, „sich an seinen Namen erinnern“, „auf seinen Namen kommen“ (= to remember/think of his name).
target_language_example: Ich kann mir seinen Namen nicht merken.
native_language_example: I can't remember his name.

meaning: his place / his seat; (figuratively) his place/role.
additional_notes: Literally means “his place” (sein + Platz). Often refers to a physical spot or seat (jemandem seinen Platz überlassen = to give someone your seat; etwas an seinen Platz stellen = to put something back where it belongs). Can also be used figuratively for someone’s role or standing (seinen Platz im Volk verdienen = to earn one’s place among the people). The possessive changes with gender/case (z.B. seinen/ihren/meinen Platz).
target_language_example: Kann ich bitte deinen Platz haben?
native_language_example: Can I please have your seat?

meaning: his umbrella (accusative: the thing being lost/forgotten/opened, etc.).
additional_notes: "seinen" is the masculine accusative form of "sein" (his). "Regenschirm" is masculine (der Regenschirm). Used when the umbrella is the direct object: *seinen Regenschirm verlieren/vergessen/öffnen/liegenlassen*. Changes with gender/case/owner: *seinen Regenschirm* (acc.), *seinem Regenschirm* (dat.), *sein Regenschirm* (nom.), and *ihren/deinen/meinen Regenschirm* for other possessors.
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Regenschirm im Zug vergessen.
native_language_example: I forgot my umbrella on the train.

additional_notes: Used when a male person owns the umbrella and it is the direct object of the sentence (after many verbs, e.g., haben, wiederhaben, ausleihen). The possessive pronoun changes with case: der Schirm (nom.) → seinen Schirm (acc.).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte seinen Schirm mitnehmen?
native_language_example: Can you please take his umbrella with you?

meaning: his son (accusative: as the direct object).
additional_notes: Used when “his son” is the direct object of the verb (e.g., sehen, nennen, verlieren, beschützen). The possessive pronoun changes with case and gender: nominative *sein Sohn*, accusative *seinen Sohn*, dative *seinem Sohn*. *sein* can mean “his” (or “its” for things).
target_language_example: Er besucht seinen Sohn jedes Wochenende.
native_language_example: He visits his son every weekend.

additional_notes: Used when “his father” is the direct object of the verb (e.g., sehen, besuchen, vertreten). It’s the accusative form of "sein Vater"; the possessive pronoun changes with case: nominative "sein Vater" (his father), accusative "seinen Vater" (his father), dative "seinem Vater" (to/for his father).
target_language_example: Er besucht seinen Vater am Wochenende.
native_language_example: He visits his father on the weekend.

additional_notes: "Wagen" is a common word for “car/vehicle” (similar to "Auto"). "Seinen" is the masculine accusative form of "sein" (“his”) and is used when the car is the direct object (e.g., "Er parkt seinen Wagen" = “He parks his car”).
target_language_example: Er hat seinen Wagen vor dem Haus geparkt.
native_language_example: He parked his car in front of the house.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "verpassen" (to miss) plus a possessive pronoun (meinen/deinen/seinen/ihren/unseren/euren/Ihren) and an object like "Zug". Often appears in the Perfekt tense: "Ich habe meinen Zug verpasst." You can add time words like "gerade (eben)" (just now) or "soeben" (just now).
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Zug verpasst und muss auf den nächsten warten.
native_language_example: I missed my train and have to wait for the next one.

meaning: "his own" (emphasizing that it belongs to him personally).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something is specifically his, not someone else’s. It changes with gender/case: z.B. „sein eigener Sohn“ (nom.), „seinen eigenen Sohn“ (acc.), „seinem eigenen Sohn“ (dat.); also „seine eigene …“ (fem.) / „sein eigenes …“ (neut.). Often used with family, name, mistakes, way, things, etc.
target_language_example: Er will seinen eigenen Schlüssel haben.
native_language_example: He wants to have his own key.

meaning: 'his work' / 'his job' (in dative or genitive form).
additional_notes: “seiner” is the masculine/neuter dative or genitive form of “sein” (his). “Arbeit” is feminine, so it becomes “Arbeit” with the ending shown by “seiner.” You often see it after certain prepositions (e.g., “außer” + dative: “außer seiner Arbeit”) or with adjectives/expressions that take the genitive (e.g., “(etwas) überdrüssig sein” + genitive: “seiner Arbeit überdrüssig”).
target_language_example: Außer seiner Arbeit hat er kaum Zeit für Freunde.
native_language_example: Besides his work, he hardly has time for friends.

additional_notes: “seiner” is the masculine/neuter form of “sein-” (“his”), and it changes depending on case. You often see “seiner Familie” in the dative after certain prepositions (e.g., mit seiner Familie = with his family; von seiner Familie = from his family; bei seiner Familie = at/with his family) or as an indirect object (e.g., seiner Familie Geld schicken = to send his family money). It can also appear in the genitive to mean “of his family,” though that’s less common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Er hat seiner Familie sofort geschrieben.
native_language_example: He wrote to his family right away.

meaning: to/from/with his wife (his wife, in the dative case).
additional_notes: "Seiner" is the dative form of "sein" (his) with the feminine noun "Frau" (wife). You’ll see it (1) with an indirect object: "Er gab seiner Frau …" and (2) after dative prepositions like "gegenüber", "vor", and "von" (as in the examples). The exact English translation depends on the verb or preposition (e.g., "to his wife", "from his wife", "in front of his wife").
target_language_example: Ich habe seiner Frau zum Geburtstag Blumen gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought flowers for his wife for her birthday.

meaning: to his girlfriend / with his girlfriend (dative: “his girlfriend”).
additional_notes: “Seiner Freundin” is the dative form of “seine Freundin” (“his girlfriend”). It’s used after certain prepositions (e.g., mit = with) and with verbs that take an indirect object in the dative (e.g., jemandem schreiben = to write to someone, jemandem einen Antrag machen = to propose to someone). Note: “Freundin” can mean “girlfriend” or “(female) friend” depending on context; here it clearly means “girlfriend.”
target_language_example: Er hat mit seiner Freundin telefoniert.
native_language_example: He talked on the phone with his girlfriend.

additional_notes:
"Seiner" is the masculine/neuter possessive form of "sein" (= his). With "Mutter" (feminine), you commonly see:
- dative: "seiner Mutter" = "to/for his mother" (e.g., "Er schrieb seiner Mutter einen Brief.")
- genitive: "seiner Mutter" = "of his mother" (e.g., "ein Bild seiner Mutter", "der Platz seiner Mutter").
Which meaning it has depends on the verb or noun it goes with.
target_language_example: Ich habe seiner Mutter gestern Blumen gegeben.
native_language_example: I gave his mother flowers yesterday.

additional_notes: This is the genitive case of *seine Rede* (“his speech”). It’s common after prepositions like **während** (“during”) and **nach** (“after”): *während seiner Rede*, *nach seiner Rede*. You may also see **in seiner Rede** (“in his speech”), where *in* takes the dative, so it’s not genitive.
target_language_example: Nach seiner Rede klatschten alle begeistert.
native_language_example: After his speech, everyone applauded enthusiastically.

additional_notes: "seiner" is the possessive pronoun “his,” declined to match the feminine noun "die Tasche" (dative/genitive feminine singular). You’ll often see it with prepositions like "in" (+ dative for location): "in seiner Tasche" = “in his pocket/bag.” "Tasche" can mean a bag (handbag, backpack pocket, etc.) and sometimes “pocket,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich habe meinen Schlüssel in seiner Tasche gefunden.
native_language_example: I found my key in his pocket/bag.

meaning: “of his life” (genitive: belonging/relating to his life).
additional_notes: Used with nouns to describe a part of someone’s life or something connected to their life. Common patterns: „zu Anfang seines Lebens“ (at the beginning of his life), „unter Einsatz seines Lebens“ (risking his life), „die Liebe seines Lebens“ (the love of his life). Changes with gender/number: „ihres Lebens“ (of her life), „deines Lebens“ (of your life), etc.
target_language_example: Das war der wichtigste Tag seines Lebens.
native_language_example: That was the most important day of his life.

meaning: for years; for many years (since years ago).
additional_notes: Used with the present tense (or present perfect) to say something started years ago and is still true now: „Ich kenne sie seit Jahren.“ In negatives it often means you haven’t done something for years up to now: „Ich war seit Jahren nicht mehr hier.“
target_language_example: Wir warten seit Jahren auf eine Lösung.
native_language_example: We’ve been waiting for a solution for years.

meaning: for three years; since three years ago (continuing until now).
additional_notes: Use **seit + time period** to say something started in the past and is still true now. It’s common with the present tense in German: *Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier.* You can swap in other durations: *seit zwei Wochen, seit einem Monat, seit vielen Jahren*.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite seit drei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been working in Berlin for three years.

meaning: for three days (since three days ago; still ongoing).
additional_notes: Used with actions or states that started three days ago and continue up to now. Typically used with the present tense in German (e.g., „Wir sind seit drei Tagen hier.“). For completed past events, German usually uses „vor drei Tagen“ (three days ago) instead.
target_language_example: Ich bin seit drei Tagen krank.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick for three days.

meaning: sick for a week; has been sick for a week.
additional_notes: Uses **seit** (“since”) + a time period to show something started in the past and is still true now. German often uses the **present tense** here: *Sie ist seit einer Woche krank.* In English you usually say “has been sick for a week.” You can also add location/position: *seit einer Woche krank im Bett liegen* = “to have been sick in bed for a week.”
target_language_example: Ich bin seit einer Woche krank und bleibe heute zu Hause.
native_language_example: I’ve been sick for a week and I’m staying home today.

meaning: since this morning (from this morning until now).
additional_notes: Used with **seit** + a point in time to say when something started and that it continues up to now. Often used with the present tense in German (e.g., *Er arbeitet seit heute Morgen.*), even though English typically uses the present perfect (“has been working since this morning”).
target_language_example: Ich warte seit heute Morgen auf deinen Anruf.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for your call since this morning.

meaning: for a long time (now); for a long time already.
additional_notes: Used with the present perfect or present tense to say an action/state started in the past and continues up to now. Often appears as "schon seit langem" (= for a long time already).
target_language_example: Wir wollen uns seit langem wiedersehen.
native_language_example: We’ve been wanting to see each other again for a long time.

meaning: since last (used with a time word).
additional_notes: Used with „seit“ to say something started in the past and is still true now. It’s followed by a time expression in the dative: „seit letztem Sonntag/Monat/Jahr/Mittwoch“. In writing and careful speech you’ll often also see „seit dem letzten …“ (same meaning).
target_language_example: Ich habe seit letztem Sommer keinen Urlaub gemacht.
native_language_example: I haven’t taken a vacation since last summer.

meaning: "for how many years" / "since how many years ago" (asking how long something has been the case).
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration from a starting point in the past up to now. Common with the present tense in German: "Seit wie vielen Jahren bist du schon …?" = "How many years have you been …?" Also appears inside longer sentences (indirect questions): "wer weiß, seit wie vielen Jahren …" = "who knows how many years …".
target_language_example: Seit wie vielen Jahren wohnst du schon in Berlin?
native_language_example: How many years have you been living in Berlin?

meaning: “for how many days (now)?” / “how many days has it been since…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about a duration starting in the past and continuing up to now. It’s commonly followed by a present-tense verb (e.g., „Seit wie vielen Tagen trägst du …?“) or appears with a perfect tense to ask how long since something last happened (e.g., „Seit wie vielen Tagen hast du nichts gegessen?“).
target_language_example: Seit wie vielen Tagen wartest du schon auf eine Antwort?
native_language_example: How many days have you been waiting for an answer?

meaning: for ten years; since ten years ago.
additional_notes: Used with the preposition „seit“ + a time period to say something started in the past and is still true now (often with present tense): „Ich lebe seit zehn Jahren hier.“ It can also appear in „zum ersten Mal seit zehn Jahren …“ = “for the first time in ten years …”.
target_language_example: Ich arbeite seit zehn Jahren bei dieser Firma.
native_language_example: I’ve been working at this company for ten years.

meaning: for two years; since two years ago.
additional_notes: Uses **seit** (+ dative) to mark a starting point in the past that **continues up to now**. Very common with the **present tense in German** where English often uses the present perfect: *Ich kenne sie seit zwei Jahren* = “I’ve known her for two years.”
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I've been living in Berlin for two years.

additional_notes: Du-imperative of **sich setzen** (“to sit down”). Used when speaking to one person you address as **du** (friends, family, kids). Polite/formal version: **Setzen Sie sich (bitte).** You can add a place: **Setz dich hierhin/auf den Stuhl/zu mir.**
target_language_example: Setz dich bitte kurz hin und ruh dich aus.
native_language_example: Sit down for a moment and rest.

additional_notes: Du-imperative of **(sich) hinsetzen**. Used when speaking to one person you address as **du** (friends, family, children). It can sound neutral, firm, or rude depending on tone/context. Polite/formal: **Setzen Sie sich hin.** Plural (to a group): **Setzt euch hin.**
target_language_example: Setz dich hin und entspann dich kurz.
native_language_example: Sit down and relax for a moment.

additional_notes: Polite/formal imperative of **sich setzen** (“to sit down”). Common when speaking to strangers, customers, or in formal situations. Often followed by a place: **Setzen Sie sich auf die Bank.** You may also hear **Setzen Sie sich (bitte) hin.** Note: in phrases like **sich mit jemandem in Verbindung setzen**, **setzen** means “to get in contact,” but that’s a different expression than “setzen Sie sich” on its own.
target_language_example: Setzen Sie sich bitte, ich komme gleich zu Ihnen.
native_language_example: Please have a seat; I’ll be with you in a moment.

meaning: “Sit down!” (spoken to two or more people).
additional_notes: Imperative of **sich setzen** for **ihr** (plural “you”). Often used when inviting people to take a seat. You’ll also hear it softened with particles like **doch** (“go on”), **nur** (“just”), or **schon** (“go ahead/already”): *Setzt euch doch/nur/schon.* Note: in phrases like **sich in Verbindung setzen** (“to get in touch”), **setzen** has a different meaning than “sit.”
target_language_example: Kommt rein und setzt euch bitte.
native_language_example: Come in and please sit down.

additional_notes: Usually used with the separable verb **aufsetzen**: **Er setzte seinen Hut auf.** In the past tense, **setzte ... auf** means “put on” (literally “set ... on”). You’ll also see **wieder** (“again/back on”) when someone puts it on again: **Er setzte seinen Hut wieder auf.**
target_language_example: Er setzte seinen Hut auf, bevor er hinausging.
native_language_example: He put on his hat before he went outside.

additional_notes: Past tense of the separable verb phrase „sich die Brille aufsetzen“ (present: „Er setzt sich die Brille auf.“). The „auf“ goes to the end in main clauses. „sich“ is reflexive, and „die Brille“ is the thing being put on.
target_language_example: Bevor er losging, setzte er sich die Brille auf.
native_language_example: Before he left, he put on his glasses.

additional_notes: Past tense (simple past) of the reflexive verb **sich setzen** (“to sit down”). It describes the action of moving into a sitting position, often with a place: **sich auf den Boden/Stuhl setzen**. Contrast: **saß** = “was sitting” (already seated).
target_language_example: Er setzte sich neben mich und wartete.
native_language_example: He sat down next to me and waited.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "sich auf etw. setzen" = to sit down on something (a bench, bed, chair, etc.). It’s reflexive: "sich" changes with the person (ich setzte mich…, du setztest dich…, er/sie setzte sich…). Often used in storytelling and written German; in everyday speech you also hear Perfekt: "Er hat sich auf die Bank gesetzt."
target_language_example: Sie setzte sich auf den Stuhl und wartete.
native_language_example: She sat down on the chair and waited.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb „sich setzen“ (to sit down). It’s used when someone moves into a sitting position next to someone/something. After „neben“ (next to), German typically uses the dative case for a fixed position: „neben mich/dir/ihn/sie …“.
target_language_example: Er setzte sich neben seine Freundin.
native_language_example: He sat down next to his girlfriend.

meaning: to make sure that … / it turns out that … (with a „dass“-clause).
additional_notes:
Used with certain reflexive verbs that are followed by a subordinate clause introduced by „dass“ (that). Common ones include:
- „sich vergewissern, dass …“ = to make sure/confirm that …
- „(es) ergibt sich, dass …“ = it turns out that … / it becomes clear that …
Word order: the verb goes to the end of the „dass“-clause (e.g., „… dass er ausgegangen war“).
target_language_example: Vergewissere dich, dass du die Tür abgeschlossen hast.
native_language_example: Make sure that you locked the door.

meaning: “(to do something) in order to …” after a reflexive verb.
additional_notes: Used to express purpose: a reflexive verb in the main clause + a comma + „um … zu“ + infinitive. The comma before „um“ is required. Example pattern: „Er bückte sich, um … zu …“ (= He bent down in order to …).
target_language_example: Ich beeile mich, um den Bus zu erwischen.
native_language_example: I’m hurrying (up) in order to catch the bus.

meaning: to present/describe/register oneself as; as (in disguise/role).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs to say what role or identity someone takes on. Common patterns: „sich als + Nomen verkleiden“ (to dress up as), „sich als + Nomen bezeichnen“ (to describe oneself as), „sich als + Nomen melden“ (to sign up/volunteer as). The noun after „als“ is usually without an article when it’s a role (e.g., „als Freiwilliger“, „als König“).
target_language_example: Sie hat sich als Lehrerin vorgestellt.
native_language_example: She introduced herself as a teacher.

meaning: reflexive + “am” (= at/on the): used to say you do something to yourself on a body part, or at a place.
additional_notes:
Common patterns:
- Body part: *sich am Kopf kratzen* (scratch yourself on the head), *sich am Bein weh tun* (hurt your leg), *sich am Handgelenk verletzen* (injure your wrist).
- Place: *sich am Empfang beklagen* (complain at reception).
- “Warming oneself” can also use it: *sich am Feuer die Hände wärmen* (warm your hands by the fire).
target_language_example: Ich habe mich am Fuß verletzt.
native_language_example: I injured my foot.

meaning: Used with many reflexive verbs to link to the thing/person involved (often: “to … / about …”).
additional_notes:
“sich an” is not usually used by itself; it’s part of common reflexive verb patterns:
- **sich an etw. erinnern** = to remember something (usually **Akk.**)
- **sich an etw. gewöhnen** = to get used to something (usually **Akk.**)
- **sich an etw. beteiligen** = to take part in something (usually **Dat.**)
- **sich an etw. halten** = to stick to / follow something (usually **Akk.**)
- **sich an jdn./etw. anschleichen** = to sneak up on someone/something (usually **Akk.**)
So the meaning depends on the main verb; “an” often corresponds to English “to/about/at,” but not word-for-word.
target_language_example: Ich erinnere mich nicht an seinen Namen.
native_language_example: I don’t remember his name.

meaning: reflexive + “an” + accusative: “to / at / onto (someone/something)”—meaning depends on the verb.
additional_notes: “sich an + Akk.” is a common pattern used with many verbs. Typical meanings: • sich an etw. gewöhnen = to get used to something • sich an jdn./etw. wenden = to turn to / contact someone (often for help or information) • sich an etw. halten = to follow / stick to rules/laws • sich an etw. machen = to get to work on something • sich an etw. fassen = to touch / grab something. The noun after “die” is in the accusative (e.g., an die Gesetze, an die Öffentlichkeit).
target_language_example: Bitte halten Sie sich an die Regeln.
native_language_example: Please follow the rules.

meaning: reflexive + “auf” (usually + accusative): used to link the verb to what you’re preparing for / looking forward to / focusing on.
additional_notes: “sich auf …” isn’t usually a standalone phrase; it’s a common pattern used with specific reflexive verbs. In the examples: sich vorbereiten auf (+Akk) = “to prepare for”, sich freuen auf (+Akk) = “to look forward to”, sich konzentrieren auf (+Akk) = “to concentrate on”. With location it can also appear in phrases like “sich auf der Straße treffen” (= to meet on/in the street), where “auf” is part of “auf + dative” for place. Case depends on the verb/expression, but with the ‘prepare/look forward/focus’ meanings it’s typically accusative.
target_language_example: Ich bereite mich auf die Prüfung vor.
native_language_example: I’m preparing for the exam.

meaning: oneself on/onto the; sometimes (with certain verbs) for the.
additional_notes: This is a pattern: a reflexive verb + „auf“ + accusative masculine („den“). Often it’s physical position or movement onto a surface (e.g., „sich setzen/legen auf den …“ = to sit/lie down on …). With some verbs it becomes more abstract: „sich auf den … vorbereiten“ = to prepare for …, and „sich auf den … auswirken“ = to have an effect on … . The noun after „den“ is masculine and in the accusative case (e.g., „den Stuhl“, „den Bauch“, „den Kampf“).
target_language_example: Ich setze mich auf den Stuhl.
native_language_example: I sit down on the chair.

meaning: (to) onto/on your back (lying with your back on the ground).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs like **sich legen** (lie down), **sich drehen** (turn over), or **sich klopfen** (pat yourself) to show the action is directed toward your own back. It takes the accusative: **auf den Rücken**.
target_language_example: Nach dem Sport lege ich mich auf den Rücken und entspanne mich.
native_language_example: After sports, I lie on my back and relax.

meaning: “(to) oneself onto/on the …” (reflexive + “auf die” = “onto/on the” with feminine/plural noun).
additional_notes: Used with many reflexive verbs and the preposition **auf**. **Auf + Accusative (auf die …)** is common for **movement/direction or focus toward something** (e.g., *sich auf die Abreise vorbereiten* = prepare for the departure; *sich auf die falschen Dinge konzentrieren* = focus on the wrong things; *sich auf die linke Seite legen* = lie down on the left side; *sich auf die Parkbank setzen* = sit down on the park bench). For location without movement, German often uses **auf + Dative** (e.g., *auf der Bank* = on the bench).
target_language_example: Ich setze mich auf die Bank.
native_language_example: I sit down on the bench.

meaning: reflexive + bei = to do something (e.g., apologize/thank/complain) to/with someone.
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs that take "bei" to mark the person you direct the action toward. Common with: sich (bei jdm.) entschuldigen (apologize to), sich (bei jdm.) bedanken (thank), sich (bei jdm.) beschweren (complain to). The person is in the dative: bei Tom, bei jemandem, bei der Chefin. Word order in questions: "Hast du dich bei Tom entschuldigt?"
target_language_example: Ich habe mich bei meiner Nachbarin entschuldigt.
native_language_example: I apologized to my neighbor.

meaning: "to/with me" (used with reflexive verbs like *sich entschuldigen*, *sich erkundigen*).
additional_notes: *Bei* + dative can mean "at/with" a person. With certain reflexive verbs, it marks the person you apologize to (*sich bei jemandem entschuldigen* = "to apologize to someone") or the person you ask/inquire with (*sich bei jemandem erkundigen* = "to ask someone / to inquire with someone"). Here *mir* is the dative form of *ich* (me).
target_language_example: Kannst du dich bitte bei mir erkundigen, ob der Laden noch offen ist?
native_language_example: Can you please ask for me/check with me whether the store is still open?

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive verb plus **beim** (= **bei dem**) to say that something happens to someone during an activity. Pattern: **sich + Verb + beim + noun/gerund** (e.g., *sich verletzen beim Tanzen* = to hurt oneself while dancing). Common with verbs like **sich übergeben** (vomit), **sich verletzen** (injure oneself), **sich amüsieren** (have fun), **sich abwechseln** (take turns).
target_language_example: Ich habe mich beim Kochen geschnitten.
native_language_example: I cut myself while cooking.

meaning: (to do something) to oneself / for oneself; or “it/that” as the object in reflexive phrases.
additional_notes: Often appears with a dative reflexive pronoun (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch) + “das” as the thing affected or chosen. Common patterns: (1) harming/affecting a body part: „Er hat sich das Knie gestoßen.“ (he hurt his knee). (2) having something done for yourself: „Sie hat sich das Klavier stimmen lassen.“ (she had the piano tuned). (3) choosing/ordering/buying something for yourself: „Ich bestelle mir das …“ (I’ll order that). In questions like „Verbessert sich das …?“ it’s not reflexive at all: „sich“ belongs to the verb „sich verbessern“ (= to improve), and „das“ is the subject (the thing that improves).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir das neue Handy gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself the new phone.

meaning: to break one’s leg (with verbs like „brechen“).
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) plus the body part in the accusative: „Ich habe mir das Bein gebrochen.“ This is the common German pattern for injuries to body parts.
target_language_example: Sie hat sich beim Skifahren das Bein gebrochen.
native_language_example: She broke her leg while skiing.

meaning: to (do something to) your hair; literally “to oneself the hair”.
additional_notes: Used with many hair-related verbs to show the action affects your own hair: e.g. sich das Haar bürsten (brush your hair), sich das Haar waschen (wash your hair), sich das Haar färben (dye your hair). German often uses a reflexive pronoun + a body part with an article (das Haar) instead of a possessive (“my/your”).
target_language_example: Ich wasche mir gerade das Haar.
native_language_example: I’m washing my hair right now.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like rasieren (to shave) or wachsen lassen (to let grow): the reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) shows whose beard it is. Common patterns: „Ich rasiere mir den Bart.“ / „Er rasiert sich den Bart.“ / „Sie lässt sich den Bart wachsen.“
target_language_example: Ich rasiere mir jeden Morgen den Bart.
native_language_example: I shave my beard every morning.

meaning: "one’s head" in a reflexive body-part expression (e.g., shave your head / bump your head); also in the idiom "sich den Kopf zerbrechen" = "to rack your brains".
additional_notes: German often uses a reflexive pronoun + a body part with a definite article: "Ich habe mir den Kopf gestoßen" (literally “I bumped myself the head”). The pronoun is usually dative (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch). With "sich den Kopf zerbrechen", it’s an idiom meaning to think very hard about a problem.
target_language_example: Ich habe mir gestern den Kopf gestoßen.
native_language_example: I bumped my head yesterday.

meaning: to be aware of the danger.
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive pronoun (sich) and usually the verb "sein": "jemand ist sich (Genitiv) bewusst" = someone is aware/conscious of something. Often appears with "müssen" or "sollten": "Er muss sich der Gefahr bewusst sein" (He has to be aware of the danger). In everyday German you may also hear the dative: "sich der Gefahr bewusst sein" vs. "sich der Gefahr bewusst sein" (Genitiv is the standard in writing).
target_language_example: Wir müssen uns der Gefahr bewusst sein, bevor wir losgehen.
native_language_example: We have to be aware of the danger before we set off.

meaning: “(to) oneself the …” — a very common reflexive pattern, often meaning “my/your/his/her/their …” or “to do … for oneself.”
additional_notes: This is not a fixed phrase by itself. It’s the reflexive pronoun (sich) + a definite article (die) used in many everyday expressions. Commonly, German uses “die” (the) with body parts and personal things where English uses a possessive: sich die Hände waschen = “wash your hands”, sich die Tränen abwischen = “wipe away your tears”. It also appears in set expressions like sich die Mühe machen = “make the effort”, and in verbs like sich die Telefonnummer aufschreiben = “write down the phone number (for yourself)”, sich die Sehenswürdigkeiten ansehen = “see the sights”.
target_language_example: Ich wasche mir schnell die Hände.
native_language_example: I’ll quickly wash my hands.

meaning: "one's hair" (used with a reflexive verb, e.g. wash/dye one’s hair).
additional_notes: Common German pattern for body parts: use a reflexive pronoun + definite article (die) instead of a possessive. You typically use it with verbs like waschen (to wash) or färben (to dye): „Ich wasche mir die Haare.“ / „Sie hat sich die Haare gefärbt.“ The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject (ich mir, du dir, er/sie sich, wir uns, ihr euch, Sie sich).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir heute Morgen die Haare gewaschen.
native_language_example: I washed my hair this morning.

meaning: to get one’s hair cut (have it cut by someone else).
additional_notes: Uses a reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) plus **lassen** to mean you arrange for someone else to do it (usually at a hair salon). Example forms: **Ich lasse mir die Haare schneiden.** / **Sie lässt sich die Haare schneiden.**
target_language_example: Ich lasse mir morgen die Haare schneiden.
native_language_example: I’m getting my hair cut tomorrow.

meaning: (to) one’s hands (used with a reflexive verb: wash/rub/wipe your hands).
additional_notes: This is the common reflexive+dative pattern for body parts: the person is the indirect object (mir/dir/sich …) and the body part takes the article (die Hände), not a possessive (*meine Hände*) in most everyday sentences. Typical verbs: sich die Hände waschen/abwischen/reiben.
target_language_example: Ich wasche mir schnell die Hände.
native_language_example: I’m quickly washing my hands.

meaning: (as in „sich die Zähne putzen“) ‘your teeth’ in the phrase ‘to brush your teeth’.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) plus a body part with a definite article: „Ich putze mir die Zähne.“ / „Er putzt sich die Zähne.“ In everyday English you usually just say “brush my/your/his teeth.”
target_language_example: Ich putze mir morgens und abends die Zähne.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth in the morning and in the evening.

meaning: a common pattern meaning “(to) oneself a …” (reflexive pronoun + “ein/eine/ein”).
additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself: it appears inside many verbs. **sich** changes with the subject (ich **mir**, du **dir**, er **sich**, wir **uns**, ihr **euch**, sie/Sie **sich**). **ein** is the indefinite article (“a/an”) and changes to **ein/eine** depending on gender/case. Often used for actions someone does for themselves (e.g., *sich ein Eis kaufen* = “buy oneself an ice cream”) or with other verbs where the reflexive is required (e.g., *sich fühlen* = “feel”).
target_language_example: Ich habe mir ein Buch gekauft.
native_language_example: I bought myself a book.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun (sich) to emphasize buying something for yourself. Often appears with another verb expressing intention/plan (e.g., beabsichtigen, vorhaben) or with um ... zu to express purpose: „Er nahm einen Kredit auf, um sich ein Auto zu kaufen.“ In a main clause the verb is split: „Ich kaufe mir ein Auto.“
target_language_example: Ich spare Geld, um mir ein Auto zu kaufen.
native_language_example: I’m saving money to buy myself a car.

meaning: "(to) get/buy/find oneself a ..." (do something for oneself).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive dative (mir/dir/sich/uns/euch/sich) plus an accusative masculine noun: "sich einen + Nomen". Common with verbs like "kaufen" (buy), "suchen" (look for), "nehmen" (take), "holen" (get). It adds the idea that you do it for your own benefit: "Tom kauft sich einen Anzug" ≈ "Tom buys himself a suit" (not just "Tom buys a suit").
target_language_example: Ich suche mir einen ruhigen Platz.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a quiet place (for myself).

meaning: "to have decided" / "to have made up one’s mind".
additional_notes: Perfect tense of the reflexive verb **sich entscheiden** (haben + sich + entschieden). Often followed by **zu + infinitive** ("decided to...") or **für + Akkusativ** ("decided on/for...").
target_language_example: Ich habe mich entschieden, heute zu Hause zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I decided to stay at home today.

meaning: reflexive + “für” (“for”), used with certain verbs (e.g., be interested in, think of oneself as, apologize for, be suitable for).
additional_notes: “sich” changes with the subject (ich mich, du dich, er/sie/es sich, wir uns, ihr euch, sie/Sie sich). “für” takes the accusative: für mich/dich/ihn/sie/es/uns/euch/sie/Sie. Common combinations: sich interessieren für (+Akk) = to be interested in; sich (für etw.) entschuldigen = to apologize for; sich (für jdn./etw.) halten = to consider oneself (to be); sich eignen für = to be suitable for.
target_language_example: Ich interessiere mich für Musik.
native_language_example: I’m interested in music.

additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs to show that two or more people do the action to one another (mutual action). It often comes after the verb: „Sie helfen sich gegenseitig.“ In subordinate clauses it can come earlier: „…, weil sie sich gegenseitig helfen.“
target_language_example: Wir unterstützen uns gegenseitig.
native_language_example: We support each other.

additional_notes: Perfect tense of the reflexive verb **sich ändern** (“to change”). It’s used when something changes (often by itself or over time), not when someone changes something on purpose (that’s **etw. ändern**). Common pattern: **etw. hat sich geändert** (“something has changed”), **Haben sich deine Pläne geändert?** (“Have your plans changed?”).
target_language_example: Seit letztem Jahr hat sich viel geändert.
native_language_example: Since last year, a lot has changed.

meaning: to do/feel/be well (with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used as an adverb with many reflexive verbs to say that something goes well or someone performs well. Common patterns: **sich gut schlagen** (do well/hold up), **sich gut verkaufen** (sell well), **sich gut machen** (do well / look good), **sich gut anfühlen** (feel good), **sich gut auskennen** (know a place/topic well), **sich gut um jdn. kümmern** (take good care of someone). The **sich** changes with the subject (ich **mich**, du **dich**, er **sich**, wir **uns**, ihr **euch**, sie **sich**).
target_language_example: Keine Sorge, ich kenne mich hier gut aus.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know my way around here well.

meaning: used with certain verbs to mean “(to) down” (e.g., “lie down”, “kneel down”).
additional_notes: This is a common pattern in German: a reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) + the particle/adverb “hin”. It often appears with verbs like **sich hinlegen** (to lie down) and **sich hinknien** (to kneel down). In commands you’ll often see **sich**: **Legen Sie sich hin!** = “Lie down!” (formal).
target_language_example: Ich bin müde und lege mich kurz hin.
native_language_example: I’m tired and I’m going to lie down for a moment.

additional_notes:
This is not a fixed expression by itself. It’s a common pattern where a reflexive verb uses **sich** and then a place/setting introduced by **im** (“in the”). **im** is the contraction of **in dem**.

Common examples:
- **sich im Nebel auflösen** = “to dissolve/vanish in the fog”
- **sich im Klaren sein (über …)** = “to be clear/aware (about …)”
target_language_example: Ich bin mir im Klaren, dass das schwer ist.
native_language_example: I’m aware that this is difficult.

meaning: (to look at) yourself in the mirror.
additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) to describe seeing or looking at yourself in a mirror. Often used with verbs like betrachten (to look at), ansehen (to look at), and anlächeln (to smile at).
target_language_example: Ich sehe mich im Spiegel und richte meine Haare.
native_language_example: I look at myself in the mirror and fix my hair.

meaning: reflexive pattern meaning “(to put/get) oneself in/into …” (used with certain verbs).
additional_notes: You’ll often see this with verbs that take a reflexive pronoun (mich, dich, sich, uns, euch, sich) plus the preposition "in". With "in" + accusative (in + einen/eine/ein), it usually means movement/change into something (e.g., sich in drei Gruppen aufteilen = divide into three groups; sich in ein Tuch/ eine Decke wickeln = wrap oneself in a cloth/blanket). With "in" + dative (in + dem/der), it can describe being within a place/context (e.g., sich in der Stadt verlaufen = get lost in the city).
target_language_example: Nach dem Baden wickelte ich mich in ein Handtuch ein.
native_language_example: After bathing, I wrapped myself in a towel.

meaning: (oneself) into the (masculine singular noun in the accusative).
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed phrase on its own; it’s a common grammar pattern: reflexive pronoun + "in den" (="into the" for masculine singular nouns in the accusative) used with many verbs. Often used for movement/positioning into something (e.g., "sich in den Sessel sinken lassen" = to sink into the armchair, "sich in den Bus setzen" = to sit down in the bus). It can also appear inside idioms (e.g., "sich in den Hintern beißen" = to regret something). If you mean location (no movement), German often uses dative: "in dem"/"im".
target_language_example: Er setzte sich in den Bus und fuhr nach Hause.
native_language_example: He sat down in the bus and rode home.

meaning: “(oneself) into a …” (masculine noun), used to show becoming/transforming into something; also “(oneself) in love with a …” with certain verbs.
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs like **sich verwandeln in …** (“to transform into …”) and **sich verlieben in …** (“to fall in love with …”). **in + accusative** often expresses a change or movement *into* something. **einen** is the accusative form of **ein** for masculine nouns (e.g., *einen Schmetterling, einen Skandal, einen Künstler*).
target_language_example: Der Prinz hat sich in einen Frosch verwandelt.
native_language_example: The prince transformed into a frog.

meaning: “(to) … every day” with a reflexive verb (doing something to yourself).
additional_notes: Used with reflexive verbs like sich rasieren, sich waschen, sich duschen, sich baden, sich wiegen. The word order is typically: verb + sich + jeden Tag (e.g., „Ich rasiere mich jeden Tag.“). It’s not a fixed phrase by itself; it depends on the verb.
target_language_example: Ich dusche mich jeden Tag vor der Arbeit.
native_language_example: I shower every day before work.

additional_notes: Used when an action happens easily/quickly to someone or by itself, often with reflexive verbs like: sich eine Erkältung einfangen/holen (to catch a cold), sich ausbreiten (to spread), sich anpassen (to adapt). The reflexive pronoun (sich) changes with the subject: ich passe mich leicht an, du passt dich leicht an, er/sie passt sich leicht an, wir passen uns leicht an, ihr passt euch leicht an, sie passen sich leicht an.
target_language_example: Kinder stecken sich leicht an.
native_language_example: Kids get infected easily.

meaning: “with” used with a reflexive verb (e.g., to meet/contact/speak with).
additional_notes: Many German verbs are reflexive and commonly take an object with **mit**. The pattern is **sich + Verb + mit + Dativ** (e.g., *sich treffen mit*, *sich in Verbindung setzen mit*, *sich unterhalten mit*, *sich umgeben mit*). In some cases it can also mean “(to change) with” (*sich verändern mit der Zeit* = “change over time”).
target_language_example: Ich treffe mich morgen mit meiner Freundin.
native_language_example: I’m meeting my girlfriend (friend) tomorrow.

meaning: “oneself … with a …” (used with many reflexive verbs; often means “with a …” or “meet with a …”).
additional_notes:
This is a common pattern: a reflexive verb + „mit“ + a thing/person. „mit“ takes the dative case, so the indefinite article is „einem“ (masculine/neuter), „einer“ (feminine), „einem“ (neuter). Meaning depends on the verb: 
- „sich beschäftigen mit …“ = to deal with / work on …
- „sich (die Stirn/das Gesicht) wischen mit …“ = to wipe … with … (instrument)
- „sich treffen mit …“ = to meet with … (person)
target_language_example: Ich treffe mich heute mit einem Freund.
native_language_example: I’m meeting a friend today.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) plus "neben" to show that someone places themselves next to someone/something. With movement/positioning (sich legen/setzen/stellen/knien) it usually takes the accusative: neben mich/ihn/das Plakat. If you are already there (no movement), "neben" often takes the dative: neben mir/ihm/dem Plakat.
target_language_example: Ich setzte mich neben meine Freundin.
native_language_example: I sat down next to my friend.

additional_notes: Used to negate reflexive verbs like sich erinnern (to remember), sich trauen (to dare), sich rühren (to move), sich an etw. halten (to stick to sth.). Word order: in main clauses, the reflexive pronoun (mich/dich/sich/uns/euch/sich) usually comes before "nicht" (Ich erinnere mich nicht.). In subordinate clauses, both are near the end (…, weil er sich nicht erinnert.). Often translates simply as "not" in English, because English usually doesn’t use a reflexive pronoun here ("He doesn’t remember").
target_language_example: Ich beeile mich nicht, weil ich noch Zeit habe.
native_language_example: I’m not hurrying because I still have time.

meaning: to get divorced (to have a divorce).
additional_notes: Used when a married person (or couple) ends the marriage. It’s a reflexive verb phrase: sich scheiden lassen = to have oneself divorced. Often used with wollen (want to) or in the past: Er hat sich scheiden lassen.
target_language_example: Nach zehn Jahren Ehe lassen sie sich scheiden.
native_language_example: After ten years of marriage, they’re getting divorced.

meaning: to get divorced (to have a divorce).
