additional_notes: Used with a subject in 3rd person singular (er/sie/es or a name): **spielt** is the present-tense form of **spielen** (“to play”). **jeden Tag** means “every day” (accusative after a time expression). Often followed by a sport or game: *spielt jeden Tag Fußball/Tennis*.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester spielt jeden Tag Klavier.
native_language_example: My sister plays the piano every day.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not important or not relevant to the situation. Often said as (1) "Das spielt keine Rolle" = "That doesn't matter" or (2) "Es spielt keine Rolle, ..." / "Spielt keine Rolle, ..." = "It doesn't matter (that/what/if) ...". "Rolle" literally means "role," but here the whole phrase means "be important / make a difference."
target_language_example: Es spielt keine Rolle, ob du heute oder morgen kommst.
native_language_example: It doesn't matter whether you come today or tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **mit jemandem sprechen** (“to speak with someone”). **Mit** is followed by the **dative** case: *sprach mit mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen*; *sprach mit Maria / mit den Freunden*. It can also be used with **mit + noun** to describe how someone spoke: *sprach mit fester Stimme* (“spoke in a firm voice”).
target_language_example: Ich sprach gestern mit meinem Lehrer über das Problem.
native_language_example: I spoke with my teacher yesterday about the problem.

additional_notes: "sprachen" is the simple past (Präteritum) of "sprechen" for "they" (or a plural subject like "Tom und Maria"). It’s commonly used in writing or storytelling. It is followed by "über" + accusative to say what the conversation topic was: "über Politik", "über mich", "über die Zukunft".
target_language_example: Wir sprachen über das Wetter, während wir warteten.
native_language_example: We talked about the weather while we were waiting.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **springen** in the simple past (**sprang**) to describe someone/something jumping out of a place/container. **aus** takes the **dative** case, so masculine/neuter nouns often appear as **aus dem** (“out of the”). For feminine nouns: **aus der**; plural: **aus den**.
target_language_example: Das Kind sprang aus dem Auto.
native_language_example: The child jumped out of the car.

additional_notes: "sprang" is the simple past of "springen" (to jump). "über" means "over/across." "den" is the accusative masculine form of "der" (the), used because the thing being jumped over is a direct object (e.g., "den Hund", "den Graben"). With other nouns, the article changes: "über das" (neuter), "über die" (feminine/plural).
target_language_example: Der Junge sprang über den Zaun.
native_language_example: The boy jumped over the fence.

additional_notes: This is the formal (Sie) form of the verb sprechen (“to speak”). It’s used when addressing strangers, customers, or in professional settings. In questions it often means “Do you speak …?” (e.g., a language). As an imperative, it can mean “Please talk/speak …” (e.g., Sprechen Sie mit ihm! = “Talk to him!”). With aus Erfahrung it means “from experience” (Sprechen Sie aus Erfahrung? = “Are you speaking from experience?”).
target_language_example: Sprechen Sie bitte langsamer.
native_language_example: Please speak more slowly.

additional_notes: Present tense of **sprechen** with **ihr** (“you all/you guys”). Often used in questions (verb first): **Sprecht ihr Deutsch?** = “Do you guys speak German?” It can also mean “are you talking (about…)” depending on what follows: **über** (about), **von** (about/which), **mit** (with), **aus (persönlicher) Erfahrung** (from (personal) experience). Uses **ihr**, not the formal **Sie**.
target_language_example: Sprecht ihr auch Englisch?
native_language_example: Do you guys also speak English?

additional_notes: Used to ask what a group of people you address as "ihr" (friends, classmates, kids, etc.) is talking about. It goes with "über" + accusative (e.g., über Tom, über sie, über etwas). You can also say: "Sprecht ihr gerade über …?" (right now) or "Worüber sprecht ihr?" (What are you talking about?).
target_language_example: Sprecht ihr über etwas Bestimmtes?
native_language_example: Are you talking about something specific?

additional_notes: From "sprechen" (to speak/talk). Used to ask someone if they speak a language (often followed by a language: „Sprichst du Deutsch?“) or to ask about what they’re talking about (e.g., „Von wem sprichst du?“ = “Who are you talking about?”). It’s informal because it uses „du“ (used with friends, family, kids, etc.); the formal version is „Sprechen Sie …?“
target_language_example: Sprichst du Englisch?
native_language_example: Do you speak English?

additional_notes: Used with the verb „sprechen“ to say what language someone speaks. It changes with the subject: ich spreche Englisch, du sprichst Englisch, er/sie spricht Englisch, wir sprechen Englisch, ihr sprecht Englisch, sie/Sie sprechen Englisch. You can add adverbs like „flüssig“ (fluently) or list multiple languages with „und“.
target_language_example: Ich spreche Englisch, aber nur ein bisschen.
native_language_example: I speak English, but only a little.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „sprechen“ (to speak) + a language. The verb changes with the subject: ich spreche, du sprichst, er/sie/es spricht, wir sprechen, ihr sprecht, sie/Sie sprechen. You can add adverbs like „auch“ (also), „natürlich“ (of course), „ziemlich gut“ (pretty well), or comparisons like „genau so gut wie …“ (just as well as …).
target_language_example: Meine Schwester spricht Französisch, aber ich spreche nur Englisch.
native_language_example: My sister speaks French, but I only speak English.

additional_notes: Used to compare language ability, often with **als** (“than”): *Er spricht besser Französisch als ich.* You can also add what it’s being compared to: *… als Englisch.* If **als** introduces a full clause, a comma is used: *…, als er glauben machen will.*
target_language_example: Sie spricht besser Französisch als Deutsch.
native_language_example: She speaks French better than German.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s language ability is the same as someone else’s. It’s typically followed by a comparison with **wie**: **Er spricht genauso gut Englisch wie du.** You can also place the language after **gut**: **Er spricht genauso gut wie du Englisch.**
target_language_example: Sie spricht genauso gut Deutsch wie ihr Bruder.
native_language_example: She speaks German just as well as her brother.

additional_notes: Used with "man" (impersonal subject meaning "people/one") to say what language is spoken in a place or in general. Common pattern: "In/Hier + spricht man + Sprache." You can also use it in questions: "Wie viele Sprachen spricht man ...?"
target_language_example: In der Schweiz spricht man Deutsch, Französisch und Italienisch.
native_language_example: In Switzerland people speak German, French, and Italian.

additional_notes: Uses the impersonal pronoun „man“ (= people/one) to talk generally about what language is spoken in a country/region. Often used in statements like „Deutsch spricht man in …“ and in questions like „Welche Sprache spricht man in …?“ In English you’d usually say “People speak … in …” or “... is spoken in ...”.
target_language_example: Deutsch spricht man in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz.
native_language_example: People speak German in Germany, Austria, and Switzerland.

spricht nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch

target_language_multi_word_term: spricht nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch
additional_notes: This uses the common pattern **nicht nur …, sondern auch …** to add extra information (“not only … but also …”). Here it’s used with **sprechen** to list more than one language. The second part (**sondern auch …**) typically names the additional language.
target_language_example: Er spricht nicht nur Englisch, sondern auch Italienisch.
native_language_example: He speaks not only English, but also Italian.

additional_notes: Used with **über + accusative** to say someone never talks about a topic. **seine** is the possessive for **his** (or **their**) with masculine/neuter nouns in the accusative (e.g., *seinen Bruder*, *seine Arbeit*, *sein Leben*). In full sentences you often add the subject first: *Er spricht nie über seine …*
target_language_example: Er spricht nie über seine Vergangenheit.
native_language_example: He never talks about his past.

additional_notes: Used with a language name after it: „spricht sehr gut Deutsch/Englisch/Japanisch“. The verb changes with the subject (ich spreche, du sprichst, er/sie spricht), but „sehr gut“ stays the same.
target_language_example: Meine Schwester spricht sehr gut Deutsch.
native_language_example: My sister speaks German very well.

additional_notes: Used with forms of „sein“ (ich bin/du bist/wir sind … spät dran) to say you’re late or don’t have much time left. Often used for appointments, meetings, deadlines, or when you need to hurry. You can intensify it with „schon“ (already) or „zu“ (too): „Ich bin schon spät dran.“ / „Wir dürfen nicht zu spät dran sein.“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, ich bin spät dran — der Bus hatte Verspätung.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm running late — the bus was delayed.

additional_notes: Used with motion verbs like kommen/gehen/fahren to say someone arrives at home late. "nach Hause" means "(to) home" (direction). Don’t confuse it with "zu Hause" = "at home" (location). You can add intensifiers like "sehr" (very) or give a time: "um Mitternacht" (at midnight).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern spät nach Hause gekommen.
native_language_example: I got home late yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or someone does something at a very late hour during the night (often implying “too late” or unusual). Often used with "bis" (bis spät nachts = until late at night) or "so" (so spät nachts = so late at night).
target_language_example: Bitte ruf mich nicht so spät nachts an.
native_language_example: Please don’t call me so late at night.

meaning: to call later; to call back later.
additional_notes: Used when you want to make a phone call at a later time. With the separable verb **anrufen**, the verb splits in a main clause: **Ich rufe dich später an.** In polite requests you often hear **Können Sie mich später anrufen?**
target_language_example: Ich rufe dich später an, ich bin gerade in einer Besprechung.
native_language_example: I’ll call you later; I’m in a meeting right now.

meaning: to come from; to originate from.
additional_notes: Used to say where a person, thing, or word originally comes from. Common with people’s origin (often like “to be originally from”) and with the origin of words/ideas. It’s usually followed by a place/country or a language: aus Australien, aus Boston, aus dem Latein(ischen).
target_language_example: Dieses Rezept stammt aus Italien.
native_language_example: This recipe comes from Italy.

additional_notes: Used to link two actions: first someone gets up (from sitting/lying), then they do the next action. It’s the simple past of the separable verb **aufstehen**: **(er/sie) stand … auf**. In sentences, **stand** comes early and **auf** goes to the end of the clause; **und** connects the next verb/action.
target_language_example: Ich stand auf und machte das Fenster auf.
native_language_example: I stood up and opened the window.

meaning: "stood up and went" (got up and left/went somewhere).
additional_notes: A common story/narration sequence in the simple past (Präteritum): **stand auf** is the Präteritum of **aufstehen** (a separable verb: *auf* goes to the end), and **ging** is the Präteritum of **gehen**. Often followed by a destination: *zur Tür*, *ans Fenster*, or used alone to mean someone left.
target_language_example: Sie stand auf und ging nach Hause.
native_language_example: She stood up and went home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone got up early with a purpose. It’s the past tense (Präteritum) of "früh aufstehen" (to get up early): "ich stand … auf", "sie/er stand … auf". "um … zu" introduces the purpose/goal (like "in order to"). In everyday speech, many people also use Perfekt: "Ich bin früh aufgestanden, um …".
target_language_example: Ich stand früh auf, um vor der Arbeit noch zu joggen.
native_language_example: I got up early to go jogging before work.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone/something being positioned next to something (often right at an edge or surface): *an der Tür* (at the door), *an der Spüle* (by the sink), *an der Straßenecke* (at the street corner). With a fixed location, *an* takes the dative case: *an der* (feminine nouns), *an dem* = *am* (masculine/neuter), *an den* (plural).
target_language_example: Sie stand an der Bushaltestelle und wartete.
native_language_example: She stood at the bus stop and waited.

meaning: “died of/from” (a cause) or “died on” (a specific day).
additional_notes: “Starb” is the simple past of *sterben* (“to die”). With **an + dative**, it often gives the cause of death: *an Krebs, an Sauerstoffmangel, an einer Krankheit*. It can also use **an + dative** for a point in time like a day/date: *an ihrem Geburtstag* (“on her birthday”).
target_language_example: Mein Großvater starb an Krebs.
native_language_example: My grandfather died of cancer.

additional_notes: "starb" is the simple past of "sterben" (to die). In German you often say "an" + illness/cause of death: "an Krebs sterben" = to die of cancer. In everyday speech you’ll also hear the perfect tense: "Er ist an Krebs gestorben."
target_language_example: Ihre Mutter starb an Krebs.
native_language_example: Her mother died of cancer.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **sterben** + **an** + dative to name the cause of death (often an illness, injury, or overdose). Here **starb** is simple past (“died”), and **einer** is dative feminine/indefinite (“a/an”), e.g. **an einer Lungenentzündung**. Other forms: **stirbt an …** (present), **ist an … gestorben** (present perfect).
target_language_example: Er starb an einer schweren Krankheit.
native_language_example: He died of a serious illness.

additional_notes: “starb” is the simple past of “sterben” (to die). With “vor” + a time period, it means “... ago” (e.g., „vor einem Jahr“ = a year ago). With “vor” + an event/noun, it means “before” (e.g., „vor meiner Ankunft“ = before my arrival).
target_language_example: Meine Großmutter starb vor drei Jahren.
native_language_example: My grandmother died three years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has sufficient strength, power, or intensity. Often followed by an infinitive with „um … zu …“: „stark genug, um … zu …“ (strong enough to …). With drinks like coffee, „stark“ means strong in taste/caffeine.
target_language_example: Ich bin noch nicht stark genug, um den Koffer allein zu tragen.
native_language_example: I'm not strong enough yet to carry the suitcase by myself.

additional_notes: Used to describe intense physical pain. Often used with haben (Ich habe starke Schmerzen …) and can be specified with a body part/location: im Rücken (in the back), im Bauch (in the stomach), im Kopf (in the head). In sentence 4, zu starke Schmerzen, um … means “too much pain to …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe starke Schmerzen im Bauch und brauche einen Arzt.
native_language_example: I have severe stomach pain and I need a doctor.

meaning: of heavy rain (genitive: “because of / despite heavy rain”).
additional_notes: “starken Regens” is the genitive form of “starker Regen” (heavy rain). It’s commonly used after prepositions that often take the genitive, especially **wegen** (because of) and **trotz** (despite): **wegen starken Regens**, **trotz des starken Regens**. In everyday speech you may also hear the dative: **wegen starkem Regen**.
target_language_example: Wegen starken Regens bleibt der Park heute geschlossen.
native_language_example: Because of heavy rain, the park is closed today.

additional_notes: Command form of the separable verb **aufstehen**. Used to tell one person (du) to stand up from a chair or to get out of bed. Often said with urgency: **Komm schon, steh auf!**
target_language_example: Steh auf, wir müssen jetzt los!
native_language_example: Get up, we have to leave now!

meaning: 'are you standing?' / 'do you stand (for/in line)?' / 'what are you into?' (depending on context).
additional_notes: "stehst du" is the 2nd-person singular form of "stehen" (you stand/are standing). The meaning depends a lot on what comes with it: (1) "Auf was/was für … stehst du?" = 'What … are you into?' (colloquial, about tastes). (2) "Auf wessen Seite stehst du?" = 'Whose side are you on?' (3) "Wie lange stehst du da …?" = 'How long have you been standing there …?' (4) "Wofür stehst du an?" uses "anstehen" = 'to queue/wait in line for'.
target_language_example: Auf welche Musik stehst du gerade?
native_language_example: What kind of music are you into right now?

meaning: gets up every morning (literally: “stands every morning”).
additional_notes: Used with "auf" as the separable verb "aufstehen" (= to get up). In a main clause, "steht" comes early and "auf" goes to the end: "Er steht jeden Morgen um acht Uhr auf." "jeden Morgen" means “every morning.”
target_language_example: Ich stehe jeden Morgen um sieben Uhr auf.
native_language_example: I get up every morning at seven o’clock.

meaning: “is/stands on the …” (location); also “is at stake” in fixed phrases (e.g., auf dem Spiel stehen).
additional_notes: Literal use: for where an object is placed, with a dative noun after „auf dem“ (e.g., auf dem Herd = on the stove). Figurative: in the idiom „auf dem Spiel stehen“ it means something important is at risk/at stake.
target_language_example: Das Glas steht auf dem Tisch.
native_language_example: The glass is on the table.

additional_notes: From the verb "stehen" (to suit, to look good on someone). Very common with clothes/colors: "Das steht dir gut." It can also be used in fixed expressions like "(Etwas) steht dir ins Gesicht geschrieben" = "(Something) is written all over your face" (your expression clearly shows it).
target_language_example: Die Farbe steht dir wirklich gut.
native_language_example: That color really suits you.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s appearance, especially clothes, colors, or accessories. The thing that looks good is the subject: "Blau steht dir gut" = “Blue suits you.” Often said as "Das steht dir gut!" (“That looks good on you!”).
target_language_example: Die Jacke steht dir gut.
native_language_example: The jacket looks good on you.

meaning: “is right at the door” (literally) / “is just around the corner; is coming very soon” (figuratively).
additional_notes: Used both literally (something is physically in front of the door) and very commonly figuratively for events or times of year that are approaching soon (e.g., Herbst, Halloween, Weihnachten). In the figurative sense, it means it will happen very soon, like “just around the corner.”
target_language_example: Die Prüfungen stehen vor der Tür, deshalb lerne ich jeden Tag.
native_language_example: The exams are just around the corner, so I study every day.

additional_notes: Du-imperative of **sich stellen** (“to stand/position oneself”). Very common with a place: **Stell dich da vorne hin.** / **Stell dich an die Wand.** / **Stell dich in die Schlange.** With a thing/person (dative) it can mean “face/confront”: **Stell dich der Sache!** Note: **Stell dich mal an!** comes from **sich anstellen** and is often colloquial for “Don’t make such a fuss / stop acting so difficult” (context decides whether it’s “line up” or “make a fuss”).
target_language_example: Stell dich bitte in die Schlange.
native_language_example: Please get in line.

additional_notes: Used in conversation to ask someone to imagine a situation or to introduce surprising news. Literally it’s “put (it) in front of yourself,” but the natural meaning is “imagine” or “just think.” Often followed by a clause (sometimes with “dass”): “Stell dir vor, (dass) …”.
target_language_example: Stell dir vor, wir haben morgen frei!
native_language_example: Imagine that—we have tomorrow off!

meaning: polite command form of „stellen“: “(please) put/place/set …” (and in some fixed phrases: “connect” / “make sure”).
additional_notes:
„Stellen Sie …“ is the formal (Sie) imperative. Very common with locations: „Stellen Sie die Eier in den Kühlschrank.“ (= put/place). Also appears in set phrases:
- „jemanden zu … durchstellen“ = to put someone through (on the phone)
- „Stellen Sie sicher, dass …“ = make sure that …
- „wegstellen“ (often as „Stellen Sie … weg!“) = put away.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, stellen Sie bitte sicher, dass das Fenster zu ist.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please make sure the window is closed.

additional_notes: This uses the formal imperative with **Sie** (used with strangers, customers, etc.). **stellen** often means to place something somewhere in an upright/positioned way, and it commonly appears with a location phrase: **auf** (+ accusative) = onto, **ins** (= in das, + accusative) = into, **dorthin/dahin zurück** = back there.
target_language_example: Stellen Sie das Buch bitte zurück ins Regal.
native_language_example: Please put the book back on the shelf.

additional_notes:
This is the polite command form (Sie) of **sich stellen**. It’s usually completed with a place or a prefix verb:
- **Stellen Sie sich an.** = Queue up.
- **Stellen Sie sich (in einer Reihe) auf.** = Line up.
- **Stellen Sie sich vor.** = Introduce yourself / Imagine (depending on context).
So **stellen Sie sich** by itself often feels unfinished; you typically add **an/auf/vor** or a location.
target_language_example: Stellen Sie sich bitte hierhin.
native_language_example: Please stand here.

additional_notes: Past tense of the common phrase „jemandem eine Frage stellen“ = “to ask someone a question.” „mir“ is dative (“to me”), used for the person you ask. In the present tense: „Sie stellt mir eine Frage.“
target_language_example: Der Lehrer stellte mir eine Frage, aber ich wusste die Antwort nicht.
native_language_example: The teacher asked me a question, but I didn’t know the answer.

meaning: “(he/she) put/placed himself/herself”; often used as: lined up, set something for himself/herself, introduced himself/herself, or pretended/acted.
additional_notes: “stellte sich” is the simple past (Präteritum) of reflexive “sich stellen”. In everyday German it commonly appears in set phrases: **sich anstellen** = to line up (Er stellte sich als letzter an.); **sich den Wecker stellen** = to set an alarm for oneself (Er stellte sich … den Wecker.); **sich vorstellen** = to introduce oneself (Er stellte sich vor. / … mit dem Namen Paul.); and sometimes **sich + adjective stellen** = to put on/act a mood (e.g., “wütend stellen” = pretend to be angry).
target_language_example: Ich stellte mich hinten an.
native_language_example: I lined up at the back.

meaning: "turned out to be" (it was revealed to be).
additional_notes:
Usually used with the separable verb "sich als … herausstellen":
- Present: "Es stellt sich als schwierig heraus." = It turns out to be difficult.
- Past (like in your examples): "Es stellte sich als schwierig heraus." 
It often describes the true nature of something after you learn more (a rumor, a person, a situation). The structure is: [subject] + (stellt/stellte) + sich + als + [noun/adjective] + heraus.
target_language_example: Die Idee stellte sich als viel besser heraus als gedacht.
native_language_example: The idea turned out to be much better than expected.

meaning: got out of the (e.g., car, elevator, plane).
additional_notes: Past tense of the separable verb **aussteigen** (ich steige aus → ich **stieg** aus). Used with **aus + dative** for leaving a vehicle or enclosed place: **aus dem** (masc./neut.), **aus der** (fem.), **aus den** (plural). Common with Auto, Wagen, Fahrstuhl, Flugzeug, Bus, Zug, etc.
target_language_example: Nachdem der Bus angehalten hatte, stieg ich aus dem Bus.
native_language_example: After the bus stopped, I got off the bus.

meaning: got off the bus / got out of the bus.
additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of the separable verb **aussteigen** (“to get off/out”). In main clauses, **aus** often appears at the end: *Sie stieg aus dem Bus aus.* In the perfect tense: *Er ist aus dem Bus ausgestiegen.*
target_language_example: Als wir an der Haltestelle ankamen, stieg sie aus dem Bus aus.
native_language_example: When we arrived at the stop, she got off the bus.

additional_notes: Past tense of the separable verb **einsteigen** (“to get in / board”). You’ll often see it split as **stieg … ein**: *Er stieg in den Zug ein.* The preposition **in** takes the accusative here (direction/movement), and **den** is used with masculine nouns like **der Zug** (train) or **der Bus** (bus). With other nouns you’ll get **in die** (feminine/plural) or **in das / ins** (neuter).
target_language_example: Sie stieg in den Bus ein und setzte sich ans Fenster.
native_language_example: She got on the bus and sat by the window.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **in seinen Wagen steigen** = “to get into his car.” Used in narratives and written German; in speech you’ll also hear **ist in seinen Wagen gestiegen** (Perfekt). **Wagen** here means “car” (not necessarily a wagon).
target_language_example: Er stieg in seinen Wagen und machte den Motor an.
native_language_example: He got into his car and started the engine.

meaning: “got out of the / got off the” (something).
additional_notes: From the separable verb **aussteigen** (“to get out / get off”). **stiegen** is the simple past (Präteritum) for **wir/sie** (we/they). It’s usually followed by **aus + dative**: **aus dem** (from the), **aus der** (from the). Used for vehicles and transport: **aus dem Bus/Auto/Zug** = “get off/out of the bus/car/train.”
target_language_example: Wir stiegen aus dem Zug und suchten ein Taxi.
native_language_example: We got off the train and looked for a taxi.

meaning: to be quiet; to keep quiet.
additional_notes: Used to ask or tell someone not to make noise. Common after verbs like „bitten“ (to ask) or „bedeuten“ (to signal/indicate), and also with „scheinen“ (to seem): „Er bat uns, still zu sein.“ Note: German „still“ often means “quiet,” not English “still” (= not moving).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte still zu sein? Ich telefoniere gerade.
native_language_example: Can you please be quiet? I’m on the phone right now.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase „jemandem zustimmen“ = to agree with someone. Word order can change depending on the sentence (e.g., „Ich stimme dir zu.“ or after an intro phrase: „Im Großen und Ganzen stimme ich dir zu.“). Often used with context phrases like „in dem Punkt / in dieser Hinsicht / im Großen und Ganzen“ to show you agree in general or only on a specific point.
target_language_example: Ich stimme dir zu, aber wir sollten trotzdem vorsichtig sein.
native_language_example: I agree with you, but we should still be careful.

meaning: 'Is it true that…?' / 'Is it correct that…?'
additional_notes: Used to ask whether a statement or rumor is true. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb). In formal situations you’ll often see „Stimmt es, dass Sie …?“; informally „Stimmt es, dass du …?“
target_language_example: Stimmt es, dass du morgen keine Zeit hast?
native_language_example: Is it true that you don't have time tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation of a statement or rumor. "Stimmt es, dass …?" = “Is it true that …?”; "Sie" makes it formal/polite (talking to a stranger, customer, official, etc.). The verb usually goes to the end of the "dass" clause: "Stimmt es, dass Sie gestern nicht da waren?".
target_language_example: Stimmt es, dass Sie nächste Woche Urlaub haben?
native_language_example: Is it true that you’re on vacation next week?

meaning: "Is it true that you…?" / "Is it correct that you…?"
additional_notes: Used to check whether a statement or rumor is true. Often introduces a yes/no question with a subordinate clause: "Stimmt es, dass du …?" (verb goes to the end in the dass-clause). You can change "du" to other subjects: "…, dass er/sie/wir …".
target_language_example: Stimmt es, dass du morgen nach Berlin fährst?
native_language_example: Is it true that you’re going to Berlin tomorrow?

meaning: "Is it true that …?" / "Is it correct that …?"
additional_notes: Used to ask whether a statement or rumor is true. It’s often followed by a full clause (subject + verb). In modern German, "dass" is the standard spelling ("daß" is older). You can also say "Stimmt es, dass …?" or more simply "Stimmt es, dass …" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Stimmt es, dass du morgen keine Zeit hast?
native_language_example: Is it true that you don’t have time tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sein" (to be): "stolz auf + accusative". The thing/person you’re proud of is in the accusative case (e.g., auf meinen Sohn, auf dich).
target_language_example: Wir sind stolz auf dich.
native_language_example: We’re proud of you.

additional_notes: Used with the adjective "stolz" + "auf" + a person/pronoun: "stolz auf dich" (informal singular), "stolz auf Sie" (formal singular), "stolz auf euch" (informal plural). Often follows "Ich bin ..." / "Wir sind ...". It can be positive encouragement, but depending on tone/context it can also sound critical ("too proud of yourself").
target_language_example: Wir sind stolz auf dich!
native_language_example: We’re proud of you!

additional_notes: Used with the adjective phrase **stolz auf + Akkusativ** (here: **auf dich**). **gewesen** is the past participle of **sein** (“to be”). Very often you’ll see it in the conditional/subjunctive form **wäre(n) … stolz auf dich gewesen** = “would have been proud of you.”
target_language_example: Ich wäre stolz auf dich gewesen, wenn du es versucht hättest.
native_language_example: I would have been proud of you if you had tried.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to more than one person (euch = “you all”). Often used with „sein“: „Ich bin stolz auf euch“ = “I’m proud of you (all).” You can also say it as advice/encouragement: „Ihr solltet/müsst stolz auf euch sein“ = “You should really be proud of yourselves.”
target_language_example: Ich bin stolz auf euch – ihr habt das wirklich gut gemacht.
native_language_example: I'm proud of you all—you really did that well.

additional_notes: Used with the adjective "stolz" + preposition "auf" to say you are proud of someone or something. The noun after "auf" is in the accusative case. "ihre" is a possessive determiner and can mean "her" or "their" depending on context (e.g., "ihre Söhne" = her sons; "ihre Brücke" = their bridge).
target_language_example: Die Eltern sind stolz auf ihre Kinder.
native_language_example: The parents are proud of their children.

additional_notes: Used with the pattern **stolz auf + Akkusativ** to say someone is proud of someone/something: **stolz auf mich/ dich/ ihn/ sie/ euch/ Sie**. You can use it in questions (**Bist du stolz auf mich?**) or statements (**Ich bin stolz auf mich.**).
target_language_example: Meine Eltern sind stolz auf mich.
native_language_example: My parents are proud of me.

meaning: 'proud of his' (proud of something that belongs to him / relates to him).
additional_notes: Used with the adjective "stolz" + "auf" + accusative (auf + Akk.). The possessive can change depending on the person: stolz auf meine/deine/seine/ihre/unsere/eure … . Often followed by a noun (e.g., "seine Pünktlichkeit") or a person/group (e.g., "seine Schüler").
target_language_example: Ich bin stolz auf meine Arbeit.
native_language_example: I'm proud of my work.

additional_notes: Used with what you’re proud of: either a noun/pronoun (e.g., "Ich bin stolz darauf" = I’m proud of it) or very often with a clause/infinitive: "stolz darauf, ... zu ..." (proud to ...) and "stolz darauf, dass ..." (proud that ...). Commonly follows "sein": "Ich bin stolz darauf ...".
target_language_example: Ich bin stolz darauf, dass ich Deutsch lerne.
native_language_example: I’m proud that I’m learning German.

additional_notes: Used to compare strength. Pattern: **X ist stärker als Y**. You can intensify with words like **viel** (much) or **ein bisschen** (a little). The word **als** is used after comparatives (stärker, größer, schneller, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich bin heute stärker als gestern.
native_language_example: I’m stronger today than yesterday.

additional_notes: A polite way to ask for permission or check if something would bother someone. Literally “Does it bother you if I … ?” and is followed by a verb clause (often in present tense): „Stört es dich, wenn ich … mache/öffne/rauche?“ You can also say „Stört es Sie, wenn ich …?“ for formal situations.
target_language_example: Stört es dich, wenn ich mich hier hinsetze?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I sit here?

additional_notes: Used with **helfen + infinitive** to say you help with an activity: **jemandem (Dat.) helfen, etwas/jemanden zu suchen**. Often you’ll also hear **beim Suchen helfen** (“help with searching”). The helper is the subject; the person being helped is in the **dative** (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen/Ihnen).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir helfen, meine Schlüssel zu suchen?
native_language_example: Can you help me look for my keys?

additional_notes: You’ll usually see this as **Zwei Leute suchen nach …** (“Two people are looking for …”). In the examples, **Da** or **Es** is put first to mean something like “There/Here …” (inverted word order): **Da/Es suchen zwei Leute nach dir.** The preposition **nach** takes the **dative**: **nach dir**, **nach euch**, **nach Ihnen**.
target_language_example: Draußen suchen zwei Leute nach dir.
native_language_example: Two people are looking for you outside.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is searching for a person with a certain skill/quality. It’s followed by a relative clause: „der“ (masculine), „die“ (feminine/plural), „das“ (neuter), depending on „jemand“/the person being referred to and the grammar of the clause (e.g., „jemanden, der … hilft“).
target_language_example: Sie sucht jemanden, der ihr beim Umzug hilft.
native_language_example: She’s looking for someone who can help her move.

meaning: “was looking for” / “searched for” (past tense of "suchen nach").
additional_notes: "suchte" is the simple past of "suchen" (to look for/search). It’s used with "nach" + dative to say you were searching for someone or something: "nach Tom" (after Tom), "nach dem Kind" (after the child), "nach einem Versteck" (for a hiding place). In speech, Germans often use the perfect tense instead: "Ich habe nach Tom gesucht."
target_language_example: Wir suchten nach einem offenen Café, aber alles war schon zu.
native_language_example: We were looking for an open café, but everything was already closed.

additional_notes: Used with "sehen" + infinitive (without "zu"): "jemanden tanzen sehen" = to watch/see someone dancing. The person is in the accusative: "Ich habe dich tanzen sehen." In the perfect tense, both verbs often appear together at the end: "hat ... tanzen sehen".
target_language_example: Ich habe sie gestern auf der Party tanzen sehen.
native_language_example: I saw her dancing at the party yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did the thing that was required, requested, promised, or said (often followed by a clause like "...von mir verlangt hat" or "...ihr gesagt wurde"). Note: German "was" means "what" (not English "was").
target_language_example: Er tat, was er konnte, um zu helfen.
native_language_example: He did what he could to help.

additional_notes: Past tense of „(Es) tut mir leid.“ Used either to apologize (“I was sorry about that”) or to express sympathy/compassion (“I felt sorry for him/her”). Often appears as „Es tat mir leid, dass …“ + clause, or with a person: „Er/Sie tat mir leid.“
target_language_example: Es tat mir leid, dass ich zu spät gekommen bin.
native_language_example: I was sorry that I arrived late.

additional_notes: This is the simple past of the phrase "so tun, als (ob) …" (= to pretend). It’s used to say someone behaved like something was true, even though it wasn’t. In present tense you often see: "Ich tue so, als ob ich zuhöre."
target_language_example: Sie tat so, als hätte sie die Nachricht nicht gehört.
native_language_example: She pretended she hadn’t heard the news.

additional_notes: Used to say someone acted as though something were true (even if it isn’t). It combines past tense of **tun** (ich **tat**) + **so** + **als** + a clause in **Konjunktiv II** (**wäre**, **hätte**). Other persons: **du tatest**, **er/sie/es tat**, **wir taten**, **ihr tatet**, **sie taten**. Common pattern: **Er/Sie tat so, als wäre …** / **… als hätte …**.
target_language_example: Er tat so, als wäre er krank, um nicht zur Arbeit zu müssen.
native_language_example: He pretended he was sick so he wouldn’t have to go to work.

meaning: “he pretended (to be) …” / “he acted as if he were …”.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is pretending or putting on an act. It’s the past tense of "so tun, als ob/als …". After "als" you often see Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) like "wäre" to express an unreal comparison (“as if”). You can change the person: "ich tat so …", "sie tat so …", "sie taten so …".
target_language_example: Er tat so, als wäre er überrascht.
native_language_example: He pretended to be surprised.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is pretending or behaving as if something were true, even though it isn’t (or may not be). Past tense of "so tun, als ob". Structure: "[Person] tat so, als würde + verb (infinitive)"; with other tenses: "Ich tue so, als würde …" (present). Often implies the speaker thinks it’s not genuine.
target_language_example: Er tat so, als würde er mich nicht kennen.
native_language_example: He pretended (like) he didn’t know me.

additional_notes: Used to compare prices. Structure: **teuer** (expensive) → **teurer** (more expensive) + **als** (than). Example pattern: **X ist teurer als Y.**
target_language_example: Das Ticket ist teurer als gestern.
native_language_example: The ticket is more expensive than yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone or something (“Das ist Bob.”), to describe/define something (“Das ist mein Haus.”), or to introduce a clause (“Das ist, was wir wollen.”). For emphasis, German often uses “Das ist so …” (“That’s so …”).
target_language_example: Das ist, was wir wollen.
native_language_example: This is what we want.

meaning: breathe in deeply (take a deep breath in).
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "atmen" in instructions or commands: "Atme/Atmen Sie tief ein!" It refers to inhaling (often paired with "und aus" / "tief aus" for exhaling). Related verb: "einatmen" (to inhale), where "ein" is a separable prefix.
target_language_example: Atme tief ein und zähl bis drei.
native_language_example: Breathe in deeply and count to three.

additional_notes: *traf* is the simple past (Präteritum) form of *treffen* for **er/sie/es**. It can mean **to meet/see** someone (often with a time/place: *am Strand*, *heute Morgen*, *vor drei Jahren*) or **to hit/strike** someone/something (often with what hit them + body part: *Der Ball traf ihn am Bein*).
target_language_example: Ich traf ihn gestern in der Stadt.
native_language_example: I met/saw him yesterday in the city.

meaning: formal: “(do) you wear …?” / “please wear …” / “please enter/fill in …”
additional_notes: "Tragen" means "to wear" (clothes, glasses/contacts, a helmet, etc.) or "to carry". With "Sie" it’s the formal form used with strangers, customers, patients, etc., and it’s also used for polite requests: "Tragen Sie eine Maske." With forms, "tragen Sie … ein" means "enter/fill in" (write information into a form). Word order changes meaning: "Tragen Sie …?" = question; "Tragen Sie …!" = polite command/request.
target_language_example: Tragen Sie bitte Ihren Namen hier ein.
native_language_example: Please enter your name here.

additional_notes: Question form with the verb **tragen** (“to wear/carry”) and **ihr** (“you” plural/informal = you all). Used to ask what someone is wearing now (**Tragt ihr gerade …?**) or what they wear in general (**Tragt ihr oft …?**). Common with clothing/accessories (Schuhe, Kontaktlinsen, Helm), and also in fixed phrases like **Kontaktlinsen tragen** (“to wear contact lenses”).
target_language_example: Tragt ihr heute Jacken oder ist es zu warm?
native_language_example: Are you all wearing jackets today, or is it too warm?

additional_notes: Used to say someone drank one glass of a drink. It’s usually followed by what was in the glass: **ein Glas Wasser / ein Glas Milch / ein Glas Rotwein**. This is **simple past** (common in writing/storytelling); in everyday speech you often hear **hat ein Glas … getrunken** (present perfect).
target_language_example: Gestern trank sie ein Glas Saft.
native_language_example: Yesterday she drank a glass of juice.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past of **trinken** (“to drink”): **er/sie trank**. Usually followed by what was in the cup (often with **eine Tasse + Getränk**, e.g. *eine Tasse Kaffee/Tee*). In everyday spoken German, you often hear the perfect tense instead: *Er hat eine Tasse Kaffee getrunken.*
target_language_example: Gestern Abend trank ich eine Tasse Tee vor dem Schlafengehen.
native_language_example: Yesterday evening I drank a cup of tea before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of "einen Schluck trinken". "ein Schluck" means a sip/small mouthful, used with drinks (Wasser, Kaffee, Milch). Often followed by what you sip: "einen Schluck Wasser" or "einen Schluck von der Milch".
target_language_example: Ich war durstig und trank einen Schluck Wasser.
native_language_example: I was thirsty and drank a sip of water.

meaning: "(he/she) stepped aside" / "moved out of the way."
additional_notes: Past tense (Präteritum) of **zur Seite treten** = to step to the side so someone can pass or enter. Often followed by **damit** (so that) or **um … zu** (in order to). In the present tense: **ich trete zur Seite**, **er/sie tritt zur Seite**.
target_language_example: Ich trat zur Seite, damit die Leute aussteigen konnten.
native_language_example: I stepped aside so that the people could get out.

additional_notes: Used with the verb „aussehen“ (to look/appear): „jmd. sieht traurig aus“ = someone looks sad. In the past: „sah traurig aus“ (looked sad). The „aus“ comes at the end in statements: „Er sieht traurig aus.“
target_language_example: Du siehst heute traurig aus.
native_language_example: You look sad today.

meaning: "are you meeting up" / "do you meet" (with someone).
additional_notes: From **sich treffen (mit + Dativ)** = to meet up. **triffst du dich** is the 2nd person singular question form (“are you meeting up?”). It’s usually followed by **mit +** a person (e.g., *mit ihm/ihr/jemandem/Tom*), and often used to ask who/when you’re meeting: *Mit wem triffst du dich? Wann triffst du dich (wieder)?*
target_language_example: Triffst du dich heute Abend mit Freunden?
native_language_example: Are you meeting up with friends tonight?

additional_notes: “trinken” = “to drink”. “Sie” is the formal/polite form of “you” (used with strangers, customers, older people, etc.). In questions it means “Do you drink…?” (Trinken Sie Kaffee?), and as an imperative it means “Drink!” (Trinken Sie es! = Drink it!). Word order often flips in questions: “Trinken Sie …?”
target_language_example: Trinken Sie normalerweise Kaffee oder Tee?
native_language_example: Do you usually drink coffee or tea?

additional_notes: From the verb "trinken" (to drink). "Trinkst" is the present-tense form for "du" (you, singular), used to ask someone directly about what they drink or their drinking habits/preferences (often with a drink or an amount: "Trinkst du Kaffee?", "Trinkst du viel Kaffee?").
target_language_example: Trinkst du heute Abend ein Bier?
native_language_example: Are you drinking a beer tonight?

meaning: 'despite the' / 'in spite of the' (with masculine or neuter nouns).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens even though there is a difficulty or opposing condition. It is followed by the genitive case: trotz des Regens, trotz des Wetters, trotz des Lärms. (For feminine or plural nouns you’ll see: trotz der …).
target_language_example: Trotz des Stresses hat er gute Laune.
native_language_example: Despite the stress, he’s in a good mood.

meaning: despite the rain / in spite of the rain.
additional_notes: Means something happens even though it’s raining. Uses the preposition "trotz" ("despite"), which is commonly followed by the genitive: "des Regens". It can go at the start of the sentence ("Trotz des Regens ...") or later ("... trotz des Regens ...").
target_language_example: Trotz des Regens haben wir einen Spaziergang gemacht.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.

additional_notes: *Trug* is the simple past (Präteritum) of **tragen** (“to carry / to wear”). **Ein** here is just the indefinite article (“a/an”) introducing the object: *ein Kind, ein Kleid, ein Jahr, ein Lächeln*. Don’t confuse this with **eintragen** (“to enter/register”), where *ein-* is a prefix.
target_language_example: Er trug einen schweren Koffer die Treppe hoch.
native_language_example: He carried a heavy suitcase up the stairs.

additional_notes: From **tragen** = “to wear/carry”; **trug** is simple past (Präteritum), common in written stories. **ein rotes** needs a noun after it (e.g., *Kleid, Hemd*) or can refer back to one already mentioned: *Elke trug das gleiche in Grün* (“Elke wore the same one in green”). The adjective ending **-es** matches a neuter noun like *das Kleid* or *das Hemd*.
target_language_example: Er trug ein rotes T-Shirt und schwarze Schuhe.
native_language_example: He wore a red T-shirt and black shoes.

additional_notes: *trug* is the simple past (Präteritum) of **tragen**. It’s used a lot in written stories and news; in speech you often hear **hat ... getragen**. **eine** is used because the noun is feminine (e.g., *eine Hose, eine Halskette*). For other genders: *trug einen* (masc.), *trug ein* (neut.). Depending on context, **tragen** can also mean “to carry,” but with clothes/accessories it usually means “to wear.”
target_language_example: Gestern trug sie eine schwarze Jacke.
native_language_example: Yesterday she wore a black jacket.

additional_notes: “trug” is the simple past (Präteritum) of “tragen” (“to wear/carry”). “einen” is the masculine accusative form of “ein” and is used with masculine nouns when they are the direct object (e.g., einen Anzug, einen Mantel, einen Rucksack). In everyday speech, many people also use the perfect: “Er hat einen Anzug getragen.”
target_language_example: Gestern trug er einen schwarzen Mantel.
native_language_example: Yesterday he wore a black coat.

meaning: 'do you wear' / 'are you carrying' (you, informal singular).
additional_notes: Form of the verb **tragen** with **du** (2nd person singular). Very common in questions with **verb-first** word order: **Was trägst du …?** It often refers to clothing/accessories (wear), but can also mean carrying or bearing something (e.g., a bag, responsibility).
target_language_example: Trägst du heute eine Jacke?
native_language_example: Are you wearing a jacket today?

meaning: 'wears a' / 'is wearing a' (or 'carries a') + feminine noun.
additional_notes: From the verb **tragen** (to wear/carry). Use **trägt eine** with a **feminine** singular noun in the accusative (e.g., *eine Maske, eine Tasche, eine Krawatte*). It can mean wearing something on your body (*Er trägt eine Perücke.*) or carrying something (*Er trägt eine Tasche auf dem Rücken.*).
target_language_example: Sie trägt eine rote Jacke.
native_language_example: She is wearing a red jacket.

additional_notes: From the verb **tragen** (“to wear/carry”) + **einen** (masculine accusative “a”). Use it for clothes and accessories (**einen Hut, einen Ring, einen Pulli**) and also for things someone has on them (**einen Regenschirm tragen**) or even facial hair (**einen Bart tragen**). The exact meaning depends on the noun.
target_language_example: Er trägt einen schwarzen Mantel.
native_language_example: He’s wearing a black coat.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to do a certain thing, usually followed by a clause: **Tu, was du für richtig hältst.** (“Do what you think is right.”) It’s the **du**-imperative of **tun**; for **Sie** (formal) you’d say **Tun Sie, was …** or more commonly **Machen Sie, was …**.
target_language_example: Tu, was du für richtig hältst.
native_language_example: Do what you think is right.

meaning: to pretend / act as if; also: “do … than …” (comparison).
additional_notes:
Two common patterns:
1) **so tun, als (ob)** + clause = “to pretend (that) / to act as if”. The verb in the clause is often in **Konjunktiv** (e.g., *als wäre…, als sei…*).
2) **mehr/weniger/… tun, als** + clause/phrase = “to do more/less/… than”.
target_language_example: Er tut so, als hätte er nichts gehört.
native_language_example: He’s pretending he didn’t hear anything.

meaning: to do (something) in order to (achieve a goal).
additional_notes: Used when an action is done with a purpose: **tun** + (what you do) + **, um** + goal (usually with **zu** + infinitive). Very common in questions: *Was kann/muss ich tun, um …?* Also often appears with *alles tun* / *alles in meiner Macht Stehende tun* to mean “do everything (I can) in order to …”.
target_language_example: Ich tue alles, um mein Deutsch zu verbessern.
native_language_example: I do everything I can to improve my German.

meaning: “do something to help” / “do (something) in order to help.”
additional_notes: Used when offering help or saying you want/need to take action to support someone. It commonly appears with pronouns like etwas/alles/irgendetwas + tun, um zu helfen (e.g., etwas tun, um zu helfen = do something to help; alles tun, um zu helfen = do everything to help).
target_language_example: Was kann ich tun, um zu helfen?
native_language_example: What can I do to help?

additional_notes: Used with a clause starting with **was** to say that someone does (or must do) a particular thing. Often appears with modal verbs: **Ich kann tun, was ich will** (I can do what I want), **Du musst tun, was …** (You must do what …). You can also strengthen it with **auch immer**: **tun, was auch immer …** = “do whatever …”.
target_language_example: Mach einfach, was du für richtig hältst.
native_language_example: Just do what you think is right.

additional_notes: Used with the pattern „tun, was + subject + wollen“ (= “do what someone wants”). The comma is typical because it introduces a subordinate clause: „…, was er will“. Often follows modal verbs like „kann/darf/soll“ (can/is allowed/should): „Er kann tun, was er will.“ With an exclamation mark it can express annoyance or emphasis (“He can just do whatever he wants!”).
target_language_example: Ich lasse ihn tun, was er will.
native_language_example: I’m letting him do what he wants.

additional_notes: Used to give someone complete freedom of choice: "You can do whatever you like." It’s a fixed pattern: "tun, was immer" + subject + verb (often in Konjunktiv in indirect speech: "sie könne tun, was immer sie wolle"). Similar to "tun, was auch immer …" (= whatever …).
target_language_example: Du darfst tun, was immer du willst.
native_language_example: You can do whatever you want.

meaning: "to do what they …" (do whatever they want/can).
additional_notes: Used with a follow-up verb at the end of the clause, e.g. **tun, was sie wollen** (do what they want) or **tun, was sie können** (do what they can). This is a relative clause with **was** (“what”) and the verb goes to the end in German.
target_language_example: In dieser Stadt können die Menschen tun, was sie wollen.
native_language_example: In this city, people can do what they want.

meaning: "(to) do ... if/when ..." (talking about what someone will/would do in a situation).
additional_notes: This is a common sentence pattern: a form of **tun** (mache/tust/tut/tun; würde tun; könnte tun) + an action, then a **wenn**-clause that gives the condition/situation. **Wenn** can mean **"if"** (condition) or **"when"** (whenever/once something happens). In hypotheticals, German often uses **würde**/**könnte** + infinitive: *Was würdest du tun, wenn ...?* / *Er könnte das tun, wenn er wollte.*
target_language_example: Was würdest du tun, wenn du im Lotto gewinnen würdest?
native_language_example: What would you do if you won the lottery?

meaning: to do what … asks (someone) to do; to do what someone requested.
additional_notes: This is a common pattern with a relative clause: **tun, worum … bitten**. The verb **bitten** is used as **jemanden um etwas bitten** (to ask someone for something / to ask someone to do something). **Worum** literally means **“what (about/for which thing)”** and refers back to that **um + thing**. In the relative clause, the verb goes to the end: **…, worum ich dich gebeten habe.**
target_language_example: Ich werde tun, worum du mich gebeten hast.
native_language_example: I will do what you asked me to do.

meaning: Formal: “do what you …” (e.g., “do what you can / what makes you happy”).
additional_notes: This is the formal (Sie) imperative of **tun** (“to do”). It’s used to introduce a relative clause with **was** (“what”) and is usually completed by a verb phrase: **Tun Sie, was Sie können.** (“Do what you can.”) / **Tun Sie, was Sie wollen.** (“Do what you want.”). The verb in the second part typically goes at the end: **… was Sie nicht lassen können** (“… what you can’t stop doing”).
target_language_example: Tun Sie, was Sie für richtig halten.
native_language_example: Do what you think is right.

meaning: 'should do' (what someone is supposed to do).
additional_notes: Usually appears in a subordinate clause after words like "was" or "dass": "was er tun soll" = "what he should do", "dass er es nicht tun soll" = "that he shouldn’t do it". It uses "sollen" to express advice, instructions, or what is expected of someone.
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich tun soll.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do.

meaning: to be supposed to do; should do (what to do).
additional_notes: Uses the modal verb „sollen“ with „tun“ (to do). Common in (in)direct questions like „Was soll ich tun?“ / „… was wir tun sollen“ = “what we should do / what to do.” In the past with Konjunktiv II: „hätte/hättest/hätten … tun sollen“ means “should have done” (often with regret or criticism).
target_language_example: Ich weiß nicht, was ich tun soll.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do.

meaning: "you do" / "do you" (2nd person singular of *tun* = “to do”).
additional_notes: Used with **du** (“you”, informal singular) in statements (**Du tust…** / **Das tust du.**) and in questions when the verb comes first (**Tust du…?**). Often followed by **es** (“it”) or another object. In some contexts, *tun* can mean “to put/add” (e.g., *Wie viel Zucker tust du dir in den Tee?* = “How much sugar do you put in your tea?”).
target_language_example: Was tust du heute Abend?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

meaning: “do you do that?” / “are you doing that?”
additional_notes: A question using the verb **tun** (“to do”) with **du** (“you”) in **yes/no question** word order (verb first). Used to ask whether someone does an action (often about habits: **oft/gerne**), or why/for whom they do it (**wieso/für wen**). In everyday German, **tun** can sound a bit informal or emphatic compared to repeating a more specific verb, but it’s still common and understandable.
target_language_example: Warum tust du das?
native_language_example: Why are you doing that?

additional_notes: Used with a relative clause introduced by **was** to mean “everything that” / “whatever.” The verb is **tun** (“to do”): **tut** = “does” (3rd person singular) or “do!” (plural imperative). Often followed by **sie/er kann** (“she/he can”) or **wir ihm/ihr sagen** (“we tell him/her”).
target_language_example: Er tut alles, was er kann, um pünktlich zu sein.
native_language_example: He does everything he can to be on time.

meaning: "does (something) to me" — used in set phrases like "es tut mir leid" (I’m sorry) and "(das) tut mir weh" (that hurts).
additional_notes: "tut" is the 3rd-person singular of **tun** (to do), and **mir** is the dative form of "me". It commonly appears with an impersonal subject (**es** or **das**): **Es tut mir leid** = “I’m sorry” (literally “It does me sorrow”), **Das tut mir weh** = “That hurts (me)”. As an imperative (to multiple people / formal "Sie"), it can mean “do (for) me”: **Tut mir einen Gefallen** = “Do me a favor.”
target_language_example: Es tut mir leid, das wollte ich nicht.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I didn’t mean that.

additional_notes: Used to apologize or to politely soften bad news/refusals. Very common in spoken German. Often at the start of a sentence: “Tut mir Leid, …”. Also written “tut mir leid” (lowercase “leid”); “Es tut mir leid” is a slightly fuller form.
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich habe das nicht verstanden.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand that.

additional_notes: A very common way to apologize or express regret (both for a mistake and for something unfortunate). Often used as a standalone phrase (“Tut mir leid!”) or followed by an explanation: “Tut mir leid, ich musste …”.
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, ich bin zu spät.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late.

additional_notes: Used to apologize and introduce the reason with a subordinate clause starting with „dass“ + verb at the end. Common in spoken and written German. Often followed by an explanation: „Tut mir leid, dass ich zu spät bin.“
target_language_example: Tut mir leid, dass ich dein Buch vergessen habe.
native_language_example: I'm sorry that I forgot your book.

additional_notes: Common, polite apology or expression of sympathy. Often used with a situation: „Das tut mir sehr leid.“ (= I’m very sorry to hear that.) You can change the person in the dative: „tut dir sehr leid“ (I’m very sorry — to you), „tut ihm/ihr sehr leid“, „tut uns/euch/ihnen sehr leid“. You can also say about someone: „Du tust mir sehr leid.“ = I feel very sorry for you.
target_language_example: Es tut mir sehr leid, dass ich zu spät bin.
native_language_example: I'm very sorry that I'm late.

additional_notes: Used to express strong regret or sympathy (often for something bad that happened, or when you caused inconvenience). It’s more emotional/stronger than just "Entschuldigung" and can be followed by a "dass…" clause: "Tut mir so leid, dass …". You’ll also hear it as "Es tut mir so leid" or simply "Tut mir leid".
target_language_example: Es tut mir so leid, dass du heute so einen stressigen Tag hattest.
native_language_example: I’m so sorry that you had such a stressful day today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone spends all their time doing one thing (often with criticism or annoyance). Conjugate "tun" to match the subject: ich tue, du tust, er/sie/es tut, wir tun, ihr tut, sie/Sie tun. Usually followed by an infinitive phrase: "..., als + Infinitiv" (e.g., "..., als den ganzen Tag fernzusehen").
target_language_example: Sie tut nichts anderes, als sich über alles zu beschweren.
native_language_example: She does nothing but complain about everything.

additional_notes: Used with a following clause to say someone behaves as though something were true. Often appears as **tut so, als ob ...** and the clause frequently uses **Konjunktiv II** (e.g., *als wäre*, *als hätte*, *als störte*). It can also refer to groups: *ihr tut so, als ...*.
target_language_example: Sie tut so, als ob sie mich nicht kennen würde.
native_language_example: She pretends as if she doesn’t know me.

additional_notes: Used to say that something causes pain. It’s the verb phrase "wehtun" (to hurt); in the present tense you often say "Das tut weh" (That hurts) or "Mein Kopf/Arm tut weh" (My head/arm hurts).
target_language_example: Aua, das tut weh!
native_language_example: Ouch, that hurts!

meaning: for forgiveness; for an apology (used with „(jemanden) um Entschuldigung bitten“ = to apologize).
additional_notes: Usually appears with the verb „bitten“: „(jemanden) um Entschuldigung bitten“ = to ask someone’s forgiveness / to apologize. Common polite forms are „Ich bitte um Entschuldigung“ (formal) and „Entschuldigung!“ (short). You can add a reason with „für …“ (for …) or a condition with „falls/wenn …“ (if …).
target_language_example: Ich möchte Sie um Entschuldigung bitten, ich bin zu spät.
native_language_example: I’d like to apologize; I’m late.

additional_notes: Usually used with **bitten** or **fragen**: **jdn. um Erlaubnis bitten/fragen** = “to ask sb for permission.” Often with **erst/immer erst** (“first”) and can contrast with **ohne um Erlaubnis zu fragen** (“without asking for permission”).
target_language_example: Kann ich dich kurz um Erlaubnis bitten?
native_language_example: Can I ask you for permission for a moment?

additional_notes: Used with verbs/expressions that take **um + Akkusativ** to show what something is about or what is requested/concerned. Common patterns: **jdn. um Geld bitten** (to ask someone for money), **(sich) um Geld sorgen** (to worry about money), **es geht um Geld** (it’s about money / it’s about the money).
target_language_example: Er hat mich um Geld gebeten.
native_language_example: He asked me for money.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like „bitten“ (to ask) or „beten“ (to pray): „jdn. um Hilfe bitten“ = to ask someone for help; „zu Gott um Hilfe beten“ = to pray to God for help. It expresses what you are requesting (help).
target_language_example: Kann ich dich um Hilfe bitten?
native_language_example: Can I ask you for help?

additional_notes: Used when you think (now) that someone made a mistake by not asking for help. Often appears as **hättest/hätte + um Hilfe bitten + sollen** (Konjunktiv II past), expressing regret or criticism/advice about the past. **jemanden um Hilfe bitten** = to ask someone for help (accusative person + „um“ + accusative thing: „Hilfe“).
target_language_example: Du hättest mich um Hilfe bitten sollen.
native_language_example: You should have asked me for help.

additional_notes: Past participle of "um Hilfe bitten" (= to ask for help). Often used with "haben": "Ich habe (jemanden) um Hilfe gebeten." Pattern: "jemanden" (accusative person) + "um" + "Hilfe" (accusative). You can also say simply: "Er hat um Hilfe gebeten" (without naming who was asked).
target_language_example: Ich habe meine Nachbarin um Hilfe gebeten.
native_language_example: I asked my neighbor for help.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive + zu, often to express purpose: "Er kam, um ..." = "He came (in order) to ...". The full verb pattern is commonly "jemanden (Akk.) um Hilfe bitten" = "to ask someone for help" (person in the accusative, and "um" + what you are asking for).
target_language_example: Ich rufe dich an, um Hilfe zu bitten.
native_language_example: I’m calling you to ask for help.

additional_notes: An emotional exclamation used to show strong urgency, shock, annoyance, or pleading. Often used at the beginning of a sentence (“Um Himmels willen, …”) or inserted as an aside with commas (“…, um Himmels willen.”). It’s not slang, but it’s quite strong; use with care in polite situations.
target_language_example: Um Himmels willen, mach das nicht!
native_language_example: For heaven’s sake, don’t do that!

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens. With clock times German often uses **um** + time: *um 8 Uhr* (at 8 o’clock), *um Mitternacht* (at midnight). It can mean exactly midnight or roughly around that time, depending on context.
target_language_example: Der Film fängt um Mitternacht an.
native_language_example: The movie starts at midnight.

meaning: for advice (as in: to ask someone for advice).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "jdn. um Rat bitten" (to ask someone for advice) or "jdn. um Rat fragen" (to ask someone for advice). Grammar: "um" takes the accusative, so you usually see it as "jemanden um Rat bitten/fragen".
target_language_example: Ich möchte dich um Rat bitten.
native_language_example: I’d like to ask you for advice.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "fragen" (to ask) in the pattern "jemanden um Rat fragen" = to ask someone for advice. The person asked is in the accusative (mich/dich/Sie/euch), and "Rat" stays the same. Often appears in regrets or wishes with Konjunktiv II (e.g., "Ich wünschte, ich hätte dich um Rat gefragt").
target_language_example: Ich habe meine Lehrerin um Rat gefragt.
native_language_example: I asked my teacher for advice.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with **bitten**: **(jdn.) um Verzeihung bitten** = “to ask (someone) for forgiveness” / “to apologize.” Similar in meaning to **Entschuldigung**, but **Verzeihung** can sound a bit more serious or formal depending on context. Grammar: **um** + accusative noun (**die Verzeihung**).
target_language_example: Ich möchte dich um Verzeihung bitten.
native_language_example: I’d like to ask you for forgiveness (I’d like to apologize).

additional_notes: Used with clock times: **um + [time]** to say when something happens (e.g., *um acht*, *um 8 Uhr*, *um halb neun*). It refers to a specific time, not a duration (*für acht Stunden* = for eight hours).
target_language_example: Der Film beginnt um acht.
native_language_example: The movie starts at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact time when something happens. "um" + clock time answers the question "Wann?" (When?): um 8:00, um 8:15 (um Viertel nach acht), etc. In speech you often hear "um acht" without "Uhr" when the meaning is clear.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns morgen um acht Uhr.
native_language_example: We’re meeting tomorrow at eight o’clock.

meaning: “around the,” “about the,” or “for the” (as in competing/fighting for something).
additional_notes: Common uses of **um den** (with masculine accusative nouns): (1) **spatial**: *um den Tisch* = around the table; (2) **topic**: *Es geht um den …* = it’s about the …; (3) **goal/competition**: *um den Sieg kämpfen* = fight for the victory. Also appears in the pattern **jdn. um den + noun bringen** = to deprive someone of something (*um den Verstand bringen* = drive someone crazy), which is not a literal “around/about” meaning.
target_language_example: Es geht heute um den neuen Vertrag.
native_language_example: Today it’s about the new contract.

additional_notes: Used to say something is positioned or wrapped around someone’s neck (e.g., a scarf) or that you put your arms around someone’s neck (often in a hug). With clothing/jewelry it often answers “where?” (Wo?): Ich trage einen Schal um den Hals. It can also describe tightness/pressure around the neck: zu eng um den Hals.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte den Schal um den Hals legen?
native_language_example: Can you put the scarf around my neck, please?

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs (gehen, wandern, laufen) to describe going around the outside/edge of a lake. It can mean a full loop (especially with "eine Runde/einmal") or simply moving along the shore area. Often reinforced with words like "herum" or "rings" ("um den See herum", "rings um den See"). "um" takes the accusative here: der See → den See.
target_language_example: Lass uns morgen um den See joggen.
native_language_example: Let’s jog around the lake tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the accusative: **um + die** (feminine singular or plural). Common uses: (1) movement/location around something: *um die ganze Welt* = around the whole world; (2) approximate numbers/ages: *um die dreißig* = about thirty; (3) approximate time: *um die Mittagszeit* = around noon. In phrases like **um … Bescheid wissen** (“to know about …”), **um** means “about/regarding” (not physical ‘around’).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um die Mittagszeit.
native_language_example: We’ll meet around noon.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "reisen" (to travel) to mean traveling all around the world (a world trip). Often appears as "um die Welt reisen" or "eine Reise um die Welt". With motion verbs it can also literally mean going all the way around the Earth.
target_language_example: Nach dem Abi will sie ein Jahr lang um die Welt reisen.
native_language_example: After graduating, she wants to travel around the world for a year.

meaning: at this time (of day); at this hour.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the particular time right now or the time being discussed (often the current time). Common in questions about opening hours or safety, and it can express surprise/disbelief as a short question: "Um diese Uhrzeit?" ("At this hour?"). Works for present and future/past contexts: "Morgen um diese Uhrzeit …" = "Tomorrow at this time …".
target_language_example: Um diese Uhrzeit fährt kein Bus mehr.
native_language_example: At this time of night, no buses are running anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact clock time when something happens. With clock times, German uses **um** + time (no preposition change), e.g., *um drei Uhr*, *um 15 Uhr*, *um halb drei*. You can add *morgens/nachmittags/abends* or *nachts* for clarity.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um drei Uhr vor dem Café.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at three o’clock in front of the café.

meaning: for a pay raise (a salary increase).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like „bitten“ or „fragen“ to say you are asking for something: „um + accusative“ = “for”. Here: „(jemanden) um eine Gehaltserhöhung bitten“ = “to ask (someone) for a raise”.
target_language_example: Ich möchte meinen Chef um eine Gehaltserhöhung bitten.
native_language_example: I’d like to ask my boss for a raise.

additional_notes: Used for polite requests. The person you’re asking is in the accusative (dich/euch/Sie), and what you’re asking for is introduced with „um“ + accusative: „um einen Gefallen“. Common openings: „Darf ich dich/euch/Sie um einen Gefallen bitten?“ or „Ich möchte/wollte …“.
target_language_example: Kann ich dich um einen Gefallen bitten?
native_language_example: Can I ask you for a favor?

additional_notes: Used to say the exact time when something happens. "um" + a clock time answers the question "Wann?" (When?): "um 7 Uhr", "um 11 Uhr", etc. Often you add "morgens" (in the morning) or "abends" (in the evening) if it’s not clear. With minutes: "um 11:15 Uhr" / "um Viertel nach elf".
target_language_example: Der Film beginnt um elf Uhr.
native_language_example: The movie starts at eleven o’clock.

additional_notes: Used with clock times to say when something happens. With an exact time, it's usually understood as precisely 5:00; with words like "etwa" it means around 5:00. Often used for appointments and schedules ("um fünf hier sein").
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um fünf vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at five in front of the cinema.

meaning: 'at half past' (i.e., 30 minutes before the stated hour).
additional_notes: Used with a following hour: "um halb neun" means 8:30 (half an hour before nine), not 9:30. It’s a very common way to say times in German.
target_language_example: Der Zug fährt um halb acht ab.
native_language_example: The train leaves at 7:30.

additional_notes: German time expressions use **halb + next hour**: **halb drei** means “half (an hour) before three,” i.e., **2:30**. **um** means “at” for clock times. Common mistake: it does **not** mean 3:30.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um halb drei vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at 2:30 in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: In German, "halb sieben" means “half to seven” = 6:30 (30 minutes before seven), not 7:30. Often used with "um" to say the exact time something happens; "(Uhr)" is optional: "um halb sieben (Uhr)".
target_language_example: Der Unterricht beginnt um halb sieben.
native_language_example: Class starts at 6:30.

additional_notes: Used to give a specific time when something happens (appointments, opening times, deadlines). Often followed by "Uhr" (um neun Uhr), and you can add parts of the day: "um neun Uhr morgens/abends".
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um neun vor dem Bahnhof.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at nine in front of the train station.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact time when something happens. "um" + time (Uhr) = “at (a certain time)”. You can add "vormittags" (a.m., in the morning) or "abends" (in the evening) for clarity. For schedules you’ll often see the 24-hour clock instead (e.g., 21 Uhr = 9 p.m.).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um neun Uhr am Bahnhof.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at nine o’clock at the train station.

additional_notes: Used with clock times to say when something happens. "um" + a time answers the question "Wann?" (When?). Often also: "um sechs Uhr".
target_language_example: Der Zug fährt um sechs (Uhr) ab.
native_language_example: The train leaves at six (o’clock).

additional_notes: Used to say the exact time when something happens. Use **um + Uhrzeit** (e.g., um sechs Uhr, um 6 Uhr). Often combined with **früh** (in the morning/early) or **abends** (in the evening) for clarity: **um sechs Uhr früh/abends**.
target_language_example: Das Meeting beginnt morgen um sechs Uhr.
native_language_example: The meeting starts tomorrow at six o’clock.

meaning: 'up at six o’clock' (as in: to get up at 6:00).
additional_notes: Used with the separable verb **aufstehen** (“to get up”). In sentences, the time phrase **um sechs Uhr** usually comes before the verb, while **auf** goes to the end: **Ich stehe um sechs Uhr auf.**
target_language_example: Am Wochenende stehe ich nicht um sechs Uhr auf.
native_language_example: On weekends I don’t get up at six o’clock.

meaning: “at six (o’clock) … up” (shows a separable verb ending in **auf**, e.g. **aufstehen** = get up, **aufhören** = stop).
additional_notes: German separable verbs split in many sentences: the main verb goes in position 2, and the prefix goes to the end. With a time phrase like **um sechs** (“at six”), you’ll often see **auf** at the very end: **Ich stehe um sechs auf.** (= *aufstehen*). It can also occur with other separable verbs like **aufhören**: **Ich höre um sechs auf zu arbeiten.** (= I stop working at six).
target_language_example: Ich stehe morgen um sechs auf.
native_language_example: I’m getting up at six tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. Often you can add "Uhr": "um sieben" = "um sieben Uhr". "um" is the common preposition for clock times (um 8, um 12, um halb drei, etc.).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um sieben (Uhr) vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at seven (o’clock) in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: Used with specific clock times. The preposition "um" means "at" for times (um 7 Uhr, um 7:30, um Viertel nach sieben). Often used with routines and appointments. Note: for days/dates you use different words (e.g., "am Montag", "am 3. Mai").
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um sieben Uhr vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: We’re meeting at seven o’clock in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact time when something happens. "um" + time = "at" (a specific clock time). You can add "morgens" (in the morning), "nachmittags" (in the afternoon), "abends" (in the evening), or "nachts" (at night) to clarify.
target_language_example: Der Zug fährt um vier Uhr ab.
native_language_example: The train leaves at four o’clock.

meaning: “At what time are you…?” / “What time did you…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific clock time. It’s usually followed by a past participle with a place/action (e.g., „… nach Hause gekommen?“) or a time/place expression (e.g., „… wieder da?“). Often written as „um wie viel Uhr bist du …?“.
target_language_example: Um wieviel Uhr bist du heute aufgestanden?
native_language_example: What time did you get up today?

additional_notes: A question used to ask the time when a group of people (“ihr” = you plural) is going somewhere or going to do something. Very common with another verb or destination after it, e.g. „… nach Hause?“, „… schlafen?“, „… ins Bett?“. You can also say „Um wie viel Uhr …?“ (same meaning).
target_language_example: Um wieviel Uhr geht ihr morgen früh zur Schule?
native_language_example: What time are you (all) going to school tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used to ask at what time someone is/was doing something. It’s usually followed by a verb phrase (e.g., gekommen, zu Hause, schlafen gegangen). Uses the formal “Sie” (you) for strangers, customers, older people, etc. Word-by-word it’s “at how many o’clock are you,” but in English you normally say “What time…?”.
target_language_example: Um wieviel Uhr sind Sie heute angekommen?
native_language_example: What time did you arrive today?

additional_notes: Use **um + Uhrzeit** for clock times: **um zehn** = “at 10:00.” It can also mean “around ten” if the context is approximate (often clarified with **etwa/gegen**). With quantities/changes, **um + Betrag/Prozent** means “by” that amount: **um zehn Prozent** = “by ten percent.”
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um zehn vor dem Kino.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at ten in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Used with clock times to say when something happens. Use **um + [time] + Uhr** for exact times: *um zehn Uhr*, *um zehn Uhr dreißig* (10:30), *um zehn Uhr vierzig* (10:40). Often used with meetings, appointments, and daily routines.
target_language_example: Der Zug fährt um zehn Uhr ab.
native_language_example: The train leaves at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Used in an **um … zu + infinitive** purpose clause to say why someone does something. It typically has the **same subject** as the main clause (e.g., *Er ging …, um … zu studieren*). Word order: **um + (object) + zu + infinitive** → *um Musik zu studieren*.
target_language_example: Sie ist nach Wien gezogen, um Musik zu studieren.
native_language_example: She moved to Vienna in order to study music.

additional_notes: Used with the purpose construction "um ... zu" to say why someone does something. It often comes at the start of the sentence (followed by a comma) or after the main clause: "..., um Zeit zu sparen." The verb goes at the end: "sparen".
target_language_example: Um Zeit zu sparen, gehen wir zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
native_language_example: To save time, we walk to work.

meaning: 'to finish it' / 'to get it done' (in order to).
additional_notes: Used to talk about having enough time to complete a task. It’s built around **mit etwas fertig werden** (“to finish something / be done with something”). **damit** refers back to the thing you need to finish (a task, project, homework, etc.). Often appears after a time expression: **genug Zeit, um ...**, **eine Stunde, um ...**.
target_language_example: Ich brauche noch zwei Tage, um damit fertig zu werden.
native_language_example: I need two more days to finish it.

meaning: 'in order to' (used with 'um … zu' + an object starting with 'das').
