native_language_example: I needed many hours for the homework.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to emphasize variety within a large number: "viele verschiedene Ursachen" (= many different causes, not just many causes). The adjective "verschieden" changes ending like other adjectives depending on the noun phrase (e.g., "viele verschiedene Sorten", "viele verschiedenen Sorten" in some contexts).
target_language_example: In der Klasse gibt es viele verschiedene Sprachen.
native_language_example: There are many different languages in the class.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions to mean “for many years / many years ago.” Common patterns: „seit vielen Jahren“ = for many years (since many years ago, continuing to now); „vor vielen Jahren“ = many years ago; „nach so vielen Jahren“ = after so many years. Note the dative plural: „in/seit/vor/nach vielen Jahren“.
target_language_example: Ich wohne seit vielen Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Berlin for many years.

additional_notes: Used when the noun phrase is in the dative plural, often after prepositions like in/aus/mit/zu: „in vielen Ländern“ (in many countries), „aus vielen Ländern“ (from many countries), „mit vielen Ländern“ (with many countries). In questions you often see „wie vielen Ländern…?“ = „in how many countries…?“
target_language_example: In vielen Ländern gibt es unterschiedliche Traditionen.
native_language_example: In many countries there are different traditions.

additional_notes: A polite, common way to thank someone. Often used alone (“Vielen Dank!”) or with a reason using “für” + noun (“Vielen Dank für deine Hilfe.”) or “dass” + clause (“Vielen Dank, dass du gekommen bist.”). In writing you may also see: “Vielen Dank!”
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für Ihre Hilfe.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help.

meaning: “Thank you very much for…” (polite/formal, addressing “you” as Sie).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely and introduce a reason with dass + a full clause. Common in formal situations or when speaking to someone you don’t know well (e.g., a customer, a neighbor, an older person). After „dass“, the verb goes to the end of the clause: „…dass Sie gekommen sind.“
target_language_example: Vielen Dank, dass Sie sich so viel Zeit genommen haben.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for taking so much time.

meaning: “Thank you very much that …” / “Thank you very much for … (doing something).”
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific action, followed by a full clause with „dass/daß“ (today usually spelled „dass“). Commonly used with polite „Sie“ or informal „du/ihr“. Often followed by the perfect tense for something already done („… dass du gewartet hast“) or present tense for something ongoing („… dass du mir hilfst“).
target_language_example: Vielen Dank, dass Sie sich Zeit genommen haben.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for taking the time.

additional_notes: Used to express strong thanks for a specific thing. It’s followed by a noun/pronoun (often in the accusative), e.g. für deine Hilfe, für alles, für die Einladung. In speaking you’ll also hear the shorter “Danke für …”; “Vielen Dank” is a bit more formal/polite.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für deine Zeit und deine Geduld.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your time and your patience.

additional_notes: Used in polite/formal situations when addressing one person with “Sie/Ihr” (e.g., in emails, at events, to customers/strangers). It is usually followed by a noun: Vielen Dank für Ihre Einladung / Ihre Unterstützung / Ihre Zeit. For informal “you,” use: „Vielen Dank für deine …“.
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für Ihre Zeit und Ihre Hilfe.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your time and your help.

additional_notes: Used to warmly thank someone for something that belongs to them or that they did. It’s followed by a feminine noun in the singular (e.g., deine Hilfe, deine Unterstützung) or a plural noun (e.g., deine Kommentare, deine Fragen). Because it uses deine (du-form), it’s for friends, family, classmates, etc. (Formal would be: „Vielen Dank für Ihre …“).
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für deine Hilfe!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

meaning: "Thanks a lot for the ..." (feminine noun or plural).
additional_notes: A very common, polite way to thank someone. It’s typically followed by a noun phrase in the accusative (e.g., die Hilfe, die Unterstützung, die schnelle Antwort). Use it in emails and everyday speech. With masculine/neuter nouns you change "die" to "den/das" (e.g., Vielen Dank für den Anruf / für das Geschenk).
target_language_example: Vielen Dank für die Einladung!
native_language_example: Thanks a lot for the invitation!

additional_notes: Used to suggest an idea gently or politely, often when making plans, offering help, or proposing a solution. It can be followed by an infinitive (e.g., helfen, reden, zusammenarbeiten) or a full clause.
target_language_example: Vielleicht können wir morgen darüber sprechen.
native_language_example: Maybe we can talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion gently and politely. It often introduces an idea without sounding too direct, and is commonly followed by a time/activity (e.g., Freitag, morgen, dieses Wochenende, zusammen lernen). Verb order: in a main clause with "vielleicht" first, the conjugated verb comes second: "Vielleicht könnten wir …".
target_language_example: Vielleicht könnten wir nach der Arbeit einen Kaffee trinken.
native_language_example: Maybe we could have a coffee after work.

additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty that something will happen or be true (often softening a statement). It commonly comes before the verb or at the end of the clause: „Ich schaffe es vielleicht nicht.“ / „Vielleicht schaffe ich es nicht.“
target_language_example: Ich kann heute Abend vielleicht nicht kommen.
native_language_example: I might not be able to come this evening.

additional_notes: Used to make a gentle suggestion about your own actions (often with a verb in the infinitive at the end): „Vielleicht sollte ich + Infinitiv …“ (e.g., „… lernen/gehen/anrufen“). „sollte“ is Konjunktiv II of „sollen“ and sounds softer/less definite than „ich soll“.
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollte ich heute früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: Maybe I should go to bed earlier today.

additional_notes: Used to soften advice or a recommendation. Grammatically, it’s often **sollten** (Konjunktiv II of **sollen**) + infinitive: **Vielleicht sollten wir gehen.** You can use it with different subjects: **Vielleicht sollten Sie … / Vielleicht sollten wir … / Vielleicht sollten sie …**.
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollten wir später noch einmal darüber sprechen.
native_language_example: Maybe we should talk about it again later.

additional_notes: Used to give advice or make a gentle recommendation in a polite/formal way. "Sie" is the formal "you" (to a stranger, customer, older person, etc.). Word order: "Vielleicht sollten Sie + infinitive" (e.g., "… anrufen", "… warten", "… hingehen").
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollten Sie den Arzt anrufen.
native_language_example: Maybe you should call the doctor.

meaning: maybe we should… / perhaps we should…
additional_notes: Used to make a gentle suggestion for what the group ("we") should do. "sollten" is the subjunctive form of "sollen" and often sounds like English "should" (a recommendation, not a strict obligation). It’s commonly followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Vielleicht sollten wir gehen."
target_language_example: Vielleicht sollten wir morgen früher losfahren.
native_language_example: Maybe we should leave earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give advice in a soft, non-direct way. It’s formed from "vielleicht" (maybe) + "solltest" (you should, subjunctive of "sollen") + "du" (you). Often followed by an infinitive at the end of the clause: "Vielleicht solltest du mit ihr reden."
target_language_example: Vielleicht solltest du morgen früher ins Bett gehen.
native_language_example: Maybe you should go to bed earlier tomorrow.

meaning: "maybe you (all) should" (a suggestion/advice to a group).
additional_notes: Used to politely suggest what a group of people ("ihr" = you plural/informal) should do. "Solltet" is Konjunktiv II of "sollen" and softens the advice (less direct than "ihr sollt"). Often followed by an infinitive at the end: "... fragen/arbeiten/unterhalten/nachdenken".
target_language_example: Vielleicht solltet ihr früher losfahren, wenn es regnet.
native_language_example: Maybe you should leave earlier if it’s raining.

additional_notes: Used to say a duration (how long something lasts: „dauerte vier Jahre“), a frequency (how often: „alle vier Jahre“ = every four years), or an age (how old someone was: „vier Jahre alt“ = four years old). With time expressions, German often uses the accusative without a preposition for duration (e.g., „Er lebte vier Jahre dort.“).
target_language_example: Ich habe vier Jahre in Berlin gelebt.
native_language_example: I lived in Berlin for four years.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s age. With "sein" (ist) it describes a current age; with "werden" (wird/werde) it means turning four (on a birthday). Often used with "schon" (already) or "erst" (only).
target_language_example: Mein Neffe ist vier Jahre alt.
native_language_example: My nephew is four years old.

additional_notes: An adverbial phrase used to emphasize total agreement, full dedication, or full availability. Common with verbs like „zustimmen“ (agree) and the expression „jdm. voll und ganz zur Verfügung stehen“ (to be fully at someone’s disposal/available).
target_language_example: Ich unterstütze dich dabei voll und ganz.
native_language_example: I fully support you in that.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "sein" (to be) or "sich fühlen" (to feel) to describe someone’s mood/condition. Grammatically it’s "voll" + genitive: "voller" is the common form before a noun ("voller Energie", "voller Freude").
target_language_example: Nach dem Kaffee bin ich wieder voller Energie.
native_language_example: After the coffee, I’m full of energy again.

additional_notes: Used with sein: „X ist/sind vom Aussterben bedroht“ = X could disappear completely. Common in news and nature contexts when talking about species/animals (Art, Tiere). Past: „war/waren vom Aussterben bedroht“.
target_language_example: Viele Insektenarten sind vom Aussterben bedroht.
native_language_example: Many insect species are endangered.

additional_notes: "vom" = "von dem" and is used for movement/starting point away from a place. Often used with verbs like "abfahren" (depart), "kommen" (come), "gehen" (go), and in distance/time phrases like "vom Bahnhof zur Schule" (from the station to the school). Also appears in "vom Bahnhof aus" = "starting from the station".
target_language_example: Vom Bahnhof aus sind es nur zehn Minuten zu Fuß bis zum Hotel.
native_language_example: From the train station, it’s only a ten-minute walk to the hotel.

additional_notes: "vom" = "von dem" (from the). Used with movement away from a tree, often when someone/something falls or takes something off it (e.g., apples). Common with verbs like "fallen" (to fall) or "(etwas) stehlen/pflücken" (to steal/pick).
target_language_example: Die Katze sprang vom Baum herunter.
native_language_example: The cat jumped down from the tree.

additional_notes: Used for something/someone hit by a lightning strike, often in the passive: „X wurde vom Blitz getroffen.“ (X was struck by lightning). You’ll also hear the related idiom „wie vom Blitz getroffen“ meaning “as if struck by lightning” (suddenly shocked/surprised).
target_language_example: Der Baum wurde letzte Nacht vom Blitz getroffen.
native_language_example: The tree was struck by lightning last night.

additional_notes: "vom" is a common contraction of "von dem" (dative). Use it to talk about a starting point (e.g., traveling from the airport) or where someone/something is picked up ("jemanden vom Flughafen abholen"). It can also mean “of the airport” in contexts like "ein Foto vom Flughafen" (= a photo of the airport).
target_language_example: Wir nehmen ein Taxi vom Flughafen zum Hotel.
native_language_example: We’re taking a taxi from the airport to the hotel.

meaning: 'off the horse' / 'from the horse' (i.e., from on top of a horse).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or accidents to describe leaving the horse: e.g. fallen/stürzen/geworfen werden (fall off/be thrown off) or steigen (get off). It’s the contraction of „von dem Pferd“ and refers to movement away from the horse’s back.
target_language_example: Nach dem Ausritt stieg sie vom Pferd.
native_language_example: After the ride, she got off the horse.

meaning: to fall off a chair (often because of laughing hard or being shocked).
additional_notes: Literally means “(to have) fallen from the chair.” Often used with **fast** (“almost”) to show something nearly happened: **…dass er fast vom Stuhl gefallen wäre** (“…that he would have almost fallen off his chair”). In the past tense it commonly uses **sein**: **Ich bin vom Stuhl gefallen.**
target_language_example: Ich musste so lachen, dass ich fast vom Stuhl gefallen wäre.
native_language_example: I laughed so hard that I almost fell off my chair.

meaning: from beginning to end; all the way through.
additional_notes: Used to say something is told, read, watched, or done completely, without skipping any parts. Often goes with verbs like erzählen (tell), lesen (read), ansehen (watch).
target_language_example: Wir haben den Film von Anfang bis Ende gesehen.
native_language_example: We watched the movie from beginning to end.

additional_notes: Used in the passive voice to say who did the abducting: **von** + dative (agent) + **entführen** (“to abduct/kidnap”). Common full forms: **Er wurde von Außerirdischen entführt.** (simple past passive) / **Er ist von Außerirdischen entführt worden.** (perfect passive).
target_language_example: Sie behauptet, sie sei von Außerirdischen entführt worden.
native_language_example: She claims she was abducted by aliens.

additional_notes: Uses the formal pronoun "Sie" in the dative form "Ihnen". Common in polite письма/emails and formal conversation, especially with nouns like "Nachricht" (news/message): "von Ihnen Nachricht haben" = "to hear from you / to have news from you".
target_language_example: Ich habe lange nichts von Ihnen gehört.
native_language_example: I haven’t heard from you in a long time.

von Ihnen sagen, was passiert ist

target_language_multi_word_term: von Ihnen sagen, was passiert ist
meaning: (Can) one of you tell me what happened?
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask someone from a group (“von Ihnen” = “one of you” in formal/polite address) to explain what happened (“was passiert ist”). Often appears as: „Kann mir jemand/irgendjemand von Ihnen sagen, was passiert ist?“ Variants like „irgendwer/wer“ are more casual than „jemand“.
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, kann mir jemand von Ihnen sagen, was passiert ist?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can one of you tell me what happened?

additional_notes: Used in two very common patterns: (1) with superlatives: „der/die/das …-ste von allen“ = “the …est of all”; (2) with passive verbs to show the agent: „von allen + Verb (Partizip II)“ = “by everyone” (e.g., „von allen bewundert“).
target_language_example: Das ist das beste Restaurant von allen.
native_language_example: This is the best restaurant of all.

meaning: "from your" / "of your" (used with a masculine or neuter noun in the dative).
additional_notes: "von" takes the dative case. "deinem" is the dative form of "dein" for masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., von deinem Wein, von deinem Schiff). It’s used for source/origin ("ein Schluck von deinem Wein"), talking about something/someone related to you ("etwas von deinem Traum" = something about your dream), and with some verbs/phrases like "abhängen von" ("hängt von deinem Erfolg ab" = depends on your success) or "sich befreien von" (free yourself from your curse).
target_language_example: Ich habe von deinem Plan gehört.
native_language_example: I heard about your plan.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "von" plus the dative form of "der" (masc./neut.): "von dem". Very often shortened in speech and writing to "vom" (e.g., "vom Brief", "vom Haken"). Common meanings include origin/source ("from"), separation/removal ("take from"), and sometimes "of the" in expressions like "Kopien von dem Brief".
target_language_example: Ich habe eine E-Mail von dem Lehrer bekommen.
native_language_example: I got an email from the teacher.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **sprechen (von)**, **hören (von)**, **erzählen (von)** to mean “about.” It takes **dative**: **von dem Unfall**. In everyday speech and writing, it’s often contracted to **vom Unfall**.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir mehr vom Unfall erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me more about the accident?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "von" plus the dative form of "der" (masc./neut.): "von dem". Very often shortened in speech and writing to "vom" (e.g., "vom Brief", "vom Haken"). Common meanings include origin/source ("from"), separation/removal ("take from"), and sometimes "of the" in expressions like "Kopien von dem Brief".
target_language_example: Ich habe eine E-Mail von dem Lehrer bekommen.
native_language_example: I got an email from the teacher.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a part/amount of something previously mentioned, especially after words like einiges (some), die Hälfte (half), kein Wort (not a word), das Doppelte (double). It connects that quantity to a clause: "von dem, was + sentence" = "of what + happened/was said/costs…". Often follows a noun phrase: "die Hälfte von dem, was ...".
target_language_example: Ich habe nur einen Teil von dem verstanden, was du erklärt hast.
native_language_example: I only understood part of what you explained.

von dem ich dir erzählt habe

target_language_multi_word_term: von dem ich dir erzählt habe
meaning: “that I told you about” (literally: “about which I told you”).
additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to refer back to a noun (person/thing) you mentioned before. You choose the form based on the noun: von dem (masculine/neuter), von der (feminine), von denen (plural). It’s common after expressions like “Das ist …,” “Der Mann …,” “Das Buch …”.
target_language_example: Das ist der Film, von dem ich dir erzählt habe.
native_language_example: That’s the movie I told you about.

meaning: 'from the' / 'of the' (used with plural or formal 'you').
additional_notes:
Combination of the preposition **von** + **den** (dative plural of **der/die/das**, or dative plural of formal **Sie**). Commonly used:
- for **partitives/selection**: *von den vier Jahreszeiten* = “of the four seasons” (among them)
- for **origin/source**: *von den Toten* = “from the dead”.
Grammar note: **von** takes the **dative**. With singular masculine/neuter you usually see the contraction **vom** (= *von dem*), but there is **no** contraction for *von den*.
target_language_example: Von den Kindern hat nur eins Zeit.
native_language_example: Of the children, only one has time.

additional_notes: Used with plural "die" to refer back to a previously mentioned group of people/things. Common uses: (1) comparison: "X unterscheidet sich von denen ..." = "X is different from those ..."; (2) partitive: "einer/eins von denen" = "one (of) those"; (3) in a relative clause: "..., von denen ..." = "..., of whom/which ...".
target_language_example: Ich kenne ein paar Leute, von denen du viel lernen kannst.
native_language_example: I know a few people you can learn a lot from.

meaning: 'from the' / 'of the' / 'about the' (von + feminine dative noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "von" plus "der" (dative feminine singular, or dative plural). Common meanings: (1) origin/source: "vom/von der Bahnhof" = from the station; (2) part of/association: "ein Freund von der Freundin" = a friend of the (female) friend; (3) topic: "von der Belohnung" = about the reward. The noun after it is in the dative case.
target_language_example: Ich komme gerade von der Arbeit.
native_language_example: I’m just coming from work.

von der Hand in den Mund

target_language_multi_word_term: von der Hand in den Mund
meaning: living hand to mouth; living paycheck to paycheck.
additional_notes: An idiom meaning you have barely enough money for basic needs, with little or no savings (you spend what you earn right away). Used with "leben": "(von der Hand in den Mund) leben".
target_language_example: Nach der Miete bleibt uns fast nichts übrig – wir leben von der Hand in den Mund.
native_language_example: After rent, we have almost nothing left—we’re living paycheck to paycheck.

additional_notes: Used to show distance or origin relative to the coastline. Common with words like "entfernt" (away) and verbs like "liegen": "X liegt ... von der Küste entfernt" = "X is ... away from the coast." It can also describe origin: "Leute von der Küste" = "people from the coast."
target_language_example: Das Hotel liegt nur fünf Minuten von der Küste entfernt.
native_language_example: The hotel is only five minutes away from the coast.

additional_notes: Used to show that something/someone is taken from a list. Common with **(jdn./etw.) von der Liste streichen** = “to cross (someone/something) off the list / remove from the list”, and with **(etw.) von der Liste wählen** = “to choose (something) from the list.”
target_language_example: Bitte streichen Sie meinen Namen von der Liste.
native_language_example: Please remove my name from the list.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has been removed from a list, often implying it was deleted or deliberately taken off. It’s the past participle of „von der Liste streichen“ (to cross off/remove from the list) and is commonly used in passive sentences: „Du wurdest von der Liste gestrichen“ (You were removed from the list).
target_language_example: Aus Versehen wurde ich von der Liste gestrichen.
native_language_example: I was accidentally crossed off the list.

additional_notes: Literally "von" = "from/by" and "der Polizei" = "the police" (dative). Very common in the passive to show who does the action: "wurde von der Polizei festgenommen" = "was arrested by the police". With "sein" it can mean belonging/working there: "Sind Sie von der Polizei?" = "Are you with the police?"
target_language_example: Er wurde von der Polizei kontrolliert.
native_language_example: He was checked by the police.

additional_notes: A common way to describe the route/direction after school. Used with verbs of movement like gehen, kommen, fahren, sein (auf dem Weg). Note the cases: von + dative (von der Schule) and nach + dative (nach Hause). You can also shorten it to „von der Schule heim(gehen)“ in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ich gehe jeden Tag von der Schule nach Hause.
native_language_example: I walk from school to home every day.

additional_notes: Used to describe where someone/something is seen or where an action comes from. The noun after "des" is in the genitive (e.g., "des Raumes", "des Zimmers"). Often appears with "aus" ("von der anderen Seite des Raumes aus" = from across the room) or with verbs like "betrachten" ("von der anderen Seite ... betrachtet" = viewed from the other side).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn von der anderen Seite des Flusses gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him from the other side of the river.

meaning: "of this" / "from this" (referring to a masculine/neuter noun).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "von" + dative to show origin, source, or relation: "von diesem Dokument" = "of/from this document". "Diesem" is the dative form of "dieser" for masculine/neuter nouns; for feminine/plural you’ll see "von dieser" / "von diesen".
target_language_example: Ich brauche eine Kopie von diesem Vertrag.
native_language_example: I need a copy of this contract.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition "von" + "dir" (dative of "du"). Common uses: (1) origin/source: "eine Antwort von dir" = an answer from you; (2) topic: "von dir erzählen / von dir reden" = talk about you; (3) depends on: "Das hängt von dir ab" = That depends on you; (4) distance from: "weit weg von dir" = far away from you; (5) separation: "sich von dir verabschieden" = say goodbye to you.
target_language_example: Das hängt ganz von dir ab.
native_language_example: That depends entirely on you.

meaning: “(I/we) expect/require (from) you to …” (introduces what is expected of you).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like **erwarten** (to expect) or **verlangen** (to demand): **[Verb] von dir, dass du + Nebensatz**. The **dass**-clause explains the expectation/requirement, and the verb in the **dass**-clause goes to the end: *… dass du pünktlich **bist***.
target_language_example: Ich erwarte von dir, dass du pünktlich bist.
native_language_example: I expect you to be on time.

meaning: 'from a' / 'by a' (introduces a masculine/neuter noun in the dative).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine or neuter singular noun (dative: einem). Common with: (1) origins/sources: "nichts von einem ..." = "nothing about a ..."; (2) size/amount comparisons: "in der Größe von einem ..." = "the size of a ..."; (3) passive/agent: "von einem Hund angegriffen" = "attacked by a dog"; (4) having something done by someone: "von einem Gepäckträger tragen lassen" = "have a porter carry it". (Feminine would be "von einer"; plural "von (den)".)
target_language_example: Der Brief wurde von einem Freund geschrieben.
native_language_example: The letter was written by a friend.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "werden" to form the passive: "jemand wird von einem Auto angefahren" = someone gets hit by a car. "fast" adds “almost/nearly”: "fast von einem Auto angefahren". Common in accident/news contexts; "anfahren" means to hit/knock someone down with a vehicle.
target_language_example: Der Mann wurde gestern Abend von einem Auto angefahren.
native_language_example: The man was hit by a car last night.

meaning: (to) have been hit/struck by a car.
additional_notes: This is the passive past form of **anfahren** (“to hit/strike (someone) with a vehicle”). It’s built with **werden**: *jdn. anfahren* → *von einem Auto angefahren werden* (present passive) → *von einem Auto angefahren worden* (“have/was been hit by a car”). **von + dative** names who/what caused it (*von einem Auto*, *von einem Bus*). Often appears with **fast / beinahe** (“almost”) or in the conditional: **wäre … angefahren worden** (“would have been hit”).
target_language_example: Sie ist gestern auf dem Zebrastreifen fast von einem Auto angefahren worden.
native_language_example: Yesterday she was almost hit by a car at the crosswalk.

meaning: to be run over by a car.
additional_notes: Passive construction: **jemand wird von einem Auto überfahren** = someone is hit and driven over by a car. Often used with **(beinahe / fast)** to mean “almost got run over.” You can replace **Auto** with another vehicle (z.B. **von einem Bus / LKW überfahren**).
target_language_example: Pass auf! Ich wurde fast von einem Auto überfahren.
native_language_example: Watch out! I almost got run over by a car.

additional_notes: Used to say the source/origin of something (a letter, help, money, a borrowed item) is a friend. It can also mark the doer in passive sentences: "Sie wurde von einem Freund betrogen" = "She was cheated on/by a friend."
target_language_example: Ich habe das Buch von einem Freund bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the book from a friend.

meaning: from another planet (often said jokingly: very strange / out of touch).
additional_notes: Literally refers to extraterrestrials (“aliens from another planet”). In everyday speech it can also be used humorously to say someone’s idea or behavior seems so odd that they must be “from another planet.” Used with verbs like kommen (“to come”): „Kommst du von einem anderen Planeten?“
target_language_example: Die Idee ist so komisch – bist du von einem anderen Planeten?
native_language_example: That idea is so weird—are you from another planet?

meaning: "from a" / "by a" (referring to a feminine noun, dative).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns in the dative case: von + einer + [feminine noun]. Often means "from" (origin/source: von einer Freundin) or "by" in the passive voice (agent: von einer süßen Kellnerin begrüßt). Common feminine nouns: die Freundin, die Universität, die Person, die Brücke, die Kellnerin.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Tipp von einer Kollegin bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the tip from a (female) colleague.

additional_notes: Used in the passive to say someone received a bee sting. Common patterns: „Wurdest du (schon mal) von einer Biene gestochen?“ (Were you ever stung by a bee?) and „Ich bin von einer Biene gestochen worden.“ (I was stung by a bee).
target_language_example: Ich bin gestern im Garten von einer Biene gestochen worden.
native_language_example: I was stung by a bee in the garden yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the informal plural pronoun euch (“you all”). Often used (1) to mean “(some) of you” in partitive expressions: *ein paar von euch* = “a few of you”; and (2) after adjectives to comment on someone’s behavior: *nett/unhöflich von euch* = “nice/rude of you (all)”. It can also mean “from you (all)” depending on context.
target_language_example: Das ist echt nett von euch, dass ihr mir helft.
native_language_example: That’s really nice of you all to help me.

meaning: of great use; very useful; of great benefit.
additional_notes: Often used with "sein" or "werden" to say something is very helpful/beneficial: "X ist/wird jemandem von großem Nutzen (sein)." The person who benefits is usually in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/uns/Ihnen), and you can also add "für" to specify who it’s useful for (e.g., "für mich").
target_language_example: Der Tipp war mir von großem Nutzen.
native_language_example: The tip was very useful to me.

meaning: 'from here to' (describing a distance, travel time, or cost).
additional_notes: Used with a destination that usually follows (often introduced by nach/zu/in), e.g. "von hier bis nach Berlin", "von hier bis zum Bahnhof", "von hier bis in die Stadt". Common in questions about how far it is, how long it takes, or how much it costs to get somewhere.
target_language_example: Wie lange dauert es von hier bis zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: How long does it take from here to the train station?

additional_notes: A distance/direction phrase: von + place (dative) + bis zu(m) + destination (dative). Often used when asking or telling how long it takes (e.g., „Wie lange braucht man …?“ / „Es dauert …“), frequently with „zu Fuß“ (on foot). „zum" = „zu dem" (masculine/neuter); with feminine destinations you’ll see „bis zur …“ (zu der).
target_language_example: Wie lange dauert es zu Fuß von hier bis zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: How long does it take on foot from here to the train station?

meaning: 'away from here' (at a distance from this place).
additional_notes: Used to say how far something is from where you are now. Very common with distances (e.g., „zwei Kilometer von hier entfernt“) and with „(nicht) weit“: „nicht weit von hier entfernt“ = not far from here. Often appears with „sein“: „X ist … von hier entfernt.“
target_language_example: Die Apotheke ist nur fünf Minuten zu Fuß von hier entfernt.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is only a five-minute walk away from here.

additional_notes: Used with movement/approach verbs, especially in phrases like „sich von hinten an jemanden heranschleichen/an jemanden anschleichen“ (= to sneak up on someone from behind). It often implies the person being approached doesn’t notice. Common word order: „Er schlich sich von hinten an sie heran.“
target_language_example: Der Hund kam von hinten an mich heran.
native_language_example: The dog came up to me from behind.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "von" + dative pronoun "ihm" (him). Common meanings: (1) source/origin: "Ich habe es von ihm erfahren." = I found out from him; "ein Brief von ihm" = a letter from him. (2) topic: "von ihm sprechen/erzählen" = talk/tell about him. (3) sometimes with passive/"lassen": "sich von ihm küssen lassen" = let him kiss you.
target_language_example: Ich habe das Geschenk von ihm bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the gift from him.

additional_notes: Used with a thing you receive: "etwas von ihm bekommen" (e.g., eine Antwort, einen Brief, ein Geschenk). Word order changes in questions: "Hast du ... von ihm bekommen?". "bekommen" here means "receive/get" (not "become").
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern eine Nachricht von ihm bekommen.
native_language_example: I received a message from him yesterday.

meaning: heard from him; heard any news about/from him.
additional_notes: Used with hören + von (+ dative) to ask/report whether you’ve had any contact or information. Very common in the pattern „(etwas) von jemandem hören“ = to hear from someone / to hear something about someone (news, updates). Often used with time expressions like „in letzter Zeit“ (lately).
target_language_example: Ich habe seit Wochen nichts von ihm gehört.
native_language_example: I haven't heard from him in weeks.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** + dative plural pronoun **ihnen** (“them”). It can mean **from them** (source: *Wir hörten es von ihnen.*) or **of them** (belonging/responsibility: *ein Fehler von ihnen* = “a mistake of theirs”). Also appears in polite phrases like **Das war recht von Ihnen!** (“That was very kind of you!”), where **Ihnen** is the formal “you” (capitalized).
target_language_example: Ich habe es von ihnen erfahren.
native_language_example: I found out about it from them.

meaning: from her; of her (away from her).
additional_notes: "von" + dative pronoun "ihr" (her). Often marks the source/origin (e.g., a message coming from her): "eine Antwort von ihr" = "an answer from her". It’s also used in some fixed verb phrases to mean “away from her,” e.g. "den Blick von ihr lassen" = "to take your eyes off her."
target_language_example: Ich habe heute eine Nachricht von ihr bekommen.
native_language_example: I got a message from her today.

additional_notes: Used to say that she is the source/giver of something. Very common with objects: „Ich habe das von ihr bekommen.“ = “I got that from her.” In questions: „Hast du was von ihr bekommen?“ = “Did you get anything from her?” Grammar tip: „von“ takes the dative case → „ihr“ (her, dative).
target_language_example: Ich habe die Nachricht von ihr bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the message from her.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** + **dative**. **ihrem** is the dative form of **ihr** (“her/its”), used with **masculine or neuter nouns** (e.g., *von ihrem Großvater*, *von ihrem Können*). **von + dative** can show (1) where something comes from (*from*), (2) what someone is distracted from, and very often (3) the agent in the passive (*by*): *Sie wurde von ihrem Chef angeschrien.*
target_language_example: Sie war von ihrem Ergebnis überrascht.
native_language_example: She was surprised by her result.

additional_notes: Uses **von** (+ dative) to show who something comes from or who is involved. **ihrem** is dative of **ihr** (“her”). **Freund** can mean either “friend” or “boyfriend” depending on context. Also used with verbs like **(sich) trennen von** (“to separate/break up with”). Word order can vary: *ein Geschenk von ihrem Freund* or *von ihrem Freund ein Geschenk*.
target_language_example: Sie hat das Buch von ihrem Freund bekommen.
native_language_example: She got the book from her boyfriend/friend.

additional_notes: "von" takes the dative case, so "ihrer" is the dative form of "sie" as a possessive meaning "her" or "their" (feminine singular noun or plural noun). It’s used for origin/source ("von ihrer neuen Arbeit erzählen" = talk about her new job), cause/experience ("bewegt von ihrer Freundlichkeit" = moved by her kindness), opinion/assessment ("halten von ihrer Entdeckung" = think of her discovery), and in passive-like meaning with people ("von ihrer Großmutter großgezogen" = raised by her grandmother).
target_language_example: Ich habe das Geschenk von ihrer Schwester bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the gift from her sister.

additional_notes:
Used with the preposition **von** + **dative** to mean:
- **source/origin**: *von meinem Freund* = from my friend
- **possession/connection** (often like “of”): *ein Bild von meinem Wagen* = a picture of my car
- **topic** after verbs like **erzählen (von)**, **sprechen (von)**: *von meinem Problem* = about my problem
**meinem** is the dative form of **mein** for **masculine or neuter singular** nouns. (Feminine: *von meiner*; plural: *von meinen*.)
target_language_example: Kannst du mir von meinem Urlaub erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about my vacation?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **von** (+ dative) to show a starting point or reference point: distance **from** your house, directions **from** your house, or location relative to it. Often appears with **aus** (e.g., **von meinem Haus aus**) meaning “starting from my house / from where my house is.” (Note: **von dem** is often shortened to **vom**, but with **meinem** you keep **von meinem**.)
target_language_example: Von meinem Haus aus dauert es nur zehn Minuten bis zum Bahnhof.
native_language_example: From my house, it only takes ten minutes to get to the train station.

meaning: by my father; from my father.
additional_notes: Uses **von + dative** (mein Vater → **meinem Vater**). Often means **“by”** to name the doer in the **passive** (Das Haus wurde von meinem Vater gestrichen = “The house was painted by my father”). It can also mean **“from”** to show the source/origin, e.g. a gift or something you received (ein Geschenk von meinem Vater = “a gift from my father”), or authorship (ein Buch von meinem Vater = “a book by my father”).
target_language_example: Der Brief ist von meinem Vater.
native_language_example: The letter is from my father.

additional_notes: "von" takes the dative case, so it becomes "von meiner" before a feminine noun (e.g., "von meiner Mutter", "von meiner Freundin"). It can mean (1) origin/source: "I got it from my…", (2) distance/avoidance with verbs like "sich fernhalten": "Stay away from my…", and (3) “of” in expressions like "überzeugt von": "convinced of my…". In "von ... sprechen", it means “talk about …”.
target_language_example: Ich habe den Rat von meiner Mutter bekommen.
native_language_example: I got the advice from my mother.

meaning: to tell (someone) about my trip; to report on my trip.
additional_notes: Used with a person in the dative (mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen) and the topic with **von + dative**: *jemandem von etwas berichten*. You can make it more polite or more forceful with **Lassen Sie mich …** (formal) / **Lass mich …** (informal singular) / **Lasst mich …** (informal plural).
target_language_example: Nach dem Urlaub möchte ich meinen Freunden von meiner Reise berichten.
native_language_example: After the vacation, I’d like to tell my friends about my trip.

meaning: from me; of mine (as the source/owner).
additional_notes: Used to say that something comes from you or belongs to you, often after a noun (e.g., ein Buch von mir = a book from me / one of my books). With verbs like leihen/ausleihen it marks the person something is borrowed from.
target_language_example: Kann ich das Fahrrad von dir ausleihen?
native_language_example: Can I borrow the bike from you?

meaning: from morning to evening; all day long.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something lasts the whole day, typically with the idea of working or doing something continuously from the morning until the evening. Often paired with verbs like arbeiten (to work) or lernen (to study).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute von morgens bis abends gelernt.
native_language_example: I studied today from morning to evening (all day long).

additional_notes: "von" + dative. "seinem" is the dative form of "sein" (= his) for masculine/neuter nouns (e.g., von seinem Text, von seinem Motorrad). Used for: (1) origin/source or “a (photo/picture) of his …”, (2) separation/movement away (e.g., getting off something), (3) being impressed/affected by something, and (4) asking an opinion: "Was hältst du von seinem …?"
target_language_example: Ich habe viel von seinem neuen Projekt gehört.
native_language_example: I’ve heard a lot about his new project.

meaning: from his father; (in passive) by his father.
additional_notes: "von" + dative shows the source/origin of something (e.g., inheriting or taking over something from someone). It can also name the agent in a passive sentence: "Er ist von seinem Vater ..." = "He was ... by his father." (Here: "seinem Vater" is dative masculine; the base form is "sein Vater".)
target_language_example: Er hat das Haus von seinem Vater geerbt.
native_language_example: He inherited the house from his father.

meaning: "from his" / "of his" (used before a plural noun).
additional_notes: "von" is a preposition that usually takes the dative case. "seinen" is the dative plural form of "sein" (his), used with plural nouns (often masculine/neuter in dative plural). Common uses: source/origin ("von seinen Händen" = from his hands), belonging/selection ("eines von seinen Autos" = one of his cars), and fixed patterns like "abhängig von seinen …" (dependent on his …) or "leben von seinen …" (live on/from his …).
target_language_example: Sie bekommt Hilfe von seinen Freunden.
native_language_example: She gets help from his friends.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition „von“ + dative to mean origin/separation or source: being independent/dependent on money or support from one’s parents („finanziell unabhängig/abhängig von …“), or living separately („getrennt von …“). „seinen“ changes with gender/number (e.g., „von seiner Mutter“, „von ihren Eltern“).
target_language_example: Sie bekommt keine Hilfe von ihren Eltern.
native_language_example: She doesn’t get any help from her parents.

additional_notes: Uses dative plural after "von" (Freunden). In passive sentences, "von" often marks the doer/agent = "by" ("Er wurde von seinen Freunden ausgelacht" = "He was laughed at by his friends"). In other contexts it can mean origin/source = "from" ("Hilfe von seinen Freunden" = "help from his friends").
target_language_example: Er hat das Geschenk von seinen Freunden bekommen.
native_language_example: He got the present from his friends.

meaning: "about his" / "of his" (von + dative; refers to something that belongs to him).
additional_notes: Used when a verb or noun takes "von" (with dative). Common patterns: **von seiner Arbeit erzählen** = talk about his job; **ein Bild von seiner Katze** = a picture of his cat. **seiner** is the dative feminine form of **sein** (“his”), used with feminine nouns like **die Arbeit**, **die Katze**, **die Vergangenheit**.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir von seiner Familie erzählen?
native_language_example: Can you tell me about his family?

meaning: by/from/about his girlfriend (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: "von" + dative. Common uses: (1) In the passive, it can mark the doer/agent: "Er wurde von seiner Freundin verlassen" = "He was left by his girlfriend." (2) It can mean "from" with receiving/getting: "eine Nachricht von seiner Freundin" = "a message from his girlfriend." (3) Some verbs take "von" to mean "about/of": "träumen von" = "to dream about." "seiner" is the masculine/neuter dative form of "sein" (his).
target_language_example: Er hat eine Nachricht von seiner Freundin bekommen.
native_language_example: He got a message from his girlfriend.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "(jdn.) von etw. überzeugen" (to convince someone of something). Literally "from his innocence" in German structure, but in English it’s usually "of his innocence". After "von" you use the dative: "von seiner Unschuld" (masc./neut. dative), "von ihrer Unschuld" (fem. dative).
target_language_example: Die Anwältin konnte den Richter von seiner Unschuld überzeugen.
native_language_example: The lawyer was able to convince the judge of his innocence.

meaning: "of us" / "from us" ("one/some/how many of us"; "away from us").
additional_notes: Very common with quantities and superlatives: "einer von uns" (one of us), "einige von uns" (some of us), "wie viele von uns" (how many of us), "der Beste von uns" (the best of us). Also used with distance: "(zwei Häuser) von uns entfernt" = "(two houses) away from us". With "wissen von" it means "to know about": "Wissen sie von uns?" = "Do they know about us?"
target_language_example: Nur einer von uns hat die Antwort.
native_language_example: Only one of us has the answer.

additional_notes: Used with a reflexive pronoun: „sich von uns helfen lassen“ = literally “to have oneself helped by us.” In practice it’s a polite way to suggest/ask someone to accept help. Conjugate „lassen“ (musst/müsst/solltest/sollten/müssen) and match the reflexive pronoun: ich lasse **mich**, du lässt **dich**, ihr lasst **euch**, Sie lassen **sich**.
target_language_example: Lassen Sie sich von uns helfen.
native_language_example: Let us help you.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "anfangen" or "beginnen" to say you will restart completely (not just continue where you left off). Often intensified as "ganz von vorne an" (right from the start) or combined with "noch mal / noch einmal" (again).
target_language_example: Können wir bitte von vorne an anfangen?
native_language_example: Can we please start over from the beginning?

meaning: to start over; to start again from the beginning.
additional_notes: Used when you want to restart a task, conversation, or explanation from the beginning (often because something went wrong or wasn’t understood). Commonly combined with "noch mal / noch einmal" (= again): "Können wir noch mal von vorne anfangen?"
target_language_example: Sorry, ich habe es nicht verstanden—können wir von vorne anfangen?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand—can we start over?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the person something comes from or originates with (a gift, an idea, information, etc.). It’s the combination of the preposition "von" (from) + "wem" (whom, dative). Often used alone as a follow-up question: "Von wem?" = "From who(m)?"
target_language_example: Von wem hast du die Nachricht gehört?
native_language_example: Who did you hear the news from?

meaning: from home; working/doing something from home.
additional_notes: Used to say you do an activity while staying at home, often with work ("von zu Hause aus arbeiten" = "to work from home"). It goes with verbs like arbeiten, lernen, telefonieren, bestellen, etc. It can be moved in the sentence like other adverbs: "Ich arbeite von zu Hause aus." / "Von zu Hause aus arbeite ich ..."
target_language_example: Ich kann heute von zu Hause aus lernen.
native_language_example: I can study from home today.

meaning: away from home (as in “run away from home”).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/leaving, especially **(weg)laufen** or **weglaufen** (“to run away”), to say someone leaves home without permission or unexpectedly. Often: **von zu Hause weglaufen**.
target_language_example: Der Teenager ist von zu Hause weggelaufen.
native_language_example: The teenager ran away from home.

meaning: from excitement / nervousness (so that you react strongly).
additional_notes: Used to say that excitement or nervousness is the cause of a reaction (e.g., jumping up and down, not being able to sleep, barely being able to control yourself). Often appears with verbs like hüpfen, nicht schlafen können, sich kaum halten können, außer sich sein. Similar: „vor Freude“ (from joy), „vor Angst“ (from fear).
target_language_example: Ich konnte vor Aufregung kaum sprechen.
native_language_example: I could hardly speak from excitement/nervousness.

meaning: before nightfall / before it gets dark.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than the moment when darkness begins (around sunset). Common with arrival/return plans and deadlines: „Wir müssen vor Einbruch der Dunkelheit zurück sein.“ Often paired with „noch“ for emphasis: „noch vor Einbruch der Dunkelheit“ = “before it gets dark (still in time)”.
target_language_example: Lass uns vor Einbruch der Dunkelheit nach Hause gehen.
native_language_example: Let’s go home before it gets dark.

meaning: with joy; out of joy (because of happiness).
additional_notes: Used to express that someone does something because they feel very happy. Often used with strong reactions like tanzen (dance), springen (jump), lachen (laugh), weinen (cry), schreien (shout). The preposition "vor" can mean "from/out of" with feelings: vor Angst (out of fear), vor Wut (with anger).
target_language_example: Die Kinder sprangen vor Freude, als sie die gute Nachricht hörten.
native_language_example: The children jumped for joy when they heard the good news.

meaning: 'in court' / 'before a court' (in a legal case).
additional_notes: Used in legal contexts for court proceedings (not the food meaning of "Gericht"). Common with verbs like "kommen" (to end up in court), "gehen" (to go to court), and "aussagen" (to testify in court).
target_language_example: Der Zeuge muss morgen vor Gericht erscheinen.
native_language_example: The witness has to appear in court tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with feelings like "Angst haben" or "ängstlich sein": "Angst vor + dative". Here, "Hunden" is dative plural of "Hund". It means being afraid of dogs (not the literal sense of "in front of dogs").
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst vor Hunden, besonders wenn sie bellen.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of dogs, especially when they bark.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a short time ago (in the recent past). Often placed near the verb, but it can also start a sentence for emphasis: "Vor Kurzem ...". Common in both spoken and written German.
target_language_example: Ich bin vor Kurzem nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: I moved to Berlin recently.

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs to show the reason or emotion behind a strong reaction, e.g. „zittern vor Wut“ (to tremble with rage), „kochen vor Wut“ (to be boiling with rage), „außer sich vor Wut“ (to be beside oneself with rage). It’s not about physical location; it expresses how strongly someone feels anger.
target_language_example: Sie schrie vor Wut und knallte die Tür zu.
native_language_example: She shouted with rage and slammed the door.

meaning: “in front of the” / “before the” (with masculine or neuter nouns).
additional_notes: “vor” takes the dative when it means location (where?): vor dem Kino (= in front of the cinema). It can also mean time: vor dem Sommer (= before the summer). “dem” is the dative form of “der/das” (masculine/neuter). Often used in fixed phrases like “vor dem Gesetz” (= before the law).
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns vor dem Restaurant.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in front of the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with an action to say it happens earlier than dinner. It’s a time phrase with the preposition "vor" + dative: "vor dem" + noun (here: "Abendessen").
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte vor dem Abendessen den Müll rausbringen?
native_language_example: Can you please take out the trash before dinner?

meaning: in front of the train station.
additional_notes: A location phrase: "vor" + dative means "in front of" (outside, near the entrance). "dem" is the dative form of "der" because "Bahnhof" is masculine (der Bahnhof). Often used for meeting points or where taxis wait.
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns vor dem Bahnhof um acht.
native_language_example: We’ll meet in front of the train station at eight.

vor dem Essen die Hände waschen

target_language_multi_word_term: vor dem Essen die Hände waschen
meaning: to wash your hands before eating.
additional_notes: Used for hygiene advice or rules. Often with modal verbs like sollten (“should”) and with the reflexive pronoun: ich wasche mir…, du wäschst dir…, wir waschen uns…, ihr wascht euch…, Sie waschen sich… The phrase can also be used as a polite question: Wo kann ich mir … waschen? (“Where can I wash my hands …?”).
target_language_example: Kinder, bitte wascht euch vor dem Essen die Hände!
native_language_example: Kids, please wash your hands before eating!

meaning: in front of the TV; watching TV.
additional_notes: Literally means “in front of the television.” Often used to describe where someone is sitting/lying (e.g., on the couch) and commonly implies they’re watching TV or spending time watching TV (e.g., Zeit vor dem Fernseher verbringen).
target_language_example: Ich habe gestern Abend zwei Stunden vor dem Fernseher gesessen.
native_language_example: I sat in front of the TV for two hours last night.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens earlier than breakfast (time expression). With the dative: vor + dem + Frühstück (das Frühstück). Often used with daily routines (shower, walk, take medicine, etc.).
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Frühstück ein Glas Wasser.
native_language_example: I drink a glass of water before breakfast.

meaning: 'in front of the house' (outside, by the house).
additional_notes: "vor" + dative (dem Haus) describes a location in front of something. Often used for where someone/something is or stops (e.g., a bus stops in front of the house). Not to be confused with "vor das Haus" (accusative), which means movement to in front of the house.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte vor dem Haus warten?
native_language_example: Can you please wait in front of the house?

meaning: from the rain; against the rain (protected from rain).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like „schützen“ or „sich schützen“ to say someone/something is protected from rain. It literally means “before the rain,” but in this context it means “from/against the rain.” Often paired with an object like „Schirm/Regenschirm“, „Jacke“, or „Dach“.
target_language_example: Wir haben die Fahrräder vor dem Regen untergestellt.
native_language_example: We put the bikes under cover to protect them from the rain.

meaning: before going to sleep; before bedtime.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do shortly before you go to bed. Often used with a regular habit (e.g., "Ich lese vor dem Schlafengehen") or a suggestion/plan ("Wollen wir ...?").
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Schlafengehen noch einen Tee.
native_language_example: I drink a tea before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is standing/doing something in front of a mirror, often while getting ready (hair, makeup, clothes) or practicing (e.g., speaking, singing, facial expressions). It commonly goes with verbs like stehen (to stand), sich fertig machen (to get ready), üben (to practice).
target_language_example: Ich mache mich vor dem Spiegel fertig.
native_language_example: I’m getting ready in front of the mirror.

meaning: "of death" (e.g., fear of death); also "before death."
additional_notes: Most often used with nouns like Angst/Furcht: **Angst/Furcht vor dem Tod** = “fear of death” (here **vor** + dative expresses what you’re afraid of). It can also be used in a more general sense meaning “before death” or “in the face of death,” e.g. **Vor dem Tod sind alle gleich** (“In the face of death, everyone is equal”).
target_language_example: Viele Menschen haben Angst vor dem Tod.
native_language_example: Many people are afraid of death.

meaning: before going to bed; before bedtime.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do as part of your evening routine. Literally “before the going-to-bed” (vor + dem + Zubettgehen). Often pairs with habits like duschen (shower), baden (bathe), lesen (read), Zähne putzen (brush teeth).
target_language_example: Ich trinke vor dem Zubettgehen immer noch einen Tee.
native_language_example: I always drink a tea before going to bed.

additional_notes: Used especially with a hand: „die Hand vor den Mund halten/nehmen“ = to cover your mouth (e.g., when coughing, sneezing, yawning, or to hide a smile). Often appears with a reflexive pronoun: „Halt dir / sich die Hand vor den Mund.“
target_language_example: Bitte halte dir die Hand vor den Mund, wenn du hustest.
native_language_example: Please cover your mouth with your hand when you cough.

meaning: "in front of the" or "before the" (also used as "of/about" after verbs like *warnen*).
additional_notes: *Vor* is a preposition that usually takes the dative for location (*vor der Disko* = in front of the club) and can mean time (*vor der Wahl* = before the election). With verbs like **warnen vor** it means “warn (someone) about/of” (*jemanden vor der Gefahr warnen*). **der** here is the dative feminine article (“the”), e.g. *die Disko* → *vor der Disko*.
target_language_example: Bitte warne mich vor der Gefahr.
native_language_example: Please warn me about the danger.

meaning: to wait for someone in front of the school.
additional_notes: Used with the verb **warten**: **vor der Schule auf jemanden warten**. **vor** + dative indicates location here (standing/being in front of the school), and **auf** + accusative is required with **warten** to say who you’re waiting for (e.g., **auf ihn/sie/euch/Sie**).
target_language_example: Ich warte vor der Schule auf meine Freundin.
native_language_example: I’m waiting for my friend in front of the school.

meaning: in front of the door; (figuratively) just around the corner / about to happen.
additional_notes: Literal: the place immediately outside a door (often used with verbs like stehen, warten). Figurative: used with things like events or time periods to mean they’re coming very soon (e.g., Die Ferien stehen vor der Tür). You’ll often also hear it with draußen: draußen vor der Tür.
target_language_example: Ich warte kurz vor der Tür.
native_language_example: I’ll wait outside the door for a moment.

additional_notes: Used with a past tense to say something happened three years before now. With "vor" + a time period (dative): vor einem Jahr, vor zwei Wochen, vor drei Monaten, etc. You can often place it at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Vor drei Jahren habe ich angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen.
native_language_example: Three years ago, I started learning German.

additional_notes: Used to say when and where something happened: "vor drei Jahren" = "three years ago" and "in" introduces the place (city/country). Word order is flexible, but this pattern is common: time phrase + in + place.
target_language_example: Ich war vor drei Jahren in Berlin.
native_language_example: I was in Berlin three years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a certain amount of time before now. Pattern: „vor + time (dative)“ (e.g., vor einem Jahr, vor zwei Wochen, vor drei Monaten). Often used with the simple past (Präteritum) or present perfect (Perfekt).
target_language_example: Wir sind vor drei Monaten umgezogen.
native_language_example: We moved three months ago.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened three hours before now (or before another reference time). Common with the simple past/perfect: „Ich habe … vor drei Stunden …“. You can place it at the start for emphasis: „Vor drei Stunden habe ich …“.
target_language_example: Wir haben vor drei Stunden gegessen.
native_language_example: We ate three hours ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened 3 days before now (or before another reference point in the sentence). With a specific past event, German often uses simple past ("ging") or present perfect ("habe gelesen"). Pattern: "vor + time period" (vor zwei Wochen, vor einem Jahr).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor drei Tagen zum letzten Mal gesehen.
native_language_example: I last saw him three days ago.

additional_notes: Time expression with **vor + dative** to say how long ago something happened. With plural time units like **Wochen**, the form stays the same in dative: **vor drei Wochen** (not *vor drei Wochens*). You can swap the number: **vor zwei Wochen**, **vor vier Wochen**, etc.
target_language_example: Wir sind vor drei Wochen umgezogen.
native_language_example: We moved three weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used with "vor" + a time expression to say how long ago something happened. Often with past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum): "Ich habe/hatte … vor ein paar Minuten …". Similar patterns: "vor einer Stunde" (an hour ago), "vor zwei Tagen" (two days ago).
target_language_example: Wir haben vor ein paar Minuten angefangen.
native_language_example: We started a few minutes ago.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened a small number of days in the past. It’s a common, neutral time phrase; you can also say "vor ein paar Wochen/Monaten" (a few weeks/months ago). In speech you may also hear "vor ein paar Tage(n)"; standard German is "vor ein paar Tagen" (dative plural after "vor").
target_language_example: Wir haben uns vor ein paar Tagen gesehen.
native_language_example: We saw each other a few days ago.

meaning: a year ago; one year earlier (than now/then).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened exactly one year before a reference point. Often paired with a time word like heute/gestern (e.g., heute vor einem Jahr = “this day a year ago”). Can also be used more loosely to mean “about a year ago.”
target_language_example: Heute vor einem Jahr habe ich meinen neuen Job angefangen.
native_language_example: This day a year ago, I started my new job.

additional_notes: "Vor" is a preposition that usually takes the dative case for location/time. "Vor einer" is used when the following noun is feminine (e.g., *vor einer Minute*, *vor einer Prüfung*, *vor einer schwierigen Entscheidung*). With time expressions it often means "ago" (*vor einer Weile* = "a while ago"). With events it can mean "before" (*vor einer Prüfung* = "before an exam"). With objects/situations it can mean "in front of" or "facing" (*vor einer Entscheidung stehen* = "to be facing a decision").
target_language_example: Ich war vor einer Stunde schon zu Hause.
native_language_example: I was already at home an hour ago.

additional_notes: Used with the dative after "vor" to say how long before now something happened. Often goes with past tense (Perfekt/Präteritum) and can come at the beginning or in the middle of the sentence.
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor einer Stunde gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him an hour ago.

meaning: a week ago (one week before now/then).
additional_notes: Used with a time point in the past to say something happened one week earlier. Often with the simple past (Präteritum) or present perfect (Perfekt): „Ich habe … vor einer Woche …“. Also used with due dates/expected events: „Es war vor einer Woche fällig“ = it was due a week ago.
target_language_example: Wir sind vor einer Woche nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: We moved to Berlin a week ago.

additional_notes: Used with past events to say something happened 30 minutes earlier. Often answers the question "Wann?" (When?) and is placed like a time expression: "Er ist vor einer halben Stunde gegangen." You can change the amount of time: "vor einer Stunde" (an hour ago), "vor zwei Stunden" (two hours ago).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihn vor einer halben Stunde gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him half an hour ago.

additional_notes: Used with a time unit in the dative plural (e.g., vor einigen Tagen/Wochen/Monaten/Jahren) to say something happened a short time ago. Often translated as “a few” or “some” in English.
target_language_example: Wir sind vor einigen Tagen nach Berlin gefahren.
native_language_example: We went to Berlin a few days ago.

additional_notes: Time expression for something that happened in the past. Uses dative plural after "vor": "vor einigen Jahren" (not *vor einige Jahre*). Often used with past tense (Perfekt or Präteritum).
target_language_example: Vor einigen Jahren habe ich in Berlin gearbeitet.
native_language_example: A few years ago, I worked in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened a few days in the past. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence (then the verb comes second: "Vor einigen Tagen habe ich ...") or later in the sentence ("... ist vor einigen Tagen passiert").
target_language_example: Vor einigen Tagen habe ich ihn in der Stadt gesehen.
native_language_example: I saw him in town a few days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long before now something happened. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis ("Vor fünf Jahren ..."), or after the verb ("... ist vor fünf Jahren ..."). In questions it can show surprise or ask for confirmation ("Vor fünf Jahren?").
target_language_example: Vor fünf Jahren bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: Five years ago I moved to Berlin.

meaning: 'in front of my house' (outside, on the street side).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "vor" (in front of) with the dative: "vor" + dative answers "where?" (location), e.g. "vor meinem Haus". For motion to a place, German often uses accusative: "vor mein Haus" (rare in everyday speech here; more common: "vor mein Haus" = to in front of my house). You can swap "meinem" for other possessives: "vor deinem Haus", "vor ihrem Haus".
target_language_example: Wir treffen uns um acht vor meinem Haus.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at eight in front of my house.

meaning: in front of me; ahead of me; (hidden) from me.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “before me.” Used for physical position (“Tom steht direkt vor mir.” = right in front of me), for things that are coming up in time/tasks (“Ich habe eine lange Fahrt vor mir.” = I have a long drive ahead of me), and with verbs like „verstecken“ to mean keeping something from you (“etwas vor mir verstecken”). Note: „vor“ can look like English “for,” but it means “before/in front of.”
target_language_example: Ich habe heute noch viel Arbeit vor mir.
native_language_example: I still have a lot of work ahead of me today.

additional_notes: Comes from the verb phrase „vor sich gehen“ (= to happen, to be going on). Very common in the question „Was geht (da/dort/hier) vor sich?“ meaning “What’s going on (there/here)?” Often used when someone wants to find out what is happening, especially something unusual.
target_language_example: Ich will wissen, was hier vor sich geht.
native_language_example: I want to know what’s going on here.

meaning: to oneself; quietly/absentmindedly (often for a while).
additional_notes: Used to show that someone is doing something on their own, not for others and often without much attention (e.g., humming/whistling, daydreaming). It can also describe something continuing for some time in a low-key way (e.g., coughing/sneezing). Common with verbs like „summen“, „pfeifen“, „träumen“, „niesen“, „husten“.
target_language_example: Er murmelte vor sich hin und suchte seine Schlüssel.
native_language_example: He mumbled to himself while looking for his keys.

additional_notes: Used with a past event to say how long ago it happened. Pattern: „vor + time period (dative)“ (e.g., vor einer Woche, vor zwei Monaten, vor sieben Jahren).
target_language_example: Ich bin vor sieben Jahren nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: I moved to Berlin seven years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened ten years before now (or before another reference point in the sentence). Often used for comparisons with the present: „… wie vor zehn Jahren“ = “…than ten years ago.”
target_language_example: Ich habe vor zehn Jahren in Berlin studiert.
native_language_example: I studied in Berlin ten years ago.

meaning: 'was ten years ago' / 'used to be ten years ago'.
additional_notes: Used to compare the present with a past state. Pattern: **vor + time period (dative) + war**. Common with comparisons like **nicht mehr das, was ... war** (“no longer what it was”) or **anders, als ... war** (“different than it was”). You can swap **zehn** for other numbers: **vor fünf Jahren war**, **vor zwei Jahren war**, etc.
target_language_example: Mein Leben ist nicht mehr so, wie es vor zehn Jahren war.
native_language_example: My life is not the way it was ten years ago.

meaning: "two ... ago" or "before two ..." (depending on what follows).
additional_notes:
Uses **vor + dative**. 
- With a **time period** (e.g., *vor zwei Monaten / vor zwei Tagen*), it means **two months/days ago**.
- With a **clock time** (e.g., *vor zwei Uhr dreißig*), it means **before 2:30**.
- With certain verbs/nouns like **Angst haben vor** (e.g., *vor zwei Sachen*), it means **afraid of two things** (not time-related).
target_language_example: Wir sind vor zwei Tagen angekommen.
native_language_example: We arrived two days ago.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. It’s built with **vor + time period** (e.g., *vor einem Jahr* = a year ago, *vor drei Tagen* = three days ago). The noun is in the dative after **vor** (*vor zwei Jahren*, not *vor zwei Jahre*).
target_language_example: Vor zwei Jahren bin ich nach Berlin gezogen.
native_language_example: Two years ago I moved to Berlin.

additional_notes: Used with the past tense to say something happened two days before now. It can appear at the start of the sentence for emphasis ("Vor zwei Tagen ...") or later in the sentence ("... vor zwei Tagen"). Related patterns: "vor einem Tag" (one day ago), "vor drei Wochen" (three weeks ago).
target_language_example: Vor zwei Tagen habe ich meinen Schlüssel verloren.
native_language_example: Two days ago I lost my key.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened two weeks before now (a point in the past). With other time amounts: vor drei Tagen (three days ago), vor einem Jahr (a year ago).
target_language_example: Wir haben uns vor zwei Wochen zum ersten Mal getroffen.
native_language_example: We met for the first time two weeks ago.

additional_notes: Used to say that something sometimes (or rarely/often) happens. Very often you’ll add an adverb like **selten** (rarely), **oft** (often), **manchmal** (sometimes): *Es kommt selten vor, dass …* = “It rarely happens that …”. The verb **vorkommen** is separable: *Es kommt … vor* + **dass**-clause.
target_language_example: Es kommt manchmal vor, dass ich den Schlüssel vergesse.
native_language_example: It sometimes happens that I forget the key.

meaning: to be careful; to be cautious.
additional_notes: Used to warn someone or to remind yourself to avoid danger or mistakes. Often with "bei" + noun (e.g., "beim Autofahren") or with "wenn" (when) / "damit" (so that) clauses. You can also specify what to be careful about with "vorsichtig sein, was ...".
target_language_example: Sei bitte vorsichtig, wenn du nachts nach Hause gehst.
native_language_example: Please be careful when you go home at night.

meaning: to be more careful; to be more cautious.
additional_notes: Used to advise or warn someone to use more care. Often appears with modal verbs like "sollen" or "müssen": "Du solltest vorsichtiger sein" (You should be more careful), "Er muss vorsichtiger sein" (He has to be more careful). "vorsichtiger" is the comparative of "vorsichtig" (careful).
target_language_example: Sei bitte vorsichtiger, wenn du die Straße überquerst.
native_language_example: Please be more careful when you cross the street.

meaning: “(to have) completely lost your mind” (said to someone: “Are you crazy?!”).
additional_notes: Used as a sharp, often rhetorical question to show shock, anger, or disbelief at what someone is doing or suggesting. It can sound quite rude or aggressive. Often appears with a pronoun/auxiliary: „Hast du völlig den Verstand verloren?“ / „Haben Sie völlig den Verstand verloren?“ (formal).
target_language_example: Willst du ohne Helm Motorrad fahren? Hast du völlig den Verstand verloren?
native_language_example: You want to ride a motorcycle without a helmet? Have you completely lost your mind?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive construction: „(zu) bleiben“ = “to stay/remain.” Very common after „versuchen“ (to try) and especially after „um … zu …“ to express purpose: „Ich trinke Kaffee, um wach zu bleiben.“ (“I drink coffee to stay awake.”).
target_language_example: Ich muss heute Abend wach bleiben, um zu lernen.
native_language_example: I have to stay awake tonight to study.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an ideal, deep, genuine kind of love (often in romantic stories). You can use it as a noun phrase ("wahre Liebe") or with "Das nennt man …" (= "That’s what you call …").
target_language_example: Sie glaubt an wahre Liebe.
native_language_example: She believes in true love.

additional_notes: Used with the pattern **jemanden dazu zwingen, etwas zu tun** = “to force someone to do something.” **dazu** points forward to the **zu + infinitive** action (often explicitly stated: *dazu zwingen, das zu tun*). Word order: modal/auxiliary + adverb (*wahrscheinlich*) + **dazu zwingen**.
target_language_example: Sie könnten ihn wahrscheinlich dazu zwingen, die Wahrheit zu sagen.
native_language_example: They could probably force him to tell the truth.

additional_notes: Used with another verb (often in invitations/plans) to say you’re going hiking: z. B. „Hast du vor, …?“ (Do you plan to…?) or „Hättest du Lust, …?“ (Would you like to…?). „wandern“ means hiking (walking in nature), not just wandering around aimlessly.
target_language_example: Hast du Lust, am Samstag wandern zu gehen?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going hiking on Saturday?

meaning: “when did you…?” / “when were you…?” (asking about a past time).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time or on what date something happened, often with the Perfekt (past) tense: "Wann bist du … gewesen/gegangen/gekommen/aufgestanden?". With verbs that use "haben" in the past, you’ll say "Wann hast du …?" instead (e.g., "Wann hast du das gemacht?").
target_language_example: Wann bist du gestern nach Hause gekommen?
native_language_example: When did you come home yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time/date someone arrived in or moved to a place. It’s typically followed by a city/country and a verb like **gekommen** (came/arrived), **gezogen** (moved), or **gefahren** (went/traveled). **nach** is used with most cities and countries (e.g., *nach Berlin, nach Australien*).
target_language_example: Wann bist du nach Berlin gezogen?
native_language_example: When did you move to Berlin?

additional_notes: Used to ask for departure time in timetables and public transport. It’s normally followed by a masculine noun like der Bus / der Zug, or you add the noun right after: „Wann fährt der Bus/Zug?“ Often paired with „ab“: „Wann fährt der Bus ab?“
target_language_example: Entschuldigung, wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin ab?
native_language_example: Excuse me, when does the train to Berlin leave?

meaning: 'when do you go / leave' (when are you going to...).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time/date someone is going somewhere or doing an activity with gehen + a destination or activity (e.g., nach Hause, zur Schule, ins Bett, mit jemandem essen). Very common in everyday planning. For a more formal/polite version (e.g., to strangers), use „Wann gehen Sie ...?“.
target_language_example: Wann gehst du heute nach Hause?
native_language_example: When are you going home today?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a past action in the polite/formal form ("Sie"). It’s typically followed by a past participle (Perfekt), e.g. "Wann haben Sie angefangen?" / "Wann haben Sie es gekauft?" In spoken German this is a very common way to ask "when did you…?"
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal Ihren Arzt gesehen?
native_language_example: When did you last see your doctor?

additional_notes: A polite/formal question using "Sie" to ask when someone began doing something. Often followed by an infinitive with "zu" (e.g., "angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen") or a main clause alone ("Wann haben Sie angefangen?").
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie angefangen, Deutsch zu lernen?
native_language_example: When did you start learning German?

wann haben Sie das letzte Mal

target_language_multi_word_term: wann haben Sie das letzte Mal
additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. It’s a formal/polite question with “Sie” (used with strangers, in service situations, interviews, etc.). The verb usually goes at the end of the clause: „Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal … gemacht/gekauft/gehört?“
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal Urlaub gemacht?
native_language_example: When was the last time you took a vacation?

target_language_multi_word_term: wann haben Sie das letzte Mal
additional_notes:
Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. Very common in conversation and interviews. After this phrase you typically use a verb in the past: 
- Perfekt: „Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal … gemacht/gegessen/getragen?“
- Or simple past for some verbs: „Wann waren Sie das letzte Mal …?“ (e.g., „Wann waren Sie das letzte Mal im Kino?“). 
Note the spelling: „das letzte Mal“ (two words; „Mal“ is capitalized).
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie das letzte Mal Deutsch gesprochen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you spoke German?

meaning: “When did you …?” (formal), often with a reflexive verb (“… yourself”).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the time of a past action in the Perfekt: **Wann haben Sie …?** The **Sie** is the polite/formal “you.” The **sich** appears with reflexive verbs (e.g., **sich rasieren** = to shave, **sich streiten** = to argue, **sich etw. zulegen** = to get/buy oneself something). Word order typically continues with the rest of the verb phrase and any objects: **Wann haben Sie sich das letzte Mal rasiert?**
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie sich entschieden, Deutsch zu lernen?
native_language_example: When did you decide to learn German?

meaning: 'when did you (all) ...?' (asking about time in the past).
additional_notes: Used to ask when something happened, addressing a group ("ihr" = you all) or using informal plural "you". Often followed by the Perfekt: "habt" + past participle (e.g., "Wann habt ihr es gemerkt?"). It can also be used with an infinitive phrase after a verb like "anfangen": "Wann habt ihr angefangen, ... zu ...?"
target_language_example: Wann habt ihr die Tickets gekauft?
native_language_example: When did you (all) buy the tickets?

target_language_multi_word_term: wann habt ihr das letzte Mal
additional_notes: Used to ask when something last happened. It’s typically followed by a past participle at the end of the clause (Perfekt): „Wann habt ihr das letzte Mal … gegessen/geschlafen/geschrieben?“ „ihr“ is informal plural “you” (addressing two or more people you’re on du-terms with). Note: correct spelling is usually „das letzte Mal“ (two words).
target_language_example: Wann habt ihr das letzte Mal im Kino einen Film gesehen?
native_language_example: When was the last time you went to the movies and saw a film?
