Also used with nouns: „zu viel Kaffee“ (too much coffee), „zu viele Leute“ (too many people). „zu viel“ for singular/uncountable; „zu viele“ for plural countable nouns.
target_language_example: Ich esse heute zu viel.
native_language_example: I'm eating too much today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is more than is wanted or acceptable. With verbs like reden/fragen/wissen, it means doing/knowing it excessively (e.g., „Du redest zu viel“ = you talk too much). Also used with nouns: „zu viel Kaffee“ (too much coffee), „zu viele Leute“ (too many people). „zu viel“ for singular/uncountable; „zu viele“ for plural countable nouns.
target_language_example: Ich esse heute zu viel.
native_language_example: I'm eating too much today.

additional_notes: Used with the separable verb **ausgeben** (to spend). In a normal sentence, the prefix **aus** goes to the end: **Er gibt zu viel Geld aus.** In infinitive form it stays together: **zu viel Geld ausgeben**. Commonly used to criticize or worry about spending.
target_language_example: Wir dürfen diesen Monat nicht zu viel Geld ausgeben.
native_language_example: We mustn't spend too much money this month.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone spends an excessive amount of time doing something. Very often used with verbs like **(Zeit) verbringen** (to spend time) or **zubringen** (to spend time). Common patterns: **zu viel Zeit mit + Dativ** (with an activity), **zu viel Zeit damit** (doing it), and **zu viel Zeit vor + Dativ** (in front of something, e.g., the TV).
target_language_example: Ich verbringe zu viel Zeit am Handy.
native_language_example: I spend too much time on my phone.

additional_notes: Used when something is more than someone can handle (physically, emotionally, mentally) or more than is reasonable (e.g., money). Often followed by a person/noun in the dative: „zu viel für mich/ihn/sie/euch“.
target_language_example: Die Aufgabe war zu viel für mich.
native_language_example: The task was too much for me.

additional_notes: Used to say you ate more than was good for you (often meaning you feel too full). Common with the verb "haben" in the perfect tense: "Ich habe zu viel gegessen." You can add a time word like "heute" (today) or "gestern" (yesterday).
target_language_example: Mir ist schlecht – ich habe wohl zu viel gegessen.
native_language_example: I feel sick — I probably ate too much.

meaning: drank too much (alcohol); had too much to drink.
additional_notes: Used to say you overdid drinking alcohol, often implying you feel drunk or unwell. Common with forms of "haben": "Ich habe zu viel getrunken" (I drank too much). Intensifiers are frequent: "ein bisschen zu viel" (a bit too much), "viel zu viel" (far too much).
target_language_example: Sorry, ich habe gestern zu viel getrunken.
native_language_example: Sorry, I drank too much yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with plural nouns to say there is an excessive number of something. The ending changes with gender/case: e.g., nominative/accusative plural often "zu viele" (zu viele Freunde), but dative plural "zu vielen" (mit zu vielen Leuten). Common in set phrases like "Mach dir nicht zu viele Gedanken/Sorgen/Hoffnungen" (“Don’t worry/think/hope too much”).
target_language_example: Wir haben zu viele Termine diese Woche.
native_language_example: We have too many appointments this week.

additional_notes: Used with the perfect tense: (jemand) hat/haben … Fehler gemacht (“someone has made … mistakes”). Often said as a criticism or regret about an outcome. "zu viele" means “too many”; "Fehler" are “mistakes/errors” (not “failures”).
target_language_example: Ich habe zu viele Fehler gemacht und muss es noch einmal versuchen.
native_language_example: I made too many mistakes and have to try again.

additional_notes: Used when someone is asking more questions than you want/expect. Very commonly used with the verb phrase „Fragen stellen“ (to ask questions): „Du stellst zu viele Fragen.“ The word „zu“ means “too” (as in “too much/many”), and comes before the adjective/quantity word: „zu viele“, „zu laut“, „zu spät“.
target_language_example: Bitte stell mir nicht zu viele Fragen.
native_language_example: Please don’t ask me too many questions.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like „gehen“ and „treiben“ to say someone has crossed a line: „Das geht zu weit“ = “That goes too far.” In „Es würde zu weit führen …“, it means “that would take us too far” (it would be too much detail / go beyond the scope).
target_language_example: Dein Witz ging mir wirklich zu weit.
native_language_example: Your joke really went too far for me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has crossed a boundary—by what they said or did (often figuratively, not literally walking too far). It’s the perfect tense of **gehen**: *jemand ist zu weit gegangen*. Can be addressed formally (*Sie sind…*) or informally/plural (*Ihr seid…*).
target_language_example: Mit diesem Kommentar bist du zu weit gegangen.
native_language_example: You went too far with that comment.

meaning: Used when a separable verb ends with „… zu“ and is followed by a „dass“ clause (“that …”).
additional_notes:
In many common separable verbs, „zu“ is the verb prefix that goes to the end of the clause (e.g. „zugeben“, „zustimmen“, „zusehen“). If the sentence continues with „dass …“, it introduces a subordinate clause (“that …”):
- „Ich stimme (euch) zu, dass …“ = “I agree (with you) that …”
- „Sie gaben zu, dass …“ = “They admitted that …”
- „(Sieh/Seht) zu, dass …“ = “Make sure that …” / “See to it that …”
Also, in sentences like „Er schlug die Tür so fest zu, dass …“, the „zu“ is the separated prefix of „zuschlagen“ and the pattern „so … dass …“ means “so … that …”.
target_language_example: Sieh zu, dass du morgen pünktlich bist.
native_language_example: Make sure you’re on time tomorrow.

meaning: to watch (someone/something) as they do something.
additional_notes: Common with "wie" to describe an action you observe in progress: "Ich sah zu, wie …" (I watched as …). "zusehen" often takes the dative for the person/thing you’re watching: "Ich sehe ihm/ihr zu" (I’m watching him/her). You may also see "dabei": "Wir sahen einem Vogel dabei zu, wie …" = we watched a bird as it … . Not to be confused with "zubereiten" in sentence 2 ("to prepare/cook").
target_language_example: Wir sahen zu, wie die Kinder im Schnee spielten.
native_language_example: We watched as the children played in the snow.

additional_notes: Used as a “zu”-infinitive clause (“to …”) after many verbs and adjectives, often to express habits, plans, or necessity. Example pattern: „Ich bin es gewohnt, … zu arbeiten“ = “I’m used to working …”. The “zu” stays directly in front of the infinitive: „viel zu arbeiten“ (“to work a lot”).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, mehr zu arbeiten.
native_language_example: I’m trying to work more.

additional_notes: Used when the verb is in the infinitive with „zu“ (often after another verb), e.g. after helping/trying/starting/asking: „Er hat uns geholfen, … zu bauen.“ With separable verbs, „zu“ goes between prefix and verb stem (e.g. „aufzubauen“).
target_language_example: Wir versuchen, eine kleine Brücke zu bauen.
native_language_example: We’re trying to build a small bridge.

additional_notes: Infinitive with „zu“, often used with adjectives like „schwer/leicht zu beantworten“ (= hard/easy to answer) or after another verb: „sich weigern, … zu beantworten“ (= refuse to answer), „versuchen, … zu beantworten“ (= try to answer). Usually used with questions („eine Frage zu beantworten“), but can also mean answering a knock/doorbell.
target_language_example: Ich kann diese Frage gerade nicht beantworten.
native_language_example: I can't answer this question right now.

meaning: to finish; to end (to bring something to an end).
additional_notes: This is the verb "beenden" used with "zu" (the "zu"-infinitive). It often follows another verb like "versuchen" (try), "sich bemühen" (make an effort), "Zeit haben" (have time), "darauf bestehen" (insist), or fixed phrases like "Es wird Zeit, ..." (It’s time to ...). It usually takes an object: "die Arbeit / das Spiel / den Krieg zu beenden".
target_language_example: Wir müssen das Gespräch jetzt zu beenden.
native_language_example: We need to end the conversation now.

additional_notes: "zu beruhigen" is the infinitive with "zu" (often used after verbs like versuchen/es gelingt, or with um … zu). Common patterns: "jemanden zu beruhigen" = to calm someone down; "sich zu beruhigen" = to calm yourself down. In commands you usually drop "zu": "Beruhigen Sie sich!" / "Beruhigt euch!"
target_language_example: Ich versuche, dich zu beruhigen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to calm you down.

additional_notes: "zu besuchen" is the infinitive "besuchen" with "zu" (often used after verbs like "vorhaben" = to plan, "bitten" = to ask, or in phrases like "der Wunsch, ..." / "das Ziel war es, ..."). "besuchen" is used for visiting people ("Oma besuchen", "Sie besuchen") and also for attending events or places ("eine Besprechung besuchen" = attend a meeting).
target_language_example: Ich plane, meine Freunde am Wochenende zu besuchen.
native_language_example: I’m planning to visit my friends this weekend.

meaning: to move; to persuade/encourage (someone) to do something.
additional_notes: “zu bewegen” is the infinitive form used after many verbs/adjectives (e.g., „ohne … zu bewegen“, „zu überrascht, um mich zu bewegen“). With „dazu … zu bewegen“ it means “to get someone to do something / to persuade someone to do something.”
target_language_example: Ich konnte ihn dazu bewegen, früher nach Hause zu gehen.
native_language_example: I managed to persuade him to go home earlier.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive "bezahlen" used with "zu" (often like English “to pay”), commonly after another verb (e.g., "bitten", "denken", "brauchen") or to express purpose with "um ... zu" (“in order to pay”). It can also show necessity/obligation, especially with "sein" (e.g., "Die Rechnung ist zu bezahlen" = “The bill has to be paid”).
target_language_example: Ich habe kein Geld, um die Rechnung zu bezahlen.
native_language_example: I don’t have any money to pay the bill.

meaning: to stay; to remain (in order to…).
additional_notes: "Zu bleiben" is the infinitive "bleiben" used with "zu" after certain verbs (e.g., beschließen, sich entscheiden, gedenken, bitten, überreden) or in purpose phrases with "um ... zu". It refers to continuing to be in a place or state: "zu Hause zu bleiben" (to stay at home), "am Leben zu bleiben" (to stay alive).
target_language_example: Ich habe beschlossen, noch ein paar Tage zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I decided to stay a few more days.

meaning: to bring (to), or to cause someone/something to become/do something.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to express purpose/result. Common patterns: (1) jemanden/etwas irgendwohin bringen = to take/bring someone/something somewhere (often like “to drive/escort”). (2) jemanden zum Lachen/Weinen bringen = to make someone laugh/cry. (3) etwas zu Ende bringen = to finish something. Often combines with "zu" + noun: zum (= zu dem), zur (= zu der).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich zum Bahnhof bringen?
native_language_example: Can you take me to the train station?

additional_notes: Used as the infinitive form after certain verbs/expressions (like “versuchen”, “aufhören”, “dazu bringen”) and often with an extra word that specifies *how/what* you think: **an jdn/etw. denken** = to think of/about someone/something; **logisch denken** = to think logically; **so denken** = to think that way; **dazu gebracht, so zu denken** = made you think that way.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, positiv zu denken.
native_language_example: I’m trying to think positively.

additional_notes: Usually used with the reflexive verb: **sich entschuldigen** = “to apologize.” Common patterns: **Denk daran, dich zu entschuldigen!** (“Remember to apologize!”) and **Ich muss dich/euch bitten, mich zu entschuldigen.** (“I have to ask you to excuse me.” = “Sorry, I have to go / interrupt”). In polite/formal contexts you may see **sich zu entschuldigen** with **Sie**.
target_language_example: Ich habe vergessen anzurufen—ich bitte dich, mich zu entschuldigen.
native_language_example: I forgot to call—please excuse me.

additional_notes: "Zu erfahren" is the infinitive with "zu" (a common structure after certain verbs/adjectives/nouns), meaning “to find out/learn.” It often refers to getting new information (sometimes surprising). Typical patterns: "es zu erfahren" = “to find it out,” "das zu erfahren" = “to learn that.” Base verb: "erfahren" (past: "erfuhr", participle: "erfahren").
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, bald mehr darüber zu erfahren.
native_language_example: I hope to find out more about it soon.

additional_notes: Often used with "sein" or "geben" to say whether there is anything that needs explaining: "Es gibt nichts zu erklären" = "There’s nothing to explain." It can also follow a noun to mean "to explain" that noun: "einen Weg, es zu erklären" = "a way to explain it."
target_language_example: Ich habe dir noch etwas zu erklären.
native_language_example: I still have something to explain to you.

meaning: 'to do' / 'to take care of' (something that needs to be done).
additional_notes: Used with "haben" or "es gibt" to say there are tasks still pending: "Ich habe noch ... zu erledigen" = "I still have ... to do." Common with words like "viel", "einiges", "etwas", "was". Often implies finishing/handling a task (e.g., errands, paperwork, homework).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute noch ein paar Dinge zu erledigen.
native_language_example: I still have a few things to do today.

meaning: to reach; to get to; (someone) to contact.
additional_notes: Infinitive form used after many verbs (e.g., versuchen, sich bemühen) and in purpose phrases with „um … zu …“. It can mean reaching a place/thing (e.g., a train, a house, a goal) or reaching someone by phone/message („jemanden erreichen“). In negative form it often means “unreachable / cannot be accessed” („nicht zu erreichen“).
target_language_example: Kannst du den Kunden heute noch zu erreichen versuchen?
native_language_example: Can you try to reach/contact the customer today?

meaning: “to tell” / “to narrate” (used as an infinitive, often “to tell (someone) about (something)”).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive form of **erzählen** used with **zu** (like “to” in English), often after verbs/phrases such as **brauchen** (need), **Zeit erfordern** (require time), or **jemanden dazu bringen** (get someone to). Common patterns: **(jemandem) etwas erzählen** = tell (someone) something; **(jemandem) von etwas erzählen / davon erzählen** = tell (someone) about something; **die Geschichte erzählen** = tell the story.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir erzählen, was passiert ist?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what happened?

additional_notes: Used with the infinitive + zu ("zu" + "essen") after certain verbs or in purpose clauses: "aufhören zu essen" = "to stop eating", "um zu essen" = "in order to eat". It can also be used like a noun phrase meaning "something to eat" (often with words like "nichts", "etwas", "genug"): "nichts zu essen" = "nothing to eat".
target_language_example: Hast du etwas zu essen dabei?
native_language_example: Do you have something to eat with you?

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase „jemandem etwas zu essen geben“ (= to give someone something to eat). „zu essen“ means “to eat” (as in “something to eat”), and „gegeben“ is the past participle of „geben“ (to give), often used in the Perfekt tense: „Ich habe … gegeben.“
target_language_example: Der Arzt hat mir nach der Untersuchung etwas zu essen gegeben.
native_language_example: The doctor gave me something to eat after the examination.

meaning: 'to travel/drive (by vehicle)' in a 'zu + infinitive' structure.
additional_notes: Used when the verb *fahren* is in the infinitive with **zu** (often after verbs like *planen, vorhaben, daran denken, träumen*, or expressions like *es wäre sicherer*). It can mean going by car/train/ship, etc., depending on context (*mit dem Zug zu fahren* = to go by train). Also used with activities like *Ski zu fahren* (“to ski”).
target_language_example: Ich habe vor, morgen früh nach Berlin zu fahren.
native_language_example: I intend to travel to Berlin tomorrow morning.

meaning: “to find” (infinitive with “zu”; often “in order to find”).
additional_notes: "Zu" + infinitive is used after many verbs to express an action as a goal, plan, or result. With "finden", it often means “to find” or “to manage/succeed in finding.” Common patterns: "um ... zu finden" = “in order to find”; "es gelingt jemandem, ... zu finden" = “someone manages to find ...”; "hoffen, jemanden zu finden" = “hope to find someone.”
target_language_example: Wir müssen einen Parkplatz zu finden versuchen.
native_language_example: We have to try to find a parking space.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive with „zu“, often used after certain verbs or expressions: „vergessen, jemanden zu fragen“ (to forget to ask someone), „sich die Mühe machen, zu fragen“ (to make the effort to ask). You’ll also commonly see „um + Akk. + zu fragen“ when asking for something: „um Erlaubnis zu fragen“ (to ask for permission), „um Rat zu fragen“ (to ask for advice).
target_language_example: Ich muss dich noch etwas zu fragen.
native_language_example: I still need to ask you something.

meaning: (for animals) to eat; used in “jemandem/etwas zu fressen geben” = to feed an animal.
additional_notes: “Fressen” is the verb for animals eating. With “zu” it’s commonly used after verbs like “geben/kaufen”: “der Katze zu fressen geben” (give the cat food) or “etwas zu fressen kaufen” (buy food for an animal). For people you usually use “essen”; saying a person “frisst” can sound rude/insulting.
target_language_example: Kannst du dem Hund bitte zu fressen geben?
native_language_example: Can you please feed the dog?

meaning: “to give” (infinitive with zu, like English “to give”).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions like versprechen (to promise), versuchen (to try), sich weigern (to refuse), or um … zu (in order to): jemanden/etwas zu geben. Often takes a dative person + accusative thing: jemandem (to someone) + etwas (something), e.g., „mir einen Ratschlag zu geben“. Common set phrases include „jemandem die Hand geben“ (to shake/give someone your hand). Note: „sich … geben“ means “to act/behave (in a certain way)”, e.g., „sich natürlich geben“ = “to act natural.”
target_language_example: Ich habe versucht, dir ein gutes Gefühl zu geben.
native_language_example: I tried to make you feel good (to give you a good feeling).

meaning: 'to go' (infinitive with 'zu', often like English 'to go').
additional_notes: Used when a verb is followed by an infinitive clause: e.g., vorhaben/versuchen/entscheiden/bitten + zu + infinitive ("Er versucht zu gehen."). With movement activities it often means “to go and do something”: "angeln zu gehen" = “to go fishing”. In "besser zu gehen", "gehen" can mean “to be doing/feeling” ("Es geht mir besser" = “I’m doing better”).
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, heute Abend zu gehen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to go tonight.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive form used after another verb (often showing a goal or plan): "versuchen, zu gewinnen" (to try to win), "um ... zu gewinnen" (in order to win). With "Zeit" it commonly means "to gain time": "Zeit zu gewinnen".
target_language_example: Wir hoffen, morgen zu gewinnen.
native_language_example: We hope to win tomorrow.

additional_notes: Infinitive with „zu“, used after many verbs/adjectives (e.g., „Es war dumm, ihm zu glauben.“ = “It was stupid to believe him.”). With people, „glauben“ often takes the dative: „jemandem glauben“ = “to believe someone.” With ideas/things, you often use „an“ + accusative: „an etwas glauben“ = “to believe in something.” The exclamation „Nicht zu glauben!“ means “Unbelievable!” / “Hard to believe!”
target_language_example: Ich kann nicht glauben, was ich gerade gehört habe.
native_language_example: I can’t believe what I just heard.

additional_notes: Used when a verb like (einen Grund haben / sich weigern / scheinen / veranlassen) is followed by an infinitive + object clause: „… zu glauben, dass …“. Often expresses belief, assumption, or (un)willingness to accept something as true. You’ll also see it in set phrases like „Kaum zu glauben, dass …“ = “Hard to believe that …”.
target_language_example: Ich finde es schwer zu glauben, dass er schon fertig ist.
native_language_example: I find it hard to believe that he’s already finished.

meaning: “to have” (used in the perfect infinitive: “… to have done”).
additional_notes: Often appears as part of the *Perfektinfinitiv* (perfect infinitive): **Partizip II + zu haben**. It’s used after verbs like *glauben, scheinen, behaupten, vergessen, sich erinnern* to say that something happened **before** the main verb: *Er scheint es nicht gewusst zu haben* = “He seems not to have known (it).”
target_language_example: Ich bereue, das nicht früher gesagt zu haben.
native_language_example: I regret not having said that earlier.

meaning: to hold; to keep (something in a certain state).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive of **halten** used with **zu** (roughly “to …”) after many verbs and expressions. It often means **to keep** something going/secret/separate/under control, e.g. **warm zu halten** (keep warm), **geheim zu halten** (keep secret), **getrennt zu halten** (keep separate), **im Zaum zu halten** (keep under control). It can also mean **to give** in set phrases like **eine Rede zu halten** (to give a speech).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, das Fenster geschlossen zu halten.
native_language_example: I’m trying to keep the window closed.

additional_notes: "zu heiraten" is the infinitive "heiraten" used with "zu" after many verbs and expressions (e.g., vorhaben, beschließen, sich entscheiden, überzeugt sein, zu jung sein), similar to English "to" + verb: "Er hat vor, sie zu heiraten" = "He plans to marry her." Often used when talking about plans/decisions or being too young/old to marry.
target_language_example: Ich habe beschlossen, nächstes Jahr zu heiraten.
native_language_example: I decided to get married next year.

additional_notes: “zu helfen” is the infinitive form used after many verbs and expressions like “bitten” (to ask), “entschließen” (to decide), “Zeit haben” (to have time), or adjectives like “freundlich” (kind): e.g., „Er war so freundlich, mir zu helfen.“ The verb „helfen“ usually takes the dative: „jemandem helfen“ (to help someone) → „mir/dir/ihm/ihr/uns/euch/ihnen helfen“.
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte helfen, den Tisch zu tragen?
native_language_example: Can you please help me carry the table?

additional_notes: "zu holen" is the "zu"-infinitive of **holen**. It’s used in structures like **um ... zu holen** (“in order to get/fetch ...”) and after certain verbs (e.g., **kommen**, **gehen**) often with **es** referring to something mentioned: **Kommst du, es zu holen?** = “Are you coming to get it?”
target_language_example: Ich gehe schnell nach Hause, um meine Jacke zu holen.
native_language_example: I’m going home quickly to get my jacket.

additional_notes: Infinitive with "zu" used after many verbs/adjectives to express the idea of hearing something: e.g. "glücklich, das zu hören" (happy to hear that), "erstaunt zu hören, dass …" (surprised to hear that). Often appears as "das zu hören" or with a noun phrase like "die Nachricht zu hören".
target_language_example: Ich bin erleichtert, das zu hören.
native_language_example: I'm relieved to hear that.

additional_notes: Usually used in the reflexive pattern **sich für + Akkusativ interessieren**: **Ich interessiere mich für Musik.** = “I’m interested in music.” With other verbs you often see the infinitive with **zu**, e.g. **anfangen, sich für … zu interessieren** (“to start to become interested in …”) or **scheinen, sich für … zu interessieren** (“to seem to be interested in …”).
target_language_example: Ich scheine mich für Deutsch zu interessieren.
native_language_example: I seem to be interested in German.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive clause is needed: many verbs take an extra action with "zu" (e.g., "vergessen, ... zu kaufen" = "to forget to buy ..."). It can also express purpose with "um ... zu" ("um ... zu kaufen" = "in order to buy ...").
target_language_example: Ich muss noch Brot zu kaufen.
native_language_example: I still have to buy bread.

meaning: to come; to arrive (and in some phrases: to get/obtain).
additional_notes: "Zu kommen" is the infinitive form "to come" used after another verb (often with modal verbs like müssen) or in common structures like "um ... zu" (in order to ...) and "es gelingt jdm., ... zu" (someone succeeds in ...). In phrases like "an etw. zu kommen", it means "to get/obtain" something (often after effort).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, morgen pünktlich zu kommen.
native_language_example: I hope to come/arrive on time tomorrow.

meaning: "to be able to" (infinitive form, used in longer sentences).
additional_notes: "Zu können" is the infinitive of the modal verb "können" used with "zu" in infinitive clauses, often when there’s another verb already conjugated in the sentence. Very common patterns: "um ... zu können" = "in order to be able to ..." and verbs like "glauben/behaupten/hoffen/versprechen + ... zu können" = "to believe/claim/hope/promise to be able to ...". The main action verb usually comes at the end: "... kaufen zu können" = "to be able to buy (it)".
target_language_example: Ich lerne jeden Tag Deutsch, um besser sprechen zu können.
native_language_example: I study German every day in order to be able to speak better.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive with „zu“, used after many verbs (like „anfangen“, „verspüren“, „sich fragen“): „Sie fing an, ihn zu küssen.“ With the reflexive pronoun „sich“ it often means “to kiss (each other)” in the plural: „Wir fingen an, uns zu küssen.“
target_language_example: Er hat versucht, sie zu küssen.
native_language_example: He tried to kiss her.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like anfangen/beginnen/aufhören to describe starting, beginning, or stopping the action of laughing: anfangen zu lachen (start laughing), beginnen zu lachen (begin laughing), aufhören zu lachen (stop laughing). Also used after “es gibt … zu …” to mean “there is … to …”: Was gibt es (noch) zu lachen? = “What’s there (left) to laugh about?”
target_language_example: Als er das gehört hat, fing er an zu lachen.
native_language_example: When he heard that, he started to laugh.

meaning: to let / allow (someone do something); to leave (something as it is).
additional_notes: Used as the infinitive of **lassen** with **zu**. Very common in the pattern **jemanden + (etwas) + Verb (Infinitiv) + lassen** = “to let/allow someone (to) do something” (e.g., *ihn abschreiben lassen* = “let him copy”). It can also mean “to leave” in expressions like **etwas so lassen** = “leave it like that / keep it as it is.” Often appears inside longer phrases: *etw. verlauten lassen* (“let something be known”), *sich etw. anmerken lassen* (“let something show / give something away”).
target_language_example: Kannst du mich bitte kurz in Ruhe zu Ende sprechen lassen?
native_language_example: Can you please let me finish speaking in peace for a moment?

meaning: to run; to walk (to a place)
additional_notes: "zu" + infinitive is used after many verbs/adjectives to mean "to" + verb in English (e.g., hassen/lieben, genug, brauchen). With distances (e.g., einen Marathon, 10.000 Meter) it usually means "to run". With destinations and "um ..." + time (e.g., zur Schule, eine halbe Stunde) it often means "to walk" (go on foot).
target_language_example: Ich brauche zwanzig Minuten, um nach Hause zu laufen.
native_language_example: I need twenty minutes to walk home.

additional_notes: “Zu leben” is the infinitive “leben” used with “zu” (“to”)—often after certain verbs (e.g., jemanden motivieren/bitten/hoffen, … zu leben) or after expressions like “in einer Stadt zu leben” (“to live in a city”). A very common pattern is “nur noch [time] zu leben haben”, meaning “to have only [time] left to live.”
target_language_example: Ich versuche, gesünder zu leben.
native_language_example: I’m trying to live more healthily.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like „bitten“ or phrases like „nett von dir/ihm/ihr“ to say someone lends something. Grammar: „jemandem (Dat.) etwas (Akk.) leihen“ = to lend someone something. Related: „ausleihen“ often means “to borrow/check out” (e.g., from a library).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir kurz deinen Stift leihen?
native_language_example: Can you lend me your pen for a moment?

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive is required with *zu*, often after another verb or expression (e.g., *Interesse haben, etwas zu lernen* = “to be interested in learning something”; *es gibt noch viel zu lernen* = “there’s still a lot to learn”). *Zu* is similar to English “to” in “to learn,” but German doesn’t use *zu* with every infinitive (e.g., after modal verbs like *können/müssen/wollen* you usually use the bare infinitive without *zu*).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, jeden Tag neue Wörter zu lernen.
native_language_example: I try to learn new words every day.

meaning: to read (in the “zu + infinitive” form: “to read”).
additional_notes: "Zu lesen" is the infinitive with "zu" and is used after certain verbs and expressions, like "anfangen" (to start), "imstande sein" (to be able), or after nouns like "das Hobby". Word order: the "zu" stays with the verb at the end ("… anzufangen, … zu lesen").
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, heute Abend zu lesen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to read tonight.

additional_notes: Infinitive form used with other verbs/expressions (often with "sein", "versprechen", "fähig", "aufhören") and in longer clauses: e.g., "nicht fähig zu lieben" (not able to love), "aufhören, mich zu lieben" (stop loving me), "versprechen, ihn zu lieben" (promise to love him). It can also be used with "jemanden/etwas" in the accusative: "jemanden zu lieben" (to love someone), "das Leben zu lieben" (to love life).
target_language_example: Ich verspreche, dich immer zu lieben.
native_language_example: I promise to always love you.

additional_notes: Used with another verb (often “versuchen”, “aufhören”, “anfangen”, etc.) to express an action in the infinitive: verb + „zu“ + infinitive. With separable verbs, „zu“ goes in the middle (e.g., „aufhören“ → „aufzuhören“), but with a normal verb like „lächeln“ it stays separate: „zu lächeln“. In negative sentences, „nicht“ usually comes right before the „zu“-infinitive: „nicht zu lächeln“.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, nicht zu lächeln.
native_language_example: I’m trying not to smile.

additional_notes: "Zu lösen" is the infinitive form of "lösen" with "zu" (often like English "to solve"). It commonly appears after adjectives or nouns (e.g., "zu schwierig zu lösen" = "too difficult to solve") and in purpose phrases with "um ... zu" ("um die Aufgabe zu lösen" = "in order to solve the task").
target_language_example: Wir haben nur noch zwei Minuten, um das Problem zu lösen.
native_language_example: We only have two minutes left to solve the problem.

meaning: to lie (to not tell the truth).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive with „zu“ (“to”), used after many verbs and expressions: e.g., „aufhören zu …“ (to stop …-ing), „versprechen, zu …“ (to promise to …), „(keinen) Grund haben, zu …“ ((no) reason to …), „die Neigung haben, zu …“ (to have a tendency to …). In commands you usually use the infinitive without „zu“: „Lüg nicht!“ (“Don’t lie!”).
target_language_example: Ich habe keinen Grund, zu lügen.
native_language_example: I have no reason to lie.

additional_notes: *Zu machen* is the infinitive of **machen** used with **zu** (like English “to …”), often after another verb or an adjective: *Es ist schwierig, das zu machen* (“It’s hard to do that”). Very common combinations include: *Übungen machen* (do exercises), *Fehler machen* (make mistakes), *Besorgungen machen* (run errands), *wahr machen* (make [a dream/plan] come true).
target_language_example: Ich habe heute noch viel zu machen.
native_language_example: I still have a lot to do today.

additional_notes: “zu nehmen” is the infinitive “nehmen” with “zu”, used after many verbs and structures: e.g. “versuchen, … zu nehmen” (to try to take), “raten, … zu nehmen” (to advise to take), “keine andere Wahl, als … zu nehmen” (no other choice than to take), and with purpose clauses “um … zu nehmen” (in order to take/capture). Depending on context it can mean taking transport (“das Flugzeug zu nehmen”), taking medicine (“ein Medikament zu nehmen”), taking/grabbing something (“den Ring an sich zu nehmen”), or capturing someone (“jemanden gefangen zu nehmen”).
target_language_example: Ich versuche, den nächsten Zug zu nehmen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to take the next train.

meaning: to smoke (used as an infinitive, often after another verb).
additional_notes: “zu rauchen” is the infinitive form used after many verbs (e.g., raten/empfehlen/versuchen/aufhören) and in some constructions like “davor warnen, zu …” (to warn someone about doing …). Often used with negation: “nicht zu rauchen” = “not to smoke.” Note: “aufhören zu rauchen” = “to stop smoking.”
target_language_example: Ich versuche, nicht zu rauchen.
native_language_example: I’m trying not to smoke.

additional_notes: “zu reden” is the infinitive “reden” used with “zu”, common after many verbs and phrases (e.g., anfangen, aufhören, versuchen, bereit sein, Zeit haben, jemanden zwingen). Often used with “mit + Dativ” (mit ihr/ihm/Ihnen reden = talk to/with her/him/you) and “über + Akkusativ” (über etwas reden = talk about something). Word order note: in longer verb phrases, “zu” comes right before the infinitive: „wieder anfangen zu reden“.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, mit meiner Schwester über das Problem zu reden.
native_language_example: I'm trying to talk to my sister about the problem.

meaning: to rain (used after another verb, e.g. “to start/stop raining”).
additional_notes: German often uses the infinitive with **zu** after verbs like **beginnen/anfangen** (to start), **aufhören** (to stop), and in patterns like **wenn** (if/when) or **sobald** (as soon as): *Es beginnt/ hört auf zu regnen.* The subject is usually **es** (“it”) when talking about weather.
target_language_example: Es hat aufgehört zu regnen, aber es ist noch kalt.
native_language_example: It stopped raining, but it’s still cold.

additional_notes: "Zu reisen" is the infinitive "reisen" used with "zu" (similar to "to" + verb in English). It commonly follows verbs like "vorschlagen" (to suggest), "ermöglichen" (to enable), "träumen" (to dream), and expressions like "Lust haben" (to feel like), e.g., "Er schlug vor, zusammen zu reisen." It can also be used after adjectives/phrases like "Es ist angenehm, ... zu reisen."
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dieses Jahr nach Deutschland zu reisen.
native_language_example: I hope to travel to Germany this year.

additional_notes: "zu retten" is the infinitive with "zu" ("to save") and is often used after phrases like "versuchen" (to try), "kommen" (to come), or with "um ... zu" (in order to). It can mean saving a person from danger (rescue) or saving something from being lost/ruined (e.g., a marriage, a project).
target_language_example: Wir tun alles, um das Kind zu retten.
native_language_example: We’re doing everything to save the child.

additional_notes: "Zu sagen" is the infinitive "sagen" used with "zu" (similar to "to" + verb in English): "Ich habe vergessen, dir etwas zu sagen" = "I forgot to tell you something." Often used with an object: "etwas zu sagen" (to say something). Common pattern: "(nichts/etwas) zu sagen haben" = to have (nothing/something) to say.
target_language_example: Ich habe dir noch etwas Wichtiges zu sagen.
native_language_example: I still have something important to tell you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or a statement after verbs like sagen (to say/tell): „… zu sagen, dass + clause“. Often appears in purpose phrases with „um … zu sagen, dass …“ = “(in order) to tell (someone) that …”. When you specify a person, use a dative pronoun/noun: „dir/ihm/ihr/Ihnen zu sagen, dass …“.
target_language_example: Ich muss dir sagen, dass ich heute keine Zeit habe.
native_language_example: I have to tell you that I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Common pattern: jemanden (Dat.) sagen, dass er … (= to tell someone that he …). "zu sagen" is the infinitive form, often used after another verb (e.g., bitten, wagen, den Mut haben). The pronoun can change: dass sie/ich/wir …
target_language_example: Ich habe vergessen, ihm zu sagen, dass er seinen Ausweis mitbringen soll.
native_language_example: I forgot to tell him that he should bring his ID.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an infinitive clause with **zu sagen** followed by a **was**-clause that specifies the content of what is said (often what someone thinks/knows). Typically appears after phrases like **das Recht/ die Erlaubnis haben** or **es ist (nicht) erlaubt**, and you usually write a comma before **was**: **… zu sagen, was man denkt**.
target_language_example: Ich habe nicht den Mut, zu sagen, was ich wirklich denke.
native_language_example: I don't have the courage to say what I really think.

meaning: to manage to do it / make it (in time); to have business somewhere.
additional_notes: Common with an object like „es“: „es schaffen“ = to succeed/manage (often about arriving on time or completing a task). In the question „Was hattest du … zu schaffen?“ it’s a fixed use meaning “What were you doing/what business did you have there?” (often suspicious or critical).
target_language_example: Wenn wir uns beeilen, schaffen wir es noch rechtzeitig.
native_language_example: If we hurry, we'll still make it in time.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive of **schließen** used with **zu** (“to …”), often after another verb (e.g. *vergessen*, *daran denken*, *bitten*). Common with doors/windows/gates: *die Tür / das Fenster / die Tore zu schließen* (“to close the door/window/gates”). In fixed phrases like *Freundschaften zu schließen*, it means “to make/form friendships.”
target_language_example: Ich habe vergessen, das Fenster zu schließen.
native_language_example: I forgot to close the window.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive is needed after another verb (often with weather): anfangen/aufhören + zu + infinitive. Snowing is usually expressed impersonally with „es“: „Es schneit.“
target_language_example: Es fängt gleich an zu schneien.
native_language_example: It’s about to start snowing.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive is needed: often after another verb/adjective/noun (e.g., *anfangen/vergessen/vorziehen/ermuntern*, or phrases like *es dauert …*). It can introduce a purpose/task (*ein Buch zu schreiben* = “to write a book”) or what someone should do (*ihm zu schreiben* = “to write to him”). In many sentences it corresponds to English “to + verb.”
target_language_example: Ich versuche, heute Abend meiner Freundin zu schreiben.
native_language_example: I’m trying to write to my girlfriend this evening.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like **anfangen** (to start), **aufhören** (to stop), or **(an)fangen** in the pattern **Verb + zu + infinitive**: *anfangen zu schreien* = “to start screaming”, *aufhören zu schreien* = “to stop screaming”. It often expresses loud, angry, or panicked shouting.
target_language_example: Bitte hör auf, zu schreien!
native_language_example: Please stop screaming!

meaning: to stay/keep silent; to not say anything.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive clause after another verb (e.g., versprechen, das Recht haben): „Ich habe versprochen zu schweigen.“ / „Sie haben das Recht zu schweigen.“ Common in formal or legal contexts.
target_language_example: Bitte versuch zu schweigen, während der Film läuft.
native_language_example: Please try to be quiet while the movie is on.

additional_notes: Used as the infinitive form of the verb “schwimmen” after another verb (e.g., versuchen/anfangen/sich anstrengen), after expressions like “Angst haben, … zu …”, and with “um … zu …” to express purpose (“in order to swim”). Also appears in idioms like “gegen den Strom schwimmen” (“to swim against the current,” meaning to go against the mainstream).
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Lust, heute zu schwimmen.
native_language_example: I don't feel like swimming today.

additional_notes: Most often used with „wissen“: „etwas an jemandem zu schätzen wissen“ / „etwas zu schätzen wissen“ = “to appreciate/value something (about someone).” It can also mean “to estimate” in the sense of making a rough guess (numbers, amounts, time).
target_language_example: Ich weiß deine Hilfe wirklich zu schätzen.
native_language_example: I really appreciate your help.

additional_notes: “Zu schützen” is the infinitive with “zu”, often used after expressions like “um … zu …” (in order to …) or verbs like “versuchen” (to try) and “müssen” (to have to). Very common patterns: “um jemanden/etwas zu schützen” (to protect someone/something) and “sich (vor + Dat.) schützen” (to protect oneself from something), e.g. “sich vor dem Regen schützen.”
target_language_example: Ich mache die Tür zu, um die Kinder zu schützen.
native_language_example: I close the door to protect the children.

additional_notes: Used when a verb requires an infinitive clause with **zu** (similar to “to + verb” in English), especially after verbs like **sich erinnern** (to remember), **erlauben** (to allow), **versuchen** (to try), **hoffen** (to hope). With films/TV, it often means “to watch.”
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dich morgen zu sehen.
native_language_example: I hope to see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used when **sein** is in an infinitive clause with **zu**, similar to English **to be**. Common after verbs like **versuchen** (to try), **scheinen** (to seem), **behaupten** (to claim), and in adjective/phrase structures like **stolz darauf, ... zu sein** (“proud to be ...”). **Zu** goes directly before the infinitive: *... zu sein*.
target_language_example: Es ist schön, hier zu sein.
native_language_example: It's nice to be here.

additional_notes: Used as a "zu"-infinitive after certain verbs, especially ones like anfangen (to start) and aufhören (to stop): anfangen, (etwas) zu singen; aufhören, (etwas) zu singen. Often refers to the action (singing) rather than a specific person doing it.
target_language_example: Er hat angefangen, im Chor zu singen.
native_language_example: He started singing in the choir.

additional_notes: Used when German requires an infinitive with „zu“, often after another verb or expression (e.g., „Lust haben, … zu spielen“ = to feel like playing; „anfangen, … zu spielen“ = to start playing). In many cases English just uses “to play,” while German adds „zu“ before the infinitive.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, heute zu spielen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to play today.

additional_notes: Used when German needs an infinitive with "zu", often after another verb or expression: "anfangen, ... zu sprechen" (to start speaking), "das Bedürfnis haben, ... zu sprechen" (to feel the need to talk), "verlangen, ... zu sprechen" (to want/long to speak). It can also be used with prepositions: "mit jemandem zu sprechen" = to talk to someone; "über jemanden/etwas zu sprechen" = to talk about someone/something.
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Zeit, mit dir zu sprechen.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to talk to you.

meaning: to put/place; to set (e.g., an alarm); (jdn) to satisfy.
additional_notes: This is the infinitive of **stellen** used with **zu** after other verbs (e.g., *vergessen, versuchen, planen*): *Ich habe vergessen, die Milch in den Kühlschrank zu stellen.* A very common fixed expression is **jdn zufriedenstellen** = “to satisfy someone / to make someone happy.” With objects, it’s often about putting something somewhere (*in den Kühlschrank stellen*) or setting a device (*den Wecker stellen*).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte die Flaschen zurück in den Kühlschrank zu stellen?
native_language_example: Can you please put the bottles back in the fridge?

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive needs "zu" (similar to English "to"), often after certain verbs/expressions (e.g., "wünschen"), or in purpose/avoidance phrases like "um ... zu" (in order to ...) and "ohne ... zu" (without ...ing). The base verb is "sterben" = "to die".
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst, allein zu sterben.
native_language_example: I'm afraid of dying alone.

meaning: to argue; to have a quarrel.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like anfangen/aufhören (e.g., „anfangen zu streiten“, „aufhören zu streiten“). Often appears with „mit + Dativ“ (argue with someone: „mit Tom streiten“) or „über + Akkusativ“ (argue about something: „über Geld streiten“). Also common as „sich streiten“ = to argue with each other.
target_language_example: Bitte fangt nicht an, über Kleinigkeiten zu streiten.
native_language_example: Please don’t start arguing about little things.

meaning: to study (usually at a university); to study/examine closely.
additional_notes: Often used with "um ... zu" to express purpose: "... um X zu studieren" = "... in order to study X." It can mean studying a subject at university (Medizin, Jura, Englisch), and it can also mean examining/observing something carefully (e.g., animals, data).
target_language_example: Ich gehe nach Berlin, um Informatik zu studieren.
native_language_example: I'm going to Berlin to study computer science.

meaning: to look for; to search for; to seek.
additional_notes: "Zu suchen" is the infinitive "suchen" used with "zu" (often after another verb or in purpose clauses like "um ... zu ..."). Common pattern: "anfangen/versuchen/planen, ... zu suchen" = "to start/try/plan to look for ...". Fixed expression: "(hier) nichts zu suchen haben" = "to have no business being (here)".
target_language_example: Ich versuche, meine Schlüssel zu suchen.
native_language_example: I’m trying to look for my keys.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive verb comes after another verb/phrase (an infinitive clause), especially after verbs like "anfangen" (to start), "(etwas) mögen" (to like), and expressions like "Lust haben" (to feel like). Often appears as "anfangen zu tanzen" = "to start dancing". You can add what you dance to/with: "zu der Musik zu tanzen" = "to dance to the music".
target_language_example: Ich habe keine Lust, heute zu tanzen.
native_language_example: I don't feel like dancing today.

meaning: 'to carry' (to take something from one place to another).
additional_notes: "zu" + infinitive is used after many verbs (e.g., helfen, versuchen, schaffen) to mean "to ...": "helfen, den Koffer zu tragen" = "help (to) carry the suitcase". Depending on context, "tragen" can also mean "to wear" (clothes), and it’s also used figuratively for burdens: "sein Kreuz zu tragen" = "to bear one's cross".
target_language_example: Kannst du mir helfen, die Kisten nach oben zu tragen?
native_language_example: Can you help me carry the boxes upstairs?

additional_notes: "zu" + infinitive is used after many verbs (e.g., hoffen, planen, sich freuen) to mean "to ...": *Ich hoffe, dich zu treffen* = "I hope to meet you." With **Entscheidungen zu treffen**, **treffen** means "to make" (a decision). Without an object, **jemanden treffen** usually means "to meet someone"; **etwas treffen** can also mean "to hit" (not shown in these examples).
target_language_example: Ich hoffe, dich morgen wieder zu treffen.
native_language_example: I hope to meet you again tomorrow.

meaning: 'to drink' (in the 'zu' infinitive form); also 'something to drink' in phrases like 'was zu trinken'.
additional_notes: 1) Used after many verbs/adjectives that require the 'zu' + infinitive: e.g., "raten/aufhören/ablehnen … zu trinken" (= to advise/stop/refuse to drink). 2) With neuter pronouns like "etwas/was/nichts" it often means a drink (something to drink): "Ich brauche was zu trinken." 3) "gut zu trinken" means "easy/pleasant to drink" (drinkable). 4) "zu viel zu trinken" can mean either "too much to drink" or "too much (alcohol) to drink" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ich hätte gern etwas zu trinken.
native_language_example: I’d like something to drink.

meaning: 'to do' (infinitive with *zu*); also 'to be connected/related' in *mit … zu tun haben*.
additional_notes: *zu tun* is *tun* (“to do”) used with *zu* in many infinitive phrases, often after another verb (e.g., *versuchen, … zu tun* = “try to do …”) or in set expressions like *nichts zu tun haben* (“have nothing to do”) and *Es bleibt nur noch … zu tun* (“All that’s left is to do …”). In *mit etwas/jemandem zu tun haben*, it means “to have something to do with” (= be related/connected), not literally “to do.”
target_language_example: Ich habe heute viel zu tun.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do today.

additional_notes: Used when you do exactly what someone wants/asks: „… zu tun, was man von ihm verlangte“ = “to do what was demanded of him.” You’ll also see it in the common expression „(nichts) mit etwas zu tun haben“ (“to have (nothing) to do with something”), followed by a „was …“ clause: „Es hat nichts mit dem Haus zu tun, was passiert ist.“ = “It has nothing to do with the house, what happened.”
target_language_example: Ich versuche einfach, zu tun, was richtig ist.
native_language_example: I'm just trying to do what's right.

meaning: “to do” / “needs to be done” (as in: what should be done).
additional_notes: Used almost always in the pattern „was … zu tun ist“ = “what to do / what needs to be done.” It’s a fixed, common way to talk about the next necessary action: „Weißt du, was zu tun ist?“ = “Do you know what to do?”
target_language_example: Wir wissen nicht, was zu tun ist.
native_language_example: We don’t know what to do.

additional_notes: "zu" + infinitive is used to express a purpose, intention, or result, often after certain nouns/adjectives (e.g., "die Absicht, ... zu ..." = "the intention to ...", "genug, um ... zu ..." = "crazy/strong/etc. enough to ..."). "töten" is a strong verb meaning to cause death; it’s more formal than "umbringen" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Er hatte nicht vor, jemanden zu töten.
native_language_example: He didn’t intend to kill anyone.

meaning: to say goodbye (to); to take leave; to see someone off.
additional_notes: Used as an infinitive with „zu“, often in purpose clauses with „um … zu …“: „Er ging zum Flughafen, um sie zu verabschieden.“ Very often the verb is reflexive: „sich verabschieden“ = to say goodbye / take leave. With an object („jemanden verabschieden“) it can mean to say goodbye to someone or to see them off (e.g., at the station/airport).
target_language_example: Ich bin gekommen, um mich zu verabschieden.
native_language_example: I came to say goodbye.

additional_notes: Infinitive with "zu" of the verb "verbergen". Common patterns: "etwas zu verbergen" (to have something to hide), "(etwas) vor jemandem zu verbergen" (to hide something from someone), and "um ... zu verbergen" (in order to hide/conceal).
target_language_example: Ich habe nichts zu verbergen.
native_language_example: I have nothing to hide.

meaning: to owe (something) to (someone/something); to be thanks to.
additional_notes:
Used with the dative to name the person/thing that caused something: 
- etwas ist jemandem/etwas zu verdanken = something is owed to / is thanks to someone/something (often for positive results, but can be neutral).
Common patterns: „Das ist dir zu verdanken.“ / „Das habe ich dir zu verdanken.“ / „… ist einem Zufall zu verdanken.“
target_language_example: Dass wir gewonnen haben, ist vor allem deinem Einsatz zu verdanken.
native_language_example: That we won is mainly thanks to your effort.

meaning: to earn (e.g., money); sometimes also “to deserve”.
additional_notes: This is the verb **verdienen** used with **zu + infinitive** (“to …”), common after many verbs and expressions (e.g., *versuchen*, *Zeit haben*, *um ... zu ...*). In money contexts it usually means “to earn”; in other contexts it can mean “to deserve” (*Das hast du verdient.* = “You deserve(d) that.”).
target_language_example: Sie arbeitet hart, um mehr Geld zu verdienen.
native_language_example: She works hard to earn more money.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive form with "zu" (like English “to leave”). It’s commonly used after other verbs (e.g., befehlen/verbieten/versuchen) and usually takes a direct object in the accusative: "den Hafen / das Zimmer / das Hotel zu verlassen".
target_language_example: Ich muss jetzt das Büro verlassen.
native_language_example: I have to leave the office now.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive with „zu“ (often like English “to + verb”). Common in phrases like „Angst haben, jemanden/etwas zu verlieren“ (to be afraid of losing someone/something) and „(laufen) Gefahr, etwas zu verlieren“ (to be in danger of losing something). In the fixed expression „ohne weitere Worte zu verlieren“ it means “without saying another word.”
target_language_example: Ich habe Angst, meinen Schlüssel zu verlieren.
native_language_example: I’m afraid of losing my key.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "versuchen" or in purpose phrases with "um … zu" to say you want to prevent something from happening. It’s the infinitive form of "vermeiden" (e.g., "Ich versuche, das zu vermeiden.").
target_language_example: Ich versuche, zu spät zu kommen, zu vermeiden.
native_language_example: I try to avoid being late.

additional_notes: Infinitive with "zu" ("to" + verb). Often used after expressions like "schwer"/"leicht" (hard/easy) or "Es fällt mir schwer, ... zu verstehen" (I find it hard to understand ...). You can also use it after some verbs like "scheinen" (to seem): "Er scheint ... zu verstehen".
target_language_example: Ich finde es schwer, dich zu verstehen.
native_language_example: I find it hard to understand you.

additional_notes: "zu + infinitive" is used after many verbs to express an action as a goal/plan (e.g., jemanden anflehen, etwas zu tun = to beg someone to do something). Very common with the reflexive form "sich verteidigen" = to defend yourself/ourselves ("uns zu verteidigen").
target_language_example: Er versuchte, sich zu verteidigen, aber niemand glaubte ihm.
native_language_example: He tried to defend himself, but nobody believed him.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive clause is needed, often after verbs like bitten/auffordern/vorschlagen: „jemanden bitten/auffordern, zu warten“ (to ask/tell someone to wait). Common patterns include „auf jemanden warten“ (to wait for someone) and „darauf warten, dass …“ (to wait for something to happen).
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte kurz hier zu warten?
native_language_example: Can you please wait here for a moment?

additional_notes: Used when you wait up to a specific moment/event. Structure: "(jemanden) bitten/entscheiden/beschließen, zu warten, bis + clause". After "bis", you use a normal verb clause (e.g., "bis er zurückkommt"). Sometimes you may see Konjunktiv I/II in reported speech or more formal/older style (e.g., "bis er zurückkomme/käme").
target_language_example: Ich habe beschlossen, hier zu warten, bis du zurückkommst.
native_language_example: I decided to wait here until you come back.

additional_notes: "zu weinen" is the infinitive "weinen" (to cry) used with "zu" after certain verbs (e.g., anfangen, aufhören, versuchen). Common patterns: "anfangen zu weinen" = to start crying; "aufhören zu weinen" = to stop crying; "nicht aufhören zu weinen" = to not stop crying.
target_language_example: Kannst du bitte aufhören zu weinen?
native_language_example: Can you please stop crying?

meaning: 'to become' / 'to be' (in the passive, e.g. 'to be chosen/praised').
additional_notes: "zu werden" is the infinitive of "werden" with "zu" (often like English "to become"). It’s used after many verbs/expressions that take an infinitive clause, e.g. "daran denken, … zu werden" (to think about becoming …). Very often it appears as a passive infinitive: "(aus)gewählt/gelobt/wertgeschätzt zu werden" = "to be (selected/praised/appreciated)".
target_language_example: Sie hofft, eines Tages Ärztin zu werden.
native_language_example: She hopes to become a doctor one day.

meaning: 'to become' / 'to be' (in the passive, e.g. 'to be chosen/praised').
additional_notes: "zu werden" is the infinitive of "werden" with "zu" (often like English "to become"). It’s used after many verbs/expressions that take an infinitive clause, e.g. "daran denken, … zu werden" (to think about becoming …). Very often it appears as a passive infinitive: "(aus)gewählt/gelobt/wertgeschätzt zu werden" = "to be (selected/praised/appreciated)".
target_language_example: Sie hofft, eines Tages Ärztin zu werden.
native_language_example: She hopes to become a doctor one day.

additional_notes: Used when *wissen* is in an infinitive clause that requires *zu* (similar to “to” in English). Common after many verbs/adjectives like *genug … zu wissen* (“smart/old enough to know”), *vorgeben … zu wissen* (“pretend to know”), and *scheinen … zu wissen* (“seem to know”).
target_language_example: Ich bin froh, das zu wissen.
native_language_example: I’m glad to know that.

meaning: 'to know what' (to claim/seem/believe to know what …).
additional_notes: Used when a verb like „scheinen“, „glauben“ or „sich einbilden“ is followed by an infinitive clause („zu wissen“) and then a „was“-clause with the specific content. Word order in the „was“-clause is typically verb-last: „… was er tut“.
target_language_example: Ich glaube zu wissen, was du meinst.
native_language_example: I think I know what you mean.

meaning: to leave something to be desired (not as good as it should be).
additional_notes: Usually used in the fixed expression „(etwas) lässt … zu wünschen übrig“ (= something isn’t good enough). Common patterns: „lässt viel zu wünschen übrig“ (is quite poor), „lässt nicht viel zu wünschen übrig“ (is pretty good), „lässt nichts zu wünschen übrig“ (is excellent / there’s nothing to criticize).
target_language_example: Der Service im Hotel lässt noch viel zu wünschen übrig.
native_language_example: The service at the hotel still leaves a lot to be desired.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive with „zu“ of the verb „zeigen“ (“to show”). It often follows another verb or expression (e.g., „vorhaben“, „freundlich sein“, „gehört sich“, „es würde dir etwas ausmachen“) or appears in purpose clauses with „um … zu …“ (“in order to …”). Depending on context, it can mean showing something to someone („jemandem etwas zeigen“) or showing/expressing a feeling („Wut/Zuneigung zeigen“).
target_language_example: Kannst du mir bitte zeigen, wie das funktioniert?
native_language_example: Can you please show me how that works?

meaning: to pull; to move/relocate (to a place).
additional_notes: "Zu ziehen" is the infinitive form used after many verbs/expressions (like English “to …”). Common uses: (1) moving house: „nach Berlin zu ziehen“ = “to move to Berlin”; (2) pulling/tugging: „an etwas zu ziehen“ = “to pull on something.” Note: in the fixed phrase „in Betracht ziehen“ it means “to consider” (literally “to pull into consideration”).
target_language_example: Sie plant, nächstes Jahr nach Hamburg zu ziehen.
native_language_example: She plans to move to Hamburg next year.

additional_notes: Used in polite or hypothetical questions about relocating. **ziehen** can mean “to pull,” but with places (e.g., *nach Australien ziehen*) it usually means “to move (to a place).” The pattern is **bereit, … zu ziehen** (“willing/ready to move”) plus a conditional clause with **wenn wir …** (“if we …”).
target_language_example: Wärst du bereit, nach Berlin zu ziehen, wenn wir dich darum bäten?
native_language_example: Would you be willing to move to Berlin if we asked you to?

additional_notes: "zu" + infinitive is used after many verbs to express "to do" something (e.g., jemanden überzeugen, etwas zu ändern = to convince someone to change something; gedenken, etwas zu ändern = to intend/plan to change something). With reflexive verbs it becomes "sich zu ändern" = to change (oneself) / to change.
target_language_example: Ich versuche, meine Gewohnheiten zu ändern.
native_language_example: I’m trying to change my habits.

additional_notes: “zu öffnen” is the infinitive “öffnen” used with “zu” (often like English “to open”). It commonly appears after adjectives (e.g., „schwer zu öffnen“ = “hard to open”) or in purpose/necessity phrases with „um … zu …“ (“in order to …”) and „brauchen/versuchen, … zu …“ (“need/try to …”). It can be used for physical objects (doors, boxes, cans) and also for letters (“to open” = “to open/read”).
target_language_example: Diese Flasche ist schwer zu öffnen.
native_language_example: This bottle is hard to open.

additional_notes: Uses "zu" + infinitive to express a task/purpose: "etwas zu übersetzen" = “something to translate.” Often appears after nouns/pronouns like "etwas/nichts" or as a clause: "Dieses Gedicht zu übersetzen, ist schwer." For the simple infinitive without "zu": "Ich übersetze das Gedicht."
target_language_example: Ich habe noch zwei E-Mails zu übersetzen.
native_language_example: I still have two emails to translate.

additional_notes: Used with an object (a person) and often with a clause showing what you want them to do or believe. Common patterns: „jemanden von etwas überzeugen“ = convince someone of something; „jemanden (davon) überzeugen, … zu …“ = convince someone to … . Often appears as an infinitive with „zu“ after verbs like „versuchen“ (to try) or „schwierig sein“ (to be difficult).
target_language_example: Ich konnte sie nicht davon überzeugen, länger zu bleiben.
native_language_example: I couldn't convince her to stay longer.

meaning: “by any chance, where …” (a polite way to ask if someone happens to know).
additional_notes: Used in questions like „Weißt du zufällig, wo …?“ to soften the request and sound less demanding. „zufällig“ means “by chance/coincidentally,” and it often goes with verbs like „wissen“ (to know): „Wissen Sie zufällig, wo …?“ It’s neutral and polite (not slang).
target_language_example: Weißt du zufällig, wo die nächste Apotheke ist?
native_language_example: Do you happen to know where the nearest pharmacy is?

additional_notes: Used to acknowledge something (often a fact, mistake, or truth), sometimes reluctantly. Common with müssen: „Du musst zugeben, dass …“ = “You have to admit that …”. The verb changes with the subject (ich gebe zu, du gibst zu, er/sie gibt zu) and „dass“ introduces a clause with the verb at the end.
target_language_example: Ich gebe zu, dass ich falsch lag.
native_language_example: I admit that I was wrong.

meaning: (jdn.) zum Abendessen einladen = to invite (someone) to dinner.
additional_notes: This is used with the separable verb **einladen** (“to invite”). In the present/past tense, **ein** often goes to the end of the sentence: **Er lädt sie zum Abendessen ein. / Er lud sie zum Abendessen ein.** The person invited is usually in the accusative (**sie/ihn**).
target_language_example: Ich lade dich morgen zum Abendessen ein.
native_language_example: I’m inviting you to dinner tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "einladen" (to invite). "zum" = "zu dem" (to the). Common patterns: "jemanden zum Abendessen einladen" (invite someone to dinner) and "zum Abendessen eingeladen sein" (to be invited to dinner).
target_language_example: Wir sind morgen zum Abendessen eingeladen.
native_language_example: We’re invited to dinner tomorrow.

additional_notes: "jemanden zum Abendessen einladen" means you ask someone to join you for dinner, usually with the idea that you host or pay. The person is in the accusative (mich/dich/Sie/euch). Common polite phrasing is "Darf ich Sie zum Abendessen einladen?"; with friends you can say "Darf ich dich/euch ...?" or "Lass mich dich ...".
target_language_example: Darf ich dich morgen zum Abendessen einladen?
native_language_example: May I invite you to dinner tomorrow?

meaning: as a farewell; when saying goodbye.
additional_notes: Used with a parting gesture or action (e.g., wave, hug, kiss, give a gift) right before leaving. Literally “to the farewell,” but in English it’s usually “as a farewell / before leaving.”
target_language_example: Zum Abschied gab sie ihm noch schnell eine Umarmung.
native_language_example: As a farewell, she quickly gave him a hug.

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs like gehen/fahren/kommen to say you’re going to a doctor’s office for medical care. Grammar: zu + dem Arzt → zum Arzt (dative). You can also say "zum Arzt gehen" = "to go to the doctor".
target_language_example: Ich muss morgen zum Arzt.
native_language_example: I have to go to the doctor tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going in the direction of a specific train station (destination). It’s a contraction of "zu dem Bahnhof" ("to the" + "train station"), used with movement verbs like fahren, gehen, bringen, nehmen (ein Taxi).
target_language_example: Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?
native_language_example: How do I get to the train station?

additional_notes: Short for „zu dem Essen“ (zu + dem). Used to talk about gathering or being invited for a meal (often like “for dinner/lunch” depending on context), or to express purpose: doing something in order to eat (e.g., catching fish to eat).
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen zum Essen vorbei?
native_language_example: Are you coming over tomorrow for a meal?

additional_notes: Short for „zu dem Essen“ (zu + dem). Used to talk about gathering or being invited for a meal (often like “for dinner/lunch” depending on context), or to express purpose: doing something in order to eat (e.g., catching fish to eat).
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen zum Essen vorbei?
native_language_example: Are you coming over tomorrow for a meal?

additional_notes: “zum” is a contraction of “zu dem” and is used with masculine/neuter nouns in the dative after “zu”. Common with movement/direction (e.g., fahren, gehen, kommen, bringen): “Ich fahre zum Flughafen.”
target_language_example: Wir fahren morgen früh zum Flughafen.
native_language_example: We’re going to the airport tomorrow morning.

meaning: “to the airport to … / in order to …”.
additional_notes: Used with a verb of motion (gehen/fahren) + destination: „zum Flughafen“ (to the airport), followed by „um … zu …“ to express purpose (“in order to”). Structure: [Ich gehe/fahre] zum Flughafen, um + infinitive + zu + verb.
target_language_example: Wir fahren zum Flughafen, um meine Schwester abzuholen.
native_language_example: We’re going to the airport to pick up my sister.

additional_notes: Means traveling to the airport. With a car/taxi it often implies driving ("fahren"), and it can be used with a direct object to say you drive someone there: "jdn. zum Flughafen fahren" (e.g., "Ich fahre dich zum Flughafen.").
target_language_example: Kannst du mich morgen früh zum Flughafen fahren?
native_language_example: Can you drive me to the airport tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used to say what you eat/drink for breakfast (often with essen/trinken). It’s also common at the start of a sentence for emphasis: "Zum Frühstück esse ich ...". Literally "zu dem Frühstück" (zu + dem → zum).
target_language_example: Zum Frühstück trinke ich Kaffee und esse ein Brötchen.
native_language_example: For breakfast I drink coffee and eat a bread roll.

meaning: for (someone’s) birthday; for a birthday (as a gift/occasion).
additional_notes: Often used with greetings and gift-giving: "Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!" (Happy birthday!). Also used to say what someone wants/gets as a birthday present: "zum Geburtstag bekommen/schenken/wünschen". Grammar: "zum" = "zu dem" + dative; it refers to the occasion (the birthday).
target_language_example: Ich habe ihr zum Geburtstag Blumen geschenkt.
native_language_example: I gave her flowers for her birthday.

meaning: to give (someone) something for their birthday.
additional_notes: Used when talking about giving a gift specifically as a birthday present. Structure: jemandem (dative) + etwas schenken + zum Geburtstag. Often with "etwas" (something) or a specific gift: „Ich schenke dir ein Buch zum Geburtstag.“
target_language_example: Ich schenke meiner Schwester zum Geburtstag einen Gutschein.
native_language_example: I’m giving my sister a voucher for her birthday.

meaning: “the hell” (strong, annoyed emphasis); also “to hell with …”.
additional_notes: A harsh, old-fashioned-sounding exclamation used to show anger, impatience, or disbelief. Often inserted into questions like: „Wer/Was/Wo zum Henker …?“ = “Who/What/Where the hell …?” As a standalone phrase with „mit“ it means rejection/hostility: „Zum Henker mit dir/euch!“ = “To hell with you!” Stronger than neutral options like „denn“ or „bloß“; use carefully.
target_language_example: Wie zum Henker soll ich das in zwei Minuten schaffen?
native_language_example: How the hell am I supposed to do that in two minutes?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like „bringen“ (to bring/cause) to say that something causes someone to laugh: „jemanden zum Lachen bringen“ = to make someone laugh. „zum“ = „zu dem“ + „Lachen“ (noun: laughing).
target_language_example: Die Szene hat mich zum Lachen gebracht.
native_language_example: That scene made me laugh.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase „jemanden zum Lachen bringen“ = to make someone laugh. It’s used with a direct object (the person): „Sie hat mich zum Lachen gebracht.“ Often expresses that you caused a laugh (e.g., with a joke, something funny).
target_language_example: Der Witz hat mich sofort zum Lachen gebracht.
native_language_example: The joke made me laugh right away.

meaning: 'for studying' / 'to study' (for the purpose of learning).
additional_notes: "zum" is a contraction of "zu dem". With an infinitive noun like "Lernen" (learning/studying), "zum Lernen" expresses purpose: why something is used or where someone goes (e.g., "ein Zimmer zum Lernen", "in die Bibliothek zum Lernen"). Often corresponds to English "to study" or "for studying" rather than a literal word-for-word translation.
target_language_example: Ich brauche einen ruhigen Platz zum Lernen.
native_language_example: I need a quiet place to study.

meaning: for reading; to read (as a purpose).
additional_notes: Uses **zum** (= **zu dem**) + **nominalized infinitive** (**Lesen**) to express purpose: *Zeit/Gelegenheit/Ort zum Lesen* = time/opportunity/place for reading. Often follows nouns like **Zeit**, **Lust**, **Gelegenheit**. It can also take an object in the genitive: **zum Lesen des Vertrags** = to read the contract.
target_language_example: Ich nehme mir abends eine halbe Stunde zum Lesen.
native_language_example: In the evening, I set aside half an hour for reading.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at lunchtime or that someone is invited for lunch. Grammar: "zum" = "zu dem" + dative, used here with the event/meal "das Mittagessen" (neutral). Common with verbs like "einladen" (invite) and with movement like "nach Hause fahren/kommen" to indicate going somewhere for lunch.
target_language_example: Kommst du morgen zum Mittagessen vorbei?
native_language_example: Are you coming by for lunch tomorrow?

meaning: "to the museum" (toward/going to the museum); sometimes "for the museum" (as a recipient).
additional_notes: "zum" is a contraction of "zu dem" and is used with the dative case. Most often it expresses destination/direction: "Ich gehe/fahre zum Museum." With certain verbs it can mean the recipient/beneficiary, e.g. "(Geld) zum Museum beitragen" = to contribute (money) to/for the museum. Contrast: "im Museum" = in the museum.
target_language_example: Wir gehen heute Nachmittag zum Museum.
native_language_example: We’re going to the museum this afternoon.

meaning: (jemanden) as a fool; in the phrase „jemanden zum Narren halten“ = to make a fool of someone / to trick someone.
additional_notes: Almost always used with „halten“: „jemanden zum Narren halten“ means you are not taking someone seriously and are deceiving them, joking at their expense, or fooling them. Commonly used in the passive too: „Ich werde nicht zum Narren gehalten.“
target_language_example: Willst du mich zum Narren halten?
native_language_example: Are you trying to make a fool of me?

additional_notes:
Comes from "zu dem Reden" and is used to express purpose or suitability: 
- "Zeit zum Reden" = time to talk
- "zu müde zum Reden" = too tired to talk
Very common with "jdn. zum Reden bringen" = to get someone to talk (make them start talking).
target_language_example: Wir brauchen einen ruhigen Ort zum Reden.
native_language_example: We need a quiet place to talk.

additional_notes: Used to say why someone goes/comes somewhere: "in den Park zum Spielen" = "to the park to play." With people, it can mean "to play with": "jemanden zum Spielen" = "someone to play with" (often used about children). "zum" = "zu dem" + noun/gerund "Spielen".
target_language_example: Hast du jemanden zum Spielen?
native_language_example: Do you have someone to play with?

additional_notes: "zum" = "zu dem" (to the). Use it with movement/direction (going/driving/walking somewhere): „Ich gehe/fahre/laufe zum Strand.“ For location (being at the beach), German usually uses „am Strand“: „Ich bin am Strand.“
target_language_example: Morgen fahren wir zum Strand.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re driving to the beach.

additional_notes: "zum" = "zu dem" (to the/for the). Used with "kommen/gehen" to say someone comes/goes to class, or with "außer" to mean "except for class". "Unterricht" can mean a school class/lesson or instruction/teaching in general.
target_language_example: Ich gehe gleich zum Unterricht.
native_language_example: I’m going to class in a moment.

additional_notes: Used to say something is being offered for sale, often with verbs like „sein“ or „stehen“: „Das Haus ist/steht zum Verkauf.“ The opposite is „nicht zum Verkauf“ (“not for sale”).
target_language_example: Dieses Fahrrad steht zum Verkauf.
native_language_example: This bicycle is for sale.

meaning: (to) cry; used in „jdn. zum Weinen bringen“ = to make someone cry.
additional_notes: Usually appears with the verb „bringen“: „jemanden zum Weinen bringen“ (to bring someone to the point of crying). It expresses that something causes a person to cry (from sadness, joy, etc.).
target_language_example: Der Film hat mich zum Weinen gebracht.
native_language_example: The movie made me cry.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **jemanden zum Weinen bringen** = “to make someone cry” (often because you hurt, upset, or moved them). In the past: **hat/haben ... zum Weinen gebracht**. With reported speech you may see **hätte ... zum Weinen gebracht** (Konjunktiv II).
target_language_example: Der Film hat mich zum Weinen gebracht.
native_language_example: The movie made me cry.

meaning: to feel like crying; to be in the mood to cry.
additional_notes: Used with **sein** and usually with a **dative person**: **Mir/Dir/Ihm/Ihr/Uns/Euch/Ihnen ist (war) zum Weinen zumute.** It describes an emotional state (sad, overwhelmed, touched) rather than an action you’re doing right now.
target_language_example: Nach dem Film war mir zum Weinen zumute.
native_language_example: After the movie, I felt like crying.

meaning: to the dentist (i.e., to a dentist appointment).
additional_notes: "zum" = "zu dem" (to the). Used with verbs of going/coming (gehen, fahren, müssen, sollen) to say you’re going to the dentist. It can imply the purpose is an appointment/checkup. Related: "beim Zahnarzt" = at the dentist’s (already there).
target_language_example: Ich muss morgen zum Zahnarzt.
native_language_example: I have to go to the dentist tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first time you met someone. It often appears with a time or place (e.g., Wann? Wo?) and can be used with an object (jdn. treffen = to meet someone) or reflexively: sich treffen = to meet each other (Wir haben uns … getroffen).
target_language_example: Ich habe sie zum ersten Mal auf einer Party getroffen.
native_language_example: I met her for the first time at a party.

meaning: for the first time in (a place).
additional_notes: Used to say it’s your first visit/experience in a city, country, etc. Common with the verb sein (“to be”) or verbs like sein/gehen/kommen. Word order: „zum ersten Mal“ usually comes before the place phrase with „in“: „Ich bin zum ersten Mal in Berlin.“
target_language_example: Ich bin zum ersten Mal in Deutschland.
native_language_example: I’m in Germany for the first time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going/coming/traveling to a specific destination for the first time. Common with verbs like gehen, kommen, reisen, fahren, fliegen. Structure: (Verb) + zum ersten Mal + nach + [place]. Use "nach" with most cities/countries; use "in die" with feminine/plural countries/regions (e.g., in die Schweiz), and "auf die" with islands (e.g., auf die Insel).
target_language_example: Ich fliege nächsten Monat zum ersten Mal nach Japan.
native_language_example: I'm flying to Japan for the first time next month.

meaning: "for the first time since" (a point in time or a period).
additional_notes: Used to say something is happening again after not happening for a long time. It’s followed by a time expression (e.g., zehn Tagen, Monaten, Jahren, Ewigkeiten/ewigen Zeiten). Often used with past tense: "Zum ersten Mal seit Monaten ..."
target_language_example: Zum ersten Mal seit zwei Jahren bin ich wieder in Berlin.
native_language_example: For the first time in two years, I’m back in Berlin.

additional_notes: Used to ask when someone last saw a person/animal/thing. Very common in questions like: „Wann hast du … zum letzten Mal gesehen?“ In formal situations use „haben Sie“ instead of „hast du“.
target_language_example: Wann haben Sie Ihren Pass zum letzten Mal gesehen?
native_language_example: When did you last see your passport?

meaning: 'went to work' / 'drove (traveled) to work' (by some means of transport).
additional_notes: "zur Arbeit" means "to work" (destination). "gefahren" is the past participle of "fahren" (to go/drive/ride). With "sein" (ist/bist/sind) it usually means you traveled to work (e.g., by car, train, taxi): "Er ist zur Arbeit gefahren." With "haben" it can mean you drove someone to work: "Er hat sie zur Arbeit gefahren." Often used with transport details like "mit dem Zug/Auto/Taxi".
target_language_example: Ich bin heute mit dem Bus zur Arbeit gefahren.
native_language_example: Today I went to work by bus.

additional_notes: Used with "sein" in the Perfekt tense (spoken past) of "gehen": "Ich bin zur Arbeit gegangen" = "I went to work." "zur" = "zu der" (to the). Often describes commuting or going in to work, not necessarily starting work itself.
target_language_example: Ich bin heute trotz Regen zur Arbeit gegangen.
native_language_example: I went to work today despite the rain.
